provenance.rightsNote: Lectio Edition (SDIT): clear modern English of Augustine's Confessions, synthesized from the public-domain translation tradition (Pusey 1838; Watts 1631) and checked against the Latin; modern critical translations consulted, not quoted. Complete, 13 books.
sourcesCited: Latin, the original text of the Confessiones
E. B. Pusey, The Confessions of S. Augustine (1838, public domain)
F. J. Sheed (1942, consulted, not quoted)

character: Plain modern English — the sense of the original, made to read with ease today.
overview: The Lectio Edition renders Augustine's Confessions in plain modern English that keeps its prayerful urgency and restless intelligence — sin and conversion, memory and time, a heart that finds no rest until it rests in God — while shedding the archaic diction.
introduction: The Confessions is the first true autobiography of an inner life: Augustine talking directly to God, and letting us overhear. It moves from a misspent youth through a long intellectual and moral struggle to conversion, then turns to memory, time, and the meaning of Genesis. Read it as one long prayer thinking out loud.

divergences.phrase: fecisti nos ad te et inquietum est cor nostrum, donec requiescat in te
divergences.older: Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee
divergences.lectio: you made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you
divergences.note: The most famous sentence in the book. The Latin binds inquietum (restless) to requiescat (rest) in a single breath; 'restless ... until it rests' keeps that echo, where Pusey's 'repose' breaks it. 'Ad te' is literally 'toward you' — made aimed at you — but 'for yourself' carries the pull of that vocation without sounding strange in English.

divergences.phrase: moriar, ne moriar, ut eam videam
divergences.older: Let me die—lest I die—only let me see Thy face.
divergences.lectio: Let me die — so that I do not die — only let me see your face.
divergences.note: Two deaths packed into four Latin words: Augustine will accept the death of his old self — even the end of this life in the vision of God — to escape the real death, which is life without him. 'Lest' now reads as mere hedging; 'so that I do not die' keeps the two deaths distinct and the paradox audible.

divergences.phrase: et vae tacentibus de te, quoniam loquaces muti sunt
divergences.older: Yet woe to him that speaketh not, since mute are even the most eloquent.
divergences.lectio: Yet woe to those who say nothing of you: even the ones who talk the most are mute.
divergences.note: Loquaces is not 'the most eloquent' but 'the talkative' — the people who produce the most words. The line closes the trap Augustine has built across the whole paragraph: all speech about God falls short, yet silence is forbidden; since the chattiest are already mute, failure is no excuse for not praising.

divergences.phrase: ut essem gratis malus
divergences.older: that I should be gratuitously evil
divergences.lectio: that I should be evil for free
divergences.note: Gratis is market language — no payment, no payoff. Augustine's whole point about the pear theft is that there was no motive to bank: sin as pure gratuity. Modern 'gratuitously' has drifted toward meaning 'excessively'; 'for free' restores the commercial shock of the Latin.

divergences.phrase: condimentum ibi peccatum erat
divergences.older: what sweetened it was the sin
divergences.lectio: the sin was its seasoning
divergences.note: Condimentum is kitchen vocabulary — the sauce or spice that makes bland food worth eating. Pusey's 'sweetened' prettifies the image; seasoning keeps Augustine's culinary joke intact: the pears themselves were flavorless, and the only flavor in his mouth was the sin.

divergences.phrase: factus sum mihi regio egestatis
divergences.older: I became to myself a barren land
divergences.lectio: I became to myself a land of famine
divergences.note: Egestas is destitution — hunger, not infertility — and the phrase deliberately echoes the prodigal son's far country where famine struck. 'Barren' turns the self into bad soil; Augustine's image is a whole country with nothing left to eat, the book's last word on gratuitous sin as self-starvation.

divergences.phrase: sartago flagitiosorum amorum
divergences.older: there sang all around me in my ears a cauldron of unholy loves (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: a cauldron of shameful loves hissed and seethed around me
divergences.note: The Latin sartago is literally a frying pan — Augustine puns on Carthago/sartago, Carthage sizzling in his ears. The pun cannot survive in English, so we keep the tradition's 'cauldron' but restore the noise the verb circumstrepebat insists on: the pan is heard before it is felt. And flagitiosus means disgraceful, scandalous — 'shameful,' not the churchier 'unholy.'

divergences.phrase: ille vero liber mutavit affectum meum
divergences.older: But this book altered my affections (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: That book changed what I loved
divergences.note: Affectus is the whole set of a person's loves and leanings. 'Altered my affections' now sounds like a line from a Victorian courtship; what Augustine says about Cicero's Hortensius is far more radical — a book reoriented his desire itself. 'Changed what I loved' keeps the shock plain, and states in five words the book's whole theory of a life: you are the history of your loves.

divergences.phrase: tu autem eras interior intimo meo et superior summo meo
divergences.older: But Thou wert more inward to me than my most inward part; and higher than my highest (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: you were more inward than my inmost part, and higher than my highest
divergences.note: The most famous sentence in Book III, and among the most famous in the Confessions. The Latin is a tight double comparative — interior intimo, superior summo — three words per limb. Pusey's reading is accurate but padded; we compress it back toward the Latin's symmetry so the paradox lands in one breath: God nearer to me than I am to myself, and higher above me than my own height.

divergences.phrase: factus eram ipse mihi magna quaestio
divergences.older: I became a great riddle to myself (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: I had become a great question to myself
divergences.note: A riddle is a puzzle with a trick answer; Augustine’s quaestio is an open inquiry. In grief he becomes the object of his own investigation — the sentence that sets the program of the whole Confessions. The pluperfect is also his: the loss did not create the condition, it exposed it.

divergences.phrase: fuderam in harenam animam meam
divergences.older: I had poured out my soul upon the dust (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: I had poured out my soul on sand
divergences.note: Harena is sand, not dust: the image is liquid poured onto a beach — instantly swallowed, impossible to hold — with an echo of the house built on sand. ‘Dust’ turns a precise image of futile pouring into a generic image of mortality.

divergences.phrase: victus cupiditate vendebam victoriosam loquacitatem
divergences.older: overcome by cupidity, made sale of a loquacity to overcome by (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: Defeated by greed, I sold the kind of speech that wins
divergences.note: Augustine’s joke is the point: the man selling victorious words is himself the loser (victus / victoriosam). Pusey keeps the repetition but buries it in syntax; the Lectio states the paradox plainly.

divergences.phrase: de manu linguae meae
divergences.older: from the ministry of my tongue
divergences.lectio: from the hand of my tongue
divergences.note: Augustine gives the tongue a hand: the confessing tongue lifts the sacrifice the way a priest's hand lifts the offering. Pusey tames the strange image into 'ministry'; the strangeness is the point, so the Lectio keeps the hand.

divergences.phrase: vident enim defectum solis futurum ante tam longe, suum autem praesentem non vident
divergences.older: they foresee a failure of the sun's light, which shall be, so long before, but see not their own, which is
divergences.lectio: they can see an eclipse of the sun coming years ahead, but their own eclipse, happening now, they cannot see
divergences.note: Defectus means both 'eclipse' and 'failure,' and Augustine's whole sentence turns on the pun. English 'eclipse' carries the same double weight — the astronomy and the moral collapse in one word — so the joke lands without a footnote.

divergences.phrase: exaudiens cardinem desiderii eius
divergences.older: hearing the main point of her desire
divergences.lectio: heard the hinge of her desire
divergences.note: Cardo is literally a hinge — the pivot a door swings on. Monica asked that the ship not sail; what her whole longing turned on was her son's salvation, and God answered the hinge rather than the door. 'Main point' flattens the image; the Lectio keeps it.

divergences.phrase: clausis foribus oculorum ... aperuit oculos
divergences.older: closing the passage of his eyes, [he] forbade his mind to range abroad after such evil ... he opened his eyes, and was stricken with a deeper wound in his soul
divergences.lectio: He shut the doors of his eyes and forbade his mind to walk out into all that evil ... he opened his eyes. And he took a worse wound in the soul than the fighter he had itched to look at took in the body
divergences.note: Augustine stages the scene as the siege of a house: the eyes are doors (fores), the crowd's roar comes in through the ears and 'unlocks' them (reseravit oculos), and only then can the wound enter. Pusey's 'passage of his eyes' drops the door, and with it the architecture of the whole metaphor. Keeping 'doors' lets the surrender of the eyes read as what Augustine wrote: a gate thrown open from the inside.

divergences.phrase: cor, ubi adhaerebat, concisum et vulneratum mihi erat et trahebat sanguinem
divergences.older: my heart which clave unto her was torn and wounded and bleeding
divergences.lectio: my heart, which had grown into her, was cut, and wounded, and it trailed blood
divergences.note: Pusey's 'bleeding' makes the wound a state; Augustine's trahebat sanguinem is an action that keeps happening — the heart drags a trail of blood behind it, the way a body does when it goes on walking after the blow. The verb matters because the paragraph is about going on living, badly, with the wound: he takes another woman precisely because the bleeding will not stop, and it festers instead of healing.

divergences.phrase: ille bene optando adquisiverat vinum, ego mentiendo quaerebam typhum
divergences.older: he, by fair wishes, had gotten wine; I, by lying, was seeking for empty, swelling praise
divergences.lectio: he had earned his wine by wishing people well, and I was chasing a swollen name by lying
divergences.note: Pusey's 'by fair wishes' is opaque to a modern ear. The beggar earned his coins the way beggars do — calling out blessings and good wishes to passers-by. Augustine's ledger is exact and damning: the beggar traded honest well-wishing for wine; the imperial orator traded lies for typhus — Greek for smoke, the swollen vapor of a reputation. Making the transaction visible restores the point that the beggar's trade was the more honest one.

divergences.phrase: o aeterna veritas et vera caritas et cara aeternitas
divergences.older: O Truth Who art Eternity! and Love Who art Truth! and Eternity Who art Love!
divergences.lectio: O eternal Truth, and true Love, and beloved Eternity!
divergences.note: Augustine's cry at the summit of the first ascent is three adjective-noun pairs whose words interlock — aeterna/aeternitas, vera/veritas, cara/caritas — each adjective handing its noun on to the next phrase. Pusey recast it as three identity-statements ('Truth Who art Eternity'), theology Augustine implies but syntax he did not write. Lectio keeps the plain braid and lets the words do the work.

divergences.phrase: dealbatiores vias saeculi cursitabat
divergences.older: ran his course through the gilded paths of life
divergences.lectio: ran up and down the whitewashed roads of the world
divergences.note: Dealbatus means whitewashed, not gilded — the white of the office-seeker's toga candida, and, to Augustine's scripture-soaked ear, of whitewashed tombs. Pusey's gold makes Firminus's success glitter; Augustine's white lets the shine carry a hint of rot. The frequentative cursitabat ('kept running about') adds the bustle Lectio keeps.

divergences.phrase: cothurno tamquam doctrinae sublimioris elati
divergences.older: lifted up in the lofty walk of some would-be sublimer learning
divergences.lectio: those who strut on the stage-boots of a supposedly loftier doctrine
divergences.note: The cothurnus is the tragic actor's platform boot. Augustine is calling the Platonists' loftiness a costume — added height, worn for an audience. Pusey abstracts the prop into a 'lofty walk'; Lectio keeps the boot, and the theater.

divergences.phrase: tolle lege, tolle lege
divergences.older: Take up and read; Take up and read.
divergences.lectio: Take it and read. Take it and read.
divergences.note: It is a child’s sing-song chant drifting over a garden wall — two clipped Latin imperatives, four syllables. “Take up and read” is Bible-margin English that no child ever chanted at play. Lectio keeps it short and singable, the way Augustine heard it — ordinary words that only he could hear as a command.

divergences.phrase: da mihi castitatem et continentiam, sed noli modo
divergences.older: Give me chastity and continency, only not yet.
divergences.lectio: Give me chastity and self-control — but not yet.
divergences.note: “Continency” has moved to the clinic since 1838; continentia is the power to hold yourself in — self-control. The line is a prayer engineered to fail, and its dark comedy survives only if every word stays ordinary, with “but not yet” dropping the punchline exactly where Augustine put it. The personified Continentia later in the book keeps her traditional name, Continence, as a proper noun.

divergences.phrase: quippe ex voluntate perversa facta est libido, et dum servitur libidini, facta est consuetudo, et dum consuetudini non resistitur, facta est necessitas
divergences.older: For of a forward will, was a lust made; and a lust served, became custom; and custom not resisted, became necessity.
divergences.lectio: For the will, twisted, becomes craving; a craving served becomes habit; and a habit unresisted becomes necessity.
divergences.note: Augustine’s four-link anatomy of addiction, centuries early. Pusey’s “forward will” and “custom” hide the mechanism from a modern ear; Lectio uses the plain ladder — twisted will, craving, habit, necessity — so the chain clicks shut link by link, as it does in the Latin.

divergences.phrase: et hoc erat totum, nolle quod volebam et velle quod volebas
divergences.older: And this Thy whole gift was, to nill what I willed, and to will what Thou willedst
divergences.lectio: And the whole of it came to this: to stop willing what I willed, and to will what you willed.
divergences.note: Pusey reaches for the dead verb 'nill' to preserve the Latin's mirrored wordplay (nolle/velle). The sentence is Augustine's entire conversion in one clause — a bare exchange of wills and nothing else — and modern English can keep that symmetry without the fossil.

divergences.phrase: attingimus eam modice toto ictu cordis
divergences.older: we slightly touched on her with the whole effort of our heart
divergences.lectio: we touched her — just barely, with one full beat of the heart
divergences.note: At the summit of the vision at Ostia, 'ictus cordis' is literally a heartbeat, not an 'effort': the contact with eternal Wisdom lasts exactly one pulse. Keeping the beat keeps Augustine's point — the touch is real, and it cannot be held.

divergences.phrase: meribibulam
divergences.older: wine-bibber
divergences.lectio: a little wine-swiller
divergences.note: The servant girl's taunt is a mocking one-off diminutive — roughly 'little guzzler of neat wine' — flung mid-quarrel. 'Wine-bibber' sounds like a pulpit word; the insult has to sting like name-calling, because the sting is what cured Monica.

divergences.phrase: sero te amavi, pulchritudo tam antiqua et tam nova, sero te amavi
divergences.older: Too late loved I Thee, O Thou Beauty of ancient days, yet ever new! too late I loved Thee!
divergences.lectio: Late have I loved you, Beauty so old and so new — late have I loved you!
divergences.note: Pusey's “too late” turns the cry into a verdict — a chance missed. Augustine's sero is simply “late”: grief at the delay, spoken from inside the arrival. And tam antiqua et tam nova is one taut paradox, “so old and so new”; “of ancient days, yet ever new” pads it into ornament. The line has to land in a few plain words, the way the Latin does.

divergences.phrase: da quod iubes et iube quod vis
divergences.older: Give what Thou enjoinest, and enjoin what Thou wilt.
divergences.lectio: Give what you command, and command what you will.
divergences.note: This is the sentence that scandalized Pelagius — the whole doctrine of grace in six Latin words: God must supply the very obedience he demands. “Enjoin” files the edge off into legal politeness; “command” keeps the sentence a demand made back at God, which is what makes it dangerous.

divergences.phrase: mihi quaestio factus sum
divergences.older: I have become a problem to myself
divergences.lectio: I have become a question to myself
divergences.note: Quaestio is an inquiry — the Roman word for a formal investigation, even an interrogation. A “problem” is an obstacle to be cleared; a “question” is an open case. Augustine means he is now the subject of his own cross-examination, conducted in God's presence, and the case is not closed.

divergences.phrase: quid est ergo tempus? si nemo ex me quaerat, scio; si quaerenti explicare velim, nescio
divergences.older: What then is time? If no one asks me, I know: if I wish to explain it to one that asketh, I know not.
divergences.lectio: What then is time? If no one asks me, I know; if I want to explain it to someone who asks, I do not know.
divergences.note: The most famous sentence in the book, and Pusey is already nearly plain. The Lectio only levels the last archaisms — 'one that asketh,' 'I know not' — so the line lands as the everyday, honest shrug Augustine intends, with no ornament to soften the paradox.

divergences.phrase: nihil esse aliud tempus quam distentionem: sed cuius rei, nescio, et mirum, si non ipsius animi
divergences.older: time is nothing else than protraction; but of what, I know not; and I marvel, if it be not of the mind itself (and at the book's close, 'my life is but a distraction')
divergences.lectio: time is nothing other than a stretching-out — but of what, I do not know. And I would be surprised if it were not of the mind itself (and later, 'my life is a stretching-apart').
divergences.note: Distentio is Augustine's one technical coin for what time is, and he strikes it again in the book's final movement — distentio est vita mea; creation happens 'without any distentio of your action.' Pusey splits it into 'protraction' and 'distraction,' breaking the thread. The Lectio keeps a single audible root, 'stretching,' so the analysis of time and the lament over a scattered life are heard as the same word — which is the book's whole point.

divergences.phrase: aliud est videre, aliud ridere
divergences.older: It is one thing to answer enquiries, another to make sport of enquirers.
divergences.lectio: Seeing is one thing; sneering is another.
divergences.note: Augustine's dismissal of the 'preparing hell for people who pry' joke is itself a joke: videre/ridere, a one-letter rhyme. Pusey paraphrases the sense and loses the sound. The Lectio keeps a click of near-rhyme so the wit survives along with the point — you can wave a hard question away with a laugh, or you can look at it.

divergences.phrase: nihil aliquid; est non est
divergences.older: Might one say, 'a nothing something', an 'is, is not,' I would say, this were it
divergences.lectio: If one could say 'a nothing-something,' or 'an is that isn't,' that is what I would call it
divergences.note: Augustine is coining deliberately impossible grammar for formless matter — a thing hovering between existence and nothing, which ordinary language cannot hold. Pusey keeps the shock but buries it in his syntax. We hyphenate 'nothing-something' and let 'an is that isn't' break English grammar exactly the way the Latin breaks Latin, so the reader feels the concept fail on the tongue — which is Augustine's point.

divergences.phrase: nec distenditur in tempora
divergences.older: nor distracted into any times
divergences.lectio: nor stretched out into time
divergences.note: The verb is distendere — the word behind Book XI's famous definition of time as a distentio animi, a stretching-out of the soul. Pusey's 'distracted' hides the cross-reference. We keep 'stretched out' so Book XI's argument can be heard running underneath: the heaven of heavens is happy precisely because it is never stretched thin across past and future the way we are.

divergences.phrase: sicut prior est sonus quam cantus
divergences.older: as the sound before the tune
divergences.lectio: as the sound is before the song
divergences.note: Pusey renders cantus as 'tune,' which now suggests a melody you could hum apart from any performance. Augustine means the actual sung sound — the sound is the matter of the song and exists only in the act of singing, which is exactly what makes his example work: matter and form arise together, prior in origin but not in time. 'Song' keeps the analogy exact throughout the passage.

divergences.phrase: pondus meum amor meus; eo feror, quocumque feror
divergences.older: My weight, is my love; thereby am I borne, whithersoever I am borne.
divergences.lectio: My weight is my love; wherever I am carried, it is love that carries me.
divergences.note: Ancient physics held that weight is not a downward pull but each thing's drive toward its proper place — fire strains up, a stone strains down, oil rises through water. Augustine turns that physics into psychology: love is the gravity of the soul, and the soul is restless until it reaches the place its love is pulling it toward. The Latin is eight words, twice four, and no English can match that compression without going dark; we unfold the second clause so the real claim survives — that whatever is moving me, it is my love doing the moving.

divergences.phrase: pacem quietis, pacem sabbati, pacem sine vespera
divergences.older: the peace of rest, the peace of the Sabbath, which hath no evening
divergences.lectio: the peace of rest, the peace of the sabbath: peace without an evening
divergences.note: In Genesis, every day of creation closes the same way — 'and there was evening' — except the seventh. Augustine reads that missing evening as the promise the whole book has been climbing toward: God's rest is the one day that never closes. Pusey tucks the phrase into a relative clause; we let it stand bare, as the Latin does, because it is the final cadence of the entire work — the rest the restless heart of Book I was made for.

divergences.phrase: omnis mihi copia quae deus meus non est egestas est
divergences.older: all abundance, which is not my God, is emptiness to me
divergences.lectio: every abundance that is not my God is, to me, poverty
divergences.note: Egestas is beggary, destitution — the strict economic opposite of copia, plenty. Pusey's 'emptiness' turns the line into a mood; Augustine's word is harder and stranger: wealth without God is not merely hollow-feeling, it is actual want. We keep the ledger language, so the paradox stays a paradox — abundance that counts as poverty.
divergences.phrase: fecisti nos ad te, et inquietum est cor nostrum, donec requiescat in te
divergences.older: Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee
divergences.lectio: you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you
divergences.note: The most famous sentence in the book and arguably in Western devotional prose. We keep it almost verbatim, shedding only the archaic "madest / repose / Thee." "Restless" is the right modern word for inquietum (restless, unquiet, unsettled), and "rests in you" preserves the requies / requiescat root that anchors the whole work's arc. Nothing here is modernized away; this line is load-bearing and stays plain and strange.

divergences.phrase: fornicabar abs te / amicitia enim huius mundi fornicatio est abs te
divergences.older: I committed fornication against Thee ... the friendship of this world is fornication against Thee
divergences.lectio: I committed adultery against you ... friendship with this world is adultery against you
divergences.note: Augustine's verb is the deliberately scandalous fornicari, echoing the prophets' charge that Israel "plays the harlot" by loving the world instead of God (cf. James 4:4, "friendship of the world is enmity with God"). "Fornication" now reads either clinical or quaint; "adultery" keeps the covenant-betrayal force — the soul is breaking faith with a God it is bound to — which is the metaphor's whole point. We chose betrayal-of-marriage over a generic "unfaithfulness" to preserve the sexual sting Augustine intends.

divergences.phrase: et flebam Didonem extinctam ... at non flebam, quod ipse moriebar
divergences.older: to weep for dead Dido, because she killed herself for love ... weeping not his own death for want of love to Thee
divergences.lectio: to weep for dead Dido because she killed herself for love ... but does not weep for his own death, dying for want of love for you
divergences.note: The Dido set-piece is the emotional engine of the book's second half: Augustine indicts his boyhood self for shedding real tears over a fictional queen's suicide while feeling nothing for his own soul's death. We keep "Dido," the Virgilian frame, and the brutal symmetry (weeping for her death / not weeping for his) intact rather than smoothing it into abstraction, because the rhetorical mirror IS the argument.

divergences.phrase: foeda erat, et amavi eam; amavi perire, amavi defectum meum
divergences.older: It was foul, and I loved it; I loved to perish, I loved mine own fault (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: It was foul, and I loved it. I loved my own undoing; I loved my falling-away — not the thing I fell toward, but the fall itself.
divergences.note: The hinge of the whole book: sin loved for its own sake. The Latin defectus is privative — a falling-short, a defecting-away from being toward nothing. Pusey's 'fault' loses the metaphysics; 'falling-away / undoing' keeps the sense that the soul loved its own diminishment, not any object. Deliberately left strange.

divergences.phrase: gratis malus … nulla causa malitiae meae nisi malitia mea
divergences.older: that I should be gratuitously evil, having no temptation to ill, but the ill itself
divergences.lectio: that I should be evil for nothing, with no cause for my malice but malice itself
divergences.note: 'Gratuitously evil' is the famous tag, but in modern English 'gratuitous' has drifted toward 'excessive/uncalled-for.' 'Evil for nothing' restores gratis — done for free, with no payoff — which is exactly Augustine's puzzle: motiveless malice. The doubling malitia/malitia is kept as 'malice … malice itself.'

divergences.phrase: foeda eram, et eram in oculis tuis
divergences.older: my beauty consumed away, and I stank in Thine eyes (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: My beauty wasted away, and I was rotten in your eyes
divergences.note: Pusey's vivid 'I stank' overtranslates; the Latin says simply 'I was foul' (foeda), the same root as the theft passage, binding the book together. 'Rotten' keeps the strong sensory disgust and the verbal echo of foeda without inventing a smell the Latin does not name. Direct address kept: 'Thine' → 'your.'

divergences.phrase: a cauldron of shameful loves seethed and crackled in my ears
divergences.older: there sang all around me in my ears a cauldron of unholy loves (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: a cauldron of shameful loves seethed and crackled in my ears
divergences.note: Augustine's Latin puns: sartago (a frying-pan or cauldron) chimes with Carthago, and circumstrepebat means it crackled and roared all around — the very sound of frying. The pun cannot survive translation, but we keep the seething, sizzling cookpot rather than Pusey's gentler 'sang,' since the noise of the cauldron is load-bearing. The famous opening 'To Carthage I came' is preserved.

divergences.phrase: the love of wisdom is what the Greek word "philosophy" means
divergences.older: the love of wisdom is in Greek called 'philosophy' (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: love of wisdom is what the Greek word "philosophy" means
divergences.note: The Hortensius turning point. We keep the etymology explicit (philo- + sophia = love of wisdom) because Augustine's whole conversion here pivots on it: a pagan book about loving wisdom turns his prayers toward God. The book's title (Hortensius) and Cicero are preserved untouched.

divergences.phrase: It cannot be that the son of these tears should perish
divergences.older: it is not possible that the son of these tears should perish (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: It cannot be that the son of these tears should perish
divergences.note: The bishop's reply to Monica, Latin 'fieri non potest, ut filius istarum lacrimarum pereat' — one of the most quoted lines in the book. Kept almost verbatim; only the archaic phrasing is smoothed. 'The son of these tears' is preserved exactly, since the whole force depends on it.

divergences.phrase: factus eram ipse mihi magna quaestio
divergences.older: I became a great riddle to myself (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: I had become a great riddle to myself
divergences.note: One of the most quoted sentences in the book, and the seed of Augustine's whole inward turn: in grief the self becomes opaque to itself. Latin quaestio is literally a "question" or "problem," but Pusey's "riddle" is exactly right — it keeps the sense that Augustine has become a thing he cannot read or answer. We keep it almost verbatim, shifting only the tense to the English pluperfect so it sits naturally in the surrounding narration. Deliberately left strange and unsoftened; nothing is added or explained away.

divergences.phrase: portabam enim concisam et cruentam animam meam, impatientem portari a me
divergences.older: For I bore about a shattered and bleeding soul, impatient of being borne by me (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: For I was carrying my soul, broken and bleeding, and it could not bear to be carried by me
divergences.note: The most physically violent image of grief in the book: the self is split in two, one part lugging the other like a wound. We keep the carrying and the blood intact (concisa = cut to pieces, cruenta = bloodied) rather than abstracting it into "distress." Pusey's "impatient of being borne" is accurate but archaic; "could not bear to be carried" preserves the bitter pun on bearing/carrying a burden that the soul itself refuses. The strangeness is load-bearing and stays.

divergences.phrase: fuderam in harenam animam meam diligendo moriturum acsi non moriturum
divergences.older: I had poured out my soul upon the dust, in loving one that must die, as if he would never die (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: I had poured out my soul upon the sand, in loving one who must die as though he would never die
divergences.note: The diagnostic line of the whole book of grief: the error was not love but the lie inside it — loving a mortal thing as though it were immortal. Augustine returns to this thought as the cure (love souls in God, who cannot be lost). Pusey's "dust" renders harena, but harena is specifically sand — the ground that swallows water and gives nothing back, the right image for a love poured out and lost. We keep the bare, aphoristic shape ("one who must die as though he would never die") because the symmetry is the argument; it is not smoothed into a general remark about loss.

divergences.phrase: Faustus quidam ... magnus laqueus diaboli
divergences.older: a certain Bishop of the Manichees, Faustus by name, a great snare of the Devil (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: a certain bishop of the Manichees, Faustus by name, a great snare of the devil
divergences.note: Kept almost verbatim, because it is load-bearing and meant to unsettle: the most celebrated teacher in Augustine's old sect is introduced not as a fraud but as a genuinely charming, decent man — and named outright as the devil's trap. The strangeness is the point, so we hold to "a great snare of the devil" and let the seductive smooth-tongued bishop (and, later, the man Augustine comes to like for his honest admission of ignorance) stand under that verdict. Only the archaic capitalization and inversion are smoothed; the image is not softened into "temptation" or "danger."

divergences.phrase: et mentitus sum matri, et illi matri, et evasi
divergences.older: And I lied to my mother, and such a mother, and escaped (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: So I lied to my mother, and to a mother like that, and got away.
divergences.note: The hinge of the book and one of its most painful confessions: Augustine slips away by night from the harbor at Carthage, leaving Monica praying at Cyprian's shrine, having told her he was only seeing a friend off. The Latin doubles matri — "to my mother, and to THAT mother" — the repetition driving home that it was not just any deception but the betrayal of the one person praying for his soul. We keep the doubling intact ("to my mother, and to a mother like that") rather than collapsing it, because the verbal stab is the confession. "Got away" preserves the furtive evasi over a flatter "escaped."

divergences.phrase: suscepit me paterne ille homo Dei ... ut ab illo ad te scienter ducerer
divergences.older: That man of God received me as a father ... that by him I might knowingly be led to Thee (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: That man of God received me like a father ... that by him I might knowingly be led to you.
divergences.note: The turn of the whole book. Augustine comes to Milan still a Manichee, despairing of the Catholic Church, drawn only by curiosity about Ambrose's reputation as an orator — and Ambrose simply receives him with fatherly kindness. We keep "like a father" and the deliberate play of unknowing/knowing (led "all unknowing" to Ambrose, that through Ambrose he might "knowingly" be led to God), because the quiet, undramatic welcome is exactly the hinge on which the conversion narrative will swing in Books VI–VIII. Nothing is heightened; the plainness of the reception is its force.

divergences.phrase: laetitia temporalis felicitatis
divergences.older: the joy of a temporary felicity ... he verily had not the true joy; but yet I with those my ambitious designs was seeking one much less true
divergences.lectio: the joy of a little patch of happiness ... His joy was not the true joy, of course; but the joy I was after, with all my ambitious designs, was a far less true one still
divergences.note: This is the moral hinge of Book VI: the drunken beggar, merry on a few begged coins, is happier than the ambitious Augustine sweating toward an emperor's panegyric he knows is a lie. The strangeness is load-bearing and must not be softened — the beggar genuinely is "beyond" Augustine, "the happier" man. We keep the brutal comparison intact (he cheerful / I anxious; he free of care / I full of fears) and preserve Augustine's own verdict that his glory was the less true of the two false joys. Pusey's "felicity" is dead vocabulary; "a little patch of happiness" keeps the smallness and contingency of temporal felicitas without inventing anything.

divergences.locus: VI.xii (Pusey seg. 27), Alypius at the amphitheater
divergences.phrase: ut vidit illum sanguinem, immanitatem simul ebibit ... hauriebat furias
divergences.older: For so soon as he saw that blood, he therewith drunk down savageness; nor turned away, but fixed his eye, drinking in frenzy, unawares, and was delighted with that guilty fight, and intoxicated with the bloody pastime
divergences.lectio: The moment he saw the blood, he drank down savagery with it, and did not turn away, but fixed his gaze, and drank in the frenzy without knowing it, taking delight in that guilty contest, drunk on the bloody pleasure
divergences.note: The most famous image in the book outside the pear theft: Alypius, dragged to the games with his eyes shut, opens them at the crowd's roar and is wounded deeper in soul than the gladiator in body. Augustine's metaphor is relentlessly liquid — ebibit (drank down), hauriebat (kept drawing/draining in), inebriabatur (was made drunk). We keep every beat of the drinking-in-of-blood image rather than abstracting it to "was corrupted," because the physiology of the addiction — savagery swallowed like wine — is the whole point. "Drinking in the savagery" is the load-bearing strangeness the brief names explicitly.

divergences.locus: VI.xv (Pusey seg. 24), the dismissal of the concubine
divergences.phrase: avulsa a latere meo ... concubina, cor, ubi adhaerebat, concisum et vulneratum mihi erat et trahebat sanguinem
divergences.older: my concubine being torn from my side as a hindrance to my marriage, my heart which clave unto her was torn and wounded and bleeding
divergences.lectio: the woman I lived with was torn from my side as a hindrance to my marriage, and my heart, which clung to her, was torn and wounded and left bleeding
divergences.note: Augustine never names her, and we keep her unnamed, as the original withholds the name — the omission is itself a wound the text carries. "Concubine" in modern English reads either legalistic or lurid and obscures that this was a years-long partnership and the mother of his son; "the woman I lived with" restores the human fact without softening the moral verdict Augustine passes on himself (he was "a slave to lust," not a "lover of marriage"). The torn / wounded / bleeding triad (concisum, vulneratum, trahebat sanguinem) is kept verbatim in force: the rawest emotional sentence in the book, and it must keep its blood.

divergences.locus: Book VII.x (Pusey seg. 15), the vision of the Light
divergences.phrase: et inveni longe me esse a te in regione dissimilitudinis ... ego sum qui sum
divergences.older: I perceived myself to be far off from Thee, in the region of unlikeness, as if I heard this Thy voice from on high ... Yet verily, I AM that I AM (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: I found that I was far away from you, in the region of unlikeness ... No — truly, I AM WHO I AM
divergences.note: The summit of the book's intellectual ascent, where the Neoplatonic climb meets the God of Exodus. Two phrases are load-bearing and must not be smoothed. "Region of unlikeness" (regio dissimilitudinis) is a technical Platonic term — the soul's distance from God measured as ontological un-likeness, not mere geography — and we keep it exactly, strange as it sounds, because it names Augustine's whole diagnosis of the fallen self. And "I AM WHO I AM" (the burning-bush name, Exod. 3:14) is kept verbatim in small capitals: the answer is not an argument but a Name, and the force depends on its bareness. We render Pusey's "I AM that I AM" with the more standard "I AM WHO I AM" but add nothing and explain nothing away.

divergences.locus: Book VII.xii (Pusey seg. 17), evil as privation
divergences.phrase: quaesivi quid esset iniquitas, et non inveni substantiam, sed ... omne quod corrumpitur privatur bono
divergences.older: all which is corrupted is deprived of good ... That evil then which I sought, whence it is, is not any substance (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: everything that is corrupted is being robbed of some good ... that evil whose origin I was searching for is not a substance
divergences.note: The metaphysical heart of Book VII and Augustine's lifelong answer to the Manichees: evil is not a thing (substantia) but a privation, a robbing-away of good. The argument is precise and must not be flattened into a vague "evil is the absence of good." We keep the active, almost violent privatur as "is being robbed of some good" rather than a static "is deprived," because Augustine's point is dynamic — corruption is a process that diminishes a real good, and a thing wholly stripped of good would simply cease to be. The conclusion ("evil is not a substance") is kept bare and load-bearing; the whole theodicy turns on it.

divergences.phrase: quaerebam viam comparandi roboris ... non tenebam ... donec amplecterer mediatorem ... Verbum caro factum est
divergences.older: Then I sought a way of obtaining strength sufficient to enjoy Thee; and found it not, until I embraced that Mediator betwixt God and men ... For, the Word was made flesh (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: I began to search for a way to gain the strength I needed to enjoy you, and I did not find it — not until I embraced that Mediator between God and men ... For the Word was made flesh
divergences.note: This is the hinge on which all of Book VII turns: the Platonists could lift Augustine to glimpse Being, but could not give him the strength to stay — only the Incarnation could, the Word stooping into flesh as "milk for our infancy." We keep "Mediator" (mediator, 1 Tim. 2:5) as a title, not softened to "go-between," and we keep "the Word was made flesh" verbatim (John 1:14), the load-bearing answer to everything the Platonist books lacked. The whole book is built so that this plain sentence lands with full weight after pages of metaphysics; nothing here is modernized away.

divergences.phrase: da mihi castitatem et continentiam, sed noli modo
divergences.older: Give me chastity and continency, only not yet (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: Give me chastity and self-control — only not yet
divergences.note: The most quoted prayer in the book, and one of the most honest sentences ever written about a divided will: Augustine begs God for chastity while secretly dreading to be heard, because he wants the disease of lust "fed full rather than snuffed out" (malebam expleri quam exstingui). We keep the prayer almost verbatim, since its whole force is in the bald confession of the trick the heart plays on itself. We render continentia as "self-control" rather than the now-archaic "continency," but the load-bearing punchline — "only not yet" — is kept exactly. Nothing is softened; the strangeness is the confession.

divergences.phrase: tolle, lege; tolle, lege
divergences.older: Take up and read; Take up and read (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: Take up and read, take up and read
divergences.note: The hinge of the whole Confessions: the child's chant in the neighboring house that sends Augustine to the book of Paul. The Latin "Tolle, lege" is so famous it is often left untranslated, and we preserve it as a touchstone here while rendering the chant itself in plain English. "Take up and read" is the load-bearing line and is kept exactly as Pusey has it (and as the tradition has fixed it), because the entire conversion turns on those four words and the verse they send him to — Romans 13:13–14, which we also keep close to the literal ("put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh and its cravings"). Nothing here is modernized away.

divergences.phrase: imperat animus corpori, et paretur statim; imperat animus sibi, et resistitur
divergences.older: The mind commands the body, and it obeys instantly; the mind commands itself, and is resisted (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: The mind commands the body, and is obeyed at once; the mind commands itself, and is resisted
divergences.note: The most influential piece of psychology in the book, and the heart of Augustine's analysis of the will that cannot obey itself: a single will, not two natures, half willing and half not, and so tearing itself apart. We keep the bare, antithetical shape (commands the body / is obeyed; commands itself / is resisted) verbatim in force, because the symmetry is the argument — it is this passage, not Manichaean dualism, that explains the agony in the garden. Pusey's "and it obeys instantly" we render as "and is obeyed at once" to match the passive of the matching clause ("and is resisted") and let the parallel ring. Deliberately left plain and strange; nothing is added or explained away.

divergences.locus: IX.10 (Pusey segs. 22–25), the vision at Ostia
divergences.phrase: et dum loquimur et inhiamus illi, attingimus eam modice toto ictu cordis
divergences.older: And while we were discoursing and panting after her, we slightly touched on her with the whole effort of our heart (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: And while we were speaking and panting after her, we touched her, a little, with one whole stroke of the heart
divergences.note: The climax of the book and one of the summits of Western mystical prose: mother and son, leaning at a window in Ostia, rise "step by step" through created things to the eternal Wisdom and brush against her for a single instant. The crux is ictu cordis. Pusey's "the whole effort of our heart" loses the decisive image: ictus is a single beat, blow, or stroke — the touch lasts exactly one heartbeat. We keep "one whole stroke of the heart" so the reader feels both the totality of the reach (toto, the whole self thrown into it) and its momentariness (one beat, then gone). We deliberately keep the strange Wisdom-as-"she" and the bare grammar of eternity ("only 'is'") rather than smoothing them; the passage's holiness is in its difficulty, and nothing in it is paraphrased away.

divergences.phrase: ponite hoc corpus ubicumque; nihil vos eius cura conturbet; tantum illud vos rogo, ut ad domini altare memineritis mei, ubiubi fueritis
divergences.older: Lay this body any where; let not the care for that any way disquiet you: this only I request, that you would remember me at the Lord's altar, wherever you be (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: Lay this body anywhere; let no care for it trouble you in the least. This one thing only I ask: that you would remember me at the Lord's altar, wherever you may be.
divergences.note: Monica, who had spent her life preparing a grave beside her husband in Africa, lets the whole earthly wish drop in a single sentence — the inward fruit of the vision she has just shared. The line is load-bearing and must stay almost verbatim; we shed only the archaic grammar ("disquiet you," "wherever you be") and keep the flat, astonishing "anywhere" (ubicumque) and the one thing she does still want — to be named at the altar. The repetition ubiubi ("wherever, wherever") is rendered plainly as "wherever you may be," matching the deliberate plainness of her dying speech. Nothing is added or softened; the renunciation is exactly as stark as Augustine wrote it.

divergences.phrase: ne reprehendat me, si aliquantulum temporis matrem... flevi, matrem... quae me multos annos fleverat, ut oculis tuis viverem
divergences.older: if he finds sin therein, that I wept my mother for a small portion of an hour (the mother who... had for many years wept for me that I might live in Thine eyes), let him not deride me (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: if he finds it a sin that I wept for my mother for one small fraction of an hour — the mother who for the time was dead to my eyes, who for so many years had wept for me that I might live in your eyes — let him not mock me
divergences.note: Augustine has spent the whole death-scene damming his tears — at the deathbed, at the prayers, at the graveside — until, alone in bed, he finally lets them "flow as freely as they would." The crux is the symmetry of weeping that closes it: he weeps for his mother for a fraction of an hour; she had wept for him for years, that he might live. This is the same logic as Book III's "the son of these tears," and the mirror is the argument, so we keep it exact: his brief tears against her long ones, his eyes against your eyes (oculis tuis). Pusey's "a small portion of an hour" is kept in sense as "one small fraction of an hour"; we do not round it off or generalize the grief, because its smallness, set against her years, is the point Augustine is confessing.

divergences.phrase: Sero te amavi, pulchritudo tam antiqua et tam nova, sero te amavi! et ecce intus eras et ego foris... vocasti et clamasti et rupisti surditatem meam
divergences.older: Too late loved I Thee, O Thou Beauty of ancient days, yet ever new! too late I loved Thee!... Thou calledst, and shoutedst, and burstest my deafness
divergences.lectio: Late have I loved you, O Beauty so ancient and so new, late have I loved you! And see, you were within, and I was outside... You called and cried aloud and broke through my deafness
divergences.note: The single most quoted passage in the Confessions and a summit of devotional prose. Pusey's "Too late" overtranslates sero ("late"); the received English of this passage is "Late have I loved you," which keeps the bare adverb and the haunting repetition (sero... sero). We preserve the chiastic engine of the whole — you within / I outside, you with me / I not with you — and the five-sense reversal of conversion (called/cried/broke deafness, flashed/shone/scattered blindness, breathed fragrance, tasted, touched/burned), where God seizes each sense Augustine had squandered on creatures. "Ancient and new" (antiqua / nova) is load-bearing paradox and stays plain and strange; nothing is smoothed.

divergences.phrase: venio in campos et lata praetoria memoriae... magna ista vis est memoriae, nimis magna, deus, penetrale amplum et infinitum
divergences.older: I come to the fields and spacious palaces of my memory... Great is this force of memory, excessive great, O my God; a large and boundless chamber
divergences.lectio: I come to the fields and vast palaces of memory... Great is this power of memory, exceedingly great, O my God, a vast and boundless inner room
divergences.note: The memory analysis is Book X's intellectual heart and the seedbed of Western interiority. We keep Augustine's central, deliberately physical image intact — memory as fields, palaces, vast halls, storehouses, even "the stomach of the mind" (venter animi) where joy and sorrow are stored like food but not tasted — because the spatial metaphor IS the argument: the self is a place larger than itself that it cannot fully enter ("the mind is too narrow to hold itself"). We resisted abstracting these into "capacity" or "faculty." The recurring refrain "I will pass beyond... that I may reach you" (transibo... ut attingam te) is preserved each time, since the ascent past memory to the God above memory is the chapter's spine.

divergences.phrase: da quod iubes et iube quod vis
divergences.older: Give what Thou enjoinest, and enjoin what Thou wilt
divergences.lectio: Give what you command, and command what you will
divergences.note: The prayer that, repeated to Augustine by report, so provoked Pelagius that it helped ignite the grace controversy. The whole theology of Book X's second half rests on it: God's command creates no obligation he does not also enable, so the commanded continence is itself a gift to be asked for, not a feat to be achieved. We render iubes/iube as "command" rather than Pusey's archaic "enjoin" (now nearly opaque), keeping the tight four-beat symmetry (give/command :: command/will) that makes the line memorable and lets it toll, as in the Latin, three times across the temptations. The paired O Love, who are forever burning and never burned out (numquam consumeris) is kept as the affective ground of the petition.

divergences.phrase: Quid est ergo tempus? si nemo ex me quaerat, scio; si quaerenti explicare velim, nescio
divergences.older: What then is time? If no one asks me, I know: if I wish to explain it to one that asketh, I know not (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: So what is time? If no one asks me, I know; if I want to explain it to someone who asks, I do not know
divergences.note: The most quoted sentence in all of Augustine's philosophy of time, and the hinge of Book XI. The strangeness is the whole point: a knowing that collapses the moment it is asked to give an account of itself. We keep it almost verbatim, shedding only Pusey's archaic 'asketh / know not' and the inverted clause order. 'I do not know' is held back to the end, as in the Latin, so the paradox lands on nescio. Nothing is smoothed away; this line stays plain and unsettling.

divergences.phrase: distentio animi / video tempus quandam esse distentionem
divergences.older: time is nothing else than protraction; but of what, I know not; and I marvel, if it be not of the mind itself ... my life is but a distraction (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: time is nothing other than a stretching-out -- but of what, I do not know, and I would be amazed if it were not a stretching of the mind itself ... my life is nothing but a being-pulled-apart
divergences.note: Augustine's answer to 'what is time' is distentio animi -- the soul stretched across past, present, and future at once, holding the no-longer of memory and the not-yet of expectation in a present attention. Pusey scatters the one Latin root (distendere) across 'protraction', 'extension', 'distraction', and 'distended', which hides that this is a single technical idea. We keep it consistent: 'stretching-out' for the neutral analysis of measured time, and the heavier 'being-pulled-apart' in 11.38 where the same word turns confessional -- the scattered soul longing to be gathered back into the One. Keeping the metaphysics precise here is the point of the whole book; we do not flatten distentio into a vague 'duration'.

divergences.phrase: Quid faciebat Deus antequam faceret caelum et terram?
divergences.older: What was God doing before He made heaven and earth? ... He was preparing hell (saith he) for pryers into mysteries (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: What was God doing before he made heaven and earth? ... He was preparing hell for those who pry into deep things
divergences.note: The mocker's question that frames the move from Genesis to the analysis of time. Augustine pointedly refuses the famous flippant retort ('preparing hell for pryers') -- 'it is one thing to answer a question, another to make sport of the questioner' -- because the real answer dismantles the question's hidden assumption: there was no 'before', since time itself is created and 'there was no then, when there was no time'. We keep both the joke and the refusal intact, and keep the answer's strangeness ('before God made heaven and earth, he was not making anything'), since softening it would lose the whole point that eternity is not merely a very long time.

divergences.phrase: caelum caeli
divergences.older: the heaven of heavens
divergences.lectio: the heaven of heavens
divergences.note: Augustine's caelum caeli (from the Psalm, caelum caeli Domino) is the metaphysical hinge of the whole book: not the visible sky but an intellectual creature, a created mind that clings to God in unbroken contemplation and so escapes the flux of time without being coeternal with God. The phrase is deliberately strange in Latin and must stay strange in English — 'the heaven of heavens,' not smoothed into 'the highest heaven' or 'the spiritual realm,' both of which would flatten the load-bearing idea that this is itself a creature, the first thing made, the 'house of God' that is eternal in measure but not without beginning. We keep Pusey's wording verbatim and let the surrounding prose carry the meaning.

divergences.phrase: terra invisibilis et incomposita / materia informis / paene nihil
divergences.older: earth invisible and without form ... formless matter ... almost nothing
divergences.lectio: earth invisible and unformed ... formless matter ... almost nothing
divergences.note: The second pillar of Book XII is the 'formless matter' (materia informis) that Augustine reads under the Genesis phrase terra invisibilis et incomposita — the near-nothing (paene nihil), made by God out of nothing, out of which the visible world is shaped. The precision here is doctrinal: it is not nothing (it has being, from God), and not a thing (it has no form), but a 'formless almost-nothing' between form and nothing. We render incomposita as 'unformed' rather than Pusey's 'without form' for plain modern rhythm, but we hold the paradox intact everywhere — 'a nothing-something, an is-and-is-not' — and never let it collapse into a tidy 'raw material,' which would lose Augustine's point that it is barely on the near side of nothing at all.

divergences.phrase: in ipsa veritate incommutabili ... non quia ipsius, sed quia verum
divergences.older: in the unchangeable Truth itself ... not because it is theirs, but because it is true
divergences.lectio: in the unchangeable Truth itself ... not because it is theirs, but because it is true
divergences.note: The long second half of the book is Augustine's defense of interpretive pluralism: a single passage of Moses may carry many true meanings, all of them genuinely in the text, because the one God 'shaped the holy Scriptures to fit the understandings of many.' The danger he names is not error but pride — loving a reading 'because it is theirs,' not because it is true — which wounds charity, the end of the whole law. The crux for a translator is to keep both halves sharp: the generous 'why not as both, if both are true?' AND the insistence that truth is common property, belonging 'to us all,' never private. We resist softening this into modern relativism; for Augustine the many readings are true precisely because they meet in 'the unchangeable Truth itself, which is above our minds.'

divergences.phrase: ecce apparet mihi in aenigmate trinitas, quod es tu, deus meus
divergences.older: Lo, now the Trinity appears unto me in a glass darkly, which is Thou my God (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: And now, look — the Trinity appears to me in a glass, darkly, and that Trinity is you, my God
divergences.note: The structural heart of the final three books: Augustine reads the Trinity out of the opening of Genesis — God the Father creating "in the Beginning" (the Son) while "the Spirit moved upon the waters." Pusey's "in a glass darkly" is Paul's phrase (1 Cor 13:12) for in aenigmate, and we keep it, because Augustine is deliberately quoting it: the Trinity is glimpsed, not grasped. We resist flattening aenigma to "dimly" or "as a riddle"; the load-bearing point is that creation itself is the dark mirror in which the triune God is half-seen. "That Trinity is you" keeps the audacious identification (quod es tu) that the rest of the book unfolds.

divergences.phrase: esse, nosse, velle ... sum enim et scio et volo
divergences.older: To Be, to Know, and to Will. For I Am, and Know, and Will (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: to be, to know, and to will. For I am, and I know, and I will
divergences.note: Augustine's analogy for the Trinity drawn from the inner self — being, knowing, willing — three that are one life and yet truly distinct. The Latin is three bare infinitives (esse, nosse, velle); we keep them bare and lower-case rather than Pusey's reverent capitals, because the whole point is that these are ordinary facts of one's own mind, a ladder to climb and then leave behind: Augustine insists they are "something altogether different from the Trinity" and only "point out where they may test themselves." The strangeness — that you can verify the triad in yourself and still not have touched God — must be preserved, not smoothed into a tidy proof.

divergences.phrase: pacem quietis, pacem sabbati, pacem sine vespera ... tu autem, domine, semper operaris et semper requiescis
divergences.older: the peace of rest, the peace of the Sabbath, which hath no evening ... But Thou, Lord, ever workest, and art ever at rest (Pusey)
divergences.lectio: the peace of rest, the peace of the Sabbath, the Sabbath that has no evening ... But you, Lord, are always at work and always at rest
divergences.note: The benediction of the whole Confessions, and the resolution of its first sentence: the restless heart (Book I) finds, at the last, the rest that has no evening. "Evening" (vespera) is literal and load-bearing: each of the six days of creation closed with "there was evening," but the seventh has none — the Sabbath of eternal life is rest without sunset, without falling-off. We keep "evening" rather than the abstract "end" so the figure stays anchored in Genesis. The closing paradox — semper operaris et semper requiescis, God always working and always resting, with rest that is God himself (requies tua tu ipse es) — is held intact and plain, because the strangeness is the consolation. The book ends as it began and as the Gospel commands: ask, seek, knock — "so will it be opened. Amen."

segments.text: Great are you, Lord, and greatly to be praised: great is your power, and your wisdom is beyond all measure. And man wants to praise you — man, one small piece of your creation; man, hauling his mortality around with him, hauling the evidence of his sin and the evidence that you resist the proud. Yet still he wants to praise you, this man, one small piece of your creation. You stir us up to delight in praising you, because you made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you. Grant me, Lord, to know and understand which comes first: calling on you, or praising you? And which first — knowing you, or calling on you? But who calls on you without knowing you? Not knowing you, he could call on something else instead of you. Or is it rather that you are called on in order to be known? Yet how will they call on one they have not believed in? And how will they believe without someone to preach him? And those who seek the Lord will praise him — for those who seek find him, and those who find him will praise him. Let me seek you, Lord, by calling on you; let me call on you by believing in you — for you have been preached to us. My faith calls on you, Lord: the faith you gave me, that you breathed into me through the humanity of your Son and the ministry of your preacher.

You are great, Lord, and greatly to be praised; great is your power, and your wisdom has no measure. And a human being wants to praise you — one small piece of your creation, a man who carries his own death about with him, who carries the evidence of his sin and the evidence that you stand against the proud. Still he wants to praise you, this small piece of your creation. You yourself stir him to take delight in praising you, because you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you. Grant me, Lord, to know and understand which comes first: to call on you or to praise you? And again — to know you or to call on you? For how can anyone call on you without knowing you? Not knowing you, he might call on something other than you. Or is it rather that we call on you in order to know you? But how can they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe without someone to preach? Those who seek the Lord will praise him, for those who seek will find him, and those who find will praise him. Let me seek you, Lord, by calling on you, and call on you by believing in you — for you have been preached to us. My faith calls on you, Lord, the faith you gave me, the faith you breathed into me through the coming of your Son in the flesh, through the work of the one who preached him.

And how will I call on my God, my God and Lord — when to call on him is, surely, to call him into myself? And what place is there in me for my God to come into? Where would God come into me — God, who made heaven and earth? Is it true, Lord my God: is there anything in me that could hold you? Do heaven and earth hold you — heaven and earth, which you made, and in which you made me? Or is it that whatever exists holds you, because nothing that exists could exist without you? Then since I exist too, why do I beg you to come into me — I, who would not exist unless you were in me? For I am not now in hell, and yet even there you are; for if I go down into hell, you are there. So I would not exist, my God — would not exist at all — unless you were in me. Or say it better: I would not exist unless I were in you, from whom all things are, through whom all things are, in whom all things are. Yes, Lord: yes. Then where do I call you to, if I am already in you? And from where would you come into me? Where could I withdraw, outside heaven and earth, so that my God could come into me from there — my God, who has said, "I fill heaven and earth"?

And how shall I call upon my God — my God and my Lord — since to call him is to call him into myself? What room is there inside me for my God to come, the God who made heaven and earth? Is there really anything in me, Lord my God, that can hold you? Can heaven and earth, which you made, and in which you made me, hold you? Or is it that, because nothing could exist without you, whatever exists holds you? Then since I too exist, why do I beg you to come into me, when I would not exist at all unless you were already in me? For I am not yet in hell — and yet you are there too. If I go down into hell, you are there. I could not exist, my God, could not exist at all, unless you were in me; or rather, unless I were in you, from whom all things come, through whom all things come, in whom all things hold together. Yes, Lord, exactly so. Where do I call you to, since I am already in you? And from where could you enter me — for where can I go beyond heaven and earth, so that from there my God might come into me, the God who said, I fill heaven and earth?

So do heaven and earth hold you, since you fill them? Or do you fill them and have some of yourself left over, since they cannot hold you? And where do you pour out what remains of you, once heaven and earth are full? Or do you need nothing to hold you — you who hold all things together — since what you fill, you fill by holding it? The vessels that are full of you give you no footing: even if they shattered, you would not spill. And when you pour yourself out over us, you do not fall down into us; you raise us up. You do not scatter; you gather us in. But you who fill everything — do you fill it with the whole of yourself? Or, since all things together cannot hold the whole of you, do they hold a part of you — all of them the same part, all at once? Or each its own part, the larger things a larger part, the smaller a smaller? Then is one part of you larger and another smaller? Or are you whole everywhere, while nothing holds you whole?

Do heaven and earth contain you, then, since you fill them? Or do you fill them and still overflow, since they cannot contain you? And when heaven and earth are full, where do you pour the rest of yourself? Or do you have no need of anything to contain you, since you contain all things — filling what you fill by holding it? The vessels you fill do not hold you up: even if they shatter, you are not spilled. And when you pour yourself out on us, you do not fall down — you lift us up. You are not scattered — you gather us together. But when you fill all things, do you fill them with the whole of yourself? Or, since all things cannot hold the whole of you, do they hold only a part — and all of them the same part at once? Or each its own part, the larger things more, the smaller less? Then is one part of you greater and another smaller? Or are you wholly everywhere, while nothing holds the whole of you?

What are you, then, my God? What, I ask, but the Lord God? For who is Lord besides the Lord? Who is God besides our God? Highest, best, most powerful, most almighty; most merciful and most just; most hidden and most present; most beautiful and most strong; constant and ungraspable; unchangeable, changing everything; never new, never old; renewing all things while quietly aging the proud, who never see it happen; always at work, always at rest; gathering, though you need nothing; carrying, filling, sheltering; creating, feeding, finishing; seeking, though you lack nothing. You love without fever; you are jealous and untroubled; you repent and feel no sorrow; you are angry and calm. You change your works without changing your plan; you take back what you find, though you never lost it. Never poor, you delight in gain; never greedy, you demand interest. We pay you more than you require, to make you our debtor — yet who has anything that is not already yours? You pay debts owing no one; you forgive debts and lose nothing. And after all that, what have we said, my God, my life, my holy sweetness? What does anyone manage to say when he speaks of you? Yet woe to those who say nothing of you: even the ones who talk the most are mute.

What are you, then, my God? What, but the Lord God? For who is Lord but the Lord, who is God but our God? Highest and best, most powerful, all-powerful; most merciful and most just; most hidden and most present; most beautiful and most strong; steady, and beyond our grasp; unchanging, yet changing all things; never new, never old, yet making all things new — and bringing old age on the proud, who never notice it. Always working, always at rest; gathering, yet lacking nothing; carrying, filling, sheltering; creating, feeding, bringing to ripeness; always seeking, though you have everything. You love, but without the fever of it; you are jealous, but without anxiety; you regret, but feel no grief; you are angry, yet stay serene; you change your works while your purpose never changes; you take back what you find, though you never lost it; you are never in need, yet you are glad of gains; never greedy, yet you charge interest. We pay you more than we owe, so that you become our debtor — yet who has anything that is not already yours? You pay debts though you owe nothing; you forgive debts and lose nothing. And what have I now said, my God, my life, my holy joy? What does anyone say when he speaks of you? Yet woe to those who say nothing, since even the most eloquent are struck dumb.

Who will give me rest in you? Who will send you into my heart to intoxicate it, so that I forget my miseries and hold on to you, my one and only good? What are you to me? Have mercy, so I can even say it. And what am I to you, that you command me to love you — and if I don't, you are angry with me and threaten me with immense miseries? Is failing to love you, then, only a small misery? Oh, by your own mercies, Lord my God, tell me what you are to me. Say to my soul, "I am your salvation." Say it so that I hear it. Look: the ears of my heart are in front of you, Lord. Open them, and say to my soul, "I am your salvation." Let me run after that voice and lay hold of you. Do not hide your face from me. Let me die — so that I do not die — only let me see your face.

Oh, let me rest in you! Let you come into my heart and make it drunk, so that I forget my troubles and embrace you, my one good. What are you to me? In your pity, teach me to say it. What am I to you, that you command me to love you, and are angry with me if I do not, and threaten me with terrible griefs? Is it a small grief, then, not to love you? Oh, for the sake of your mercies, tell me, Lord my God, what you are to me. Say to my soul, I am your salvation. Say it so that I hear it. Look, Lord — my heart is here before you; open its ears and say to my soul, I am your salvation. Let me run after that voice and lay hold of you. Do not hide your face from me. Let me die — so that I do not die — only let me see your face.

The house of my soul is cramped — too small for you to come into. Enlarge it. It is in ruins: rebuild it. It holds things that will offend your eyes: I admit it, I know it. But who is going to clean it? Who else can I cry out to but you? Cleanse me from my hidden faults, Lord, and spare your servant from the sins of others. I believe, and that is why I speak — Lord, you know it. Haven't I laid my offenses out before you, testifying against myself, my God — and you forgave the wickedness of my heart? I do not go to court against you, for you are truth itself; and I have no wish to deceive myself, letting my own wrongdoing lie to itself. So no — I do not go to court against you. For if you kept a record of sins, Lord — Lord, who could stand?

The house of my soul is too narrow for you to enter; widen it. It is falling down; rebuild it. It holds things that must offend your eyes; I confess it, I know it. But who will clean it out? To whom but you should I cry? Lord, cleanse me from the faults I cannot see, and keep your servant from the power of the enemy. I believe, and so I speak. Lord, you know. Have I not confessed my wrongs against myself to you, and have you not, my God, forgiven the guilt of my heart? I do not go to law against you, who are the truth; I am afraid of deceiving myself, of letting my own sin lie to itself. So I will not go to law against you — for if you, Lord, kept a record of sins, Lord, who could stand?

Still, let me speak in front of your mercy — me, dust and ashes — still let me speak. It is your mercy I am speaking to, after all, not some man who would laugh at me. Maybe you laugh at me too; but you will turn and have compassion on me. Because what is it I want to say, Lord, except that I do not know where I came from into this place — this dying life, should I call it, or this living death? I don't know. What met me were the consolations of your mercies, as I heard from the parents of my flesh — the father you formed me from, the mother you formed me in; for I remember none of it myself. So the consolations of human milk received me; but it was not my mother or my nurses who filled their own breasts. You were giving me an infant's food through them, by your own design, out of the riches you have laid down at the very foundation of things. You gave me the gift of wanting no more than you gave, and you gave my nurses the will to pass on to me what you gave to them: by an affection you had set in order, they were glad to give me what they had in such abundance from you. For the good they did me was a good for them — a good not from them, but through them; for every good thing is from you, God, and from my God comes the whole of my rescue. I learned this only later, with you calling out to me through these very gifts of yours, inside me and around me. For back then, all I knew was how to suck, to settle when something pleased me, and to cry at whatever hurt my flesh — nothing more.

Yet let me speak before your mercy — me, dust and ashes. Let me speak, since I am speaking to your mercy and not to a man who would sneer. Perhaps you too look down on me — yet you will turn back and have compassion on me. For what would I say, Lord my God, except that I do not know where I came from when I came into this — what shall I call it — dying life, or living death? The comforts of your compassion took me up at once: I have it from the parents of my flesh, out of whose substance you shaped me in time, for I do not remember it myself. So the comforts of a woman's milk welcomed me. My mother and my nurses did not fill their own breasts; you gave the food of my infancy through them, by the order you have set, by which you hand out your riches through the hidden depths of all things. You also gave me to want no more than you gave, and gave my nurses the will to give me what you had given them. For with an instinct planted by you they wanted to give me what they had in abundance from you. The good I had from them was good for them, too. Yet it was not really from them but through them; for from you, God, come all good things, and from my God comes all my well-being. This I learned later, when you cried out to me through these gifts, inside me and around me. Back then I knew only how to suck, to settle into what pleased me and to cry at whatever hurt my body — nothing more.

Later I began to smile as well — first in my sleep, then awake. So I was told about myself, and I believed it, since we see the same in other infants; of myself I remember none of it. And little by little I began to sense where I was, and to want to show my wants to the people who could satisfy them — and I couldn't, because the wants were inside me and the people were outside, and no sense of theirs could reach into my soul. So I flailed my limbs and threw out sounds — signs, the few I could manage, such as I could manage — and they were nothing much like what I meant. And when I was not obeyed at once, either because I hadn't been understood or because obeying would have harmed me, I raged at my elders for not submitting to me, raged at free people for not being my slaves, and avenged myself on them by crying. That this is what infants are, I have learned from every infant I have been able to watch; and those babies, knowing nothing, have shown me better that I was the same than my nurses ever could, who knew me.

Later I began to smile, first in my sleep, then awake. So I was told of myself, and I believed it, for we see the same in other infants, though I do not remember it of myself. Little by little I began to notice where I was, and to want to make my wishes known to those who could meet them — and I could not, for the wishes were inside me, and they were outside, and no sense of theirs could reach into my spirit. So I would fling my limbs and my voice about at random, making the few signs I could, as best I could, that were like — though really very little like — what I wanted. And when I was not obeyed at once (my wishes being either harmful or unintelligible), I was furious at my elders for not giving in to me, at people who owed me nothing for not serving me, and I took revenge on them by crying. That infants are like this, I have learned from watching them; and that I was once like this, they have shown me — these infants who knew nothing of it — better than my nurses, who did.

And look — my infancy died long ago, and I am alive. But you, Lord, live forever, and nothing in you dies. Before the first beginnings of the ages, before everything that can even be called "before," you are; and you are God and Lord of everything you have created. In you stand fast the causes of all unstable things; in you the sources of all changing things remain unchanged; in you live the eternal reasons of everything unreasoning and everything that passes. So tell me, God — tell your suppliant; in your mercy, tell your miserable one: did my infancy come after some other age of mine that had already died? Was it the age I spent inside my mother's womb? I have been told a little about that, and I have seen pregnant women with my own eyes. And before even that, God my sweetness — what? Was I anywhere? Was I anyone? I have no one who can tell me: not father or mother, not the experience of others, not my own memory. Or are you laughing at me for asking, and commanding me instead to praise you and confess you for what I do know?

And look — my infancy died long ago, and I am alive. But you, Lord, live forever, and nothing in you dies; for before the foundation of the worlds, and before everything that can be called "before," you are, and you are God and Lord of all that you have made. In you stand fixed forever the first causes of all unstanding things; in you the springs of all changing things hold unchanging; in you live the eternal reasons of all the reasonless, passing things. Tell me, Lord — I am your suppliant — tell me, you who pity all, for I am pitiable: did my infancy follow some earlier age of mine that died before it? Was that age the time I spent in my mother's womb? Of that I have heard something, and I have myself seen pregnant women. And before that, my God, my joy — what then? Was I anywhere, was I anyone?
