I have no one to tell me this — not father, not mother, not the experience of others, not my own memory. Do you laugh at me for asking, and tell me instead to praise you and acknowledge you for what I do know?

So I confess you, Lord of heaven and earth, and I praise you for my first beginnings and for my infancy, which I do not remember. You have arranged for a man to guess much about himself from others, and to believe much about himself on the word of ordinary women. Even then I existed and lived, and by infancy's end I was already hunting for signs to make what I felt known to other people. Where could a living creature like that come from, if not from you, Lord? Is anyone the craftsman of his own making? Is there some channel running from anywhere else through which being and living pour into us — other than you making us, Lord, you for whom being and living are never two different things, because to be supremely and to live supremely are one and the same? You are supreme, and you do not change; today never runs its course in you — and yet in you it does run its course, because all times are in you too, and they would have no way to pass unless you held them. And because your years do not fail, your years are one single today. How many of our days, and of our fathers' days, have already passed through this today of yours, taking from it their measure and the manner of the existence they had; and others will pass through too, and take their own measure and manner of existing. But you are the same, always; and everything of tomorrow and after, everything of yesterday and before, you will do in this today, you have done in this today. What is it to me if someone cannot grasp this? Let him rejoice anyway and say, "What is this?" Let him rejoice even so — and let him love to find you by not finding the answer, rather than find the answer and not find you.

I acknowledge you, Lord of heaven and earth, and I praise you for the first beginnings of my being and for my infancy, of which I remember nothing — since you have arranged that a person should learn much about himself from others, and believe much on the word of mere women. Even then I existed and was alive, and toward the end of infancy I was already looking for signs by which to make my feelings known to others. Where could such a creature come from, Lord, but from you? Can anyone be his own maker? Is there any other stream from which being and life could flow into us, except from you, Lord, in whom being and life are one? For you yourself are supremely Being and Life. You are most high, and you do not change, and in you today never comes to an end — and yet in you it does come to an end, since all such things are also in you; they would have no way to pass at all unless you held them. And since your years do not fail, your years are one single today. How many of our years, and our fathers' years, have flowed away through your today, taking from it the measure and the shape of whatever being they had — and still others will flow away, and take the shape of their own degree of being. But you stay the same; and all of tomorrow, and all beyond it, and all of yesterday, and all behind that, you have done today. What does it matter to me if someone does not grasp this? Let him rejoice even so, and say, What is this? Let him rejoice, and be content to find you by not finding you out, rather than by finding you out to miss you altogether.

Hear me, God. How miserable is the sin of men! A man says so, and you have mercy on him — because you made the man, and did not make the sin in him. Who reminds me of the sin of my infancy? For in your sight no one is clean of sin, not even the infant whose life is one day old on the earth. Who reminds me? Doesn't every tiny infant do it, in whom I see what I cannot remember of myself? So what was my sin back then? That I cried and grabbed so greedily at the breast? If I did that now — grabbed that greedily at food fit for my age — I would be laughed at and told off, and rightly. So what I did then deserved a telling-off; but since I could not have understood one, custom and common sense forbade my being told off. After all, we root those habits out and throw them away as we grow — and I have never seen a man of sense throw away anything good when he prunes a plant. Or was it good, even for a moment, to cry for something that would have harmed it if given? To seethe with rage at free people — grown people, its own parents — because they would not be its slaves; at people far wiser than itself, because they would not jump at its every whim; to fight back, striking and hurting as hard as it could, because they refused commands it could only have obeyed to its own cost? So the innocence of infants is in the weakness of their limbs, not in any innocence of will. I have watched a jealous baby with my own eyes. He could not speak yet, but he went pale and turned a bitter stare on the child who shared his milk. Who hasn't seen this? Mothers and nurses will tell you they charm it away with remedies of their own. But is it really innocence — when the spring of milk is running full and overflowing — to refuse to share it with a companion in utter need, whose whole life still hangs on that one food? We bear with all this gently — not because it is no evil, or a small one, but because it will fall away as the years come on. And here is the proof: the very same behavior, met in someone older, cannot be borne for a moment.

Hear me, God. Alas for the sin of man! So a man says, and you pity him, for you made him, but the sin in him you did not make. Who reminds me of the sins of my infancy? For in your sight no one is free of sin, not even the infant whose life on earth is a single day. Who reminds me? Does not every little child, in whom I see what I no longer remember of myself? What, then, was my sin? Was it that I cried for the breast? If I cried now for food fit to my age, I would rightly be laughed at and corrected. What I did then deserved correction, but since I could not have understood it, neither custom nor reason allowed me to be corrected; for such habits we root out and throw away as we grow. No one who is pruning knowingly throws away what is good. Was it then good, even for a moment, to scream for what would have done me harm if I had got it? To rage bitterly at free people — my own elders, the very authors of my birth — for not serving me? To strike out and try to hurt the many wiser than me who would not obey my every whim, because they would not obey commands that would have harmed me? So the innocence of infants lies in the weakness of their limbs, not in their will. I have seen and known a jealous baby myself: it could not yet speak, but it went pale and looked daggers at the other child at the breast. Everyone knows this. Mothers and nurses say they can soothe it somehow. But is even this innocent — that when the fountain of milk is flowing in plenty, the child will not let another share it, though that other is in the greatest need and its very life depends on it for now? We are gentle with all this, not because it is no evil or only a small one, but because it will pass with the years — for though we tolerate it now, the very same temper is completely unbearable when we find it in grown men.

So you, Lord my God — you who gave the infant its life and its body; who fitted it, as we see, with senses, jointed it with limbs, graced it with a shape, and wove into it every drive a living whole needs for its wholeness and its safety — you command me to praise you in all this, to confess to you and sing to your name, Most High. For you are God, almighty and good, and you would be so had you made nothing but this — this, which no one else can make: you, the One, from whom comes all measure; you, most beautiful, who give all things their form and set all things in order by your law. So this stretch of my life, Lord — which I do not remember living, which I take on other people's word, and infer from watching other infants that I must have passed through, likely as the inference is — I am reluctant to count as part of this life of mine that I live in this world. As far as the darkness of my forgetting goes, it is one with the age I spent in my mother's womb. But if I was conceived in iniquity, and in sin my mother nourished me inside her womb — then where, I beg you, my God, where, Lord, and when was I, your servant, ever innocent? But look, I leave that time behind. What is it to me now, when I cannot recover a single trace of it?

You, then, Lord my God, who gave life to me in my infancy and fitted the body you gave with senses, set its limbs in order, gave its parts their beauty, and for its general good and safety planted in it all the powers of a living thing — you command me to praise you in these things, to confess to you and sing to your name, Most High. For you are God, almighty and good, even if you had done nothing but this, which no one but you could do — you whose oneness is the pattern of all things, who out of your own beauty make all things beautiful, and order all things by your law. So this age, Lord, of which I have no memory, which I take on others' word and guess at from other infants — true as the guess may be — I am still reluctant to count it as part of this life of mine that I live in this world. For it is as hidden from me, in the shadows of forgetting, as the time I spent in my mother's womb. And if I was shaped in wrongdoing, and in sin my mother conceived me — then where, I beg you, my God, where, Lord, or when, was I, your servant, free of guilt? But there — I let that time go by; what have I now to do with it, when I can recall no trace of it?

Out of infancy I moved on into boyhood — or rather boyhood moved into me, taking infancy's place. And infancy did not leave — where would it have gone? — and yet it was no longer there. For I was no longer an infant, with no speech in me, but a boy, talking. This I do remember; and how I learned to talk, I worked out only later. It was not that grown-ups taught me, handing me words in some fixed order of instruction, as they did the alphabet a little afterward. I taught myself — with the mind you gave me, my God — because the grunts and cries and flung-about limbs I was using to get my wishes across could not carry everything I meant, or reach everyone I meant it for. So I began to seize words and hold them in my memory. When people named a thing, and turned toward it as they made the sound, I watched, and I grasped it: that thing was called by the sound they uttered whenever they meant to point it out. And that this was what they meant was plain from the motion of their bodies — the natural vocabulary of the whole human race, made of facial expressions and glances of the eyes, gestures of the limbs and tones of the voice, showing what the mind feels as it seeks, keeps, rejects, or recoils. So, hearing the same words again and again in their places in different sentences, I gradually gathered what things they were signs of; and once I had trained my mouth to those signs, I used them at last to say what I wanted. In this way I traded the signs of our wants with the people around me, and waded out deeper into the stormy shared life of human beings — still hanging on the authority of my parents and the beck and call of my elders.

Leaving infancy behind, I came to boyhood — or rather it came to me and took the place of infancy. And infancy did not depart (where would it go?), and yet it was no longer there. For I was no longer a speechless infant but a speaking boy. This I remember, and I have since noticed how I learned to speak. It was not that my elders taught me words by any set method, as they soon taught me other lessons. No — longing to make my thoughts known by cries and broken sounds and the various motions of my limbs, so as to get my way, and unable to express all I wanted or to whom I wanted, I drilled the sounds in my memory by the understanding you gave me, my God. When people named some thing and turned toward it as they spoke, I saw it and grasped that the thing they wanted to point out was called by the sound they made. Their meaning was plain from the motion of their bodies — the natural language, you might say, of every nation, made of the face, the glance of the eye, the gestures of the limbs, the tone of the voice, all showing the mind's state as it reaches for things, holds them, refuses them, or shuns them. And so, by hearing words again and again in their places in different sentences, I gradually worked out what they stood for, and having trained my mouth to these signs, I used them to speak my will. So I traded these current coins of our wishes with the people around me, and launched out deeper into the stormy commerce of human life — still under the authority of my parents and the orders of my elders.

God, my God, what misery I met there, what mockery. The right way to live, I was told as a boy, was to obey my instructors — so that I might get on in this world and shine in the arts of the tongue, arts that win the honor of men and serve up counterfeit riches. So I was sent to school to get my letters. What use they were, I — poor wretch — could not see; and yet if I slacked in learning, I was beaten. Our ancestors approved this system; the crowds who had walked that road before us had laid down the paths of misery we were forced along, multiplying labor and grief for the sons of Adam. But we also found men who prayed to you, Lord, and from them we learned — imagining you as far as our powers reached — that you were someone great, someone who could hear us and help us even though our senses could not find you. So as a boy I began praying to you, my help and my refuge; I broke the knots of my tongue calling on you; and small as I was, it was with no small feeling that I prayed not to be beaten at school. And when you did not hear me — which was no foolishness in me — the grown-ups laughed at my stripes, my own parents along with the rest, who wished me no harm at all; and those beatings were, at the time, my great and grievous harm.

O God, my God, what miseries and mockeries I now went through, when as a boy it was set before me that the right thing was to obey my teachers, so that I might get on in this world and excel in the arts of the tongue — which would serve to win the praise of men and false riches. Next I was sent to school to get learning, though I, poor wretch, could not see what it was good for; and yet if I was lazy at it, I was beaten. Our elders judged this right; many before us had marked out the same weary paths, and we were made to tread them, with toil and grief piled on the children of Adam. But, Lord, we found that men called on you, and from them we learned to think of you, as well as we could, as some great One who could hear us and help us, though hidden from our senses. So as a boy I began to pray to you, my help and my refuge, and broke the bonds of my tongue to call on you, and prayed — small as I was, but with no small earnestness — that I might not be beaten at school. And when you did not hear me (which was not to leave me to my folly), my elders, even my own parents, who wished me no harm, laughed at my beatings — which were then my great and grievous trouble.

Is there anyone, Lord, so great in soul, holding to you with a love so enormous — is there anyone (for a certain thick-headedness can produce the same effect), is there anyone whose devout attachment to you runs so deep that he counts as trifles the racks and the hooks and the rest of the torturer's inventory, which men everywhere beg you in terror to be spared — that he can laugh at the people who dread those things most bitterly, the way our parents laughed at the torments our schoolmasters dealt us as boys? For we were no less afraid of ours, and prayed to you no less to escape them. And we sinned all the same, by writing or reading or thinking over our lessons less than was demanded of us. It was not memory or intelligence we lacked, Lord — you willed us enough of those for our age. But we loved to play; and we were punished for it by men who were doing the very same thing. Except that adult play is called "business." When boys do it, it is exactly the same thing, and the grown-ups punish them for it, and nobody pities the boys, or the men, or both. Would any fair judge of things say I was rightly beaten, as a boy, for playing ball — because the games slowed my learning of letters, letters I was going to use, as a man, to play a far uglier game? And the man who beat me — what else was he doing? If some colleague got the better of him in a petty scholarly quarrel, he was more racked by bile and envy than I ever was when a playmate beat me at ball.

Is there anyone, Lord, with a soul so great, who clings to you with such fierce love — for a kind of dullness can manage it too — but is there anyone who, from devotion to you, is given so great a spirit that he can make as light of the racks and hooks and other torments that men dread and pray to escape from all over the world, mocking those who fear them most bitterly, as our parents mocked the torments we suffered as boys at our masters' hands? For we feared our torments no less, and prayed no less to you to escape them. And yet we sinned, by writing or reading or studying less than was demanded of us. It was not, Lord, that we lacked memory or ability — your will gave us enough for our age. The trouble was that we loved nothing but play, and for this we were punished by men who were doing the very same. But the idling of grown men is called "business"; when boys do the same, those very men punish them — and no one pities either the boys or the men. For will any sound judge approve of my being beaten as a boy because playing ball kept me from studies I was supposed to learn, so that as a man I might play at worse things? And the one who beat me — what else was he doing? If he came off worse in some petty argument with a fellow teacher, he was more soured and jealous than I was when a playmate beat me at ball.

And yet I sinned in this, Lord God — you who order and create everything in nature, though sin you do not create, only order — Lord my God, I sinned by disobeying the commands of my parents and of those masters. For whatever motive my elders had for wanting me to learn, I could later have put the learning to good use. I disobeyed not because I had chosen something better, but out of love of play: I loved the swagger of winning my contests; I loved having my ears tickled by made-up stories, which only made them itch the hotter; and the same curiosity glittered more and more in my eyes for the shows and the games of grown men. The men who stage those games stand so high in public esteem that nearly everyone wishes the same eminence for their little children — and is perfectly content to have those children beaten if the shows keep them from the studies that are supposed to lead them, someday, to be the men who stage the shows. Look on all this with mercy, Lord, and set free those of us who now call on you; set free those who do not yet call on you, so that they may call on you, and you may set them free.

And yet I did sin in this, Lord God, the maker and the ruler of all things in nature, though of sins only the ruler — I sinned, Lord my God, by disobeying the commands of my parents and my masters. For whatever they wanted me to learn, with whatever motive, I could have put to good use later. I disobeyed not from a better choice but from love of play: I loved the pride of winning my matches, and to have my ears tickled with made-up stories until they itched the more; and the same hunger flashed brighter and brighter in my eyes for the shows and games of grown men. Yet the very people who put on these shows are held in such honor that almost everyone wants the same for their children — and are still glad to have them beaten if those games keep them from the studies by which they hope their children will become the givers of such shows. Look with pity, Lord, on all this, and rescue us who call on you now; rescue too those who do not yet call on you, so that they may call on you, and you may rescue them.

While still a boy, I had already heard of the eternal life promised to us through the humility of the Lord our God, coming all the way down to our pride; and I was signed with the sign of his cross, and seasoned with his salt, fresh from the womb of my mother, who set great hope in you. You saw, Lord, how once, while still a boy, I was seized one day with a sudden cramping fever of the stomach and came close to death — you saw, my God, for you were already my keeper, with what feeling and what faith I begged for the baptism of your Christ, my God and Lord, appealing to the devotion of my mother and of the mother of us all, your Church. The mother of my flesh was shaken — for with a heart chaste in your faith, she was in labor even more lovingly for my eternal salvation — and she would have rushed to have me initiated and washed in the sacraments of salvation, confessing you, Lord Jesus, for the forgiveness of sins, if I had not suddenly recovered. So my cleansing was deferred — as though, if I lived, I was bound to be dirtied again; and because after that washing, the guilt of sin's filth would be greater and more dangerous. So: I already believed, and so did my mother and the whole household — except my father alone. Yet he did not defeat, in me, the claim my mother's devotion had on me: he could not stop me believing in Christ just because he did not yet believe himself. For she strained every nerve so that you, my God, would be my father rather than him; and in this you helped her win out over her husband — she, the better one, serving him, because in serving him she was serving you, who commanded it.

As a boy I had already heard of an eternal life promised us through the humility of the Lord our God, who stooped to our pride; and from my mother's womb — for she greatly hoped in you — I was marked with the sign of his cross and seasoned with his salt. You saw, Lord, how once, while still a boy, I was suddenly seized with a stomach fever and came close to death — you saw, my God, for you were already my keeper, with what eagerness and faith I begged, from the devout care of my mother and of your Church, the mother of us all, for the baptism of your Christ, my God and Lord. And the mother of my flesh, deeply troubled — for with a heart pure in your faith she was laboring all the harder to give birth to my salvation — would have hurried to have me consecrated and cleansed by the saving sacraments, confessing you, Lord Jesus, for the forgiveness of sins, had I not suddenly recovered. So my cleansing was put off, on the grounds that if I lived I was bound to be defiled again, and the stains of sin after that washing would bring greater and more dangerous guilt. I already believed then — and so did my mother, and the whole household, except my father. But he did not win out over the strength of my mother's devotion in me, so as to make me an unbeliever as he still was. For it was her great care that you, my God, should be my father rather than he; and in this you helped her to prevail over her husband, whom she, the better of the two, obeyed — and in obeying him she was also obeying you, who had so commanded.

I beg you, my God — I would love to know, if you are willing to tell me — to what end was my baptism deferred? Was it for my good that the reins were slackened on me, so to speak, to let me sin? Or were they not slackened? If not, why does it still ring in our ears from every side, about this person and that: "Leave him alone, let him do it; he isn't baptized yet"? Yet when it is the body's health, we never say, "Let him be wounded worse; he isn't healed yet." How much better, then, if I had been healed at once — if my own diligence and my family's had seen to it that the recovered health of my soul was kept safe in your keeping, who gave it. How much better, truly. But my mother could already see the waves of temptation, how many and how great, massing over me beyond boyhood; and she preferred to let them break on the clay from which I could still be shaped afterward, rather than on the finished image itself.

I beg you, my God, I long to know, if it is your will: why was my baptism put off just then? Was it for my good that the rein was, so to speak, loosened on me, to let me sin? Or was it not loosened? If not, then why does it still ring in our ears on every side — "Leave him alone, let him do as he likes, he isn't baptized yet"? And yet, where bodily health is concerned, no one says, "Let him be wounded worse, he isn't healed yet." How much better, then, had I been healed at once, and my soul's recovered health kept safe, with my friends' help and my own, in your keeping, who gave it. Far better, truly. But how many great waves of temptation seemed to hang over me after boyhood! My mother foresaw them, and chose to expose to them the clay from which I might later be shaped, rather than the finished cast.

In boyhood itself, though — which gave less cause for fear on my account than adolescence did — I had no love of study, and I hated being forced to it. And I was forced, and it was good for me; but I was not good, for I would never have learned unless I was made to. And no one does well against his will, even when what he does is good. Nor were the people forcing me doing well: the good that came to me came from you, my God. For they never looked past their own aim for the learning they crammed into me: the glutting of appetites that cannot be filled — appetites for a wealthy kind of poverty and a shameful kind of glory. But you, who have counted every hair on our heads, used the error of everyone who pushed me to learn for my profit; and my own error — my not wanting to learn — you used for my punishment, which I richly deserved: so small a boy, and so great a sinner. So through people who were not doing good, you did good for me; and for my own sin, you paid me back justly. For you have decreed it, and so it stands: every disordered soul is its own punishment.

In boyhood itself, though — so much less feared on my behalf than the youth to come — I did not love study, and hated being forced to it. Yet I was forced, and this was done well to me, though I did not do well; for unless forced, I would not have learned. But no one does well against his will, even if what he does is good. Nor did those who forced me do well — but the good that came to me came from you, my God. For they cared nothing for how I might use what they forced me to learn, except to feed the bottomless appetite of a rich beggary and a shameful glory. But you, by whom the very hairs of our head are numbered, used for my good the error of all who pressed me to learn, and my own error, in refusing to learn, you used to punish me — a fitting penalty for one so small a boy and so great a sinner. So through those who did not do well you did well for me, and through my own sin you justly punished me. For you have commanded, and so it is, that every disordered love is its own punishment.

But why did I so hate the Greek literature I was steeped in as a small boy? Even now I have not quite got to the bottom of it. For Latin I loved — not what the first teachers gave, but what the ones called grammarians teach. Those first lessons — reading, writing, arithmetic — I found as much a burden and a punishment as all my Greek. And yet where did even that come from, if not from sin and the emptiness of this life, since I was flesh, a breath that goes out and does not come back? Those first lessons were the better ones, because they were the surer: through them I got, and keep to this day, the power to read whatever I find written and to write whatever I want myself. In the others, I was forced to memorize the wanderings of some man called Aeneas — forgetting my own wanderings the while — and to weep for the death of Dido, who killed herself for love; while all the time, in the middle of these things, I endured my own wretched self dying far away from you, God my life, and my eyes stayed dry.

But why did I so hate Greek, which I studied as a boy? I still do not fully know. For I loved Latin — not the lessons of my first teachers, but what the so-called grammarians taught me. Those first lessons — reading, writing, and arithmetic — I felt to be as heavy a burden and penalty as any Greek. And where did this come from, too, but from the sin and emptiness of this life, since I was flesh, and a breath that goes and does not come back? Those first lessons were certainly better, because surer: by them I gained, and still keep, the power to read what I find written and to write what I want. The others forced me to memorize the wanderings of a certain Aeneas, forgetting my own wanderings, and to weep for dead Dido because she killed herself for love — while I, with dry eyes, endured my own miserable self dying among these things, far from you, O God, my life.

For what is more pitiful than a pitiful man with no pity for himself — a man weeping over the death of Dido, which came from loving Aeneas, and not weeping over his own death, which came from not loving you, God? Light of my heart, bread for the inner mouth of my soul, strength wedded to my mind and to the deep lap of my thought: I did not love you. I went whoring away from you, and as I whored, from every side came the cry, "Well done! Well done!" For the friendship of this world is whoring away from you, and "Well done! Well done!" is shouted until one is ashamed not to be that kind of man. And over none of this did I weep. I wept for Dido, "dead, gone by the sword to her uttermost end" — while I myself forsook you and went after the uttermost and lowest of the things you made: earth sinking back into earth. And had I been forbidden to read those stories, I would have grieved that I could not read what made me grieve. Madness of this kind passes for a more honorable and a richer education than the lessons by which I learned to read and write.

For what is more miserable than a miserable man who has no pity on himself — who weeps for Dido's death, dying for love of Aeneas, but does not weep for his own death, dying for want of love for you, O God? You, light of my heart; you, bread of my inmost soul; you, the Power that gives vigor to my mind and quickens my thoughts — I did not love you. I committed adultery against you, and all around me, in the same adultery, voices cheered, "Well done! Well done!" For friendship with this world is adultery against you, and the "Well done! Well done!" goes on until a man is ashamed not to be one of the crowd. And for all this I did not weep — I who wept for slain Dido, who "sought by the sword her bitter, mortal wound" — while I myself sought the bitterest, lowest end among your creatures, having forsaken you, earth slipping back into earth. And if I had been forbidden to read all this, I would have grieved that I could not read what grieved me. Such madness is thought a higher and richer learning than the lessons by which I learned to read and write.

But now let my God cry out in my soul, and let your truth tell me: "Not so. Not so. The first learning was far better." Look — I would sooner forget the wanderings of Aeneas and all the rest of it than forget how to read and write. Yes, curtains hang across the doorways of the grammar schools; but they stand less for the honor of a mystery than for the covering of an error. And let the men I have stopped fearing not shout me down while I confess to you whatever my soul wants to confess, my God, and consent to the condemnation of my own bad roads, so that I may love your good ones. Let the buyers and sellers of literature not shout me down either. For if I put the question to them — is it true, as the poet says, that Aeneas ever came to Carthage? — the less educated will answer that they don't know; the more educated will say flatly that it never happened. But if I ask which letters spell the name "Aeneas," everyone who has learned to read will give me the right answer, according to the agreement and convention by which human beings settled those signs among themselves. And if I ask which would do more damage to a person's life to forget — reading and writing, or those poetic fictions — who does not see what anyone would answer who has not completely forgotten himself? So I sinned, as a boy, in loving the empty studies above the useful ones — or rather, in hating the useful and loving the empty. "One and one is two, two and two is four" — that, to me, was a hateful chant; and the sweetest of all spectacles to my vanity was the wooden horse full of armed men, and Troy burning, and the very ghost of Creusa.

But now, my God, cry aloud in my soul, and let your truth tell me, "Not so, not so. That first study was far better." For look — I would more readily forget the wanderings of Aeneas and all the rest than how to read and write. True, there is a curtain hung over the door of the grammar school — yet this is not so much a sign of something hidden as a cloak for error. Let them not cry out against me, those I no longer fear, while I confess to you, my God, whatever my soul wills, and find peace in condemning my own bad ways, that I may love your good ways. Let neither the buyers nor the sellers of grammar-learning cry out against me. For if I ask them whether it is true that Aeneas once came to Carthage, as the poet says, the less learned will answer they do not know, and the more learned that he never did. But if I ask how the name "Aeneas" is spelled, everyone who has learned it will answer me rightly, according to the signs men have agreed on by convention. And if I ask which could be forgotten with less harm to one's life — reading and writing, or these poetic fictions — who does not see what everyone must answer, unless he has utterly forgotten himself? So I sinned, as a boy, when I preferred those empty studies to the more useful ones — or rather, loved the one and hated the other. "One and one is two"; "two and two is four" — this was to me a hateful singsong, while "the wooden horse packed with armed men," "the burning of Troy," and "Creusa's ghost, her sad and shadowy likeness" were the chosen spectacle of my vanity.

Then why did I hate the Greek classics, which sing the same kind of songs? For Homer too was skilled at weaving such tales — he is delicious in his emptiness — and yet to me as a boy he tasted bitter. I suppose Virgil is exactly that to Greek boys, when they are forced to learn him the way I was forced to learn Homer. It was the difficulty — the sheer difficulty of mastering a foreign language at all — that splashed gall, as it were, over the whole sweetness of the Greek tales of wonder. For I did not know one word of the language, and I was pressed hard, with savage terrors and punishments, to make me know it. There was a time, in infancy, when I knew no Latin either; yet Latin I learned just by paying attention, without any fear or torture at all, amid the endearments of my nurses, the jokes of people smiling at me, the delight of people playing with me. I learned it with no drum-beat of punishment driving me on, because my own heart drove me to bring out what it had conceived — and I could not have done that without learning words: taken not from instructors but from anyone who talked with me, into whose ears, in turn, I delivered whatever I was feeling. It is plain enough from this that for learning such things, free curiosity has more power than fearful compulsion. But compulsion reins in curiosity's wandering — through your laws, God: your laws, from the schoolmaster's cane to the martyr's trials, your laws with their power to mix us a wholesome bitterness, calling us back to yourself away from the poisoned pleasure that first drew us from you.

Why then did I hate the Greek classics, which tell the same kind of tales? For Homer too is skilled at weaving such fictions, and is most sweetly empty — and yet he was bitter to my boyish taste. And so, I suppose, Virgil would be to Greek children, forced to learn him as I was forced to learn Homer. The difficulty — yes, the difficulty of a foreign tongue — splashed bitterness, like gall, over all the sweetness of the Greek story. For I understood not one word of it, and to make me understand I was driven hard with cruel threats and punishments. There was a time, too, when as an infant I knew no Latin; yet I learned it without fear or pain, by mere observation, amid the caresses of my nursery and the laughter of friends, who smiled and played and urged me on. I learned it without the pressure of any punishment, for my heart pressed me to bring its own thoughts to birth, which I could only do by learning words — not from those who taught me, but from those who talked with me, in whose ears I was likewise giving birth to whatever I conceived. There is no doubt, then, that a free curiosity has more power to make us learn these things than a fearful compulsion. Yet this compulsion checks the wanderings of that freedom, by your laws, my God — your laws, from the schoolmaster's cane to the martyr's trials — being able to mix for us a wholesome bitterness that calls us back to you from the deadly pleasure that lures us away.

Hear my prayer, Lord: do not let my soul collapse under your discipline, and do not let me collapse in confessing to you all the mercies by which you dragged me out of every one of my worst roads — so that you might grow sweeter to me than all the seductions I used to chase; so that I might love you with all my strength and clasp your hand with everything my heart has; and so that you might rescue me from every temptation, all the way to the end. For look, Lord: you are my king and my God. Let whatever useful thing I learned as a boy be at your service; let it serve you that I speak and write and read and count. For while I was learning emptiness, you were giving me discipline; and my sin of delighting in that emptiness, you have forgiven. In those studies I did learn many a useful word — but the same words can be learned in studies that are not empty, and that is the safe road children ought to walk.

Hear my prayer, Lord; let not my soul faint under your discipline, nor let me faint in confessing to you all your mercies, by which you have drawn me out of all my worst ways — so that you may grow sweeter to me than all the allurements I once chased; that I may love you with all I am, and clasp your hand with my whole heart, and that you may yet rescue me from every temptation, all the way to the end. For look, Lord, my King and my God: let whatever useful thing I learned as a child be put to your service — that I speak, write, read, and reckon for your service. For you gave me discipline while I was learning empty things, and the sin of delighting in those empty things you have forgiven. In them, I admit, I learned many a useful word — but those can just as well be learned in things that are not empty, and that is the safe path for the steps of the young.

But how horrible you are, you river of human custom! Who can stand against you? How long before you run dry? How long will you keep sweeping the children of Eve into that vast and dreadful sea, which even those who have climbed aboard the wood of the cross barely manage to cross? Wasn't it in your current that I read of Jove, thunderer and adulterer at once? Both he could not be, of course; but both he was made, so that fake thunder could stand as authority and play the pimp for real adultery. And which of our gowned masters lends a sober ear to a man formed of the same dust as themselves when he calls out: "Homer invented these stories, and carried the human up to the gods — I would rather he had brought the divine down to us"? But it is truer to say: yes, he invented them — but he did it by conferring divinity on depraved men, so that depravity would no longer count as depravity, and whoever practices it could seem to be imitating, not degenerate men, but the gods of heaven themselves.

But woe to you, torrent of human custom! Who can stand against you? How long until you run dry? How long will you keep rolling the sons of Eve into that vast and dreadful ocean, which even those who climb the cross can barely cross over? Did I not read in you of Jove the thunderer — and the adulterer? Both he could not truly be; but the pretended thunder was invented to give cover and license to real adultery. And now, which of our gowned masters lends a sober ear to a man who cries out, from their own school, "These were Homer's fictions; he brought human things up to the gods — if only he had brought divine things down to us!" Truer still would he have said, "These are indeed his fictions, but he gave a divine nature to wicked men, so that their crimes might no longer count as crimes, and whoever committed them might seem to be imitating not abandoned men but the gods of heaven."

And still, you river out of hell, the sons of men are flung into you, fees and all, to learn these things; and it becomes a great public affair when the business is transacted in the forum, in full view of laws that vote the teachers a state salary on top of the students' fees. You slap your rocks and roar: "Here is where words are learned! Here is where men acquire the eloquence essential to persuasion and to unfolding their opinions!" Really? We would never have known the words "golden shower," "lap," "trick," "temples of heaven," and the other words written in that passage, if Terence had not brought a worthless young man onto the stage, holding up Jupiter as the model for his own seduction.

And yet, you torrent of hell, into you the sons of men are thrown, with rich rewards, for mastering such learning; and a great ceremony is made of it, conducted in the public square, in full view of laws that grant a salary on top of the students' own fees. And you lash your rocks and roar, "Here words are learned; here eloquence is learned, so necessary to get your way and to win your arguments." As if we would never have known such words as "golden shower," "lap," "beguile," "the temples of heaven," and the rest of that passage, unless Terence had brought a worthless youth onto the stage, setting up Jupiter as his model for seduction —
"He looked up at a painting on the wall, where the story was pictured: Jove, as they tell it, once sent a golden shower into Danae's lap — the trick he played on the woman."
"Gazing at a painting where the tale was told / of Jove sending down a golden shower / into Danaë's lap, a woman to beguile" —
And watch how he whips himself up to lust, as if with heaven's own coaching:
and then see how he stirs himself to lust as if by heavenly warrant:
"And what a god!" he says. "The one who shakes the highest temples of heaven with his thunder."
"And what god? The great one / who shakes the highest temples of heaven with his thunder.
"And should I, one little man, not do the same? I did it — and I did it gladly."
And I, a poor mortal man, should I not do the same? I did it, and gladly I did it."

The words are not one bit easier to learn for all this filth; but by the words, the filth is committed with more confidence. I bring no charge against the words themselves — they are like choice and costly vessels — but against the wine of error in them, which drunken teachers poured out for us; and if we would not drink, we were beaten, with no appeal to any sober judge. And yet, my God — before whose eyes my memory can now rest safe — I learned all of it willingly; I enjoyed it, wretch that I was; and for that, they called me a boy of great promise.

The words are learned no more easily for all this filthiness; rather, by means of the words the filthiness is done with less shame. I do not blame the words — they are like choice and precious vessels — but the wine of error that drunken teachers pour out for us in them; and if we do not drink it too, we are beaten, with no sober judge to whom we may appeal. And yet, my God — in whose presence I can now remember this without harm — all of it, sadly, I learned willingly and with great delight, and for it I was called a promising boy.

Bear with me, my God, while I say something about the intelligence you gave me, and the ravings I wore it out on. For a task was set me that gave my soul no peace — the prize was praise, the threat was disgrace and the cane: I was to recite the speech of Juno, raging and grieving that she could not

Bear with me, my God, while I say something of my cleverness — your gift — and the follies I wasted it on. I was set a task troubling enough to my soul, with praise or shame and the fear of a beating riding on it: to speak the words of Juno as she raged and grieved that she could not
"turn the Trojan king away from Italy."
"turn this Trojan prince away from Italy" —

Words which, I had heard, Juno never spoke. But we were forced to go astray in the footprints of poetic make-believe, and to say in loose prose the kind of thing the poet had said in verse. And the boy whose speaking won the most applause was the one in whom the passions of rage and grief stood out most convincingly, matched to the dignity of the character he was impersonating and dressed in the most fitting words. What was any of it to me, my true life, my God? Why did my recitation earn more applause than those of the many boys my own age, in my own class? Isn't the whole thing smoke and wind? Was there really nothing else on which to exercise my mind and my tongue? Your praises, Lord — your praises rising through your Scriptures could have staked up the young vine of my heart, and it would not have been dragged off through this empty trash, filthy plunder for the birds of the air. For there is more than one way of sacrificing to the angels who fell.

words I had heard that Juno never said; but we were made to wander in the footsteps of these poetic fictions and to say in prose roughly what the poet had said in verse. And the boy whose speech won most applause was the one in whom the passions of rage and grief stood out most strongly, dressed in the most fitting words, keeping up the dignity of the character. What is it to me, my true life, my God, that my speech was applauded above so many of my own age and class? Is not all of it smoke and wind? Was there nothing else for me to exercise my wit and tongue on? Your praises, Lord — your praises might have propped up the still tender shoot of my heart with the support of your Scriptures, so that it would not have trailed away among these empty trifles, a defiled prey for the birds of the air. For there is more than one way in which men sacrifice to the rebel angels.

But what wonder is it that I was swept away into emptiness like that, and went out and away from you, my God — when the men held up for me to imitate were men who, if they were caught in a barbarism or a slip of grammar while reporting some perfectly innocent act of their own, were covered in confusion; but when they narrated their own lusts in rich, ornamented, well-built sentences and were praised for it, they gloried? You see all this, Lord, and you keep silent — patient, and rich in mercy and truth. Will you be silent forever? Even now you are drawing up out of that monstrous pit the soul that seeks you, that thirsts for your delights, whose heart says to you: "I have sought your face; your face, Lord, I will keep seeking." For I was far from your face, deep in the darkness of my passions. It is not on foot, not by distance in miles, that we go away from you or come back to you. That younger son of yours in the story did not hire horses or chariots or ships; he did not fly on any visible wing or wear out his legs walking, so as to live in a far country and pour away like a prodigal what you had given him when he set out. You were a sweet father, because you gave it — and sweeter still to him when he came back destitute. To live in lustful passion, then — which is to say, in darkened passion — that is what it is to be far from your face.

But what wonder that I was carried away to empty things and went out from your presence, my God, when the men set before me as models were these: men who, if they made some slip of grammar in telling of an action of theirs that was not in itself bad, were ashamed when corrected — but who, when they told of their own disordered lives in rich, polished, well-ordered words, and were praised for it, gloried in it? You see all this, Lord, and keep silent — patient, and full of mercy and truth. Will you keep silent forever? Even now you are drawing out of this horrible pit the soul that seeks you, that thirsts for your delights, whose heart says to you, I have sought your face; your face, Lord, will I seek. For to be far from your face is to be in the dark of disordered loves. It is not on our feet, or by changing place, that men leave you or return to you. Did that younger son of yours look for horses or chariots or ships, fly off on visible wings, or travel by moving his limbs, in order to squander in a far country all you had given him at his departure — a loving Father when you gave it, and more loving still when he came back with empty hands? So it is in lustful, that is, in darkened loves that the true distance from your face is measured.

Look, Lord God — and look patiently, the way you always look — at how exactly the sons of men keep the compacts of letters and syllables received from the speakers who came before them, while they neglect the eternal compacts of everlasting salvation received from you. It goes so far that a man who holds or teaches the old agreed rules of sounds will offend people more by dropping the "h" and saying "uman being," against the discipline of grammar, than if he — a human being — hates a human being, against yours. As if any human enemy could do a man more damage than the hatred itself with which he burns against him; as if anyone could wreck another person, by hounding him, more thoroughly than he wrecks his own heart by the hating. And surely no science of letters is written deeper in us than the writing of conscience: that he is doing to another what he would refuse to suffer himself. How hidden you are, dwelling in silence on the heights, you the only great God — scattering blindness, by a law that never tires, as punishment on lawless desires! A man hunting a reputation for eloquence stands before a human judge, ringed by a crowd of human beings, denouncing his enemy with the most inhuman hatred — and keeps the most vigilant watch that his tongue not slip and kill the word "human being," while he loses no sleep over whether the fury of his mind might kill an actual human being.

Look, Lord God — and look patiently, as you always do — at how carefully the sons of men keep the agreed rules of letters and syllables handed down from those who spoke before them, while they neglect the eternal covenant of everlasting salvation that they have from you. So much so that a man who knows or teaches the inherited rules of speech will offend people more by saying, against the laws of grammar, "a uman being" without the breath of the h, than if, against your laws, he, a human being, hates a human being. As if any enemy could do him more harm than the hatred with which he burns against him; as if he could wound the man he persecutes more deeply than he wounds his own soul by hating him. Surely no knowledge of letters is as deeply woven into us as the record written on the conscience: that he is doing to another what he would hate to suffer himself. How hidden are your ways, O God — you, the only great One, who sit silent on high and by a tireless law deal out a blinding punishment to lawless desires! A man chasing the fame of eloquence, standing before a human judge, ringed by a human crowd, raging at his enemy with the fiercest hatred, will watch most anxiously that no slip of the tongue lets him "murder" the word "human being" — and takes no care at all that, in the fury of his spirit, he does not murder a real human being.

This was the threshold of the world where I lay, a wretched boy; this was the training-floor where I wrestled — more afraid of committing a barbarism than on guard, if I did commit one, against envying the boys who hadn't. I say it, and I confess it to you, my God: this is what I was praised for, by the people whose approval was then my entire definition of living well. For I did not see the whirlpool of shame into which I had been thrown, out of the sight of your eyes. For in your sight, what was fouler by then than I was? — I even displeased people like myself, deceiving tutor and masters and parents with lie upon countless lie, out of love of play, a craving for trashy shows, and a restless itch to mimic what I watched on the stage. I stole, too, from my parents' pantry and their table, sometimes with gluttony giving the orders, sometimes to have something to hand the other boys, who charged me for their games even though they enjoyed the playing as much as I did. And in the games themselves I would often grab a cheat's victory, because I was already beaten myself — by the empty craving to come first. And what was I so unwilling to have done to me, what did I attack so ferociously when I caught anyone at it, as the very thing I was doing to the others? And when I was caught and attacked myself, I chose to fight rather than give way. Is that the innocence of boyhood? It is not, Lord; it is not — let me say it, my God. For these are the very things — these exactly — that pass on, as tutors and masters give way to governors and kings, and nuts and balls and pet sparrows give way to gold and estates and slaves, and heavier punishments take over from the cane. So it was the small stature of childhood, our King, that you were commending as the emblem of humility when you said, "The kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these."

This was the world at whose gate I lay, poor wretch, in my boyhood; this was the arena where I feared more to commit a grammatical blunder than, having committed one, to envy those who had not. I say and confess these things to you, my God — the things for which I was praised by those whom it then seemed the whole of virtue to please. For I did not see the pit of vileness into which I had been flung, away from your eyes. In their sight, what was fouler than I already was, displeasing even people like myself, deceiving my tutor, my masters, and my parents with countless lies, all from love of play, an itch to watch worthless shows, and a restlessness to act them out myself? I committed thefts, too, from my parents' cellar and table, driven by greed, or to have something to give the boys who sold me their play — which all the while they enjoyed no less than I did. And in this play I often sought to win by cheating, mastered all the while by an empty craving to come out on top. And what could I bear less, and rebuke more fiercely when I caught it, than the very thing I was doing to others? And if I was caught and rebuked for it myself, I would rather pick a fight than give in. Is this the innocence of boyhood? Not so, Lord, not so — I cry for your mercy, my God. For these very sins, as the riper years come on, pass over from tutors and masters, from nuts and balls and pet sparrows, to magistrates and kings, to gold and estates and slaves, just as harsher punishments take the place of the cane. It was the small stature of childhood, then, that you our King commended as an emblem of lowliness, when you said, Of such is the kingdom of heaven.

And yet, Lord — to you, most excellent and most good creator and governor of the universe, our God — thanks would still be owed even if you had willed that I not live past boyhood. For even then I existed; I lived and I felt; and I cared for my own wholeness — a trace of that deeply hidden Oneness from which I came. With an inner sense I stood guard over the wholeness of my outer senses; and in my small thoughts, about small things, I came to delight in truth. I hated to be deceived; my memory was vigorous; I was gaining command of speech; friendship softened me; I fled pain, humiliation, ignorance. In a living creature like that, what was not wonderful, not worth praising? And all of it the gifts of my God. I did not give them to myself. They are good, and all of them together are me. So the one who made me is good, and he himself is my good; and I leap up to him in thanks for every good thing that was in me even as a boy. My sin was this: that I looked for pleasures, for greatness, for truth not in him but in the things he made — in myself and the rest — and so pitched headlong into pains, humiliations, and errors. Thanks be to you, my sweetness and my honor and my confidence; thanks be to you, my God, for your gifts. Only keep them for me. For then you will keep me too, and the things you have given me will grow and be perfected, and I myself will be with you — because even that I exist at all is your gift.

And yet, Lord — to you, the Creator and Governor of the universe, most excellent and most good — thanks were owed to you, our God, even if you had granted me boyhood only. For even then I existed, I was alive, and I had feeling; I had within me a care for my own well-being, a trace of that mysterious Oneness from which I came; I kept watch, by an inner sense, over the wholeness of my senses; and in these small pursuits, and in my thoughts about small things, I learned to take delight in truth, I hated to be deceived, I had a strong memory, I was furnished with speech, I was soothed by friendship, I shrank from pain, from baseness, from ignorance. In so small a creature, what was not full of wonder, full of praise? But all these are gifts of my God; I did not give them to myself. They are good, and all together they are myself. Good, then, is he who made me, and he is my good; and before him I will exult for every good I had as a boy. For this was my sin: that I sought my pleasures, my heights, my truths, not in him but in his creatures — in myself and others — and so fell headlong into sorrows, confusions, and errors. Thanks be to you, my joy and my glory and my confidence, my God — thanks be to you for your gifts; but keep them for me. For so you will keep me, and the things you have given me will be enlarged and made perfect, and I myself will be with you, since even my existence is your gift.

I want to remember now my past foulness and the carnal corruptions of my soul — not because I love them, but so that I can love you, my God. For love of your love I do this: I go back over my most vicious ways in the very bitterness of the remembering, so that you may turn sweet to me — you sweetness that never fails, sweetness happy and secure — you who gather me back from the scattering in which I was cut into pieces when, turned away from you, the One, I dissolved into the many. For in my adolescence there was a time when I burned to gorge myself on the lowest things, and I dared to run wild in one shadowy love after another. My beauty wasted away, and I rotted in your sight — pleased with myself, and eager to please the eyes of men.

Now I want to call to mind the ugliness of my past, the corruptions my soul fed on the flesh — not because I love them, but so that I may love you, my God. I do this for love of your love, going back over my most wicked ways in the very bitterness of remembering, so that you may grow sweet to me: you, sweetness that never fails, blissful and sure sweetness, gathering me again out of the scattering in which I was torn to pieces, when, turned away from you, the one Good, I lost myself among many things. For in my youth I had burned to be filled with the things below, and I dared to run wild with these tangled, shadowy loves. My beauty wasted away, and I was rotten in your eyes, while I pleased myself and longed to please the eyes of men.

And what was it I delighted in, except to love and be loved? But I did not hold to the measure of mind reaching to mind, that bright boundary-line of friendship. Instead, out of the muddy lust of the flesh and the bubbling spring of adolescence, mists steamed up that clouded and darkened my heart, until I could not tell the clear sky of love from the fog of lust. Both boiled in me together, confused, and dragged my unsteady young self over the cliffs of desire and drowned me in a whirlpool of disgrace. Your anger had built up over me, and I did not know it. I had gone deaf from the clanking of the chain of my own mortality — the punishment for the pride of my soul — and I moved further from you, and you let me go. I was tossed about, poured out, scattered in every direction; I boiled over in my fornications — and you said nothing. O my joy, how slow you were in coming! You said nothing then, and I traveled further and further from you, into more and more sterile seedbeds of sorrow, proud in my dejection, restless in my exhaustion.

And what was it I took such delight in, except to love and be loved? But I did not keep love within its measure, mind to mind, the bright border where friendship ends. Out of the muddy craving of the flesh, out of the bubbling-up of youth, a fog rose and clouded my heart over, so that I could not tell the clear brightness of love from the haze of lust. Both boiled in me, confused together, and swept my unsteady youth over the cliff of unholy desire and sank me in a gulf of disgraces. Your anger had gathered over me, and I did not know it. I had been deafened by the rattling chain of my mortality — the punishment of my soul's pride — and I strayed further from you, and you let me go. I was tossed about, spilled out, scattered, boiling over in my fornications, and you held your peace, O you my joy so slow in coming. You held your peace, and I wandered further and further from you, into more and more barren fields where only sorrows grow, in a proud dejection and a restless exhaustion.

If only someone back then had set my chaos in order — had taken the fleeting loveliness of these lowest things, the far edge of your creation, and turned it to some use; had fixed a limit to their sweetness, so that the surf of my youth, if it could not come to calm, might at least have spent itself on the shore of marriage, content to raise children, as your law prescribes, Lord. For that is how you shape the offspring of our mortality, able to lay a gentle hand on thorns that never grew in your paradise, and blunt them; your omnipotence is not far from us even when we are far from you. Or else I should have listened more sharply to the voice out of your clouds: 'Still, those who marry will have trouble in the flesh, and I would spare you.' And: 'It is good for a man not to touch a woman.' And: 'The unmarried man thinks about the things of the Lord, how to please the Lord; but the married man cares about the things of this world, how to please his wife.'

If only someone, back then, had eased my disorder and put the fleeting beauties of these things — the outermost edge of your creation — to good use, and set a limit to their pleasure, so that the tides of my youth might have cast themselves up on the shore of marriage, if they could not be calmed; that the restlessness might have been kept within the purpose of raising a family, as your law prescribes, O Lord — you who shape even the offspring of this our dying, and can with a gentle hand blunt the thorns shut out of your paradise. For your power is not far from us, even when we are far from you. Otherwise I should have listened more carefully to the voice from the clouds: "Such will have trouble in the flesh, but I would spare you," and "It is good for a man not to touch a woman," and "The unmarried man thinks about the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord; but the married man cares about the things of this world, how he may please his wife."

I should have listened harder to those words. I should have made myself a eunuch for the kingdom of heaven's sake and waited, happier, for your embrace. But instead I seethed, poor wretch, like a sea churning after its own current; I abandoned you and overran every limit you had set — and I did not escape your lash. What mortal can? You were with me the whole time, mercifully severe, sprinkling the bitterest disappointments over every one of my forbidden delights, so that I would learn to look for delight with no bitterness in it — and find that nowhere could I find it but in you, Lord. Nowhere but in you, who use sorrow to teach, and wound us to heal us, and kill us so that we will not die away from you. Where was I? How far was I exiled from the delights of your house, in that sixteenth year of the age of my flesh, when the madness of lust took up the scepter over me — lust licensed by human shamelessness, unlicensed by your laws — and I handed it both my hands? Meanwhile my family took no care to catch me as I fell by marrying me off; their one care was that I learn to make the finest speeches and to persuade with words.

I should have listened to those words more closely, and made myself a eunuch for the kingdom of heaven's sake, and waited more happily for your embrace. But I, poor wretch, foamed like a storming sea, following the rush of my own tide, abandoning you, and broke past every one of your limits. Yet I did not escape your lashes — for what mortal can? You were always with me, mercifully severe, sprinkling the bitterest taste over all my forbidden pleasures, so that I might go looking for a pleasure with no bitterness in it. And where to find that, I could not discover, except in you, O Lord — you who teach by sorrow, and wound us in order to heal, and kill us so that we will not die away from you. Where was I, and how far an exile from the joys of your house, in that sixteenth year of my body's life, when the madness of lust — which human shamelessness is given free rein to, though your law gives it no license — took command of me, and I handed myself over to it completely? My family meanwhile took no trouble to save me from falling by marriage; their only concern was that I should learn to speak well and become a persuasive speaker.

That year my studies were interrupted. I was back from Madaura — the neighboring city where I had gone to study literature and public speaking — while the money for the longer journey to Carthage was being scraped together, more by my father's determination than by his means, for he was a citizen of Thagaste with very little to his name. Who am I telling this to? Not to you, my God. But in your presence I am telling it to my own kind — to the human race, or whatever tiny fraction of it may happen upon these pages. And why? So that whoever reads this may consider how deep the pit is from which we must cry out to you. For what comes closer to your ears than a heart that confesses and a life of faith? Back then, who did not have praise for my father — a man spending beyond the strength of his estate to outfit his son for a distant journey, all for the sake of study? Many citizens far richer did nothing of the kind for their children. Yet this same father never troubled himself with how I was growing toward you, or how chaste I was — only that I turn out fluent, however much of a desert I was, untilled by you, O God, the one true and good landlord of that field of yours, my heart.

That year my studies were on hold. After I came back from Madaura, a nearby town where I had gone to study grammar and rhetoric, the money was being gathered for a longer journey to Carthage — gathered more by my father's determination than his means, for he was only a poor freeman of Thagaste. Who am I telling this to? Not to you, my God, but in your presence to my own kind, to that small share of humankind who may come upon these writings of mine. And why? So that whoever reads this may consider out of what depths we have to cry to you. For what is nearer to your ears than a heart that confesses, and a life of faith? Everyone praised my father for furnishing his son with everything needed for a long journey for the sake of his studies, far beyond what his means allowed — for many far wealthier citizens did no such thing for their children. Yet this same father gave no thought to how I was growing toward you, or whether I was chaste, so long as I was rich in speech, however barren I might be of your cultivation, O God, the one true and good Lord of your field, which is my heart.

But during that sixteenth year, home with my parents, out of school for a while — a season of idleness forced on us by the family's thin finances — the briers of lust grew up over my head, and there was no hand to root them out. Worse: when my father saw me at the baths, becoming a man now, dressed in a restless adolescence, he told my mother about it delightedly, as if he were already dreaming of grandchildren — delighted with that drunkenness in which the world forgets you, its Creator, and falls in love with your creature instead of you, drunk on the invisible wine of a will bent and tilted toward the bottom. But in my mother's breast you had already begun your temple and laid the first foundation of your holy dwelling — my father was still only a catechumen, and a recent one at that. So she startled up with a holy fear and trembling; and though I was not yet baptized, she was afraid for me — afraid of the crooked roads walked by those who turn toward you their backs and not their faces.

But while in that sixteenth year I lived at home with my parents, free of school for a while — an idle season forced on us by the narrowness of my parents' fortune — the briars of unclean desire grew rank over my head, and there was no hand to root them out. And when my father saw me at the baths, now growing into manhood and clothed in a restless youthfulness, he was delighted, as if already imagining grandchildren, and gladly told my mother — rejoicing in that surge of the senses by which the world forgets you, its Creator, and falls in love with your creature instead of with you, drunk on the invisible wine of its own self-will, turning aside and bowing down to the basest things. But in my mother's heart you had already begun your temple and laid the foundation of your holy dwelling, while my father was still only a catechumen, and that only recently. So she was shaken with a holy fear and trembling, and though I was not yet baptized, she was afraid for me of those crooked paths walked by people who turn their backs to you and not their faces.

Misery! Do I dare to say that you were silent, my God, while I wandered further from you? Were you really silent to me then? Then whose words were they, if not yours, that you sang in my ears through my mother, your faithful one? Not that any of them sank into my heart deep enough to act on. She wanted — I remember how privately, how anxiously she warned me — that I keep clear of fornication, and above all that I never sleep with another man's wife. This sounded to me like women's advice; I would have blushed to obey it. But the advice was yours, and I did not know it. I decided you were silent and she was the one talking — she, through whom you were not silent to me; and in her it was you being despised, by me, her son, the son of your servant woman, and your servant. But I did not know it. I went headlong, so blind that among boys my own age I was embarrassed to be less shameless than they were, hearing them brag about their outrages — bragging louder the filthier they got. I came to like doing the thing not only for the pleasure of it, but for the praise. What deserves contempt, if not vice? Yet to duck contempt I made myself out more vicious than I was; and where I had not sinned up to the level of the worst of them, I would claim to have done what I had not done — terrified of seeming more despicable for being more innocent, and cheaper the more chaste I was.

O misery — and dare I say that you held your peace, my God, while I wandered further from you? Did you truly hold your peace toward me then? And whose were those words, if not yours, that you sang in my ears through my mother, your faithful one? Nothing of them sank into my heart so as to make me act. For she wished — and I remember her warning me privately, with great anxiety — that I should never commit fornication, and above all never defile another man's wife. These struck me as womanish bits of advice that I would have blushed to obey. But they were yours, and I did not know it. I thought you were silent and that it was only she who spoke — she through whom you were not silent to me, and in whom you were despised by me, her son, the son of your handmaid, your servant. But I did not know it, and ran headlong with such blindness that among the boys my age I was ashamed to be less shameless. I heard them boasting of their disgraces, and the more degraded the boast, the louder it was, and I took pleasure not only in the act but in the praise of it. What deserves blame, if not vice? Yet to escape blame I made myself out worse than I was, and where I had not sinned as the lost ones had, I would claim I had done what I had not done, so that I would not seem contemptible for being more innocent, or cheaper for being more chaste.

Look at the companions I ran with through the streets of Babylon — how I rolled in its filth as though in cinnamon and precious perfumes. And to fasten me all the tighter to Babylon's dead center, the invisible enemy trampled me and seduced me, because I was easy to seduce. The mother of my flesh had already fled the center of that Babylon herself — though she still went slowly along its outskirts. She had counseled me to chastity; but what her husband had told her about me — this thing she could feel was diseased already and dangerous for the years ahead — she did not take care to hem inside the boundary of married love, if it could not be cut back to the quick. She let it be, because she feared a wife would be a shackle on my hopes. Not that hope of the world to come, which my mother rested in you — the hope of my education, which both my parents wanted for me far too much: my father, because he gave you next to no thought, and had only empty ambitions for me; my mother, because she reckoned the usual course of studies would be no obstacle on my way to you and might even be some help. So I guess, at least, recalling as well as I can what my parents were like. Meanwhile the reins were slackened on me far beyond any just strictness, and I was left to play — play shading into dissipation — at whatever I had a taste for. And over all of it, my God, hung a fog that shut me off from the clear sky of your truth; and my iniquity came oozing out of me, as if out of fat.

Look at the company I kept as I walked the streets of Babylon and wallowed in its mire as though in a bed of spices and costly perfumes. And to make me stick faster at its very center, the invisible enemy trod me down and seduced me, for I was easy to seduce. The mother of my flesh, who had by now fled the heart of Babylon but lingered in its outskirts — even she, though she urged chastity on me and had heard from her husband what I was becoming, did not think to rein it in within the bounds of married love, if it could not be cut away to the quick. She did not see how dangerous all this was, both now and for what was coming, because she was afraid that a wife might prove a weight and a hindrance to my prospects — not the hope of the world to come, which she rested in you, but the hope of learning, which both my parents were too eager for me to gain: my father because he had next to no thought of you, and only empty notions of me; my mother because she reckoned that the usual course of studies would be no obstacle, but even some help, toward reaching you. So I gather, recalling as best I can what my parents were like. Meanwhile the reins were slackened on me past all proper firmness, to spend my time in amusement, even in dissolution, in whatever I fancied. And over all of it lay a fog, cutting me off, O my God, from the brightness of your truth, and my wrongdoing burst out as if from sheer fatness.

Theft is punished by your law, Lord — by the law written in human hearts, which not even iniquity itself can rub out. For what thief calmly puts up with being robbed? Not even a rich thief puts up with one who steals from need. Yet I chose to steal, and steal I did, driven by no need — unless the need was my poverty of justice, my disgust with doing right, my glut of iniquity. For I stole what I already had plenty of, and better. And I had no wish to enjoy the thing I stole: what I wanted to enjoy was the theft itself, the sin itself. There was a pear tree near our vineyard, loaded with fruit that tempted nobody, in color or in taste. In the dead of night — having strung out our street games till then, in our pestilent fashion — a pack of us worthless young men went to shake it down and haul it off. We carried away enormous loads, not for our own eating — though we tasted a few — but to throw, in the end, to the pigs; and all of it just to do a thing that pleased us because it was not allowed. Look at my heart, O God, look at my heart, which you pitied at the bottom of the bottomless pit. Let my heart tell you now what it was after down there: that I should be evil for free — that my evil should have no cause but the evil itself. The thing was foul, and I loved it. I loved my own ruin; I loved my own falling — not the thing I fell toward, the falling itself. A filthy soul, leaping off your firmament into sheer destruction — reaching for nothing through the shame, but for the shame.

Theft is punished by your law, O Lord, and by the law written in human hearts, which not even our wrongdoing can erase. For what thief will put up with another thief? Not even a rich thief will bear with one who steals out of need. Yet I wanted to steal, and did, driven by no hunger, no poverty, but by a glut of well-being and a bloated craving for sin. For I stole something I already had plenty of, and far better. I did not even want to enjoy what I stole — I enjoyed the theft and the sin themselves. There was a pear tree near our vineyard, loaded with fruit that was nothing special to look at or to taste. Late one night — having dragged out our games in the streets till then, as our rotten habit was — a gang of us reckless young fellows went to shake the tree and carry off the pears. We took huge loads, not to eat, but to fling to the pigs, after barely tasting a few. We did it purely to do what was forbidden, simply because it was forbidden. Look at my heart, O God, look at my heart, which you took pity on at the bottom of the bottomless pit. Now let my heart tell you what it was looking for there, that I should be evil for nothing, with no cause for my malice but malice itself. It was foul, and I loved it. I loved my own undoing; I loved my falling-away — not the thing I fell toward, but the fall itself; my disgraced soul falling away from your firmament into utter ruin, seeking nothing through the shameful act but the shame itself.

There is a real allure in beautiful bodies, in gold and silver, in all of it; in the sense of touch, bodily affinity counts for much, and every other sense finds objects fitted exactly to it. Worldly honor has its own grace, and so do the power to command and the power to prevail — which is also where the thirst for revenge springs from. And yet, to get any of these things, we are not to walk away from you, Lord, or swerve from your law.
