Even this life we live here has its enchantment, through a certain proportion of its own and its harmony with all these lower beauties. And human friendship is a sweet knot, dear to us, because it ties many souls into one. Sin gets committed on account of all this and things like it: in an immoderate lunge toward these goods of the lowest order, the better and higher goods are abandoned — you, our Lord God, and your truth, and your law. The lowest things have their delights, but nothing like my God, who made everything; for in him the righteous man delights, and he is the joy of the upright in heart.

There is a certain beauty in lovely bodies, in gold and silver and all such things; in the touch of the body there is a powerful answering pleasure, and each of the other senses has its own object fitted to it. Worldly honor too has its appeal, and the power to win and to master, out of which springs also the thirst for revenge. Yet to get any of these we must not turn away from you, O Lord, or stray from your law. The life we live here has its own charm, by a certain proportion of its own and a fitness to all the beautiful things below. Human friendship, too, is sweet, bound by a dear tie, for the way it makes one out of many souls. It is over these things and the like that sin is committed, when through an unchecked leaning toward these lowest goods, the better and higher goods are abandoned — you, our Lord God, and your truth, and your law. For these lower things have their delights, but not like my God, who made them all; for in him the righteous one delights, and he is the joy of the upright in heart.

So when we ask why a particular crime was committed, we do not usually believe the answer unless it turns out there was an appetite to get one of those goods we called lower — or a fear of losing one. For they are beautiful; they do become us; even if, next to the higher goods, the goods that make life blessed, they are shabby and small. A man has murdered another man. Why did he do it? He was in love with the man's wife, or wanted his land; or he meant to rob him and live off it; or he was afraid the man would take some such thing from him; or he had been wronged, and burned to be avenged. Would anyone commit murder over nothing, delighted by the murder alone? Who would believe it? Even for that raging, savage man of whom it was written that he was evil and cruel for no reason, a reason is given a sentence later: 'so that idleness,' the historian says, 'should not slow his hand or his mind.' And why even that? So that by this daily rehearsal of crimes he might take the city, and grab honors, commands, and wealth; and be free of the fear of the laws, and of the money troubles and the guilty knowledge of his own villainies that were pressing him. No — not even Catiline loved his crimes. He loved something else, and the crimes were for its sake.

So when we ask why a crime was done, we do not believe the answer unless it appears there might have been some desire to gain one of those things we called lower goods, or some fear of losing them. For they are beautiful and pleasing, though set against the higher, blessed goods they are cheap and low. A man has murdered another — why? He loved his victim's wife, or his estate; or he wanted to rob him to live; or he was afraid of losing something to him; or, wronged, he was on fire for revenge. Would anyone commit murder for no cause at all, taking simple delight in the killing? Who would believe it? Even that wild and savage man who was said to be cruel and evil for nothing — even for him a cause is given: "so that hand and heart should not grow slack through idleness." And to what end? So that, by all that practice in crime, he might seize the city and gain office, power, and riches, and be free of the fear of the law and the strain of his debts at home and the knowledge of his own villainy. So not even Catiline loved his own crimes — he loved something else, and that was why he did them.

So what did I love in you, my theft — you crime of mine committed at night, in the sixteenth year of my life? There was nothing beautiful about you: you were theft. Are you even a thing at all, that I should be talking to you? The pears were beautiful, those pears we stole — because they were made by you, the most beautiful of all, Creator of all, good God: God the highest good, and my true good. The pears were beautiful; but they were not what my miserable soul wanted. I had plenty of better ones. I picked those only to be stealing; once picked, I threw them away. My only meal there was the wickedness itself, and I ate it with relish. If any bite of those pears entered my mouth, the sin was its seasoning. And now, Lord my God, I ask what it was in that theft that delighted me — and look: it has no loveliness at all. I do not mean the loveliness that lives in justice and prudence, or in the human mind, in memory, in the senses, in the life that quickens us; not the beauty of the stars, glorious in their stations, or of the earth and the sea, teeming with newborn lives that replace, by being born, the lives that die. It does not even have that stunted, shadowy beauty that belongs to the vices when they deceive us.

What, then, did wretched I love in you, my theft, my deed of darkness, in that sixteenth year of my life? You were not beautiful, since you were theft. But are you anything at all, that I should speak to you like this? The pears we stole were beautiful, because they were your creation, you the most beautiful of all, Maker of all, good God, God the highest good and my true good. The pears were beautiful, but it was not them my miserable soul wanted — I had a store of better, and I picked these only in order to steal. Once I had picked them, I threw them away; my whole feast was my own sin, and that was what I took pleasure in. If any bit of those pears did pass my lips, what sweetened it was the sin. And now, O Lord my God, I ask what it was in that theft that delighted me. Look — it has no loveliness. I do not mean such loveliness as there is in justice and wisdom; nor as in the mind and memory and senses and animal life of a person; nor the glory of the stars, beautiful in their courses; nor the earth and sea, teeming with new life that replaces by birth what dies away. It has not even that false and shadowy beauty that belongs to the deceiving vices.

For pride is a counterfeit of height — while you alone are God, high above everything. And what does ambition hunt but honors and glory — while you alone are to be honored before all things, and glorious forever? The cruelty of the powerful wants to be feared — but who should be feared except God alone? From his power what can be snatched or smuggled away — when, or where, or to where, or by whom? The wanton's caresses want to pass for love — but nothing caresses more tenderly than your charity, and no love is healthier than the love of your truth, beautiful and luminous past everything. Curiosity poses as a passion for knowledge — while it is you who supremely know all things. Even ignorance and sheer stupidity dress up in the names of simplicity and harmlessness — because nothing simpler than you can be found; and what is less harmful than you, since it is a sinner's own works that come back against him? Sloth presents itself as a longing for rest — but what rest is sure, except the Lord? Self-indulgence would rather be called fullness and plenty — but you are the fullness, the never-failing store of pleasure that cannot spoil. Wastefulness throws the shadow of generosity — but you are the most lavish giver of every good. Greed wants to own many things — and you own everything. Envy litigates over excellence — and what is more excellent than you? Anger demands vengeance — and who avenges more justly than you? Fear flinches at the strange and the sudden, threats to the things it loves, and scrambles to keep them safe — but to you what is strange? What is sudden? Who can take from you what you love? And where, except with you, is safety that cannot be shaken? Grief pines over lost things its desire once fed on with delight, wishing nothing could ever be taken from it — the way nothing can be taken from you.

For pride too plays at being lofty, while you alone are God lifted high over all. Ambition — what does it seek but honor and glory, while you alone are to be honored above all, and glorious forever? The cruelty of the powerful wants to be feared, but who is to be feared except God alone, from whose power what can be torn or kept back, and when, or where, or to where, or by whom? The caresses of the lustful want to pass for love, while nothing is more tender than your love, and nothing is loved more wholesomely than your truth, bright and beautiful above everything. Curiosity puts on the look of a thirst for knowledge, while you supremely know all things. Even ignorance and stupidity hide under the name of innocence and harmlessness — because nothing is found more single than you, and what could do less harm, since it is the sinner's own deeds that harm him? Sloth wants to look like rest, but what steady rest is there except in the Lord? Self-indulgence longs to be called plenty and abundance, but you are the fullness and the never-failing abundance of pleasures that do not rot. Extravagance throws up a shadow of generosity, but you are the most overflowing Giver of every good. Greed wants to own many things, and you own all things. Envy fights for first place — but what is higher than you? Anger goes after revenge — but who takes revenge more justly than you? Fear shrinks from things strange and sudden, threats to what it loves, and takes thought for their safety; but to you what is strange or sudden, and who can separate from you what you love, and where, except with you, is safety unshakable? Grief wastes away over things lost, the delights it craved, because it would have nothing taken from it — as nothing can be taken from you.

This is how the soul commits fornication: it turns away from you and looks outside you for what it can never find pure and unclouded until it comes back to you. All those who put themselves far from you and raise themselves up against you are imitating you — perversely. But even by imitating you that way, they admit that you are the Creator of the whole of nature, and that therefore there is nowhere to withdraw from you altogether. So what did I love in that theft? In what way was I imitating my Lord — even viciously, even perversely? Did it please me to break your law by fraud, since I could not break it by force — to play at a cripple's freedom, prisoner that I was, by getting away with what was not allowed, in a shadow-play of omnipotence? Look at him: a slave running from his master, and what he catches is a shadow. What rottenness! What a monstrosity of life, what a depth of death — that I could like a thing I was not allowed to do, for no reason except that I was not allowed!

So the soul commits fornication when it turns away from you and seeks outside you what it cannot find pure and clean until it comes back to you. All who go far from you and rise up against you are imitating you in a twisted way. But even by imitating you like this, they show that you are the Maker of all that is, and that there is nowhere they can go to get away from you entirely. So what did I love in that theft, and how was I, even corruptly and perversely, imitating my Lord? Did I want, by stealth, to do something against your law — because I could not do it by power — so that, a prisoner, I might act out a crippled freedom, doing what was not allowed me with no consequence, a darkened likeness of your all-powerfulness? Look at the servant running from his Lord and catching nothing but a shadow. O rottenness, O monstrous life and depth of death — could I love what was not allowed, for no reason except that it was not allowed?

What can I give back to the Lord for this — that my memory can revisit all of it and my soul feel no terror? I will love you, Lord, and thank you, and confess to your name, because you have forgiven me such evils, such unspeakable acts of mine. I put it down to your grace and your mercy that you melted my sins away like ice. And I put down to your grace, too, all the evil I did not do. What was I not capable of — I, who could love a crime for nothing? I confess it has all been forgiven me: the evils I did by my own choice, and the evils that, with you steering, I did not do. Where is the man who will weigh his own weakness and still dare to credit his purity and innocence to his own strength — and so love you less, as though he had less need of that mercy of yours by which you forgive the sins of everyone who turns to you? A man you called, who followed your voice and kept clear of the things he now reads me remembering and confessing about myself — let him not laugh at me. I was sick, and I was healed by the same Physician who kept him from falling sick, or rather kept him less sick. Let him love you for that as much as I do — no, more: for he sees that the one who pulled me out of so deep a wasting sickness of sin is the very one who kept him from wasting that way at all.

What shall I give back to the Lord, that my memory can call these things up and my soul is not terrified by them? I will love you, O Lord, and thank you, and confess to your name, because you have forgiven me these great and wicked deeds. To your grace I credit it, and to your mercy, that you melted my sins away like ice. To your grace I credit, too, whatever evil I did not do — for what might I not have done, I who loved a sin for its own sake? Yes, I confess that all of it has been forgiven me: both the evils I committed by my own will and those I did not commit because you held me back. What man, weighing his own weakness, dares to credit his purity and innocence to his own strength, and so love you the less, as though he had needed less of your mercy, by which you release the sins of those who turn to you? Whoever has been called by you and followed your voice and avoided the things he hears me recalling and confessing about myself — let him not laugh at me, the sick man healed by that Physician, by whose help it was that he himself was not sick, or was less sick. Let him love you just as much, and more — seeing that the same one by whom he sees me recovered from so deep a wasting of sin is the one by whom he sees himself kept safe from a wasting just as deep.

What harvest did I ever get, wretched as I was, from the things I blush now to remember — above all from that theft, in which the theft itself was all I loved? The theft itself was nothing — and I was that much more wretched for loving it. And yet, alone, I would not have done it. I remember what I was then: alone, I would never have done it. So I also loved the company of the ones I did it with. Then I did love something besides the theft after all? No — nothing besides; because the company, too, was nothing. What is it really? Who can teach me, except the one who lights up my heart and clears out its dark corners? What is this thing that has come into my mind to be asked about, argued, weighed? If I had loved the pears I stole, and wanted the taste of them, I could have done it alone — if the wrong itself had been enough to deliver my pleasure. I would not have needed to kindle the itch of my desire against the friction of accomplice minds. But my pleasure was not in those pears. It was in the crime itself, and the crime was made by the company of us sinning together.

What harvest did I have then, wretched man, in those things I am now ashamed even to remember? Above all in that theft, which I loved only for the theft's sake — a theft that was itself nothing, which made me, who loved it, the more wretched. Yet I would not have done it alone; that was what I was then, I remember — alone I would never have done it. So I loved in it also the company of those who did it with me. Then I did not love only the theft? No, rather I loved nothing else — because that company was itself nothing too. What is the truth here? Who can teach me, except the one who lights up my heart and lays bare its dark corners? Why has this come into my mind to ask and weigh and consider? For if I had loved the pears I stole and wanted to enjoy them, I could have done it alone, had the mere act of theft been enough to get my pleasure; I would not have needed to rub up the itch of my desire against the company of accomplices. But since my pleasure was not in the pears, it was in the offense itself, which the company of fellow-sinners brought about.

What was that state of mind? Whatever it was, it was foul beyond words, and misery on me for having it. But what was it? Who understands his own faults? It was laughter — a kind of tickle in the heart at the thought that we were fooling people who never suspected us and would have hated what we were doing. Why, then, did it delight me that I was not doing it alone? Is it that nobody laughs easily alone? Not easily, no — and yet laughter will sometimes overpower a person who is completely alone, with no one else anywhere near, if something funny enough strikes his senses or his mind. But this — I would not have done this alone. Alone, I would never have done it. Here it is before you, my God: the living memory of my soul. By myself I would not have committed that theft — a theft in which what I stole gave me no pleasure, only the stealing did; and stealing by myself would have given me none, and I would not have stolen. Unfriendly friendship! Seduction of the mind that no one can trace: out of games and jokes, a greed to do harm; an appetite for another's loss, with nothing in it for me — no gain, no grudge. Just someone saying, 'Come on — let's do it,' and the shame of not being shameless.

What, then, was this feeling? It was truly too foul, and woe to me who had it. But what was it? Who can grasp his own errors? It was the game of it, the way it tickled our hearts to fool people who had no idea what we were doing and would have hated it. Why, then, was my pleasure such that I would not do it alone? Because no one usually laughs by himself? Usually no one — and yet laughter does sometimes overtake a man alone and by himself, when no one at all is with him, if something truly absurd strikes his senses or his mind. Still, I would not have done this alone; alone I would never have done it. Look, my God, here before you is the living memory of my soul: alone I would never have committed that theft, in which what pleased me was not what I stole but that I stole — and it would not have pleased me to do it alone, and I would not have done it. O friendship too unfriendly, you baffling seducer of the mind, you hunger to do harm for sport and mischief, you craving for another's loss with no appetite for my own gain or revenge — when the word goes round, "Come on, let's do it," we are ashamed not to be shameless.

Who can untangle that twisted, matted knot? It is foul. I do not want to keep staring at it; I do not want to see it. I want you — Justice, Innocence, beautiful and honorable to honest eyes, a fullness no one ever tires of. With you is rest, rest to the very bottom, and life that nothing disturbs. Whoever enters into you enters into the joy of his Lord; he will not be afraid, and he will be at his best in the One who is best. I drained away from you and I wandered, my God — too far off every path from you, my steadiness, in those years of my youth — and I became to myself a land of famine.

Who can untangle that knotted, twisting snarl? It is foul; I hate to think of it, to look at it. But it is you I long for, O Righteousness and Innocence, lovely and fair to all clear eyes, a satisfaction that never cloys. With you is rest entire and a life that nothing disturbs. Whoever enters into you enters into the joy of his Lord, and shall not be afraid, and shall stand at his best in the Best of all. I slipped away from you and wandered, O my God, far astray in the days of my youth from you, my support, and I became to myself a barren land.

I came to Carthage, and a cauldron of shameful loves hissed and seethed around me. I was not in love yet, but I was in love with loving, and out of a deeper, hidden need I hated myself for not needing more. I hunted for something to love, in love with loving itself; I hated safety, hated a road without traps. For inside me was a famine of the inner food — of you yourself, my God — yet the famine gave me no hunger. I had no appetite for the food that does not spoil, not because I was full of it, but because the emptier I was, the more it turned my stomach. That is why my soul was sick, and broke out in sores, and flung itself wretchedly outward, itching to be scratched by the touch of things of sense. Yet if those things had no soul in them, they would not be loved at all. To love and to be loved was sweet to me, and sweeter if I could also enjoy the body of the one who loved me. So I fouled the spring of friendship with the dirt of lust; I clouded its brightness with a hell of desire; and, foul and disgraceful as I was, in my overflowing vanity I longed to pass for elegant and refined. I fell headlong into the love I was aching to be caught by. My God, my mercy, how much gall you sprinkled over that sweetness — and what goodness it was to do it! For I was loved in return; I came in secret to the bond of enjoying; and I was glad to be tied up in chains of misery, so that I could be flogged with the burning iron rods of jealousy and suspicion, of fear and anger and quarrels.

To Carthage I came, and all around me a cauldron of shameful loves seethed and crackled in my ears. I was not yet in love, but I was in love with loving, and out of a hunger deep inside me I despised myself for not being hungrier still. I went searching for something to love, in love with loving, and I hated safety, hated a road without snares. For inside me was a famine for that inner food, which is you yourself, my God — and yet that famine left me feeling no hunger. I had no appetite for the bread that cannot rot, not because I was full of it but because the emptier I grew the more it sickened me. So my soul was diseased, broken out in sores, and it flung itself wretchedly at the world of the senses, craving to be scratched by the touch of physical things. And yet, if those things had no soul in them, they could never be loved at all. To love and to be loved was sweet to me, sweeter still if I could possess the body of the one I loved. So I fouled the clear spring of friendship with the filth of lust, and I clouded its brightness with the smoke of desire. Foul and disgraceful as I was, in my craving to be elegant and sophisticated I plunged headlong into the very love I longed to be caught in. My God, my Mercy, with how much bitterness, out of your great goodness, you sprinkled that sweetness for me. For I was loved, and secretly I reached the bond of two bodies enjoying each other, and joyfully I let myself be chained in misery, so that I might be flogged with the red-hot iron rods of jealousy and suspicion and fear and anger and quarrels.

Stage shows swept me away too, full of images of my own miseries and fuel for my own fire. Why is it that a man in the theater wants to feel grief, watching sorrowful and tragic things he would never willingly suffer himself? Yet as a spectator he wants to suffer grief at them, and the grief itself is his pleasure. What is that but wretched madness? The more a man is stirred by these performances, the less he has recovered from such passions himself — though when he suffers in his own person we call it misery, and when he feels with someone else we call it compassion. But what sort of compassion is there for fictions on a stage? The listener is not being called to help; he is only being invited to grieve, and the more he grieves, the louder he applauds the actor of those fictions. And if these human calamities — ancient ones, or pure inventions — are played so that the spectator feels no sorrow, he walks out disgusted and muttering criticism; but if sorrow is stirred in him, he stays riveted to his seat, weeping for joy.

The stage and its plays carried me away too, full of images of my own misery, more fuel for my fire. Why is it that a person wants to be made sad by watching grief and tragedy that he would never want to suffer himself? And yet he wants, as a spectator, to feel the sorrow of it, and the sorrow itself is his pleasure. What is this but a pitiable madness? For a man is moved by these scenes the more, the less he is cured of such feelings in his own life. When he suffers in his own person we call it misery; when he suffers along with others we call it compassion. But what kind of compassion is this, for things acted out and invented? The audience is not asked to step in and help, only to grieve — and the more it grieves, the more it praises the actor of these fictions. If the disasters on stage, whether ancient history or pure invention, are performed so badly that the spectator is not moved to tears, he leaves bored and complaining; but if he is moved and made to suffer, he stays riveted, and weeps, and enjoys it.

So griefs are loved too? Surely joy is what everyone wants. Or is it this — that though no one likes to be miserable, we do like to be merciful, and since mercy cannot exist without grief, for this one reason griefs are loved? This too springs from that vein of friendship. But where does it go? Where does it flow? Why does it run down into a torrent of boiling pitch, into those monstrous tides of foul lust into which it is changed and twisted — by its own choice bent and hurled down out of its heavenly clearness? Should compassion be thrown out, then? By no means. Let griefs, then, sometimes be loved. But beware of uncleanness, my soul — with my God for your guardian, the God of our fathers, to be praised and exalted above all forever — beware of uncleanness. Even now I have not stopped pitying. But in those days, in the theaters, I rejoiced with the lovers when they wickedly enjoyed one another, though it was all make-believe in the play; and when they lost one another I grieved with them as if I were deep in compassion — and both delighted me all the same. Now I pity the man who rejoices in his wickedness far more than the man who is thought to have suffered hardship because he missed some ruinous pleasure and lost some miserable happiness. This is surely the truer mercy, but there is no delight in its grief. For though a man who grieves for the wretched is commended for his act of love, the man who is genuinely compassionate would far rather there were nothing to grieve about. Only if goodwill could be ill will — which can never be — could a man who truly and sincerely pities wish for wretched people to exist so that he could pity them. Some sorrow, then, can be approved; none can be loved. For this is your way, Lord God: you love souls far more purely than we do, and pity them more incorruptibly, because no sorrow can wound you. And who is equal to these things?

So are griefs themselves loved? Surely everyone wants joy. Or is it that, though no one likes being miserable, a person still likes being moved to pity — and because pity cannot exist without some pain, the pain is loved for the pity's sake alone? This too springs from that same vein of friendship in us. But where does that vein run? Where does it flow? Why does it pour itself into a boiling river of pitch, those monstrous swells of foul desire, into which, by its own choice, it twists and changes itself, dragged down and corrupted from its native, heavenly clearness? Should pity then be thrown out? By no means. So let some griefs be loved, after all. But beware of filth, my soul — under the keeping of my God, the God of our fathers, who is to be praised and lifted up above all forever — beware of filth. I have not stopped feeling pity even now. But back then, in the theaters, I rejoiced with lovers when they sinfully enjoyed each other, even though it was only make-believe in the play; and when they lost each other I grieved with them, as if full of compassion — and either way I had my pleasure. Now I pity the man who delights in his wickedness far more than the man who is thought to suffer hardship by going without some ruinous pleasure, the loss of some wretched happiness. This is surely the truer mercy, but grief takes no delight in it. For though a person who grieves for the miserable is rightly praised for his charity, anyone who is genuinely compassionate would far rather there were nothing to grieve over. If goodwill could wish someone ill — which it never can — then a person who is truly and sincerely full of pity might wish there were someone miserable, so that he could pity him. So some sorrow can be permitted, but none can be loved. For this is how you are, O Lord God, who love souls far more purely than we do, and pity them more incorruptibly, and yet are wounded by no grief at all. And who is equal to such things?

But I, wretched then, loved to grieve, and went looking for something to grieve over. In another man's misery — faked, staged — the performance I liked best, the one that pulled at me hardest, was the one that shook tears out of me. Was it any wonder that an unhappy sheep, straying from your flock, sick of your keeping, broke out in an ugly mange? That was where my love of griefs came from — not griefs that would cut me deep, since I had no wish to suffer the things I loved to watch, but griefs that, heard and invented, scraped me lightly on the surface. And after them, as after raking fingernails, came the hot swelling, the abscess, the festering sore. That was my life — but was it life, my God?

But I, wretch that I was, loved to grieve in those days, and went looking for things to grieve at. In another person's misery — invented, performed by an actor — what pleased me most, what drew me in hardest, was whatever drew the tears out of me. No wonder, then, that I, an unhappy sheep straying from your flock and refusing to be kept by you, broke out in this disgusting disease. Hence my love of griefs — not the kind that would cut deep into me, since I had no wish to suffer what I loved to watch, but the kind that, when I heard these stories, would lightly scratch the surface. And on that scratch, as if from poisoned fingernails, came swelling and inflammation and festering and rot. Was such a life a life at all, my God?

And your faithful mercy circled over me, far off. On what enormous iniquities I wasted myself! I followed a sacrilegious curiosity, so that, having deserted you, it might drag me down to the treacherous depths, to the cheating service of demons — and to them I sacrificed my evil deeds. And in all of it you were flogging me. I even dared, while your solemn rites were being celebrated inside the walls of your own church, to feel desire, and to set about a piece of business whose fruit was death. For that you lashed me with heavy punishments, but nothing next to my fault, O you, my exceedingly great mercy, my God, my refuge from the terrible destroyers among whom I wandered, stiff-necked, drawing further and further away from you — loving my own ways and not yours, loving a runaway's freedom.

And your faithful mercy hovered over me, far off. On what monstrous wrongs I wore myself out, chasing a sacrilegious curiosity that, having abandoned you, was dragging me down toward the treacherous abyss and the lying service of demons, to whom I made offerings of my own bad deeds — and in all of it you were scourging me. I even dared, while your solemn rites were being celebrated inside the walls of your Church, to lust after a woman and to set in motion an affair whose fruit was death; for which you punished me with heavy blows, though nothing compared to my fault, O my exceeding mercy, my God, my refuge from those terrifying destroyers among whom I roamed with my head held stiff, drawing further and further from you, in love with my own ways and not yours, in love with a runaway freedom.

Those studies too, the ones people called honorable, had their eye on the law courts: I was to excel in them, and the more crooked I was, the more I would be praised. So great is the blindness of men, who glory even in their blindness. And I was now the senior student in the rhetoric school, and I rejoiced in it proudly and swelled with conceit — though I was far quieter, Lord, you know it, and stood completely apart from the wrecking done by the "Wreckers." That crooked, devilish name was worn like a badge of sophistication. I lived among them, ashamed with a shameless shame that I was not one of them. I was with them; at times I enjoyed their friendships; but their doings I always abhorred — their "wreckings," the insolent way they hounded the shyness of strangers, tormenting it with unprovoked mockery and feeding their own malicious glee on it. Nothing could be more like the conduct of demons. So what truer name could they have than Wreckers? — wrecked and twisted themselves first, while the lying spirits secretly laughed at them and seduced them in the very thing they loved to do: laughing at others, and deceiving them.

My studies, too, the ones thought respectable, were aimed at excelling in the law courts — and the more praised I was, the more cunning. Such is human blindness, that men glory even in being blind. By now I was top of the school of rhetoric, and I was proud and pleased with myself and swollen with conceit, though (Lord, you know) far quieter than, and entirely apart from, the wreckings of those self-styled "Wreckers" — for that grim and devilish name was their badge of sophistication — among whom I lived in a kind of shameless shame at not being one of them. I lived among them, and sometimes I enjoyed their company, while I always loathed what they did: their "wreckings," the way they would wantonly hound the modesty of newcomers, throwing them off balance with pointless mockery, feeding their own malice on it. Nothing is more like the very work of demons than this. What truer name could they be given than "Wreckers"? — themselves first of all wrecked and utterly twisted, with the deceiving spirits secretly laughing at them and luring them on, in the very act of luring and laughing at others.

Among such men, at that impressionable age, I studied the books of eloquence, in which I longed to stand out — a damnable and windy purpose, aimed at the joys of human vanity. Following the usual course of study, I came to a book by one Cicero, whose tongue almost everyone admires; his heart, not so much. That book contains his exhortation to philosophy, and it is called the Hortensius. That book changed what I loved. It turned my prayers toward you yourself, Lord, and gave me new purposes, new desires. All at once every vain hope was worthless to me; I longed for the immortality of wisdom with an unbelievable burning of the heart; and I had begun to rise, so that I might return to you. For it was not to sharpen my tongue — the thing I was supposedly buying with my mother's money, in my nineteenth year, my father two years dead — it was not to sharpen my tongue that I took up that book. What had won me was not the way it spoke, but what it said.

Living among people like that, at that unsteady age, I studied books of eloquence, in which I longed to shine — for a damnable, empty-headed reason: delight in human vanity. In the ordinary course of study I came upon a book by a certain Cicero, whose tongue almost everyone admires, though not his heart. This particular book of his is an exhortation to philosophy, and it is called the Hortensius. That book changed how I felt. It turned my prayers toward you, Lord, and gave me new purposes and longings. Suddenly every empty hope looked worthless to me, and with an unbelievable fire in my heart I began to long for the immortality that wisdom is, and I began to get up and start back toward you. For it was not to sharpen my tongue that I used that book — sharpening my tongue was what I seemed to be buying with my mother's money, in that nineteenth year of mine, my father having died two years before — it was not for its style that I read it, but for what it said.

How I burned then, my God — how I burned to fly up from earthly things back to you! And I did not know what you were doing with me. For wisdom is with you. The love of wisdom has a Greek name, "philosophy," and that book set me on fire with it. There are men who use philosophy to seduce, coloring and painting over their own errors with that great, smooth, honorable name; and nearly all who did so, in Cicero's day and before it, are marked and exposed in that book. It even makes plain that saving warning of your Spirit, spoken through your good and devout servant: "See to it that no one takes you captive through philosophy and empty deceit, following human tradition, following the elements of this world and not Christ; for in him the whole fullness of deity dwells in bodily form." And at that time — you know it, light of my heart — those words of the apostle were still unknown to me. What delighted me in Cicero's exhortation was just this: that his words roused me, kindled me, set me ablaze to love and seek and win and hold and strongly embrace not this school or that school, but wisdom itself, whatever it might be. Only one thing dampened the blaze: the name of Christ was not there. For that name, by your mercy, Lord — the name of my Savior, your Son — my tender heart had drunk in devoutly with my mother's milk, and it stayed deep in me; and whatever came without that name, however learned, however polished, however true, could not carry me away entirely.

How I burned then, my God, how I burned to fly up from earthly things back to you, and I had no idea what you were going to do with me. For with you is wisdom. And love of wisdom is what the Greek word "philosophy" means, and it was with this love that the book set me ablaze. There are people who use philosophy to lead others astray, dressing up their own errors under that great, smooth, respectable name — and almost everyone who did so in that age and earlier ages is named and exposed in that book. There, too, stands out that healthy warning given by your Spirit through your good and devoted servant: See to it that no one takes you captive through philosophy and empty deceit, following human tradition and the elementary principles of the world, and not Christ; for in him the whole fullness of God dwells in bodily form. And since at that time (you, the light of my heart, know it) I had no knowledge of the apostolic Scriptures, this is all the exhortation delighted me to do: it roused and kindled and inflamed me to love and seek and win and hold and embrace not this or that school of thought, but wisdom itself, whatever it might be. One thing alone held back my blaze: that the name of Christ was not in it. For this name, by your mercy, Lord, this name of my Savior, your Son, my tender heart had drunk in devoutly with my mother's milk and stored away deep — and whatever lacked that name, however learned and polished and true, could never take complete hold of me.

So I resolved to turn my mind to the holy Scriptures, and see what kind of thing they were. And what I see there is a thing not opened to the proud, not laid bare to children: lowly at the threshold, lofty as you go deeper in, and veiled in mysteries. I was not the kind of man who could enter it, or bend my neck to walk at its pace. When I first turned to Scripture, I did not feel what I am saying now. It seemed to me unworthy to stand beside the stateliness of Cicero. My swollen pride recoiled from its plainness, and my sharp eye could not pierce its depths. Yet Scripture is exactly the thing that grows up with a little child. But I sneered at being a little child; puffed up with self-importance, I took myself for a great man.

So I made up my mind to turn to the holy Scriptures and see what they were like. But look — here was something the proud cannot grasp and yet is not laid bare to children; lowly to enter, but in its depths towering, and veiled in mystery. And I was not the kind of person who could enter into it, or bend my neck to walk its path. For I did not feel about those Scriptures, when I first turned to them, what I am saying now. They struck me as unworthy to be set beside the grandeur of Cicero. My swollen pride recoiled from their plainness, and my sharp wit could not pierce to their inner meaning. Yet they were exactly the kind of thing that grows along with a little child. But I scorned to be a little child, and, puffed up with pride, I took myself for someone great.

And so I fell in with men proudly raving, all flesh and all talk, whose mouths held the devil's snares — a birdlime mixed from the syllables of your name, and of the Lord Jesus Christ, and of the Paraclete, our Comforter, the Holy Spirit. These names never left their mouths, but only as sound, as the noise of the tongue; their hearts were empty of truth. "Truth! Truth!" they kept saying, and they said it to me constantly, and it was nowhere in them. They spoke falsehoods — not only about you, who truly are the Truth, but even about the elements of this world, your creation. Even the philosophers who say true things about such matters I should have passed by, for love of you, my Father, supremely good, beauty of all things beautiful. O Truth, Truth — how the marrow of my soul sighed for you, even then, from the inside, while those men sounded your name at me over and over, in many ways, with the voice alone and with many enormous books! Those books were the platters on which — while I starved for you — they served me the sun and the moon in your place: beautiful works of yours, but works of yours all the same. Not you. Not even your first works: for your spiritual works come before these bodily ones, bright and heavenly though they are. But I was hungry and thirsty not even for those first works, but for you yourself, the Truth, in whom there is no change, no shadow of turning. And still they kept setting glittering fantasies before me on those platters. Better to love this actual sun — real at least to these eyes — than those falsehoods that use the eyes to cheat the mind. And yet, because I took them for you, I ate — not eagerly, since in my mouth you had no taste of what you are (you were not those empty fictions), and I was not nourished by them; I was drained. Food in dreams looks exactly like the food of waking life; yet the sleeping are not fed by it — they are asleep. But those doctrines were not like you in any way, as you have now spoken to me, for they were bodily fantasies — false bodies. More certain than they are these true bodies we see with the sight of the flesh, in the sky or on the earth. The beasts and the birds see them just as we do, and they are more certain than when we picture them in the mind; and again, we picture them with more certainty than when we start from them and guess at other bodies, vaster and infinite, that do not exist at all. Such were the empty husks I was fed on then — and I was not fed. But you, my Love, for whom I grow faint so that I may grow strong — you are neither those bodies we see, though they are in heaven, nor those we do not see there; for you created them, and you do not even count them among your greatest works. How far you are, then, from those fantasies of mine, fantasies of bodies that have no being at all! More certain than those are the images of bodies that do exist, and more certain than the images the bodies themselves — and even they are not you. Nor are you the soul, which is the life of bodies — and the life of bodies is better and more certain than the bodies. No: you are the life of souls, the life of lives, alive by your own self, and you do not change — O life of my soul.

So I fell in with men full of proud nonsense, utterly carnal and talkative, in whose mouths were the snares of the Devil — birdlime smeared together out of the syllables of your name, and of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, our Comforter. These names never left their mouths, but only as sound, as the noise of the tongue; their hearts were empty of truth. And still they kept crying "Truth! Truth!" and saying much about it to me, and it was never in them. They spoke falsehood not only about you, who truly are the Truth, but even about these elements of the world, your creatures. And I should have walked right past even the philosophers who spoke truth about such things, for love of you, my Father, supreme good, Beauty of all things beautiful. O Truth, Truth, how deeply even then the marrow of my soul ached for you, while these men kept dinning your name in my ears, again and again, in many ways, in many huge books — and it was only an echo. And these were the dishes on which, while I starved for you, they served me up the sun and moon instead of you — beautiful works of yours, yes, but works, not you, and not even your first works. For your spiritual works come before these physical ones, splendid and shining though they are. But I hungered and thirsted not even for those first works of yours; I hungered for you yourself, the Truth, in whom there is no change, not even the shadow of turning. And still they set before me in those dishes their glittering fantasies, when it would have been better to love this very sun, which is at least real to our eyes, than those fantasies that deceive the mind through the eyes. Yet because I thought they were you, I fed on them — not eagerly, for in them you did not taste to me as you really are. You were not those empty things, and I was not nourished by them; I was drained instead. Food in a dream looks just like food when we are awake, yet sleepers are not fed by it, for they are asleep. But those fantasies were not even like you in the way you have now spoken to me; for they were bodily fantasies, false bodies — and the real bodies we see with our eyes of flesh, in the sky or on the earth, are far more certain than they. The beasts and birds see these real bodies as well as we do, and they are more certain than the bodies we merely imagine; and the ones we imagine are in turn more certain than the vaster, endless bodies we go on to guess at from them, which have no existence at all. On such empty husks I was being fed in those days, and not fed. But you, the Love of my soul, in seeking whom I grow weak so that I may grow strong, you are not those bodies we see, even up in heaven, nor the ones we do not see there; for you made them, and you do not even count them among your highest works. How far, then, you are from those fantasies of mine, fantasies of bodies that do not exist at all — when the images of bodies that do exist are far more certain than my fantasies, and the bodies themselves more certain still, which yet you are not; nor are you even the soul, which is the life of bodies. So the life of bodies is better and more certain than the bodies. But you are the life of souls, the life of lives, alive in yourself, and you do not change, O life of my soul.

Where were you then, for me? How far away? I was wandering far from you, shut out even from the husks of the pigs whom I was feeding on husks. How much better are the little fables of the poets and the schoolmasters than those traps! Verses, songs, "Medea in flight" — these are truly more useful than those men's five elements, painted up in different disguises to match their five dens of darkness: things that do not exist at all, and that kill whoever believes in them. A verse and a song I can turn into real food. And though I sang of Medea flying, I never claimed it happened; though I heard it sung, I never believed it. But those things I believed. Woe, woe! By what steps was I dragged down into the depths of hell — toiling and seething for lack of the truth! For I was seeking you, my God — to you I confess it, who took pity on me before I could yet confess — I was seeking you not by the understanding of the mind, by which you willed me to stand above the beasts, but by the senses of the flesh. And all the while you were more inward than my inmost part, and higher than my highest. I had walked into that brazen woman of Solomon's riddle, poor in prudence, who sits on a stool at her door and says, "Eat hidden bread gladly, and drink sweet stolen water." She seduced me, because she found me living outside, in the eye of my flesh, chewing over in myself the food I had gulped down through it.

Where, then, were you to me in those days, and how far off? Far indeed I was wandering from you, shut out even from the husks of the pigs I was feeding with husks. For how much better are the stories of poets and grammar-teachers than these snares of theirs? Verses and poems and "Medea taking flight" are honestly more useful than these men's five elements painted in different disguises, answering to five dens of darkness — things that have no existence, yet kill whoever believes in them. Verses and poems I can turn into real food; and though I once recited "Medea taking flight," I never claimed it was true, and though I heard it recited, I never believed it — but those Manichaean things I did believe. What a pity, what a pity, by what steps I was led down into the depths of hell, sweating and straining for lack of Truth — for I was seeking you, my God (to you I confess it, you who had mercy on me even before I confessed), not with the understanding of the mind, by which you meant me to surpass the beasts, but with the sense of the flesh. But you were more inward to me than my innermost self, and higher than the highest in me. I stumbled upon that brazen woman, foolish and knowing nothing, sketched in Solomon's proverb, sitting at her door and saying, Eat the bread of secrecy gladly, and drink the sweet stolen waters. She seduced me, because she found my soul living outside itself, in the eye of my flesh, chewing over the food I had swallowed through it.

For I did not know that other thing, the one that truly is. And I was subtly nudged — sharp fellow that I was — to side with fools and deceivers when they put their questions to me: Where does evil come from? Is God bounded by a bodily shape — does he have hair and nails? Are men to be counted righteous who had several wives at once, and killed men, and sacrificed animals? In my ignorance these questions shook me, and while I was walking away from the truth I imagined I was walking toward it. For I did not yet know that evil has no being of its own — that it is nothing but the privation of good, thinning down toward the point where nothing at all is left. How could I have seen that, when my eyes' seeing stopped at bodies, and my mind's seeing stopped at a phantasm? And I did not know that God is spirit: not something with limbs stretched out in length and breadth, not something whose being is bulk. For bulk is smaller in its part than in its whole; and if it were infinite, it would be smaller in any part you marked off by a fixed space than in its whole infinity — so it is not whole everywhere, the way spirit is, the way God is. And what there is in us by which we exist, and by which Scripture rightly says we are made in the image of God — of that I was completely ignorant.

For I knew nothing else than this — than what really is I had no knowledge — and I was talked into agreeing, as though by sheer cleverness, with stupid deceivers when they asked me: "Where does evil come from?" "Is God bounded by a bodily shape, with hair and nails?" "Are men to be counted righteous who had many wives at once, and killed men, and sacrificed living animals?" At all this I, in my ignorance, was badly shaken, and while moving away from the truth I imagined I was moving toward it — because I did not yet know that evil is nothing but a lack of good, right down to the point where a thing ceases to exist at all. And how was I to see this, when the sight of my eyes reached only as far as bodies, and the sight of my mind only as far as a phantom? I did not know that God is Spirit, with no parts stretched out in length and breadth, no being that is sheer bulk — for every bulk is less in a part than in the whole, and if it were infinite it would be less in any part marked off by a given space than in its whole infinity, and so could not be wholly everywhere, as Spirit is, as God is. And as for what it is in us by which we resemble God, so that we can rightly be called made in the image of God, I had no idea at all.

Nor did I know the true inner righteousness, which judges not by custom but by the perfectly straight law of almighty God — the law by which the moral codes of regions and ages were shaped to fit those regions and ages, while the law itself is the same always and everywhere, not one thing in one place and something else in another. By that law Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and Moses and David were righteous — all those men praised by the mouth of God himself. It is fools who judge them unrighteous, judging by man's judgment and measuring the moral conduct of the whole human race against the yardstick of their own small habits. It is as if a man in an armory, with no idea what fits which limb, tried to cover his head with a shin-guard and put a helmet on his foot, and then complained that nothing fits. Or as if, on a day when trade is publicly banned after noon, a shopkeeper fumed that he could not sell in the afternoon, since he had been allowed to in the morning. Or as if, in a single house, a man watched one servant handle something the cup-bearer is not allowed to touch, or saw a thing done behind the stables that is forbidden at the dinner table, and grew indignant that in one dwelling, in one household, the same thing is not granted to everyone everywhere. Such are the people who bristle when they hear that something was lawful for righteous men in that age which is not lawful in this one, or that God commanded those men one thing and these men another, for reasons belonging to the times — though both alike were obeying the same righteousness. Yet they can see that in one man, one day, one house, different things fit different members; that a thing lawful for years may cease to be lawful; that something permitted or commanded in one corner is justly forbidden and punished in another. Is justice then fickle and changeable? No. But the times over which justice presides do not run alike — they are times, after all. And men, whose life on earth is short, cannot stitch together by their own experience the circumstances of earlier ages and other nations, which they never knew, with what they know first-hand — though within a single body, a single day, a single household, they can easily see what suits each member, each moment, each part and person. At the one they take offense; to the other they submit.

Nor did I know that true, inward righteousness which judges not by custom but out of the perfectly right law of God Almighty — the law by which the moral ways of different places and times were each fitted to their own time and place, while the law itself stays one and the same always and everywhere, not one thing here and another there. By this righteousness Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and Moses and David were righteous, and all those praised by the mouth of God, even though shallow men, judging by human judgment and measuring the moral practice of the whole human race by their own narrow habits, counted them unrighteous. It is as if someone who knew nothing about armor, ignorant of which piece fits which part of the body, were to put the leg-guards on his head and try to wear the helmet on his feet, and then complain that they did not fit. Or as if, on a day when business is shut down for the afternoon, a man were furious at not being allowed to keep his shop open, just because he had been allowed to in the morning. Or as if, in one household, he saw a servant handle something the wine-steward is not permitted to touch, or saw something allowed out in the yard that is forbidden at the dinner table, and grew angry that within one house and one family the same thing is not allowed everywhere and to everyone. Such are the people who fume to hear that something was lawful for righteous men long ago which is not lawful now, or that God for certain temporal reasons commanded those men one thing and these men another, while both obeyed one and the same righteousness — when in a single body, a single day, a single household, they plainly see different things fitting for different parts, and a thing once lawful unlawful a little later, permitted or commanded in one corner but rightly forbidden and punished in another. Is justice, then, changeable and inconsistent? No — but the times it presides over do not run all alike, precisely because they are times. Men, though, whose days on earth are few, cannot piece together by their senses how the causes of things in earlier ages and other nations, which they have no experience of, fit with the causes they do have experience of; and so, while in one body or day or family they easily see what suits each part and season and person, they take offense at the one and submit to the other.

All this I did not know then, and did not notice. It struck my eyes on every side, and I did not see it. I wrote verses, and in them I was not free to set any foot in any position; each meter demanded something different, and even within one meter the same foot could not stand in every place. Yet the art by which I composed did not have one rule here and a different rule there; it held them all at once. And still I could not see that the righteousness which good and holy men obeyed held everything it commands together in one — far more excellently, far more sublimely — varying in no part of itself, and yet, for varying times, distributing and prescribing not everything at once, but what was proper to each. Blind as I was, I faulted the devout fathers — not only for using the things of their own day as God commanded and inspired them, but also for foretelling what was to come, as God revealed it through them.

These things I did not yet know or notice. They struck my eyes on every side and I did not see them. When I composed verses, I could not put just any metrical foot just anywhere; I had to place them differently in different meters, and even within a single meter I could not put the same foot in every position. Yet the art of poetry itself, by which I composed, did not have different principles for these different cases; it held them all in one. And still I could not see how that righteousness which good and holy men obeyed contained, far more excellently and loftily, in one single principle, all the things God commanded, never varying in any part — even though in varying times it did not prescribe everything at once, but assigned to each its own. And I, in my blindness, condemned the holy fathers, not only where they used the things of their own time as God commanded and inspired them, but even where they were foretelling things to come, as God was revealing them through them.

Can it ever, anywhere, be unjust to love God with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole mind — and to love your neighbor as yourself? So the offenses that are against nature are everywhere and always to be detested and punished; such were the offenses of Sodom. If every nation on earth committed them, all would stand guilty of the same crime under God's law, which did not make human beings to use one another so. For the very fellowship that ought to hold between God and us is violated when the nature of which he is the author is defiled by perverted lust. But offenses against the customs of men are to be avoided according to the customs of each place, so that a compact settled among themselves by a city's or a nation's custom or law may not be broken at the whim of anyone, citizen or foreigner. For any part that will not fit its own whole is ugly. When God commands something contrary to the custom or the compact of any people, however, then even if it was never done there, it must be done; if it has lapsed, it must be restored; if it was never instituted, it must be instituted now. For if a king, in the city he rules, may lawfully command what no one before him — nor he himself until then — had ever commanded, and obeying him is no offense against the community of that city (indeed it is an offense not to obey him, since the general compact of human society is to obey its kings), then how much more must God, the ruler of all his creation, be obeyed without hesitation in whatever he commands. For just as, among the powers of human society, the greater authority is set above the lesser and is obeyed first, so God is set above all.

Can it ever, anywhere, be wrong to love God with all your heart and all your soul and all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself? And so those foul offenses against nature are everywhere and always to be detested and punished, such as the offenses of the men of Sodom; if every nation committed them, they would all stand guilty of the same crime under the law of God, which did not make human beings to abuse one another like that. For even the fellowship that ought to exist between God and us is violated when the very nature he authored is polluted by twisted lust. But offenses against the customs of men are to be avoided according to whatever customs are in force; so that what has been agreed and confirmed by the custom or law of any city or nation is not to be broken at the lawless whim of anyone, whether citizen or foreigner. For any part that does not fit with its whole is offensive. But when God commands a thing against the customs or agreements of any people, even something never done among them before, it is to be done; and if it has lapsed, it is to be restored; and if it was never established, it is now to be established. For if a king is allowed, in the realm he rules, to command something neither he nor anyone before him had ever commanded, and obeying him is not against the common good of the state — indeed it would be against it not to obey, since obedience to rulers is a general compact of human society — how much more unhesitatingly ought we to obey God, the Ruler of all his creatures, in everything he commands? For just as, among the powers in human society, the greater authority is obeyed in preference to the lesser, so must God be obeyed above all.

The same holds for acts of violence, where there is an appetite to hurt — by insult or by injury — and either for revenge, as enemy against enemy; or to seize some advantage that belongs to another, as robber against traveler; or to ward off an evil, against someone who is feared; or out of envy, as the wretched envy the fortunate, or a man who has prospered envies the one he fears will pull level with him, or aches to see already level; or for the sheer pleasure of another's pain, like the spectators at the gladiators, or the people who mock and jeer at whomever they please. These are the chief heads of iniquity, and they sprout from the lust to rule, the lust to look, the lust to feel — from one of them, or two, or all three at once. And so men live evil lives against the three and the seven — that harp of ten strings, your Ten Commandments, O God most high, most sweet. But what can foul offenses do to you, who cannot be defiled? What violence can reach you, who cannot be harmed? What you avenge is what men do to themselves; for even when they sin against you, they are doing wicked harm to their own souls. Iniquity lies to itself — whether by corrupting and perverting its own nature, which you made and set in order; or by using permitted things without measure; or by burning for forbidden things, for that use which is against nature; or men stand guilty of raging against you in heart and word, kicking against the goad; or, bursting the fences of human society, they brazenly exult in private alliances and private feuds, as this or that tempts or offends them. And all of it happens when you are forsaken, O fountain of life, the one true creator and ruler of the universe — when, in private pride, some single false thing is loved in the part. So the way back to you is a humble devotion: and you cleanse us of our evil habit; you are merciful to the sins of those who confess; you hear the groaning of the shackled, and you loose us from the chains we made for ourselves — if only we stop lifting against you the horns of a false liberty, greedy to have more at the risk of losing everything, and loving our own private good more than you, the good of all things.

So too with acts of violence, where there is a wish to do harm, whether by insult or injury: done either for revenge, as one enemy against another; or for some gain belonging to someone else, as a robber against a traveler; or to escape some evil, as against a man one fears; or out of envy, as the less fortunate against the more fortunate, or a man doing well in some area against another whose mere equality he fears or resents; or for the sheer pleasure of another's pain, like the spectators at the gladiators, or the mockers and sneerers at other people. These are the chief headings of sin, and they spring from the lust of the flesh, or of the eye, or of power — singly, or two combined, or all three together. And so men live badly against the three, and the seven, that ten-stringed harp, your Ten Commandments, O God, most high and most sweet. But what foul offenses can there be against you, who cannot be defiled? What acts of violence against you, who cannot be harmed? What you avenge is what men commit against themselves, for even when they sin against you they are doing wickedness against their own souls, and their wrongdoing gives itself the lie — by corrupting and perverting the nature you created and ordered, whether through an excessive use of what is allowed, or by burning, in things not allowed, with a use against nature; or they are found guilty of raging with heart and tongue against you, kicking against the goads; or, bursting through the bounds of human fellowship, they brazenly delight in self-willed alliances or splits, depending on what they hope to gain or take offense at. And all this is done when you are forsaken, O Fountain of Life, the one true Maker and Ruler of the whole universe, and by self-willed pride some single false thing is picked out and loved. So it is by a humble devotion that we come back to you; you cleanse us of our bad habits, you are merciful to the sins of those who confess, you hear the groaning of the prisoner and free us from the chains we forged for ourselves — provided we do not raise against you the horns of a counterfeit freedom, losing everything through greed for more, by loving our own private good more than you, the Good of all.

And yet among these offenses of foulness and of violence and so many iniquities, there are the sins of people who are making progress. Those who judge rightly fault these sins by the rule of perfection, but praise the persons in hope of the harvest, as one praises the green blade for the grain to come. And there are certain acts that look like foul or violent offenses and are not sins at all, because they offend neither you, our Lord God, nor the bond of society: as when a man gathers things suited to his season of life for its use, and we cannot tell whether a lust for owning drove him; or when established authority punishes in order to correct, and we cannot tell whether a lust for hurting drove it. Many an act, then, that seems blameworthy in men's sight is approved by your testimony, and many an act praised by men is condemned with you as witness — because the look of the deed is one thing, the mind of the doer another, and the hidden hinge of the moment another still. But when you suddenly command something unaccustomed and unforeseen — even a thing you once forbade — and for the time being keep the reason of your command hidden, and it cuts against the compact of some human society, who can doubt that it must be done? — for the only human society that is just is the one that serves you. But blessed are those who know that it is you who command. For everything your servants did was done either to show what the present hour needed, or to foreshadow what was to come.

In among these offenses of foulness and violence, these many wrongs, there are the sins of men who, on the whole, are making progress — sins which those who judge rightly, by the standard of perfection, disapprove of, while still commending the persons, in hope of future fruit, as in the green blade of growing grain. And there are some acts that look like offenses of foulness or violence and yet are not sins, because they wrong neither you, our Lord God, nor human society: as when something fitting for a particular moment is acquired for the service of life — and we cannot tell whether out of a craving to possess; or when something is punished, for the sake of correction, by lawful authority — and we cannot tell whether out of a craving to do harm. So many an action disapproved of in men's eyes is, by your testimony, approved; and many an action praised by men is, with you as witness, condemned — because the look of the deed, and the mind of the doer, and the hidden need of the moment, each vary. But when you suddenly command some unaccustomed, unthought-of thing — yes, even something you once forbade, and even while you keep the reason for your command hidden for a time, and even though it goes against the agreement of some human society — who can doubt that it is to be done, since a human society is only just when it serves you? But blessed are those who know your commands! For all the things your servants did were done either to display something needed for the present, or to foreshadow things to come.

Ignorant of all this, I laughed at those holy servants and prophets of yours. And what did my laughing accomplish, except that you laughed at me? For little by little, step by step, I was drawn into absurdities like these: that a fig weeps when it is picked, and that its mother the tree sheds tears of milk. And yet if some Manichaean "saint" ate that fig — picked, naturally, by someone else's guilt, not his own — he would blend it into his guts and breathe angels out of it; better still, as he groaned and moaned in prayer, he would belch up particles of God — particles of the most high and true God that would have stayed locked in that fruit forever had they not been freed by the teeth and belly of one of the Elect. And I, wretch that I was, believed that more mercy was owed to the fruits of the earth than to the human beings for whose sake they grow. If a hungry man who was not a Manichee had asked for a bite, giving it to him would have seemed like sentencing that morsel to death.

Ignorant of all this, I mocked those holy servants and prophets of yours. And what did I gain by mocking them, except to be mocked by you, as I was insensibly drawn on, step by step, into such follies as believing that a fig tree weeps when its fruit is picked, that the tree, its mother, sheds milky tears? And yet, if some Manichaean "saint" had eaten that fig — picked by another man's sin, not his own — and digested it, he would breathe out angels from it; indeed, particles of divinity would burst out at every groan and sigh of his prayer, particles of the most high and true God that would have stayed trapped in that fig if they had not been set free by the teeth and belly of some "Elect" one. And I, poor fool, believed that more mercy was owed to the fruits of the earth than to the human beings they were created for. For if some hungry man who was not a Manichaean had asked for one, that mouthful would have been treated as good as condemned to death the moment it was handed over to him.

And you sent down your hand from on high and drew my soul out of that deep darkness — because my mother, your faithful one, wept to you for me, more than mothers weep over the bodies of dead children. By the faith and the spirit she had from you, she saw my death; and you heard her, Lord. You heard her, and did not despise her tears when they streamed down and watered the ground beneath her eyes in every place where she prayed. You heard her. For where else did that dream come from, by which you comforted her, so that she consented to live with me and share the same table in her house? She had begun to refuse it, turning away in loathing from the blasphemies of my error. In the dream she saw herself standing on a kind of wooden rule, and a radiant young man coming toward her, cheerful and smiling at her, while she grieved, crushed under her grief. He asked her the causes of her sorrow and her daily tears — asking, as such visitors do, to teach and not to learn — and she answered that she was mourning my perdition. Then he told her to rest easy, and bade her look and see: where she was, there I was also. And she looked, and saw me standing beside her on the same rule. Where did this come from, if not that your ears were bent to her heart? O good Omnipotent — you who care for each one of us as if you cared for that one alone, and care for all as if for one.

And you reached down your hand from above and drew my soul out of that deep darkness, while my mother, your faithful one, wept to you for me more than mothers weep over the bodily death of their children. For by the faith and the spirit she had from you, she saw the death I was lying in; and you heard her, O Lord. You heard her, and you did not despise her tears, when they streamed down and watered the ground beneath her eyes in every place where she prayed. Yes, you heard her. For where else did that dream come from, by which you comforted her, so that she agreed to live with me and to share the same table at home — something she had begun to refuse, shrinking back in horror and disgust from the blasphemies of my error? In the dream she saw herself standing on a wooden plank, and a young man coming toward her, radiant, cheerful, smiling at her, while she herself was grieving and crushed with grief. He asked her the reasons for her sorrow and her daily tears — asking, as such messengers do, in order to teach, not to be taught — and when she answered that she was mourning my ruin, he told her to be at peace, and bade her look and see "that where she was, there I was too." And when she looked, she saw me standing beside her on the same plank. Where did this come from, but that your ears were turned toward her heart, O Good and Almighty, who care for each one of us as if you cared for him alone, and for all as if each were the only one?

And where did this come from too? When she told me the vision, and I tried to twist it to mean that she should not despair of one day being what I was, she answered at once, without a moment's hesitation: "No. It was not said to me, Where he is, there you will be. It was said, Where you are, there he will be." I confess to you, Lord, what I remember of it — and I have told it often: that answer of yours through my wide-awake mother — that she was not rattled by my false reading, plausible as it was, and saw in an instant what had to be seen, which I certainly had not seen until she said it — even then that moved me more than the dream itself, in which the joy of that devout woman, to be fulfilled so long afterward, was foretold so long in advance to console her present anguish. For almost nine years followed, in which I wallowed in the mud of that deep pit and in the darkness of falsehood — often trying to rise, and slammed down all the harder. And through all that time, that chaste, devout, and sober widow — the kind you love — brisker now with hope, but no slacker in weeping and mourning, never stopped lamenting over me to you in every hour of her prayers. Her prayers came into your presence — and still you let me roll, and roll again, in that darkness.

And where did this come from, too: that when she had told me the vision, and I tried to twist it to mean that she should not despair of one day becoming what I was, she answered at once, without a moment's hesitation: "No. I was not told, 'where he is, there you will be,' but 'where you are, there he will be'"? I confess to you, Lord, that as far as I can remember — and I have often spoken of this — your answer through my waking mother moved me more than the dream itself: that she was not thrown off by the plausibility of my false reading, and so quickly saw what was there to be seen, which I certainly had not seen before she spoke. By that dream a joy was promised to a holy woman long before it came true, to console her in her present anguish; for almost nine years were still to pass in which I wallowed in the mud of that deep pit and the darkness of falsehood, often trying to rise and being slammed down all the harder. All that time, that chaste, devout, level-headed widow — the kind you love — now more cheered with hope but no less steady in her weeping and mourning, never stopped pleading your case for me to you at every hour of her prayers. And her prayers reached your presence, and still you let me go on rolling and re-rolling in that darkness.

Meanwhile you gave her another answer, one I remember — for I am passing over much, hurrying toward the things that most press me to confess to you, and much I have simply forgotten. You gave her another answer, then, through a priest of yours, a certain bishop reared in the church and well trained in your books. When that woman begged him to be so kind as to talk with me — to refute my errors, unteach me my evils and teach me what was good (he did this whenever he found people fit for it) — he refused, and wisely, as I understood afterwards. He answered that I was still unteachable: I was puffed up with the newness of that heresy, and had already needled plenty of untrained people with my little trick questions, as she herself had told him. "Leave him alone for a while," he said. "Only pray to the Lord for him. Reading on his own, he will discover what that error is, and how great its impiety." At the same time he told her how he himself, as a small boy, had been handed over to the Manichees by his mother, who had been led astray; how he had not only read but copied out nearly all their books; and how it had become plain to him, with no one arguing or persuading him, that the sect was to be fled — and he had fled it. When he had said this and she still would not be satisfied, but pressed him harder, pleading and weeping freely, that he would see me and talk with me, he lost patience a little at her insistence and said: "Go now, leave me — and as you live, it cannot be that the son of these tears should be lost." In her talks with me afterward she often recalled that she had received those words as if they had sounded from heaven.

Meanwhile you gave her another answer, which I remember — for I am passing over much, hurrying on to the things that press me harder to confess to you, and much I do not remember. You gave her, then, another answer, through a priest of yours, a certain bishop raised in your Church and well-read in your books. When this woman begged him to be so good as to talk with me, refute my errors, unteach me what was bad, and teach me what was good — which he was in the habit of doing when he found people ready for it — he refused, wisely, as I later understood.
