For he answered that I was still unteachable, swollen with the novelty of that heresy, and that I had already tangled a number of unskilled people with my tricky questions, as she herself had told him. "But leave him alone for a while," he said. "Only pray to God for him. By his own reading he will discover what that error is, and how great its impiety." At the same time he told her how he himself, as a small boy, had been handed over to the Manichees by his own seduced mother, and had not only read but copied out almost all their books, and had come to see — without anyone arguing or proving it to him — how thoroughly that sect was to be shunned, and had shunned it. But when he had said this and she still would not be satisfied, pressing him harder with her pleading and her many tears to see me and have it out with me, he grew a little impatient with her insistence and said: "Go your way, and God bless you. It cannot be that the son of these tears should perish." And she took this answer, as she often told me later in our talks together, as though it had sounded from heaven.

For nine years — from my nineteenth year to my twenty-eighth — we lived seduced and seducing, deceived and deceiving, through one desire after another: openly, by way of the studies they call liberal; secretly, under a false name of religion. Proud on the one side, superstitious on the other, empty everywhere. On the one hand we chased the hollowness of popular glory, right down to applause in the theater, prize poems, contests for garlands of hay, the trash of the shows, the appetites that keep no measure. On the other we wanted to be scrubbed clean of all that filth by carrying food to the people called ‘elect’ and ‘holy,’ so that in the workshop of their own stomachs they could manufacture angels and gods for us — the gods who were supposed to set us free. That is what I pursued; that is what I practiced with my friends — friends deceived by me, and deceived along with me. Let the arrogant laugh at me, and all those you have not yet struck down and broken for their own healing, my God: I will still confess my shame to you, and make it your praise. Let me do it, I beg you; give me the grace to walk back, in present memory, around the old loops of my wandering, and to offer you a sacrifice of rejoicing. For what am I to myself, without you, but a guide leading myself off the cliff? And what am I even at my best but a creature suckling your milk, feeding on you, the food that never spoils? And what kind of man is any man, seeing that he is a man? Let the strong and the powerful laugh at us, then. We are weak and poor, and we will confess to you.

For nine years — from my nineteenth year to my twenty-eighth — we lived seduced and seducing, deceived and deceiving, in every kind of lust. Openly, by way of the studies they call liberal; in secret, under the cover of a religion that lied about its own name. On the one side proud, on the other superstitious, and on every side empty. On the one side, chasing the emptiness of popular acclaim, right down to the applause of the theater, the prizes for poems, the contests for crowns of grass, the foolishness of the shows, the runaway appetites. On the other side, hoping to be cleansed of these very stains by carrying food to those who were called the "elect" and the "holy," so that in the workshop of their stomachs they might forge for us the angels and gods who were to cleanse us. These were the things I went after, and practiced with my friends — friends deceived by me, and along with me. Let the arrogant laugh at me, and all who have never yet been struck down and laid low by you, my God, for the saving of their souls; still I will confess to you my own shame, to your praise. Bear with me, I beg you, and give me grace to go back over the wanderings of my past life in my present memory, and to offer you the sacrifice of thanksgiving. For what am I to myself without you, but a guide steering my own way to ruin? Or what am I even at my best, but an infant sucking the milk you give, feeding on you, the food that does not perish? And what is any man, seeing he is only a man? Let the strong and the mighty laugh at us; let us, poor and needy, confess to you.

In those years I taught rhetoric. Defeated by greed, I sold the kind of speech that wins. Even so — Lord, you know this — I preferred to have good students, as students are reckoned good, and without deceit I taught them deceit: not the kind to be used against an innocent man’s life, though sometimes for a guilty man’s. And you, God, watching from far off, saw my good faith stagger on that slippery ground and throw off a few sparks through all the smoke — the good faith I kept in teaching men who loved emptiness and went hunting for lies, I their fellow traveler. In those years I had a woman. She was not mine in what is called lawful marriage; a restless passion, empty of prudence, had found her out. But she was the only one, and I kept faith with her bed. And with her I learned firsthand the distance between the covenant of marriage, entered for the sake of children, and the bargain of a lustful love — where a child is born against the parents’ wishes, though once born, it makes them love it.

In those years I taught rhetoric, and, beaten down by greed, I put up for sale a skill in speech meant for beating others down. Yet I preferred — you know it, Lord — honest students, or those reckoned honest; and these, without any trickery, I taught the tricks of the trade, not to be used against the life of an innocent man, though sometimes to be used for the life of a guilty one. And you, God, watched me from far off, stumbling along that slippery road, and out of all that smoke sending up a few sparks of good faith, which I showed in guiding those who loved vanity and went looking for lies — I, their companion in it. In those years I had a woman, not one joined to me in what is called lawful marriage, but one my reckless and unthinking passion had hunted out. Yet she was the only one, and I stayed faithful even to her; and in her I learned for myself the difference between the restraint of the marriage covenant, entered into for the sake of children, and the bargain of a lustful love, where children are born against their parents' will — though, once born, they force you to love them.

I remember, too, that when I had decided to enter a competition for theatrical verse, some soothsayer sent word to ask what I would pay him to win it. I loathed and detested those filthy rites, and I answered that even if the garland were made of gold that never perishes, I would not let a fly be killed to win it — for he was going to kill living creatures in his sacrifices, and by those honors, it seemed, to recruit demons to back me. But even this evil I refused not out of any pure love for you, God of my heart. I did not know how to love you; I did not know how to conceive of anything beyond material light. And a soul that sighs after fictions like those — isn’t it breaking faith with you, trusting in shams, feeding the winds? I would not have sacrifices offered to demons on my behalf; yet by my superstition I was offering myself to them all the while. For what else is ‘feeding the winds’ but feeding the demons themselves — becoming, by our straying, their entertainment and their joke?

I remember, too, that when I had decided to compete for a prize in the theater, some sorcerer asked me what I would pay him to win. But I loathed and shrank from those foul rites, and I answered that even if the crown were of imperishable gold, I would not let a single fly be killed to win it for me. For he was to slaughter living creatures in his sacrifices, and by those offerings to invite the demons to favor me. But even this evil I refused, and not out of any pure love for you, God of my heart — for I did not know how to love you, I who could conceive of nothing beyond a brightness of the body. And does not a soul that sighs after such fictions commit adultery against you, trust in things that are not real, and feed the wind? So I would not, it seems, have sacrifices offered to demons on my behalf — while by that very superstition I was sacrificing myself to them. For what is it to feed the wind, but to feed them — to become, by going astray, their pleasure and their sport?

But those frauds they call astrologers I consulted without a scruple, because they seemed to use no sacrifice and to aim no prayer at any spirit for their divinations. Christian and true devotion rejects that art too, and condemns it — consistently. For it is a good thing to confess to you and to say, Have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you; not to twist your mercy into a license to sin, but to remember the Lord’s words: Look, you have been made well. Sin no more, or something worse may happen to you. All that healthy counsel the astrologers labor to kill, telling us, ‘The cause of your sin is fixed, inescapably, in the sky,’ and ‘Venus did this, or Saturn, or Mars’ — so that man, this flesh and blood, this proud rot, might carry no blame, while the blame lands on the maker and orderer of heaven and the stars. And who is that but our God — the very sweetness and wellspring of justice, who repays each of us according to our works, and does not despise a broken and contrite heart?

So I went without scruple to consult those impostors they call astrologers, because they seemed to offer no sacrifice and to pray to no spirit for their fortune-telling — though true Christian devotion rightly rejects and condemns that art as well. For it is good to confess to you and to say, Have mercy on me, heal my soul, for I have sinned against you; and not to take your mercy as a license to sin, but to remember the Lord's words: See, you are made whole, sin no more, in case something worse should happen to you. All this saving counsel the astrologers labor to undo, when they say, "The cause of your sin is fixed beyond escape in the heavens," and "This was the work of Venus, or Saturn, or Mars" — so that a man, mere flesh and blood and rotting pride, should bear no blame, and the blame fall instead on the Maker and Orderer of heaven and the stars. And who is that but our God, the very sweetness and well-spring of righteousness, who pays back each man according to his deeds, and will not despise a broken and contrite heart?

There was in those days a shrewd man, deeply skilled in medicine and famous in it, who as proconsul had set that contest garland, with his own hand, on my head — my sick head, though he did not set it there as a doctor. For that disease you alone cure — you who resist the proud and give grace to the humble. But did you fail me even through that old man? Did you leave off healing my soul? I came to know him better, and I hung steadily, intently, on what he said; the words were plain, but the talk was quick, alive, and serious. When he gathered from my conversation that I was devoted to the books of the horoscope-casters, he advised me — kindly, like a father — to throw them away, and not to waste on that nonsense the care and effort that useful things need. He had studied the art himself, he said, in his early years, wanting to make it his living: if he had understood Hippocrates, he could certainly have understood that. And yet he had given it up and taken to medicine for one reason only — he had found it utterly false, and, being a serious man, he would not earn his bread by fooling people. ‘But you have rhetoric to live on,’ he said, ‘so you follow this thing by free choice, not by necessity. All the more reason, then, to believe me about it, since I worked to master it so completely that I meant to live by it alone.’ I asked him how it was, then, that so many true things were foretold by it. He answered, as well as anyone could, that the force of chance, scattered through the whole order of things, brought it about. If a man opens the pages of some poet at random — a poet singing and thinking of something else entirely — a line often falls out that fits his present business wonderfully. So it was no marvel, he said, if from the soul of a man, by some higher instinct and without the soul’s knowing what happens inside it, an answer should come out that chimes with the asker’s business and doings — by luck, not by art.

In those days there was a wise man, very skilled and famous in medicine, who, in his office as proconsul, had with his own hand set the winner's crown on my disordered head — though not as a physician, for this sickness of mine is one that you alone can cure, you who resist the proud and give grace to the humble. And yet did you fail me even through that old man, or hold back from healing my soul? For I came to know him better, and hung steadily and closely on his words, which, though plainly spoken, were vivid and alive and earnest. When he gathered from my talk that I was given to the books of the horoscope-casters, he advised me, kindly, like a father, to throw them away, and not to waste on these empty things the care and effort that real and useful matters need. He told me that in his own early years he had studied that art with a mind to make it the trade he would live by; that since he had understood Hippocrates, he could easily have mastered this too — and yet he had given it up and turned to medicine, for no other reason than that he found it utterly false, and being a serious man, he would not earn his bread by fooling people. "But you," he said, "have rhetoric to support yourself by, so you follow this thing by free choice, not by need. All the more, then, should you take my word for it, since I worked to master it so thoroughly as to make my whole living from it." When I asked him how it was, then, that many true things were foretold by it, he gave me the best answer he could: that it was the power of chance, spread through the whole order of things, that brought this about. For if a man, opening at random the pages of some poet who had been singing and thinking of something else entirely, often lights on a verse that fits his present situation wonderfully well — it should be no wonder, he said, if out of the human soul, by some higher prompting it knows nothing of, an answer comes up, by luck and not by art, that matches the affairs and doings of the one who asks.

That much you procured for me from him, or through him, and you traced into my memory what I would later search out for myself. But at the time, neither he nor my dearest Nebridius — a young man singularly good and singularly clean of heart, who laughed at the whole business of divination — could persuade me to throw it away. The authority of the authors still weighed more with me, and I had not yet found the certain proof I was looking for: proof that would show, past all doubt, that when these consulted men said true things, it was chance speaking, not the art of the star-readers.

And so, either from him or through him, you conveyed this to me and traced it in my memory, for me to look into later for myself. But at that time neither he, nor my dearest Nebridius — a young man wholly good and full of holy reverence, who laughed at the whole business of divination — could talk me into casting it aside. The authority of the writers still swayed me more, and as yet I had found no sure proof, the kind I was looking for, that would show beyond all doubt that whatever those consultations foretold truly came about by chance and not by the stargazers' art.

In those years — the time when I first began to teach in the town where I was born — I had made a friend, too dear to me, my own age, sharing my studies, flowering with me in the first flower of young manhood. He had grown up with me as a boy; we had gone to school together, played together. But he was not yet my friend the way he later became — and even then, not the way true friendship is. For there is no true friendship unless you glue it together, between people who hold fast to you, with the love poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who is given to us. Still, it was something almost too sweet, ripened in the heat of shared enthusiasms. I had even bent him away from the true faith — which as a youth he had never taken in deeply or thoroughly — toward those superstitious, soul-destroying fables my mother wept over in me. With me, now, the man wandered in his mind; and my soul could not do without him. But look: you were right behind your runaways — God of vengeance and fountain of mercies at once, who turn us back to you by astonishing means — look: you took the man out of this life when he had scarcely filled one whole year of a friendship sweeter to me than every sweetness of that life of mine.

In those years, when I first began to teach rhetoric in my home town, I had made a friend who was too dear to me — drawn together by a shared love of the same things — a man of my own age, and, like me, in the first opening flower of youth. He had grown up alongside me from childhood; we had gone to school together and played together. But he was not yet my friend in the way he later became, and even then it was not friendship in its truest sense; for true friendship cannot exist unless you bind it fast among those who cling to you, by the love poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who is given to us. Still, it was sweet to me, all too sweet, ripened in the warmth of shared studies. For I had turned him aside from the true faith — which, being young, he had not soundly and deeply taken in — and led him into those superstitious and ruinous fables over which my mother wept for me. With me he now wandered in his mind, and my soul could not be without him. But you were close behind your runaways, at once a God of vengeance and a fountain of mercy, turning us back to yourself by ways we could not have foreseen. You took that man out of this life when he had barely rounded out a single year of friendship with me — a friendship sweeter to me than all the sweetness of my whole life.

Who can count up all your praises — even those a single man has felt in his single self? What did you do then, my God? How unsearchable is the abyss of your judgments! For a long time he lay senseless in a death-sweat, burnt through with fever, and when they gave up hope for him, he was baptized — knowing nothing of it. I hardly cared. I took it for granted that his soul would keep what it had learned from me, and not whatever had been done to a body that could not feel it. It turned out very differently: he rallied; he was saved. And the moment I could talk with him — which was the moment he could talk, for I never left him, and we hung on each other far too much — I tried joking with him, expecting him to laugh with me about that baptism he had received while absent in mind and sense, though by now he had learned that he had received it. He recoiled from me as if from an enemy. With a sudden, startling freedom he told me that if I wished to stay his friend, I would stop saying such things to him. I was astonished; I was shaken; and I buried every feeling I had until he should be well again, strong enough for me to handle as I pleased. But he was snatched away from my madness, to be kept safe with you for my consolation. A few days later, while I was away, the fever came back, and he died.

Who can tell all your praises that he has known in his own one self? What did you do then, my God, and how unsearchable is the deep abyss of your judgments? For he was long and gravely sick with a fever, and lay senseless in a death-sweat. When they gave up hope of his recovery, he was baptized while unconscious — and I gave it little thought, taking it for granted that his soul would hold on to what it had received from me rather than to what had been done to his unknowing body. But it turned out far otherwise. For he rallied and was restored to health; and the moment I could speak with him — which was as soon as he was able, since I never left his side, and we leaned on each other too heavily — I tried to make a joke of it, as though he would laugh with me at the baptism he had been given while utterly absent in mind and feeling, but which he had now learned that he had received. But he drew back from me as if I were an enemy, and with a sudden, astonishing independence he told me, as I valued his friendship, never to speak to him like that again. Dumbfounded and shaken, I held back all I felt until he should grow stronger, well enough in health for me to handle him as I pleased. But he was snatched away from my madness, to be kept safe with you for my consolation. A few days later, while I was away, the fever returned, and he died.

At that grief my heart went black. Everything I looked at was death. My own country was a torture to me, my father’s house a strange unhappiness; and everything I had shared with him became, without him, one immense torment. My eyes looked for him everywhere, and he was not given to them. I hated all places because he was not in them — because they could no longer tell me, ‘Look, he’s coming,’ as they could when he was alive and only away. I had become a great question to myself. I kept asking my soul why it was sad, and why it troubled me so deeply, and it had no answer to give me. And if I said, ‘Hope in God,’ it rightly refused to obey — because the man it had lost, that dearest man, was truer and better than the phantasm it was being ordered to hope in. Only weeping was sweet to me, and tears took my friend’s place among the delights of my heart.

At this grief the whole of my heart went dark, and everything I looked at was death. My home town was a torment to me, and my father's house a strange misery; and everything I had shared with him became, without him, an excruciating torture. My eyes searched for him everywhere, and he was not given to them; and I hated every place, because none of them held him, nor could any of them say to me now, "Look, he is coming," as they could when he was alive and only away. I had become a great riddle to myself, and I kept asking my soul why it was so downcast and why it disturbed me so. But it had no answer to give me. And if I said, Trust in God, it rightly would not, for the friend it had lost, dear as he was, was a truer and better thing than the phantom it was being told to trust. Only weeping was sweet to me, for it had taken the place of my friend in the dearest of my affections.

And now, Lord, all that has passed, and time has softened my wound. May I hear from you, who are Truth — may I put the ear of my heart against your mouth — and will you tell me why weeping is sweet to the miserable? Have you, though present everywhere, flung our misery far away from you? You abide in yourself, while we are rolled through trial after trial. And yet, if we could not cry into your ears, nothing of our hope would be left at all. How is it, then, that sweet fruit is picked from life’s bitterness — from mourning, weeping, sighing, complaint? Is the sweetness this, that we hope you hear? In prayer, yes, rightly so: prayer carries the longing to reach you. But in grief for a lost thing — in the sorrow that had buried me then? I had no hope he would come back to life; my tears were not begging for that. I simply grieved, and wept: I was miserable, and I had lost my joy. Or is weeping a bitter thing after all, which pleases us only out of revulsion — only in the moment we recoil from the things we used to enjoy?

And now, Lord, these things are long past, and time has eased my wound. May I learn from you, who are Truth, and bring the ear of my heart close to your mouth, that you may tell me why weeping is sweet to the wretched. Have you, present everywhere, cast our misery far from yourself? You remain at rest in yourself, while we are tossed about from trial to trial. And yet, unless we mourned in your ears, no hope would be left to us. So where does this sweet fruit come from, gathered out of the bitterness of life, out of groaning and tears and sighing and complaint? Is it sweet because we hope you hear us? That is true of prayer, since prayer is a longing to come near you. But is it also true of grief over a thing lost, of the sorrow that overwhelmed me then? For I had no hope he would come back to life, nor was that what my tears asked for; I only wept and grieved. For I was wretched, and I had lost my joy. Or is weeping really a bitter thing after all, sweet to us only in our loathing of the things we used to enjoy, when now we shrink back from them?

But why am I saying all this? Now is no time for questions; now is the time to confess to you. I was miserable, and every soul is miserable that is tied by friendship to mortal things: it is shredded when it loses them, and only then does it feel the misery that was in it even before it lost them. That is how it was with me then. I wept with utter bitterness, and I rested in the bitterness. So miserable was I that I held that miserable life dearer than my friend himself. However much I might have wished to change it, I was less willing to lose it than to lose him — I doubt I would have given it even for him, in the way tradition tells (if it is not invention) of Orestes and Pylades, who wanted to die for each other, or die together, since to them not living together was worse than dying. In me a feeling had risen up quite contrary to that, and I could not explain it: a crushing weariness of being alive, and at the same time a fear of dying. I believe that the more I loved him, the more I hated death, which had taken him from me, and the more I feared it, as the most savage of enemies; and I imagined it would suddenly devour every human being, since it had been able to devour him. That is how it was with me — I remember. Look at my heart, my God; look inside it and see, for I do remember, O my Hope, you who wash me clean of the uncleanness of such affections, turning my eyes toward you, pulling my feet out of the snare. For I marveled that the rest of the mortals went on living, when the man I had loved as though he would never die was dead; and I marveled more that I, his other self, was alive when he was dead. Someone once called his friend ‘the half of my soul,’ and said it well. For I felt that my soul and his soul had been one soul in two bodies; and that is why living horrified me — I refused to live as a half. And that, perhaps, is why I was afraid to die: so that the man I had loved so much would not die entirely.

But why do I talk of these things? This is no time to ask questions; it is time to confess to you. I was wretched, and wretched is every soul bound fast to things that must perish. It is torn apart when it loses them, and only then feels the wretchedness it was already in before it lost them. So it was then with me. I wept most bitterly, and found my rest in bitterness. So wretched was I that I held that wretched life of mine dearer than my friend. For though I would gladly have changed that life, I was even more unwilling to lose it than to lose him; in fact I do not know whether I would have given it up even for him — as the old story tells (whether true or made up) of Pylades and Orestes, who would gladly have died for each other, or both together, since for them not to live together was worse than death. But some strange feeling had risen in me, the very opposite of theirs: at one and the same time I loathed to be alive and was terrified to die. I suppose the more I loved him, the more I hated and feared, as my cruelest enemy, the death that had robbed me of him; and I imagined that death would suddenly devour all human beings, since it had been able to take him. Yes, that is how it was with me, I remember it. Look into my heart, my God, look and see right into me; for I remember it well, my Hope, you who cleanse me of the filth of such feelings, turning my eyes toward yourself and pulling my feet out of the snare. For I was amazed that other mortals went on living, since the one I had loved as though he would never die was dead; and I was more amazed still that I, who had been a second self to him, could go on living while he was gone. Well did someone say of his friend, "You, the half of my soul" — for I felt that my soul and his had been one soul in two bodies; and so my life was a horror to me, because I would not live as a half. And perhaps that is also why I feared to die: so that he whom I had loved so much would not then be wholly dead.

What madness — not to know how to love human beings as human beings! What a fool, to take the human lot with so little measure! That was what I was then. So I seethed, I sighed, I wept, I was in turmoil; there was no rest, and no counsel. For I was carrying my soul around cut open and bloodied — a soul that could not stand being carried by me — and I could find nowhere to lay it down. Not in pleasant groves; not in games and songs; not in sweet-scented places; not in elegant banquets; not in the pleasures of bedroom and bed; not, finally, in books or in poetry would it rest. Everything looked ghastly, even light itself; and whatever was not what he had been was repellent and hateful — all of it, except groaning and tears. In those alone was there a little relief; and whenever my soul was taken from them, a huge freight of misery weighed me down. To you, Lord, it should have been lifted, for you to lighten it. I knew that. But I neither would nor could — all the less because, when I thought of you, you were nothing solid or firm to me. It was not you at all: my god was an empty phantasm, my own error. If I tried to lay my burden down on it, to let it rest, it slid through the void and came crashing back down on me; and I had been left to myself an unhappy place, where I could not stay and from which I could not get away. For where could my heart run from my heart? Where could I run from myself? Where would I not follow myself? And yet I fled my own country. My eyes would look for him less, I thought, in places where they were not used to seeing him. And so I left the town of Thagaste and came to Carthage.

O madness, that does not know how to love human beings as human beings! O foolish man that I then was, raging against the lot that belongs to every man! So I fretted and sighed and wept; I was torn to pieces; I had neither rest nor good sense. For I was carrying my soul, broken and bleeding, and it could not bear to be carried by me — yet where to set it down, I could not find. Not in cool groves, not in games and song, not in sweet-scented places, not in fine banquets, not in the pleasures of the bed and the couch, not, in the end, in books or in poetry, could it find its rest. Everything was hideous to me, even the light itself; whatever was not what he was, was loathsome and hateful to me — except for groaning and tears, for in those alone I found a little relief. But the moment my soul was drawn away from them, a huge weight of misery pressed me down. To you, Lord, it ought to have been lifted up, for you to lighten; I knew it, but I neither could nor would. The more so since, when I thought of you, you were nothing solid or substantial to me. For it was not you, but an empty phantom, and my error was my god. If I tried to set my load down there for rest, it slid through the emptiness and came rushing back down on me; and I remained to myself an unhappy place where I could neither stay nor leave. For where could my heart flee from my heart? Where could I flee from myself? Where would I not follow myself? And yet I fled my home town, so that my eyes would look for him less in the places where they were not used to seeing him. And so I came from Thagaste to Carthage.

Time is not idle; it does not roll uselessly over our senses. It works strange operations in the mind. Look — the days came and went, one after another, and coming and going they slipped other hopes into me, other memories, and little by little they patched me back together out of the old kinds of pleasure. To those my grief gave way. But what followed was not other griefs; it was the causes of other griefs. For why had that grief gone into me so easily and so deep, if not because I had poured out my soul on sand, loving a man who was going to die as if he would never die? What restored me most, what remade me, was the comfort of other friends — friends with whom I loved what I loved instead of you. And that was one enormous fable, one long-drawn lie, and its adulterous friction was corrupting our minds, whose itch was in the ears. But that fable would not die for me, however many of my friends died. There were other things in friendship that took a deeper hold on the mind: to talk together and laugh together; to trade kindnesses turn by turn; to read sweet-tongued books together; to be silly together and serious together; to disagree now and then without hatred, the way a man may disagree with himself, and to find those rarest disagreements the seasoning of countless agreements; to teach one another something, or learn something from one another; to miss the absent with impatience, and to welcome them home with joy. These signs, and a thousand like them, rising from the hearts of people who love and are loved in return — spoken by the mouth, the tongue, the eyes, and countless gestures of pleasure — were the kindling that fused our souls together and made, out of many, one.

Time takes no time off; it does not roll idly by. Through our senses it works strange changes on the mind. It came and went, day after day, and by its coming and going it planted other imaginings and other memories in me, and little by little patched me up again with the old kinds of delight, before which my grief gave way. Yet what followed was not other griefs, exactly, but the causes of other griefs. For why had that first grief pierced so easily to the very depths of me, except that I had poured out my soul upon the sand, in loving one who must die as though he would never die? What restored and revived me most was the consolation of other friends, with whom I loved what I was loving in the place of you — and this was one great fable, one drawn-out lie, whose adulterous coaxing kept defiling our soul as it lay itching in our ears. Yet that fable did not die in me, however often one of my friends died. There were other things in them that took hold of my mind even more: to talk and laugh together; to do each other kindnesses by turns; to read sweet books together; to fool around together and to be serious together; to disagree at times without any ill will, as a man might with his own self, and by the very rareness of such disagreements to give a flavor to our far more frequent agreements; to teach one another and to learn from one another; to miss the absent with longing, and to welcome them back with joy. By these and the like signs, breaking out of the hearts of those who loved and were loved in return — through the face, the tongue, the eyes, a thousand pleasing gestures — our souls were kindled together as if by so much fuel, and out of many were made one.

That is what we love in friends — and we love it so, that a man’s conscience convicts itself if he fails to love the one who loves him, or to love back the one who loved him first, asking of the other’s person nothing but the signs of his goodwill. From this comes the mourning when a friend dies: the darkness of sorrows; the heart soaked through, its sweetness turned to bitterness; and, from the lost life of the dying, the death of the living. Blessed is the one who loves you — who loves his friend in you, and his enemy for your sake. For he alone loses no one dear to him, to whom everyone is dear in the One who is never lost. And who is that but our God — the God who made heaven and earth, and who fills them, since it was by filling them that he made them? No one loses you who does not let you go. And the one who lets you go — where does he go? Where can he run, except from you at peace with him to you set against him? For where will he not find your law waiting in his own punishment? And your law is truth, and truth is you.

This is what is loved in friends, and so loved that a man's own conscience condemns him if he does not love one who loves him back, or does not love in return one who loves him, asking nothing of that other but signs of his love. From this comes the mourning when someone dies, the darkening of sorrows, the heart steeped in tears, all sweetness turned to bitterness; and at the death of the dying, the death of the living. Blessed is the one who loves you, and loves his friend in you, and his enemy for your sake. For he alone loses no one dear to him, to whom all are dear in the One who cannot be lost. And who is that but our God, the God who made heaven and earth and fills them — for by filling them he made them? You no one loses, unless he leaves you. And whoever leaves you, where does he go, where does he flee, but from you in your favor to you in your displeasure? For where does he not run into your law, in his own punishment? And your law is truth, and you are truth.

Turn us, God of hosts; show us your face, and we will be saved. For wherever the soul of man turns, it is nailed to sorrows unless it turns to you — nailed even when it fastens on beautiful things. And those beautiful things, outside you and outside the soul, would not exist at all unless they came from you. They rise and they set: rising, they begin, as it were, to be; they grow, toward their completion; completed, they age, and they perish. Not everything ages — but everything perishes. So when they rise and reach toward being, the faster they grow into being, the harder they hurry toward not-being. That is their law. You gave them that much, because they are pieces of a whole whose pieces do not all exist at once: by giving way and taking over, all of them together act out the whole universe of which they are pieces. Our own speech is carried out the same way, through signs that sound: there is no whole sentence unless each word passes away, once it has sounded its part, so that the next may take its place. For all of this let my soul praise you, God, creator of all — but let it not be stuck fast to these things by the glue of love, through the senses of the body. For they go where they were always going: toward not-being; and they tear the soul with pestilent longings, because the soul wants to be — and it loves to rest in the things it loves. But in them there is nowhere to rest, because they do not stay. They flee: and who can follow them with the senses of the flesh? Who can grasp them even while they are near? The sense of the flesh is slow, because it is the sense of the flesh: that is its boundary. It is enough for what it was made for; it is not enough to hold things as they run their course from their appointed start to their appointed end. For in your Word, through whom they are created, they hear their orders: ‘Start here; end here.’

Turn us back, God of hosts, show us your face, and we shall be whole. For wherever the human soul turns itself, unless it turns toward you, it is nailed fast to sorrows — even when it is nailed to beautiful things. And yet those things, outside you and outside the soul, would not exist at all unless they came from you. They rise and set; by rising, they begin, as it were, to be; they grow toward their fullness, and having reached it they grow old and wither; and not all reach old age, but all wither. So, when they rise and reach toward being, the faster they grow toward being, the faster they hurry toward not-being. This is the law of them. So much you have granted them, because they are parts of things that do not exist all at once, but by passing away and following one another make up the whole universe of which they are the parts. And this is how our own speech is completed by audible signs: it would never be a whole unless each word, having sounded its part, passed away so that another could follow. Let my soul praise you out of all these things, God, Maker of all; but let my soul not be stuck fast to these things by the glue of love, through the body's senses. For they go where they were always going — into not-being — and they tear the soul apart with sick longings, because the soul wants to be, and loves to rest in what it loves. But in these things there is no place of rest, for they do not stay; they flee; and who can follow them with the senses of the flesh? Or who can grasp them even when they are close at hand? For the flesh's sense is slow, because it is the sense of the flesh, and there it has its limit. It is enough for the purpose it was made for, but it is not enough to hold things back as they run their course from their appointed beginning to their appointed end. For in your Word, by which they are created, they hear the decree: "From here, and no farther."

Don’t be empty, my soul; don’t let the ear of your heart go deaf with the racket of your own emptiness. Listen — you too. The Word himself is crying out for you to return, and there is the place of rest that cannot be disturbed, where love is not abandoned unless it abandons first. Look: these things pass away so that other things may take their place, so that this lowest order of the universe may be complete in all its parts. ‘But do I go anywhere?’ says the Word of God. Fix your dwelling there. Whatever you have from there, my soul, place it there in trust — now at least, tired out as you are with deceptions. Entrust to the Truth whatever the truth has given you, and you will lose nothing. The rot in you will flower again; all your diseases will be healed; all in you that drains away will be formed anew, made new, bound close around you. It will not drop you where it descends, but will stand with you, and hold, before the God who stands and holds forever.

Do not be foolish, my soul, and do not let the ear of your heart be deafened by the uproar of your folly. Listen, you too. The Word itself calls you back; and there is the place of rest that nothing can disturb, where love is not abandoned unless it abandons first. Look — these things pass away so that others may take their place, and so this lower universe may be made complete in all its parts. "But do I go anywhere?" says the Word of God. Fix your dwelling there; entrust to it whatever you have from it, my soul, weary at last as you are of your empty pursuits. Entrust to Truth whatever you have from the Truth, and you will lose nothing; and what has decayed in you will bloom again, and all your sicknesses be healed; what is mortal in you will be made over and made new, bound fast around you. These things will not drag you down with them where they themselves go down; rather, they will stand firm with you and last forever before God, who himself stands firm and lasts forever.

Why keep following your own flesh, turned backwards? Turn around, and let it follow you. Whatever you sense through the flesh is a part; the whole to which the parts belong, you do not know — yet the parts delight you. But if the flesh’s senses were fit to take in the whole — if they had not, for your punishment, been justly confined to a part of it — you would want whatever exists in the present moment to pass away, so that the whole could please you more. When we speak, you hear us through that same sense of flesh — and you certainly do not want the syllables to stand still; you want them to fly past, so that others can come and you can hear the whole. That is how it always is, when one thing is made of many parts that do not exist all at once: all of it, could all of it be perceived, would please more than the pieces do. But better by far than all of it is he who made all of it: he is our God. And he does not pass away, because there is nothing to take his place.

Why, then, be twisted and follow your flesh? Let it instead be turned around and follow you. Whatever you sense through it, you sense only in part; and the whole, of which these are parts, you do not know — and yet they delight you. But if the sense of your flesh were able to take in the whole, and had not, for your punishment, been justly held to a part of the whole, you would wish that whatever exists at this present moment would pass on, so that the whole might please you all the more. For what we speak, you also hear by this same sense of the flesh; yet you would not want the syllables to stand still, but to fly away, so that others may come and you may hear the whole. And so it always is: whenever one thing is made up of many that do not all exist together, all of them together would please more than they do one by one — if only all of them could be taken in together. But far better than all these is the One who made them all; and he is our God, and he does not pass away, for nothing comes after him to take his place.

If bodies please you, praise God for them and turn your love back around, onto their maker — lest in the things that please you, you displease. If souls please you, love them in God; for they too are changeable, and only fixed in him do they stand firm — otherwise they would go, and be gone. Love them in him, then, and sweep up with you to him every soul you can, and say to them: ‘Let us love him — let us love him! He made these things, and he is not far away. He did not make them and then leave; they are from him, and they are in him. Look where he is: he is wherever truth is savored. He is inmost in the heart itself — but the heart has strayed from him. Come back to your heart, you deserters, and hold fast to the one who made you. Stand with him, and you will stand. Rest in him, and you will be at rest. Where are you going, over such rough ground? Where are you going? The good you love is from him — and turned toward him it is good and it is sweet; but it will turn bitter, and justly so, because whatever is from him is loved unjustly if he is deserted for its sake. What do you want, walking on and on down these hard and weary roads? There is no rest where you are seeking it. Seek what you seek — but it is not where you are seeking it. You seek a happy life in the country of death, and it is not there. How can there be a happy life where there is no life at all?

If bodies please you, praise God on their account, and turn your love back upon their Maker, in case, through the things that please you, you should be displeasing to him. If souls please you, let them be loved in God; for they too are changeable, and only in him are they firmly fixed — otherwise they would pass on and pass away. Let them, then, be loved in him; and carry off to him along with you whatever souls you can, and say to them: "Let us love him, let us love him. He made these things, and he is not far off. For he did not make them and then go away; they come from him and are in him. Look, there he is, wherever truth is loved. He is deep within the heart, but the heart has strayed away from him. Return to your heart, you sinners, and cling fast to him who made you. Stand with him, and you will stand firm. Rest in him, and you will be at rest. Where are you going, by these rough roads? Where are you going? The good that you love is from him; but it is good and pleasant only by reference to him, and justly will it turn bitter, because anything that comes from him is unjustly loved if he is forsaken for it. Why, then, do you keep on walking these hard and weary roads? There is no rest where you are looking for it. Seek what you seek, but it is not there where you seek it. You are looking for a happy life in the land of death; it is not there. For how can there be a happy life where there is no life at all?

‘But our true Life came down here and carried our death away, and killed it out of the abundance of his own life. And he thundered, calling us to return from here to him — back into that secret place from which he first came forth to us: into the Virgin’s womb itself, where the human creature was wedded to him, mortal flesh, that it might not be mortal forever; and from there, like a bridegroom coming out of his chamber, he exulted like a champion to run his race. He did not linger — he ran, shouting by his words, his deeds, his death, his life, his descent, his ascent, shouting to us to return to him. And he withdrew from our eyes, so that we would return into our own hearts and find him there. He went away — and look: he is here. He would not stay long with us, and he has not left us. He went back to the place he never departed from, because the world was made through him; and he was in this world, and he came into this world to save sinners. To him my soul confesses, and he heals it, because it sinned against him. You sons of men, how long will you be so heavy of heart? Even now, after Life itself has come down to you, will you not climb up and live? But where can you climb, when you are already high, with your mouths set against the heavens? Come down, so that you can climb — climb, this time, to God. For you fell when you climbed against him.’ Tell them this, my soul, and let them weep in the valley of weeping — and so carry them up with you to God; for it is by his Spirit that you say this to them, if you say it burning with the fire of love.

"But our true Life came down here, and bore our death, and killed it out of the abundance of his own life. And he thundered, calling out to us to come back from here to him, into that hidden place from which he came out to us — first into the Virgin's womb, where he wedded himself to our human nature, our mortal flesh, so that it would not be mortal forever; and from there, like a bridegroom coming out of his chamber, he rejoiced as a strong man to run his course. For he did not linger, but ran, calling aloud by words, by deeds, by death, by life, by descent, by ascent, crying out to us to come back to him. And he passed out of our sight, so that we might return into our heart and find him there. For he went away, and look — he is here. He would not stay long with us, and yet he did not leave us; for he went away to the place he had never left, because the world was made through him. He was in this world, and into this world he came to save sinners — to whom my soul confesses, and he heals it, for it has sinned against him. O sons of men, how long will you be so slow of heart? Even now, after Life has come down to you, will you not rise up and live? But where will you climb, when you are already on the heights and have set your mouths against heaven? Come down, so that you may rise — rise up to God. For you fell by trying to climb against him." Tell them this, so that they may weep in the valley of tears, and so carry them up with you to God — because it is out of his Spirit that you speak to them like this, if you speak burning with the fire of love.

None of this did I know then. I loved the lower beauties, and I was sinking toward the bottom, and I would say to my friends: ‘Do we love anything except the beautiful? Then what is the beautiful? And what is beauty? What is it in the things we love that pulls us and binds us to them? Unless there were some grace in them, some form, they could not possibly draw us.’ And I looked, and I noticed that in bodies themselves there is one beauty that comes of being a kind of whole, and another that comes of fitting — of answering well to something else, as a part of the body answers to its whole body, or a shoe to a foot, and so on. This thought welled up in my mind from the bottom of my heart, and I wrote some books — ‘On the Beautiful and the Fitting,’ I think — two of them, or three. You know, God; it has slipped from me. I no longer have them; they wandered away from me, I don’t know how.

These things I did not yet know; I loved those lower beauties, and I was sinking to the very bottom. And I would say to my friends: "Do we love anything but the beautiful? What, then, is the beautiful? And what is beauty? What is it that attracts us and binds us to the things we love? For unless there were a grace and beauty in them, they could never draw us to them at all." And I noticed and worked out that in bodies themselves there is one kind of beauty that comes from a thing's being a whole, and another that comes from a fitting correspondence — as of a part of the body to its whole, or a shoe to a foot, and the like. And this line of thought rose up in my mind out of the depths of my heart, and I wrote a book — two or three books, I think — On the Beautiful and the Fitting. You know, Lord, for it has gone from me; I no longer have it, but it has wandered off, I do not know how.

But what was it, Lord my God, that moved me to dedicate those books to Hierius, an orator of the city of Rome? I did not know him by sight. I loved the man for his reputation for learning, which was brilliant, and for a few sayings of his I had heard and liked. But he pleased me more because he pleased others: people praised him to the skies, amazed that a Syrian, schooled first in Greek eloquence, should afterward have turned into a marvelous speaker of Latin too, and one supremely learned in everything that belongs to the pursuit of wisdom. A man is praised, and, sight unseen, he is loved. Does the love enter the hearer’s heart from the mouth of the one praising? No. One lover kindles another. That is why a man who is praised gets loved: because we believe the praise comes from an undeceiving heart — that is, that the one praising already loves him.

But what moved me, Lord my God, to dedicate those books to Hierius, an orator of Rome whom I did not know by sight, but loved for the fame of his learning, which was outstanding in him, and for some words of his I had heard, which pleased me? But he pleased me more because he pleased others, who praised him to the skies, marveling that out of a Syrian, first trained in Greek eloquence, there should later have come a wonderful master of Latin and a man deeply learned in matters of philosophy. So a man is praised, and, never seen, is loved. Does this love enter the listener's heart from the mouth of the one who praises? Not at all. Rather, one who loves kindles another. For this is why the man who is praised is loved: when the one praising him is believed to praise him with an honest heart — that is, when the one who praises him truly loves him.

That is how I loved men then: on the judgment of men, not on yours, my God, in which no one is deceived. Still — why not love him the way one loves a famous charioteer, or a beast-fighter adored by the crowds, instead of so very differently, so seriously — exactly the way I wanted to be praised myself? For I would not have wanted to be praised and loved the way actors are — though I myself praised and loved actors. I would sooner have been unknown than known like that; sooner hated than loved like that. Where does one soul store the weights of so many different and contrary loves? Why do I love in another man what — since we are equally men — I would detest and throw off from myself, if I did not hate it? A good horse may be loved by a man who would not choose to be that horse even if he could; but you cannot say the same of an actor, who shares our nature. Do I then love in a man what I would hate to be, though I am a man? Man himself is a vast deep. You, Lord, keep the count of his very hairs, and not one of them is lost in you; and yet the hairs of his head are easier to number than his feelings — than the movements of his heart.

For that is how I loved men in those days, by the judgment of men, not by yours, my God, in whom no one is deceived. But why was it not as one admires a famous charioteer, or a fighter of beasts in the arena, known far and wide by the cheering of the crowd? It was something quite different, and earnest — the way I would have wanted to be admired myself. For I would not have wanted to be praised and loved the way actors are loved, though I myself praised and loved them; I would sooner be unknown than known like that, sooner even hated than loved like that. Where in one soul are all these powers toward so many different and clashing loves stored up? Why do I love in another man — since we are equally men — what, if I did not hate it, I would push away from myself in disgust? It does not hold that, just as a good horse is loved by one who would not want to be that horse even if he could, the same could be said of an actor, who shares our human nature. Do I, then, love in a man what I would hate to be, who am myself a man? Man himself is a great deep, whose very hairs you have numbered, Lord, and they do not fall to the ground without you. And yet the hairs of his head are easier to count than his feelings and the stirrings of his heart.

That orator was of the kind I loved in the way of wanting to be him. And I strayed, swollen with conceit, carried around by every wind — and all the while, in deepest secret, you were steering me. And how do I know — how can I confess it to you as a certainty — that I loved him more in the love of his praisers than for the things they praised? Because if those same men, instead of praising him, had torn him down — if they had reported the very same facts about him with scorn and contempt — I would never have caught fire for him, never been stirred. And yet the facts would have been no different; the man himself no different; only the feeling of the tellers. Look where the strengthless soul lies, when it is not yet fastened to the solidity of truth: as the gusts of tongues blow out of the chests of the opinionated, the soul is carried and turned, twisted and twisted back; the light clouds over, and it cannot make out the truth. And look — the truth is right in front of us. To me, back then, it was a very great matter that my style and my studies should become known to that man. If he approved them, I would blaze all the hotter; if he disapproved, my heart — hollow, void of your solidity — would have taken the wound. And yet that ‘beautiful and fitting’ I had written to him about, I liked turning over in my mind, gazing on it and admiring it, with no one to praise it with me.

But that orator was of the kind I loved because I wished to be such a man myself; and I went astray through a swelling pride, tossed about by every wind, and yet steered by you, though very secretly. And how do I know, how do I confess it to you with such confidence, that I had loved him more for the love of those who praised him than for the very things for which he was praised? Because if those same men had run him down instead of praising him, and had told the very same things about him in scorn and contempt, I would never have caught fire and been stirred to love him. And yet the things themselves would have been no different, nor he himself any different — only the feelings of those reporting them. See where the helpless soul lies sprawled, when it is not yet held up by the solidity of truth! Just as the gusts of speech blow from the breasts of people sure of their opinions, the soul is carried this way and that, driven forward and back; the light is overclouded to it, and the truth is not seen — and yet it is right there before us. And it seemed a great thing to me that my work and my labors should be known to that man. If he approved them, I would burn the brighter; but if he disapproved, my empty heart, void of your solid truth, would have been wounded. And yet I dwelt with pleasure on that work On the Beautiful and the Fitting which I wrote to him, and looked it over, and admired it, with no one else to share in it.

But I did not yet see the hinge on which this great question turns: your craftsmanship, Almighty — you who alone do wonders. My mind moved among bodily forms. The ‘beautiful’ I defined as what pleases in itself; the ‘fitting’ as what pleases by suiting something else; and I shored up the distinction with examples drawn from bodies. Then I turned to the nature of the mind — and the false notion I held of spiritual things would not let me see what was true. The sheer force of the truth kept beating against my eyes, and I kept turning my quivering mind away from bodiless reality toward outlines and colors and swollen masses; and since I could not see such things in the mind, I concluded that I could not see my mind. And since in virtue I loved peace, and in vice I hated discord, I noted in the one a unity, in the other a kind of division; and it seemed to me that in that unity lay the rational mind and the very nature of truth and of the highest good, while in that division — this was my misery — there was some substance of irrational life, and the nature of a highest evil: not merely a substance, but genuinely a life, and yet not from you, my God, from whom all things are. The first I called a Monad — a mind, as it were, without any sex; the second a Dyad: anger in crimes of violence, lust in crimes of the flesh. I did not know what I was saying. For I had not known, and had not learned, that evil is not a substance at all — and that our own mind is not the highest and unchangeable good.

But I did not yet see the hinge on which this whole weighty matter turned in your wisdom, almighty one, who alone work wonders. My mind ranged among bodily forms, and I defined and marked off the "beautiful" as what is so in itself, and the "fitting" as what is beautiful in its correspondence to something else; and I backed this up with examples drawn from bodies. I turned to consider the nature of the mind, but the false notion I had of spiritual things would not let me see the truth. And yet the very force of truth flashed before my eyes, and I turned my panting soul away from bodiless reality toward shapes and colors and swelling bulks; and because I could not see these in the mind, I thought I could not see my mind. And whereas I loved peace in virtue and hated discord in vice, in the one I noticed a unity, and in the other a kind of division. And in that unity I imagined the rational soul to lie, and the nature of truth and of the highest good; while in that division I wretchedly imagined there to be some substance of irrational life, and the very nature of the highest evil — which I took to be not only a substance but a real life of its own, and yet not derived from you, my God, from whom all things come. And the first of these I called a Monad, as if it were a soul without sex; the second a Duad — anger in deeds of violence, and lust in shameful acts — not knowing what I was talking about. For I had neither known nor learned that evil is not a substance at all, nor that our soul is not that highest and unchangeable good.

For as crimes of violence arise when the surge of the soul from which action springs is corrupted and hurls itself forward, insolent and turbid; and as crimes of the flesh arise when the soul’s appetite for drinking in bodily pleasures runs unbridled: just so do errors and false opinions poison a life when the reasoning mind itself is corrupt. And so it was then in me — a mind that did not know it must be lit by another light in order to share in the truth, since it is not itself the nature of truth. For you will light my lamp, Lord; my God, you will turn my darkness to light; and from your fullness we have all received. For you are the true light, which gives light to every man who comes into this world; and in you there is no changing — not even the shadow thrown by turning.

For just as deeds of violence arise when the impulse of the soul is corrupted from which vehement action springs, when it stirs itself up insolently and out of control; and lusts arise when that affection of the soul is ungoverned by which bodily pleasures are drunk in — so do errors and false opinions defile the way one lives, when the reasonable soul itself is corrupted. So it was then in me, who did not know that it must be lit by another light if it is to share in the truth, since it is not itself the nature of truth. For you will light my lamp, Lord my God; you will brighten my darkness; and of your fullness we have all received, for you are the true light that lights every man coming into the world — for in you there is no change, nor any shadow of turning.

I strained toward you, and was pushed back from you so that I might taste death — for you resist the proud. And what is prouder than to claim, with unbelievable madness, that I was by nature what you are? I was changeable, and I knew it — plainly, since the very fact that I wanted to become wise meant I wanted to go from worse to better. Yet I preferred to imagine even you changeable, rather than admit that I was not what you are. So you pushed me back; you set yourself against my stiff, wind-filled neck. And I went on imagining bodily shapes; flesh myself, I put flesh on trial; a wind that walks away and does not come back, I did not return to you, but wandered on and on, toward things that have no being at all — not in you, not in me, not in the body. None of it was created for me by your truth; all of it was invented by my vanity out of body. And I used to say to your faithful little ones, my fellow citizens — from whom, without knowing it, I was living in exile — I used to say to them, glib and fatuous: ‘Why does the soul go wrong, if God made it?’ But I did not want anyone to say to me, ‘Why does God go wrong, then?’ And I argued that your unchangeable substance erred under compulsion, sooner than confess that my changeable substance had swerved of its own free will, and that its erring now was punishment.

But I was pressing toward you, and was thrust back from you, so that I might taste death; for you resist the proud. And what was prouder than for me, in a strange madness, to claim that I was by nature what you are? For though I was subject to change — and that much was plain to me, since my very wish to grow wise was the wish to become better out of worse — I chose instead to imagine you subject to change, rather than admit that I was not what you are. So I was driven back, and you stood against my empty stubbornness; and I went on imagining bodily forms, and, being flesh myself, I accused flesh; and, a wind that passes and does not return, I did not turn back to you, but passed on and on toward things that have no being at all — neither in you, nor in me, nor in any body — things not created for me by your truth, but invented out of bodily things by my own emptiness. And I used to ask your faithful little ones — my fellow citizens, from whom, without knowing it, I stood exiled — I used to ask them, prattling and foolish: "Why, then, does the soul go astray, when God created it?" But I would not let myself be asked, "Why, then, does God go astray?" And I would maintain that your unchangeable substance went astray under compulsion, rather than confess that my own changeable substance had gone astray of its own free will, and now, in punishment, lay in error.

I was perhaps twenty-six or twenty-seven years old when I wrote those volumes — turning over inside me bodily fictions that drummed at the ears of my heart. And I was straining those ears, sweet Truth, for your inward melody, thinking on the beautiful and the fitting, longing to stand still and hear you and to rejoice with joy at the voice of the Bridegroom — and I could not. The voices of my own error dragged me outward, and under the weight of my own pride I kept sinking toward the lowest place. You did not give joy and gladness to my hearing; and the bones did not exult, because they had not been humbled.

I was about twenty-six or twenty-seven when I wrote those books, turning over inside me those bodily fictions that buzzed in the ears of my heart — that heart which I was straining, sweet Truth, toward your inward music, meditating on the "beautiful and the fitting," longing to stand still and listen to you and rejoice greatly at the Bridegroom's voice; but I could not, for by the voices of my own errors I was hurried away outside, and by the weight of my own pride I was sinking into the lowest pit. For you had not yet made me to hear joy and gladness, nor did the bones rejoice that had not yet been humbled.

And what good did it do me that at about twenty, when a certain work of Aristotle fell into my hands — they call it the Ten Categories, and at the bare name of it I would stand open-mouthed, as before something great and divine, whenever my rhetoric master at Carthage, and others reckoned learned, pronounced it with their cheeks bursting with pride — I read it alone, and understood it? I compared notes with others, who said that even with the most erudite teachers — teachers who did not just lecture on it, but drew diagram after diagram in the sand — they had barely understood it; and they could tell me nothing about it that I had not already gathered reading it by myself. The book seemed to me to speak plainly enough about substances, such as ‘a man,’ and about what is in them: the figure of a man, what it is like; his stature, how many feet; his kinship, whose brother he is; where he is placed; when he was born; whether he stands or sits; whether he is shod or armed; whether he is doing something or having something done to him — and all the innumerable things that fall under those nine categories, of which I have set down a few samples, or under the chief category, substance itself.

And what did it profit me that, when I was scarcely twenty, a book of Aristotle's that they call the Ten Categories fell into my hands — at whose very name I hung as on something great and divine, every time my teacher of rhetoric at Carthage and others reckoned learned would mouth it with cheeks bursting with pride — and I read it and understood it on my own, with no help? When I compared notes with others, who said they had barely understood it even with very able teachers, who not only explained it aloud but drew many diagrams in the sand, they could tell me no more about it than I had learned reading it by myself. And the book seemed to me to speak quite clearly of substances, such as "man," and of their qualities — the shape of a man, what sort it is; his height, how many feet tall; his kinship, whose brother he is; where he is placed; when he was born; whether he is standing or sitting; whether he is shod or armed; whether he is doing something or having something done to him — and of all the countless things that can be ranged under those nine categories, of which I have given a few samples, or under that chief category of Substance.

What good was this to me — when in fact it did me harm? For, supposing that those ten categories covered absolutely everything that is, I tried to understand even you that way, my God — you, wonderfully simple, wonderfully unchanging — as though you too were the subject in which your greatness or your beauty resided, existing in you as they exist in a body. But your greatness and your beauty are you yourself; whereas a body is not great or beautiful simply by being a body — were it less great and less beautiful, it would be a body still. What I was thinking about you was falsehood, not truth: the fictions of my own misery, not the firm ground of your blessedness. For you had commanded it, and so it was being done in me: the earth was bearing me briars and thorns, and I was reaching my bread by the sweat of my face.

What did all this advance me — when in fact it held me back? For, imagining that whatever exists is taken in under those ten categories, I tried in the same way to understand your own wonderful and unchangeable Oneness, my God — as if you too were laid out under your own greatness or beauty, so that they should exist in you as their subject, the way they do in bodies; whereas you yourself are your own greatness and beauty, while a body is not great or beautiful by being a body, since even if it were less great or beautiful it would still be a body. For what I thought of you was falsehood, not truth — the fictions of my misery, not the realities of your blessedness. For you had commanded, and it was done in me, that the earth should bring forth thorns and briars for me, and that with the sweat of my brow I should eat my bread.

And what good did it do me that I read on my own, and understood, every book I could lay hands on of the arts they call liberal — I, at that time the vile slave of vile desires? I delighted in the books, and had no idea where whatever in them was true and certain came from. For I had my back to the light and my face to the things the light fell on; and so my face, by which I saw the lit things, caught no light itself. Whatever was written on rhetoric or on logic, on the measuring of figures, on music, on numbers, I understood without much difficulty, without any man to teach me — you know it, Lord my God, because quickness of understanding and sharpness of analysis are your gift. But I offered you no sacrifice from it. So it worked not for my use but rather for my ruin, since I fought to keep so good a part of my inheritance in my own power, and did not keep my strength for you, but set out from you into a far country, to squander my substance there on whoring passions. For what good was a good thing to me, when I did not use it well? I never realized how hard those arts are — hard even for the studious and the gifted — until I tried to explain them to the studious and the gifted, and found that the most brilliant of them was simply the one who was not too slow in following me.

And what did it profit me that all the books I could get hold of on what they call the liberal arts, I — the vile slave of vile desires — read and understood by myself? I took delight in them, but I did not know where all that was true or certain in them came from. For I had my back to the light and my face to the things lit by it; so that my face, with which I looked at the things lit, was not itself lit. Whatever was written on rhetoric or logic, on geometry, music, and arithmetic, I understood, you know it, Lord my God, without much trouble and with no instructor — for both quickness of understanding and sharpness of discernment are your gift. But for this I offered no sacrifice to you. So it served not my benefit but my ruin, since I was trying to get so good a portion of my substance into my own keeping; and I did not keep my strength for you, but wandered away from you into a far country, to squander it on harlotries. For what did good abilities profit me, if I did not put them to good use? For I did not feel how hard those arts were to master, even for the diligent and gifted, until I tried to explain them to such people — and the best among them was the one who could keep up with me without falling too far behind.

But what good was any of it to me, while I supposed that you, Lord God of truth, were a vast and luminous body, and I a broken-off piece of that body? Perversity past all measure! But that is what I was. And I am not ashamed now, my God, to confess to you your mercies over me, and to call upon you — I who then was not ashamed to profess my blasphemies in front of men, and to bark at you. What use to me, then, was a mind so nimble in those sciences — all those knotted volumes untied with no help from any human teacher — when in the teaching of true devotion I was going ugly, sacrilegiously wrong? And what harm was a far slower mind to your little ones, who never wandered far from you — who could grow their feathers in safety in the nest of your Church, and feed the wings of love on the food of a sound faith? O Lord our God, let us hope in the shelter of your wings: protect us, and carry us. You will carry us — you will carry us when we are small, and when our hair is white you will carry us still; for when our strength is you, it is strength, and when it is our own, it is weakness. Our good lives always with you, and because we have turned away from it, we have gone wrong. Let us turn back now, Lord, so that we are not overturned — because our good lives with you, lacking nothing; and that good is you yourself. And we need not be afraid that there is no place to come back to, just because we fell out of it: in our absence, our house does not fall down — our house, which is your eternity.

But what did this advance me, while I imagined that you, Lord God, the Truth, were a vast and shining body, and I a fragment of that body? Perverseness too great! But that is what I was. And I do not blush, my God, to confess to you your mercies toward me, and to call upon you — I who did not blush then to profess my blasphemies to men, and to bark against you. What good to me then was my nimble wit in those studies, all those most knotty books unraveled by me without any help of human teaching, when in the teaching of true devotion I went so foully and sacrilegiously astray? And what harm was a far slower wit to your little ones, since they did not depart far from you, but in the nest of your Church grew their feathers in safety, and nourished the wings of love on the food of a sound faith? Lord our God, let us hope under the shadow of your wings; protect us and carry us. You will carry us — you will carry us when we are small, and even to gray hairs you will carry us. For when our firmness is you, then it is firmness; but when it is our own, it is weakness. Our good lives forever with you, and when we turn away from it, we are turned aside. Let us now return, Lord, so that we are not overturned, since with you our good lives on without any decay — and that good is you. And we need not fear that there is no place to return to, just because we fell from it; for in our absence our home did not fall — your eternity.

Accept the sacrifice of my confessions from the hand of my tongue — you formed that tongue, and you stirred it up to confess your name. Heal all my bones, and let them say: Lord, who is like you? A man who confesses to you is not telling you anything new about himself; a closed heart does not shut out your eye, and the hardness of a human heart cannot push back your hand. You melt it whenever you choose, in mercy or in vengeance, and nothing can hide from your heat. Let my soul praise you, so that it may love you; let it confess your mercies to you, so that it may praise you. Your whole creation never stops praising you, never falls silent: every human spirit turns its voice toward you, and every animal and lifeless thing praises you through the mouths of those who contemplate them — so that our souls may rouse themselves out of weariness and rise toward you, leaning on the things you have made and passing beyond them to you, who made them so wonderfully. And there is refreshment there, and real strength.

Accept the sacrifice of my confessions from the labor of my tongue, which you yourself shaped and stirred up to confess to your name. Heal all my bones, and let them say, Lord, who is like you? For the one who confesses to you is not teaching you what goes on inside him; a closed heart does not shut out your eye, and a man's hardness cannot push back your hand. You dissolve that hardness whenever you please, in pity or in punishment, and nothing can hide itself from your heat. But let my soul praise you, so that it may love you; let it confess your own mercies to you, so that it may praise you. Your whole creation never stops, never falls silent in your praises — not the spirit of a man whose voice is turned toward you, nor anything alive or lifeless, by the voice of those who consider it — so that our souls may rise up out of their weariness toward you, leaning on the things you have made and passing on through them to you, who made them so wonderfully. There is refreshment, and there is the true strength.
