Let the restless and the wicked run; let them flee from you. You see them anyway; you divide the shadows. And look — the whole, with them inside it, is beautiful, though they themselves are ugly. What harm have they done you? How have they disgraced your rule, which is just and whole from the heavens down to the lowest things of earth? Where did they run, when they ran from your face? Where will you fail to find them? They ran so they would not see you seeing them — ran blind, and blundered into you, because you abandon nothing you have made. The unjust blundered into you and were justly hurt: pulling away from your gentleness, striking against your straightness, falling on their own jaggedness. They do not know, evidently, that you are everywhere, that no place contains you, that you alone stay near even to those who put themselves far away. Then let them turn and look for you. You have not abandoned your creation the way they abandoned their Creator. Let them turn — and look, there you are, in their heart, in the heart of everyone who confesses to you, who throws himself on you and weeps into your breast after all his hard roads. And you gently wipe away the tears, and they weep the more, and are glad in the weeping — because it is you, Lord, not some human being of flesh and blood, but you, Lord, their maker, who remake them and console them. And where was I, when I was looking for you? You were right in front of me; but I had walked away — even from myself. I could not find myself. How much less you.

Let the restless and the godless leave you and run; still you see them and divide the darkness. And look — with them in it, the universe is beautiful, though they themselves are foul. How have they hurt you? How have they disgraced your rule, which from the heavens down to this lowest earth is just and complete? Where did they flee to, when they fled from your presence? Where would you not find them? They fled so as not to see you seeing them, and, blinded, stumble against you — for you forsake nothing you have made. They stumble against you, the unjust, and are justly hurt: drawing back from your gentleness, tripping over your uprightness, falling on their own roughness. They do not know, in truth, that you are everywhere, that no place can hold you, and that you alone are near even to those who take themselves far from you. So let them turn and look for you. For you have not forsaken your creation the way they have forsaken their Creator. Let them turn and look for you, and there you are, in their heart — in the heart of those who confess to you and throw themselves on you and weep on your breast after all their rugged ways. Gently you wipe away their tears, and they weep the more, and rejoice in their weeping; because you, Lord — not some man of flesh and blood, but you, Lord, who made them — remake them and comfort them. And where was I, when I was looking for you? You were there in front of me, but I had gone away from myself, and could not even find myself, much less you.

Let me lay open before my God my twenty-ninth year. A Manichee bishop named Faustus had just arrived in Carthage — a great snare of the devil, and many people were tangled in him, caught by the lure of his smooth talk. I admired the talk too, but I could tell it apart from the truth of the things I was hungry to learn: I cared less for the serving-dish of his rhetoric than for the knowledge this Faustus, so celebrated among them, was supposed to set in front of me. His reputation had reached me ahead of him: superbly trained in every honorable study, an expert in the liberal arts. And since I had read a good deal of the philosophers and kept it in memory, I compared some of their claims with the endless fables of the Manichees, and the philosophers seemed to me more probable — men with strength enough to take the measure of this world, though they never found its Lord. Because you are great, Lord, and you look kindly on the lowly, but the proud you know only from far off. You come near to the broken-hearted alone; the proud do not find you — not even if their exacting skill could count the stars and the grains of sand, survey the fields of the sky, and trace out the paths of the planets.

Let me lay open before my God that twenty-ninth year of my life. There had come to Carthage by then a certain bishop of the Manichees, Faustus by name, a great snare of the devil, and many were caught in it by the bait of his smooth tongue. I admired that tongue myself, and yet I could tell it apart from the truth of the things I was so eager to learn. It was not the serving-dish of his rhetoric I cared about, but the knowledge that this Faustus, so famous among them, was supposed to set before me to feed on. Rumor had run ahead of him: he was a master of every worthwhile study, deeply skilled in the liberal arts. And since I had read a good deal of the philosophers, and kept it well, I held some of their findings up against the long fables of the Manichees, and found the philosophers more believable — even though their reach went only so far as to take the measure of this lower world; the Lord of that world they could not find at all. For you are great, Lord, and you look on the lowly, but the proud you see only from far off. You come near to none but the contrite in heart; the proud do not find you, not even if by some clever skill they could count the stars and the sands, chart the shining heavens, and trace the courses of the planets.

With the mind and the intelligence you gave them, they investigate these things, and they have found out a great deal. They predicted eclipses of the sun and the moon years in advance — the day, the hour, how much of the light would go — and the arithmetic did not fail them: it happened exactly as they foretold. They wrote down the rules they discovered, and the rules are read to this day, and from them others still predict the year, the month, the day, the hour, and what fraction of its light the moon or the sun is going to lose — and it goes dark on schedule. People who do not know the art marvel and are dumbfounded; people who know it exult and are puffed up. In their godless pride they draw back from you, and your light fails inside them; and they can see an eclipse of the sun coming years ahead, but their own eclipse, happening now, they cannot see. Because they never ask, reverently, where the intelligence came from that they use to investigate all this. And when they do discover that you made them, they do not hand themselves over to you, so that you can preserve what you made; they do not slaughter for you what they have made of themselves. They do not kill their soaring pretensions, like birds of the air; or their diving curiosities, like fish of the sea that wander the hidden paths of the deep; or their appetites, like beasts of the field — so that you, God, a devouring fire, could burn up their dead preoccupations and re-create the men themselves for immortality.

With the mind and wit you gave them they search these things out, and much they have discovered: they foretold eclipses of those great lights, the sun and moon, years ahead — the very day, the hour, how far the shadow would reach — and their reckoning did not fail; it happened just as they said. They wrote down the rules they had worked out, and those rules are read to this day, and from them others foretell in what year and month, on what day and at what hour, and to what depth, the sun or moon will be darkened, and so it comes to pass exactly as foreshown. People who do not know this art are astonished and amazed; those who do know it crow and swell with pride. For by a godless pride they slip away from you and lose your light: they foresee, so long beforehand, a coming failure of the sun's light, and cannot see the failure of their own, here and now. They make no reverent search into where they got the very wit they search with. And when they find that you made them, they do not hand themselves over to you to keep what you made; they do not put to death, as a sacrifice to you, the selves they have made of themselves. They do not slaughter their own soaring presumptions, like birds of the air, nor their prying curiosities, by which, like the fish of the sea, they wander the trackless deep, nor their own self-indulgence, like the beasts of the field — so that you, Lord, a devouring fire, might burn up those dead concerns of theirs and remake the men themselves for life that does not end.

But they did not know the way: your Word, through whom you made the things they count, and the men who do the counting, and the senses by which they perceive what they count, and the mind they count with. And of your wisdom there is no counting. The Only-begotten himself was made wisdom for us, and righteousness, and sanctification; he was counted as one of us, and he paid his tax to Caesar. They did not know this way — the way down from themselves to him, and through him up to him. They did not know it; they thought themselves high and shining among the stars, and look, they crashed to the earth, and their foolish heart went dark. They say many true things about the creation, but the Truth, the master craftsman of creation, they do not seek reverently, and so they do not find him. Or if they find him, and know that he is God, they do not honor him as God or give thanks; they evaporate into their own speculations and call themselves wise, crediting to themselves what is yours — and then, with the most perverse blindness of all, they work to charge you with what is theirs, pinning lies on you, who are the Truth, and swapping the glory of the incorruptible God for an image shaped like corruptible man, like birds and four-footed animals and snakes — trading your truth for a lie, worshiping and serving the creature instead of the Creator.

But they did not know the way, your Word, by whom you made the very things they count, and the counters themselves, and the sense by which they perceive what they count, and the understanding out of which they count — for of your wisdom there is no number. Yet the Only-Begotten was made, for us, wisdom and righteousness and holiness, and was counted among us, and paid his tax to Caesar. They did not know this way, by which to climb down from themselves to him and by him climb up to him. They did not know it, and reckoned themselves high among the stars and shining; and look — they fell to earth, and their foolish heart was darkened. They say many true things about the creation, but the Truth who crafted the creation they do not look for in the right spirit, and so do not find — or if they do find him, and know him to be God, they do not honor him as God, nor give thanks, but lose themselves in their own notions, and call themselves wise, claiming for their own what is yours. And so, with the most twisted blindness, they go on to charge you with what is theirs, telling lies about you who are the Truth, trading the glory of the incorruptible God for an image made like corruptible man, and birds, and beasts, and crawling things — swapping your truth for a lie, and worshiping and serving the creature in place of the Creator.

Still, I held onto many true things these men said about creation, and I saw the reasoning behind them — the calculations, the ordered sequence of the seasons, the visible testimony of the stars — and I set it all against the sayings of Mani, who had written on these subjects at enormous length, raving. And in him I found no account of solstices, or equinoxes, or eclipses of the sun and moon, nothing of what I had learned in the books of ordinary philosophy. I was simply ordered to believe it; and it did not square with what calculation and my own eyes had established. It was flatly contrary.

Even so, I held on to many true things about the created world that I had from these men, and I saw the reason of them in the calculations, the succession of seasons, and the visible witness of the stars. I set them beside the sayings of Manichaeus, who in his ravings had written at huge length on these very subjects, and I could find in him no account of the solstices, or the equinoxes, or the eclipses of the greater lights, nor anything of the kind I had learned in the books of ordinary philosophy. Yet I was ordered to believe him — and it did not square with what calculation and my own eyes had settled; it ran flat against them.

Lord God of truth — is knowing such things enough to please you? A man who knows them all and does not know you is unhappy; a man who knows you, though he knows none of them, is happy. And whoever knows both you and them is not the happier for them; he is happy for you alone — if, knowing you, he honors you as God and gives thanks, and does not evaporate into his own thoughts. A man who owns a tree and thanks you for the use of it is better off — though he cannot say how tall it stands or how wide it spreads — than the man who can measure it and count every branch, but does not own it, and neither knows nor loves its maker. Just so, a believer has the whole world of riches for his own, and having nothing, possesses everything, by holding fast to you, whom all things serve; and even if he cannot trace the wheel of the Great Bear, it is folly to doubt that he is better off than the man who can measure the sky, count the stars, and weigh the elements — and neglects you, who arranged all things by number, weight, and measure.

Does anyone, then, Lord God of truth, please you just because he knows these things? Surely the man who knows all of that and does not know you is wretched, and the man who knows you, even if he knows none of it, is happy. And the man who knows both you and them is no happier for knowing them, but happy in you alone — if, knowing you, he glorifies you as God, and gives thanks, and does not lose himself in his own notions. For just as a man is better off who knows how to own a tree and thank you for the use of it, though he cannot say how many feet high it stands or how wide it spreads, than one who can measure it and count every branch but neither owns it nor knows and loves the One who made it — so a believer, to whom all this wealth of a world belongs, who having nothing yet possesses all things by clinging to you, whom all things serve, even if he does not know so much as the turning of the Great Bear, it is folly to doubt that he is better off than the man who can measure the sky and number the stars and weigh the elements, yet has no thought for you, who made all things in number and weight and measure.

But who asked this Mani to write about these subjects in the first place? Skill in them is no part of holiness. For you have said to man: Behold, reverence — that is wisdom. He could have been ignorant of all the science and still have had the wisdom; but since he knew none of it and still had the gall to teach it, he plainly could not have had the wisdom either. Parading a knowledge of worldly things is vanity even when the knowledge is real; confession to you is holiness. So this wanderer talked at length about the heavens to his own undoing: refuted by those who had truly studied them, he showed exactly what his judgment was worth on the harder, deeper matters. He would not settle for being thought a small man. He went about persuading people that the Holy Spirit — the Comforter, the Enricher of your faithful — dwelt in him personally, with full authority. So when he was caught teaching falsehoods about the sky and the stars and the motions of the sun and moon — matters that are no part of religious doctrine — the sacrilege of his presumption stood exposed clearly enough: he was delivering things he not only did not know but had gotten wrong, with a vanity so deranged by pride that he tried to have them credited to himself as to a divine person.

But still — who told that Manichaeus to write on these matters too, when skill in them is no part of devotion? For you have said to man, Behold, devotion and wisdom are this. Of astronomy he might have been ignorant and still had wisdom; but these things, of which he knew nothing, he shamelessly dared to teach, and so plainly could have no knowledge of devotion. For to make a show of these worldly matters, even when you do know them, is vanity; but to confess to you is devotion. That is why this wanderer talked so much about them: so that, once he was caught out by people who had truly learned them, it would be clear how little understanding he had in the deeper, more hidden things. For he would not be thought a small man; he went about persuading people that the Holy Spirit, the Comforter and Enricher of your faithful, was present in his own person, with full authority. So when he was caught teaching falsely about the heavens and the stars and the movements of sun and moon — though such things have nothing to do with the teaching of religion — even so his blasphemous nerve stood exposed, since he handed out things he not only did not know but had got plainly wrong, and with such a mad swollen pride that he tried to ascribe them to himself, as to a divine person.

When I hear some Christian brother who is ignorant of these matters, or mistaken about them, I can watch him hold his opinion patiently. So long as he believes nothing unworthy of you, Lord, Creator of all things, I do not see that it hurts him to be ignorant of the layout and workings of the physical creation. It does hurt him if he decides this belongs to the very form of holy teaching, and insists too stubbornly on what he does not understand. And even that weakness, in the infancy of faith, is carried by charity, our mother, until the new man grows up to maturity and is no longer blown about by every wind of doctrine. But a man who presumed to set himself up as teacher, source, guide, and chief of everyone he could persuade — so that his followers believed they were following not a man but your Holy Spirit — who would not judge that such madness, once it was caught teaching anything false, deserved detestation and total rejection? But I had not yet settled for certain whether the lengthening and shortening of days and nights, the alternation of day and night itself, the eclipses, and everything else of the kind I had read in other books could somehow be squared with what Mani said. If they could, whether he was right would still remain an open question for me; but I could rest my belief on his authority, because of his reputation for holiness.

For when I hear some Christian brother who knows nothing of these matters and has them confused, I can look on his mistakes with patience; I do not see how any ignorance about the place or make-up of the physical world can harm him, as long as he believes nothing unworthy of you, Lord, the Creator of all. It does harm him if he takes such things to belong to the body of devout teaching, and stubbornly insists on what he does not know. Yet even such a weakness, in the infancy of faith, our mother Charity carries, until the newborn grows up to a full-grown man, no longer blown about by every wind of doctrine. But in a man who set himself up as the teacher, the source, the guide, the head of all he could persuade — so that whoever followed him thought he was following not a mere man but your Holy Spirit — who would not judge that so vast a madness, once caught teaching anything false, was to be loathed and utterly thrown off? Still, I had not yet made out for certain whether the changing lengths of days and nights, and of day and night themselves, and the eclipses of the greater lights, and whatever else of the kind I had read of, could be squared with his sayings; so that, if they somehow could, it would still be an open question to me whether it was so or not, and I might rest my belief on his authority for the sake of his supposed holiness.

For almost all of those nine years in which I drifted as their hearer, I had waited for this Faustus with an eagerness that was too much. The other Manichees I happened to meet, whenever they failed against my objections, kept promising me this Faustus: once he came, and I could talk with him, these difficulties — and greater ones, if I had them — would be untangled with the greatest of ease. Then he came. I found a charming man, pleasant with words, chattering the very things the rest of them always say — only much more sweetly. But what good is the most elegant of waiters to a man thirsty for a costlier drink? My ears were already stuffed with that fare. It did not seem better to me for being better said, or true for being eloquent; the soul did not seem wise because the face was attractive and the language graceful. The people who kept promising him to me were not good judges of things: to them he seemed prudent and wise because his talk delighted them. I have noticed another breed, meanwhile, that suspects even the truth, and refuses to accept it if it arrives in fluent, ample speech. But you had already taught me, my God, by wonderful and hidden ways — and I believe it was you who taught me, because it is true, and there is no other teacher of truth besides you, wherever and from whatever quarter it dawns. From you I had already learned this: a thing is not true because it is said eloquently, or false because the sounds from the lips come out awkward; and not true because it is roughly delivered, or false because the language is splendid. Wisdom and folly are like foods, one nourishing, one worthless; and ornate words or plain are like dishes, fine or homely — and either kind of food can be served on either kind of plate.

And for nearly all those nine years in which, with an unsettled mind, I had been their student, I had been longing for the coming of this Faustus, too intensely. For the others of the sect, the ones I happened to fall in with, when they could not answer my questions about these things, kept holding out this Faustus to me, by whose coming and by talking with whom these difficulties and any greater ones would be cleared up most easily and fully. So when he came, I found a man of pleasant conversation, who said the very same things they all said, but in better and smoother words. But what good was the most elegant cupbearer to a thirst that wanted a more precious drink? My ears were already glutted with all this, and it did not seem any better to me for being better said, nor true for being eloquent, nor the soul wise because the face was handsome and the speech well-turned. But those who held him out to me were no judges of such things, and so to them he seemed thoughtful and wise, because he was pleasant to listen to. I had noticed, though, that there are people who grow suspicious even of the truth, and will not give their assent to it, if it is delivered in a smooth and copious style. But you, my God, had already taught me by wonderful, hidden ways — and I believe it was you who taught me, because it is true, and there is no teacher of truth but you, wherever and from wherever it may shine on us. So from you I had already learned that nothing should seem true just because it is well said, nor false because the words come out rough; nor, again, true because plainly put, nor false because richly worded. Wisdom and folly are like wholesome and unwholesome food, and polished or plain phrases are like fine or common dishes: either kind of food may be served in either kind of dish.

The hunger with which I had waited so long for that man was fed, all right, by the energy and feeling of his performance in debate, and by the apt words that came so readily to clothe his thoughts. I was delighted; along with many others — more than most of them — I praised him and sang his praises. But it galled me that in the crowd of his listeners I was not allowed to put forward the questions that troubled me and trade them back and forth with him in real conversation. When at last I could — when my friends and I began to claim his ears at hours when a mutual discussion was not out of place, and I laid out the things that were pressing on me — I found, first of all, a man ignorant of the liberal arts except literature, and of that he knew only the ordinary amount. He had read some of Cicero's speeches, a very few books of Seneca, some scraps of the poets, and whatever volumes of his own sect happened to be written in decent Latin; add daily practice at speaking, and out of that came his eloquence — the more pleasing, and the more seductive, because a good native wit steered it and a kind of natural grace attended it. Is it as I remember it, Lord my God, judge of my conscience? My heart and my memory lie open before you. You were working on me even then, in the hidden secret of your providence, turning my shameful errors around to face me, so that I would see them and hate them.

So the hunger with which I had waited so long for that man was delighted, true enough, by his energy and warmth in debate, and by the apt, ready words he found to dress his ideas. I was delighted, and along with many others — more than they — I praised and exalted him. It troubled me, though, that in the crowd around him I could never get my turn to bring forward the questions that were troubling me, in a real exchange with him. When at last I could, and began with my friends to engage his attention at times when it was not unfitting for him to talk it over with me, and laid before him the things that moved me, I found him first of all ignorant of the liberal arts, except for grammar, and that only in an ordinary way. But because he had read a few of Cicero's speeches, a very few books of Seneca, some of the poets, and the handful of his own sect's volumes that were written in good Latin, and because he practiced speaking every day, he had picked up a certain eloquence, the more pleasing and seductive for being guided by a good wit and a kind of natural grace. Is it not so, as I recall it, Lord my God, judge of my conscience? Before you lie my heart and my memory — you who were guiding me even then by the hidden working of your providence, and setting those shameful errors of mine before my face, that I might see them and hate them.

Once it was plain enough that he was untrained in the very arts I had believed him to excel in, I began to despair of his ever opening and untying the knots that bound me. A man could be ignorant of all that, it is true, and still hold the truths of reverence — if he were not a Manichee. Their books are stuffed with interminable fables about the sky and the stars, the sun and the moon; and I no longer believed he could do what I urgently wanted — weigh the calculations I had read elsewhere against what stood in Mani's books, and show me with any precision that Mani's account was the better one, or even that it held up equally well. When I put this on the table for discussion, he — modestly enough — did not even dare to take up the load. He knew that he did not know these things, and he was not ashamed to admit it. He was not one of those talkers, of whom I had endured so many, who undertook to teach me and said nothing. This man had a heart — not right toward you, but not altogether false to himself either. He was not entirely ignorant of his own ignorance, and he would not rashly let himself be boxed into an argument with no exit and no honorable retreat. I liked him better for it. The modesty of a mind that admits its limits is a fairer thing than the knowledge I was after; and that is how I found him in every harder and subtler question.

For once it was clear that he knew nothing of the arts I had thought him a master of, I began to despair of his opening up and solving the difficulties that perplexed me — though, ignorant of all that as he was, he might still have held the truths of devotion, had he not been a Manichee. Their books are stuffed with long-winded fables about the heavens, the stars, the sun and moon; and I no longer thought him able to settle what I so badly wanted settled: whether, when these things were set against the calculations I had read elsewhere, the account in the books of Manichaeus was the better, or at least as good. When I put this up to be weighed and discussed, he, modestly enough, shrank from the load. He knew that he did not know these things, and was not ashamed to admit it. For he was not one of those many talkers I had put up with, who undertook to teach me these matters and said nothing. This man had a heart, not right toward you, and yet not altogether false to himself: he was not wholly ignorant of his own ignorance, and would not rashly let himself be drawn into an argument from which he could find no honest retreat or way out. And for that I liked him the better. For the modesty of a candid mind is a fairer thing than the very knowledge I was after — and that is how I found him in all the harder and subtler questions.

So the enthusiasm I had flung into Mani's writings was broken. And despairing all the more of their other teachers — since the famous one had turned out this way on the many points that perplexed me — I began instead to spend time with Faustus on the studies he himself was burning for: the literature I was then teaching, as professor of rhetoric, to the young men of Carthage. We read together whatever he wanted to hear, or whatever I judged suited to a mind like his. But every plan I had made for rising in that sect collapsed completely once I knew that man. Not that I cut myself off from them altogether; it was rather that, having found nothing better than the thing I had somehow stumbled into, I decided to stay put for the time being, unless something preferable showed itself. And so this Faustus, who had been a trap of death for so many, had begun — neither willing it nor knowing it — to loosen the trap that held me. For your hands, my God, in the secrecy of your providence, did not desert my soul; and out of my mother's heart's blood, through the tears she poured out day and night, a sacrifice was being offered to you for me; and you dealt with me in astonishing ways. You did it, my God — for by the Lord a man's steps are directed, and it is he who makes the way sure. And what other securing of salvation is there than your hand, remaking what it made?

With my zeal for the writings of Manichaeus thus blunted, and despairing all the more of their other teachers now that the famous one had turned out so, I began to spend my time with him in the study of literature, which he too was keen on — and which, as a teacher of rhetoric, I was then teaching young men at Carthage — reading with him either what he wanted to hear or what I judged suited to his talent. But all the efforts by which I had meant to advance in that sect came utterly to an end once I knew the man — not that I broke with them altogether, but, finding nothing better, I had settled to make do for the time with whatever I had stumbled into, unless by chance something more worth choosing should dawn on me. So that Faustus, who to so many had been a snare of death, had now, without willing or even knowing it, begun to loosen the snare that held me. For your hands, my God, in the secret purpose of your providence, did not let go of my soul; and out of the blood of my mother's heart, through her tears poured out for me day and night, a sacrifice was being offered to you on my behalf, and you dealt with me in wonderful ways. You did it, my God — for a man's steps are ordered by the Lord, and he shall direct his way. And how else are we to find salvation, except from your hand, remaking what it made?

You dealt with me so that I would be persuaded to go to Rome, and to teach there instead what I was teaching at Carthage. And how I came to be persuaded I will not fail to confess to you, because in this too the deepest workings of your wisdom, and your mercy always so near to us, deserve to be pondered and declared. It was not because my friends promised higher earnings and higher standing — though those things did tug at my mind at the time. The chief reason, almost the only one, was this: I kept hearing that students in Rome were quieter, held in check by a stricter and more orderly discipline; that they did not barge insolently, whenever they pleased, into the classroom of a teacher who was not their own, and were not admitted at all without his leave. At Carthage, by contrast, the license of the students is disgraceful and past all restraint. They burst in shamelessly and, looking half-crazed, wreck whatever order a teacher has established for his pupils' good. They commit outrage after outrage, with an astonishing obtuseness — conduct the law would punish, if custom did not stand as its patron. And the custom only proves them the more pitiable: they now do, as if it were lawful, what by your eternal law will never be lawful, and they think they do it with impunity — when the very blindness with which they do it is the punishment, and they suffer something incomparably worse than what they inflict. So the habits I had refused to make my own as a student, I was forced as a teacher to endure in others; and that is why it suited me to go to a place where, everyone who knew it assured me, such things were not done. But it was you — my hope, my portion in the land of the living — who, so that I would change countries for my soul's health, set the goad at Carthage that pried me loose, and hung the lure at Rome that drew me on; and you did it through men in love with a dying life — the ones doing insane things, the others promising empty ones — and, to straighten my steps, you secretly used their crookedness and mine. Because the men wrecking my peace were blind with a squalid frenzy, and the men beckoning me elsewhere had the taste of earth in their mouths. And I, who detested a real misery here, chased a false happiness there.

You dealt with me, then, so that I was talked into going to Rome, to teach there what I was teaching at Carthage. And how I was talked into it I will not fail to confess to you, because here too the deepest folds of your wisdom and your ever-present mercy toward us must be weighed and confessed. I did not want to go to Rome because of the higher pay and higher standing my friends promised me — though even those things did have a hold on my mind at the time. My chief, almost my only, reason was that I had heard the young men studied there more quietly, kept in check by a stricter and steadier discipline, so that they did not, whenever they pleased, come bursting brazenly into the lecture room of a teacher whose pupils they were not, and were not even let in without his leave. At Carthage, by contrast, there reigns among the students a most disgraceful, unbridled license. They break in shamelessly, and with almost crazed faces overturn whatever order a man has set up for his pupils' good. They commit any number of outrages, with an astonishing stupidity, that the law should punish, if custom did not shield them — custom proving them all the more wretched, in that they now do as if lawful what by your eternal law will never be lawful, and think they go unpunished, when the very blindness in which they do it is their punishment, and they suffer beyond all measure worse than they inflict. So the manners I would not make my own as a student, I had now as a teacher to endure in others; and so I was glad to go where all who knew assured me such things were not done. But you, my refuge and my portion in the land of the living — that I might change my dwelling on earth for the saving of my soul — at Carthage you used the goad on me, to tear me away, and at Rome you held out lures to draw me there, working through men in love with a dying life: the one sort doing crazy things, the other promising empty ones; and to set my own steps straight, you secretly turned both their perverseness and mine to account. For both those who disturbed my peace were blinded with a shameful frenzy, and those who beckoned me elsewhere had the taste of earth in them; while I, who here loathed a real misery, there went chasing a false happiness.

But why I left the one place and went to the other — you knew, God, and you showed it neither to me nor to my mother, who grieved terribly over my going and followed me all the way to the sea. She held onto me by force, to pull me back or to sail with me; and I deceived her. I pretended I had a friend I could not leave until the wind rose and he could sail. I lied to my mother — to that mother — and slipped away. Even this you have mercifully forgiven me: you kept me, brimming as I was with unspeakable filth, safe from the waters of the sea, and brought me through to the water of your grace — the washing that would dry the rivers running from my mother's eyes, with which, day after day, she watered the ground beneath her face for my sake. She refused to go home without me, and it was all I could do to persuade her to spend that night in a place close by our ship, a shrine to the memory of blessed Cyprian. That night I stole away; she stayed behind, praying and weeping. And what was she begging of you, my God, with all those tears, but that you would not let me sail? But you, in the depth of your counsel, heard the hinge of her desire: you ignored what she was asking then, in order to make of me what she was asking always. The wind blew and filled our sails and pulled the shore out of our sight — the shore where, come morning, she stood out of her mind with grief, filling your ears with complaints and groans. And you disregarded them, because you were using my own desires to haul me toward the end of all desiring, and chastening the earthly part of her love for me with the just whip of sorrows. She loved having me with her, as mothers do — only far more than most mothers; and she did not know what joy you were going to make for her out of my absence. She did not know. So she wept and wailed, and in that agony the inheritance of Eve showed itself in her: seeking in sorrow what in sorrow she had brought into the world. And yet, when she had finished accusing my deceit and my cruelty, she turned back to pleading with you for me. She went home to her accustomed life; and I went to Rome.

But why I left here and went there, you knew, God, and you showed it neither to me nor to my mother, who wept bitterly over my going and followed me all the way to the sea. There she clung to me, to hold me back or come with me, but I lied to her — to such a mother — pretending I had a friend I could not leave until he caught a fair wind and sailed. So I lied to my mother, and to a mother like that, and got away. This too you have mercifully forgiven me, keeping me, full of execrable filth as I was, from the waters of the sea, for the water of your grace — by which, once I was washed, the streams from my mother's eyes were to be dried, the streams with which day after day she watered the ground beneath her face for me. And since she refused to go back without me, I barely talked her into staying the night in a place near our ship, where there was a shrine in memory of the blessed Cyprian. That night I slipped away in secret; she stayed behind, weeping and praying. And what was she begging of you, Lord, with all those tears, but that you would not let me sail? Yet you, in the depth of your designs, hearing the true point of her longing, took no notice of what she asked just then, so that you might make me into what she was always asking for. The wind blew and filled our sails and drew the shore out of our sight; and in the morning there she stood, frantic with grief, filling your ears with complaints and groans — which you then disregarded, while through my own cravings you were hurrying me on to put an end to craving, and the earthly part of her love for me was chastened by the appointed lash of sorrows. For she loved having me with her, as mothers do, but far more than most mothers; and she did not know what great joy you were about to make for her out of my going. She did not know it, and so she wept and wailed, and in that agony showed the inheritance of Eve, seeking in sorrow what in sorrow she had brought to birth. And yet, after blaming my treachery and my hardness of heart, she turned back to interceding with you for me, went back to her usual place, and I went on to Rome.

And look what received me at Rome: the whip of bodily sickness. I was on my way down to hell, carrying all the evils I had committed against you and against myself and against others — many, and grave, over and above the bond of that original sin by which we all die in Adam. For you had forgiven me none of them in Christ, nor had he dissolved on his cross the enmity my sins had built up between me and you. How could he dissolve it by the crucifixion of a phantom — which is what I believed him to be? The death of my soul was exactly as real as the death of his flesh seemed to me unreal; and the life of my soul was exactly as false as his death in the flesh was true — because my soul did not believe it. The fevers were climbing; I was on my way out, and on my way to ruin. If I had gone then, where would I have gone but into fire and torments that fit my deeds, in the truth of your order? My mother knew nothing of this — and, far away, she went on praying for me. And you, present everywhere, heard her where she was, and pitied me where I was, so that I got back the health of my body — while my sacrilegious heart stayed frantic and sick. Even in all that danger, I did not want your baptism. I was better as a boy, when I begged for it from my mother's devotion, as I have already recalled and confessed. But I had grown up into my own disgrace, and in my madness I laughed at the prescriptions of your medicine — you, who would not let me, in that condition, die twice over. Had that wound gone through my mother's heart, she would never have healed. For I cannot say enough what she carried in her heart for me — with how much harder an anguish she was now in labor with me in the spirit than she had ever been in the flesh.

And there I was met by the lash of bodily sickness, and I was going down toward hell, carrying all the sins I had committed against you, against myself, and against others — many and grievous — over and above that bond of original sin by which we all die in Adam. For you had forgiven me none of them in Christ, nor had he undone, by his cross, the enmity I had brought on myself with you by my sins. How could he, by the crucifixion of a phantom — for that is what I believed him to be? As real, then, as I thought the death of his flesh was false, so real was the death of my soul; and as false as I thought the death of his body, so real was the death of my own soul, which did not believe it. And now, with the fever climbing, I was going, going, on my way out for good. For if I had gone out then, where would I have gone but into the fire and the torments my deeds deserved, in the truth of your ordering? And this she did not know, yet far away she was praying for me. But you, present everywhere, heard her where she was, and where I was you had compassion on me, so that I got back the health of my body, still frenzied as I was in my godless heart. For in all that danger I did not long for your baptism — and I was better as a boy, when I begged for it from my mother's devotion, as I have already recounted and confessed. But I had grown up to my own shame, and in my madness I mocked the prescriptions of your medicine, you who would not let one such as I was die a double death. Had that wound struck my mother's heart, it could never have been healed. For I cannot put into words the love she bore me, and with how much more fierce an anguish she was now in labor with me in the spirit than she had been at my birth in the flesh.

I do not see how she could have been healed if a death like that — my death, in that state — had run through the very core of her love. And where would they have been then, all those prayers — so many of them, so constant, offered to no one but you? Would you, God of mercies, have despised the contrite and humbled heart of a chaste and sober widow, generous with alms, dutiful in the service of your saints, letting no day pass without an offering at your altar; coming to your church twice a day, morning and evening, without fail — and not for idle gossip and old wives' tales, but to hear you in your words, and to be heard by you in her prayers? Could you have despised the tears of such a woman, and turned her away from your help — when what she begged of you was not gold or silver, not any shifting, perishable good, but the salvation of her son's soul — she, whom your own gift had made what she was? Never, Lord. No: you were there, hearing and acting, in the order you had determined long before that it should be done. Far be it from you to have deceived her in those visions and those answers of yours — the ones I have mentioned and the ones I have not — which she kept in her faithful heart, and in her constant prayer pressed upon you like bonds signed in your own hand. Because your mercy endures forever, you condescend, with those whose debts you have wholly forgiven, to make yourself a debtor in turn — by your promises.

I cannot see, then, how she could have been healed, had such a death of mine pierced clean through the bowels of her love. And where would all those strong, ceaseless prayers of hers have gone, that never let up toward you alone? But would you, God of mercies, despise the contrite and humbled heart of that chaste and sober widow — so quick to give alms, so dutiful in her service to your holy ones, never letting a day pass without bringing her offering to your altar, coming morning and evening, without a break, to your church, not for idle gossip and old wives' tales, but so that she might hear you in your sermons and you might hear her in her prayers? Could you despise and turn away from your help the tears of a woman like that — tears with which she begged you not for gold or silver, not for any changing, passing good, but for the salvation of her son's soul — you, by whose gift she was such a woman? Never, Lord. No, you were at hand, and you were hearing and acting, in the very order in which you had determined beforehand it should be done. Far be it from you to have deceived her in your visions and your answers — some of which I have set down, some I have not — which she stored up in her faithful heart, and, ever praying, pressed on you as your own handwriting. For you, because your mercy lasts forever, make yourself a debtor by your own promises to those whose every debt you forgive.

So you brought me back from that sickness. You healed the son of your handmaid — in body, for the time being — so that he would be alive for you to give him a better and surer health. And even then, in Rome, I attached myself to those 'saints' — deceived men, and deceivers; and not only to their hearers, one of whom was the man in whose house I had fallen sick and recovered, but even to the ones they call the Elect. For I still believed that it is not we who sin, but some other nature — who knows what — sinning inside us. It flattered my pride to stand outside the fault: when I had done something evil, not to confess that I had done it, so that you could heal my soul for sinning against you, but to excuse the soul and accuse — I never knew what — some other thing that was with me and was not me. But of course it was all me. My own impiety had split me against myself. And my sin was the more incurable precisely because I did not count myself a sinner; and it was a damnable perversity to prefer that you, you, God almighty, be defeated inside me to my ruin, rather than that I be defeated by you and saved. You had not yet set a guard on my mouth and a door of restraint around my lips, to keep my heart from sliding into wicked words and making excuses for sins in the company of men who deal in evil — and so I still kept company with their Elect.

So you brought me back from that sickness, and healed the son of your handmaid — for the time, in body — that he might live, and you might give him a better and more lasting health. And even then, at Rome, I joined myself to those deceiving and deceived "holy ones" — not only their hearers, of whom the man was one in whose house I had fallen sick and recovered, but also those they call the "Elect." For I still thought it was not we who sin, but some other nature, I knew not what, that sins in us; and it flattered my pride to be free of blame, and when I had done some evil, not to confess that I had done it, so that you might heal my soul because it had sinned against you — no, I loved to excuse myself and to accuse some other thing, I knew not what, that was with me but was not me. But in truth it was wholly I, and my own godlessness had split me against myself; and that sin was the more incurable for my not judging myself a sinner. It was an execrable wickedness, that I would rather have you, you, God almighty, be defeated in me to my own ruin, than be defeated by you for my salvation. You had not yet set a watch over my mouth and a door of guarding around my lips, that my heart might not slide off into wicked words to make excuses for sins, in company with men who do iniquity; and so I was still bound up with their Elect.

But I had given up hope of getting anywhere in that false doctrine, and even the positions I had resolved to settle for — failing anything better — I now held loosely and carelessly. For a thought was half-forming in me that the shrewdest of the philosophers had been the ones they call Academics, because they taught that everything must be doubted, and ruled that no truth can be grasped by man. That, at least, is what they plainly seemed to me to hold — the common opinion of them — though I did not yet understand what they were really after. And I did not hesitate to talk my host out of the overconfidence I could see he had in the fabulous stuff that fills Mani's books. Still, I stayed on closer terms of friendship with the Manichees than with people outside that heresy. I no longer defended it with my old fire; but intimacy with the sect — Rome quietly shelters a good many of them — made me slower to look for anything else. Above all, I had no hope that the truth could be found in your Church, Lord of heaven and earth, maker of all things visible and invisible, because they had turned me away from it: it seemed to me outright shameful to believe that you had the shape of human flesh and were bounded by the bodily outline of our limbs. And since, whenever I wanted to think about my God, I could think of nothing but masses of body — nothing else seemed to me to exist at all — this was the greatest, and almost the only, cause of my error; and the error could not be escaped.

But now, despairing of getting anywhere in that false doctrine, I held even the things I had decided to rest content with, if I could find nothing better, more loosely and carelessly. For a thought half rose in me that those philosophers they call Academics had been wiser than the rest, in holding that men ought to doubt everything and laying it down that no truth can be grasped by a human being. For so they are commonly reported, and that is how I took them, not yet understanding even what they meant. And I openly discouraged my host from the over-confidence I saw he had in those fables that fill the books of Manichaeus. Even so, I lived on more familiar terms with the Manichees than with people outside that heresy. I no longer defended it with my old eagerness, yet my closeness to the sect — and Rome was secretly harboring many of them — made me slower to look for any other way, especially since I despaired of finding the truth, from which they had turned me aside, in your Church, Lord of heaven and earth, Maker of all things visible and invisible. It seemed to me a most unfitting thing to believe that you had the shape of human flesh and were bounded by the bodily outline of our limbs. And because, whenever I tried to think of my God, I could not conceive of anything but a mass of bodies — for whatever was not such a mass did not seem to me to be anything at all — this was the greatest, almost the only, cause of my inescapable error.

From the same root, I believed that evil too was a substance of that kind, with its own foul, misshapen bulk — either dense, the kind they call earth, or thin and fine like the body of the air, which they picture as a malignant mind crawling through that earth. And because such piety as I had forced me to believe that a good God never created any evil nature, I set up two masses facing each other, both infinite — the evil one narrower, the good one vaster — and from that diseased starting-point the rest of my sacrileges followed. When my mind tried to run back to the Catholic faith, it was thrown back, because what I took for the Catholic faith was not the Catholic faith. And I felt more devout believing you infinite on every side but one, my God — to whom your own mercies confess out of my mouth — even though on the side where the mass of evil stood against you I was forced to call you finite, than if I had imagined you bounded on all sides by the shape of a human body. And it seemed better to believe that you had created no evil — which in my ignorance I took to be not just a substance but a bodily one, since I could not think of mind except as a fine sort of body, spread out through space — better that, than to believe that the nature of evil, as I conceived it, could come from you. Even our Savior himself, your Only-begotten, I imagined as something stretched out for our rescue from the mass of your most luminous bulk — so that I believed nothing about him except what my vanity could picture. A nature like that, I reasoned, could not be born of the Virgin Mary without being mixed into flesh; and how what I had imagined could be mixed in and not be defiled, I could not see. So I was afraid to believe him born in the flesh, or I would have had to believe him dirtied by the flesh. Your spiritual ones will smile at me now, gently and with love, if they read these confessions of mine. But that is what I was.

For from this I believed evil too to be some such substance, with its own foul and hideous bulk: either gross, which they called earth, or thin and fine, like the body of the air, which they imagine to be some malignant mind creeping through that earth. And because a kind of devotion, such as it was, made me believe that the good God created no evil nature, I framed two masses opposed to each other, both unbounded — the evil one narrower, the good one wider. And from that diseased beginning the other blasphemous fancies followed in me. For when my mind tried to fall back on the Catholic faith, it was driven back, since what I took to be the Catholic faith was not. And I thought myself more reverent in believing you, my God — to whom your mercies confess out of my mouth — to be unbounded on all sides but the one, where the mass of evil stood opposed to you, where I was forced to confess you bounded, than if on every side I were to imagine you bounded by the shape of a human body. And it seemed better to me to believe that you had created no evil — which to my ignorance seemed not just some evil but a bodily substance, since I could not conceive of mind except as a fine sort of body spread out through definite spaces — than to believe that the nature of evil, such as I conceived it, could come from you. Our Savior himself, your Only-Begotten, I believed had been put forth, as it were, for our salvation out of the mass of your most shining substance, and so could believe nothing of him but what I could picture in my emptiness. His nature, being such, could not, I thought, be born of the Virgin Mary without being mingled with the flesh; and how what I had so pictured could be mingled and not defiled, I did not see. So I was afraid to believe him born in the flesh, for fear I should be forced to believe him defiled by the flesh. Your spiritual ones will now smile on me gently and lovingly, if they read these confessions of mine. Yet that is what I was.

Besides, I did not think the things the Manichees attacked in your Scriptures could be defended. Yet now and then I genuinely wanted to sit down over each disputed point with someone deeply versed in those books, and find out what he thought. Already at Carthage the words of a man named Elpidius, who spoke and argued face to face against the Manichees, had begun to work on me: he brought material out of the Scriptures that was not easy to resist, and their answer to it seemed feeble to me. They did not like giving that answer in public, but only to us in private. It was that the Scriptures of the New Testament had been tampered with by persons unknown, who wanted to graft the law of the Jews onto the Christian faith — and yet the Manichees themselves could produce no uncorrupted copies. But it was those 'masses' that chiefly held me down. Thinking of nothing but bodies, I lay pinned under them, half-suffocated — and panting for the air of your truth, I could not breathe it pure and clean.

Furthermore, what the Manichees had found fault with in your Scriptures I thought could not be defended; and yet at times I truly wished I could talk these various points over with someone really well versed in those books, and find out what he thought. For the words of one Helpidius, speaking and arguing face to face against the Manichees, had begun to stir me back at Carthage, in that he brought out of the Scriptures things not easily withstood; and the Manichees' reply seemed to me feeble — a reply they did not like to give in public, but only to us in private. It was that the Scriptures of the New Testament had been tampered with by someone, they could not say who, who wanted to graft the law of the Jews onto the Christian faith — yet they produced no uncorrupted copies themselves. But I, conceiving only of bodily things, was held down most of all, weighed on and all but suffocated, by those "masses," gasping under them for a breath of your truth, and unable to breathe it pure and untainted.

So I set to work at the thing I had come to Rome to do: teach rhetoric. First I gathered a few students at my lodgings, and with them, and through them, my name began to be known. And behold — I discovered that Rome had abuses of its own, which I had not had to swallow in Africa. The wreckings by degenerate young men did not happen there, it was true, just as I had been told. But instead, they warned me, a pack of students will suddenly conspire to dodge paying their teacher's fee, and decamp together to another master — breakers of faith, who hold justice cheap and money dear. My heart hated them too, though not with a perfect hatred: I probably hated them more for what I stood to lose by them than for the wrong they did to anyone at all. Still, such people are foul. They go whoring away from you; they love the passing mockeries of time, and dirty money, which fouls the hand that closes on it; they hug a world that is running through their fingers, and despise you — you, who remain, who call back, who pardon the prostituted human soul when it returns to you. And I hate such warped and crooked men now, too; but I love them as men who can be corrected — men who might come to prefer the learning to the money, and to the learning, you, God: the truth, the fullness of certain good, the purest peace. Back then, though, I simply did not want them to be bad, for my own sake; I had not yet learned to want them good for yours.

So I set diligently about the work I had come to Rome for, the teaching of rhetoric, and first gathered a few to my house, to whom and through whom I was beginning to be known — when, look, I found other wrongs being done at Rome that I had not been exposed to in Africa. True, those "wreckings" by profligate young men were not practiced here, I was told; but all at once, they said, to dodge paying their teacher his fee, a band of youths would plot together and transfer to another — breakers of faith, who for love of money hold justice cheap. These too my heart hated, though not with a perfect hatred; for perhaps I hated them more because of what I would suffer through them than because of the wholly unlawful thing they did. Such people are surely base, and they go whoring away from you, loving these fleeting mockeries of passing things, and the filthy money that fouls the hand that grips it, hugging the fleeting world and despising you, who abide, and call back, and forgive the adulterous soul of man when she returns to you. And now I do hate such crooked and twisted people, though I love them if they can be set right, so as to prefer to their money the learning they acquire, and to that learning, you, God, the truth and the fullness of sure good and the purest peace. But back then I disliked them as bad more for my own sake than I liked and wished them good for yours.

Then word came from Milan to Rome, to the prefect of the city, asking that a professor of rhetoric be furnished for Milan, with travel at public expense. I applied for the post — through those same men, drunk on Manichean vanities; I was going, though neither they nor I knew it, in order to be rid of them — and Symmachus, then prefect, tested me with a set speech and sent me. And I came to Milan, to Ambrose the bishop, known across the whole world as one of the best of men, your devout servant, whose eloquence in those days was strenuously serving your people the finest of your wheat, the gladness of your oil, and the sober drunkenness of your wine. I was led to him, unknowing, by you, so that by him I might be led, knowing, to you. That man of God took me in like a father; he welcomed this stranger's coming the way a bishop should. And I began to love him — not, at first, as a teacher of the truth, which I had utterly despaired of finding in your Church, but simply as a man who was kind to me. I listened closely whenever he preached to the people — not with the intent I should have had, but sampling his eloquence, so to speak: testing whether it lived up to its fame, whether it ran fuller or thinner than report made it. I hung on his words, attentive; toward the substance I stood aloof, a scornful bystander. And I enjoyed the sweetness of his speech — more learned than Faustus's, though in delivery less sparkling, less caressing. In substance, there was no comparison: the one was straggling through Manichean tricks; the other was teaching salvation, and teaching it soundly. But salvation is far from sinners, and that is what I was, standing there. And yet I was drawing closer, little by little, and did not know it.

So when the people of Milan sent to the prefect of the city of Rome, asking him to supply them a teacher of rhetoric for their city, with the journey paid from public funds, I made application — through those very men, drunk on Manichaean emptiness, to be freed from whom I was, all unknowing, on my way, and they no more knowing it than I — that Symmachus, then prefect of the city, would test me by setting me a subject and so send me. And to Milan I came, to Ambrose the bishop, known throughout the world as among the best of men, your devout servant, whose eloquent preaching was then richly handing out to your people the flour of your wheat, the gladness of your oil, and the sober intoxication of your wine. To him I was led, all unknowing, by you, that by him I might knowingly be led to you. That man of God received me like a father, and showed me a bishop's kindness at my coming. From then on I began to love him — at first not as a teacher of the truth, which I utterly despaired of finding in your Church, but as a man kind to me. And I listened carefully to him preaching to the people, not with the intent I should have, but as it were testing his eloquence, to see whether it lived up to its fame, or flowed fuller or thinner than report had it; and I hung on his words attentively, but stood as a careless and scornful onlooker over what he said. I was charmed by the sweetness of his speech, which was more learned, though less coaxing and warm in manner, than Faustus's. As for the matter, there was no comparison: the one was wandering among Manichaean delusions, the other teaching salvation most soundly. But salvation is far from sinners, such as I then stood before him; and yet, little by little, and without knowing it, I was drawing nearer.

For although I took no trouble to learn what he was saying, only to hear how he said it — that hollow interest was all I had left, since I despaired of any road lying open to you for man — still, along with the words I loved, the matter I meant to ignore kept arriving in my mind. I could not pry them apart. And while I was opening my heart to take in how eloquently he spoke, there entered, in the same motion, how truly he spoke — though only by degrees. First it began to dawn on me that these positions could actually be defended: the Catholic faith, for which I had thought nothing could be said against the Manichees' attacks, I now judged could be held without embarrassment — especially once I had heard one hard place in the Old Testament after another untangled, and so often 'in a figure.' Taken literally, those passages had been killing me. So when many texts of those books had been opened up in their spiritual sense, I began to fault that old despair of mine — the belief that the Law and the Prophets simply could not stand against those who hated and mocked them. Yet I did not therefore feel that the Catholic way was the one to take, just because it too could field learned defenders, who could answer objections at length and without absurdity; nor that what I held stood condemned, just because the defenses had come out even. The Catholic side seemed to me not beaten — but not yet the winner, either.

For though I took no trouble to learn what he said, but only to hear how he said it — that empty concern was all I had left, despairing of any road open to a man to reach you — still, along with the words I was prizing came also the matter I was dismissing, for I could not keep them apart. And while I opened my heart to take in how eloquently he spoke, there entered, by degrees, how truly he spoke. For first these things began to seem to me capable of being defended; and the Catholic faith, on whose behalf I had thought nothing could be said against the Manichees' objections, I now saw might be upheld without absurdity — especially after I had heard one or two passages of the Old Testament unraveled, which, taken often "in a figure," had been killing me spiritually when I understood them literally. Many places in those books being thus explained, I now blamed my own despair for having believed that no answer at all could be given to those who hated and scoffed at the Law and the Prophets. Yet I did not therefore see that the Catholic way was the one to hold, just because it too could find learned defenders who could answer objections at length and with some show of reason; nor that what I held was to be condemned, just because both sides could be defended. The Catholic cause seemed to me not so much beaten as not yet victorious.

Then I bent my whole mind to the question of whether I could, by any decisive proof, convict the Manichees of falsehood. If I had been able to conceive of a spiritual substance, all their contraptions would have come apart at once and been thrown out of my mind. But I could not. Even so, where the physical world was concerned — the whole of nature that the senses of the flesh can reach — considering and comparing more and more, I judged that most of the philosophers had held views far more probable. So, doubting everything in the manner attributed to the Academics, wavering among all the options, I did settle this much: the Manichees had to go. Even in a season of doubt, I decided, I could not stay in a sect to which I now preferred certain of the philosophers — though to those philosophers, because they were without the saving name of Christ, I flatly refused to hand over the cure of my sick soul. So I determined to remain a catechumen in the Catholic Church — the church my parents had set before me — until some certainty should light the way I ought to steer.

On this I bent my mind hard, to see whether by any sure proof I could convict the Manichees of falsehood. Could I once have conceived of a spiritual substance, all their strongholds would have been thrown down and cast clean out of my mind. But I could not. And yet, concerning the frame of this world and the whole of nature that the senses of the flesh can reach, the more I considered and compared, the more I judged the views of most of the philosophers far more probable. So, after the manner of the Academics, as they are supposed to be — doubting everything and wavering between all things — I settled this much at least: that the Manichees were to be abandoned, judging that, even in my doubting, I ought not to stay in that sect, to which I now preferred some of the philosophers. To those philosophers, all the same, because they were without the saving Name of Christ, I utterly refused to hand over the cure of my sick soul. I resolved, therefore, to be a catechumen in the Catholic Church, to which my parents had commended me, until something certain should dawn on me by which to steer my course.

My hope from my youth — where were you all that time, and where had you gone? Wasn't it you who made me, you who set me apart from the four-footed beasts and made me wiser than the birds of the air? Yet I was walking through darkness, on slick ground, and looking for you outside myself; and I did not find the God of my own heart. I had gone down into the deep of the sea, and I had lost confidence, and despaired of ever finding truth. By now my mother had come to me — strong in her devotion, following me over land and sea, and in every danger of the road certain of you. In the storms at sea it was she who steadied the sailors, the very men who usually steady frightened passengers new to the deep: she promised them they would come through safe, because you had promised her so in a vision. She found me in a graver danger of my own — despair of ever tracking truth down. But when I told her that I was no longer a Manichee, though not yet a Catholic Christian either, she did not jump for joy as if the news were unhoped-for. About that half of my misery she was already calm. She had wept over me as over a dead man — but a dead man you would raise; she had been carrying me out to you on the bier of her thought, so that you might say to the widow's son, Young man, I say to you, get up — and he would revive and begin to speak, and you would give him back to his mother. So her heart did not shake with any wild exultation when she heard that what she begged of you daily, with tears, was already in such large part done: I had not yet reached truth, but I had been pulled clear of falsehood. Certain that you, who had promised the whole, would give what remained, she answered me very calmly, out of a heart brimming with confidence: she believed in Christ that before she left this life she would see me a faithful Catholic. That much she said to me. To you, fountain of mercies, she poured out prayers and tears redoubled, that you would hurry your help and light my darkness; and she ran the more eagerly to church and hung on Ambrose's lips, on the spring of water leaping up into everlasting life. She loved that man as an angel of God, because she knew it was he who had brought me, for the moment, to this wavering middle state — and she was fully confident that through it I would pass from sickness to health, once the fever had spiked the way it does just before recovery, at what physicians call the crisis.

You, my hope from my youth — where were you to me, and where had you gone? Was it not you who created me, and set me apart from the beasts of the field and the birds of the air? You had made me wiser than they, yet there I walked in the dark, on slippery ground, searching for you outside myself and not finding the God of my own heart. I had gone down into the depths of the sea, and I distrusted and despaired of ever finding the truth. By now my mother had come to me, made resolute by her devotion, following me over sea and land, trusting you in every danger. For when storms rose at sea, it was she who comforted the very sailors — the ones who usually comfort the passengers when they panic, the passengers who know nothing of the deep. She assured the sailors of a safe landing, because you had assured her of it in a vision. She found me in grave danger, despairing of ever finding the truth. But when I told her I was no longer a Manichee — though not yet a Catholic Christian — she was not overjoyed as at some surprise. She was already at rest about that part of my misery, the part for which she had wept over me as over a dead man, though a man you would raise again; she had been carrying me out on the bier of her thoughts, so that you might say to the widow's son, "Young man, I say to you, arise," and I might come back to life and begin to speak, and you might give me back to my mother. So her heart was shaken by no wild rejoicing when she heard that what she had begged of you in tears, day after day, was in such great part already done — that though I had not yet reached the truth, I had been rescued from the lie. Instead, certain that you who had promised the whole would one day give the rest, she answered me quite calmly, her heart full of confidence, that she believed in Christ she would see me a Catholic believer before she left this life. That much she said to me. But to you, Fountain of mercies, she poured out still more prayers and tears, begging you to hurry your help and lighten my darkness; and she hurried all the more eagerly to church, hanging on the lips of Ambrose, praying for that spring of water that wells up to everlasting life. She loved that man like an angel of God, because she knew it was through him that I had been brought, for now, to the wavering, in-between state of faith I was in — through which, she was sure, I would pass from sickness to health, after a sharper attack of fever, the kind doctors call "the crisis."

In Africa my mother had been used to bringing food — a dish and bread and unmixed wine — to the memorial shrines of the saints. When she tried it here, the doorkeeper stopped her; and the moment she learned it was the bishop who had forbidden it, she took the ruling so devoutly and so obediently that I marveled at her — how readily she turned accuser of her own custom rather than critic of his ban. No thirst for wine had her spirit under siege; no love of drink goaded her into hating truth, the way it does so many, men and women both, who gag at a hymn to sobriety like drunkards at a watered cup. When she brought her basket of festival food, to taste and then give away, she never set out for herself more than one small cup, watered to the strength of her own very sober palate, and sipped from it only for courtesy. And if there were many shrines of the dead to be honored that way, it was the same single cup she carried round to all of them — not only watered thin by now but grown lukewarm from the carrying — and she shared it out in little sips to those around her. She was there for devotion, not pleasure. So as soon as she found that this famous preacher, this most devout bishop, had banned the custom even for those who kept it soberly — so that drunkards would get no license to soak, and because these rites, like a yearly feast for the dead, looked all too close to pagan superstition — she gave it up with all her heart; and in place of a basket full of the fruits of the earth she learned to bring the shrines of the martyrs a breast full of purer offerings. She gave what she could to the poor; and so the communion of the Lord's body was celebrated rightly there — there, where the martyrs, after the pattern of his passion, had been sacrificed and crowned. And yet it seems to me, Lord my God — and this is how my heart weighs it in your sight — that she might not have bent so easily to the cutting off of that custom if it had been forbidden by some other man, one she did not love as she loved Ambrose. Him she loved above all men for the sake of my salvation; and he loved her for her deeply devout way of living — for the good works and the fervor of spirit that kept her always at church — so that when he saw me he would often break out in her praises and congratulate me on having such a mother. He did not know what a son she had: a man who doubted all of it, and did not believe the way to life could be found.

Once my mother brought to the churches built over the saints' graves, as she used to do in Africa, some little cakes and bread and wine, and the doorkeeper turned her away. When she learned that the bishop himself had forbidden this, she embraced his ruling so devoutly and obediently that I marveled at how readily she condemned her own custom rather than argue against his ban. For her spirit was under no siege from wine; no love of drink stirred her to hate the truth, the way it does so many, men and women alike, who gag at a lesson on sobriety the way a heavy drinker gags at watered wine. When she had brought her basket with the usual feast-day food, to be tasted by her and then given away, she never set out more than a single small cup of wine, diluted to her own sober taste, which she would sip for courtesy's sake. And if there were many shrines of departed saints to be honored in that way, she carried that same one cup around to be used everywhere; and though by then it was thoroughly watered and gone unpleasantly warm from being carried about, she would share it out in tiny sips to those around her, for she came there for devotion, not pleasure. So as soon as she found that this custom had been forbidden by that famous preacher and most devout bishop — forbidden even to those who would keep it soberly, in case it gave the heavy drinkers an excuse, and because these yearly graveside rites were too much like the superstition of the pagans — she gladly gave it up. In place of a basket loaded with the fruits of the earth, she had learned to bring to the shrines of the martyrs a heart loaded with purer prayers, and to give what she could to the poor, so that the sharing of the Lord's body might be rightly kept there, in the place where the martyrs had been sacrificed and crowned in the likeness of his Passion. Yet it seems to me, Lord my God — and this is how my heart reads it in your sight — that perhaps she would not have given up the custom so readily had it been forbidden by someone she did not love as she loved Ambrose; and she loved him utterly, for my salvation's sake. He, in turn, loved her for her deeply religious life, in which, fervent in spirit, she was constant in her good works and her churchgoing — so that when he saw me, he often broke into praise of her, congratulating me on having such a mother, not knowing what a son she had in me: one who doubted all these things and supposed there was no finding the road to life.

And I was not yet groaning in prayer for your help. My mind was bent on inquiry and restless for debate. Ambrose himself I counted a fortunate man as the world reckons fortune — so much honor from such important people; only his celibacy looked like a hardship to me.
