What hope he carried inside him, what battles he fought against the temptations that came with his very eminence, what comfort he had in adversity, what sweet joys your bread held for the hidden mouth of his heart when he chewed it over — that I could not guess, and had never tasted. Nor did he know my seethings, or the pit gaping under me. I could not ask him what I wanted the way I wanted, because crowds of people with business — men whose weaknesses he served — walled me off from his ear and his mouth. And the little time he was not with them, he was restoring either his body with necessary food or his mind with reading. When he read, his eyes traveled the pages and his heart hunted out the sense, but his voice and tongue were still. Often when we came in — no one was ever turned away, and it was not his custom to have visitors announced — we found him reading like that, silently; never any other way. We would sit a long time in silence (who would dare intrude on a man so absorbed?) and then slip out, guessing that in the small interval he was granted for restoring his mind, on furlough from the din of other men's business, he did not want to be called away — and perhaps he was wary that if his author put something obscurely, some rapt or puzzled listener would make him stop and explain it, or argue out the knottier questions, and with his time spent that way he would get through fewer books than he wished. Though a truer reason for reading silently may have been to spare his voice, which broke down easily. But whatever his reason was, in such a man it was a good one.

I was not yet groaning in prayer for you to help me; my whole spirit was bent on learning and restless to argue. As for Ambrose, I counted him a happy man by the world's reckoning, since people of such standing held him in such honor; only his celibacy seemed to me a hard road. But what hope he carried within, what battles he fought against the temptations that come precisely with his gifts, what comfort he found in hardship, what hidden joys your Bread held for the secret mouth of his spirit as he chewed it over — none of this I could guess at, because none of it I had tasted. Nor did he know the tides of my feeling or the abyss I was in danger of. I could not ask him what I wanted to ask, the way I wanted to ask it: both his ear and his speech were walled off from me by crowds of busy people whose troubles he attended to. The little time he was not taken up with them he spent restoring his body with the food it strictly needed, or his mind with reading. And when he read, his eyes ran down the page and his heart searched out the sense, but his voice and tongue stayed still. Often, when we came in — for no one was barred, and it was not his habit to have visitors announced — we found him reading like this, silently, never any other way; and after sitting a long while without a word (for who would dare break in on such concentration?), we would leave again, guessing that in the little space he got free from the din of other people's affairs, to refresh his mind, he did not want to be interrupted. Perhaps too he was afraid that if the author he was reading said anything obscurely, some intent or puzzled listener would want it explained, or want to thrash out some harder question, and so his time would go, and he would get through fewer of the books he longed to read. Though the truer reason for reading to himself may have been to save his voice, which the least speaking wore out. But whatever his reason, in such a man it was surely good.

So there was no chance to ask what I longed to ask of that holy oracle of yours, his heart — nothing, unless it could be answered briefly. My surging troubles needed him fully at leisure before I could pour them out, and they never found him so. But every Sunday I heard him expounding the word of truth rightly among the people, and I grew surer and surer that every knot of cunning slander our deceivers had tied around the divine books could be untied. And when I discovered that man made by you in your own image was not understood by your spiritual children — the ones you have brought to second birth by grace, out of our Catholic mother — as though they believed you penned inside the shape of a human body (even though what a spiritual substance might be I could not conceive, even faintly, even in shadow), I blushed, and gladly: all those years I had been barking not at the Catholic faith but at the figments of a mind that could think only in flesh. I had been reckless and impious: things I ought to have asked about and learned, I had pronounced on and condemned. For you — highest and nearest, most hidden and most present — have no limbs, some larger and some smaller; you are whole everywhere, and nowhere confined in space; you are certainly not this bodily shape of ours. Yet you made man in your own image — and look at him: head to foot, he fits inside space.

Still, I found no chance to ask that holy oracle of yours — his heart — what I wanted, unless the thing could be answered briefly. The tides in me that needed to be poured out to him required his full leisure, and never found it. I did hear him every Lord's Day, rightly laying open the word of truth before the people, and I grew more and more convinced that all the knots of cunning slander our deceivers had tied against the holy books could be untied. And when I came to understand that "man, created by you in your own image" was not taken by your spiritual sons — those you have given new birth, through grace, out of our Catholic Mother — to mean that they imagined you bounded by a human shape (though what a spiritual substance might be I had not even the faintest shadow of an idea), I blushed for joy that for so many years I had been barking not against the Catholic faith but against the inventions of fleshly imaginations. For I had been so rash and irreverent that what I should have learned by asking, I had pronounced upon and condemned. You, Most High and most near, most hidden and most present, who have no limbs some larger and some smaller, but are wholly everywhere and nowhere in space — you are not of any such bodily shape, and yet you made man in your own image, and look, from head to foot he is contained in space.

Not knowing how this image of yours could be, I should have knocked and put the question — how is this to be believed? — instead of jeering at it and fighting it, as if it were believed the crude way I imagined. So the anxiety over what to hold on to gnawed my heart all the harder for the shame: that I had been strung along so many years by the promise of certainties, and had prattled out so many uncertainties as if I knew them, with a child's error and a child's heat. That they were flat falsehoods only became clear to me later. What was already clear was that they were uncertain — and that I had once held them for certain, in the days when I attacked your Catholic Church with a blind pugnacity. I had not yet discovered that she taught the truth; but I had discovered that she did not teach the things I had so bitterly charged her with. So I was confounded, and I was turning; and I rejoiced, my God, that your one and only Church, the body of your only Son — the Church in which the name of Christ was laid on me as an infant — had no taste for infantile nonsense, and nowhere in her sound teaching would cram you, the creator of all, into any space, however vast, however wide, that was still bounded on every side by the outline of a human body.

Not knowing, then, how this image of yours could exist, I should have knocked and asked how it was to be believed, instead of jeering at it as if it were already believed in that crude form. And so doubt — about what I could hold for certain — gnawed all the more sharply at my heart, and I was all the more ashamed that for so long I had been fooled and deceived by the promise of certainties, and had babbled with a child's recklessness about so many uncertain things as though they were sure. That they were falsehoods became clear to me only later; but I was already certain that they were uncertain, and that I had once counted them certain, when with blind contentiousness I accused your Catholic Church. I did not yet find her teaching the truth, but at least I now saw that she did not teach the thing for which I had so harshly condemned her. So I was put to shame, and I was turned around; and I rejoiced, my God, that the one and only Church, the body of your only Son — the Church in which the name of Christ had been laid on me as an infant — had no taste for childish fancies, and held no doctrine in her sound teaching that would shut you, the Creator of all, inside any space, however vast and wide, yet everywhere bounded by the outline of a human body.

I rejoiced too that the old scriptures, the law and the prophets, were now set before me to be read with a different eye than before, when they had looked absurd to me and I would attack your saints for holding opinions they never held. And it gladdened me to hear Ambrose, in his sermons to the people, commend this text again and again, most diligently, as a rule: The letter kills, but the spirit gives life. And when he drew back the veil of mystery and laid open the spiritual sense of passages that, taken by the letter, seemed to teach something warped, nothing he said offended me — though whether what he said was true, I did not yet know. I was holding my heart back from assenting to anything, afraid of a headlong fall — and the hanging was killing me instead. I wanted to be as certain about things I could not see as I was certain that seven and three are ten. I was not so far gone as to think even that was beyond knowing; but I wanted everything else exactly that clear — bodily things not present to my senses, and spiritual things, which I had no way of conceiving except as bodies. Believing could have healed me: the eyesight of my mind, cleared, might then have been turned toward your truth, which abides forever and fails in nothing. But it was with me as with a man who has known a bad doctor and is afraid afterward to trust himself to a good one. The health of my soul could not be healed except by believing — and it refused to be healed, for fear of believing falsehoods; and it fought your hands, though you are the one who mixed the medicines of faith, and spread them over the diseases of the whole world, and vested them with such authority.

I rejoiced too that the old Scriptures of the Law and the Prophets were now set before me to be read with a different eye than before — when they had seemed to me absurd, and I had reviled your holy ones for thinking as I supposed they did, though in fact they did not. And it was a joy to hear Ambrose, again and again in his sermons to the people, recommend most earnestly this rule: "The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life." He would draw back the veil of mystery and lay open spiritually what, taken by the letter, seemed to teach something monstrous. Nothing in this offended me, though what he taught I did not yet know to be true. For I held my heart back from giving its assent to anything, afraid of falling headlong; and by hanging there in suspense, I was the more surely killed. I wanted to be as certain of the things I could not see as I was that three and seven make ten. I was not so far gone as to think even that could not be grasped; but I longed to have everything else as clear as that — whether bodily things not before my senses, or spiritual things, which I had no way of conceiving except as bodies. By believing I might have been healed, so that the eye of my soul, once cleared, might somehow be aimed at your truth, which stands forever and fails in nothing. But it was with me as with a man who, having once trusted a bad doctor, is then afraid to trust himself even to a good one: my soul's health, which could be healed only by believing, refused to be cured for fear of believing what was false — and so it fought off your hands, the hands that mixed the medicines of faith and laid them on the diseases of the whole world, and gave them such great power to heal.

From this point I began to prefer the Catholic teaching. Here, I felt, there was more modesty and no fraud in her asking belief for things not demonstrated — whether they were demonstrable in themselves though not to everyone, or not demonstrable at all — while over there a rash promise of knowledge first mocked our credulity, and then a mountain of the most fabulous and absurd things was ordered to be believed, precisely because they could not be demonstrated. Then you, Lord, little by little, with your most tender and most merciful hand touching my heart and settling it, persuaded me. I considered how innumerable were the things I believed without ever seeing them or being there when they happened — so much in the history of nations, so much about places and cities I had never laid eyes on, so much taken on trust from friends, from doctors, from this man and that — things we could do nothing at all in this life without believing; and last, how unshakably fixed I held it which two parents I came from, which I could not possibly have known without believing what I was told. Considering all this, you persuaded me that the blame lay not with the people who believed your books — books you have established with such authority through nearly all the nations — but with the people who refused to believe them; and that I need not listen to anyone who said, 'How do you know those books were given to the human race by the spirit of the one true and truthful God?' That was the very thing that deserved belief most of all. For no siege of quibbling questions, out of the whole crowd of philosophers I had read contradicting one another, had ever been able to wring from me the belief that you are — whatever you are, and I did not know what — and that the government of human affairs is yours.

Drawn from this, though, to prefer the Catholic teaching, I felt that here she went about it more modestly and honestly: she asked that things not proved should be believed — whether because they could be proved, though not to just anyone, or could not be proved at all — whereas among the Manichees our trust was mocked with a promise of sure knowledge, and then a heap of the most fabulous, absurd things was forced on us to believe, just because they could not be proved. Then you, Lord, little by little, with the most gentle and merciful hand, touched and settled my heart. I considered how countless were the things I believed that I had not seen and was not present at when they were done: so much in secular history, so many reports of places and cities I had never visited, so much I took on the word of friends, of doctors, of one person after another — things that, unless we believed them, we could do nothing at all in this life. And, last of all, with how unshakable an assurance I believed which parents I was born to, which I could never have known except by believing what I was told. So you persuaded me that the ones to be blamed were not those who believed your books, which you have established with such great authority among almost every nation, but those who did not believe them; and that I should not listen to anyone who asked me, "How do you know those Scriptures were given to mankind by the Spirit of the one true and truthful God?" For this above all was to be believed, since no amount of quarrelsome, blasphemous questioning in all those self-contradicting philosophers I had read could wring from me the belief that you exist — whatever you are, which I did not know — and that the governing of human affairs belongs to you.

This I believed sometimes more strongly, sometimes more faintly; but I always believed both that you are and that you care for us, even though I did not know what to think about your substance, or which road leads to you and back to you. And so, since we were too weak to find truth by pure reasoning, and for that very reason needed the authority of the holy writings, I now began to believe that you would never have conferred such towering authority on that scripture through every land unless you had willed to be believed through it, and sought through it. The strange-sounding passages that used to trip me in those pages — now that I had heard so many of them explained, and explained credibly — I referred to the depth of the mysteries. And its authority seemed to me the more venerable, the more worthy of sacred trust, for this: that it lay open for everyone to read, yet kept the dignity of its secret for a deeper understanding — offering itself to all in the plainest words and the humblest style, while stretching to the utmost the attention of those who are not light of heart — so that it might gather everyone into its wide-open lap, and through narrow passages bring a few through to you: a few, but far more than if it did not stand on such a peak of authority, or draw the crowds into the lap of its holy lowliness. These were my thoughts, and you were beside me; I sighed, and you heard me; I wavered, and you steered me; I drifted down the broad way of the world, and you did not abandon me.

This I believed, sometimes more strongly, sometimes more weakly; but I always believed both that you exist and that you care for us, even while I was ignorant both of what to think about your nature and of which way led to you, or back to you. Since we were too weak to find the truth by pure reasoning, and for that very reason needed the authority of holy Scripture, I had now begun to believe that you would never have given that Writing such towering authority across all lands unless you had willed to be believed and to be sought through it. As for the things in Scripture that used to strike me as strange and offend me, now that I had heard several of them well explained I traced them back to the depth of their mysteries; and its authority looked all the more worthy of reverence and faith to me, in that while it lay open for everyone to read, it kept the majesty of its mysteries in its deeper meaning — stooping to all in the great plainness of its words and the lowliness of its style, yet calling out the closest attention of those who are not light of heart; so that it might take all comers into its open lap, and through narrow ways ferry a few across toward you, yet far more than if it did not stand on such a height of authority and did not draw the crowds into its embrace by its holy lowliness. These were my thoughts, and you were with me. I sighed, and you heard me. I wavered, and you steadied me. I wandered down the broad road of the world, and you did not abandon me.

I was gaping after honors, after money, after marriage — and you were laughing. In those cravings I suffered the bitterest reversals, and in this you were the kinder to me, the less you allowed anything to grow sweet that was not you. Look at my heart, Lord — you willed that I remember this and confess it to you. Let my soul cleave to you now, now that you have pulled it free of that clinging birdlime of death. How wretched it was! And you kept needling the raw place in its wound, so that it would leave everything else and turn to you — you who are above all things, and without whom all things would be nothing — turn, and be healed. How wretched I was, then, and how you worked on me, that one day, to make me feel my wretchedness. I was preparing to deliver a speech in praise of the emperor — a speech in which I would tell plenty of lies, and be applauded for the lying by men who knew — and my heart was panting under those anxieties, boiling with the fever of thoughts that were eating me alive, when, crossing one of the streets of Milan, I noticed a beggar — his belly full by then, I imagine — joking and glad. And I groaned, and said to the friends who were with me: look at the sorrows our madness buys us. All this straining of ours — like the load I was dragging that day, hauling my own unhappiness along under the whip of desire, and making it heavier by the hauling — and the whole of what we wanted was only to arrive at some carefree gladness. That beggar had beaten us to it, and we might never arrive at all. What he had gotten with a few begged coins, I was scheming toward through wretched twists and turnings: the joy of a happiness that passes. He did not have true joy — granted; but what I was hunting with those ambitions of mine was far falser still. And there was no arguing with this much: he was merry, I was anxious; he was carefree, I was afraid. If anyone had asked me whether I would rather be glad or scared, I would have answered, glad. But if he had asked next whether I would rather be that beggar or myself, I would have chosen myself, worn out with cares and fears as I was — and chosen out of sheer perversity. For where was the truth in it? I had no right to set myself above him because I was more educated, since the education gave me no joy: I used it to court men's approval — not even to teach them, only to please. Which is why you kept breaking my bones with the rod of your discipline.

I panted after honors, money, marriage; and you laughed at me. In these cravings I went through the bitterest frustrations, you being the kinder the less you let anything grow sweet to me that was not you. Look at my heart, Lord — you who wanted me to remember all this and confess it to you. Let my soul cling to you now that you have pulled it free from that gripping birdlime of death. How wretched it was! And you irritated the raw edge of its wound, so that, leaving everything else, it might turn to you, who are above all things, without whom all things would be nothing — turn, and be healed. How miserable I was then, and how you went to work to make me feel my misery, on the day I was getting ready to deliver a speech in praise of the emperor, in which I would tell many a lie, and lying, be applauded by people who knew I was lying! My heart was pounding with all this strain, boiling with the fever of consuming thoughts. And then, walking down one of the streets of Milan, I noticed a poor beggar — joking and merry, with, I suppose, a full belly. I sighed, and said to the friends with me how many sorrows come of our own madness. For with all our efforts — exactly the kind I was sweating at just then, dragging along the load of my own unhappiness under the goad of desire, and only adding to the load by dragging it — we were laboring to reach the very same lightness of heart that the beggar had reached ahead of us, and that we might never reach at all. What he had got with a few coins begged from passersby — the joy of a little patch of happiness — I was scheming for by so many weary windings and turnings. His joy was not the true joy, of course; but the joy I was after, with all my ambitious designs, was a far less true one still. And he, at least, was cheerful, and I was anxious; he had no cares, and I was full of fears. Yet if someone had asked me whether I would rather be merry or afraid, I would have said merry. And if he had asked whether I would rather be the man that beggar was, or the man I then was, I would have chosen to be myself, worn out as I was with cares and fears — but the choice would have been wrong. For was it really truer? I had no business preferring myself to him on the ground that I was better educated, since I took no joy in that, but only used it to please people — not to teach them, just to please them. And so you broke my bones with the rod of your correction.

So away from my soul with those who tell it, 'It matters where a man's joy comes from. That beggar rejoiced in drunkenness; you wanted to rejoice in glory.' What glory, Lord? A glory not in you. For just as his was no true joy, mine was no true glory — and it did the deeper damage to my mind. He would sleep off his wine that very night. I had gone to bed with mine and gotten up with it, and I would go to bed with it and get up with it again — how many days more, you, God, knew. Yes: it does matter where a man's joy comes from. I know it; and the joy of a faithful hope stands incomparably far from all that emptiness. But even then the beggar stood ahead of me. He was plainly the happier man — not only because he was drenched in cheerfulness while I was being gutted by worry, but because he had earned his wine by wishing people well, and I was chasing a swollen name by lying. I said much along these lines to my dear friends at the time, and through them I often took my own measure; and I found that it went badly with me, and I grieved, and doubled the badness by grieving; and if some piece of fortune smiled on me, I could hardly rouse myself to catch it, because it flew off almost before it could be held.

Away, then, from my soul with those who say to her, "It makes all the difference where a man's joy comes from. That beggar took his joy in drunkenness; you wanted to take yours in glory." What glory, Lord? A glory not in you. For just as his was no true joy, so that was no true glory — and it unsettled my soul the more. He would sleep off his drunkenness that very night; but I had gone to sleep with mine and risen again with it, and was to sleep with it and rise with it again, day after day, for how many days you, God, know. Still, "it does make a difference where a man's joy comes from." I know it. The joy of a faithful hope lies beyond all comparison above such emptiness. And in that way the beggar was indeed beyond me even then; for he truly was the happier — not only because he was soaked in good cheer while I was gutted with cares, but because he had earned his wine with honest good wishes, while I was chasing an empty, swollen glory with my lying. Much to this effect I said to my friends then; and I often watched how it fared with me in their faces, and found that it went badly with me, and grieved, and so doubled the very badness; and if any bit of good fortune smiled on me, I had no heart to grab at it, for it flew away almost before I could close my hand.

All this we mourned over together, those of us who lived as friends, but I talked it through most, and most intimately, with Alypius and Nebridius. Alypius was born in the same town I was, to parents of the first rank there, and was younger than I. He had studied under me, both when I first taught in our town and later at Carthage, and he was very attached to me, because I seemed to him good and learned; and I to him, because of the great bent toward virtue that showed in him so young. And yet the whirlpool of Carthaginian morals — where the frivolous shows run at full boil — had sucked him into the madness of the circus races. While he was being tumbled about in that misery, I had a public school there and was teaching rhetoric; but he was not yet coming to me, because of a quarrel that had sprung up between his father and me. I had found out how ruinously he loved the circus, and it grieved me deeply that so much promise seemed about to be thrown away — if it had not been thrown away already. But I had no means of warning him or hauling him back, no claim on him through a friend's goodwill or a teacher's authority; I assumed he felt about me the way his father did. He was not like that. So, setting his father's feelings aside in the matter, he began to greet me, and to drop into my lecture room — listen a little, and leave.

These were the things we groaned over together, we who were living as friends; but I spoke of them most of all, and most intimately, with Alypius and Nebridius. Alypius was born in my own town, of leading families there, but younger than I. He had studied under me, both when I first taught at home and later at Carthage, and he loved me deeply, because I struck him as kind and learned; and I loved him for his great leaning toward goodness, plain enough in someone so young. Yet the whirlpool of Carthaginian habits — where those idle spectacles are followed so hotly — had dragged him into a madness for the games at the Circus. While he was being miserably tossed about in that, I was teaching rhetoric there in a public school of my own, but he was not yet my student, because of some ill-feeling that had risen between his father and me. I had found out how fatally he doted on the Circus, and it grieved me badly that he seemed likely to throw away — or had already thrown away — such great promise. But I had no way to advise him, or to reclaim him by any sort of friendly pressure, since I supposed he thought of me as his father did. But he did not; setting aside his father's mind in the matter, he began to greet me, to come sometimes into my lecture room, hear a little, and go.

Still, it had slipped my mind to deal with him at all — to keep a mind that good from being wrecked by a blind, headlong passion for empty games. But you, Lord, whose hand is on the tiller of everything you have created, had not forgotten him — a man who would one day stand among your sons as priest and steward of your sacrament. And so that his correction would be credited plainly to you, you worked it through me, and I knew nothing. One day, as I sat in my usual place with my students before me, he came in, greeted me, sat down, and gave his mind to what I was handling. I happened to have a text in hand, and as I expounded it a comparison from the circus races occurred to me — a way to make the point sweeter and plainer, salted with biting mockery for the men that madness had enslaved. You know, our God, that curing Alypius of that plague was the last thing on my mind. But he took it wholly to himself, and believed I had said it purely for his sake. What another man would have taken as grounds for anger at me, that honest young man took as grounds for anger at himself — and for loving me more warmly. You said it long ago, and wove it into your book: Rebuke a wise man, and he will love you. It was not I who had rebuked him. You use us all, knowing and unknowing, in the order you know — and that order is just — and out of my heart and my tongue you made burning coals, to sear a promising mind that was wasting away, and heal it. Let the man who does not weigh your mercies keep silent about your praise — those mercies confess to you out of my very marrow. For at those words he wrenched himself up out of the pit he had chosen to sink into, where the pleasure kept him in the dark; he shook his mind with a hard grip of self-command, and all the filth of the circus fell away from him, and he never went back. Then he wore down his reluctant father until he was allowed to be my student: the father gave way, and gave in. But once he began to hear me again, he got tangled with me in the same superstition. What he loved in the Manichees was their show of self-denial, which he took to be true and unfeigned. In fact it was a senseless, seducing self-denial — a snare for precious souls not yet able to touch the depth of virtue, and easily taken in by the surface of what was only a shadowed, counterfeit virtue.

I had, in fact, neglected to work on him, to keep him from wrecking so fine a mind through a blind and headlong craving for empty amusements. But you, Lord, who steer the course of everything you have made, had not forgotten him, who was one day to be among your children, a priest and a steward of your Sacrament; and so that his cure might plainly be credited to you, you worked it through me, without my knowing it. For one day, as I sat in my usual place with my students before me, he came in, greeted me, sat down, and turned his attention to the matter I was handling. I happened to have a passage in hand, and as I was explaining it a comparison from the races at the Circus came to me as a way to make my point pleasanter and clearer, seasoned with biting mockery of those whom that madness had enslaved. God, you know that I had no thought of curing Alypius of his infection. But he took the whole thing to himself, and believed I had said it for his sake alone. Where another man would have found grounds to be angry with me, that right-minded young man found grounds to be angry with himself, and to love me the more warmly. For you had said it long ago, and set it down in your book: "Rebuke a wise man, and he will love you." But I had not rebuked him; you had — you who put everyone, knowing or not knowing, to use in the order that you alone know, and that order is just. Out of my heart and tongue you made burning coals to set on fire that hopeful, languishing mind, and so heal it. Let anyone who does not weigh your mercies keep silent about your praises — those mercies that confess to you out of my inmost soul. For on hearing that, he burst up out of the deep pit into which he had willingly plunged himself, blinded by its wretched amusements, and with a strong act of self-command he shook his mind clear; and all the filth of the Circus games flew off him, and he never went back. After this he won over his unwilling father to let him become my student again. His father gave way and gave in. And Alypius, coming once more to hear me, was caught up in the same superstition as I was, loving in the Manichees that show of self-restraint which he took to be true and unforced — though it was a mindless, deceiving restraint, snaring precious souls not yet able to reach the depth of real virtue, and easily taken in by the surface of a shadowy, counterfeit one.

He had gone ahead of me to Rome to study law — not dropping the worldly career his parents had sung into his ears — and there, unbelievably, an unbelievable appetite for the gladiator shows carried him away. He had been utterly opposed to such things; he detested them. But one day a band of his friends and fellow students, running into him on their way back from dinner, dragged him — refusing hard, resisting — with that friendly violence of theirs into the amphitheater, on a day of the cruel and lethal games. He kept telling them: 'You can drag my body into that place and sit it down, but can you point my mind and my eyes at the show? I will be there and be absent — and beat both you and it.' They heard him out and took him along anyway, curious, perhaps, to see whether he could actually do it. They arrived; they found what seats they could; and the whole place was seething with its monstrous pleasures. He shut the doors of his eyes and forbade his mind to walk out into all that evil. If only he had stopped his ears too! For at some turn in the fight a man went down, and a huge roar from the whole crowd struck him so hard that curiosity got the better of him. Ready, he thought, to despise the sight whatever it was — to see it and stay above it — he opened his eyes. And he took a worse wound in the soul than the fighter he had itched to look at took in the body; he fell more pitiably than the man whose fall had raised the roar. The noise came in through his ears and unlocked his eyes, and there was the way in — the opening for striking down and toppling a mind that was still bold rather than strong, and all the weaker because it had counted on itself when it ought to have counted on you. The instant he saw the blood, he drank down savagery with it. He did not turn away; he fixed his stare; he was gulping the madness and did not know it; he relished the crime of the combat and got drunk on its bloody pleasure. And he was no longer the man who had come, but one of the crowd he had come to — a true accomplice of the men who had brought him. What more is there to say? He watched, he shouted, he caught fire; he carried away with him a madness that goaded him to come back — not only with the friends who had first hauled him in, but ahead of them, hauling in others. And yet from all this too you plucked him out, with a hand most strong and most merciful, and taught him to put his confidence not in himself but in you. But that came long afterward.

Not abandoning the worldly career his parents had charmed him into pursuing, he had gone ahead of me to Rome to study law, and there he was swept away — past all belief — by an unbelievable passion for the shows of the gladiators. He had been utterly set against such spectacles and loathed them; but one day some of his friends and fellow students, meeting him by chance on their way back from dinner, hauled him off — for all his hard refusal and resistance — with friendly force, into the amphitheater, in the days of those cruel and deadly shows. He kept protesting: "Even if you drag my body into that place and plant me there, can you force me to turn my mind and my eyes onto those shows? I will be absent while present, and so will get the better of both you and them." Hearing this, they led him on all the same — wanting, perhaps, to test that very thing, whether he could do as he said. When they had come to the place and taken whatever seats they could, the whole arena was ablaze with that savage sport. He shut the gates of his eyes and forbade his mind to go out after such evil. If only he had stopped his ears too! For at one point in the fight, when a man fell, a great roar went up from the whole crowd and struck him hard; overcome by curiosity, and as if ready to despise and rise above whatever it was, even once he had seen it, he opened his eyes — and was struck with a deeper wound in his soul than the fighter he wanted to see was struck in his body. He fell more wretchedly than the man whose fall had raised that roar — the roar that came in through his ears and unlocked his eyes, opening a way for the striking down and beating flat of a soul more reckless than strong, the weaker because it had presumed on itself when it should have leaned on you. The moment he saw the blood, he drank down savagery with it, and did not turn away, but fixed his gaze, and drank in the frenzy without knowing it, taking delight in that guilty contest, drunk on the bloody pleasure. He was no longer the man who had come in, but one of the crowd he had joined — a true companion of those who had brought him. Why say more? He watched, he shouted, he caught fire, and carried away with him a madness that would goad him to come back — not only with the friends who had first dragged him, but ahead of them, and dragging in others. And yet from that too you plucked him out, with the strongest and most merciful hand, and taught him to trust not in himself but in you — though that came later.

That day, though, was already being laid up in his memory as medicine for the future. So was another: while he was still my student at Carthage, he was in the forum at midday, turning over in his head a speech he had to give from memory — the usual school drill — when you let him be seized by the officers of the market as a thief. And I think you let it happen, our God, for one reason only: that a man who was to become so great should begin learning early how rashly a man can be condemned by a man on credulous suspicion. He was walking by himself in front of the tribunal with his tablets and pen when a young man — one of the students, and the real thief — carrying a hidden hatchet, slipped in without Alypius noticing, got as far as the lead gratings that fence off the silversmiths' row, and began chopping out the lead. At the ring of the hatchet the silversmiths below began to stir, and sent men up to seize whomever they found. The thief heard their voices, dropped the hatchet, and ran, terrified of being caught holding it. Alypius, who had not seen him come in, did see him leave, and saw how fast he went; and wanting to know why, he stepped into the place, found the hatchet, and was standing there wondering at it, turning it over, when the men who had been sent found him — alone, iron in hand, the very iron whose ringing had startled them into coming. They seize him; they haul him off; and gathering the market crowd around them, they brag that they have caught a thief in the act. And from there he was led away, to be handed to the judge.

But all this was already being stored up in his memory as a medicine for later. So was something else. While he was still studying under me at Carthage, and was going over at midday in the marketplace a piece he had to deliver from memory, as students do for practice, you let him be seized by the market officers as a thief. For no other reason, I think, did you, our God, allow it, except that this man, who was one day to be so great, should already begin to learn that in judging a case one ought not to condemn a fellow man too quickly, out of rash belief. For as he was walking up and down by himself in front of the judgment seat, with his notebook and pen, look — a young man, a law student, the real thief, came in secretly with a hatchet, unseen by Alypius, as far as the lead gratings that fence in the silversmiths' shops, and began to cut the lead away. But the silversmiths underneath, hearing the chop of the hatchet, raised an alarm and sent men to seize whomever they should find. The thief, hearing their voices, ran off and left his hatchet behind, afraid of being caught with it. Alypius, who had not seen him come in, did see him leave, and noticed the speed of his flight; and wanting to know what was going on, he went into the spot, where he found the hatchet and stood examining it, wondering. Then the men who had been sent found him there alone, hatchet in hand — the very noise of which had startled them and brought them running. They grabbed him, hauled him off, and, gathering the loiterers of the marketplace, made their boast of having caught a notorious thief; and so he was being led off to the judge.

But this far, and no farther, was the lesson to go. For at once, Lord, you came to the rescue of his innocence — you, its only witness. As he was being marched off to prison or punishment, they were met by a certain architect, the man with chief charge of the public buildings. The crowd was especially glad it was he, because he had a way of suspecting them of the goods that kept vanishing from the forum: now at last, they thought, he could see who had really been doing the stealing. But this man had often seen Alypius at the house of a certain senator whose receptions he used to attend. Recognizing him at once, he took him by the hand, drew him out of the mob, asked how so great a calamity had come about, and heard the story; then he ordered the whole rabble — churning around him, shouting threats — to come with him. They came to the house of the young man who had done it. There in front of the door stood a slave boy, young enough to blurt the whole thing out with no thought of what trouble it might bring his master — for he had gone with his master to the forum. Alypius remembered him and told the architect; the architect showed the hatchet to the boy and asked whose it was. 'Ours,' he said at once — and, questioned further, he gave up everything. So the charge crossed over to that house; the mob that had already begun its victory strut over Alypius was put to shame; and the future steward of your word, the future examiner of so many cases in your church, went away more experienced, and better instructed.

But this was as far as Alypius was meant to be schooled in it. For at once, Lord, you came to the rescue of his innocence, of which you alone were witness. As he was being led off either to prison or to a beating, they were met by a certain architect who had the chief charge of the public buildings. They were especially glad to meet him, since he was the very man who used to suspect them of stealing the goods that went missing from the marketplace; now, they thought, they could show him at last who was behind the thefts. But the architect had often seen Alypius at the house of a certain senator, where Alypius regularly went to pay his respects; and recognizing him at once, he took him by the hand, drew him aside, and asked how this disaster had come about. He heard the whole story, and ordered the whole shouting, threatening crowd to come along with him. They came to the house of the young man who had done it. At the door stood a boy, young enough not to grasp any danger to his master, and so likely to let the whole thing out; he had gone with his master to the marketplace. Alypius recognized him and told the architect, who showed the boy the hatchet and asked, "Whose is this?" "Ours," the boy answered at once; and on further questioning he gave away everything. So the crime was shifted onto that house, the crowd that had begun to crow over Alypius was put to shame, and he who was to be a steward of your word and a judge of many cases in your Church went away the wiser and better taught.

This was the man I had found again at Rome. He fastened himself to me with the strongest of ties and went with me to Milan — partly so as not to leave me, partly to make some use of the law he had studied, more to please his parents than himself. Three times already he had sat as an assessor, with an incorruptibility that amazed everyone else — while he was more amazed at men who could set gold above honesty. And his character was tested with more than the bait of greed; it was tested with the goad of fear. At Rome he was assessor to the count of the Italian treasury. There was at that time a certain senator of enormous power, a man who had half the city bound to him by favors and the other half afraid of him. He wanted, in the usual style of such power, something the law did not allow. Alypius refused. A bribe was offered: he laughed at it from the bottom of his heart. Threats were raised: he trampled them. And everyone marveled at so rare a spirit, which neither wanted so great a man for a friend nor feared him as an enemy — a man renowned for his countless ways of helping or hurting. The judge Alypius counseled did not want to grant the thing either, but he would not refuse it to the man's face: he shifted the whole business onto Alypius, claiming that Alypius would not permit him — and truly, if the judge had done it, Alypius would have walked out. In one thing only, and that through his love of learning, was he nearly seduced: he could have had books copied for himself at the cut rates court officials paid. But he took counsel with justice and turned his thought the better way, judging the fairness that forbade it worth more than the privilege that allowed it. Small things, all this — but he who is faithful in a little is faithful also in much; and what came from the mouth of your Truth can never stand void: If you were not faithful with dishonest wealth, who will trust you with true riches? And if you were not faithful with what belongs to another, who will give you what is your own? Such was the man who held close to me then, and wavered along with me over what course of life to take.

Him, then, I had found at Rome, and he attached himself to me by the strongest of ties and came with me to Milan — both so as not to leave me, and to practice some of the law he had studied, more to please his parents than himself. At Milan he had three times sat as an assessor on the bench, with an honesty that astonished others, while he in turn was astonished at others who could prefer gold to honesty. His character was tested not only with the bait of greed but with the spur of fear. At Rome he had been assessor to the count of the Italian treasury. There was at that time a very powerful senator, to whom many were bound by favors and many bound by fear. He insisted, by his usual show of power, on having something granted to him that the laws did not allow. Alypius resisted. A bribe was promised; with all his heart he scorned it. Threats were made; he trampled on them. Everyone marveled at so unusual a spirit, that neither sought the friendship nor feared the enmity of a man so great and so famous for his countless ways of doing good or harm. And the judge himself, whose counselor Alypius was, though he too was unwilling that the thing be granted, would not openly refuse it, but put it off onto Alypius, claiming that Alypius would not permit it — when in truth, had the judge granted it, Alypius would have walked off the bench. One thing alone in the way of his beloved learning nearly tempted him: that he might have books copied for him at the official rates. But, consulting justice, he changed his mind for the better, judging the fairness that held him back more profitable than the power that would have let him do it. These are small things, but he who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much; and that cannot be void which came from the mouth of your Truth: "If you have not been faithful in the dishonest mammon, who will entrust to you the true riches? And if you have not been faithful in what is another's, who will give you what is your own?" Such was the man who clung to me at that time, and wavered along with me over what way of life we should take.

Nebridius too. He had left his birthplace near Carthage, and Carthage itself, where he had mostly lived; left behind a fine family estate, and the house, and a mother who would not follow — and had come to Milan for no other reason on earth than to live with me in a burning search for truth and for wisdom. He sighed as I sighed; he wavered as I wavered — an ardent seeker of the happy life, and the sharpest of examiners of the hardest questions. So there were three hungry mouths, sighing out their want to one another, and waiting on you, that you might give them their food in due season. And in all the bitterness that, by your mercy, trailed our worldly doings, whenever we looked toward the end of it — asked why we should suffer all this — darkness met us; and we turned away groaning, and saying, 'How long shall it be like this?' We said it constantly — and saying it, we did not quit those doings, because nothing certain had yet shown itself that we could grasp once we let them go.

Nebridius, too, had left his home country near Carthage — yes, and Carthage itself, where he had mostly lived — leaving behind a fine family estate and house and a mother who would not follow him, for no other reason than to live with me in a most ardent search for truth and wisdom. Like me he sighed, like me he wavered: a passionate seeker of the true life, and a most acute examiner of the hardest questions. So there were three hungry mouths, sighing out their need to one another, and waiting on you to give them their food in due season. And in all the bitterness that, by your mercy, followed our worldly dealings, whenever we looked toward the end — toward why we should suffer all this — darkness met us, and we turned away groaning, and said, "How long will these things go on?" We said this often; and saying it, we still did not forsake those things, because as yet nothing certain had dawned that we might forsake them for and embrace.

And I, turning it all over and over, was amazed above everything at the stretch of time since that nineteenth year of mine, when I first caught fire with a passion for wisdom and resolved that once I found her I would abandon all the empty hopes and lying lunacies of vain desire. And here I was going on thirty, stuck fast in the same mud, greedy for the enjoyment of present things that slipped away and scattered me, all the while saying: 'Tomorrow I will find it. It will show itself plainly, and I will hold it fast. Faustus will come and explain everything. — You great men, you Academics! So nothing certain can be grasped for the conduct of life? — No: search harder, and do not despair. Look, the things in the church's books that used to seem absurd are not absurd now; they can be read another way, and honorably. I will plant my feet on the step where my parents set me as a boy, until the clear truth is found. But where is it to be looked for? When is it to be looked for? Ambrose has no spare time; there is no spare time to read. And where do we even hunt for the books? Where do we get them, and when? Who lends them? No — appoint set times; portion out hours for the health of the soul. A great hope has dawned: the Catholic faith does not teach what we thought it taught; our accusations were empty. Her learned men hold it blasphemy to believe God bounded by the shape of a human body. And we hesitate to knock, so that the rest may be opened? Our students take the mornings; what do we do with the hours that are left? Why not this? — But then when do we wait on our great friends, whose backing we need? When do we write what the students will pay for? When do we recover ourselves, and let the mind go slack from its strain of cares?'

And I, looking back over things again and again, was most amazed at the length of time since that nineteenth year of mine, when I had first caught fire with the desire for wisdom and resolved that once I found her I would let go of all the empty hopes and lying frenzies of vain desires. And here I was, now in my thirtieth year, still stuck in the same mud, greedy to enjoy the things of the present, which slipped away and laid my soul waste, while I kept telling myself: "Tomorrow I'll find it; it will show itself plainly and I'll grasp it. Look — Faustus the Manichee will come, and he will clear everything up. O you great men, you Academics, is it really true, then, that no certainty can be had for the ordering of one's life? No — let us search the harder, and not despair. See, the things in the Church's books are not absurd to us now, as they once seemed; they can be taken otherwise, in a good sense. I will take my stand where my parents set me as a child, until the clear truth is found. But where is it to be sought, and when? Ambrose has no free time; we have no free time to read; and where are we even to find the books? When, or where, do we get hold of them? From whom do we borrow them? Let set times be appointed, and certain hours set aside for our soul's health. A great hope has dawned: the Catholic faith does not teach what we thought, what we vainly accused it of; her instructed members hold it irreverent to believe God to be bounded by the figure of a human body. So why do we hesitate to knock, that the rest may be opened? The mornings our students take up; what are we doing with the rest of the day? Why not this? But then, when do we pay our respects to the powerful friends whose favor we need? When do we prepare what we sell to our students? When do we refresh ourselves and unbend our minds from this strain of care?

'Let it all perish! Dismiss this hollow emptiness, and turn wholly to the one search — for truth. Life is wretched; death may come any hour. If it creeps up suddenly, in what state will we leave this world? And where will we learn what we neglected here — or rather, won't we pay the penalty of the neglect? But what if death itself cuts off every care, and ends it along with the feeling that feels it? Then that must be looked into too. — No; God forbid it should be so. It is not for nothing, it is not empty, that the towering authority of the Christian faith stands spread across the whole world. Such great things would never have been worked for us by God if the soul's life ended with the body's death. Why then do we delay to drop our worldly hope and give ourselves wholly to seeking God and the blessed life? — But wait: these things are pleasant too; they carry a sweetness of their own, and not a small one. We must not cut ourselves off from them lightly, because it would be shameful to come crawling back. And look how little it would take now to land some post of honor — and what more, in this line, could a man wish for? We have a crowd of powerful friends; if nothing else offers and we press hard, at least a governorship might be handed us. And a wife should be taken, with a little money of her own, so she does not swell the expenses; and that will be the boundary of desire. Many great men, well worth our imitation, have given themselves to the study of wisdom with a wife at their side.'

"To ruin with all of it — let us send these empty vanities packing, and turn ourselves to the one search for truth. Life is short, death is uncertain; if it steals on us suddenly, in what state will we go from here, and where will we learn what we neglected here, and will we not rather pay the penalty for this neglect? And what if death itself cuts off and ends all care and feeling? That too must be settled. But God forbid it should be so! It is no empty, hollow thing that the surpassing dignity of the Christian faith's authority has spread over the whole world. God would never have done such and so great things for us if the life of the soul ended with the death of the body. Why then do we delay to throw off our worldly hopes and give ourselves wholly to seeking God and the blessed life? But wait — these things are pleasant too; they have a sweetness of their own, and no small one. We must not be quick to break with them, for it would be a shame to slink back to them again. See, it is no great matter now to land some post; and then what more could we wish? We have plenty of powerful friends. If nothing better turns up, and we are in a real hurry, at the very least a governorship could be had — and a wife with some money, so she does not add to our expenses; and that would be the limit of our desires. Many great men, well worth imitating, have given themselves to the pursuit of wisdom while married."

While I said all this, and the winds shifted and shoved my heart now this way, now that, time was passing, and I delayed turning to the Lord. From day to day I put off living in you; I did not put off dying, daily, in myself. In love with the happy life, I feared it in the very place where it lives, and hunted for it by running away from it. I thought I would be miserable beyond bearing without a woman's arms around me; and of your mercy's medicine for curing that weakness I never thought at all, because I had never tried it. Continence, I assumed, was a matter of a man's own strength — and I knew no such strength in myself. I was fool enough not to know what is written: that no one can be continent unless you grant it. And grant it you would have, if with inward groaning I had knocked at your ears, and with settled faith had cast my care upon you.

While I turned these things over, and these winds shifted and drove my heart this way and that, time kept passing, and I put off turning to the Lord; from one day to the next I deferred living in you, while I did not defer dying, day by day, in myself. Loving a happy life, I feared it in its own home, and fled from it in the very act of seeking it. I thought I would be far too miserable without a woman's arms around me, and never gave a thought to the medicine of your mercy that might have cured that weakness, because I had never tried it. As for continence, I supposed it lay within our own power — though in myself I found no such power — being foolish enough not to know what is written, that no one can be continent unless you give it, and that you would give it if with inward groans I knocked at your ears and with a settled faith cast my care on you.

Alypius, it is true, kept me back from taking a wife. His refrain was that if I did, there was no chance of our living together at undistracted leisure in the love of wisdom, the way we had long wanted. In this matter he was even then astonishingly pure. At the very door of his youth he had gone through that experience — and had not stuck in it; he had grieved over it instead, and scorned it, and lived from then on in complete continence. I countered him with the examples of men who had cultivated wisdom inside marriage, and served God well, and kept their friends and loved them faithfully. I was a long way short of their greatness of soul. Bound by the disease of the flesh and its deadly sweetness, I dragged my chain, dreading to have it struck off; and as if he were jarring the wound, I pushed away his good words like the hand of a man come to unchain me. Worse than that: the serpent used me to speak to Alypius himself. My tongue wove sweet snares and strewed them along his path, to tangle those honest, unbound feet of his.

It was Alypius, in fact, who kept me from marrying, arguing that if I did, we could by no means live together in untroubled leisure in the love of wisdom, as we had long wanted to. For he himself was at that point remarkably pure in this regard — the more remarkably since at the very start of his youth he had had a taste of it, but had not stuck fast there; rather he had felt remorse and revulsion, and from then on had lived in the strictest continence. But I argued back with the examples of married men who had cherished wisdom, served God acceptably, and kept and loved their friends faithfully. Of their greatness of spirit I fell far short. Bound by the disease of the flesh, with its deadly sweetness, I dragged my chain along, dreading to be unchained, and pushed away his good advice as though it were the hand of someone trying to loose me, when my wound chafed at being touched. What is more, through me the serpent spoke to Alypius himself: through my tongue it wove and strewed across his path the pleasurable snares in which his virtuous and free feet might be tangled.

For he could not understand it: I, a man he did not weigh lightly, stuck so fast in the glue of that pleasure that whenever we discussed it I swore I could not possibly live unmarried. And when I saw him wondering, I defended myself: what he had tasted was a snatched and furtive thing, which he could barely remember and so could despise without a struggle — nothing like the settled delight of my own habit; and if the honorable name of marriage were added to that habit, he had no business being surprised that I could not throw such a life away. Hearing all this, he began to want marriage himself — not overcome by any appetite for the pleasure, but out of curiosity. He wanted to know, he said, what this thing could be, without which my life — a life that pleased him so — seemed to me not a life but a punishment. His mind, free of that chain, was astounded at my slavery; and from astonishment he was moving toward a desire to try it, and from there he might have come to the trial itself, and from the trial, perhaps, fallen into the very slavery that astounded him — since he was willing to strike a covenant with death; and the man who loves danger will fall into it. Whatever honor there is in the office of marriage — in the ordering of a household and the raising of children — moved us both only faintly. What tortured me, mostly, and held me captive, was the habit of glutting an appetite that could never be filled; what was leading him toward captivity was wonder. So we stood — until you, Most High, who do not abandon our clay, in pity for the pitiful came to our help, by hidden and wonderful ways.

For he was amazed that I, whom he held in no small esteem, should be so stuck fast in the birdlime of that pleasure that whenever we discussed it I would insist I could never lead a single, celibate life; and when I saw him amazed, I defended myself by saying there was a great difference between his momentary, barely remembered brush with that life, which he could easily despise, and my long-standing acquaintance with it, to which — if the honorable name of marriage were added — he ought not to wonder that I could not give it up. At that he began to want to be married himself — not because he was overcome by any craving for the pleasure, but out of curiosity. For he wanted, he said, to know what this thing was, without which my life, so pleasant to him, would seem to me no life at all but a punishment. His mind, free of that chain, was astonished at my bondage, and through that astonishment was moving on toward a desire to try it, and from the desire to the trial itself, and from there perhaps to sink into the very bondage that so amazed him — for he was willing to make a bargain with death, and whoever loves danger will fall into it. Neither of us was much moved by whatever honor there is in the office of running a marriage and a household well. What held me captive, mostly, was the habit of feeding an appetite that could never be satisfied; what was leading him captive was an admiring wonder. So it was with us, until you, Most High, not abandoning our dust, in pity for our misery came to our help by wonderful, hidden ways.

The push to get me married never slackened. I was already asking; the promise was already made. My mother worked at it hardest, hoping that once I was married, the baptism that saves would wash me clean; she rejoiced that I was daily growing fitter for it, and saw in my faith the answering of her prayers and the keeping of your promises. All that while — at my asking, and out of her own longing — she begged you every day, with a great cry of the heart, to show her in a vision something of my future marriage. You never would. She saw certain vain, fantastic things instead, the kind the human spirit's own straining sweeps together when it is bent hard on a question; and she told me of them, but dismissively, without the confidence she had when it was you who showed her. For she could tell, she said, by a certain savor she could not put into words, the difference between your revealing and the dreaming of her own soul. Still the matter was pressed, and a girl was asked for — about two years short of the age for marrying; and since she pleased, she was waited for.

There was constant effort to get me married. I proposed, I was accepted — chiefly through my mother's pains, her hope being that once I was married the saving waters of baptism might wash me clean; and she rejoiced to see me growing daily readier for it, and noticed that her prayers and your promises were being fulfilled in my coming to faith. At this time, both at my request and out of her own longing, she begged you daily, with strong cries of the heart, to show her in a vision something about my coming marriage; but you never would. She did see certain empty, fanciful things, of the sort that the human spirit, busy with such matters, throws together; and she told me of them, but not with the confidence she had when you showed her something — she made light of them. For she could tell, she said, by a certain sense she could not put into words, the difference between your revelations and the dreams of her own soul. Still, the matter was pressed; a girl was asked for in marriage, two years under the marriageable age, and since she was acceptable, it was a matter of waiting for her.

And a whole company of us friends, talking together and detesting the storm and grind of human life, had considered — had all but firmly resolved — to withdraw from the crowds and live in quiet. The quiet was to be arranged like this: whatever each of us could bring, we would pool into one household fund, so that in the honesty of friendship nothing would be this man's or that man's, but one purse made out of everything — the whole of it belonging to each of us, and all of it to all. It seemed there might be some ten of us in this fellowship, and some very rich men among us — above all Romanianus, from our own town, an intimate friend of mine from childhood, whom the grave tangles of his affairs had brought up to court. He was the hottest of all for the plan, and his word carried the greatest weight, because his ample fortune towered over everyone else's. We had settled, too, that two of us at a time, like annual magistrates, would see to all the practical needs, leaving the rest in peace. But then the question arose whether the wives would put up with it — the wives some of us already had, and the ones we meant to get — and the whole plan, so beautifully shaped, burst apart in our hands, and was broken, and thrown away. Back we went to our sighing and groaning, and our steps to the broad and beaten roads of the world; for many plans were in our heart, but your counsel stands forever. And out of that counsel you laughed at ours, and made ready your own — meaning to give us food in due season, to open your hand, and to fill our souls with blessing.

And many of us friends, talking it over together, and loathing the turbulent troubles of human life, had debated and all but resolved to live apart from business and the bustle of men. We were to get this by pooling whatever each of us could bring together, and making one household of it all, so that, in the trueness of our friendship, nothing would belong to any one of us alone, but the whole, drawn from all, would belong wholly to each, and all to all. It seemed there might be some ten of us in this fellowship, some of them very rich — above all Romanianus, a fellow townsman of mine and a close friend from boyhood, whom the heavy tangles of his affairs had brought up to court. He was the keenest of all for the plan, and his voice carried great weight in it, because his ample estate far exceeded any of ours. We had even settled that two of us each year would, like officers, see to everything needful, leaving the rest undisturbed. But once we began to ask whether the wives — which some of us already had, and others hoped to have — would put up with it, the whole scheme, so beautifully shaped, fell to pieces in our hands and was utterly smashed and thrown away. So we turned back to sighing and groaning, and our steps to following the broad, well-trodden ways of the world; for many thoughts were in our hearts, but your counsel stands forever. And out of that counsel you laughed at ours, and were preparing your own, meaning to give us food in due season, and to fill our souls with blessing.

Meanwhile my sins were multiplying. The woman I had shared my bed with for so long was torn from my side as an obstacle to the marriage; and my heart, which had grown into her, was cut, and wounded, and it trailed blood. She went back to Africa, vowing to you that she would never know another man, and leaving with me the natural son I had by her. But I, in my misery, could not manage even a woman's example. Impatient of the delay — it would be two years before I could have the girl I was promised — and being no lover of marriage but a slave of lust, I procured another woman, no wife, of course: someone to keep the disease of my soul alive, whole or even fattened, and to escort it, under the guard of unbroken habit, into the kingdom of a wife. And the wound where the first was cut away did not heal. After the raging heat of the pain, it began to fester; and the pain went colder — and more desperate.

Meanwhile my sins were multiplying, and the woman I lived with was torn from my side as a hindrance to my marriage, and my heart, which clung to her, was torn and wounded and left bleeding. She went back to Africa, vowing to you that she would never know another man, and leaving with me the son she had borne me. But wretched as I was, and unable to match even a woman, I could not bear the delay; since it would be two years before I could have the girl I had asked for, and since I was not so much a lover of marriage as a slave to lust, I got myself another woman — no wife — so that by the servitude of an unbroken habit the disease of my soul might be kept going at full strength, or even fed, all the way into the realm of marriage. And the wound made by the cutting away of the first woman was not healed; after the burning and the sharpest pain, it festered, and though the pain grew duller, it grew the more hopeless.

To you be praise, to you be glory, fountain of mercies! The more wretched I became, the nearer you came. Your right hand was ready — again and again it was ready — to pull me out of the mud and wash me clean, and I knew nothing of it. And nothing called me back from the still deeper pit of the flesh's pleasures except the fear of death and of your judgment to come, which, through every change of my opinions, never once left my breast. I used to argue with my friends Alypius and Nebridius about the ends of good and evil, and in my private judgment Epicurus would have carried the palm, had I not believed what Epicurus refused to believe: that after death a life remains for the soul, and a reckoning by deserts. And I would ask: suppose we were immortal, and lived in unbroken bodily pleasure with no fear of ever losing it — why shouldn't we be happy? What else would there be to want? I did not know that exactly this was part of my great misery: that I was sunk so low, so blind, that I could not even conceive the light of an excellence and a beauty to be embraced for its own sake — a light the eye of the flesh cannot see; it is seen from within. Nor did I stop to ask, wretch that I was, out of what spring it flowed that even these discussions, foul as they were, were sweet to me only in the company of friends; or that not even by my own idea of happiness could I be happy without friends, however deep the flood of the flesh's pleasures ran. For those friends I loved for themselves alone, for nothing — and I felt that they loved me the same way, for nothing back.

Praise be to you, glory to you, Fountain of mercies. I was growing more wretched, and you were drawing nearer. Your right hand was constantly ready to pluck me out of the mire and wash me clean, and I did not know it; and nothing called me back from a still deeper gulf of bodily pleasures but the fear of death and of your judgment to come, which, through all my changes, never left my breast. And in my arguments with my friends Alypius and Nebridius about the nature of good and evil, I held that Epicurus, to my mind, would have carried off the prize, had I not believed that after death there remained for the soul a life and a settling of accounts according to what each had deserved — which Epicurus refused to believe. And I would ask: "If we were immortal, and were to live in unending bodily pleasure with no fear of losing it, why should we not be happy — what else should we even seek?" I did not see that this very thing was itself a great misery: that, so sunk and so blinded, I could not make out the light of an excellence and beauty to be embraced for its own sake, which the eye of flesh cannot see and which is seen only by the inner man. Nor did I, unhappy that I was, consider the source from which it sprang that even about these things, foul as they were, I took pleasure in talking with my friends; for I could not be happy, even by the notions of happiness I then held, without friends, however great a heap of bodily pleasures I might have. And these friends I truly loved for their own sake, and I felt that I in turn was loved by them for my own sake.

Crooked, crooked roads! Woe to the reckless soul that hoped, by pulling away from you, to find something better. It has turned and turned again — onto its back, onto its sides, onto its belly — and every surface is hard. You alone are rest. And look: you are here. You free us from our miserable wanderings, and you set us on your way, and you comfort us, and you say: 'Run — I will carry you. I will bring you all the way through; and there, at the end, I will still be carrying you.'

O crooked paths! Woe to the reckless soul that hoped, by forsaking you, to find some better thing! It turned and turned again, onto its back, its sides, its belly, and everything was hard — and you alone are rest. And see, you are close at hand, and you free us from our wretched wanderings and set us in your way, and comfort us, and say: "Run, I will carry you; yes, I will see you through; and there too I will carry you."

sections.label: Book VII
sections.title: The unchangeable light
The Books of the Platonists and the Word Made Flesh

segments.text: By now my adolescence was dead — that evil, unspeakable adolescence — and I was passing into manhood: the older in years, the uglier in emptiness. I could not conceive of any substance except the kind these eyes are used to seeing. I did not picture you in the shape of a human body, God; from the moment I first heard anything of wisdom, I always fled that thought, and I was glad to find the same refusal in the faith of our spiritual mother, your Catholic Church. But what else to think you were, I did not know. I — a man, and such a man — was trying to think of you, the supreme, the only, the true God; and from my inmost marrow I believed you incorruptible, inviolable, unchangeable. How I knew this, or from where, I could not say; but I saw plainly, and was certain, that what can be corrupted is worse than what cannot; what cannot be violated I set without hesitation above what can be; what suffers no change is better than what can be changed. My heart cried out violently against all my phantoms, and with that one blow I tried to beat off the swarm of unclean images circling the eye of my mind. And they were scarcely scattered before, in the blink of an eye, they massed again, hurled themselves against my sight, and clouded it — so that even if I did not imagine you in the shape of a human body, I was still forced to imagine you as something bodily, spread through space: whether poured into the world, or diffused beyond it through the infinite. Even that incorruptible, inviolable, unchangeable being that I set above everything corruptible, violable, and changeable — even that I imagined this way. For whatever I stripped of such space seemed to me to be nothing — nothing at all, not even an emptiness. If a body is taken out of its place, and the place remains empty of every body — of earth, of water, of air, of sky — it still remains an empty place: a spacious nothing, as it were.

By now my evil and disgraceful youth was dead, and I was passing into early manhood — the older I grew, the more soiled by empty things, since I could not imagine any substance except the kind these eyes are used to seeing. I no longer pictured you, my God, in the shape of a human body; from the moment I first heard anything of wisdom I had always shrunk from that, and I was glad to find the same rule in the faith of our spiritual mother, your Catholic Church. But what else to make of you I did not know. And I, a man, and such a man, set myself to conceive of you, the sovereign, the only, the true God; and from the depths of my soul I did believe you to be beyond corruption, beyond injury, beyond change. For though I could not say how or why, I saw plainly, and was sure, that whatever can be corrupted is lower than what cannot; what cannot be harmed I set without hesitation above what can be harmed; the unchanging above what is subject to change. My heart cried out furiously against all my phantoms, and with this one blow I tried to beat away from the eye of my mind the whole unclean swarm that buzzed around it. And the moment they were brushed off, in the blink of an eye they were thick about me again, flying into my face, clouding it over — so that, though no longer under the shape of a human body, I was still forced to imagine you (that incorruptible, unharmable, unchanging thing I had set above all that can be corrupted, harmed, changed) as something spread out in space, whether poured through the world or stretching out infinitely beyond it. For whatever I tried to conceive without that space seemed to me nothing — utterly nothing, not even an emptiness, as if you took a body out of its place and left the place standing empty of every body, of earth and water, air and sky, and yet still an empty place, a kind of roomy nothing.

So gross was my heart — I was not clear even to my own sight — that whatever was not stretched over some expanse of space, or diffused through it, or packed into it, or swollen out into it, whatever did not have or could not have some such dimension, I judged to be nothing at all.
