Over shapes like the shapes my eyes range over, my heart then ranged; and I did not see that the very act of mind by which I formed those images was not itself anything of that kind — and yet it could not have formed them unless it were something great. So I tried to think of you too, Life of my life, as vast: penetrating the whole mass of the world through infinite space on every side, and beyond it in every direction through immensity without end — so that the earth would have you, the sky would have you, all things would have you, and they would be bounded in you, and you bounded nowhere. For as the body of the air above the earth does not block the sunlight, which passes through it and penetrates it, not by breaking it or cutting it but by filling the whole of it — so I supposed the body not only of sky and air and sea but of the earth itself lay open to you, penetrable in all its parts, greatest and smallest alike, to receive your presence: a hidden breath, within and without, governing everything you have made. This was my guess, because I could conceive of nothing else; and it was false. For in that case a larger part of the earth would hold a larger portion of you, and a smaller part a smaller; and all things would be full of you in such a way that an elephant's body would contain more of you than a sparrow's, by just so much as it is bigger and takes up more room; and so you would deal yourself out piecemeal to the pieces of the world — much of you to the large parts, little to the little. And that is not what you are. But you had not yet lit up my darkness.

So gross was my heart, so unclear even to myself, that whatever was not stretched out over some space, or spread, or packed together, or swollen out — whatever did not or could not take on some of these dimensions — I judged to be simply nothing. My heart ranged over the same shapes my eyes were used to ranging over; and I did not yet see that this very act of the mind, by which I shaped those images, was itself nothing of that kind — and yet it could not have shaped them unless it were itself some great thing. In the same way I tried to picture you, the Life of my life, as enormous, reaching on every side through infinite spaces, soaking through the whole bulk of the universe and out beyond it, every way, through measureless, boundless space — so that earth had you, sky had you, all things had you, and they were bounded in you, and you were bounded nowhere. For just as the body of the air over the earth does not block the sun's light from passing through it, but lets it through by filling it whole, not by tearing or cutting — so I thought the body, not of sky and air and sea only but of the solid earth as well, was open to you all the way through, in its greatest parts and its smallest, ready to take your presence in by a secret breath, within and without, steering everything you have made. This was my guess, only because I could conceive of nothing else, and it was false. For on that reckoning a larger piece of the earth would hold a larger piece of you, and a smaller a lesser — and all things would be full of you in such a way that an elephant's body would hold more of you than a sparrow's, simply by being bigger and taking up more room; and you would dole out the several portions of yourself to the several portions of the world, in fragments, much to the large and little to the little. But that is not what you are. You had not yet lit up my darkness.

Against those deceived deceivers, those talkative mutes — mute, because your word never sounded out of them — it was enough for me, Lord, to hold the argument that Nebridius used to put forward long ago, back in Carthage, which staggered all of us who heard it. That race of darkness which the Manichees like to set against you as an opposing mass: what would it have done to you if you had refused to fight it? If they answered, "It would have done you some harm," then you would be subject to violation and corruption. If, "It could have done you no harm," then no reason remained for fighting at all — and fighting in such a way that some portion of you, some member of you, some offspring of your very substance, gets mixed in with hostile powers, with natures you never created, and is corrupted by them and changed for the worse, driven out of happiness into misery, needing help to be pulled free and cleansed. And this offspring of your substance, they said, was the soul: enslaved, defiled, corrupted, waiting for your Word to come to its rescue — your Word free, pure, and whole; though that Word, being of one and the same substance, must be every bit as corruptible. So then: if they called you — whatever you are, the substance by which you are — incorruptible, then all these tales were false and detestable; if corruptible, that was false on its face, to be abhorred the moment it was spoken. This argument, then, was enough against men who deserved to be vomited up whole from an overloaded stomach; for they had no way out of it that did not commit a horrible sacrilege of heart and tongue, thinking and saying such things about you.

It was enough for me, Lord, to set against those deceived deceivers and dumb chatterers — for your word did not sound out of them — the argument Nebridius used to put forward, long ago when we were still at Carthage, which staggered all of us who heard it. That so-called nation of darkness, which the Manichees love to set up as a hostile mass over against you: what could it have done to you, had you refused to fight it? If they answered that it could have done you some harm, then you would be open to injury and corruption. But if it could do you no harm, then no reason at all was left for your fighting it — fighting in such a way that some portion or member of you, some offspring of your very substance, was mixed into hostile powers and natures you had not made, and was so corrupted and changed for the worse by them as to be turned from happiness into misery, and to need rescue to be set free and made clean again. And this offspring of your substance was, they said, the soul — which, once enslaved, defiled, corrupted, your Word might come to relieve; but that Word would itself be corruptible too, being one and the same substance with it. So if they granted that you, whatever you are — your substance, that is, the thing by which you are — are incorruptible, then all these claims of theirs were false and damnable; but if they called you corruptible, the claim was self-evidently false and revolting. This argument of Nebridius was enough against people who deserved to be vomited up out of a sickened stomach; for they had no way out except by a horrible blasphemy of heart and tongue, thinking and speaking of you in such terms.

But I, too — though I held and firmly believed that you, our Lord, the true God, maker not only of our souls but of our bodies, and not only of our souls and bodies but of all beings and all things, are undefilable and unalterable and in no way changeable — I still had no clear, untangled grasp of the cause of evil. Whatever it was, I saw this much: the search for it must not force me to believe the unchangeable God changeable, or I would myself become the very thing I was searching for. So I searched with an easy mind on that score, certain that what those men said was untrue. I fled them with my whole heart, because I saw that in asking where evil comes from, they had filled up with evil themselves: they preferred to believe that your substance suffers evil rather than that their own commits it.

But even now, though I held it firmly settled that you, our Lord and the true God — who made not our souls only but our bodies, and not our souls and bodies only but every being and every thing — were undefilable, unalterable, in no way subject to change, still I did not understand, clearly and without strain, the cause of evil. Yet whatever that cause might be, I saw it had to be sought in a way that would not force me to believe the unchanging God to be changeable, lest I become the very evil I was searching for. So I searched, free at least of that anxiety, certain that what those people taught was untrue — people I now shrank from with my whole heart. For I saw that in asking where evil came from, they had filled themselves with evil, since they would rather believe that your substance suffered ill than that their own committed it.

And I strained to understand what I was now hearing: that free will is the cause of our doing evil, and your just judgment the cause of our suffering it. But I could not see it clearly. I would struggle to lift the eye of my mind out of the pit, and I would sink back in; as often as I struggled, so often I sank. One thing, though, raised me a little toward your light: I knew that I had a will as surely as I knew that I was alive. When I willed a thing or refused it, I was absolutely certain that it was I who willed and I who refused — no one else — and I was beginning to see that there lay the cause of my sin. What I did against my will, I saw that I suffered rather than did; and I counted it not guilt but punishment — and since I held you to be just, I quickly confessed that the punishment was not unjust. But then I said: Who made me? Was it not my God, who is not only good but goodness itself? Then where did I get this willing of evil and refusing of good, which so justly earns the punishment? Who set it in me? Who grafted this seedling of bitterness into me, when the whole of me was made by my most sweet God? If the devil is the author — then where does the devil come from? And if he too, by his own perverse will, was turned from a good angel into a devil, where did the evil will in him come from, when the whole angel had been made by a Creator wholly good? These thoughts pushed me down again and smothered me; but they never dragged me down into that hell of error where no one confesses to you — the belief that you suffer evil rather than that man does it.

And I strained to make out what I now kept hearing — that free will is the cause of our doing evil, and your just judgment the cause of our suffering it; but I could not see it clearly. So when I tried to lift my soul's gaze out of that deep pit, I sank back down; and trying again and again, I sank again and again. But this much raised me a little into your light: I knew that I had a will as surely as I knew that I was alive. So when I willed or refused something, I was utterly sure that it was no one but myself who willed and refused — and I was on the very edge of seeing that here was the cause of my sin. But what I did against my will I saw I was suffering rather than doing, and I judged it to be not my fault but my punishment; and since I held you to be just, I quickly admitted I was not being punished unjustly. But then again I said: Who made me? Was it not my God, who is not only good but goodness itself? Where, then, did it come from, this willing of evil and refusing of good, so that I am justly punished? Who planted this in me, who grafted into me this slip of bitterness, when I was wholly made by my most sweet God? If the devil is the author of it — where did the devil himself come from? And if he too, by his own twisted will, turned from a good angel into a devil, where did that evil will come from in him by which he became a devil, when the whole nature of angels was made by that most good Creator? By such thoughts I was dragged down again and choked — yet never dragged so far as that hell of error where no one confesses to you, the error of thinking that you suffer evil rather than that man does it.

I was straining to work out the rest as a man who had already found this much: that the incorruptible must be better than the corruptible; and therefore you, whatever you were, I confessed to be incorruptible. For no soul ever has been able, or ever will be able, to conceive anything better than you, the supreme and best good. And since, most truly and most certainly, the incorruptible ranks above the corruptible — as I now ranked it — then if you were not incorruptible, I could have reached in thought something better than my God. Seeing, then, that the incorruptible stands above the corruptible, I should have sought you there; and from there I should have traced where evil is — that is, where corruption comes from, which cannot violate your substance in any way at all. For corruption cannot touch our God in any way — by no will, by no necessity, by no unforeseen chance — because he is God, and what he wills is good, and he himself is that good; and to be corrupted is not good. Nor are you forced to anything against your will, since your will is not greater than your power. It would be greater only if you were greater than yourself — for the will of God and the power of God are God himself. And what can take you by surprise, when you know all things? No nature exists at all except because you know it. Why should we go on asking why the substance that God is cannot be corruptible? If it were, it would not be God.

For I was struggling to work out the rest like a man who had already found that the incorruptible must be better than the corruptible; and so I confessed you, whatever you were, to be incorruptible. For no soul ever was, or ever will be, able to conceive of anything better than you, who are the sovereign and the best good. And since most truly and certainly the incorruptible is to be set above the corruptible — as I now did set it — then, were you not incorruptible, I could have arrived in thought at something better than my God. So where I saw the incorruptible was to be preferred to the corruptible, there I ought to look for you, and there to mark out where evil itself was — that is, where the corruption comes from by which your substance can in no way be impaired. For corruption cannot impair our God in any way: not by any will, not by any necessity, not by any unlooked-for chance. For he is God, and what he wills is good, and he himself is that good; but to be corrupted is not good. You are not driven against your will to anything, for your will is not greater than your power. It would have to be greater only if you were greater than yourself — for the will and the power of God are God himself. And what can take you by surprise, you who know all things? There is no nature in all of being that you do not know. Why say more about why the substance which God is should not be corruptible, when, if it were, it would not be God?

And I asked where evil comes from, and I asked it badly, and failed to see the evil in my own asking. I set the whole creation before the eyes of my spirit: everything in it that we can see — sea, earth, air, stars, trees, mortal creatures — and everything in it that we cannot, the firmament of heaven above, and all the angels, and all its spiritual inhabitants. But even these, as if they were bodies, my imagination arranged in places; and I made of your creation one great mass, sorted by kinds of bodies — some of them real bodies, some the bodies I had invented for spirits — and I made this mass huge: not as it really was, which I had no way of knowing, but as big as suited me, though bounded on every side. And you, Lord, I imagined surrounding the mass on every side and soaking through it, but infinite in every direction — as if there were a sea, one single sea, everywhere and everywhere boundless through unmeasured space; and in the sea a sponge, as huge as you like, but finite; and the sponge filled in every one of its parts from the immeasurable sea. That is how I conceived your creation: finite, and full of you, the infinite. And I said: Here is God, and here is what God has created; and God is good, most mightily and incomparably better than all of it; yet being good he created good things — and see how he surrounds them and fills them. Then where is evil? Where did it come from, and by what crack did it creep in? What is its root, what is its seed? Or does it have no being at all? Then why do we fear and guard against what is not? And if our fear is groundless, then the fear itself is evil — the fear that goads and tortures the heart for nothing; an evil all the heavier because there is nothing to fear, and we fear anyway. So either evil is the thing we fear, or the evil is that we fear. Where does it come from, then, since God made all these things — the good God, and all of them good? He, the greater and highest good, made lesser goods; but maker and made alike, all are good. Where does evil come from? Was there some evil matter he worked from — forming it and ordering it, but leaving something in it that he did not turn to good? But why? Was he unable — the Almighty — to turn and change the whole of it, so that no evil would remain in it? And why would he choose to make anything out of it at all, rather than use that same almightiness to make it simply not exist? Could it have existed against his will? And if it was eternal, why did he leave it alone through the endless reaches of time gone by, and only so much later decide to make something out of it? Or, if he did suddenly resolve to act, would not the Almighty rather have acted to make that evil matter cease to be, so that he alone would be — the whole, true, supreme, infinite good? Or, if it was not good that he who is good should fail to frame and found something good, then why not take away the evil matter, reduce it to nothing, and himself establish good matter, and from that create all things? For he would not be almighty if he could not create something good without the help of matter he had not created. Such things I turned over in my miserable heart, weighed down with gnawing worries and the fear of dying before I had found the truth. But the faith of your Christ, our Lord and Savior, professed in the Catholic Church, stood firm in my heart — a faith still unshaped on many points, swaying off the rule of doctrine; yet my mind did not let go of it, and day by day it drank in more.

And I kept searching, Where does evil come from? — and I searched in an evil way, and did not see the evil in my very searching. I set before my spirit's eye the whole of creation, all that we can see in it: sea, earth, air, stars, trees, mortal creatures — and all that we cannot see, the firmament of the sky, all the angels, and all the spiritual creatures up there. But even these I laid out in places, as though they were bodies, in my imagination. I made one great mass of your creation, sorted by the kinds of bodies in it — some real bodies, some the bodies I had invented in place of spirits. I made this mass huge, not as huge as it really is (which I could not know) but as huge as I pleased, yet bounded on every side. And you, Lord, I imagined surrounding it and piercing it through on every part, but yourself infinite in every direction: as if there were a sea, everywhere and on all sides, through measureless space, one single boundless sea, and within it a sponge, huge but finite, and that sponge filled in all its parts from the unmeasured sea. So I conceived your creation, finite, full of you, the Infinite; and I said: Here is God, and here is what God created; and God is good, mightily and beyond all comparison better than these. Yet he, the Good, made them good, and see how he surrounds them and fills them. Then where is evil, and where does it come from, and how did it creep in here? What is its root, what is its seed? Or does it have no being at all? Then why do we fear and shun a thing that is not? Or if our fear is groundless, then the fear itself is the evil, the thing that goads and racks the soul for nothing — and a worse evil, in that we have nothing to fear and yet fear. So either there is an evil that we fear, or else our fearing is itself the evil. Where, then, does it come from, since God, the Good, made all these things good? The greater and chief Good made these lesser goods, but creator and created are all good. Where does evil come from? Or was there some evil matter out of which he made and shaped and ordered all this, but left in it something he did not convert into good? But why would he, when he is all-powerful and could have turned and changed the whole, so that no evil remained? Indeed, why would he make anything at all out of such matter, and not rather, by that same all-power, see to it that the matter did not exist at all? Could it have stood against his will? Or if it was from eternity, why did he let it lie idle through endless stretches of past time, and only so long after decide to make something of it? Or if he suddenly decided to act, surely the all-powerful would rather have brought it about that the evil matter should not be, and that he alone should be, the whole, true, sovereign, and infinite Good. Or if it was not good that one who was good should not also frame and create something good, then he might have done away with the evil matter, reduced it to nothing, and made good matter of his own to create all things from — for he would not be all-powerful if he could not create something good without the help of matter he had not made himself. Such thoughts I turned over in my wretched heart, weighed down with the most gnawing fears that I would die before I found the truth. And yet the faith of your Christ, our Lord and Savior, as the Catholic Church holds it, stood firm in my heart — on many points still unformed and wavering from the rule of doctrine, but my mind never quite let it go, and day by day drank in more and more of it.

By this time I had also rejected the lying divinations and godless ravings of the astrologers. For this too, my God, let your own mercies confess to you from the depths of my soul! For it was you — you and wholly you (for who else calls us back from the death of every error but the Life that does not know how to die, the Wisdom that lights up minds in need of light while needing none itself, the Wisdom that governs the world, down to the leaves fluttering on the trees?) — you who dealt with the stubbornness I set against Vindicianus, that sharp old man, and against Nebridius, a young man of admirable soul: the one declaring vehemently, the other saying often, though with some hesitation, that no art exists for seeing the future — that men's guesses are a kind of lottery, and out of the many things they say, some come to pass; the speakers never know which; they simply stumble into it by never keeping quiet. So you provided me a friend: no lazy consulter of astrologers, and not really versed in their literature either, but, as I said, a curious consulter — and yet he knew a story, heard from his father, which he did not realize went far toward overthrowing the whole reputation of that art. This man, Firminus, educated in the liberal arts and well trained in rhetoric, consulted me as one of his dearest friends about certain affairs of his in which his worldly hopes were riding high: what did I think, given his "constellations," as they call them? I, already beginning to lean toward Nebridius's view of the matter, did not refuse to make my guesses and to say what came into my undecided mind — but I added that I was almost persuaded by now that the whole thing was empty, laughable nonsense. Then he told me that his father had been a passionate student of such books, and had had a friend who pursued them just as hotly; studying together, talking together, they fanned each other's ardor for this rubbish, to the point of watching for the very moments when the dumb animals around their houses gave birth, and noting the position of the sky at each — gathering, as it were, the data of this so-called art. So he said he had heard from his father that when his mother was pregnant with him — with Firminus — a slave woman of his father's friend was carrying a child at the same time; which could hardly escape her master, a man who took care to know, with scrupulous exactness, even the litters of his dogs. And so it fell out, as the two men counted the days and the hours and the smaller fractions of the hours — the one for his wife, the other for his servant — that both women delivered at the same instant: so that both men were forced to cast the identical horoscope, down to the minutest point, the one for his son, the other for his newborn slave. For as soon as the women went into labor, each man sent word to the other of what was under way in his house, and each had messengers standing ready to be dispatched the moment the birth was announced — and each, master in his own domain, had arranged to hear of it instantly. The messengers, he said, met at a point so precisely halfway between the two houses that neither man could record any different position of the stars, any different moment of time. And yet Firminus, born to high standing among his own people, ran up and down the whitewashed roads of the world, growing in wealth, rising in honors; while that slave went on serving his masters, the yoke never once loosened. Firminus knew him, and said so.

By this time, too, I had thrown off the lying guesswork and the godless nonsense of the astrologers. Let your own mercies confess to you for this also, my God, out of the very depths of my soul. For it was you — wholly you, since who else calls us back from the death of all our errors but the Life that cannot die and the Wisdom that needs no light to light up the minds that need it, by which the universe is steered down to the whirling of the leaves on the trees? You made provision for my stubbornness, the stubbornness with which I fought against Vindicianus, a shrewd old man, and against Nebridius, a young man of admirable gifts — the one fiercely declaring, the other often saying (though with some hesitation), that there was no such art for foreseeing things to come, but that men's guesses were a kind of lottery, and that out of the many things they predicted some did in fact come true, unknown to the men who said them, who simply stumbled on the hit by talking so often. So you provided me a friend who was no careless consulter of the astrologers — not well versed in those arts, but, as I said, a curious dabbler in them, and yet who knew one thing he said he had heard from his father, and did not realize how far it went toward overturning the whole estimate of the art. This man, Firminus by name, had had a liberal education and was well trained in rhetoric. He consulted me, as a dear friend, about what I thought, according to his so-called constellations, of certain affairs of his in which his worldly hopes had risen; and I, who had now begun to lean toward Nebridius's view, did not altogether refuse to guess and tell him what came into my unsettled mind — but added that I was now nearly convinced these were empty and laughable follies. At that he told me his father had been deeply devoted to such books, and had a friend just as keen on them, who fed the flame of his fascination with these toys by studying and comparing notes with him. They went so far as to note the very moment the dumb animals bred about their houses gave birth, and then observe the position of the heavens, to gather fresh evidence for this so-called art. And he said he had heard from his father that, just as his mother was about to give birth to him, Firminus, a servant-woman of that friend of his father's was also pregnant — which could not escape her master, who took the most exact care to know even the births of his puppies. And so it came about that, the one for his wife and the other for his servant, with the most careful reckoning of days, hours, and the smaller fractions of hours, both women were delivered at the same instant — so that both men were forced to grant the very same constellation, down to the finest point, the one for his son, the other for his newborn slave. For as soon as the women went into labor, each man told the other what was happening in his house, and each had a messenger ready to send the moment the birth occurred, which they could easily arrange, each in his own domain, to report at once. The messengers of the two parties met, he swore, at such an exactly equal distance from the two houses that neither could make out any difference in the position of the stars or in the least detail. And yet Firminus, born to high estate in his parents' house, ran his course down the gilded paths of life, grew rich, and rose to honors, while that slave went on serving his masters with the yoke never loosened — as Firminus, who knew him, told me himself.

When I heard this and believed it — the teller being the man he was — all my resistance melted and collapsed. And first I tried to pull Firminus himself back from that curiosity. I told him that if I had inspected his constellations and meant to predict truly, I should certainly have seen in them parents eminent among their neighbors, a noble family of its city, good birth, honorable education, liberal learning. But if that slave had consulted me about the same constellations — for they were his too — then to tell him truly, I should have seen in them, in turn, the meanest of households, the condition of a slave, and everything else utterly different from the first reading and utterly remote from it. So it followed that, looking at the same charts, I would have to say different things if I spoke truly; and if I said the same things, I would speak falsely. From which it followed with total certainty that whatever is said truly from the study of constellations is said not by art but by luck; and whatever is said falsely comes not from ignorance of the art, but from luck telling lies.

Hearing and believing all this, from a man so trustworthy, every shred of my resistance gave way. First I tried to draw Firminus himself back from that obsession. I told him that if, on inspecting his constellations, I were to predict truly, I should have read in them parents prominent among their neighbors, a noble family in its own city, high birth, a good upbringing, liberal learning. But if that servant had consulted me about the same constellations — for they were his too — then, to tell him truly, I should read in them a lineage utterly mean, a slave's condition, and everything else completely at odds with the first reading. From which it followed that, telling the truth, I would say opposite things from one and the same constellation, and if I said the same thing of both, I would be lying. So it was as certain as could be that whatever was said truly from a reading of the constellations was said not by art but by luck, and whatever was said falsely came not from any failure of skill in the art but from the failure of the luck.

With that opening made, I chewed the matter over with myself, so that none of those dotards who make their bread by this trade — men I was itching to attack and refute and laugh out of the room — could object that Firminus had told me a false story, or his father a false one to him. I turned my attention to twins. Most of them come out of the womb so close upon one another that the small interval between them — whatever force people claim it carries in the nature of things — cannot be caught by human observation, or written down at all in the charts the astrologer must inspect before he can pronounce the truth. And truth it will not be: for looking into the same charts, he would have had to say the same things about Esau and Jacob — and the same things did not happen to them. So he would speak falsely; or, if he spoke truly, he would have to give different answers while looking at the same charts. Not by art, then, but by luck would he speak the truth. For you, Lord, most just ruler of the universe, know how to work — while consulters and consulted know nothing of it — by your hidden prompting, so that each man who asks hears what he ought to hear, according to the hidden deserts of souls, out of the abyss of your just judgment. Let no man say to you, "What is this? What is that for?" Let him not say it — let him not say it. For he is a man.

Once that opening was made, I turned the same things over in my mind, so that none of those fortune-telling fools — who lived by the trade, and whom I longed to fall upon and laugh out of court — could object that Firminus had told me wrongly, or his father him. I fixed my thoughts on twins, who for the most part come out of the womb so close together that the small interval between them — whatever force people may pretend it holds in the nature of things — cannot be marked by human observation, nor set down at all in the figures the astrologer must inspect if he is to pronounce truly. And those pronouncements cannot be true: for, reading the same figures, he would have had to predict the same things of Esau and Jacob, and yet the same things did not befall them. So either he must speak falsely, or, if truly, then from the same figures he must give different answers. Therefore he speaks truly not by art but by luck. For you, Lord, most just Ruler of the universe, while the one who consults and the one consulted know nothing of it, by your hidden working bring it about that the one who asks hears what, according to the hidden deservings of souls, he ought to hear, out of the unsearchable depth of your just judgment — to whom let no one say, What is this? Why that? Let him not say it; for he is only a man.

By now, my helper, you had freed me from those chains; and still I was asking where evil comes from, and finding no way out. But you did not let any surge of thought carry me away from the faith by which I believed that you are; that your substance is unchangeable; that you care for men and will judge them; and that in Christ your Son, our Lord, and in the holy scriptures which the authority of your Catholic Church commends, you have laid down the way of man's salvation into the life that comes after this death. With these things safe, fixed immovably in my mind, I searched in a fever for the source of evil. What labor pains in my heart, what groaning, my God! And your ears were there, and I did not know it. As I searched hard in silence, the mute contritions of my soul were loud cries to your mercy. You knew what I suffered; no man knew it. How little of it my tongue managed to drop into the ears of my closest friends! Could the whole tumult of my soul reach them, when neither my time nor my mouth was equal to it? Yet the whole of it went up into your hearing — everything I roared out from the groaning of my heart; and my desire lay open before you, and the light of my own eyes was not with me. For the light was within, and I was outside it. The light was not in space; but I kept my mind on things that are contained in space, and I found among them no place to rest. They did not receive me in any way that let me say, "It is enough; it is well"; nor did they let me turn back to where it might have been well enough. For I stood above these things, and below you; and you are my true joy when I am subject to you, just as you had made subject to me the things you created beneath me. This was the right balance, the middle country of my salvation: to remain in your image, and, by serving you, to be master of my own body. But when I reared up in pride against you — when I charged my Lord, stiff-necked, behind the thick boss of my shield — then even those lowest things rose over me and pressed me down, and nowhere was there slack, nowhere breath. They swarmed my sight from every side, in masses and heaps; and when I tried to think my way back, the images of bodies flung themselves across the road, unbidden, as if to say: "Where do you think you are going, unworthy and unclean?" All this had grown out of my wound; for you humble the proud like a man run through with wounds. My swelling separated me from you, and my face, swollen too far, was closing my eyes.

By now, then, my Helper, you had loosed me from those chains; and I went on searching, Where does evil come from? — and found no way through. But you did not let any tossing of my thought carry me off from the faith by which I believed that you exist, and that your substance is unchanging, and that you care for human beings and will judge them, and that in Christ your Son, our Lord, and in the holy Scriptures, which the authority of your Catholic Church urged on me, you had set the way of our salvation toward the life that is to come after this death. With these things kept safe and immovably fixed in my mind, I searched in anguish: Where does evil come from? What pangs my heart was in labor with, what groans, my God! And even there your ears were open, and I did not know it; and when in silence I searched with all my strength, those silent griefs of my soul were loud cries to your mercy. You knew what I suffered, and no one else did. For how little of it could my tongue distill into the ears of even my closest friends! Could the whole tumult of my soul, for which I had neither the time nor the words, reach them? Yet all of it reached your hearing, all that I roared out from the groaning of my heart, and my longing was laid out before you, and the light of my own eyes was not with me. For that light was within, and I was without; that light was not in any place, but I was straining after things held in places, and there I found no resting place, nor did they so receive me that I could say, This is enough, this is well; nor did they let me turn back, where it might be well enough with me. For I was above these things, but below you; and you are my true joy when I am subject to you, and you had made subject to me the things you created below me. This was the right balance, the middle country of my safety — to stay in your image, and by serving you to rule the body. But when I rose up against you in pride and charged at the Lord with the thick bosses of my shield held high, even these lower things rose over me and bore down on me, and nowhere was there relief or room to breathe. They met my sight on every side in heaps and crowds, and when I tried to turn back to you their images thrust themselves on my thought unbidden, as if to say, Where are you going, unworthy and defiled? And all this had grown out of my wound, for you humble the proud like a man cut down; and through my own swelling I was cut off from you; my face was so puffed with pride that it swelled my eyes shut.

But you, Lord, abide forever, and you will not be angry with us forever, because you take pity on dust and ashes; and it was pleasing in your sight to re-form what was deformed in me. You goaded me from within, and I was restless under the goading until you should stand certain before my inward sight. My swelling went down under the hidden hand of your medicine; and the troubled, darkened eyesight of my mind was healed, day after day, by the stinging salve of healthy griefs.

But you, Lord, abide forever, and you are not angry with us forever, because you pity our dust and ashes; and it was your pleasure to reshape my deformities. By inward goads you stirred me, so that I could find no rest until you stood clear to my inward sight. By the secret hand of your healing my swelling went down, and the troubled and darkened eyesight of my mind, under the stinging salve of healthful sorrows, was healed from day to day.

And first — wanting to show me how you resist the proud and give grace to the humble, and with how great a mercy of yours the way of humility was shown to men when your Word became flesh and lived among them — you procured for me, through a certain man bloated with the most monstrous pride, some books of the Platonists, translated out of Greek into Latin. And in them I read — not in these words, but the very same thing, urged with many arguments of many kinds — that in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; that he was in the beginning with God; that all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made; that what was made is life in him, and the life was the light of men, and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not laid hold of it. And that the soul of man, though it bears witness to the light, is not itself the light — but the Word, God himself, is the true light that enlightens every man who comes into this world. And that he was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him. But that he came to what was his own, and his own did not receive him — and that to all who did receive him he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name: that, I did not read there.

And willing first to show me how you resist the proud but give grace to the humble, and by how great an act of your mercy you had marked out for men the way of humility — in that your Word was made flesh and lived among men — you procured for me, through a man swollen with the most monstrous pride, certain books of the Platonists, translated from Greek into Latin. And in them I read, not in these very words but to exactly this effect, urged by many and various reasons: that in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; the same was in the beginning with God; all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made; in him was life, and the life was the light of men, and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it. And that the soul of man, though it bears witness to the light, is not itself that light; but the Word of God, being God, is the true light that lights every man who comes into the world. And that he was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him. But that he came to his own, and his own did not receive him; and that to as many as received him he gave the power to become children of God, to as many as believed in his name — this I did not read there.

Again, I read there that the Word, God, was born not of flesh, not of blood, not of the will of a man nor the will of the flesh, but of God. But that the Word became flesh and lived among us — that I did not read there. I traced it in those books, said in many ways and many turns of phrase, that the Son, being in the form of the Father, did not count it robbery to be equal with God, because by nature he is that very thing. But that he emptied himself, taking the form of a slave, made in the likeness of men and found in condition as a man; that he humbled himself, becoming obedient all the way to death, even death on a cross; that God therefore exalted him from the dead and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father — those books do not have. For that your only-begotten Son abides before all times and above all times, unchangeable, coeternal with you; that souls receive of his fullness in order to be blessed; that by sharing in the wisdom that abides in them they are renewed in order to be wise — that is there. But that at the appointed time he died for the ungodly; that you did not spare your only Son but handed him over for us all — that is not there. For you have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to little children, so that those who labor and are burdened might come to him and be restored by him, because he is meek and lowly of heart; and he guides the meek in judgment, and teaches the gentle his ways, looking on our lowliness and our toil, and forgiving all our sins. But those who strut on the stage-boots of a supposedly loftier doctrine do not hear him say, "Learn from me, for I am meek and lowly of heart, and you will find rest for your souls." Even if they know God, they do not glorify him as God or give him thanks; they evaporate into their own thinking, and their foolish heart goes dark; claiming to be wise, they become fools.

Again I read there that God the Word was born not of flesh nor of blood, nor of the will of man, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God. But that the Word was made flesh and lived among us — this I did not read there. For I traced in those books that it was said, in many ways and various, that the Son was in the form of the Father and did not count it robbery to be equal with God, since by his very nature he was that same substance. But that he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men, and found in fashion as a man humbled himself and became obedient even to death, the death of the cross; for which God raised him from the dead and gave him a name above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father — those books do not have. For that before all times and above all times your Only-Begotten Son stays unchanging, co-eternal with you, and that of his fullness souls receive so that they may be blessed, and that by sharing in the wisdom that abides in them they are made new and so made wise — that is there. But that in due time he died for the ungodly, and that you did not spare your own Son but handed him over for us all — that is not there. For you have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to little children, so that those who labor and are heavy laden might come to him, and he might give them rest, because he is gentle and lowly in heart; and he guides the gentle in judgment, and teaches the meek his ways, looking on our lowliness and our trouble and forgiving all our sins. But those who are lifted up on the high road of some would-be loftier learning do not hear him saying, Learn of me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you shall find rest for your souls. For though they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but grew empty in their reasonings, and their foolish heart was darkened; claiming to be wise, they became fools.

And so I read there, too, that they had traded the glory of your incorruptible nature for idols and images of every kind — for the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds and beasts and crawling things: that Egyptian dish, in fact, for which Esau lost his rights as the firstborn; since your own firstborn people honored the head of a four-footed beast in your place, turning back in their hearts toward Egypt, bending your image — their own soul — before the image of a calf that eats hay. These things I found there, and I did not eat them. For it pleased you, Lord, to lift from Jacob the reproach of being the lesser, that the elder should serve the younger; and you called the Gentiles into your inheritance. And I had come to you out of the Gentiles; and I set my mind on the gold you willed your people to carry out of Egypt, because it was yours, wherever it was. And to the Athenians you said, through your apostle, that in you we live and move and have our being — as some of their own writers had said; and beyond question these books came from there. But I did not set my mind on the idols of Egypt, which men were serving with gold that was yours — men who traded the truth of God for a lie, and worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator.

And so I also read there that they had traded the glory of your incorruptible nature for idols and various shapes, for the likeness of the image of corruptible man, of birds and beasts and creeping things — that Egyptian food for which Esau lost his birthright. For your firstborn people worshiped the head of a four-footed beast in your place, turning back in their hearts toward Egypt, and bowing your image, which is their own soul, before the image of a calf that eats hay. These things I found there, but I did not feed on them. For it pleased you, Lord, to take the reproach of his lesser standing from Jacob, so that the elder should serve the younger, and you called the Gentiles into your inheritance. And I had come to you from among the Gentiles, and I fixed my mind on the gold that you willed your people to carry off out of Egypt, since it was yours wherever it lay. And to the Athenians you said, through your apostle, that in you we live and move and have our being, as one of their own poets had said — and these books did come from there. But I did not fix my mind on the idols of Egypt, which they served with your gold, those who exchanged the truth of God for a lie and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator.

Warned by these books to return to myself, I entered into my own depths, with you leading me; and I could enter, because you had become my helper. I entered, and with the eye of my soul, dim as it was, I saw — above that same eye of my soul, above my mind — the unchangeable light. Not this common light, which all flesh can look at; nor a greater light of the same kind, as if this daylight were to shine brighter and brighter until it filled the whole of space. Not that. Something else — utterly other than every light we know. Nor was it above my mind the way oil stands above water or the sky stands above the earth. It was higher, because it made me; and I was lower, because it made me. Whoever knows the truth knows that light; and whoever knows that light knows eternity. Love knows it. O eternal Truth, and true Love, and beloved Eternity! You are my God; to you I sigh day and night. When I first knew you, you lifted me up, so that I could see that there was something to see — and that I was not yet the man who could see it. And you beat back the weakness of my gaze, pouring your light into me with such force that I trembled with love and with dread; and I found that I was far away from you, in the region of unlikeness, as though I heard your voice from the height: "I am the food of the full-grown. Grow, and you will feed on me. And you will not change me into you, the way you change the food of your flesh; you will be changed into me." And I understood that you discipline man for his sin — that you made my soul waste thin as a spider's web — and I said, "Is truth nothing at all, then, just because it is not spread out through space, finite or infinite?" And you cried out from far away: "No indeed. I AM WHO I AM." And I heard it the way the heart hears, and there was no room left for doubting. I could sooner doubt that I am alive than doubt that truth exists — the truth that is seen and understood through the things that are made.

And being warned by these books to return into myself, I entered into my own inmost self, with you for my guide; and I could, because you had become my helper. I went in, and with the eye of my soul, such as it was, I saw above that same eye of my soul, above my mind, the Light Unchangeable. Not this ordinary light, which all flesh can look upon; nor a greater light of the same kind, as if this one shone many times brighter and filled all space with its size. It was not that; it was other, utterly other than all these. Nor was it above my mind the way oil floats above water, or the sky stands over the earth; it was above me because it made me, and I was below it because it made me. Whoever knows the truth knows that Light, and whoever knows the Light knows eternity. Love knows it. O eternal Truth, and true Love, and beloved Eternity! You are my God; to you I sigh day and night. And when I first knew you, you lifted me up so that I might see there was something to see, and that I was not yet the kind of thing that could see it. And you beat back the weakness of my gaze, blazing your beams upon me too strongly, and I trembled with love and dread; and I found that I was far away from you, in the region of unlikeness — as though I heard your voice from on high: I am the food of grown men; grow, and you shall feed on me. And you will not change me into yourself, as you change the food of your body, but you shall be changed into me. And I learned that you school a man for his wrongdoing, and make his soul waste away like a cobweb. And I said, Then is truth nothing, because it is not spread out through space, whether finite or infinite? And you cried to me from far off: No — truly, I AM WHO I AM. And I heard, as the heart hears, and there was no longer any room to doubt; I could more easily have doubted that I am alive than that Truth is — Truth that is clearly seen, understood through the things that are made.

And I considered the other things, the things below you, and I saw that they neither absolutely are nor absolutely are not. They are, because they are from you; they are not, because they are not what you are. For that truly is which abides unchangeably. But for me it is good to hold close to God; for if I do not remain in him, I cannot remain in myself either. He, remaining in himself, renews all things. And you are my Lord, because you have no need of any good of mine.

And I looked at the other things below you, and I saw that they neither altogether are nor altogether are not: they are, since they are from you; but they are not, because they are not what you are. For that truly is which abides unchanging. And it is good for me to hold fast to God, for if I do not abide in him, neither can I abide in myself; but he, abiding in himself, makes all things new. And you are the Lord my God, since you have no need of any good of mine.

And it was made plain to me that things which suffer corruption are good. If they were supremely good, they could not be corrupted; and if they were not good at all, there would be nothing in them to corrupt — for corruption harms, and unless it diminished some good, it would do no harm. So either corruption harms nothing, which cannot be; or — and this is beyond question — everything that is corrupted is being robbed of some good. But if things are robbed of all their good, they will not exist at all. For if they still exist, and can no longer be corrupted, they will be better than they were, because they now abide incorruptible — and what could be more monstrous than to say that things are made better by losing everything good in them? So: if they are stripped of all good, they will simply be nothing. Therefore, as long as they are, they are good. Therefore whatever is, is good. And this evil whose origin I was hunting is not a substance; for if it were a substance, it would be good. It would be either an incorruptible substance — a great good indeed — or a corruptible substance, which could not even be corrupted unless it were good. So I saw, and it was made plain to me, that you made all things good, and that there is no substance whatever that you did not make. And because you did not make all things equal, therefore all things are: each single thing good, and all things together very good, because our God made all things very good.

And it was made plain to me that the things which are corrupted are nonetheless good: they could not be corrupted if they were either the sovereign good, or no good at all. For if they were the sovereign good, they would be incorruptible; and if there were no good in them at all, there would be nothing in them to corrupt. For corruption does harm, and unless it lessened a thing's goodness it could do it no harm. So either corruption does no harm — which cannot be — or, as is most certain, everything that is corrupted is being robbed of some good. But if they were robbed of every good, they would cease to be entirely. For if they were to go on existing and could no longer be corrupted, they would be better than before, since they would now abide incorruptibly — and what is more monstrous than to say that things become better by losing all their good? So if they were stripped of all good, they would be nothing at all. As long, then, as they are, they are good; therefore whatever is, is good. And that evil whose origin I was searching for is not a substance; for if it were a substance, it would be good. It would have to be either an incorruptible substance, which is a great good, or a corruptible substance — which could not be corrupted at all unless it were good. So I saw, and it was made plain to me, that you made all things good, and that there is no substance whatsoever that you did not make; and because you did not make all things equal, therefore all things are, for each is good, and all together very good, since our God made all things very good.

And for you there is no evil at all — and not only for you but for the whole of your creation, because outside it there is nothing that could break in and corrupt the order you have laid upon it. In its parts, some things are counted evil because they clash with certain others; but those same things agree with others still, and there they are good — and they are good in themselves. All these things that quarrel with one another still fit the lower portion of the world we call earth, which has its own cloudy and windy sky, suited to it. Far be it from me now to say, "These things should not be." If I saw nothing but these, I would indeed long for something better; but even for these alone I would owe you praise. For that you must be praised, the things of earth declare: dragons, and all the deeps; fire, hail, snow, ice, and the storm-wind that performs your word; mountains and every hill; fruit trees and all the cedars; wild beasts and all the cattle; things that creep, and birds that fly; kings of the earth and all the peoples, princes and all the judges of the earth; young men and girls, the old together with the young — let them praise your name. And since from the heavens too they praise you — praise you, our God, in the heights: all your angels, all your hosts, sun and moon, all the stars and the light, the heaven of heavens and the waters above the heavens, praising your name — I no longer longed for anything better, because I was thinking of the whole; and with a sounder judgment I held that the higher things are better than the lower, but that all things together are better than the higher things alone.

And to you nothing whatsoever is evil — not to you only, but to your whole creation, since there is nothing outside it that could break in and corrupt the order you have set on it. But within its parts, some things, because they do not fit with certain others, are reckoned evil; yet those same things fit with others, and are good, and in themselves are good. And all these things that do not fit together among themselves do fit with the lower part of creation, which we call earth, with its own clouded and windy sky to match it. Far be it from me, then, to say, These things ought not to be. For if I could see nothing but these, I would indeed long for better; but even for these alone I ought to praise you. For that you are to be praised, the earth shows — dragons and all the deeps, fire, hail, snow, ice, and stormy wind that fulfill your word; mountains and all hills, fruit trees and all cedars; beasts and all cattle, creeping things and flying birds; kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all the judges of the earth; young men and maidens, old men and children, let them praise your name. And when from the heavens these praise you — praise you, our God, in the heights, all your angels, all your hosts, sun and moon, all the stars and light, the heaven of heavens, and the waters above the heavens — let them praise your name. I no longer longed for better things, because I now took all things into account; and with a sounder judgment I grasped that the higher things were better than the lower, but that all things together were better than the higher by themselves.

There is no health in those whom anything you have created displeases — as there was none in me, when many of the things you made displeased me. And because my soul did not dare to be displeased with my God, it refused to admit that anything that displeased it was yours. That is how it had drifted into the doctrine of two substances; and there it had no rest, and raved in words not its own. And doubling back from that, it had made itself a god stretched through the infinite measures of all space, and thought that this god was you, and set it up in its heart — and became once again the temple of its own idol, an abomination to you. But after you had stroked my head, without my knowing it, and closed my eyes so that they would stop looking at emptiness, I let go of myself a little, and my madness was lulled to sleep; and I woke in you, and saw you infinite in another way altogether — and that seeing did not come from the flesh.

There is no health in those whom any part of your creation displeases — as there was none in me, when so much that you had made displeased me. And because my soul did not dare to be displeased with my God, it refused to count as yours whatever displeased it. From there it had wandered off into the opinion of two substances, and found no rest, but talked empty nonsense. And turning back from that, it had made for itself a god stretched through infinite reaches of all space, and thought this was you, and lodged it in its heart, and so had become once more the temple of its own idol, a thing you abhor. But after you had soothed my head, all unknown to me, and shut my eyes so that they should not look on emptiness, I let go a little of my old self, and my madness was lulled to sleep; and I woke in you, and saw you as infinite — but in another way, and this seeing did not come from the flesh.

And I looked back over the rest of things, and I saw that they owe it to you that they are, and that in you all of them are bounded — not as in a place, but bounded otherwise: because you hold all things in your hand, in your truth. And all things are true insofar as they are; and falsehood is nothing but this — when what is not is thought to be. And I saw that each thing agrees not only with its place but with its time; and that you, who alone are eternal, did not begin to work after unnumbered stretches of time had gone by — for all the stretches of time, those that have passed and those that will pass, could neither go nor come except because you work and you abide.

And I looked back at the other things, and I saw that they owed their being to you, and were all bounded in you — but in a different way: not as being held in space, but because you hold all things in your hand by your truth, and all things are true insofar as they are, and there is no falsehood except where something is thought to be that is not. And I saw that all things fit not only with their places but with their seasons. And that you, who alone are eternal, did not begin to work only after countless ages had been spent; for all the stretches of time, both those that have gone by and those still to come, neither come nor go except through you, who work and abide.

And I found by experience — and saw nothing strange in it — that the same bread that delights a healthy palate is punishment to a sick one, and that light, hateful to sore eyes, is lovely to clear ones. Your justice displeases the wicked — how much more the viper and the worm! Yet these you created good, fitted to the lower parts of your creation; and the wicked themselves are fitted to those lower parts, the more unlike you they become, and to the higher, the more they come to be like you. And I asked what wickedness is, and I found not a substance, but the twistedness of a will wrenched away from the highest substance — away from you, God — toward the lowest things: a will that throws its own inmost self out of doors and swells toward the outside.

And I came to understand, and found it no strange thing, that bread which is pleasant to a healthy palate is loathsome to a sick one, and that to sore eyes the light is hateful which to sound ones is a delight. Your justice, too, displeases the wicked — and even more so the viper and the worm, which you have made good, fitted to the lower parts of your creation, with which the wicked themselves are fitted, and the more so the more unlike they are to you, just as they are fitted to the higher creatures the more they grow like you. And I asked what wickedness was, and found it to be no substance at all, but the swerving of the will away from you, God, the Supreme, toward these lower things — a will throwing its own inward parts away and swelling itself up on the outside.

And I marveled that I now loved you — you, and no phantom in place of you. But I could not stand still to enjoy my God. Your beauty swept me up to you, and my own weight promptly tore me away from you, and I fell back groaning among the lower things. That weight was the habit of the flesh. But the memory of you stayed with me; and I did not doubt in the least that there was one to whom I ought to cling — only that I was not yet the man who could cling to you. For the body, which is corrupted, weighs down the soul, and this earthly dwelling presses down the mind and its swarm of thoughts. And I was fully certain that your invisible things, ever since the creation of the world, are seen and understood through the things that are made — your eternal power also, and your divinity. For when I asked myself why I approved the beauty of bodies, in the heavens or on earth, and what I had at hand when I judged soundly about changeable things and said, "This ought to be so; that ought not" — asking, that is, why I judged as I judged, since judge I did — I had found the unchangeable and true eternity of truth, standing above my changeable mind. And so I climbed, step by step: from bodies to the soul that perceives through the body; from there to the soul's inner power, to which the body's senses report the world outside — the highest that the beasts can reach; from there again to the reasoning power, before whose judgment everything taken in by the bodily senses is brought. And this power, finding that in me it too was a changeable thing, raised itself up toward its own understanding. It led my thinking out of the rut of habit; it drew itself back from the mobs of contradictory phantoms, to find what light it was that had been sprinkled on it when it cried out — with no shred of doubt — that the unchangeable is to be preferred to the changeable; for it must somehow have known the unchangeable itself, or it could never have preferred it with such certainty. And it arrived at THAT WHICH IS, in the stroke of one trembling glance. Then indeed I saw your invisible things, understood through the things that are made. But I had no strength to hold my gaze there. My weakness was beaten back, and I was returned to my old habits, carrying with me only a loving memory — the longing, so to speak, for a dish I had caught the fragrance of, but could not yet eat.

And I marveled that I now loved you, and no phantom in your place. And yet I did not press on to enjoy my God; instead I was carried up to you by your beauty, and soon carried down from you again by my own weight, and fell with grief into these lower things. That weight was the habit of the flesh. Yet there stayed with me a remembrance of you, and I no longer doubted at all that there was one to whom I should cling — only that I was not yet the kind of thing that could cling to you, for the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and this earthly tent presses on the mind heavy with many thoughts. And I was most certain that your invisible things, from the foundation of the world, are clearly seen, understood through the things that are made — yes, your eternal power and your Godhead. For when I asked why I admired the beauty of bodies, whether of the heavens or of the earth, and what it was that helped me judge soundly of changing things and pronounce, This ought to be so, this not so — when I asked, I say, where this judging of mine came from, since I did judge, I found above my changeable mind the unchangeable and true eternity of truth. And so, step by step, I rose from bodies to the soul that perceives through the body, and from there to the soul's inward power, to which the bodily senses report things outside (and this far the beasts can reach), and from there again to the reasoning power, to which what is taken in from the bodily senses is referred for judgment. And this power, finding even itself in me to be a changeable thing, lifted itself up to its own understanding, and drew my thought away from the grip of habit, pulling itself clear of the swarming crowds of contradictory phantoms, so that it might find what light it was that was sprinkled upon it when, without any doubt, it cried out that the unchangeable was to be preferred to the changeable — for unless it had somehow known the unchangeable, it could never have been so sure to set it above the changeable. And so, in the flash of one trembling glance, it arrived at THAT WHICH IS. Then indeed I saw your invisible things, understood through the things that are made. But I could not hold my gaze there; my weakness was struck back, and I was thrown again upon my old habits, carrying away with me only a loving memory, and a craving for what I had, as it were, caught the scent of, but was not yet able to feed on.

So I looked for a way to gather strength enough to enjoy you, and I did not find it until I embraced the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who is over all things, God blessed forever — calling to me and saying, "I am the way, the truth, and the life" — and mixing into our flesh the food I was too weak to take. For the Word became flesh so that your Wisdom, through whom you created all things, might become milk for our infancy. I did not yet hold my Lord Jesus — I was not yet humbled enough to hold the humble one — and I did not yet know what his weakness had to teach. For your Word, the eternal Truth, towering above the highest parts of your creation, lifts up to itself those who have been brought low; and here below it built itself a humble house out of our clay, so that those who needed bringing low might be pulled loose from themselves and carried across to it: healing their swelling, feeding their love, so that they would not stride on farther in self-confidence, but rather consent to grow weak, seeing at their feet the Godhead made weak by taking our coat of skin — and so that, worn out at last, they would throw themselves down on that weakness, and it would rise, and lift them up.

Then I began to search for a way to gain the strength I needed to enjoy you, and I did not find it — not until I embraced that Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who is over all, God blessed forever, calling to me and saying, I am the way, and the truth, and the life; and mingling with our flesh that food which I was not yet able to take. For the Word was made flesh so that your wisdom, by which you made all things, might become milk for our infancy. For I did not yet hold on to my Lord Jesus Christ, I, humbled, to the Humble; nor did I yet know what his weakness had to teach. For your Word, the eternal Truth, towering above the highest parts of your creation, raises up to itself those it has brought low; but in this lower world it built itself a lowly dwelling out of our clay, to pull down from themselves those who would be brought low, and bring them over to itself — to ease their swelling and feed their love, so that they should go no further in self-confidence, but rather grow weak, seeing at their feet the Godhead made weak by taking on our coat of skin, and, worn out, might throw themselves down on him, who, rising, would lift them up.

But I thought otherwise. I thought of Christ my Lord only as a man of surpassing wisdom, whom no one could equal — above all because, being wonderfully born of a virgin to give an example of despising temporal things for the sake of immortality, he seemed, through God's care for us, to have earned so towering an authority as a teacher. But what mystery there was in "the Word became flesh," I could not even begin to guess. From what has been handed down in writing about him — that he ate, drank, slept, walked, was glad, was sorrowful, taught — I had learned only this much: that flesh did not cleave to your Word without a human soul and a human mind. Everyone knows this who knows the unchangeableness of your Word; and I knew it now, as well as I could, and did not doubt it at all. For now to move the limbs of the body by will, and now not; now to be moved by some feeling, and now not; now to deliver wise judgments through signs, and now to keep silence — these belong to a soul and mind that change. And if the writings said these things of him falsely, the whole of them would stand accused of lying, and no faith that saves mankind would be left in those books. But because they were written truthfully, I acknowledged in Christ a complete man: not a man's body only, nor a body with a soul that senses but does not reason, but a whole man; and I judged him greater than everyone else, not as Truth in person, but by some great excellence of his human nature and a more perfect share in wisdom. Alypius, for his part, supposed that Catholics believed in a God so clothed in flesh that in Christ, besides God and flesh, there was no soul at all — he did not think they ascribed a human mind to him. And since he was firmly persuaded that the deeds recorded of Christ could only have been done by a living and reasoning creature, he moved the more slowly toward the Christian faith itself. Later, when he understood that this was the error of the Apollinarian heretics, he rejoiced in the Catholic faith and settled into it. And I confess it was later still that I learned how, in the words "the Word became flesh," Catholic truth is pried apart from the falsehood of Photinus. The refutation of heretics throws into relief what your Church holds and what sound doctrine contains. For there had to be heresies, too, so that the tested might stand out among the weak.

But I thought otherwise. I conceived of my Lord Christ only as a man of surpassing wisdom, whom no one could be equal to — especially because, being wonderfully born of a virgin, he seemed, by God's care for us, to have reached that great height of authority precisely in order to set us an example of holding temporal things in contempt for the sake of immortality. But what mystery lay hidden in The Word was made flesh, I could not even begin to imagine. I had only learned, from what is handed down in writing of him, that he ate and drank, slept, walked, rejoiced in spirit and was sorrowful, and spoke; and that the flesh did not cleave to your Word by itself, but together with a human soul and mind. Everyone knows this who knows the unchangeableness of your Word, which I now knew as well as I could, and did not doubt at all. For to move the limbs of the body by will and now to leave them still, to feel some emotion and now not to feel it, to utter wise sayings through human signs and now to keep silence — these belong to a soul and mind that change. And if these things had been written of him falsely, then everything else would be in danger of the same charge, and there would remain in those books no saving faith for the human race. Since, then, they were written truly, I acknowledged a complete man in Christ — not the body of a man only, nor a body with a sensitive soul but no rational one, but a true man — whom I judged to be set above all others, not only as being a form of the truth but for a certain great excellence of human nature and a fuller share in wisdom. But Alypius supposed that Catholics believed God to be so clothed in flesh that, besides God and flesh, there was no soul at all in Christ, and he did not think a human mind was ascribed to him; and because he was sure that the actions recorded of Christ could only be done by a living, rational creature, he moved the more slowly toward the Christian faith. Later, learning that this was the error of the Apollinarian heretics, he rejoiced and fell in with the Catholic faith. As for me, I confess it was somewhat later still that I learned how, in that saying The Word was made flesh, the Catholic truth is marked off from the falsehood of Photinus. For the rejecting of heretics makes the teaching of your Church and the soundness of true doctrine stand out the more clearly; for there must indeed be heresies, so that those who are approved may be made plain among the weak.

But at that time, after reading those books of the Platonists, once they had prompted me to look for a truth without a body, I caught sight of your invisible things, understood through the things that are made; and though I was driven back, I sensed the thing that the darkness of my soul would not let me contemplate. I was certain that you are, and that you are infinite — yet not poured out through space, finite or infinite; that you truly are, always the same, never becoming other or otherwise in any part or by any motion; and that all other things are from you, on this single surest proof: that they are. Of all this I was certain — and far too weak to enjoy you. I chattered away like an expert; and if I had not gone looking for your way in Christ our Savior, I would have ended not expert but expired. For I had begun by now to want to seem wise. Full of my own punishment, I shed no tears; I swelled, instead, with knowledge. Where was the love that builds on the foundation of humility, which is Christ Jesus? When would those books have taught me that? I believe you willed me to run into them before I had studied your scriptures, so that the way they marked me would be stamped into my memory; so that later, when I had been gentled by your books and your fingers were dressing my wounds, I could tell apart, and know the distance between, presumption and confession — between those who see where they must go but not how to get there, and the way itself, which leads not just to a sight of the country of blessedness but to a home in it. For if I had been formed first by your holy scriptures, and you had grown sweet to me in the long familiar use of them, and I had fallen on those volumes afterward — they might have torn me off the solid ground of piety. Or, even if I had held on to the healthy disposition I had drawn in, I might have supposed that a man could draw the same from those books alone, if those alone he studied.

But having read those books of the Platonists, and being taught by them to search for a truth that has no body, I saw your invisible things, understood through the things that are made; and though I was thrown back, I caught sight of what it was that the darkness of my mind kept me from contemplating. I was sure that you exist, and are infinite, and yet are not spread out through space, finite or infinite; and that you truly are, you who are always the same, never varying in any part or any motion; and that all other things are from you, on this one most certain ground, that they are. Of these things I was sure, yet too unsteady to enjoy you. I chattered like an expert; and yet, had I not sought your way in Christ our Savior, I would have proved to be not an expert but an expiring man. For I had now begun to want to seem wise — full of my own punishment, and yet I did not grieve over it; rather, I was puffed up with knowledge and full of scorn. For where was that love that builds on the foundation of humility, which is Christ Jesus? When would those books have taught me that?
