On these books, I believe, you willed that I should fall before I took up your Scriptures, so that it might be stamped on my memory how they affected me; and that afterward, when I had been tamed by your books and had my wounds touched by your healing fingers, I might tell the difference, and know it, between presumption and confession — between those who see where they must go but not the way there, and the Way that leads not only to see the land of blessedness but to live in it. For had I first been formed by your holy Scriptures, and had you grown sweet to me through long use of them, and had I then come upon those other books, they might perhaps have torn me away from the solid ground of devotion; or, if I had held on to the healthy frame of mind I had drunk in from Scripture, I might have thought that frame could be had from the study of those books alone.

So I seized — how greedily! — the venerable writings of your Spirit, and before all the rest, the apostle Paul. And the hard questions died away: the places where he had once seemed to me to contradict himself, where the run of his words seemed to quarrel with the testimony of the law and the prophets. That pure speech showed me a single face, and I learned to rejoice with trembling. I began; and whatever truth I had read in those other books, I found here with the praise of your grace added: so that the man who sees may not boast as though he had not received — not only what he sees, but the very power of seeing (for what does he have that he did not receive?) — and so that he may be not only warned to see you, who are always the same, but also healed, so that he can hold you; and so that the man who cannot see from far off may still walk the road by which he will come, and see, and hold. For though a man delights in the law of God in his inmost self, what will he do with that other law in his members, which fights against the law of his mind and drags him captive under the law of sin that is in his members? For you are just, Lord; and we have sinned, we have done wrong, we have dealt wickedly, and your hand has grown heavy upon us, and we have justly been handed over to the old sinner, the warden of death — because he talked our will into the likeness of his own will, that will by which he did not stand fast in your truth. What is wretched man to do? Who will free him from the body of this death, except your grace, through Jesus Christ our Lord — whom you begot coeternal with you, and created at the beginning of your ways; in whom the prince of this world found nothing that deserved death, and killed him anyway; and so the bond of debt that stood against us was wiped out? None of this is in those books. Those pages nowhere carry the face of this devotion: the tears of confession; your sacrifice — a troubled spirit, a broken and humbled heart; the salvation of your people; the city made ready as a bride; the pledge of the Holy Spirit; the cup of our ransom. No one sings there: "Shall not my soul be still under God? For from him comes my salvation; he is my God and my savior, my defender: I shall not be shaken anymore." No one there hears him calling: "Come to me, all you who labor." They scorn to learn from him, because he is meek and lowly of heart; for you have hidden these things from the wise and the clever, and revealed them to little children. For it is one thing to see the country of peace from a wooded ridge, and find no road to it, and struggle toward it in vain through trackless ground, ambushed on every side by runaways and deserters with their captain, the lion and the dragon; and another thing to hold the road that leads there, guarded by the care of the heavenly commander, where no deserters from the heavenly army lie in wait to rob — for they shun that road like torment. All this went down into the marrow of me, in wonderful ways, as I read the least of your apostles; and I had gazed long at your works, and trembled.

So I seized most eagerly on the venerable writing of your Spirit, and above all on the apostle Paul. And those difficulties melted away in which he had once seemed to me to contradict himself, and the text of what he said to disagree with the witness of the Law and the Prophets. The face of that pure word appeared to me now as one and the same, and I learned to rejoice with trembling. So I began; and whatever truth I had read in those other books, I found here too, but set within the praise of your grace — so that whoever sees should not so boast as though he had not received both what he sees and the very seeing of it (for what does he have that he has not received?), and so that he might be not only warned to look toward you, who are always the same, but also healed, to hold on to you; and that one who cannot see from far off might still walk the road by which he may come, and see, and hold you. For though a man delight in the law of God after the inner man, what is he to do with that other law in his members, which fights against the law of his mind and takes him captive under the law of sin that is in his members? For you are just, Lord, but we have sinned and done wrong and acted wickedly, and your hand has grown heavy upon us, and we are justly handed over to that ancient sinner, the king of death, because he talked our will into being like his own will, by which he did not stand fast in your truth. What shall wretched man do? Who shall free him from the body of this death, except your grace, through Jesus Christ our Lord, whom you begot co-eternal with yourself and formed at the beginning of your ways — in whom the prince of this world found nothing worthy of death, and yet killed him, and so the record of debt that stood against us was wiped out? None of this is in those other books. Those pages do not hold the face of this devotion, the tears of confession, your sacrifice, a troubled spirit, a broken and contrite heart, the salvation of your people, the Bridal City, the pledge of the Holy Spirit, the Cup of our redemption. No one sings there, Shall not my soul be subject to God? For from him comes my salvation; he is my God and my salvation, my defender; I shall be moved no more. No one there hears him call, Come to me, all you who labor. They are too proud to learn from him, because he is gentle and lowly in heart; for these things you have hidden from the wise and prudent, and revealed them to little children. For it is one thing, from a wooded mountaintop, to catch sight of the land of peace and find no road to it, struggling in vain through trackless ways, set upon and waylaid by runaways and deserters under their captain the lion and the dragon; and it is another thing to keep to the road that leads there, guarded by the care of the heavenly Commander, where those who have deserted the heavenly army do not lie in wait to rob — for they shun that road as a torment. All this sank wonderfully deep into me when I read that least of your apostles, and pondered your works, and was filled with trembling.

sections.label: Book VIII
sections.title: Take It and Read
The Garden: Take Up and Read

segments.text: My God, let me remember your mercies to me with thanksgiving, and confess them to you. Let my bones be drenched in your love and say: Lord, who is like you? You have torn my chains apart — let me offer you a sacrifice of praise. How you tore them I will tell, and everyone who worships you will hear it and say: Blessed be the Lord in heaven and on earth; great and wonderful is his name. Your words had lodged deep in my heart, and on every side you had me walled in. Of your eternal life I was now certain, though I had seen it only in a riddle, as in a mirror; and every doubt about an incorruptible substance — the substance every other substance comes from — had been taken from me. I no longer wanted to be more certain of you, only more steady in you. But in my temporal life everything was still swaying, and my heart had yet to be cleared of the old yeast. The Way — the Savior himself — pleased me well; but the narrow passage he led through still made me flinch. And you put it into my mind, and it seemed good in my sight, to go to Simplicianus, who looked to me like a good servant of yours: your grace shone in him. I had heard, too, that from his youth up he had lived in complete devotion to you. He was an old man now, and in a long life spent following your way with such earnestness, I guessed he had learned much — and he had. Out of that store I wanted him, once I had laid my agitations in front of him, to draw out and show me the fittest way for a man in my condition to walk in your path.

My God, let me remember and confess your mercies to me, with thanksgiving. Let my bones be drenched in your love, and let them say to you: Who is like you, Lord? You have snapped my chains; I will offer you the sacrifice of thanksgiving. How you snapped them I will tell, and all who worship you, when they hear it, will say: Blessed be the Lord, in heaven and on earth; great and wonderful is his name. Your words had stuck fast in my heart, and on every side I was fenced in by you. Of your eternal life I was now sure, though I saw it only as a riddle, as in a dim mirror. I had stopped doubting that there is an incorruptible substance from which every other substance comes; and I no longer wanted to be more certain of you, only more steady in you. But about my life in time everything was still wavering, and my heart had to be swept clean of the old leaven. The Way itself, the Savior himself, pleased me well — and yet I still shrank from going through its narrow gate. And you put it into my mind, and it seemed good in my eyes, to go to Simplicianus, who seemed to me a good servant of yours, with your grace clearly shining in him. I had heard, too, that from his earliest youth he had lived wholly devoted to you. He was an old man now, and after so many years spent following your ways so closely, he seemed likely to have learned a great deal — and so he had. Out of that store I wanted him to tell me — once I had laid my anxieties before him — which was the best way for a man in my state to walk in your paths.

For I saw the church full, and one man went this way and another that. But my own life in the world had gone sour on me. It was a heavy load now: desire no longer burned me on, as it once did, with hopes of honor and money, making the slavery bearable. Next to your sweetness, and the beauty of your house, which I loved, those things had lost their savor. But I was still bound tight by my need for a woman. The Apostle did not forbid me to marry, though he urged something better and wished all men could live as he lived. I was weak, so I picked the softer place; and because of that one thing everything else in me pitched and rolled — I was going limp, drying out with cares I could not shed — because married life, to which I had bound myself over, would force compliance from me in matters where I had no wish to comply. From the mouth of the Truth himself I had heard that there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven — but, he says, let him accept it who can. Surely all men are hollow who lack the knowledge of God — who could not, from the good things in front of their eyes, find the One who is good. But I was out of that hollowness. I had climbed past it, and by the joint testimony of your whole creation I had found you, our Creator, and your Word — God with you, and with you one God — through whom you created all things. There is a second breed of the godless: the ones who know God and do not glorify him as God, or give him thanks. I had fallen into that as well; and your right hand took hold of me, lifted me out, and set me down where I could get well. For you have said to man, The fear of the Lord — that is wisdom, and, Do not be eager to seem wise: the people who declared themselves wise became fools. And I had already found the pearl of great price. I should have sold everything I had and bought it. And I hesitated.

For I saw the church was full, and one went this way, another that. But I was unhappy that I was leading a worldly life — now that my old cravings no longer fired me, as they once had, with hopes of honor and money, it was a heavy burden to carry so heavy a bondage. For set against your sweetness, and the beauty of your house, which I loved, those things had no charm for me anymore. But I was still held fast by the love of a woman. The Apostle did not forbid me to marry, though he urged me toward something better, wishing above all that everyone were as he was. But I, being weak, chose the easier ground, and for that one reason was tossed about in everything else, worn thin and wasted with cares that ate at me, because in all other matters I was forced, against my will, to fit myself to a married life I had given myself over to and was enslaved by. I had heard from the mouth of Truth that there are some who make themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven — but, he says, let the one who can receive this receive it. Empty indeed are all people who do not know God, who could not, from the good things they see, find out the One who is good. But I was no longer in that emptiness; I had climbed past it, and by the shared witness of all your creatures I had found you, our Creator, and your Word, God with you, and together with you one God, by whom you made all things. There is another kind of ungodly person, who knows God and yet does not glorify him as God, nor give thanks. Into this too I had fallen; but your right hand caught me up and carried me out of it, and set me where I could get well again. For you have said to a human being, Behold, the fear of the Lord is wisdom; and, Do not wish to seem wise — because those who called themselves wise became fools. I had now found the priceless pearl, which I ought to have bought by selling all I had — and I hesitated.

So I went to Simplicianus, who had been a father to Ambrose — a bishop now — in the receiving of your grace, and whom Ambrose loved like a father in truth. I laid out for him the winding maze of my wanderings. But when I mentioned that I had read certain books of the Platonists, translated into Latin by Victorinus — once professor of rhetoric in the city of Rome, who had died a Christian, as I had heard — he congratulated me on not falling in with the writings of other philosophers, crowded with fallacies and frauds after the elements of this world, while the Platonists’ pages point in every way toward God and his Word. Then, to bend me toward the humility of Christ — hidden from the wise, revealed to little children — he began to talk about Victorinus himself, whom he had known intimately at Rome; and what he told me of him I will not pass over in silence, because it holds a great confession of praise to your grace: how that old man, immensely learned, expert in every liberal art, who had read and weighed so many works of the philosophers, the teacher of so many distinguished senators — a man whose brilliance in his office had earned him, and been granted, what the citizens of this world count a summit of honor, a statue in the Roman Forum — that man, a worshiper of idols into his old age, a partner in the sacrilegious rites that almost the whole nobility of Rome then breathed like air, a nobility that had taught the people to sigh after

So I went to Simplicianus, who had been a father to Ambrose (now a bishop) in the receiving of your grace, and whom Ambrose loved as a father indeed. I told him the whole maze of my wanderings. But when I mentioned that I had read certain books of the Platonists, which Victorinus — once a professor of rhetoric at Rome, who had died a Christian, as I had heard — had translated into Latin, he was glad I had not stumbled onto the writings of other philosophers, full of frauds and deceits in keeping with the elements of this world, whereas the Platonists in many ways led toward belief in God and his Word. Then, to draw me toward the humility of Christ, hidden from the wise and revealed to little ones, he spoke of Victorinus himself, whom he had known intimately at Rome; and what he told me I will not keep back. For it holds great praise of your grace, and ought to be confessed to you: how that old man, deeply learned, skilled in all the liberal arts, who had read and weighed so many of the philosophers, the teacher of so many noble senators, who as a monument to his distinguished career had even earned and received a statue in the Roman Forum — a thing the men of this world count a high honor — and who all his life had been a worshipper of idols and a sharer in the unholy rites to which nearly all the nobility of Rome were given, breathing into the people their love of the monstrous gods of every kind, the barking dog Anubis and the rest, who once took up arms against Neptune and Venus and Minerva — gods that Rome had once conquered and now adored, and that the old Victorinus had defended for so many years with thundering eloquence — that this man was not ashamed to become a child of your Christ, an infant newly born at your font, bowing his neck to the yoke of humility and his proud forehead to the disgrace of the Cross.
Anubis the barking dog-god, and monster gods of every breed, weapons leveled against Neptune, against Venus, against Minerva —

Lord, Lord — you who bowed down the heavens and came down, who touched the mountains and they smoked — by what road did you make your way into that man's heart? He used to read the holy Scripture, Simplicianus told me, and searched out and pored over all the Christian writings most carefully; and he said to Simplicianus — not in public, but privately, as a friend — "You should know that I am already a Christian." And Simplicianus answered, "I will not believe it, nor will I count you among the Christians, until I see you in the church of Christ." Victorinus replied, mocking, "So is it walls that make Christians?" He said this often — that he was already a Christian — and as often Simplicianus gave the same answer, and as often the joke about the walls came back. For he was afraid of offending his friends, those proud demon-worshippers, from the height of whose Babylonian dignity — like cedars of Lebanon the Lord had not yet brought down — he expected a great weight of hatred to come crashing onto him. But after reading and hard thought he gathered his courage, and grew afraid that Christ would deny him before the holy angels if he were now afraid to confess Christ before men; and he saw himself guilty of a grave offense, ashamed of the sacraments of your Word's humility while feeling no shame at the unholy rites of those proud demons whose pride he had copied and whose rites he had taken up. So he hardened his face against vanity, and softened it before the truth, and suddenly, when no one expected it, he said to Simplicianus (as Simplicianus told me), "Let us go to the church; I want to be made a Christian." And Simplicianus, beside himself with joy, went with him. He was admitted to the first sacrament and became a catechumen, and not long after gave in his name to be reborn by baptism — Rome marveling, the Church rejoicing. The proud watched, and were enraged; they gnashed their teeth and melted away. But the Lord God was the hope of your servant, and he paid no heed to vanities and lying follies.

gods Rome had once defeated in battle and then bowed down to; gods the old Victorinus had thundered in defense of for so many years with that terrifying eloquence — this same man was not ashamed to become a child of your Christ, an infant at your font: to bend his neck under the yoke of humility and lower his forehead to the disgrace of the cross.

And so, when the hour came for him to make his profession of faith — which at Rome those about to come to your grace deliver from a raised place, in a set form of words learned by heart, before all the faithful — the presbyters, Simplicianus said, offered Victorinus the chance to make it more privately, as they did for those who seemed likely to be flustered by shyness. But he chose instead to profess his salvation before the holy crowd. "For it was not salvation that he taught in rhetoric, and yet he had professed that in public; how much less, then, should he be afraid of your meek flock while pronouncing your word, when he had not feared a crazed mob while delivering his own." So when he went up to make his profession, everyone who knew him whispered his name to one another with the sound of congratulation. And who there did not know him? A low murmur ran through all the mouths of the rejoicing crowd: Victorinus! Victorinus! As suddenly as they had burst out for joy at the sight of him, just as suddenly they fell silent to hear him. He pronounced the true faith with magnificent boldness, and they all longed to gather him into their very hearts — and with their love and their joy they did gather him: those were the hands that drew him in.

Lord, Lord, you who bowed the heavens and came down, who touched the mountains and they smoked — by what paths did you make your way into that man’s chest? He read holy Scripture, Simplicianus told me; he hunted out all the Christian writings and searched them with the greatest care; and he kept saying to Simplicianus — not openly, but privately, friend to friend — “You should know that I am already a Christian.” And Simplicianus kept answering, “I will not believe it, and I will not count you among the Christians, until I see you in the church of Christ.” And Victorinus would laugh at him: “So it’s walls that make Christians?” He said it often, that he was already a Christian; Simplicianus often gave the same answer; and often the joke about the walls came around again. The truth is he was afraid of offending his friends — proud worshipers of demons — and expected their hostility to come crashing down on him from the height of their Babylonian dignity, as from cedars of Lebanon the Lord had not yet shattered. But once steady reading and thirst had drawn firmness into him, a different fear took hold: that Christ might deny him before the holy angels if he was afraid to confess Christ before men. Being ashamed of the sacraments of the humility of your Word, while feeling no shame at the sacrilegious rites of those arrogant demons — rites he had accepted as their proud imitator — came to look to him like an enormous crime. So he turned brazen toward vanity and shy before the truth, and suddenly, without warning, he said to Simplicianus, as Simplicianus told it, “Let’s go to the church. I want to be made a Christian.” And Simplicianus, hardly able to contain his joy, went with him. Not long after he had been admitted to the first instruction of the faith, he gave in his name to be reborn through baptism — while Rome stared and the Church rejoiced. The proud looked on and seethed; they ground their teeth and wasted away. But the Lord God was your servant’s hope, and he had no eyes for vanities and lying madness.

Good God, what is it that happens in a person, that he rejoices more over the salvation of a soul that was despaired of, freed from a greater danger, than if there had always been hope of it, or the danger had been less? For you too, merciful Father, rejoice more over one who repents than over ninety-nine righteous people who need no repentance. And we listen with great gladness whenever we hear how the lost sheep is carried home on the shepherd's shoulders, how the coin is restored to your treasury while the neighbors rejoice with the woman who found it. And the joy of the solemn service in your house forces tears from us when in your house we read of your younger son, that he was dead and is alive again, was lost and is found. For you rejoice in us, and in your holy angels, holy through holy love. For you are always the same, since all the things that do not stay the same, and do not last, you know forever in the same unchanging way.

At last the hour came for his profession of faith. In Rome those about to approach your grace deliver the profession in fixed words, learned by heart, from a raised platform, in full sight of the faithful people; and the priests, Simplicianus said, offered Victorinus the chance to recite it more privately — an offer they used to make to anyone who seemed likely to panic from shyness. But he chose to declare his salvation in front of the holy crowd. What he had taught all those years in rhetoric was not salvation — and he had professed that in public. If he had never feared a mob of madmen when performing his own words, why should he fear your gentle flock when pronouncing yours? So when he climbed up to make the profession, everyone who knew him — and who there did not? — passed his name along with a hum of congratulation, and a low murmur ran through every mouth in the rejoicing crowd: Victorinus! Victorinus! A sudden roar at the sight of him; a sudden hush to hear him. He pronounced the true faith with superb confidence, and all of them wanted to pull him bodily into their hearts — and they did pull him in, by loving him and rejoicing over him. Those were the hands they used.

What is it, then, that happens in the soul, that it takes more delight in finding or recovering the things it loves than if it had always had them? Yes, and everything else bears witness to this; all things are crowded with witnesses crying out, "So it is." The conquering general celebrates his triumph — yet he would not have conquered unless he had fought, and the more danger there was in the battle, the more joy there is in the triumph. The storm tosses the sailors and threatens shipwreck; they all go pale at the nearness of death; then sky and sea grow calm, and they are overjoyed, just as they had been overafraid. A loved one is sick, and his pulse warns of danger; everyone who longs for his recovery is sick in heart along with him. He gets better, though he cannot yet walk with his old strength — and there is more joy than there was before, when he walked sound and strong. Even the ordinary pleasures of human life people buy with hardship: not only the troubles that fall on us unasked and against our will, but troubles we choose, that we go looking for, for the pleasure's sake. Eating and drinking give no pleasure unless the pinch of hunger and thirst comes first. Heavy drinkers eat something salty to work up an uncomfortable dryness, which the drink then relieves, and the relief is the pleasure. And it is the custom that a bride, once promised, is not handed over at once, so that her husband will not hold cheap, as a wife, the woman he did not have to sigh for as a betrothed.

Good God — what is it in a man, that he rejoices more over a soul saved after despair, delivered out of the thick of danger, than over one who never lost hope, never stood in such peril? You too, merciful Father — even you rejoice more over one sinner repenting than over ninety-nine righteous who need no repentance. And what gladness we feel whenever we hear how the straying sheep comes home on the shepherd’s rejoicing shoulders, and the small coin goes back into your treasury while the neighbors celebrate with the woman who found it. The joy of the liturgy in your house forces out tears, when the reading in your house tells of your younger son — he was dead, and came to life; he was lost, and is found. You are rejoicing in us then, and in your holy angels, who are holy with holy love. For you are always the same; and all the things that do not stay the same, and do not stay at all, you know forever in the same way.

This law holds in foul and forbidden joy; it holds in joy that is permitted and lawful; it holds in the purest perfection of friendship; it held in the one who was dead and came to life again, was lost and was found. Everywhere the greater joy is heralded by the greater pain. What does this mean, O Lord my God — you, who are everlasting joy to yourself, and around whom some things forever rejoice in you? What does it mean, that this region of things keeps ebbing and flowing, falling out of favor and being reconciled? Is this the measure you have set them? Is this all you have given them — when, from the highest heavens to the lowest earth, from the world's beginning to the end of the ages, from the angel to the worm, from the first stirring to the last, you set each thing in its place and bring each to pass in its season, every good thing after its kind? Alas for me — how high you are in the heights, and how deep in the depths! And you never leave us, and we so barely make our way back to you.

What is happening in the soul, then, when it takes more delight in finding or getting back what it loves than if it had held it all along? Everything else agrees; the world is packed with witnesses shouting, “That’s how it is!” The victorious general has his triumph — and there is no victory without a battle; the greater the danger in the fight, the greater the joy in the parade. A storm batters the sailors and threatens shipwreck; every face goes white at oncoming death; then sky and sea grow calm, and their joy runs as high as their fear did. A friend is sick, and his pulse says danger, and everyone who wants him well is sick at heart with him; he mends — he cannot yet walk with his old vigor — and already there is a joy in the house that was never there when he walked well and strong. Even the ordinary pleasures of human life men purchase with difficulty — and not only the difficulties that fall on us unlooked-for and unwanted, but difficulty chosen and arranged on purpose. Eating and drinking are no pleasure at all unless the pinch of hunger and thirst comes first. Drinkers eat salty things to raise an uncomfortable burn, and the pleasure comes when the drink puts it out. And custom rules that a promised bride is not handed over at once — so that as a husband a man will never hold cheap the woman he did not sigh for, waiting, as her betrothed.

Up, Lord, and act: rouse us and call us back; kindle us and seize us; set us on fire and grow sweet to us. Let us love now, let us run. Do not many people return to you out of a deeper hell of blindness than Victorinus knew — come near, and are enlightened, receiving the Light, and with it the power to become your sons? Yet if they are less known to the world, even those who know them rejoice less over them. For when many rejoice together, each one's joy is the richer, since they catch fire and warm one another. And again, those who are widely known carry more weight toward others' salvation, and lead the way for many to follow; and so even those who went before them rejoice greatly in them, because they do not rejoice in them alone. Far be it from us that in your tabernacle the rich should be welcomed before the poor, or the noble before the lowborn — since you have rather chosen the weak things of the world to shame the strong, and the base things and the despised things of this world, and the things that are not, to bring to nothing the things that are. And yet that least of your apostles, by whose tongue you sounded out these very words, when through his campaign the proconsul Paulus had his pride beaten down and was brought under the easy yoke of your Christ, a subject now of the great King — even he was glad to be called Paul, dropping his old name Saul, in token of so great a victory. For the enemy is more thoroughly beaten in a man through whom he held more, and through whom he held many. And he holds the proud more, on account of their high birth, and through them holds many more, on account of their authority. So the more dear the heart of Victorinus was reckoned — the heart the devil had held as an unbreachable stronghold, the tongue of Victorinus, that mighty, keen weapon with which he had slain so many — the more abundantly ought your sons to rejoice, because our King has bound the strong man, and they saw his vessels seized from him and cleansed and made fit for your honor, and turned to good use for the Lord, for every good work.

This law holds in joy that is filthy and damnable; it holds in joy that is permitted and lawful; it holds in the purest honesty of friendship; it held for the son who was dead and came to life, was lost and found. Everywhere the greater joy comes in behind the greater pain. What does it mean, Lord my God — you who are eternally joy to your own self, you yourself, with the beings around you rejoicing in you forever — what does it mean that this lower region of things ebbs and flows, alternately offended and reconciled? Is that the mode you allotted them? Is that all you granted them — while from the heights of heaven to the depths of the earth, from the first of the ages to the end of the ages, from the angel down to the worm, from the first stir of motion to the last, you were setting every kind of good thing and every one of your just works each in its proper place, and bringing each to pass at its proper hour? How high you are in the highest, and how deep in the deepest! You are never anywhere absent — and how slowly, how barely, we come back to you.

But when that man of yours, Simplicianus, told me this about Victorinus, I was on fire to imitate him — which was the very reason he had told it. And when he added that under the emperor Julian a law had been passed forbidding Christians to teach literature and oratory, and that Victorinus, obeying it, had chosen to give up his wordy school rather than your Word, by which you make eloquent the tongues of the speechless — he seemed to me not so much resolute as blessed, in having found a way to wait on you alone. And that was the very thing I was sighing for, bound as I was — not with another man's irons, but by my own iron will. The enemy held my will, and out of it had made a chain for me, and bound me with it. For out of a crooked will comes lust, and serving the lust becomes a habit, and the habit, not resisted, becomes a compulsion. By these links, joined together like a chain — which is why I called it a chain — a harsh bondage held me fast. But the new will, just beginning in me, the will to serve you freely and to enjoy you, my God, the only sure delight, was not yet strong enough to overcome the old will, grown tough with age. So my two wills — one old, one new, one of the flesh, one of the spirit — fought it out inside me, and by their quarrel they tore my soul apart.

Move, Lord; act. Wake us and call us back, kindle us and seize us, blaze up, grow sweet to us: let us love, let us run. Don’t many come back to you out of a deeper hell of blindness than Victorinus’s? They approach, and they are lit — and whoever receives that Light receives from you the power to become your child. But if such people are less known to the crowd, even those who do know them rejoice less over them; for when many rejoice together, the joy in each of them is richer — they heat and kindle one another. And the widely known carry many with them toward salvation; where they lead, the crowd follows; which is why those who got there before them rejoice over them so — because the rejoicing is not over them alone. May it never be that in your tent the rich would be welcomed ahead of the poor, or the highborn ahead of the low — when you chose instead the weak things of the world to shame the strong, chose the base and despised things of this world, the things that are nothing, to unmake the things that are. And yet even the least of your apostles, the man through whose tongue you sounded out those very words — when the proconsul Paulus had his pride beaten down by the apostle’s campaign and was sent under the easy yoke of your Christ, a plain subject now of the great King — even he was glad to drop his former name, Saul, and be called Paul, the banner of that great victory. For the enemy is more soundly beaten in a man he gripped more tightly, and gripped many others through; and he grips the proud more tightly by their rank, and by their authority he grips the many. So the more prized the heart of Victorinus was — the devil had held it like an impregnable fortress — and the tongue of Victorinus, the great keen blade he had used to cut down so many, the more abundant the joy your children owed: because our King had bound the strong man, and they were watching his weapons wrenched away, scrubbed clean, and made fit for your honor — serviceable to the Lord, for every good work.

In this way I came to understand, from my own experience, what I had read: how the flesh wars against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. I was in both, of course — yet I was more in what I approved of in myself than in what I disapproved of. For in that disapproved part it was now, for the most part, no longer truly I, since I was suffering it against my will more than doing it willingly. And yet it was through me that habit had won this power to fight against me, because I had come willingly to a place I now did not will to be. And who has any right to complain, when just punishment dogs the sinner? Nor did I have my old excuse any longer — that the reason I still held back from leaving the world to serve you was that the truth had not been made fully sure to me; for now it was. Yet I was still in service to the earth, and refused to enlist under your banner, and dreaded being freed from every burden as much as one ought to dread being weighed down by it. With the baggage of this present world I was held down, comfortably, as if in sleep; and my thoughts about you were like the efforts of someone trying to wake who, overcome by a heavy drowsiness, sinks back under again. No one wants to sleep forever, and every sober judgment agrees that waking is better; yet a man often puts off shaking off sleep when a heavy sluggishness lies in his limbs, and though it is past time to get up, gives in to it gladly, even while half-annoyed at himself. In just this way I was certain it was far better to give myself up to your love than to give in to my own craving; but while the first pleased me and won my mind, the second still pleased me too, and kept me its prisoner. And I had nothing to answer you when you called to me, Awake, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ will give you light. While you were showing me, on every side, that what you said was true, and I, convicted by the truth, had nothing at all to answer — nothing but those slow, drowsy words, "In a moment," "just a moment," "leave me a little while." But the "moment, moment" never came to any moment, and the "little while" stretched on and on. In vain I delighted in your law in my inmost self, while another law in my members fought against the law of my mind and dragged me captive under the law of sin that was in my members. For the law of sin is the sheer force of habit, by which the mind is hauled along and held fast even against its will — and deservedly so, since it was by willing that it slid into the habit in the first place. Who, then, would free me, wretched as I was, from this body of death — who but your grace, through Jesus Christ our Lord?

But when your man Simplicianus had told me all this about Victorinus, I was on fire to do the same — which was exactly why he had told it. And when he added that in the days of the emperor Julian, when a law forbade Christians to teach literature and oratory, Victorinus had obeyed the law and chosen to give up his school of words rather than your Word, which makes even the tongues of infants eloquent — he seemed to me not so much brave as lucky: he had found his opening to be free for you alone. That was the very thing I was sighing for — I, tied down not by anyone else’s irons but by my own iron will. The enemy held my power of willing, and out of it he had forged a chain for me, and it bound me. For the will, twisted, becomes craving; a craving served becomes habit; and a habit unresisted becomes necessity. By links like these, hooked one onto the next — that is why I have called it a chain — a hard slavery kept me pinned. And the new will just beginning in me, the will to worship you with no wage in view and to enjoy you yourself, God, the only sure sweetness — it was not yet able to overpower the old will, hardened in me by the years. So two wills of mine, one old, one new; one of the flesh, one of the spirit; fought each other, and their war laid waste my soul.

And how you freed me from the chains of desire, by which I was bound so tightly to the lust of the flesh, and from the drudgery of worldly business, I will now tell, and confess to your name, Lord, my helper and my redeemer. Amid mounting anxiety I went about my usual work, and day after day I sighed to you. I went to your church whenever I was free of the business under whose weight I groaned. Alypius was with me, off duty now after his third turn on the bench, and waiting for someone to buy his legal advice, just as I sold the skill of speaking, if such a thing can really be passed on by teaching. Nebridius, for our friendship's sake, had agreed to assist in the teaching of Verecundus, a citizen and grammar teacher of Milan and a close friend of us all, who badly wanted — and by the right of friendship claimed from our circle — the faithful help he so much needed. Nebridius was not drawn to this by any hope of gain, for he could have made far more of his learning had he wished; but, the kindest and gentlest of friends, he would not refuse a good turn or slight our request. He went about it very carefully, keeping clear of becoming known to the great men of this world and the distraction of mind that comes with it, wanting his own mind free and at leisure for as many hours as he could, to seek and read and hear something about wisdom.

So I came to understand from my own experience what I had read: the flesh craves against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. I was on both sides — but more myself on the side I approved of than on the side I condemned. On that second side it was mostly no longer really I: so much of it I suffered against my will rather than did with my will. And yet it was my own doing that habit had grown this warlike against me; I had arrived, willingly, where I now did not will to be. And who has any standing to complain when just punishment follows the sinner? Nor was my old excuse left to me — that the reason I had not yet thrown over the world and served you was that my sight of the truth was uncertain. By now it was certain. But I was still bound fast to the earth, and refused to soldier for you; and I feared being freed of all the baggage as much as a man ought to fear the baggage itself. So the freight of the world weighed me down — sweetly, the way sleep does; and the thoughts I tried to fix on you were like the struggles of men trying to wake, who go under again, drowned in the depth of drowsiness. No one wants to sleep forever; every sober judgment says waking is better; yet a man usually delays shaking sleep off when his limbs are thick and heavy with it — he takes it back gladly even though it has stopped agreeing with him, even when it is time to get up. Just so, I was certain it was better to give myself over to your love than to give in to my own craving; but the first course persuaded me and kept winning the argument, while the second pleased me and kept winning me. I had no answer at all when you said to me, Wake, you who sleep; rise from the dead, and Christ will give you light. On every side you were showing me your words were true, and, convicted by the truth, I could answer nothing back — only those slow, sleepy words: “In a minute.” “Look — any minute now.” “Just let me be a little longer.” But “any minute” never came to a minute, and “a little longer” stretched on and on. It did me no good to delight in your law in my inmost self, while a different law in my body made war against the law of my mind and marched me off, a prisoner of the law of sin in my own members. For the law of sin is the raw violence of habit, dragging the mind along and holding it, even unwilling — and deservedly, since it slid in willing. Wretched man that I was! Who was going to free me from this body of death — who but your grace, through Jesus Christ our Lord?

One day, then, when Nebridius happened to be away — I forget why — a man named Ponticianus came to see me and Alypius, a countryman of ours in that he was African, and holding high office at the emperor's court. What he wanted with us I do not know, but we sat down to talk, and he happened to notice on a gaming table in front of us a book. He picked it up, opened it, and found, to his surprise, that it was the Apostle Paul — for he had expected one of the books I was wearing myself out teaching. Smiling, and looking at me, he said how glad and how astonished he was to have come upon this book, and this one only, lying before my eyes. For he was a Christian, baptized, and often bowed himself before you, our God, in the church, in long and constant prayers. When I told him that I gave great care to those Scriptures, a conversation started — prompted by his telling of it — about Antony, the Egyptian monk, whose name stood in high honor among your servants, though up to that hour it was unknown to us. When he discovered this, he lingered all the more on the subject, filling us in and astonished at our ignorance of so great a man. And we stood amazed, hearing your wonderful works so fully attested, in times so recent, almost in our own day, worked in the true faith and the Catholic Church. We all wondered: we, that the works were so great; he, that they had never reached our ears.

And how you freed me from the chain of sexual craving that had me lashed down so tight, and from my slavery to worldly business, I will now tell, and confess to your name, Lord, my helper and my redeemer. I was going about my usual work, with the anxiety climbing, sighing to you every day, going to your church as often as I could get free of the business under whose weight I groaned. Alypius was with me — done, after his third term, with his legal post as assessor, and waiting for clients to buy his counsel, the way I sold skill in speaking, so far as teaching can supply such a thing. Nebridius, as a kindness to our friendship, had agreed to serve as assistant teacher under Verecundus, a citizen of Milan, a teacher of grammar, and a very close friend of us all, who had badly wanted — and by the rights of friendship had demanded from our circle — the dependable help he needed. Nebridius was not drawn to it by profit; he could have made much more from his learning if he had wished. He was simply too kind and gentle a friend to refuse a good turn or wave away our request. And he handled it with great discretion, keeping clear of the notice of the people this world calls important, and so keeping clear of the disquiet of mind that comes with them: he wanted his mind free, and at leisure for as many hours as could be, to search out something of wisdom, to read of it, to hear of it.

From there his talk turned to the communities in the monasteries, and their holy ways, a sweet fragrance to you, and the fruitful deserts of the wilderness, of which we knew nothing. There was even a monastery at Milan, outside the city walls, full of good brothers under Ambrose's fatherly care, and we had not known of it. He went on talking, and we listened in rapt silence. Then he told us how once, one afternoon at Trier, when the emperor was busy with the games at the circus, he and three companions went out to walk in some gardens near the city walls; and as they happened to pair off, one went apart with him, and the other two wandered off on their own. These two, in their wandering, came upon a cottage where some of your servants lived, poor in spirit, to whom the kingdom of heaven belongs; and there they found a little book holding the life of Antony. One of them began to read it, and to marvel, and to take fire, and as he read, to imagine taking up such a life himself, giving over his worldly service to serve you. (These two were of the men they call agents of imperial affairs.) Then suddenly, filled with a holy love and a sober shame, angry at himself, he turned his eyes on his friend and said, "Tell me, please — what are we trying to reach with all this toil of ours? What are we after? What do we serve for? Can our hopes at court rise any higher than to become the emperor's favorites? And even there, what is not brittle, what is not full of dangers? And through how many dangers do we arrive at a greater danger? And when do we even get there? But if I want it, I can become a friend of God right now, this very moment." So he spoke; and in the labor pains of a new birth he turned his eyes back to the book, and read on, and was changed within, where you were watching, and his mind was stripped clean of the world, as soon became clear. For as he read, and the waves of his heart rose and fell, every so often he stormed at himself; then he saw the better way, and chose it, and being now yours, he said to his friend, "Now I have broken loose from those hopes of ours; I have made up my mind to serve God, and I begin it from this hour, in this place. If you do not care to imitate me, do not stand in my way." The other answered that he would stay by him, to share so glorious a reward, so glorious a service. So both of them, now yours, were building the tower at the necessary cost — leaving all they had to follow you. Then Ponticianus and the man who had walked with him in another part of the garden came looking for them, found them, and reminded them it was time to go back, for the day was far gone. But those two told them what they had resolved and purposed, and how that will had risen and settled in them, and begged the others, if they would not join, at least not to trouble them. And the others, though no different from their old selves, wept for themselves (so he told us), and reverently wished their friends well, commending themselves to their prayers; and then, with hearts still trailing on the earth, went off to the palace. But the other two, with hearts fixed on heaven, stayed there in the cottage. Both had brides promised to them, who, when they heard of it, dedicated their own virginity to God.

One day, then, when Nebridius was away — I forget why — a man named Ponticianus came to the house to see me and Alypius: a countryman of ours in the loose sense, being African, and holding high office at the emperor’s court. He wanted something or other from us, and we sat down to talk; and it happened that on the game table in front of us he noticed a book. He picked it up, opened it — and found, to his complete surprise, the apostle Paul. He had assumed it was one of the books I was grinding myself down teaching. He smiled, looked up at me, and told me how glad he was, and how amazed, to have stumbled on this book, and only this book, there at my elbow. For he was a Christian, and baptized; he bowed often before you, our God, in church, in long and frequent prayers. When I told him that I spent the most serious effort on those Scriptures, a conversation began — he telling it — about Antony, the monk of Egypt, whose name stood high in honor among your servants, though up to that hour we had never heard it. When he realized that, he stayed on the subject, introducing the great man to two ignorant listeners, and marveling at the ignorance. We were stunned to hear of your wonders, so fully attested, so recent — practically our own times — done in the true faith and the catholic Church. All of us marveled: we, that these things were so great; he, that we had never heard of them.

Such was the story Ponticianus told. But you, Lord, while he was speaking, were turning me back toward myself — taking me from behind my own back, where I had stationed myself so as not to look at myself, and setting me in front of my own face, so that I might see how foul I was, how crooked and filthy, how stained and ulcered. And I looked, and was horrified, and there was nowhere to flee from myself. If I tried to turn my gaze away from myself, he kept on with his story, and again you set me over against myself and forced me before my own eyes, so that I might find out my own wrongdoing and hate it. I had known it all along, but I had pretended not to see it, had winked at it, and let it slip from my mind.

From there his talk turned to the flocks of the monasteries, and their way of life that is a sweet fragrance to you, and the fruitful deserts of the wilderness — and we knew nothing of any of it. There was even a monastery at Milan, outside the city walls, full of good brothers under Ambrose’s care — and we had not known it. He kept on, talking the subject out, and we listened in intent silence. And so he came to tell how once at Trier, one afternoon while the emperor was held by the races in the circus, he and three companions went out to walk in the gardens along the city walls. As they happened to stroll in pairs — one man going off with him, the other two wandering away by themselves — those two, drifting, came on a hut where certain servants of yours lived, poor in spirit, the kind the kingdom of heaven belongs to; and there they found a little book with the life of Antony written in it. One of the two began to read it — and to marvel, and to catch fire; and while he was still reading, to think of laying hold of such a life himself and leaving his worldly service to serve you. The two of them belonged to the corps they call agents of the imperial administration. Then, filled all at once with holy love and a sober shame, furious at himself, he threw his eyes on his friend and said to him: “Tell me something. All this striving of ours — what are we actually trying to reach? What are we after? Whose interest are we serving? Could we hope for anything higher at court than to be friends of the emperor? And at that height, what is not brittle? What is not crawling with danger? How many dangers do we climb, just to reach a bigger one? And how long will the climb take? But a friend of God — if I want it: look. I become one here and now.” He said it, and — in labor with the new life coming to birth in him — he turned his eyes back to the page and went on reading; and he was changed inwardly, where you alone could see, and his mind was shedding the world, as soon appeared. For while he read, and the waves rolled in his heart, he raged at himself a while; then he saw the better course, and decided for it; and, already yours, he said to his friend: “I have just now torn free of those hopes of ours. I have decided to serve God, and I begin this hour, in this place. If you can’t bring yourself to do the same, don’t stand against me.” The other answered that he would stay at his side, for such pay, in such a service. And both of them, yours now, were building the tower at the only cost that counts: leaving everything they had, and following you. Then Ponticianus and the man walking with him, who had wandered through other parts of the gardens, came looking for them in that same place, and, finding them, suggested they head back — the day was going. But they told what they had resolved and undertaken, how such a will had risen in them and set firm, and asked the others, if they would not join them, not to stand in their way. Ponticianus and his friend, in no way changed from what they had been, still wept over themselves — so he told us — and devoutly congratulated the two, and asked to be remembered in their prayers; then, dragging their hearts along the ground, they went off to the palace. The other two, hearts fixed on heaven, stayed in the hut. And each of them was engaged to be married; and when their brides-to-be heard what had happened, they too dedicated their virginity to you.

But now, the more warmly I loved those two men whose healthful choice I was hearing of — that they had handed themselves wholly over to you to be cured — the more I loathed myself by comparison. For many years had run out with me — some twelve — since my nineteenth, when on reading Cicero's Hortensius I was first stirred to a serious love of wisdom; and still I kept putting off the renouncing of mere earthly happiness, to give myself to the search for that wisdom whose mere seeking — never mind the finding — was to be preferred above the treasures and kingdoms of the world, and above the pleasures of the body lying spread around me at my whim. But I, a wretch, a most pitiful wretch, in the very dawn of my youth had even begged you for chastity, and had said, "Give me chastity and self-control — only not yet." For I was afraid you would hear me too soon, and too soon cure me of the disease of lust, which I would rather have had fed full than snuffed out. And I had wandered down crooked roads in an unholy superstition — not even sure of it, but preferring it to the alternatives, which I did not search out in reverence but attacked in spite.

That was Ponticianus’s story. But while he spoke, Lord, you were wrenching me around to face myself. You pulled me out from behind my own back, where I had stationed myself all the years I refused to look at me, and you planted me in front of my own face, so I would see how foul I was — how twisted and grimy, how stained, how covered in sores. I looked, and horror took me — and there was nowhere to run from myself. If I tried to turn my gaze away, there was Ponticianus, going on with his story, and there you were again, holding me up against myself, shoving me into my own line of sight, so that I would find my sin at last and hate it. I had known it all along — and looked away, and winked at it, and let it slip.

I had believed, too, that the reason I kept putting off, day after day, the renouncing of this world's hopes to follow you alone, was that nothing certain showed itself by which to set my course. But now the day had come when I was to be laid bare to myself, and my own conscience was to round on me. "Where are you now, my tongue? You used to say that you would not cast off the baggage of vanity for an uncertain truth. Well — now it is certain, and that burden still weighs you down, while these others, who have not worn themselves out searching for it, nor brooded on it for ten years and more, have had their shoulders lightened, and been given wings to fly." So I was gnawed from within, and thrown into a terrible, scalding shame, while Ponticianus went on talking. When he had finished his tale and the errand he had come on, he went his way, and I went into myself. What did I not say against myself! With what lashes of self-condemnation did I not flog my soul, to make it follow me as I struggled to go after you! And it pulled back; it refused, and made no excuse for itself. Every argument was used up and beaten; there was left only a speechless dread, and it feared, as if it were death itself, to be held back from the river of the habit by which it was wasting to death.

But now, the more ardently I loved those two men, hearing of the health in their passion — how they had handed themselves whole to you for healing — the more bitterly I loathed myself beside them. Twelve years and more of my life had run out since my nineteenth year, when Cicero’s Hortensius stirred me to the love of wisdom — and I was still postponing the day I would despise this world’s happiness and clear myself for the search: the search whose mere seeking, let alone finding, should have outweighed every treasure and kingdom of the world already in hand, outweighed all the pleasures of the body laid out around me at a nod. But I — a wretched young man, wretched beyond wretched at the very start of my youth — I had even asked you for chastity. I had said: “Give me chastity and self-control — but not yet.” I was afraid you might hear me too quickly — heal me too quickly — of the disease of desire, which I preferred to have satisfied rather than put out. And I had gone down crooked roads, in a sacrilegious superstition — not because I was sure of it, but because I preferred it to the teachings I never examined in good faith, only attacked out of spite.

Then, in the high pitch of this struggle in the house of my inmost self — a struggle I had violently stirred up against my own soul, in the chamber of my heart — troubled in mind and face alike, I rounded on Alypius and cried out, "What is wrong with us? What is this? What did you hear? The unlearned rise up and seize heaven, and we, with all our learning and no heart — look at us, wallowing in flesh and blood! Is it because they have gone ahead of us that we are ashamed to follow, and not rather ashamed that we do not even follow?" Some such words I said, and the fever of my mind tore me away from him, while he, staring at me, astonished, kept silent. For it was not my usual voice; and my forehead, my cheeks, my eyes, my color, the pitch of my voice, spoke my mind more than the words did. There was a little garden belonging to our lodging, which we had the use of, as of the whole house, for the owner, our host, was not living there. To the garden the uproar in my breast had driven me, where no one could break in on the burning quarrel I had taken up with myself, until it should come to an end you knew of, though I did not. Only I was wholesomely going mad, and dying so as to live, knowing what an evil thing I was and not yet knowing what good thing I was soon to become. So I went off into the garden, and Alypius came at my heels — for his being there was no loss of privacy to me; and how could he abandon me in such a state? We sat down as far from the house as we could. I was in turmoil of spirit, raging with the fiercest indignation that I was not entering into your will and your covenant, my God, which all my bones cried out to me to enter, praising it to the skies. And to go in there takes no ships or chariots or feet — it is not even as far as I had come from the house to where we sat. For to go there, and to arrive there, was nothing but the willing to go — but willing it strongly and through and through, not heaving the half-wounded, half-divided will this way and that, with one part rising as the other sank.

And I had told myself that the reason I kept deferring, day after day, the moment of despising this world’s hopes and following you alone, was that nothing certain had shown itself for me to steer toward. But now the day had come when I stood stripped bare in front of myself, and my conscience took up the prosecution: “Where is that tongue of yours? You’re the one who kept saying you wouldn’t drop your pack of vanities for an uncertain truth. Well: now it is certain — and the pack is still crushing you, while other men, who never wore themselves down searching, who never spent ten years and more brooding on all this, have shrugged the weight off their shoulders and been given wings.” So I was gnawed inside, and drowned in a horrible shame, while Ponticianus talked on. And when the talk was done, and the business he had come about, he went his way — and I went into myself. What did I not say against myself? With what whips of judgment did I not flog my soul, to make it follow me now that I was straining to go after you! And it dug in its heels. It refused, and it offered no excuse. Every argument had been spent and answered. What remained was speechless dread: my soul feared, as it would fear death itself, being pulled out of the current of habit — the current in which it was wasting away toward death.

At last, in the very fever of my wavering, I made many of the bodily gestures that men sometimes want to make and cannot, if they have lost the limbs, or the limbs are tied, or slackened by sickness, or hindered in some other way. So if I tore my hair, or struck my forehead, or locked my fingers and hugged my knee — I willed it, and did it. But I could have willed it and not done it, if the power of movement in my limbs had not obeyed. So I did many things where willing was not the same as being able; and yet I did not do the one thing that I longed beyond all comparison more to do, and could have done the moment I willed it — because the moment I willed it, I would have willed it wholly. For in that thing the ability was one with the will, and to will was to do it; and yet it was not done. My body obeyed the faintest wish of my soul more readily — moving its limbs at a nod — than my soul obeyed itself, to bring about, in the will alone, this one great act of will.

Then, in the middle of that great brawl of my inner house — the fight I had forced on my own soul in the room where we lived, my heart — with my mind as ravaged as my face, I rounded on Alypius and cried out: “What is wrong with us? What is this? What did you just hear? The unschooled are rising up and taking heaven by force, and here we are with our learning and no heart — look at us, wallowing in flesh and blood! Are we ashamed to follow because they went first — and not ashamed that we can’t even follow?” I said something like that, and then my agitation ripped me away from him while he stared at me, stunned, and said nothing. I did not sound like myself; and my forehead, my cheeks, my eyes, my color, the pitch of my voice, said more than the words did. There was a little garden attached to our lodging, which we had the use of, as we had the whole house — our host, the owner, was not living there. The storm in my chest had swept me out to it, where no one could interfere with the burning case I had brought against myself — until it should end however you knew it would end; I knew nothing. I only knew that my madness was working toward sanity, my dying toward life: I knew the evil thing I was, and did not know the good thing I was about to become. So I withdrew into the garden, and Alypius followed on my heels; his being there took none of my solitude from me — and how could he abandon me in that state? We sat down as far from the house as we could get. I was groaning in spirit, shaking with fury at myself for not going — not entering into your will and your covenant, my God, when every bone in me was shouting to enter it, praising it to the sky. And the way there is not by ship or carriage or on foot; it is not even as far as I had walked from the house to where we were sitting. To go there — to arrive fully — required nothing at all except the will to go: but to will it strongly and completely, not to heave and pitch, this way and that, a will half-wounded, one part rising while the other part fell.

Where does this monstrous thing come from? And why? Let your mercy shine out, so that I may ask — perhaps the hidden punishments of human beings, the darkest agonies of the sons of Adam, may give me some answer. Where does this monstrous thing come from, and why? The mind commands the body, and is obeyed at once; the mind commands itself, and is resisted. The mind commands the hand to move, and so ready is the hand that you can scarcely tell the command from the obedience. Yet the mind is mind, and the hand is body. The mind commands the mind — its own self — to will, and it does not do it. Where does this monstrous thing come from, and why? It commands itself, I say, to will — it would not command unless it willed — and what it commands is not done. But it does not will the thing wholly; therefore it does not command the thing wholly. For it commands only so far as it wills, and the thing commanded is left undone only so far as it does not will. For the will is commanding a will to exist — not some other will, but itself. But it is not the whole will that commands, and so the thing it commands does not come to be. For if the will were whole, it would not even command the will to be, since it would already be. It is no monstrous thing, then, partly to will and partly not to will, but a sickness of the mind: that it does not rise wholly, lifted by the truth but borne down by habit. And so there are two wills in us, because neither one of them is whole, and what is missing in one is present in the other.

At last, in the fever of my paralysis, I was making all sorts of movements with my body — the kind men sometimes want to make and cannot, if they are missing the limbs, or their limbs are roped down, or slack with sickness, or somehow blocked. If I tore my hair, if I struck my forehead, if I laced my fingers and gripped my knee — I willed it, and it happened. But I could have willed it and had nothing happen, if the power of movement in my limbs had refused to obey. So I was doing all these many things, where willing was not the same as being able — and I was not doing the one thing my longing set beyond all comparison above the rest: the thing I could do the moment I willed it, because the moment I truly willed it, I would will it indeed. In that act the power is one with the will; the willing itself is the doing. And still it was not done. And my body obeyed the thinnest willing of my soul, moving its limbs at a nod, more readily than my soul obeyed itself, to carry out — in the will alone — this, its own great act of will.

Let them perish from your presence, my God, as empty talkers and seducers of the mind do perish — those who, seeing that there were two wills in this weighing of choices, claim that there are in us two minds of two different natures, one good and one evil. They themselves are truly evil while they hold these evil opinions; and they will become good only when they hold the truth and consent to the truth, so that your Apostle may say to them, You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. But they, wanting to be light in themselves and not in the Lord, imagining the soul's nature to be what God is, are made into a thicker darkness by their dreadful arrogance, since they backed away even farther from you, the true Light that gives light to everyone coming into the world. Let them take heed what they say, and blush with shame; let them draw near to him and be enlightened, and their faces will not be ashamed. As for me — when I was deliberating about serving the Lord my God now, as I had long meant to, it was I who willed it, I who refused it; I, my own self. I neither willed it wholly nor refused it wholly. And so I was at war with myself, and torn apart by myself. And this tearing happened to me against my will, and yet it showed not the presence of some second mind but the punishment of my own. So it was no longer I who did it, but the sin that lived in me — the punishment of a sin more freely committed, in that I was a son of Adam.

Where does this monstrous thing come from? And why? Let your mercy shine on me while I ask, in case the answer lies in the hidden punishments of men, in the darkest griefs of the sons of Adam. Where does the monstrous thing come from — and why? The mind orders the body, and is obeyed on the instant; the mind orders itself, and is resisted. The mind orders the hand to move, and it goes so smoothly you can barely tell the order from the doing — and mind is mind, while hand is body. The mind orders the mind to will — it is not another thing; it is itself — and it does not do it. Where does this monstrous thing come from? And why? The mind orders itself to will, I say — it would not be giving the order unless it willed — and what it orders does not happen. The answer is that it does not will it whole, so it does not order it whole. It orders exactly as far as it wills, and what it orders fails exactly as far as it does not will. For what the will is ordering is that there be a will — not some other will: itself. And it is not ordering with its whole self; therefore what it orders is not. If the will were whole, it would not order itself into being — the will would already be there. So this is no monster after all, this willing partly and partly not willing. It is a sickness of the mind: lifted by truth, it cannot rise all the way, because habit drags at its weight. There are two wills, then, because one of them is not whole; and what the one lacks, the other has.

For if there were as many contrary natures as there are conflicting wills, there would be not just two of them but many. Suppose someone is deliberating whether to go to their secret meeting or to the theater — these Manichees cry out, "Look, here are two natures: a good one drawing this way, a bad one dragging back the other!" For where else, they ask, does this hesitation between conflicting wills come from? But I say both wills are bad: the one that draws toward their meeting as much as the one that draws back to the theater. They cannot believe that the will which draws toward them might be anything but good. Well then — suppose one of us were deliberating, and amid the clash of two wills were torn over whether to go to the theater or to our church: would not these men too be torn over what to answer? For either they must admit — which they would hate to do — that the will drawing a man to our church is good, just as good as the will of those who have received their own mysteries and are held by them; or they must suppose two evil natures and two evil souls battling in one man, and then it will not be true, as they say, that one is good and the other bad; or they must be converted to the truth and stop denying that, when a person deliberates, it is one single soul tossing between contrary wills.

Let them perish from your presence, God, as the empty talkers perish, the seducers of the mind — the men who noticed the two wills in our deliberating and decided that we contain two minds with two natures, one good, one evil. They are the evil ones, while they believe those evil things; and the same men will be good if ever they believe the truth and give the truth their yes, so that your apostle may say to them, You were darkness once; now you are light, in the Lord. But they want to be light in themselves rather than in the Lord — they imagine the soul’s nature is what God is — and so they became a thicker darkness: in the horror of their arrogance they backed still farther away from you, the true Light that lights every man coming into the world. Watch what you say — and blush; come near him and be lit, and your faces will not be ashamed. When I was deliberating about serving the Lord my God at last, as I had long intended, it was I who willed it, and I who refused it. I. I was the one. I neither willed it whole nor refused it whole. So I fought myself, and I was torn apart by myself; and the tearing happened against my will — yet what it showed was not the presence of some second mind, but the punishment of my own. It was no longer I producing it, but the sin that lived in me — the punishment of a sin committed more freely than mine, because I was a son of Adam.

So let them stop saying, when they notice two conflicting wills in one man, that the conflict is between two contrary souls, of two contrary substances, from two contrary first principles, one good and one bad. For you, the true God, disprove them, check them, convict them — as when, both wills being bad, a man deliberates whether to kill someone by poison or by the sword; whether to grab this estate of another's or that one, when he cannot have both; whether to spend his money on pleasure or hoard it out of greed; whether to go to the circus or the theater, if both are open the same day; or, a third thing, to rob a house, given the chance; or, a fourth, to commit adultery, if the opportunity is there too — all of these falling together in the same span of time, all equally wanted, though they cannot all be done at once. For they tear the mind apart among four wills, or even more, given the vast variety of things a man can crave — and yet the Manichees do not claim there are that many different substances in us. The same holds for good wills. For I ask them: is it good to take pleasure in reading the Apostle? Is it good to take pleasure in a quiet Psalm? Is it good to discuss the Gospel? To each they will answer, "It is good." Well then — what if all of them give equal pleasure, and all at the same moment? Do not the different wills pull the mind apart while it deliberates which to choose? Yet all are good, and they are at odds until one is chosen, and the whole will, that was split into many, can move toward that one. So too, when eternity above delights us, and the pleasure of a passing good holds us down below, it is one and the same soul that does not will this or that with its whole will, and so is torn apart by heavy distress, since out of the truth it puts the one first, but out of habit it does not put the other aside.

Besides, if there are as many contrary natures in us as there are wills in conflict, we will have to count not two but a crowd. Suppose a man is turning over whether to go to their meeting or to the theater. The Manichees shout: “There — two natures! The good one pulls him this way, the bad one pulls back that way. What else could explain this standoff of will against will?” But I say both wills are bad — the one that pulls toward them and the one that pulls back to the theater alike. They, of course, cannot imagine the will that pulls their way to be anything but good. Very well: suppose one of ours is deliberating, torn between two wills wrestling — go to the theater, or go to our church? Won’t the Manichees be torn over the answer? Either they admit what they have no wish to admit — that the will leading a man to our church is good, just as good as they claim for the will that leads to theirs the men who have received their mysteries and are held by them; or they conclude that two evil natures and two evil minds are locked in combat inside one man — and that ruins their doctrine of the one good and the one evil; or they will have to be converted to the truth, and stop denying that when a man deliberates, it is one soul, surging between different wills.

So I was sick at heart and tormented, accusing myself far more bitterly than usual, twisting and turning in my chain until it should be wholly broken — the chain that now held me only by a thread, but held me still. And you, Lord, pressed hard on my inmost parts with a severe mercy, doubling the lashes of fear and shame, so that I would not give way again, and so that the last thin thread, not yet snapped, would not knit itself back together and bind me tighter than before. For I kept saying to myself, "Let it be done now, let it be done now." And as I spoke I was on the very edge of doing it — I all but did it, and did not; yet I did not slide back to my old state, but kept my footing close by, and caught my breath. And I tried again, and came a little nearer, and a little nearer still, and all but touched it, all but grasped it; and yet I did not reach it, did not touch or take hold, hanging back from dying to death and living to life — the worse, which I was used to, having more power over me than the better, which I was not. And the very instant in which I was to become something other than I was — the nearer it came, the greater the horror it struck into me; yet it did not strike me back, did not turn me away, but held me hanging there.

So let them stop saying, when they feel two wills fighting in one man, that two hostile minds are at war, out of two hostile substances, from two hostile first principles — one good, one evil. For you, God of truth, refute them, expose them, catch them out. Take a case where both wills are bad. A man deliberates: kill his victim with poison, or with a blade? Seize this piece of another man’s property, or that one, when he cannot take both? Buy pleasure with extravagance, or hold on to his money out of greed?
