The circus or the theater, if both open on the same day? Add a third pull — rob a house, if the chance is standing open; and a fourth — commit adultery, if that door too is open at the same moment. Let them all converge on one point of time, all craved equally, and impossible to do at once: they tear the mind four ways among four wills at war — or more than four, given the enormous range of things men want — and even here the Manichees do not claim a separate substance for each. The same holds for good wills. I ask them: is it good to delight in a reading from the Apostle? Good to delight in the gravity of a psalm? Good to discuss the Gospel? To each they will answer: good. What then, if they all delight equally, all at the same time? Aren’t different wills straining the human heart while we deliberate which to seize first? All of them good — and all in contest, until one is chosen, and the whole will, split into many before, comes to rest there, one. So it is when eternity delights us from above and the pleasure of a temporal good tugs from below: it is one and the same soul, willing neither with its whole will; and that is why the soul is torn apart, and the tearing grieves it — truth teaching it to put the one first, habit refusing to lay the other down.

The trifles of trifles, the vanities of vanities, my old mistresses, still held me back; they plucked at the garment of my flesh and whispered softly, "Are you sending us away? From this moment, will we never be with you again, ever? From this moment, will this thing and that be forbidden you forever?" And what was it they were hinting at in what I have called "this and that" — what were they hinting at, my God? Let your mercy turn it away from the soul of your servant! What filth they hinted at, what disgraces! And now I was hearing them far less than half as loud; they no longer faced me openly to argue, but muttered, as it were, behind my back, and slyly tugged at me as I was leaving, to make me look back at them. Still they held me up, so that I hung back from tearing myself loose and shaking myself free of them and leaping over to where I was being called — while a violent habit kept saying to me, "Do you really think you can live without them?"

That is how sick I was, and how tortured — and I accused myself more bitterly than I had ever done, twisting and wrenching in my chain until the last of it should break: only a little held me now, but it held. And you, Lord, kept up the pressure in my hidden places — mercy severe — doubling the whips of fear and shame so that I would not go slack again, so that the thin last tether would not survive the strain, thicken, and tie me down harder than before. I kept saying inside myself, “Now — let it happen now,” and with the words I was already at the edge of doing it. I was that close — and I did not do it. But I did not fall back to where I had been, either; I stood one step off, and caught my breath. And I tried again, and I was a little nearer, and a little nearer still; I was all but touching it; I was holding it — and I was not there at all; I touched nothing; I held nothing. I hung back from dying to death and living to life, and the worse, worn deep into me, had more power than the better I had never tried; and the closer it came, that exact point of time when I would become someone else, the more horror it drove into me. But the horror did not knock me backward, and it did not turn me aside. It held me hanging.

But now it spoke very faintly. For on that side toward which I had set my face, and which I trembled to cross to, there appeared to me the chaste dignity of Continence — serene, but not slack in her gladness, honorably coaxing me to come and not to hesitate, stretching out holy hands to take me in and embrace me, hands full of crowds of good examples. There were so many boys and girls there, a multitude of the young and of every age, grave widows and gray-haired virgins; and in all of them Continence herself, not barren but the fruitful mother of children of joy, by you, her Husband, O Lord. And she smiled at me with a coaxing mockery, as if to say: "Can you not do what these young men and these young women can? Or can any of them do it of themselves, and not rather in the Lord their God? The Lord their God gave me to them. Why do you stand on your own feet, and so not stand at all? Throw yourself on him; do not be afraid. He will not draw back and let you fall. Throw yourself on him without fear; he will catch you and heal you." And I blushed deep, for I still heard the muttering of those trifles, and hung there in suspense. And again she seemed to say, "Stop your ears against your unclean members on the earth, that they may be put to death. They tell you of delights — but not such delights as the law of the Lord your God." This whole quarrel in my heart was self against self alone. And Alypius, sitting close beside me, waited in silence for the outcome of my strange agitation.

And what held me were the trifles of trifles, the vanities of vanities, those old girlfriends of mine: plucking softly at my garment of flesh and murmuring, “You’re sending us away?” and “From that moment we will never be with you again — not ever,” and “From that moment this and that will be forbidden you — forever.” And what things they meant by “this and that” — what things, my God! May your mercy keep it all far from your servant’s soul. What filth they held up, what outrages! But I heard them now at far less than half strength: they no longer came out to face me and contradict me, but muttered, as it were, behind my back, and pinched furtively at a man already leaving, trying to make him look around. And still they slowed me. I could not bring myself to tear loose, to shake them off, to make the jump to where I was being called — while habit, that bully, kept asking me, “Do you really think you can live without them?”

But when a deep self-searching had dredged up out of the secret depths of my soul all my misery and heaped it before the eyes of my heart, a mighty storm broke, bringing a mighty downpour of tears. And to pour them out in full, with all their natural cries, I got up and left Alypius — solitude seemed fitter for the business of weeping — and went off far enough that even his presence would not weigh on me. So it was with me then, and he sensed it; for I suppose I had said something in which the sound of my voice was already thick with weeping, and so had risen. He stayed where we had been sitting, utterly amazed. I flung myself down — how, I do not know — under a certain fig tree, and let my tears run free; and the floods of my eyes broke out, an acceptable sacrifice to you. And I said much to you — not in these words, but to this effect: And you, Lord — how long? How long, Lord? Will you be angry forever? Do not remember our old wrongs against us. For I felt I was still held fast by them, and I sent up these grieving cries: How long, how long? Tomorrow, and tomorrow? Why not now? Why not this very hour an end to my uncleanness?

But even the bully’s voice was faint now. For on the side I had turned my face toward — the side I trembled to cross to — there opened before me the chaste dignity of Continence: serene, cheerful without a hint of looseness, honorably coaxing me to come and doubt no more, and stretching out to receive and embrace me holy hands full of flocks of good examples. So many boys and girls were with her, so many young people, every age of life, grave widows, women grown old in virginity — and in every one of them Continence herself, in no way barren, but a fruitful mother of children, of joys, by you, Lord, her husband. And she smiled at me — a mocking smile that made me braver — as if she were saying: “Can’t you do what these men have done, what these women have done? Or do you think they do it in themselves, and not in the Lord their God? The Lord their God gave me to them. Why do you keep standing on yourself — and standing on nothing? Throw yourself onto him. Don’t be afraid: he will not step aside and let you fall. Throw yourself without fear. He will catch you, and he will heal you.” And I was blushing hard, because I could still hear the murmuring of those trifles, and I hung there, dangling. And again she seemed to say: “Go deaf to those unclean members of yours upon the earth, and let them die. They tell you of delights — but not like the delights of the law of the Lord your God.” All this was the quarrel in my heart: myself, against myself, and no one else. And Alypius sat close at my side, silently waiting out my strange agitation, to see where it would end.

So I was speaking, and weeping, in the bitterest contrition of my heart, when suddenly I heard a voice from a nearby house — a boy's voice, or a girl's, I do not know — chanting, and over and over repeating, "Take up and read, take up and read." At once my face changed, and I began to think hard whether children sang anything like this in any kind of game, and I could not remember ever having heard it. So I checked the flood of my tears and stood up, taking it to be nothing other than a command from God to open the book and read the first passage I came upon. For I had heard of Antony, that he had once come in during the reading of the Gospel and taken the words as if spoken to him: Go, sell all that you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me. And by such an oracle he was at once converted to you. So I went back quickly to where Alypius was sitting, for there I had laid down the book of the Apostle when I got up. I snatched it, opened it, and read in silence the first passage my eyes fell on: Not in rioting and drunkenness, not in lust and wantonness, not in strife and envy; but put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh and its cravings. I had no wish to read further, and no need. For instantly, as I came to the end of that sentence, it was as if a light of assurance had been poured into my heart, and all the dark of doubt scattered away.

But when deep reflection had hauled up the whole of my misery from its secret bottom and heaped it in the sight of my heart, an enormous storm broke, bringing an enormous rain of tears. And so that I could pour all of it out, with the sounds that belonged to it, I got up and left Alypius — solitude seemed to me better suited to the business of weeping — and I moved far enough away that even his presence could not weigh on me. That was my state, and he sensed it: I think I had said something, in a voice already swollen with crying, and then had risen. So he stayed where we had been sitting, astonished past words. I dropped down — how, I do not know — under a certain fig tree, and gave my tears free rein; and the floods burst from my eyes, an offering you accept. And I said to you — not in these words, but this was the sense of it — “And you, Lord — how long? How long, Lord? Will you be angry to the very end? Do not remember our old sins against us.” For I felt it was those sins that still held me, and I kept flinging out these miserable cries: “How long? How long — tomorrow, and tomorrow? Why not now? Why not, this very hour, an end to my filth?”

I was saying this and weeping in the most bitter contrition of my heart — and then I heard a voice from the house next door: a chant, repeated over and over, in a voice like a young boy’s or a girl’s, I couldn’t tell: “Take it and read. Take it and read.” My face changed at once, and I began to think as hard as I could: did children sing anything like that in any of their games? I could not remember ever hearing it anywhere. I dammed the rush of tears and stood up, taking the chant for nothing less than a command from God: open the book, and read the first passage I found. For I had heard how Antony had walked in on a reading of the Gospel and taken the words as an admonition spoken straight to him — Go, sell all you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me — and by that oracle he had been converted to you on the spot. So I went back quickly to the place where Alypius was sitting, because I had left the volume of the Apostle there when I got up. I snatched it, opened it, and read in silence the first passage my eyes fell on: Not in carousing and drunkenness, not in beds and indecencies, not in quarreling and jealousy — no: clothe yourselves in the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no plans to satisfy the cravings of the flesh. I did not want to read further, and there was no need. The instant the sentence ended, it was as if a light of peace poured into my heart, and all the darkness of doubt scattered.

Then I put my finger in the page, or some other marker, closed the book, and with a face gone calm at last I told Alypius. And this is how he showed me what had been happening in him, which I knew nothing about: he asked to see what I had read. I showed him, and he read past the place where I had stopped — I did not know what came next. This came next: Welcome the man whose faith is weak. He took it to himself, and told me so. That word steadied him; and with a good resolve, and no storm of hesitation — entirely like his character, which had long been far, far better than mine — he joined me. From there we go in to my mother. We tell her: she is filled with joy. We lay out how it happened: she exults, she triumphs, and she blessed you, who are able to do more than everything we ask or understand — because she saw that you had granted her, in me, so much more than her pitiful, grief-worn groaning had ever begged. For you converted me to yourself so fully that I no longer looked for a wife, or for any hope this world offers — standing now on that rule of faith where you had shown me to her, so many years before, in her vision. And you turned her mourning into a joy far richer than the one she had wanted, and far dearer and purer than the joy she had once looked for from grandchildren of my flesh.

Then, marking the place with my finger, or with something else, I closed the book, and with a calm face told Alypius. And he told me, in turn, what had been happening in him, which I had not known. He asked to see what I had read. I showed him; and he looked beyond what I had read, to what came next, which I had not seen. It was this: Receive the one who is weak in faith. He took it to himself, and told me. And by that word of counsel he was strengthened; and with a good resolve and purpose, fully in keeping with the character in which he had always — and far for the better — differed from me, he joined me, without any agitated delay. From there we go in to my mother. We tell her. She rejoices. We relate, in order, how it came about, and she leaps for joy and triumphs, and blesses you, who are able to do above all that we ask or imagine. For she saw that you had given her, in my case, far more than she had been used to begging for with her pitiful, grief-stricken groans. For you converted me to yourself, so that I sought neither a wife nor any hope of this world, but stood firm on that rule of faith where, so many years before, you had shown me to her in a vision. And you turned her mourning into a joy far richer than she had wished, and far dearer and purer than the joy she had once asked for in grandchildren of my body.

sections.title: Baptism, and the Death of Monica
Monica's Death

segments.text: Lord, I am your servant — I am your servant, and the son of your handmaid. You have broken my chains. I will offer you a sacrifice of praise. Let my heart and my tongue praise you; let all my bones say, Lord, who is like you? Let them say it, and answer me, and say to my soul: I am your salvation. Who am I? What kind of thing am I? What evil have my deeds not been — or if not my deeds, my words, or if not my words, my will? But you, Lord, are good and merciful. Your right hand reached into the depth of my death and drained the pit of corruption from the bottom of my heart. And the whole of it came to this: to stop willing what I willed, and to will what you willed. But where had my free will been through all those years? Out of what deep, secret hiding place was it called up in a single moment, so that I could bend my neck to your easy yoke and my shoulders to your light burden, Christ Jesus, my helper and my redeemer? How sweet it suddenly was to give up the sweetness of those toys! I had been terrified of losing them; now it was a joy to let them go. For you were casting them out of me, you the true, the highest sweetness — casting them out, and coming in to take their place, sweeter than any pleasure, though not to flesh and blood; brighter than any light, and deeper inside me than any secret; higher than any honor, though not to those who stand high in their own eyes. Now my mind was free of the gnawing cares of ambition and acquisition, of wallowing in filth and scratching the itch of lust. And I babbled like a child to you — my brightness, my wealth, my health: the Lord my God.

O Lord, I am your servant; I am your servant, and the son of your handmaid. You have broken the chains that bound me; I will offer you the sacrifice of praise. Let my heart and my tongue praise you; let all my bones say, O Lord, who is like you? Let them say it, and answer me, and say to my soul, I am your salvation. Who am I, and what am I? What evil has there not been, whether in my deeds, or, if not my deeds, then my words, or, if not my words, then my will? But you, Lord, are good and merciful; your right hand reached down into the depth of my death and from the bottom of my heart emptied out that pit of corruption. And the whole of your gift was this: that I should stop willing what I had willed, and begin to will what you willed. But where, through all those years, and out of what low and hidden recess, was my free will called forth in a single moment, so that I bent my neck to your easy yoke and my shoulders to your light burden, O Christ Jesus, my Helper and my Redeemer? How sweet it suddenly became to me to go without the sweetness of those trifles! What I had been afraid to lose, it was now a joy to let go. For you cast them out of me, you who are the true and highest sweetness; you cast them out, and in their place you entered in yourself, sweeter than every pleasure, though not to flesh and blood; brighter than every light, yet more hidden than every depth; higher than every honor, but not to those who are high in their own eyes. Now my soul was free from the gnawing cares of campaigning and getting, of wallowing in filth and scratching the itch of lust. And like a child I spoke freely to you, my brightness, my riches, my health, the Lord my God.

And I decided, in your sight, not to make a scene of quitting but to withdraw the service of my tongue quietly from the talking-market — so that boys who were studying not your law, not your peace, but lying follies and courtroom combat, should no longer buy weapons for their madness from my mouth. Conveniently, only a few days remained before the vintage vacation, and I decided to endure them and then step down in the regular way — bought back by you, never again to put myself up for sale. Our plan was known to you, but not to men, apart from our own circle. We had agreed among ourselves not to let it spread — although to us, climbing up from the valley of weeping and singing the song of ascents, you had given sharp arrows and burning coals against the treacherous tongue: the tongue that pretends to advise while it opposes, and that consumes you out of love the way it consumes a meal.

And I resolved, in your sight, not to tear myself loose all at once with a great noise, but quietly to withdraw the service of my tongue from the marketplace of hired speech, so that the young — students not of your law, not of your peace, but of lying fantasies and courtroom skirmishes — should no longer buy from my mouth the weapons for their madness. It fell out conveniently: there were only a few days left before the vintage holidays, and I decided to endure them, and then to take my leave in good order, since, having been bought by you, I would no longer put myself up for sale. So our plan was known to you, but among men it was known only to our own circle of friends. For we had agreed not to let it out to anyone else — though to us, now climbing up out of the valley of tears and singing the song of ascents, you had given sharp arrows and burning coals against the cunning tongue, the tongue that would block our way under the show of giving us good advice, and out of love would devour us, the way a man devours his food.

You had shot our heart through with arrows of your love, and we carried your words fixed deep in our gut. The examples of your servants — whom you had turned from black to shining, from dead to alive — lay heaped in the storehouse of our thoughts, and there they caught fire and burned away our heavy sluggishness, so that we would not sink back toward the pit; and they set us so fiercely alight that every blast of contradiction from some cunning tongue only fanned the flame — it could not blow us out. All the same, since your name, which you have made holy across the earth, would win our vow and purpose admirers of its own, it looked like showing off not to wait for the vacation that was so close — abandoning, ahead of time and in front of everyone, a public position. Every eye would be on the gesture; everyone would note how near the vintage was that I could not wait out; and there would be a great deal of talk about me wanting to look like somebody great. And what good would it have done me, for people to speculate and argue over my motives — and for our good to be spoken of as evil?

You had pierced our hearts with your love, and we carried your words fixed deep inside us; and the examples of your servants, whom you had turned from black to shining and from dead to living, were heaped up in the storehouse of our thoughts and set fire to our heavy sluggishness, so that we should not sink down into the abyss. They kindled us so fiercely that every gust from the cunning tongues of those who argued against us could only fan the flame the hotter, not put it out. And yet, because for the sake of your Name, which you have made holy throughout the earth, this vow and purpose of mine might also find people to praise it, it began to look like showing off — not to wait for the holiday now so near, but to quit ahead of time a public office that stood before everyone's eyes; so that everyone, watching what I did and noting how close the vintage was that I had wanted to anticipate, would have a great deal to say about me, as though I had wanted to be seen as someone important. And what would it have gained me, that people should pore over my motives and dispute about them, and that the good we were doing should be spoken of as evil?

There was something else. That same summer my lungs had begun to give way under the strain of too much teaching. Breathing came hard; pains in my chest showed the damage; a full or sustained voice was more than they could manage. This had troubled me at first, because it was all but forcing me to lay down the burden of teaching — or at least, if I could be cured and made strong again, to set it aside for a while. But once the full desire to be still and see that you are the Lord had risen in me and taken hold — my God, you know this — I even began to be glad that I had this second, unfeigned excuse, one that might soften the offense taken by men who wanted me never to be free, for their sons' sake. Full of that joy, then, I held out until the interval had run — some twenty days, perhaps — but holding out took strength; the greed that used to carry its share of the heavy load had left me, and I would have been crushed under it alone if patience had not stepped into its place. Some of your servants, my brothers, may say I sinned in this — that with my heart fully enlisted in your service, I let myself sit even one more hour in the chair of lies. I won't argue the point. But you, most merciful Lord — did you not pardon this sin too, and wash it away with the rest of my horrible, deadly sins, in the holy water?

There was something else, too, that had troubled me. That very summer, under the strain of too much literary work, my lungs had begun to fail; I breathed deeply only with difficulty, and the pain in my chest showed they were injured and refused me any full or lengthy speaking. This had troubled me, for it all but forced me, of necessity, to set down the burden of teaching, or at least, if I could be cured and recover, to set it aside for a while. But once the full longing for the quiet in which I might come to see that you are the Lord had risen in me and settled firm, then — my God, you know it — I began even to be glad that I had this second excuse, and a true one, not invented, which might somewhat soften the offense of those who, for their sons' sake, wished I would never have the freedom of your sons. So, full of that gladness, I held out until the stretch of time should run its course — some twenty days it may have been; yet they were borne with effort. The greed that used to help carry this heavy work had left me, and I was alone, and I would have been crushed, had not patience taken its place. Perhaps some of your servants, my brothers, will say I sinned in this, that with a heart fully set on serving you I let myself sit even one hour longer in the chair of lies. I will not argue the point. But have you not, O most merciful Lord, pardoned and forgiven this sin too, along with my other most horrible and deadly sins, in the holy water of baptism?

Verecundus was eaten up with worry over this happiness of ours, because he saw that the ties that bound him so tightly would cut him off from our company. He was not yet a Christian; his wife was a believer — and precisely she, more than any other shackle, held him back from the journey we had begun. He would not be a Christian, he said, on any terms but the ones closed to him. Still, he kindly offered us his country place for as long as we stayed in the area. You will repay him, Lord, at the resurrection of the just — indeed you have already given him the portion of the just. While we were away, by then at Rome, he was seized by bodily illness, and in it he was made a Christian, one of the faithful, and departed this life. So you had mercy not only on him but on us — for it would have been an unbearable grief to remember our friend's extraordinary kindness toward us and not be able to count him in your flock. Thanks be to you, our God! We are yours. Your promptings and consolations tell us so: faithful to your promises, you now repay Verecundus for that country house at Cassiciacum — where we rested in you from the fever of the world — with the everlasting freshness of your paradise; for you have forgiven him his sins on earth, on the rich mountain, the mountain flowing with milk, your own mountain.

Verecundus was worn down with worry over this happiness of ours, for, held back by bonds that bound him most tightly, he saw that he would be cut off from us. He was not yet a Christian; his wife was one of the faithful, and it was she, more than any other chain, that fastened him and held him back from the journey we had now set out on. For he would not, he said, be a Christian on any terms but the one open to him, which was the one he could not take. Still, he kindly offered us the use of his country house for as long as we should stay there. You, Lord, will reward him in the resurrection of the just, for you have already given him the portion of the righteous. While we were away, now back in Rome, he fell sick in body, and in that sickness he was made a Christian and one of the faithful, and so departed this life. And you had mercy not only on him, but on us, lest, remembering the great kindness of our friend toward us and yet unable to count him among your flock, we should be torn apart by unbearable grief. Thanks be to you, our God; we are yours. Your hints and your comforts tell us so. Faithful to your promises, you now repay Verecundus for his country house at Cassiciacum — where, away from the fever of the world, we found our rest in you — with the everlasting freshness of your Paradise; for you have forgiven him his sins upon earth, on that rich mountain, the mountain that flows with milk, your own mountain.

So he had sorrow then; but Nebridius had joy. He too, not yet a Christian, had fallen into that pit of deadly error, believing the flesh of your Son, the Truth, to be a phantom; but he had climbed out of it and believed what we believed — not yet steeped in any sacraments of your church, but a white-hot searcher after truth. Not long after our conversion and our rebirth through your baptism, he too became a faithful Catholic, serving you in perfect chastity and continence among his own people in Africa, his whole household made Christian through him — and then you released him from the flesh. And now he lives in Abraham's embrace. Whatever that phrase means, there my Nebridius lives — my sweet friend, and your son, Lord: a freedman adopted into your family. There he lives. What other place could hold such a soul? He lives in the very country he used to question me about — me, an ignorant, inexperienced man. He no longer puts his ear to my mouth; he puts the mouth of his spirit to your fountain and drinks all the wisdom he can hold, thirsty and endlessly happy. And I do not think he drinks so deep that he forgets me — since you, Lord, whom he drinks, remember us. So this was our life then: comforting Verecundus in his sadness, as far as friendship allowed, since our conversion had not broken it, and urging him toward the faith that fit his own state — married life; and waiting for Nebridius to follow us, which he was on the very edge of doing. And so those days finally rolled past. They felt long, and there were many of them, because of my longing for free, unhurried days in which to sing to you from the very marrow of my being: My heart has said to you, I have sought your face; your face, Lord, I will keep seeking.

He, then, was sorrowing at that time, but Nebridius was rejoicing. For although he too was not yet a Christian, and had fallen into the pit of that most poisonous error, believing the flesh of your Son to be a phantom, he had climbed out of it and come to believe as we did; and though he had not yet received any of the sacraments of your Church, he was a most ardent seeker after truth. Not long after our conversion and our rebirth in your baptism, when he too was a faithful member of the Catholic Church and was serving you in perfect chastity and self-control among his own people in Africa — his whole household having through him first been made Christian — you released him from the flesh, and now he lives in Abraham's bosom. Whatever that bosom may mean, there my Nebridius lives, my sweet friend, your child, O Lord, adopted now from a freedman. There he lives; for what other place could there be for such a soul? There he lives, in that place about which he used to ask me so many questions — me, a poor inexperienced man. Now he no longer lays his ear to my mouth, but lays the mouth of his spirit to your fountain, and drinks in as much wisdom as he can hold, as much as his thirst can take, endlessly happy. And I do not think he is so drunk on it that he forgets me; for you, Lord, whom he drinks, are mindful of us. So we were then, comforting Verecundus in his sorrow — as far as friendship allowed, given that our conversion had taken that turn — and urging him to be faithful within the bounds of his own condition, which was the married state; and we were waiting for Nebridius to follow us, which, being so near, he was all but ready to do. And so, at last, those days rolled by; long and many they seemed, for the love I bore to that easeful freedom in which I might sing to you from my inmost marrow: My heart has said to you, I have sought your face; your face, Lord, will I seek.

And the day came when I was released from the professorship of rhetoric in fact, as I had already been released from it in thought. It was done. You rescued my tongue as you had already rescued my heart, and I blessed you, rejoicing, and went off to the villa with all my own. What I did there in writing — writing now enlisted in your service, though still panting from the school of pride, like a runner catching his breath — my books can testify: the debates with friends, and the debates with myself alone before you; and what passed with the absent Nebridius, my letters can testify. And when would I ever have time to record all your great kindnesses to us in that season, especially when I am hurrying on to greater ones? My memory calls me back, and it is sweet to me, Lord, to confess to you the inward goads by which you finally tamed me: how you leveled me, bringing down the mountains and hills of my thoughts, straightening what was crooked in me and smoothing what was rough; and how you also subdued Alypius, my heart's brother, to the name of your Only-Begotten, our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ — a name he at first refused to allow into our writings. He wanted them to smell of the schools' lofty cedars, which the Lord has since broken to pieces, rather than of the church's healing herbs, the antidote to serpents.

Now the day had come on which I was in fact to be set free from my professorship of rhetoric, the day from which, in my mind, I was already free. And it was done. You rescued my tongue, as you had already rescued my heart. And I blessed you, rejoicing, and retired with all my household to the villa. What I did there in writing — writing that was now enlisted in your service, though it still panted, in this breathing-space, with the fumes of the school of pride — my books bear witness: both what I argued out with others present, and what I argued with myself alone, before you; and what I set down for Nebridius, who was absent, my letters bear witness. And when will I have time enough to recount all your great kindnesses to us in those days, especially as I am hurrying on toward still greater mercies? For my memory calls me back, and it is sweet to me, O Lord, to confess to you by what inward goads you tamed me — how you leveled me, lowering the mountains and hills of my high imaginings, straightening my crookedness and smoothing my rough ways; and how you also subdued the brother of my heart, Alypius, to the name of your Only-Begotten, our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, a name he would not at first allow to be put into our writings. For he preferred them to taste of the lofty cedars of the schools, which the Lord has now broken down, rather than of the wholesome herbs of the Church, the antidote against serpents.

What cries I raised to you, my God, when I read the Psalms of David — those songs of faith, those sounds of devotion that leave no room for a swollen spirit — still a raw beginner in real love of you, a catechumen resting at a villa with Alypius, a catechumen too, and my mother staying close beside us: a woman in dress, a man in faith; with an old woman's calm, a mother's love, a Christian's devotion. What cries I raised to you in those psalms, and how they kindled me toward you, and how I burned to recite them, if I could, to the whole world, against the pride of the human race! And in fact they are sung in the whole world, and no one can hide from your heat. How fierce and bitter my anger at the Manichees was — and then again I pitied them, because they did not know those sacraments, those medicines, and raged like madmen against the very antidote that could have cured their madness. I wish they could have been somewhere near me then, without my knowing it, and watched my face and heard my voice when I read the fourth Psalm in that time of quiet — and seen what that psalm did to me: When I called, the God of my justice heard me; in my distress you gave me room. Have mercy on me, Lord, and hear my prayer. I wish they could have heard what I said over those words without my knowing they heard, so they would not think I was performing for them. And in truth I would not have said the same things, or said them the same way, if I had known they were watching and listening; and if I had said them, they would not have received them as they were — spoken by myself and for myself, in front of you, out of the most intimate feeling of my soul.

Oh, in what voices I spoke to you, my God, when I read the Psalms of David, those faithful songs, those sounds of devotion that leave no room for a swelling spirit — still only a catechumen and a beginner in your true love, resting at that villa with Alypius, also a catechumen, and my mother holding fast to us, a woman in dress but with a man's faith, with the calm of her years, a mother's love, a Christian's devotion. Oh, what voices I sent up to you in those Psalms, and how they kindled me toward you and set me on fire to recite them, if I could, through the whole world, against the pride of the human race! And in fact they are sung through the whole world, and no one can hide himself from your heat. With what fierce and bitter sorrow I was angry at the Manichees! And then again I pitied them, for they did not know those sacraments, those medicines, and raged like madmen against the very cure that might have healed them of their madness. How I wished they could have been near me then, without my knowing they were there, that they might have watched my face and heard my words as I read the fourth Psalm in that time of my rest, and seen what that Psalm worked in me: When I called, the God of my righteousness heard me; in my distress you set me free. Have mercy on me, O Lord, and hear my prayer. I wish they could have heard what I said over those words, without my knowing whether they heard, so that they would not think I spoke it for their sake. For in truth I would not have said the same things, nor in the same way, if I had known they were listening and watching me; and even if I had said them, they would not have taken them in as I did when I spoke by myself and for myself, before you, out of the natural feeling of my soul.

I shuddered with fear, and in the same breath I caught fire with hope and with exultation in your mercy, Father. And all of it came pouring out through my eyes and my voice, when your good Spirit turned to us and said: Sons of men, how long will your hearts be heavy? Why do you love emptiness and chase after lies? For I had loved emptiness and chased after lies. And you, Lord, had already glorified your Holy One, raising him from the dead and seating him at your right hand, from where he would send the one he had promised, the Comforter, the Spirit of truth. He had sent him already — and I had not known it. He had sent him because he was now glorified, risen from the dead and ascended into heaven; until then the Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus was not yet glorified. And the prophet cries: How long, heavy hearts? Why do you love emptiness and chase after lies? Know this: the Lord has glorified his Holy One. He cries How long. He cries Know this. And I, for so long, not knowing, had loved emptiness and chased after lies. So I heard, and I trembled, because these words were spoken to exactly the kind of man I remembered having been. In those phantoms I had held for truth there was emptiness and there were lies; and in the bitterness of remembering, I said many things out loud, with force and from the heart. I wish the men who still love emptiness and chase after lies could have heard me. It might have shaken them; they might have vomited it all up; and then you would have heard them when they cried to you — because he who now intercedes with you for us died for us a true death in the flesh.

I trembled with fear, and then again was kindled with hope and with joy in your mercy, O Father; and it all poured out through my eyes and my voice when your good Spirit, turning toward us, said: O you sons of men, how long will you be slow of heart? Why do you love emptiness and chase after lies? For I had loved emptiness and chased after lies. And you, O Lord, had already glorified your Holy One, raising him from the dead and setting him at your right hand, from where, on high, he would send his promise, the Comforter, the Spirit of truth. And he had already sent him, though I did not know it; he had sent him, because he was now glorified, risen from the dead and ascended into heaven. For until then the Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus was not yet glorified. And the prophet cries out: How long will you be slow of heart? Why do you love emptiness and chase after lies? Know this, that the Lord has glorified his Holy One. He cries How long? He cries Know this. And I, for so long, not knowing, had loved emptiness and chased after lies; and so I heard, and trembled, because these words were spoken to the very kind of man I remembered I had been. For in those phantoms that I had held to be the truth, there was nothing but emptiness and lies; and I spoke many things aloud, earnestly and forcefully, in the bitterness of my remembering. I wish they could have heard it, those who still love emptiness and chase after lies! Perhaps they would have been shaken, and would have vomited it up, and you would have heard them when they cried out to you — for he who now intercedes with you for us died for us by a true death in the flesh.

I read on: Be angry, and do not sin. And how that moved me, my God — I who had now learned to be angry at myself for what was past, so that I would not sin in the time to come. And rightly angry: because it was no alien nature out of some tribe of darkness that had been sinning on my behalf, as they say who are not angry at themselves, and who store up wrath for the day of wrath, when your just judgment is revealed. By now my good was no longer outside me, no longer hunted with the eyes of flesh under that earthly sun. People who want their joy from outside go hollow fast: they spill themselves out on what is visible and temporary, and in their starving imagination they lick the mere images of things. If only they would wear out with hunger and say, Who will show us good things? Then we would answer, and they would hear: The light of your face, Lord, is stamped upon us. For we are not ourselves the light that enlightens every man; we are lit by you, so that we who were once darkness may be light in you. If only they could see the eternal that is within! I had tasted it, and it grieved me that I could not show it to them, as long as they came to me carrying their hearts in their eyes — eyes roving everywhere away from you — and saying, Who will show us good things? For it was there, in the room where I had been angry at myself, inside, where I had been pierced, where I had made my sacrifice — slaughtering the old man in me, and staking the new-begun hope of my life on you — it was there that you began to grow sweet to me, and put gladness in my heart. And I cried out as I read it outside and recognized it inside. And I had no wish to be multiplied in earthly goods, devouring time and devoured by time, when in your eternal simplicity I had other grain, other wine, other oil.

I read on: Be angry, and sin not. And how I was moved, O my God, I who had now learned to be angry at myself for the things of the past, that I might not sin in the time to come! And rightly angry; for it was not some other nature, a people of darkness, that had sinned instead of me — as those say who are not angry at themselves, and so store up wrath against the day of wrath and of the revealing of your just judgment. Nor were my good things outside me any longer, nor sought with the eyes of flesh in that earthly sun. For those who would have their joy from outside themselves soon grow empty, and spill themselves out on the things that are seen and passing, and in their starving thoughts lick at the mere shadows of them. Oh, that they were worn out at last with their hunger, and would say, Who will show us any good? And we would answer, and they would hear: The light of your countenance is sealed upon us. For we are not that light which gives light to every man, but we are given light by you, so that, having once been darkness, we may be light in you. Oh, that they could see the eternal that is within, which, having tasted it, I grieved that I could not show them, so long as they brought me their heart in their eyes, which roved abroad away from you, while they said, Who will show us any good? For there, where I was angry within myself, in my own room, where I was inwardly pierced, where I had offered my sacrifice, killing my old self and beginning to plan a new life, putting my trust in you — there you had begun to grow sweet to me, and had put gladness in my heart. And I cried out as I read this on the page, finding it within. Nor would I be multiplied with worldly goods, wasting time and wasted by time, when I had, in your eternal and undivided Being, another corn and wine and oil.

And at the next verse I shouted from the depth of my heart: In peace! In the Selfsame! What a thing to say — I will lie down and sleep. For who will stand against us when the written word comes true: Death is swallowed up in victory? And you, supremely, are the Selfsame — you who do not change; and in you is the rest that forgets every labor, since there is no other beside you, and we were not made to chase the many other things that are not what you are. No: you, Lord — you alone have settled me in hope. I read, and I burned; and I could find nothing to do for the deaf and the dead, one of whom I had been: a walking plague, a bitter, blind barker against the very Scriptures that drip with the honey of heaven and blaze with your own light. And I was eaten alive with zeal over the enemies of that book.

And with a loud cry of my heart I cried out at the next verse: O, in peace! O, for the Selfsame! O, what did he say — I will lie down and sleep — for who shall stop us, when that saying comes to pass which is written, Death is swallowed up in victory? And you, surpassingly, are the Selfsame, who do not change; and in you is the rest that forgets all toil, for there is no one else with you, and we are not to seek the many other things that are not what you are. You alone, Lord, make me dwell in hope. I read, and I caught fire; and I could not find what to do with those who were deaf and dead, among whom I myself had been — a plague of a man, a bitter and a blind ranter against those writings that are made sweet with the honey of heaven and bright with your own light. And I was consumed with zeal against the enemies of this Scripture.

When will I ever recall everything from those days of rest? But I have not forgotten — and I will not pass over — the sting of your whip and the astonishing swiftness of your mercy. You tormented me then with a toothache, and when it grew so bad I could not speak, it rose up in my heart to ask all my friends who were there to pray for me to you, the God of every kind of health. I wrote this on wax and gave it to them to read. The moment we had gone down on our knees in simple supplication, the pain fled. But what pain it was — and how did it flee? I was terrified, my Lord, my God; nothing like it had happened to me since my earliest years. And deep inside me I felt your nod — the mere motion of your will — and rejoicing in faith, I praised your name. And that same faith would not let me rest easy about my past sins, which had not yet been forgiven me in your baptism.

When shall I recall all that happened in those holy days? Yet I have not forgotten, nor will I pass over, the severity of your scourge and the wonderful swiftness of your mercy. You tormented me then with a pain in my teeth; and when it had grown so fierce that I could not speak, it came into my heart to ask all my friends who were present to pray for me to you, the God of every kind of health. I wrote this on wax and gave it to them to read. And the moment we had bowed our knees in humble devotion, the pain went away. But what pain it was! And how it went! I was frightened, O my Lord, my God; for from my infancy I had never known anything like it. And the power of your slightest nod sank deep into me, and rejoicing in faith I praised your Name — though that faith would not let me be at ease about my past sins, which were not yet forgiven me by your baptism.

When the vintage vacation ended, I sent the Milanese notice to find their students another seller of words, because I had chosen to serve you, and because my failing breath and the pain in my chest were not equal to the professorship. And I wrote to your bishop, the holy man Ambrose, telling him my old errors and my present resolve, and asking his advice: which of your Scriptures should I read, to make me readier and fitter to receive so great a grace? He recommended Isaiah the prophet — because, I believe, Isaiah is the plainest herald of the gospel and of the calling of the nations. But I did not understand the opening of him, and assuming the whole book was like it, I set it aside, to be taken up again when I had more practice in the Lord's way of speaking.

When the vintage holidays were over, I gave notice to the people of Milan to find their students another seller of words, both because I had chosen to serve you, and because, with my difficulty in breathing and the pain in my chest, I was no longer fit for the work. And by letter I made known to your bishop, the holy man Ambrose, my former errors and my present longings, asking his advice on which of your Scriptures I should best read to make myself readier and fitter to receive so great a grace. He recommended Isaiah the prophet — I believe because Isaiah, more clearly than the rest, foreshows the Gospel and the calling of the Gentiles. But I did not understand the first passage of him, and, imagining the whole book to be like it, I laid it aside, to be taken up again when I was better practiced in the Lord's own words.

Then, when the time came to hand in my name for baptism, we left the countryside and returned to Milan. Alypius decided to be reborn in you along with me. He had already put on the humility that fits your sacraments, and he was the bravest of tamers of his own body — daring, beyond all custom, to walk the frozen ground of Italy barefoot. We took with us the boy Adeodatus, my son in the flesh, born of my sin. You had made him well. He was barely fifteen, and in intelligence he outstripped many grave and learned men. I am confessing your own gifts to you, Lord my God, creator of all things and abundantly able to reshape our deformities — for I had no part in that boy except the sin. That we brought him up in your discipline — that was you and no one else prompting us. I am confessing your own gifts. There is a book of mine called The Teacher: a dialogue between him and me. You know that every idea placed there in the mouth of the person talking with me was his, at sixteen years old. I saw much more in him, and more astonishing still. That mind of his put a kind of awe into me — and who but you could be the craftsman of such wonders? Soon you took his life from the earth; and I remember him now with no anxiety at all, with nothing to fear for his childhood, or his youth, or the whole man he was. We took him with us, our contemporary in your grace, to be brought up in your discipline — and we were baptized, and all anxiety over our past life fled away. In those days I could not get enough of the wonderful sweetness of pondering the depth of your design for the salvation of the human race. How I wept at your hymns and canticles, pierced to the quick by the voices of your sweet-singing church! The voices flowed into my ears, and the truth was distilled into my heart, and feeling for you welled up hot and overflowed, and the tears ran down — and they did me good.

When the time came at last to give in my name for baptism, we left the country and returned to Milan. Alypius too was pleased to be reborn in you along with me, already clothed in the humility that befits your sacraments, and a most valiant tamer of his own body, so that he ventured, against all custom, to walk the frozen ground of Italy with his bare feet. And we took with us the boy Adeodatus, my son after the flesh, born of my sin. You had made him well. He was not yet fifteen, and in quickness of mind he outdid many grave and learned men. I confess to you your own gifts, O Lord my God, Maker of all things, and well able to reshape what is misshapen in us — for I had no part in that boy but the sin. That we brought him up in your discipline, it was you, no one else, who breathed it into us. I confess to you your gifts. There is a book of ours called The Teacher; it is a dialogue between him and me. You know that all the thoughts there put into the mouth of the one talking with me were his, in his sixteenth year. Much more, and still more remarkable, I found in him. That gift of his struck awe into me. And who but you could be the maker of such wonders? Soon you took his life from the earth, and now I remember him without anxiety, fearing nothing for his childhood or his youth or his whole self. We joined him to us, our companion in grace, to be brought up in your discipline; and we were baptized, and all anxiety about our past life fled from us. In those days I could not get my fill of the wondrous sweetness of pondering the depth of your design for the salvation of the human race. How I wept at your hymns and canticles, cut to the quick by the voices of your sweet-singing Church! Those voices flowed into my ears, and the truth was distilled into my heart, and out of that the feeling of my devotion overflowed, and the tears ran down, and I was happy in them.

The church of Milan had only recently begun to worship with this kind of consolation and encouragement, the brothers singing together with great fervor, voices and hearts as one. It was about a year earlier, not much more, that Justina, mother of the boy emperor Valentinian, had persecuted your servant Ambrose in the interest of the heresy the Arians had seduced her into. The devout people kept watch in the church, ready to die with their bishop, your servant. There my mother, your handmaid, holding a front place in those anxieties and vigils, lived on prayer. Even we, still cold, still unwarmed by the heat of your Spirit, were stirred by the sight of the city in alarm and turmoil. That was when the practice began — after the custom of the Eastern churches — of singing hymns and psalms, so the people would not grow faint under the grinding weight of sorrow. It has been kept from that day to this, and taken up by many — by now almost all — of your flocks across the rest of the world.

The Church of Milan had not long begun to practice this kind of comfort and encouragement, the brothers singing together with one accord of voice and heart. For it was about a year before, or not much more, that Justina, the mother of the boy-emperor Valentinian, had persecuted your servant Ambrose on behalf of her heresy, into which the Arians had seduced her. The devout people kept watch in the church, ready to die with their bishop, your servant. There my mother, your handmaid, bearing a leading part in those anxieties and vigils, lived for prayer. We ourselves, still not warmed through by the heat of your Spirit, were nonetheless stirred by the sight of the city, amazed and shaken. It was then that it was first set in place, after the manner of the Eastern churches, that hymns and psalms should be sung, so that the people should not grow faint under the weariness of their sorrow; and from that day to this the custom has been kept, and many — almost all — of your congregations in the other parts of the world have followed it.

Then, in a vision, you revealed to your bishop where the bodies of the martyrs Gervasius and Protasius lay hidden. You had kept them incorrupt for all those years in your secret treasury, so that you could bring them out at the right moment to check the fury of a woman — a woman, but a royal one. When they had been found and dug up and carried with due honor to the Ambrosian basilica, not only were those tormented by unclean spirits healed, the demons themselves confessing it; there was also a man of the city, blind for many years and well known there, who asked what all the crowd's tumbling joy was about, heard the answer, and sprang up, begging his guide to lead him there. Brought to the place, he asked to be allowed to touch with his handkerchief the bier of your saints, whose death is precious in your sight. He touched it, and put the cloth to his eyes — and at once they opened. From there the story raced outward; from there your praises glowed and blazed; from there the mind of that hostile woman, though not turned to the health of belief, was at least turned back from the madness of persecution. Thanks be to you, my God! From where, and to where, have you led my memory, that I should confess these things to you too — great things I had passed over and forgotten? And yet even then, when the fragrance of your ointments hung so heavy in the air, we did not run after you. That is why I wept the more when your hymns were sung: I had sighed after you for so long, and at last I could breathe you — as far as air can move through this house of grass.

It was then, too, that you revealed in a vision to that same bishop the place where the bodies of the martyrs Gervasius and Protasius lay hidden, whom you had kept uncorrupted so many years in your secret treasury, so that you might bring them out at the right moment to check the fury of a woman — but an empress. For when they were found and dug up and carried with due honor to the Ambrosian basilica, not only were those healed who were tormented by unclean spirits, the demons themselves confessing it, but a certain man, a citizen well known to the city, who had been blind for many years, asked why the people were rejoicing in such confusion, and when he heard the reason, he sprang up and begged his guide to lead him there. Led there, he asked to be allowed to touch with his handkerchief the bier of your saints, whose death is precious in your sight. When he had done so, and put it to his eyes, they were opened at once. From there the news spread; from there your praises blazed and shone; from there the mind of that enemy, though not turned to the soundness of belief, was at least turned back from her fury of persecuting. Thanks be to you, O my God. From where, and to where, have you led my memory, that I should confess these things too to you — things which, great as they were, I had let slip in forgetfulness? And yet even then, when the fragrance of your ointments was so sweet, we did not run after you. And so I wept the more among the singing of your hymns, who had once only sighed after you, and was now at last breathing you in, so far as the breath can enter this house of ours that is made of grass.

You, who make those of one mind dwell together in one house, joined to our company Euodius as well, a young man of our own town. He had been an officer of the imperial service; he was converted to you and baptized before we were; he quit the state's warfare and buckled on yours. We were together, meaning to live together in our holy resolve. We were looking for the place where we could serve you most usefully, and were making our way back, together, to Africa. And when we had gotten as far as Ostia on the Tiber, my mother died. I pass over many things, because I am in great haste. Receive my confessions and my thanksgivings, my God, for countless things I say nothing of. But I will not pass over whatever my soul can bring to birth about that servant of yours who brought me to birth — in her flesh, so that I was born into this daylight; in her heart, so that I might be born into eternal light. Not her gifts, but your gifts in her, are what I will tell; for she did not make herself, and she did not raise herself. You created her — her father and mother did not know what kind of person would come from them — and it was the scepter of your Christ, the discipline of your only Son, that reared her in your fear, in a believing house, a good member of your church. Yet she used to credit her upbringing less to her mother's diligence than to a certain aged servant woman, who had carried her father on her back when he was a baby, the way little children are carried by the bigger girls. Because of that, and because of her great age and impeccable character, the heads of that Christian household held her in real honor; and so the care of the master's daughters was placed in her hands. She took the charge seriously: fierce with a holy severity in restraining the girls when it was needed, sober and shrewd in teaching them. Outside the hours when they were fed, very moderately, at their parents' table, she would not let them drink so much as water, even if they were burning with thirst. She was heading off a bad habit, and she added the sensible word: "You drink water now because you don't have wine within reach. But when you're married, and find yourselves mistresses of the pantries and the cellars, water will seem beneath you — and the habit of drinking will still be there." By this way of teaching, and the authority she carried, she reined in the greed of a tender age and shaped the girls' very thirst to so decent a measure that what they should not do, they no longer even wanted.

You who make those of one mind dwell together in one house joined Euodius to us as well, a young man of our own city. While serving as an officer at court, he had been converted to you and baptized before us, and, laying down his worldly soldiering, he had girded himself for yours. We were together, and meant to live together in our devout purpose. We looked for the place where we might serve you most usefully, and together we were on our way back to Africa; and when we had come as far as Ostia, my mother departed this life. Much I leave out, for I am hurrying on. Receive my confessions and thanksgivings, O my God, for the countless things about which I keep silent. But I will not leave out whatever my soul would bring forth concerning your handmaid, who brought me forth — both in the flesh, that I might be born into this temporal light, and in her heart, that I might be born into the light eternal. Not her gifts, but yours in her, would I speak of; for she did not make herself, nor did she rear herself. You created her; and neither her father nor her mother knew what kind of woman would come from them. It was the scepter of your Christ, the discipline of your only Son, in a Christian house, a sound member of your Church, that brought her up in the fear of you. And yet, for her good upbringing, she used to give the credit not so much to her mother's care as to that of a certain aged servant, who had carried her own father as a child on her back, the way little ones are often carried by older girls. For that reason, and for her great age and excellent character, she was well respected by the heads of that Christian household. And so the care of her master's daughters was entrusted to her, and she gave it diligent heed, holding them back firmly when she had to, with a holy strictness, and teaching them with a grave good sense. For except at the hours when they were fed, very temperately, at their parents' table, she would not let them drink even water, however parched with thirst they were, heading off a bad habit and adding this wholesome word: "You drink water now, because you have no power over the wine; but when you come to be married, and are made mistresses of the storerooms and cellars, you will look down on water, but the habit of drinking will hold." By this way of teaching, and the authority she had, she reined in the greediness of childhood and shaped their very thirst to such fine moderation that they no longer even wanted what they should not have.

And yet — as your handmaid told me, her son — a love of wine had crept up on her. Her parents, trusting her as a sober girl, used to send her in the usual way to draw wine from the cask. She would dip the cup in at the opening, and before she poured the wine into the flagon she would sip just a little, with the tips of her lips — no more than that, because more than that her own taste refused. She did it not out of any craving for drink, but out of the boiling-over energy of youth, which vents itself in playful impulses and is usually held down, in children, by the weight of their elders. And so, adding to that little a daily little more — for whoever despises small things falls, little by little — she slid into the habit of greedily draining her small cups nearly full of undiluted wine. Where then was the shrewd old woman and her stern forbidding? Would anything be strong enough against a hidden disease, if your medicine, Lord, were not keeping watch over us? Father, mother, guardians absent — you present, who created us, who call us, who work good for the health of our souls even through the people set over us — what did you do then, my God? How did you cure her? How did you heal her? Did you not draw out of another soul a hard, sharp insult, like a surgeon's blade out of your hidden stores, and with one cut take off all the rot? A servant girl who used to go with her to the cellar fell to quarreling, as happens, with her little mistress when the two of them were alone, and threw this fault in her face with the bitterest scorn, calling her a little wine-swiller. The taunt went in like a barb. She saw her own foulness, condemned it on the spot, and stripped it off. As flattering friends corrupt, so needling enemies mostly correct. Yet you repay them not for what you do through them, but for what they themselves intended. That girl, in her anger, wanted to wound her little mistress, not to heal her — and she did it in private, either because that just happened to be where the quarrel caught them, or because she herself might have been in trouble for having kept quiet so long. But you, Lord, ruler of everything in heaven and on earth, who bend the deepest torrents to your own uses and give order to the churning flood of the centuries — out of one soul's sickness you healed another; so that no one who notices this should credit his own power when someone he wanted corrected is corrected through a word of his.

And yet — as your handmaid told me, her son — a love of wine had crept up on her even so. For when, as the custom was, she was sent by her parents, like the sober girl she was, to draw wine from the cask, she would hold the cup under the open spout, and before pouring the wine into the flagon she would wet the tip of her lips with a little of it; for more than that her instinct refused. She did this not out of any craving for drink, but out of the overflow of youth, which bubbles up in playful little tricks that the gravity of their elders usually keeps down in young spirits. And so, by adding to that little drop a little more, day by day — for whoever despises small things falls little by little — she fell at last into the habit of greedily draining little cups almost brimful of wine. Where now was that wise old woman and her stern forbidding? Would anything have availed against a hidden disease, if your healing hand, O Lord, had not watched over us? Father, mother, and overseers absent, and you present — you who create, who call, who also through those set over us work something toward the saving of our souls — what did you do then, my God? How did you cure her? How did you heal her? Did you not draw out of another soul a hard and cutting taunt, like a surgeon's lancet from your secret store, and with a single stroke cut away all that rottenness? For a maidservant, with whom she used to go down to the cellar, quarreling one day, as servants do, with her little mistress when the two of them were alone, threw this fault in her face, with the most bitter insult, calling her a wine-bibber. Stung to the quick by that taunt, she saw the foulness of what she did, and at once condemned it and gave it up. As flattering friends pervert us, so spiteful enemies most often set us right. Yet you repay them not for what you accomplish through them, but for what they themselves intended. For that servant, in her anger, sought to wound her young mistress, not to mend her, and did it in private, either because the time and place of their quarrel happened to find them so, or for fear of getting into trouble herself for telling it so late. But you, Lord, Ruler of all things in heaven and on earth, who turn to your own purposes the deepest currents and the ordered turbulence of the flooding stream of time, by the very sickness of one soul healed another — so that no one who sees this should credit it to his own power, even when another, whom he wished to set right, is set right through some word of his.

Raised in this modesty and sobriety — made obedient to her parents by you, rather than to you by her parents — when she reached full marriageable age she was given to a husband, and she served him as her lord. And she worked to win him for you, preaching you to him by what she was; for with that you had made her beautiful — a wife her husband could respect, admire, and love. She bore the wrongs done to her bed in such a way that no quarrel over them ever came between her and her husband. She was waiting for your mercy on him: that he might believe in you, and be made chaste. And besides this, he was as hot in temper as he was warm in kindness. But she knew not to cross an angry husband — not in act, not even in a word. Only when he had settled and grown quiet, and the moment was right, would she explain what she had done, if it happened that he had flared up without thinking. In short: while many wives with far milder husbands carried the marks of beatings on their disfigured faces, and in the gossip of friends would blame their husbands' conduct, she blamed their tongues — telling them, as if in jest but in dead earnest, that from the moment they heard the marriage contract read out, they should have understood it as the deed that made them servants; they should keep their station in mind, and not set themselves up against their lords. The women were amazed — knowing what a violent temper she lived with — that it had never been heard, and no mark had ever shown, that Patricius struck his wife, or that a single day's domestic quarrel had come between them; and when they asked her privately why, she taught them her rule, the one I have just given. Those who took it up proved it, and thanked her. Those who did not stayed under the yoke, and went on suffering.

Brought up in this modest and sober way, and made obedient to her parents more by you than by her parents to you, as soon as she was of marriageable age she was given to a husband, and served him as her lord. She worked hard to win him over to you, speaking of you to him by her way of life, by which you made her beautiful, and revered, and lovely, and admired by her husband. And she so bore his being unfaithful to her bed that she never had a quarrel with him over it; for she was waiting for your mercy upon him, that by believing in you he might be made chaste. And besides this, he was as hot in temper as he was warm in his affections. But she had learned not to stand up against an angry husband, not in deed only, but not even in word. Only when he had grown calm and quiet, and was in a state to take it, would she give him an account of what she had done, in case he had been too hasty in taking offense. And so, while many wives, who had gentler husbands, yet carried the marks of blows on their disfigured faces, and in friendly talk would blame their husbands' way of life, she would blame their tongues, giving them, as if in jest, this earnest advice: that from the moment they heard the marriage contract read out to them, they should think of it as the deed that made them servants, and so, remembering their station, should not set themselves up against their lords. And when they, knowing what a hot-tempered husband she put up with, were amazed that it had never been heard, nor shown by any sign, that Patricius had struck his wife, or that there had been so much as one day's quarrel between them, and asked her, in confidence, the reason, she taught them the practice I have described. Those who took it up found it good, and gave thanks; those who did not found no relief, and suffered.

Her mother-in-law, too, was set against her at first by the whisperings of malicious servants. But she won her over by sheer attentiveness, by unbroken patience and mildness, until the older woman, of her own accord, went to her son to expose the meddling tongues that had been poisoning the household peace between herself and her daughter-in-law, and demanded punishment. So, after he — obeying his mother, and looking to the good order of the house — had whipped the servants who had been exposed, just as she who exposed them wished, she promised the same reward to anyone else who tried to please her by speaking ill of her daughter-in-law. No one dared; and from then on they lived together in a sweetness of goodwill that people remembered.

Her mother-in-law, too, who at first had been set against her by the whispers of malicious servants, she so won over by attentiveness and steady endurance and meekness, that the older woman of her own accord disclosed to her son the meddling tongues that had disturbed the household peace between herself and her daughter-in-law, and asked him to put a stop to it. So, in obedience to his mother and for the good order of the house, he had those servants whipped, at the will of the one who had exposed them; and she promised the same reward to anyone who, to please her, should speak ill of her daughter-in-law. And after that no one dared, and they lived together with a remarkable sweetness of mutual kindness.

This great gift too you gave, my God, my mercy, to that good servant of yours in whose womb you created me: that wherever she could, between any souls at odds and in discord, she showed herself such a peacemaker that, hearing from each side the bitterest things about the other — the kind of stuff that swollen, undigested discord belches up, when raw hatred hisses itself out in sour talk to a present friend about an absent enemy — she would never pass on anything from one to the other except what would work toward their reconciliation. That might seem to me a small virtue, if I did not know, to my grief, the numberless crowds of people who — through some horrible, far-spreading contagion of sin — not only report the words of angry enemies to angry enemies, but pad them with words never spoken; whereas to an ordinarily humane person it ought to be a small thing not to feed and fan human hatreds by speaking evil, unless he is also working to put them out by speaking good. Such a woman she was — and her teacher was you, the innermost instructor, in the school of her heart.

This great gift also you bestowed, O my God, my mercy, on that good handmaid of yours, in whose womb you created me: that wherever she could, between people at odds and out of all harmony, she showed herself such a peacemaker that, hearing on both sides the most bitter things — the kind that swollen and undigested anger spills out, when the rawness of enmity is breathed out in sour talk to a friend who is present, against an enemy who is not — she would never disclose anything from the one to the other except what might tend toward their reconciling. This might seem a small good to me, did I not know, to my grief, countless people who, through some horrible and far-spreading plague of sin, not only repeat to those already angry the things said in anger, but even add things that were never said at all; whereas, for human beings, it ought to seem a slight thing not to feed or fan ill will by ill words, unless one also takes pains, by good words, to quench it. Such was she — and you, her most inward Teacher, taught her in the school of the heart.

Finally she won her own husband for you, at the very end of his earthly life; and once he believed, she never again had to mourn in him what she had endured before he believed. She was also the servant of your servants. Any of them who knew her found in her much reason to praise you, and honor you, and love you; for they could feel your presence in her heart, and the fruit of her holy way of living testified to it. She had been the wife of one husband; she had repaid the debt she owed her parents; she had governed her house devoutly; her good works spoke for her. She had brought up children, going into labor for them all over again every time she saw them straying from you. Last of all, Lord — since by your gift you allow us to speak as your servants — for all of us who, before she fell asleep in you, were living together as companions in the grace of your baptism, she cared as though every one of us were her child, and served us as though every one of us were her parent.

In the end she won even her own husband over to you, near the very close of his life on earth; nor did she have to complain of him, now that he was a believer, as she had borne with him before he believed. She was also the servant of your servants; whoever of them knew her praised and honored and loved you in her, for they felt your presence in her heart through the witness of a holy life and its fruits. For she had been the wife of one man, had repaid her parents, had governed her house piously, was well spoken of for good works; she had brought up her children, going into labor over them again and again, each time she saw them swerving away from you. And finally, of all of us your servants, O Lord — for by your own gift you let us speak — us, who before her falling asleep in you lived united together, having received the grace of your baptism, she cared for as though she had been the mother of us all, and served as though she had been the child of us all.

The day was now approaching when she would depart this life — a day you knew, though we did not. It came about, I believe by your hidden arrangement, that she and I stood alone, leaning at a window that looked onto the garden inside the house where we were staying, at Ostia on the Tiber. There, away from the crowds, after the strain of a long journey, we were gathering strength for the sea voyage. So we were talking, just the two of us, and it was very sweet; and forgetting what lay behind, straining toward what lay ahead, we asked each other, in the presence of the Truth, which is you, what the eternal life of the saints will be like — the life eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it risen into the heart of man. But with the mouth of the heart we strained wide open toward the streams that fall from your fountain on high, the fountain of life which is with you — hoping to be sprinkled from it, each to our capacity, and somehow to think about a thing so great.

The day was now drawing near on which she was to depart this life — the day you knew well, though we did not — and it came about, by your secret arranging, as I believe, that she and I stood alone, leaning at a certain window that looked out onto the garden of the house where we were staying, at Ostia. There, far from the noise of the crowd, we were resting after the strain of a long journey, in readiness for the voyage.
