We were talking together, alone, very sweetly; and forgetting the things that were behind and reaching out to the things that were ahead, we asked each other, in the presence of the Truth, which is you, what the eternal life of the saints would be like — which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man. And yet we panted with the mouth of our heart after those heavenly streams of your fountain, the fountain of life that is with you, that, sprinkled from it according to our small capacity, we might in some way turn our minds toward so great a mystery.

And our talk arrived at this point: that the delight of the body's senses, however great, in however bright a bodily light, seemed unworthy — beside the joy of that life — not just of comparison, but even of mention. Then, rising with a more burning love toward the Selfsame, we moved step by step up through all bodily things, up to heaven itself, from which sun and moon and stars shine down on the earth. And we climbed higher still, by inward thought and speech and wonder at your works; and we came into our own minds, and passed beyond them, to reach that region of unfailing plenty where you feed Israel forever on the food of truth — where life is that Wisdom through whom all these things are made, everything that has been and everything that will be. And she herself is not made: she is as she was, and so she will be always. Or rather: 'has been' and 'will be' are not in her at all — only 'is,' because she is eternal, and 'has been' and 'will be' are not eternal. And while we talked, and panted for her, we touched her — just barely, with one full beat of the heart. And we sighed, and left the first fruits of the spirit bound there, and came back down to the noise of our own mouths, where a word has a beginning and an ending. And what is like your Word, our Lord — who remains in himself without growing old, and makes all things new?

And when our talk had come to this — that the very highest delight of the bodily senses, in the very purest bodily light, set beside the sweetness of that life, was not worth comparing with it, or even worth mentioning — we lifted ourselves up with a more burning longing toward the Selfsame, and rose, step by step, through all bodily things, and through heaven itself, from which the sun and moon and stars shine down upon the earth. And still we climbed higher, in inward thought and speech and wonder at your works; and we came to our own minds, and went beyond them, to reach that region of never-failing plenty, where you feed Israel forever on the food of truth, and where life is the Wisdom by whom all these things are made, both what has been and what is to come — and she herself is not made, but is, as she has been, and so will be forever; or rather, in her there is no "has been" and no "will be," but only "is," for she is eternal, since to "have been" and to "be hereafter" are not eternal. And while we were speaking and panting after her, we touched her, a little, with one whole stroke of the heart; and we sighed, and left there, bound to her, the firstfruits of the Spirit, and came back down to the noise of our own mouths, where a word both begins and ends. And what is there like your Word, our Lord, who abides in himself without growing old, and makes all things new?

So we said: if for anyone the tumult of the flesh fell silent; silent every image of earth and water and air; silent the wheeling sky; silent the very soul to itself, passing beyond itself by not thinking of itself; silent all dreams and imagined revelations, every tongue, every sign, everything that exists only in passing — if all of it, for that person, fell completely silent (since, if you can hear them, all these things are saying one thing: We did not make ourselves; he made us, who abides forever) — if, having said that, they too fell quiet, having pricked our ear toward their Maker, and he alone spoke: not through them, but by himself, so that we heard his word not through any tongue of flesh, not through the voice of an angel, not through thunder out of a cloud, not through the dark riddle of a likeness — but heard him, himself, whom we love in all these things; himself, without them — the way the two of us, just now, reached out and in one racing thought touched the eternal Wisdom that abides over all things — if that could last, and every other vision of a far lesser kind be withdrawn, and this one seize its beholder, and swallow him, and fold him into inward joys, so that eternal life were exactly like that one moment of understanding we had just sighed for — would that not be: Enter into the joy of your Lord? And when will it come? When we all rise again — though we shall not all be changed?

We were saying, then: If for anyone the tumult of the flesh fell silent; silent the images of earth and water and air; silent the heavens; and the soul itself fell silent, and passed beyond itself by no longer thinking of itself; silent all dreams and every imagined revelation, every tongue and every sign, and whatever comes to be only by passing away — for if anyone could listen, all these things say, We did not make ourselves; he made us who abides forever — if, having said this, they too should fall silent, having turned our ear toward him who made them, and he alone should speak, not through them but by himself, so that we might hear his Word, not through any tongue of flesh, nor an angel's voice, nor a clap of thunder, nor in the dark riddle of a likeness, but might hear his very Self, whom in all these things we love, hear him without them, as we two were just now straining toward him, and in a flash of thought touched that eternal Wisdom which abides over all — if this could be made to last, and all other visions of a far lower kind be withdrawn, and this one alone seize and absorb and enfold its beholder in these inward joys, so that life forever might be like that one moment of understanding for which we had just been sighing — would not this be: Enter into your Master's joy? And when will that be? When we shall all rise again, though we shall not all be changed?

I was saying something like this — even if not in just this way, and not in these words. But you know, Lord, that on that day, while we talked, this world with all its delights grew cheap to us in the middle of our own speaking; and my mother said: "Son, as for me, nothing in this life delights me anymore. What I am still doing here, and why I am here, I do not know. My hope in this world is spent. There was one thing I wanted to stay alive a little longer for: to see you a Catholic Christian before I died. My God has given me that, and given more than that — I see you now his servant, with earthly happiness thrown aside. What am I doing here?"

Such things I was saying, and even if not in just this manner and these same words, yet you know, Lord, that on that day, while we were speaking of these things, and this world with all its delights was growing cheap to us as we spoke, my mother said: "Son, for my own part I no longer find any delight in anything in this life. What I am still to do here, and why I am here, I do not know, now that my hopes in this world are all fulfilled. There was one thing only for which I wished to linger a little while in this life: to see you a Catholic Christian before I died. My God has granted me this beyond my asking, for I see you now his servant, and despising even earthly happiness. What am I doing here?"

What I answered her, I do not remember. Hardly five days later, or not much more, she went down with a fever. One day, in the middle of her illness, she fainted, and for a little while was drawn away from everything around her. We came running. She was quickly conscious again, and looked at me and my brother standing over her, and said, like someone searching for something, "Where was I?" Then, watching us struck dumb with grief, she said: "Here you will bury your mother." I stayed silent and fought down my tears. But my brother said something about hoping she would die not in a foreign country but in her own land — the happier lot. When she heard it her face turned anxious, and her eyes rebuked him for still having a taste for such things; then she looked at me: "Listen to what he says," she said. And soon, to us both: "Lay this body anywhere. Don't let the care of it trouble you in the least. I ask only this: that you remember me at the altar of the Lord, wherever you are." When she had gotten this thought out in what words she could, she fell silent, and the sickness, worsening, worked at her.

What I answered her to this, I do not remember. For scarcely five days later, or not much more, she fell ill of a fever. And one day in that sickness she fainted away and was for a while withdrawn from the things around her. We hurried to her; but she was soon brought back to her senses, and, looking at me and at my brother who stood by, she said to us, as though asking: "Where was I?" And then, looking steadily at us, stricken with grief, she said: "Here you will bury your mother." I kept silent and held back my tears; but my brother said something, wishing for her — as the happier lot — that she might die not in a strange land but in her own. At this she gave him an anxious look, checking him with her eyes for still tasting such things, and then, looking at me, she said: "See what he says"; and soon after, to us both: "Lay this body anywhere; let no care for it trouble you in the least. This one thing only I ask: that you would remember me at the Lord's altar, wherever you may be." And when she had spoken this thought in what words she could, she fell silent, struggling now with her worsening sickness.

But I, thinking of your gifts, unseen God — the gifts you plant in the hearts of your faithful, out of which such marvelous fruit springs up — I rejoiced and gave you thanks. For I knew, I remembered, how she had always burned with anxiety about her burial place, which she had provided and prepared for herself beside her husband's body. Because the two of them had lived in such harmony, she had wanted — so little can the human mind grasp things divine — one more happiness added to that one, and remembered among men: that after her pilgrimage across the sea, it be granted her that the earthly remains of husband and wife lie joined under the same earth. When this empty wish had begun, through the fullness of your goodness, to leave her heart, I did not know; and I rejoiced, amazed, that she had shown me it was gone — though indeed in our talk at the window, when she said, "What am I still doing here?" there had been no sign of any desire to die in her own country. I heard later, too, that while we were at Ostia, one day when I was elsewhere, she had been talking with a mother's frankness to some of my friends about the contempt of this life and the good that death is; and when they stood amazed at such courage in a woman — courage you had given her — and asked whether she was not afraid to leave her body so far from her own city, she said: "Nothing is far from God. There is no fear that at the end of the world he won't know the place from which to raise me up." And so, on the ninth day of her illness, in the fifty-sixth year of her life and the thirty-third of mine, that devout and holy soul was released from the body.

But I, considering your gifts — you, the unseen God — which you pour into the hearts of your faithful ones, and from which wondrous fruits spring up, rejoiced and gave thanks to you, recalling what I had known before: how anxious and careful she had always been about her place of burial, which she had provided and made ready for herself beside the body of her husband. For because they had lived together in great harmony, she had wished also — so little can the human mind grasp the things of God — to add this to her happiness, and to have it remembered among men that, after her wandering across the seas, what was earthly of this united pair had been allowed to rest, united, beneath the same earth. When that empty wish had begun to fade from her heart through the fullness of your goodness, I did not know; and I rejoiced, marveling that she had disclosed herself to me in this way — though indeed in that talk of ours at the window too, when she said, "What am I doing here any longer?", she showed no desire to die in her own country. I heard afterward, as well, that while we were at Ostia she spoke one day, with a mother's openness, when I was not there, to some of my friends, about the contempt of this life and the blessing of death; and when they were amazed at such courage, which you had given to a woman, and asked whether she was not afraid to leave her body so far from her own city, she answered: "Nothing is far from God; nor need I fear that at the end of the world he will not know the place from which to raise me up." And so, on the ninth day of her sickness, in the fifty-sixth year of her age and the thirty-third of mine, that devout and holy soul was set free from the body.

I closed her eyes. And an enormous sorrow came flooding into my heart and was about to overflow into tears — and at the same moment my eyes, under the mind's violent command, drank the spring back down until it was dry; and that struggle went very hard with me. Then, at the instant she breathed her last, the boy Adeodatus burst out wailing; we all hushed him, and he went quiet. In the same way something childish in me, too, that was sliding toward sobs, was hushed by the heart's young voice, and went quiet. For we did not think it right to mark that death with wet laments and groaning — that is how people usually mourn a death they think of as misery, or as total extinction. But she was not dying in misery, and she was not wholly dying. Of that we were certain — from the evidence of how she had lived, from her faith that was no pretense, from reasons that were sure.

I closed her eyes; and a vast sorrow welled up into my heart and was overflowing into tears, when at the same time, by the violent command of my mind, my eyes drank their own fountain dry again; and it went bitterly with me in that struggle. But when she breathed her last, the boy Adeodatus broke out in a loud wail; then, checked by all of us, he grew quiet. And in the same way a childish thing in me, that was finding its vent in weeping through the young voice of my heart, was checked and silenced. For we did not think it fitting to mark that funeral with tearful laments and groans, since by these people usually mourn the dead as though they were wretched, or wholly dead; but she was neither wretched in her death, nor at all dead. Of this we were sure, on good grounds — the witness of her good life and her unfeigned faith.

Then what was it that ached so heavily inside me? It was the fresh wound, torn open by the sudden breaking of that sweetest, dearest habit — the habit of living together. I treasured her testimony: how in that last illness she folded her tenderness into my acts of care and called me her devoted son, remembering with great love that she had never once heard from my mouth a hard or contemptuous word thrown at her. And yet, my God, who made us — what possible comparison is there between the honor I paid her and the slavery she served for me? So, because I was left stripped of so great a comfort, my soul was wounded, and my life torn apart — the life that had been made one life out of hers and mine.

What, then, was it that hurt me so grievously within, but the fresh wound made by the sudden tearing-apart of that sweetest and dearest habit of living together? I rejoiced indeed in her testimony, when, in that last sickness, mingling her endearments with my dutiful care, she called me "dutiful," and said, with great affection, that she had never heard a single harsh or reproachful word come from my mouth against her. And yet, O my God, who made us, what comparison could there be between the honor I paid her and her servitude to me? Being then bereft of so great a comfort in her, my soul was wounded, and that life of ours was torn apart, the life that had been made one out of hers and mine together.

When the boy had been quieted, Euodius picked up the psalter and began to sing — the whole household answering him — the psalm: Of mercy and judgment I will sing to you, Lord. And hearing what was happening, many brothers and devout women gathered; and while those whose duty it was prepared the burial in the usual way, I withdrew to a part of the house where I decently could, with those who thought I should not be left alone, and talked about something suited to the hour. With that balm of truth I eased a torment known to you — they did not know it; they listened intently, and supposed I felt no grief at all. But in your ears, where none of them could hear, I was rebuking the softness of my own feeling and holding back the flood of sorrow. It gave way to me a little; then it came on again in its own surge — never as far as tears, never as far as a change of face — but I knew what I was pressing down in my heart. And because it upset me deeply that these human things had such power over me — things which, in the due order of nature and the lot we are dealt, must come to pass — I grieved over my grief with another grief, and was worn down by a double sorrow.

When the boy had been quieted from weeping, Euodius took up the Psalter and began to sing — our whole house answering him — the Psalm, I will sing to you, O Lord, of mercy and judgment. And when they heard what we were doing, many of the brothers and the religious women gathered; and while those whose office it was made ready for the burial, as the custom is, I, in another part of the house where I might fittingly do so, talked with those who thought it not right to leave me alone, on a subject suited to the time; and with this balm of truth I eased the torment that you knew of, and they did not, as they listened intently, supposing that I was without any feeling of grief at all. But in your ears, where none of them could hear, I blamed the weakness of my feeling, and held back the flood of grief; and it gave way to me a little, but then came surging back like a tide — yet not so as to burst into tears, nor to change my face. Still I knew what I was holding down in my heart. And being very much displeased that these human things had such power over me, things that in the due order and appointment of our condition must of necessity come to pass, I grieved over my grief with a fresh grief, and so was worn down by a double sorrow.

And then the body was carried out. We went; we came back; without tears. Even during the prayers we poured out to you while the sacrifice of our redemption was offered for her — the body resting beside the grave before being laid in, as the custom there is — even during those prayers I did not weep. But all that day I was heavy with a secret sadness, and with a mind in turmoil I begged you, as well as I could, to heal my pain. You did not. I think you were fixing in my memory, by this one lesson, how strong the chain of habit is, even on a mind that no longer feeds on lying words. It also seemed good to me to go and bathe, because I had heard that the bath got its name — balneum, from the Greek balaneion — because it drives anxiety out of the mind. And this too I confess to your mercy, Father of the fatherless: I bathed, and I was exactly the man I had been before I bathed. The bitterness of grief did not sweat out of my heart. Then I slept; and I woke; and I found my sorrow softened, more than a little. And lying alone in my bed, I remembered the true verses of your Ambrose. For you are —

And look — the body was carried out to burial, and we went and came back without tears. Not even in the prayers we poured out to you, when the Sacrifice of our ransom was offered for her, the body now set beside the grave before being laid in it, as the custom there is — not even during those prayers did I weep. Yet the whole day long I was secretly and heavily sad, and with a troubled mind I begged you, as best I could, to heal my sorrow; and you did not — impressing on my memory, I believe, by this one instance, how strong is the grip of every habit, even upon a soul that now feeds on no deceiving word. It seemed good to me, too, to go and bathe, having heard that the bath got its name — the Greek word for it — because it drives anxiety from the mind. And this also I confess to your mercy, Father of the fatherless: I bathed, and I was the same after as before. For the bitterness of my sorrow could not be sweated out of my heart. Then I slept, and woke again, and found my grief somewhat softened; and as I lay alone on my bed, I remembered those true verses of your Ambrose. For you are:

"God, creator of all things, ruler of the sky: you clothe the day in beautiful light, the night in the grace of sleep, so that rest may hand our slackened limbs back to the use of work, and lift up minds when they are tired, and loosen the knots of anxious grief."

Maker of all, the Lord, and Ruler of the height, who, robing the day in light, have poured soft slumbers over the night, that to our limbs the power of toil may be renewed, and weary hearts be lifted that sink and cower, and sorrows be subdued.

And then, little by little, I began to recover my old sense of your handmaid: her devout walk with you; her holy gentleness and patience with us — all of it suddenly gone from me. And I wanted to weep in your sight, about her and for her, about myself and for myself. And I let go of the tears I had been holding in — let them flow as freely as they wanted, spreading them like a bed under my heart. And my heart rested on them, because the ears there were yours — not the ears of some man who would have read my weeping with contempt. And now, Lord, I confess it to you in writing. Let anyone read it who wants to, and make of it what he will; and if he finds it a sin that I wept for my mother for a small fraction of an hour — the mother who was, for that hour, dead to my eyes, and who for so many years had wept for me, that I might live in yours — let him not sneer. Rather, if his charity is large, let him weep for my sins himself, to you: the Father of all the brothers of your Christ.

And then, little by little, I came back to my old thoughts of your handmaid, her holy life toward you, her holy tenderness and attentiveness toward us, of which I was so suddenly deprived. And I longed to weep in your sight, for her and for myself, on her behalf and on my own. And I let go the tears I had been holding back, to flow as freely as they would, spreading them out as a bed for my heart, and on them it rested, for it was in your ears, not in those of men, who would have read my weeping with scorn. And now, Lord, in writing I confess it to you. Let him read it who will, and interpret it how he will; and if he finds it a sin that I wept for my mother for one small fraction of an hour — the mother who for the time was dead to my eyes, who for so many years had wept for me that I might live in your eyes — let him not mock me, but rather, if he is a man of large charity, let him weep himself, for my sins, to you, the Father of all the brothers of your Christ.

But now, with a heart healed of that wound — in which there was perhaps too much of the flesh's affection to be blameless — I pour out to you, our God, on behalf of that servant of yours, a very different kind of tears: tears that flow from a spirit shaken by the thought of the danger facing every soul that dies in Adam. She had been made alive in Christ even before she was released from the flesh; she lived so that your name is praised in her faith and in her conduct. And yet I do not dare to say that from the moment you gave her rebirth in baptism, no word ever left her mouth that crossed your commandment. Your Son, the Truth, has said: whoever calls his brother a fool will answer for it in the fire of hell. And it would go badly even with the most praiseworthy human life, if you set mercy aside and examined it. But because you do not hunt our faults down ferociously, we hope with confidence for some place with you. And anyone who lists his real merits before you — what is he listing but your gifts? If only human beings would know themselves to be human — and let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.

But now, with a heart healed of that wound in which it might have seemed blameworthy for an earthly feeling, I pour out to you, our God, on behalf of that handmaid of yours, a far different kind of tears, flowing from a spirit shaken by the thought of the dangers that beset every soul that dies in Adam. For although she had been made alive in Christ even before she was released from the flesh, and had lived to the praise of your name in her faith and her conduct, yet I do not dare to say that from the time you reborn her in baptism, no word ever came from her mouth against your commandment. Your Son, the Truth, has said: Whoever shall say to his brother, You fool, shall be in danger of the fire of hell. And woe even to the praiseworthy life of men, if you should examine it with mercy laid aside! But because you are not strict to seek out our sins, we confidently hope to find some place with you. And whoever counts up his real merits to you, what is he counting up but your own gifts? Oh, that men would know themselves to be men, and that the one who boasts would boast in the Lord!

So I — my Praise and my Life, God of my heart — setting aside for this moment her good deeds, for which I give you thanks with joy, I now plead with you for my mother's sins. Hear me, I beg, through him who is the Medicine of our wounds, who hung on the tree, and who now, seated at your right hand, intercedes with you for us. I know she acted mercifully, and from her heart forgave her debtors their debts. Forgive her too her debts — whatever she contracted in all those years after the water of salvation. Forgive her, Lord; forgive, I beg you; do not enter into judgment with her. Let mercy triumph over judgment — for your words are true, and you have promised mercy to the merciful. That they are merciful at all was your gift: you, who will have mercy on whom you have mercy, and will show compassion to whom you have shown compassion.

And so, O my Praise and my Life, God of my heart, laying aside for a while her good deeds, for which I give you thanks with joy, I now beg you for the sins of my mother. Hear me, I entreat you, through the Medicine of our wounds, who hung upon the tree, and who now, seated at your right hand, makes intercession to you for us. I know that she dealt mercifully, and from her heart forgave her debtors their debts; forgive her too her debts, whatever she may have run up in all those years since the water of salvation. Forgive her, Lord, forgive, I beg you; do not enter into judgment with her. Let your mercy be lifted high above your justice, since your words are true, and you have promised mercy to the merciful — whom you made to be merciful, you who will have mercy on whom you will have mercy, and will have compassion on whom you have had compassion.

And I believe you have already done what I am asking — but accept, Lord, this willing offering of my mouth. As the day of her release drew near, she gave no thought to having her body wrapped in splendor or embalmed in spices; she craved no choice monument, and she no longer cared for a tomb in her own land. None of that did she charge us with. She wanted only this: to be remembered at your altar, which she had served without missing a single day — the altar from which she knew that holy Victim is dispensed by whom the writ of debt that stood against us was wiped out; by whom the enemy was triumphed over — the enemy who tallies our offenses, and hunts for something to charge us with, and finds nothing in him in whom we conquer. Who will pour back to him his innocent blood? Who will refund him the price he paid to buy us, and so take us away from him? To the sacrament of that price of ours, your handmaid bound her soul with the bond of faith. Let no one tear her from your protection. Let neither the lion nor the dragon put himself in her way, by force or by fraud. For she will not answer that she owes nothing — she would be convicted and seized by that cunning prosecutor. She will answer that her debts were forgiven by him to whom no one can repay the price that he, owing nothing, paid for us.

And I believe you have already done what I ask; but accept, O Lord, the free offerings of my mouth. For when the day of her dissolution was now at hand, she took no thought to have her body sumptuously wrapped, or embalmed with spices, nor did she long for a choice monument, or to be buried in her own land. None of this did she charge us with. She desired only that her name be remembered at your altar, which she had served without missing a single day, knowing that from it the holy Sacrifice is dispensed, by which the bond that stood against us is canceled — the Sacrifice through which the enemy was conquered, who, reckoning up our offenses and looking for something to charge us with, found nothing in him in whom we conquer. Who shall give him back the innocent blood? Who shall repay him the price with which he bought us, and so take us away from him? To the Sacrament of this our ransom your handmaid bound her soul by the bond of faith. Let no one tear her away from your protection; let neither the lion nor the dragon come between, by force or by craft. For she will not answer that she owes nothing, lest she be caught out and seized by the cunning accuser; but she will answer that her debts are forgiven her by him to whom no one can repay that price which he, who owed nothing, paid for us.

Let her rest, then, in peace, with the husband before whom and after whom she had no other; whom she served, bringing forth fruit for you with patience, so that she might win him too for you. And inspire, Lord my God — inspire your servants my brothers, your sons my masters, whom I serve with voice and heart and pen — that as many as read these confessions may remember at your altar Monica, your servant, together with Patricius, once her husband, through whose flesh you brought me into this life, how, I do not know. Let them remember with devout affection my parents in this passing light, and my brothers and sisters under you, our Father, within our Catholic mother; and my fellow citizens in the eternal Jerusalem, which your pilgrim people sighs for from its going out until its coming home — so that my mother's last request of me may be granted her more richly through the prayers of many, called up by these confessions, than through my prayers alone.

May she rest, then, in peace with her husband — before whom and after whom she had no other — whom she obeyed, with patience bringing forth fruit to you, that she might win him too for you. And inspire, O Lord my God, inspire your servants my brothers, your sons my masters, whom I serve with voice and heart and pen, that as many of them as read these confessions may remember at your altar Monica, your handmaid, together with Patricius, her husband of old, through whose bodies you brought me into this life, though how I do not know. May they remember with devout affection those who were my parents in this passing light, and my brothers under you, our Father, in our Catholic Mother, and my fellow citizens in that eternal Jerusalem for which your pilgrim people sighs from their setting out until their return. So shall my mother's last request of me be more abundantly fulfilled for her, through the prayers of many, by means of my confessions even more than by my prayers.

sections.label: Book X
sections.title: The palaces of memory
Memory, and Late Have I Loved You

segments.text: Let me know you, Lord — you who know me. Let me know you as I am fully known. Strength of my soul, enter it and shape it to yourself, so that you can have and hold it without spot or wrinkle. This is my hope; that is why I am speaking, and in this hope I rejoice, whenever my joy is a healthy joy. As for the other things of this life — the more we weep over them, the less they deserve our tears; and the more they deserve our tears, the less we weep. Look: you love the truth, and the one who does the truth comes to the light. I want to do the truth — in my heart, before you, in confession; and in this writing, before many witnesses.

Let me know you, O Lord, you who know me; let me know you, as I am known. Power of my soul, enter into it, and fit it to yourself, that you may have it and hold it without spot or wrinkle. This is my hope, and so I speak; and in this hope I rejoice, whenever I rejoice as I should. As for the other things of this life, the more we grieve over them, the less they deserve our grief; and the less we grieve, the more they deserve it. For look, you love the truth, and whoever does the truth comes into the light. This I would do, in my heart, before you, in confession; and in my writing, before many witnesses.

And from you, Lord, before whose eyes the pit of human conscience lies naked, what could stay hidden in me even if I refused to confess it? I would be hiding you from myself, not myself from you. But now — my groaning is the proof that I am sick of what I am — you shine out, and you please me, and I love and long for you; so that I blush at myself, and throw my old self away, and choose you, and please neither you nor myself except in you. To you, then, Lord, I lie open, whatever I am. What I gain by confessing to you, I have said already. And I do not make the confession with the body's words and sounds, but with the soul's words, with the shout of my thinking, which your ear knows. When I am evil, confessing to you is nothing but being displeased with myself; when I am good, confessing to you is nothing but refusing to take the credit — because you, Lord, bless the righteous, but first you take the unrighteous and make them righteous. So my confession, my God, is made in your sight silently — and not silently. In sound it is silent; in feeling it cries out. For I never say a true word to other people that you have not heard from me first, and you never hear such a word from me that you have not first said to me.

And from you, O Lord, to whose eyes the depths of a man's conscience lie bare, what could be hidden in me, even if I refused to confess it? I would be hiding you from myself, not myself from you. But now, since my groaning bears witness that I am displeased with myself, you shine out, and are pleasing, and beloved, and longed for, so that I am ashamed of myself, and turn away from myself, and choose you, and please neither you nor myself except in you. To you, then, O Lord, I lie open, whatever I am; and with what gain I confess to you, I have already said. I do it not with the words and sounds of the body, but with the words of my soul and the cry of my thought, which your ear knows. For when I am evil, to confess to you is nothing but to be displeased with myself; and when I am good, it is nothing but to claim no credit for myself, since you, O Lord, bless the godly, but first you make him godly when he was ungodly. So my confession, O my God, is made in your sight silently, and not silently. In sound it is silent; in feeling it cries aloud. For I say nothing right to other people that you have not already heard from me, nor do you hear anything from me that you have not first said to me.

Then what do other people have to do with it? Why should they hear my confessions, as though they were going to heal everything that is sick in me? A curious breed, eager to know someone else's life, lazy about mending their own. Why do they want to hear from me what I am, when they refuse to hear from you what they are? And when they hear me talk about myself, how do they know I am telling the truth, since no one knows what goes on in a person except that person's own spirit within? But if they heard from you about themselves, they could not say, “The Lord is lying.” For what is hearing from you about themselves except coming to know themselves? And who can come to know a thing and say, “It is false,” unless he himself is lying? But because love believes all things — at least among those it binds together into one — I too, Lord, will confess to you in such a way that people can hear it, though I cannot prove to them that my confession is true. Those whose ears love opens to me — they will believe me.

What, then, have I to do with other people, that they should hear my confessions, as if they could heal all my diseases — a race curious to pry into the lives of others, and slow to mend their own? Why do they want to hear from me what I am, when they will not hear from you what they themselves are? And when they hear about me from me, how do they know whether I tell the truth, since no one knows what is in a man but the spirit of the man that is in him? But if they were to hear from you about themselves, they could not say, "The Lord is lying." For what is it to hear from you about themselves but to know themselves? And who knows himself and says, "It is false," unless he himself is lying? But because love believes all things — among those at least whom it binds to itself and makes one — I too, O Lord, will so confess to you that other people may hear, people to whom I cannot prove that I confess the truth; yet they believe me, those whose ears love opens to me.

But you, physician of my inmost self, make clear to me what good comes of doing this. When the confessions of my past sins — sins you have forgiven and covered over, to make me blessed in you, remaking my soul by faith and by your sacrament — when those confessions are read and heard, they rouse the heart out of the sleep of despair, out of saying “I can't,” and wake it in the love of your mercy and the sweetness of your grace — the grace by which every weak person is made strong, once it brings home to him his own weakness. And good people love to hear about the past sins of those who are rid of them now: not because the sins are evils, but because they were, and are no more. So with what profit, my Lord and God — you to whom my conscience confesses every day, more secure in the hope of your mercy than in its own innocence — with what profit, I ask, do I confess in this book, before you and before other people too, not what I was, but what I am now? The profit of the first kind I have seen and described. But what I am now, right now, in the very moment of these confessions — this is what many want to know: people who have known me and people who have not, who have heard something from me or about me. Their ear is not pressed to my heart, where I am whatever I am. So they want to hear me confess what I am inside, where neither their eye nor their ear nor their mind can reach; and they are ready to believe it — but will they know it? Love, which makes them good, tells them I am not lying about myself; and the love in them believes me.

But you, my inmost Physician, make plain to me what good I may gain by doing this. For the confessions of my past sins — which you have forgiven and covered over, that you might make me blessed in you, changing my soul by faith and by your sacrament — when they are read and heard, they stir up the heart, so that it does not sleep in despair and say, "I cannot," but wakes in the love of your mercy and the sweetness of your grace, by which whoever is weak is made strong, once through that grace he has come to know his own weakness. And the good love to hear of the past evils of those who are now free of them — not because the evils are evils, but because they once were and now are no longer. With what gain, then, O Lord my God, to whom my conscience makes its confession daily, trusting more in the hope of your mercy than in its own innocence — with what gain, I ask, do I, by this book, confess to other people as well, in your presence, what I now am, not what I have been? That other gain I have seen and spoken of. But what I now am, at this very moment of confessing, many wish to know, whether they have known me or not, who have heard from me or about me; but their ear is not at my heart, where I am, whatever I am. They wish to hear me confess what I am within, where their eye and ear and understanding cannot reach. They wish it, ready to believe — but will they truly know? For love, by which they are good, tells them that in my confessions I am not lying, and that same love in them believes me.

But what do they gain by hearing it? Do they want to celebrate with me, when they hear how near to you I have come by your gift — and to pray for me, when they hear how far I am dragged back by my own weight? To people like that I will show myself. It is no small profit, my Lord and God, if thanks are offered to you by many on our account, and many plead with you for us. Let a brother's mind love in me what you teach is worth loving, and grieve in me what you teach is worth grieving. Let it be a brother's mind that does this — not an outsider's, not the minds of those alien children whose mouths speak emptiness and whose right hand is a right hand of fraud — but a brother's mind, which rejoices over me when it approves of me and grieves over me when it does not, because approving or not, it loves me. To such people I will show myself. Let them breathe easy at my good and sigh at my evil. My good deeds are your arrangements and your gifts; my evil ones are my own faults and your judgments. Let them breathe easy at the one and sigh at the other, and let hymn and weeping rise together into your sight from my brothers' hearts, your censers. And you, Lord, delighting in the incense of your holy temple — have mercy on me according to your great mercy, for your own name's sake; and since you never abandon what you have begun, complete what is incomplete in me.

But for what gain would they want to hear this? Do they wish to rejoice with me, when they hear how near, by your gift, I come to you, and to pray for me, when they hear how much I am held back by my own weight? To such people I will reveal myself. For it is no small gain, O Lord my God, that thanks should be given to you by many on our behalf, and that you should be entreated by many for us. Let the brotherly mind love in me what you teach it to love, and lament in me what you teach it to lament. Let it be a brotherly mind that does this, not a stranger's — not the mind of those alien children whose mouth speaks emptiness and whose right hand is a right hand of falsehood — but the brotherly mind that, when it approves of me, rejoices for me, and when it disapproves, is sorry for me; because whether it approves or disapproves, it loves me. To such I will reveal myself; they will breathe easier at my good deeds and sigh over my bad ones. My good deeds are your doing and your gifts; my bad ones are my offenses and your judgments. Let them breathe easier at the one and sigh over the other; and let hymns and weeping rise into your sight out of the hearts of my brothers, your censers. And you, O Lord, be pleased with the incense of your holy temple; have mercy on me according to your great mercy, for your own name's sake; and never forsaking what you have begun, complete what is unfinished in me.

This is the profit of confessing not what I was, but what I am: to confess it not only before you, in a hidden gladness with trembling and a hidden sorrow with hope, but in the ears of the believing children of men as well — companions in my joy and sharers in my mortality, my fellow citizens, fellow pilgrims with me: those who went ahead, those who will follow, those walking beside me on the road. They are your servants and my brothers, whom you have willed to be your sons — my masters, whom you have commanded me to serve if I want to live with you and from you. And this word of yours would be a small thing if it only gave the command and did not lead the way in doing it. So I do the same, in deed and in word; I do it under your wings — and the danger would be far too great, if my soul were not sheltered under your wings and my weakness known to you. I am a small child, but my Father lives forever, and my protector is enough for me. For he who begot me is the same one who keeps me safe; you yourself are all my good — you, the Almighty, who are with me even before I am with you. To those you command me to serve, then, I will show not what I was, but what I am now, and what I still am. But I do not even judge myself. This is how I want to be heard.

This is the gain of confessing what I am, not only what I have been: to confess it not before you alone, in a hidden joy mixed with trembling and a hidden sorrow mixed with hope, but also in the ears of the believing children of men, sharers in my joy and partners in my mortality, my fellow citizens and fellow pilgrims, those who have gone before and those who are to follow, companions on my road. These are your servants, my brothers, whom you have willed to be your sons, my masters, whom you command me to serve, if I would live with you and from you. But this word of yours would have been small, had it only commanded by speaking and not gone before by doing. This, then, I do in deed and in word; this I do under your wings — in too great a danger, were not my soul subdued to you under your wings, and my weakness known to you. I am a little one, but my Father lives forever, and my Guardian is enough for me. For he is the same who begot me and who defends me; and you yourself are all my good, you, the Almighty, who are with me before I am with you. To such people, then, whom you command me to serve, I will reveal not what I have been, but what I now am and what I still am. But neither do I pass judgment on myself. In this way, then, let me be heard.

For you, Lord, are the one who judges me. No one knows what is in a person except the person's own spirit within him — and yet there is something in a person that even his own spirit does not know. But you, Lord, know everything about him, for you made him. As for me: though in your sight I despise myself and count myself dust and ashes, I know something about you that I do not know about myself. Truly, we see now through a glass, darkly — not yet face to face. So as long as I am journeying away from you, I am more present to myself than to you; and yet I know that you can in no way be violated, while I do not know which temptations I can withstand and which I cannot. And there is hope, because you are faithful: you do not let us be tempted beyond what we can bear, but with the temptation you make a way out as well, so that we can stand it. So let me confess what I know of myself, and confess too what I do not know — because even what I know of myself I know only because you shine on me, and what I do not know I will not know until my darkness turns to noon before your face.

For you, Lord, are the one who judges me; because, although no one knows the things of a man but the spirit of a man that is in him, yet there is something of a man that not even the spirit of the man that is in him knows. But you, Lord, know everything in him, you who made him. As for me, though in your sight I despise myself and reckon myself dust and ashes, yet I know something of you that I do not know of myself. Truly, now we see through a glass, darkly, not yet face to face. So as long as I am away from you, I am more present to myself than to you; and yet I know that you cannot suffer any harm, while I do not know which temptations I can resist and which I cannot. But there is hope, because you are faithful, you who will not let us be tempted beyond our strength, but with the temptation will also make a way of escape, that we may be able to bear it. I will confess, then, what I know of myself; I will confess also what I do not know of myself. For what I do know of myself, I know by your shining upon me; and what I do not know of myself, I do not know until my darkness is made like noonday before your face.

Not with a wavering but with a settled certainty, Lord, I love you. You struck my heart with your word, and I loved you. And heaven and earth and everything in them — look, from every side they tell me to love you, and they never stop telling everyone, so that no one has an excuse. But deeper than that: you will have mercy on whom you will have mercy, and show compassion to whom you will show compassion — otherwise heaven and earth are singing your praises to the deaf. And what do I love when I love you? Not the beauty of a body, not the glory of a season, not the brightness of light — so kind to these eyes — not the sweet melodies of every kind of song, not the fragrance of flowers and oils and spices, not manna or honey, not limbs that welcome the body's embrace. These are not what I love when I love my God. And yet I do love a kind of light, a kind of voice, a kind of fragrance, a kind of food, a kind of embrace when I love my God: light, voice, fragrance, food, embrace of the self inside me — where a light shines into my soul that no place can hold, where a voice sounds that time cannot snatch away, where a fragrance drifts that no wind can scatter, where a flavor stays that no eating makes less, where a closeness holds that no having-enough can pull apart. This is what I love when I love my God.

It is not with doubt, but with sure knowledge, that I love you, Lord. You struck my heart with your word, and I loved you. Heaven and earth too, and all that is in them — look, on every side they tell me to love you, and they never stop telling everyone, so that no one has any excuse. But, more deeply, you will have mercy on whom you will have mercy, and will have compassion on whom you have had compassion; otherwise heaven and earth speak your praises to deaf ears. But what do I love when I love you? Not the beauty of any body, nor the rhythm of passing time, nor the brightness of light, so dear to these eyes, nor the sweet melodies of every kind of song, nor the fragrance of flowers and ointments and spices, not manna and honey, not the limbs that the body delights to embrace. None of these do I love when I love my God. And yet there is a kind of light I love, and a kind of voice, and a fragrance, and a food, and an embrace, when I love my God — the light, the voice, the fragrance, the food, the embrace of my inner self, where there shines into my soul a light no space can hold, and there sounds what no time carries off, and there breathes a fragrance no wind scatters, and there is a taste that no eating lessens, and there clings a closeness that no fullness pulls apart. This is what I love when I love my God.

And what is this? I asked the earth, and it said, “I am not he,” and everything in it confessed the same. I asked the sea and the deeps and the creatures that crawl and swim, and they answered, “We are not your God. Look above us.” I asked the blowing winds, and the whole air with all its inhabitants answered, “Anaximenes was wrong. I am not God.” I asked the sky, the sun, the moon, the stars: “Neither are we,” they said, “the God you are looking for.” And I said to all these things standing around the doors of my flesh, “Tell me about my God — you who are not he — tell me something about him.” And they cried out with a great voice: “He made us.” My question was my gazing at them; their answer was their beauty. Then I turned toward myself and said to myself, “And you — who are you?” And I answered: “A man.” Here at my disposal are body and soul, one outside, one within. Which of these should I have used to look for my God? I had already searched for him with the body, from earth to sky, as far as I could send the rays of my eyes out as messengers. But the inner one is better. All the body's messengers report back to it; it presides and judges over the answers of sky and earth and everything in them, all of them saying, “We are not God,” and, “He made us.” The inner self knows these things through the service of the outer self. I, the one within, knew them — I, the mind, through my body's senses. I asked the whole huge frame of the world about my God, and it answered me: “I am not he, but he made me.”

And what is this? I asked the earth, and it answered, "I am not he"; and everything in it confessed the same. I asked the sea and the deeps and the living, crawling things, and they answered, "We are not your God; look above us." I asked the gusting air, and the whole air with all that lives in it answered, "Anaximenes was wrong; I am not God." I asked the heavens, the sun, the moon, the stars: "Neither are we," they said, "the God you are looking for." And I said to all these things that crowd at the gateways of my flesh: "You have told me about my God, that you are not he; tell me something about him." And they cried out with a great voice, "He made us." My questioning of them was simply my attending to them, and their beauty was their answer. And I turned to myself and said, "Who are you?" And I answered, "A man." And here, present to me, are body and soul, the one outside, the other within. Through which of these should I seek my God? I had already sought him in the body, from earth up to heaven, as far as I could send the rays of my eyes for messengers. But the inner part is the better, for to it, as ruler and judge, all the bodily messengers brought back the answers of heaven and earth and all that is in them, who said, "We are not God, but he made us." These things my inner self came to know through the service of the outer; I, the inner self, knew them, I, the mind, through the senses of my body. I asked the whole frame of the world about my God, and it answered me, "I am not he, but he made me."

Doesn't this beauty stand visible to everyone whose senses are sound? Then why doesn't it say the same thing to all? Animals small and great see it, but they cannot question it, because no reason has been set over their senses to judge what the senses report. Human beings can question it — so that the invisible things of God are seen and understood through the things he has made — but by loving those things they fall under them, and once under them, they can no longer judge. And the world does not answer its questioners unless they judge. It does not change its voice — that is, its look — appearing one way to this person who merely sees and another way to that person who sees and questions; it appears the same to both. But to one it is mute, and to the other it speaks. Or rather, it speaks to everyone, but only they understand who take its voice in from outside and compare it with the truth inside. For the truth tells me: your God is not heaven or earth or any body at all. Their own nature says it. Anyone can see: a body is a mass, smaller in the part than in the whole. Even you, my soul, are better than that — I am telling you — for you animate the mass of your body, giving it life, and no body can do that for a body. But your God is the life even of your life.

Is not this beauty of bodies plain to everyone whose senses are sound? Then why does it not say the same to all? Animals great and small see it, but they cannot question it, because no reason is set over their senses to judge what the senses report. But human beings can question it, so that, by the things that are made, they may clearly perceive the invisible things of God — though by loving those made things they make themselves subject to them, and subjects cannot judge. Nor do these things answer those who question them unless those who question can judge. Yet they do not change their appearance, showing one face to a man who only looks and another to a man who looks and questions, so as to seem one thing to this one and another to that; appearing the same to both, they are mute to one and eloquent to the other — or rather, they speak to all, but only those understand who compare the voice received from outside with the truth within. For truth tells me, "Neither heaven nor earth nor any other body is your God." Their very nature says this to whoever sees them: "We are a mass; a mass is less in a part than in the whole." Now to you I speak, O my soul, for you are my better part, since you give life to the whole mass of my body, breathing life into it, which no body can give to another body. But your God is, even for you, the Life of your life.

What then do I love when I love my God? Who is he, there above the summit of my soul? Through my soul itself I will climb up to him. I will pass beyond the power that fastens me to my body and fills its frame with life: that is not the power by which I could find my God. If it were, then the horse and the mule, which have no understanding, could find him too, since the same power gives life to their bodies as well. There is another power, by which I not only give life to the flesh the Lord fashioned for me but give it sense: ordering the eye not to hear and the ear not to see, but giving me the one to see through and the other to hear through, and to each of the other senses its own post and its own duty; and through all their different offices I act — I, the one mind. But I will pass beyond this power of mine as well, for the horse and the mule have this one too: they also perceive through the body.

What, then, do I love when I love my God? Who is he, high above the head of my soul? By my very soul I will climb up to him. I will pass beyond that power by which I am joined to my body and fill its whole frame with life. By that power I cannot find my God, for then the horse and the mule, which have no understanding, might find him too, since it is by the same power that even their bodies live. But there is another power, not only the one by which I give life, but the one by which I give feeling to my flesh, which the Lord has made for me, telling the eye not to hear and the ear not to see, but the eye that through it I should see, the ear that through it I should hear, and to the other senses, each in its place and office, their own work, which, though they differ, I, the one mind, carry out through them all. I will pass beyond this power of mine too; for the horse and the mule have it as well, since they too perceive through the body.

So I will pass beyond this power of my nature too, climbing step by step toward him who made me. And I come to the fields and vast palaces of memory, where the treasures of countless images are stored, carried in from everything the senses have perceived. There too is laid up all our thinking — whatever enlarges or shrinks or otherwise rearranges the things the senses touched — and everything else that has been handed over there for safekeeping, everything that forgetting has not yet swallowed and buried. When I am in there, I call for whatever I want brought out. Some things come at once. Some take longer, as if they were being fetched up from deeper vaults. Some come charging out in a mob, and while something else entirely is being asked for, they leap into the middle, as if to say, “Maybe you want us?” I wave them away from the face of my remembering with the hand of my heart, until the thing I want comes clear of the cloud and steps out of hiding into view. Other things come easily, in unbroken sequence, exactly as called for — each one in front giving way to the one behind, and giving way, sinking out of sight, ready to come again when I want it. All of which happens whenever I recite something by heart.

I will pass, then, beyond this power of my nature as well, rising by stages toward him who made me. And I come to the fields and vast palaces of memory, where lie the treasures of countless images, carried in from things of every kind that the senses have met. There is stored too whatever else we think out by enlarging or shrinking or in any way altering the things our senses have reached, and whatever else has been entrusted and laid up there that forgetting has not yet swallowed and buried. When I go in there, I call for whatever I want to be brought out, and some things come at once; others have to be sought longer, hauled as it were out of some deeper hiding place; others come rushing out in crowds, and while I am wanting and looking for one thing, they leap forward as if to say, "Maybe it's me?" These I drive away with the hand of my heart from the face of my remembering, until what I want is uncovered and steps out of its hiding place into view. Other things come up readily, in unbroken order, just as they are called for, the ones in front making way for those behind, and as they make way they sink out of sight, ready to come again when I will. All this happens whenever I recite anything from memory.

There everything is kept sorted by kind, each thing carried in through its own entrance: light and all colors and the shapes of bodies through the eyes; every sort of sound through the ears; every smell through the door of the nostrils; every taste through the door of the mouth; and by the sense that runs through the whole body, what is hard and what is soft, hot or cold, smooth or rough, heavy or light, outside the body or inside it. The great harbor of memory takes all of this in, in its countless secret, unmappable folds, to be brought out and reclaimed when needed — everything entering by its own gate and laid away. Not that the things themselves go in: only the images of the things perceived stand ready in there, for thought to recall. And who can say how these images were formed, even though it is plain which sense caught each one and stored it? Sitting in darkness and in silence, I can bring out colors in my memory if I like, and tell white from black and any shade from any other; sounds do not come barging in to disturb the picture my eyes drew in and I am now considering — though the sounds are there too, lying apart in their own storage, as it were. I can call for them as well, and they appear at once; and with my tongue still and my throat silent I sing as much as I please, and those images of color, present all the while, do not push in and interrupt while I am handling this other treasure, the one that flowed in through my ears. And so with everything else the other senses hauled in and piled up: I recall each one at will. I tell the breath of lilies from violets while smelling nothing. I prefer honey to sweet wine, smooth to rough, while tasting nothing, touching nothing — only remembering.

There everything is kept apart and under its own heading, each having entered by its own doorway: light and all colors and shapes of bodies by the eyes; every kind of sound by the ears; all smells by the doorway of the nostrils; all tastes by the mouth; and by the feeling of the whole body, what is hard or soft, hot or cold, smooth or rough, heavy or light, whether outside the body or within it. All these the great harbor of memory takes in, with its numberless secret and unspeakable folds and recesses, to be ready and brought out when needed, each entering by its own gate and there laid up. And yet the things themselves do not go in; only the images of the things perceived are there, ready for thought to recall. How those images are formed, who can say, though it is plain by which sense each was brought in and stored? For even while I sit in darkness and silence, I can bring out colors in my memory if I want, and tell black from white and any other shades I please; nor do sounds break in and disturb the image drawn in through my eyes, which I am going over, although they too are there, lying dormant, stored apart. For these too I call for, and at once they appear. And though my tongue is still and my throat silent, I can sing whatever I want; nor do those images of colors, which are nonetheless there, push in and interrupt when another store, the one that flowed in through the ears, is called for. So with the rest, heaped in and up by the other senses, which I recall at will. I tell the scent of lilies from violets, though I am smelling nothing; I prefer honey to sweet wine, smooth to rough, while at that moment I am neither tasting nor touching anything, but only remembering.

All this I do inside, in the enormous hall of my memory. There I have sky and earth and sea at hand, with everything I have ever perceived in them — except what I have forgotten. There I meet myself, too: I recall myself — what I did, when and where I did it, and how I felt while doing it. Everything is there that I remember, whether from my own experience or on someone else's word. And out of the same hoard I stitch together, over and over, new and ever newer likenesses of things I have experienced, or believed on the strength of experience, into what is past; and from these I spin out future actions, events, hopes — and I contemplate all of it, again, as present. “I will do this, and I will do that,” I say to myself, inside this huge inward space of my mind, crowded with the images of so many great things, “and this or that will follow.” “Oh, if only this would happen — or that!” “God keep this away — and that!” I say these things to myself, and as I say them, the images of everything I name stand by, out of the same treasury of memory. If they were missing, I could say none of it at all.

All this I do within, in that vast court of my memory. For there are present to me heaven, earth, sea, and whatever I can think of in them, besides what I have forgotten. There too I meet myself, and recall myself, and what I have done, and when and where, and with what feelings I did it. There is everything I remember, whether from my own experience or on the word of others. Out of the same store I myself draw out, and combine with the past, fresh and fresh likenesses of things I have experienced or, from what I have experienced, have believed; and from these in turn I work out future actions and events and hopes, and all of these I think over again, as if present. "I will do this or that," I say to myself, in that great chamber of my mind, stocked with the images of so many and such great things, "and this or that will follow." "O that this or that might be!" "God forbid this or that!" So I speak to myself, and when I speak, the images of everything I speak of are present, drawn from the same storehouse of memory; nor could I speak of any of them at all, if the images were missing.

Great is this power of memory — immensely great, my God: a vast, unbounded inner chamber. Who has ever touched its floor? And yet this is a power of my own mind, and belongs to my nature — and I myself cannot hold all that I am. So the mind is too narrow to contain itself. Then where does the part it doesn't contain go? Outside itself rather than in itself? Then how is it not contained? Wonder rises up in me at this; astonishment takes hold of me. And people go traveling to marvel at the heights of mountains, the enormous waves of the sea, the broad falls of rivers, the circuit of the ocean, the wheeling of stars — and pass themselves by without a second look. It does not amaze them that while I was naming all those things I was not seeing them with my eyes; and yet I could not have named them unless I were seeing, inwardly, in my memory, the mountains and waves and rivers and stars I have seen, and the ocean I take on trust — and seeing them at the same enormous scale as if I were looking at them outside. But I did not swallow them into myself by looking at them when I saw them with my eyes. It is not the things that are in me, but their images. And I know which sense of my body impressed each one.

Great is this power of memory, exceedingly great, O my God, a vast and boundless inner room. Who has ever reached its bottom? Yet this is a power of my mind and belongs to my nature, and I myself cannot grasp all that I am. Then is the mind too narrow to hold itself? And where can that part be which it does not hold? Is it outside it, and not within? How, then, does it not hold itself? Enormous wonder rises in me at this; amazement seizes me. And people go off to marvel at the heights of mountains, the huge waves of the sea, the broad currents of rivers, the reach of the ocean, and the circling of the stars — and they pass themselves by, and do not marvel that, while I was speaking of all these things, I did not see them with my eyes, and yet could not have spoken of them unless I were inwardly seeing, in my memory, those mountains and waves and rivers and stars that I have seen, and that ocean which I take on trust, and seeing them with the same vast distances between them as if I were looking at them out in the world. Yet I did not draw them into myself by seeing them, when with my eyes I beheld them; they themselves are not within me, only their images. And I know by which sense of the body each was stamped on me.

And even these are not all that the immeasurable capacity of my memory carries. Here too is everything from the liberal arts that I have learned and not yet forgotten, set back somewhere further in — in a place that is not a place. And here it is not images I carry, but the things themselves. What grammar is, what skill in debate is, how many kinds of questions there are — whatever I know of such things is in my memory in a peculiar way: not as an image left behind while the thing stays outside; not like a voice that sounded and faded, leaving a trace through the ears by which it can be replayed as if it were sounding when it sounds no more; not like a smell that passes and thins into the wind, brushing the nostrils and dispatching an image of itself into memory, which remembering renews; not like food, which has no taste at all once in the belly and yet still tastes, in a fashion, in memory; not like anything the body feels by touch, which memory can still shape once the thing is far away. None of these things is taken into memory. Only their images are seized, with astonishing speed, laid away in astonishing storerooms, and by remembering — astonishingly — brought out.

And yet it is not only these that the unmeasured capacity of my memory holds. Here too is everything I have learned of the liberal arts and not yet forgotten, withdrawn as it were to some inner place that is no place; and it is not the images of these that I hold, but the things themselves. For what literature is, what the art of debate is, how many kinds of questions there are — whatever of this I know exists in my memory in such a way that I have not taken in an image and left out the thing. It is not as if a sound had echoed and passed away, leaving its print on the ear so that it could be recalled as though still sounding when it sounds no longer; nor as a smell, while it passes and vanishes into the air, stirs the sense of smell and from there sends an image of itself into the memory, which we renew by remembering; nor as food, which has no taste left in the belly and yet in a way still tastes in the memory; nor as anything the body perceives by touch and which the memory still pictures when it has been taken away from us. For these things are not carried into the memory; only their images are caught up, with wonderful swiftness, and stored as in marvelous compartments, and from there wonderfully brought out again by the act of remembering.

But when I hear that there are three kinds of questions — whether a thing is, what it is, and what kind it is — I hold the images of the sounds those words are made of, and I know the sounds crossed the air with a noise and now no longer exist. But the things themselves that the sounds signify, I never touched with any sense of my body, never glimpsed anywhere but in my mind — and what I laid up in memory was not their images but the things themselves. Let them tell me, if they can, how they got in. I go around all the doorways of my flesh and find none they could have entered by. The eyes say, “If they had color, we announced them.” The ears say, “If they made a sound, we reported it.” The nostrils say, “If they had a smell, they came through us.” The sense of taste says, “If there was no flavor, don't ask me.” Touch says, “If it wasn't a body, I never handled it; and if I never handled it, I never gave word of it.” Then where did these things come from? How did they get into my memory? I do not know. When I learned them, I was not trusting another mind's word for them: I recognized them in my own, approved them as true, and gave them into its keeping, setting them where I could bring them out whenever I wished. So they were there even before I learned them — but not in my memory. Where, then? And why did I recognize them when they were spoken, and say, “That's it — that's true,” unless they were already in my memory, but so far back, so buried in its deepest recesses, that if someone had not prodded them up I might never have been able to think them at all?

But now, when I hear that there are three kinds of question — whether a thing is, what it is, of what sort it is — I do hold the images of the sounds of which those words are made, and I know that those sounds passed with a noise through the air and now are gone. But the things themselves, which those sounds signify, I never reached with any bodily sense, nor ever perceived anywhere but in my mind; and yet it is not their images that I have stored in my memory, but the things themselves. How they got into me, let them say if they can; for I have gone over all the gateways of my flesh and cannot find by which they entered. For the eyes say, "If they had color, we reported them." The ears say, "If they made a sound, we gave word of them." The nostrils say, "If they had a smell, they passed by us." The taste says, "Unless they had a flavor, do not ask me." The touch says, "If it had no size, I did not handle it, and if I did not handle it, I gave no notice of it." From where, then, and how did these things enter my memory? I do not know how. For when I learned them, I did not trust another man's mind, but recognized them in my own; and approving them as true, I entrusted them to my mind, laying them up as if where I might bring them out when I wished. So they were in me even before I learned them, but they were not in my memory. Where, then? And why, when they were spoken, did I recognize them and say, "So it is, it is true," unless they were already in the memory, but so pushed back and buried in its deeper recesses that, had not someone else's prompting drawn them out, I might never have been able to think of them at all?

So we find that learning things like these — things whose images we do not drink in through the senses, but which we perceive within, by themselves, as they are, without images — amounts to just this: by thinking, we gather up what memory held here and there and in no order, and by attending we see to it that these things are set, so to speak, within easy reach in the same memory where they had lain scattered and ignored — so that now they come readily to a mind grown familiar with them. And how many things of this kind my memory carries — things already found and set within reach, things we are said to have learned and to know! If I stop revisiting them for even a short stretch of time, down they sink again, gliding off into the deeper recesses, and they have to be thought out again, as good as new, from the same place — there is no other home for them — and rounded up again so they can be known. In other words, they have to be collected out of their scattering. Hence the Latin word for thinking, cogitation: cogo — I gather — stands to cogito — I keep gathering — as ago stands to agito, as facio to factito. But the mind has claimed this word as its own: what is collected — that is, pulled together — in the mind, and nowhere but the mind, is what we properly say is cogitated: thought.

And so we find that to learn these things — the ones whose images we do not drink in through the senses, but perceive within, in themselves, without images, as they are — is nothing but to gather up, by thinking, and by careful attention to set ready at hand, as it were, those things which the memory already held scattered and unsorted, so that, now placed where before they lay unknown, neglected, and dispersed, they readily come to a mind grown familiar with them. How many things of this kind my memory carries, things already found out and, as I said, set ready at hand, which we are said to have learned and come to know — and if for some short stretch of time I stop calling them to mind, they sink again and slip back into the deeper recesses, so that they must be thought out again from there, as if new, for they have no other home, and must be gathered together once more in order to be known. That is, they must be collected, as it were, out of their scattering; from which the word cogitation, thinking-together, comes. For cogo, to collect, and cogito, to re-collect, stand to each other as ago and agito, facio and factito. But the mind has claimed this word for itself, so that not whatever is collected anyhow, but only what is re-collected, that is, gathered together, in the mind, is properly said to be thought.

The memory also holds the relations and laws of numbers and dimensions, past counting — and none of them was stamped in by any bodily sense, for they have no color, no sound, no smell, no taste, no feel. I have heard the sounds of the words that name them when they are discussed, but the sounds are one thing and the things another: the sounds are different in Greek than in Latin, but the things are not Greek or Latin or any tongue at all. I have seen the lines architects draw, fine as a thread of spider's silk; but the lines themselves are something else — not images of the ones my body's eye showed me. Whoever knows them, knows them inside himself, without any thought of a body of any kind. I have perceived with every sense of my body the numbers of the things we count; but the numbers we count with are something else again. They are not images of the counted things; they simply, and in their own right, are. Let whoever cannot see them laugh at me for saying so; and while he laughs at me, I will feel sorry for him.

The memory also holds the countless reasonings and laws of numbers and measurements, none of which any bodily sense has stamped on it, since they have neither color nor sound nor taste nor smell nor touch. I have heard the sounds of the words by which they are named when we discuss them; but the sounds are one thing, the things another. For the sounds are different in Greek and in Latin, but the things are neither Greek nor Latin nor any other language. I have seen the lines drawn by architects, fine as a spider's thread; but those mathematical lines are still something else, they are not the images of the lines my bodily eye showed me; whoever recognizes them within himself, without thinking of any body at all, knows them. I have perceived too the numbers we count with in all the senses of my body; but the numbers by which we count are different, and are not the images of those, and therefore they truly are. Let the man who does not see them laugh at me for saying these things, and I will pity him, while he laughs at me.

All these things I hold in memory, and how I learned them I hold in memory too. And I have heard, and hold in memory, many arguments falsely urged against them — false arguments, but my remembering of them is not false; and I remember, further, that I have told the true apart from the false, and I see that telling them apart now is a different thing from remembering that I told them apart often before, each time I thought them over.
