I resist the seductions of the eyes, so that these feet that walk your road are not snared; and I raise invisible eyes to you, asking you to pull my feet out of the snare. Again and again you pull them free, for again and again they are snared. You never stop pulling them out, while I keep catching fast in the traps laid on every side — because you who keep Israel will neither slumber nor sleep.

O Light, which Tobias saw when, with these eyes closed, he taught his son the way of life, and himself went before him with the feet of charity, never straying; or which Isaac saw, when his fleshly eyes, heavy and closed by old age, were granted the grace, unknowingly, to bless his sons, but by blessing to know them; or which Jacob saw, when he too, blind through great age, with an enlightened heart shed light, in the persons of his sons, on the future tribes of his people foreshadowed in them, and laid his hands, mystically crossed, on his grandsons by Joseph — not as their father by his outward eye corrected him, but as he himself inwardly discerned! This is the light; it is one, and all are one who see and love it. But that bodily light of which I spoke seasons the life of this world for its blind lovers with an enticing and dangerous sweetness. But those who know how to praise you for it — O God, Creator of all — take it up into your hymns, and are not taken up by it in their sleep. Such would I be. These seductions of the eyes I resist, lest the feet by which I walk on your way be ensnared; and I lift up my invisible eyes to you, that you would pluck my feet out of the snare. You pluck them out, again and again, for they are ensnared. You do not cease to pluck them out, while I often entangle myself in the snares laid on every side, because you who keep Israel will neither slumber nor sleep.

And what an uncountable host of things men have added to tempt their own eyes — things made by every art and every craftsman: clothes, shoes, vessels, manufactures of every kind, paintings and images of all sorts — far past any necessary or modest use, past any devout meaning. Outwardly they chase what they make; inwardly they abandon the one by whom they were made, destroying what they themselves were made to be. But I, my God and my glory — I take even these things as a reason to sing you a hymn, and I offer praise as a sacrifice to the one who offered sacrifice for me: because the beautiful designs that travel through souls into skillful hands all come down from that Beauty which stands above souls — the Beauty my soul sighs for day and night. The makers of outward beauties, and their devotees, draw from it their standard for judging them, but not their standard for using them. And it is there, though they do not see it — there, so that they need not wander so far; so that they might keep their strength for you, instead of scattering it out on delights that end in exhaustion. And I, saying all this and seeing it clearly, still tangle my steps in these beauties — but you pull me out, Lord; you pull me out, because your mercy is before my eyes. I am caught, pitifully; and you pull me out, in pity — sometimes without my even feeling it, when I had only brushed the trap; sometimes with pain, when I had already stuck fast.

What countless trifles, made by all kinds of arts and crafts — in our clothes, shoes, vessels, and works of every sort, in pictures too and all kinds of images, far exceeding any necessary and moderate use or any pious meaning — have people added to tempt their own eyes, outwardly chasing what they themselves make, inwardly forsaking him by whom they themselves were made, and destroying what they themselves were made to be! But I, my God and my Glory, even from this raise a hymn to you, and consecrate praise to him who consecrates me, because those beautiful patterns which through people's souls pass into their skilled hands come from that Beauty which is above our souls, the Beauty for which my soul sighs day and night. But the makers and lovers of these outward beauties draw from there the rule for judging them, but not for using them. And he is there, though they do not perceive him — so that they might not wander off, but keep their strength for you, and not scatter it abroad on pleasures that wear the soul out. But I, though I say this and see it, entangle my steps in these outward beauties; yet you pluck me out, O Lord, you pluck me out, because your loving-kindness is before my eyes. For I am caught, to my misery, and you mercifully pluck me out — sometimes without my feeling it, when I had only lightly brushed against them, sometimes with pain, because I had stuck fast.

To this, another form of temptation is added — one dangerous in more ways still. Besides the lust of the flesh, which lies in the enjoyment of all the senses and all pleasures, and whose slaves rot away as they wander far from you, there is in the soul a certain hollow, itching craving that works through those same bodily senses: dressed up in the names of knowledge and learning, it is a lust not for pleasure in the flesh, but for experiments through the flesh. It is rooted in the appetite for knowing; and since the eyes are the chief of the senses for gaining knowledge, the word of God calls it the lust of the eyes. Seeing belongs, strictly, to the eyes; but we use the word of the other senses too, whenever we put them to work finding things out. We do not say, “Listen how it glitters,” or “Smell how it gleams,” or “Taste how it shines,” or “Feel how it flashes”: all of these, we say, are seen. We say not only “See how it shines” — which only the eyes can perceive — but “See how it sounds,” “See how it smells,” “See how it tastes,” “See how hard it is.” So the whole business of the senses, as I said, is called the lust of the eyes: because the office of seeing, in which the eyes hold first rank, is borrowed by the other senses too, by a kind of likeness, whenever they go prospecting after some piece of knowledge.

To this is added another kind of temptation, dangerous in still more ways. For besides that lust of the flesh which lies in the delight of all the senses and pleasures — and its slaves, going far from you, waste away and perish — the soul has, through the same bodily senses, a certain empty and prying desire, cloaked under the name of knowledge and learning, which delights not in the flesh but in making experiments through the flesh. Since this has its seat in the appetite for knowledge, and the eyes are the sense chiefly used for gaining knowledge, it is called, in the language of Scripture, the lust of the eyes. For seeing belongs properly to the eyes; yet we use this word of the other senses too, when we put them to the search for knowledge. We do not say, "Listen how it flashes," or "Smell how it glows," or "Taste how it shines," or "Feel how it gleams"; for all these are said to be seen. And yet we say not only "See how it shines," which the eyes alone can perceive, but also "See how it sounds," "See how it smells," "See how it tastes," "See how hard it is." And so the general experience of the senses, as I said, is called the lust of the eyes, because the office of seeing, in which the eyes hold first place, the other senses claim for themselves by way of likeness, whenever they go searching after any knowledge.

And here the difference between pleasure and curiosity in the senses shows itself plainly. Pleasure goes after the beautiful, the melodious, the fragrant, the savory, the soft; curiosity goes after their opposites too — to test them — not to take on discomfort, but out of the sheer itch of experiencing and knowing. What pleasure is there in looking at a mangled corpse and shuddering? Yet let one lie somewhere, and people come running — to be saddened, to turn pale. They are even afraid of seeing it again in their dreams — as if anyone had forced them to look at it awake, or some rumor of its beauty had drawn them there! So too with the other senses, though it would take long to go through them all. From this disease of curiosity come the freak shows exhibited in the theater. From it people go on to pry into the hidden workings of nature — the ones beyond our concern — which it profits nothing to know, and which men want to know for no reason but the knowing. From it, too, with the same perverted aim of knowledge, come the inquiries of magic. From it, even in religion, God is put to the test: signs and portents are demanded of him — not wanted for anyone's salvation, but purely for the experience.

From this we can tell more clearly where pleasure and where curiosity is at work upon the senses; for pleasure seeks objects that are beautiful, melodious, fragrant, savory, soft, but curiosity seeks even the opposite of these, for the sake of trying them out — not to suffer annoyance, but out of the lust of making trial and knowing. For what pleasure is there in seeing, in a mangled corpse, something that makes you shudder? And yet, if one is lying nearby, people flock to it, to be made sad, to turn pale. They are afraid to see it even in their sleep — as though, when awake, anyone had forced them to see it, or any report of its beauty had drawn them there! So too with the other senses, which it would take long to go through. From this disease of curiosity come all those strange sights put on in the theater. From it people go on to search out the hidden powers of nature, which is beyond our purpose, knowledge that profits nothing, and which they desire for nothing but the knowing. From it too, with that same end of perverted knowledge, magical arts are pursued. From it, even in religion itself, God is tempted, when signs and wonders are demanded of him not desired for any good end, but merely to make trial.

In this immense forest, so full of traps and dangers, look how much I have cut away and swept out of my heart — as you have enabled me to do, God of my salvation. And yet, with so many things of this kind buzzing around our daily life on every side, when can I dare to say — when? — that nothing of the sort makes me stop and stare, or catches me in idle fascination? True, the theaters no longer carry me off; I do not bother to know the courses of the stars; my soul has never gone asking answers of the shades of the dead; every sacrilegious rite I detest. But from you, Lord my God, to whom I owe humble and single-hearted service — with what elaborate suggestions the enemy keeps working on me to demand from you some sign! By our King I beg you, and by Jerusalem our homeland, pure and chaste: as consenting to such things has been far from me, so may it always be farther and farther away. But when I pray to you for someone's salvation, what I am aiming at is different altogether; and you, doing what you will, give me — and will give me — the grace to follow you willingly.

In this so vast wilderness, full of snares and dangers, see how many of these I have cut off and thrust out of my heart, as you have given me to do, O God of my salvation. And yet when do I dare to say — since so many such things buzz on every side about our daily life — when do I dare to say that nothing of this sort holds my gaze or stirs an idle interest in me? True, the theaters no longer carry me away, nor do I care to know the courses of the stars, nor did my soul ever consult the spirits of the dead; all sacrilegious mysteries I detest. From you, O Lord my God, to whom I owe humble and single-hearted service, by what tricks and suggestions does the enemy work on me to make me desire some sign! But I beg you, by our King and by our pure and holy homeland, Jerusalem, that as all consenting to this is far from me, so may it ever be further and further still. And when I pray to you for the rescue of anyone, my aim and intention are far different. You give, and will give, that I should follow you willingly, doing what you will.

Even so, who can count the tiny, contemptible ways our curiosity is tempted every day, and how often we slip? How often we begin by putting up with people telling empty tales, so as not to wound the weak — and then, little by little, find ourselves attending with relish! I no longer watch a dog chase a hare at the circus games; but if I happen to be crossing a field and the chase is on, it may well tug me away from some serious thought and gather me to itself — forcing no swerve from the body of my mount, but a swerve of the heart. And unless you showed me my weakness and warned me quickly — either to lift myself toward you by some reflection rising out of the very sight, or to scorn the whole thing and pass on — I would stand there gaping, gone dull. And what about when a lizard catching flies, or a spider wrapping them up as they blunder into her web, stops me in my tracks as I sit at home? Is the thing any different because the animals are small? From them I move on, yes, to praising you, the marvelous creator and arranger of everything — but that is not what first caught my attention. It is one thing to get up quickly, another never to fall. And my life is packed full of such moments, and my one hope is your enormous mercy. For when our heart becomes the bin for things like these, hauling its crowds of teeming vanity, then our very prayers are cut short and disturbed by them; and while, in your presence, we direct the voice of the heart toward your ears, that great business is broken off by frivolous thoughts rushing in from I know not where. Shall we file this too under things that don't matter? Or shall anything lead us back to hope but your mercy, known and tried — since you have begun to change us?

And yet, in how many of the pettiest and most contemptible things our curiosity is daily tempted, and how often we give way, who can count? How often we begin as if we were merely tolerating people telling pointless stories, so as not to offend the weak, and then by degrees we take an interest in them! I no longer go to the circus to watch a dog chasing a hare; but if, passing through a field, that chase happens to be going on, it may pull me away even from some weighty thought and draw me after it — not that I turn the body of my horse aside, yet I incline my mind that way. And unless you, having made me see my weakness, quickly warned me either to rise toward you out of that sight by some reflection, or to despise it altogether and pass on, I stand there dully fixed. What of this — when, sitting at home, a lizard catching flies, or a spider wrapping them up as they rush into her nets, often catches my attention? Is the thing different because these are small creatures? I go on from them to praise you, the wonderful Creator and Orderer of all things; but it was not this that first drew my attention. It is one thing to rise quickly, another not to fall. And of such things my life is full; and my one hope is your great and wonderful mercy. For when our heart becomes a storehouse of such things, and is loaded with crowds of this abundant emptiness, then our prayers too are often broken off and distracted by them, and while in your presence we direct the voice of our heart to your ears, this so great matter is cut short by the rushing in of who knows what idle thoughts.

And you know how far you have already changed me — you who first healed me of the passion for revenge, so that you might then forgive all the rest of my iniquities, heal all my diseases, redeem my life from corruption, crown me with mercy and compassion, and satisfy my desire with good things: you who curbed my pride with your fear, and tamed my neck to your yoke. And now I carry the yoke, and it is light on me — because that is what you promised, and what you have made it; and truly it was so all along, and I did not know it, back when I was afraid to put it on.

And you know how far you have already changed me, you who first healed me of the lust to vindicate myself, that you might then forgive all the rest of my sins, and heal all my diseases, and redeem my life from corruption, and crown me with mercy and pity, and satisfy my desire with good things; you who curbed my pride with your fear and tamed my neck to your yoke. And now I bear it, and it is light to me, because so you promised, and so you have made it; and truly so it was, and I did not know it, when I was afraid to take it up.

But Lord, you who alone rule without arrogance, because you alone are the true Lord, who have no lord above you — has this third kind of temptation left me? Can it leave me at all in this life: the wish to be feared and loved by men for no reason but the joy of it — a joy that is no joy? A wretched life, that, and an ugly showing-off. Here above all is why men fail to love you and fear you purely; and so you set your face against the proud and give grace to the humble: you thunder down on the world's ambitions, and the foundations of the mountains shake. Now, because certain offices in human society make it necessary to be loved and feared by men, the adversary of our true happiness presses his advantage, strewing his snares everywhere with “Well done! Well done!” — hoping that as we snatch at the praise we will be caught off guard, unhook our joy from your truth and hang it on men's flattery, and come to enjoy being loved and feared not for your sake but in your place; so that, having made us like himself, he can keep us for his own — not bound together in love, but bound together in punishment: he who decided to set his throne in the north, so that in the dark and the cold they might slave for him as he apes you in his warped, crooked way. But we, Lord — look, we are your little flock. Keep us; we are yours. Spread your wings, and let us run under them. Be our glory yourself. Let us be loved for your sake; let it be your word that is held in awe in us. Whoever wants men's praise while you find fault will not be defended by men when you judge, or rescued by men when you condemn. And when it is not the sinner being praised in the desires of his soul, nor the doer of wrong being blessed, but a man being praised for some gift you gave him — if he takes more joy in the praising than in having the gift he is praised for, then he is praised while you find fault; and the one who praised is better than the one who was praised: for the one delighted in God's gift in a man, while the other delighted more in the gift of men than in the gift of God.

But, O Lord, you who alone are Lord without pride, because you are the one true Lord, who has no lord over you — has this third kind of temptation also ceased in me, or can it cease through this whole life? I mean the wish to be feared and loved by others for no other end than that we may have in it a joy that is no joy. A miserable life, and an ugly boastfulness! From this above all it comes that people neither purely love nor purely fear you. And therefore you resist the proud and give grace to the humble; yes, you thunder down upon the ambitions of the world, and the foundations of the mountains tremble. For because certain offices of human society make it necessary to be loved and feared by others, the enemy of our true blessedness presses hard upon us, spreading everywhere his snares of "Well done, well done," so that, greedily snatching at them, we may be taken off guard, and sever our joy from your truth and set it in the deceptions of men, and find pleasure in being loved and feared not for your sake but in your place; and so, made like him, he may have us for his own, not in the bonds of love but in the bonds of punishment — he who set out to place his throne in the north, that dark and chilled we might serve him, perversely and crookedly imitating you. But we, O Lord, see, we are your little flock; possess us as yours, stretch your wings over us, and let us fly beneath them. Be our glory; let us be loved for your sake, and let your word be feared in us. Whoever would be praised by men when you blame him will not be defended by men when you judge him, nor delivered when you condemn him. But when a man is praised — not the sinner praised in the cravings of his soul, nor the man blessed who does wickedly, but a man praised for some gift you have given him — and he rejoices more in the praise of himself than that he has the gift for which he is praised, he too is praised while you find fault with him; and better is the one who praised than the one who is praised. For the one took pleasure in God's gift in a man; the other was better pleased with a man's gift than with God's.

By these temptations we are tested every day, Lord — tested without rest. Our daily furnace is the human tongue. And in this matter too you command us to master ourselves: give what you command, and command what you will. In this matter you know the groans of my heart toward you, and the rivers that run from my eyes. For I cannot easily make out how far I am cleansed of this plague, and I am very afraid of my hidden faults — the ones your eyes see and mine do not. In other kinds of temptation I have at least some way of examining myself; in this one, almost none. With the pleasures of the flesh, and with useless curiosity, I can see what I have managed in reining my mind back: I do without the thing — by choice, or because it isn't there — and then ask myself how much or how little it troubles me to be without it. Riches, too, which people want in order to feed one of the three lusts, or two of them, or all three: if the soul cannot tell whether it despises them while holding them, it can throw them away and put itself to the test. But praise? To do without praise in order to test our powers — must we live so badly, so viciously and monstrously, that everyone who knows us detests us? Can a greater madness be spoken or imagined? No: if praise is the usual and rightful companion of a good life and good works, we should no more walk away from its company than from the good life itself. And yet, whether I can be calm or in pain at being without a thing, I have no way of knowing until it is gone.

By these temptations we are assailed daily, O Lord; without ceasing we are assailed. Our daily furnace is the tongue of men. And in this matter too you command us to be continent: give what you command, and command what you will. You know on this the groans of my heart and the floods of my eyes. For I cannot learn how far I have been cleansed of this plague, and I greatly fear my hidden sins, which your eyes know and mine do not. For in other kinds of temptation I have some means of examining myself; in this, scarcely any. For in restraining my mind from the pleasures of the flesh and from idle curiosity, I see how much I have gained when I do without them, foregoing them, or simply not having them; for then I ask myself how much more or less it troubles me not to have them. Riches, too, which are desired so that they may serve one or two or all of the three lusts — if the soul cannot tell whether, while it has them, it despises them, they can be cast aside, so that it may put itself to the test. But to be without praise, and so test our strength there, must we live badly — so abandonedly and atrociously that no one could know us without detesting us? What greater madness could be said or thought? But if praise is and ought to be the companion of a good life and good works, we ought as little to give up its company as the good life itself. And yet I do not know whether I can be well or ill without anything, unless it is taken from me.

So what do I confess to you, Lord, in this kind of temptation? What, except that praise delights me? — but truth delights me more than praise. If I were given the choice — to be out of my mind, wrong about everything, and praised by every man alive, or to be steady and grounded in the truth and abused by all of them — I know which I would choose. And yet I could wish that another person's approval added nothing to my joy over whatever good is in me. But it does add to it, I confess — and not only that: blame subtracts from it. And when this wretchedness of mine rattles me, an excuse slides in — you know what it is worth, God; it leaves me unsure. For you have commanded of us not only self-mastery — that is, what things to withhold our love from — but righteousness too — that is, where to bestow it — and you willed that we love not only you but our neighbor as well. And so I often tell myself that what pleases me is my neighbor's progress or promise, when I am pleased by his intelligent praise; and that it is his fault that grieves me, when I hear him tear down what he does not understand, or what is good. For sometimes I really am grieved by praise of myself — when things are praised in me that displease me, or when small and trivial goods are weighed as heavier than they should be. But again, how do I know whether I feel this only because I do not want the man who praises me to disagree with me about myself — not moved by any care for his good, but because the same goods that please me in myself please me more when they please someone else too? For somehow I am not praised at all when my judgment of myself goes unpraised — when what gets praised is what displeases me, or what gets more praise is what pleases me less. So am I not simply unsure of myself in this whole affair?

What, then, do I confess to you in this kind of temptation, O Lord? What, but that I am delighted by praise — yet by truth itself more than by praise? For if it were put to me whether I would rather, raving in error about everything, be praised by everyone, or, steady and most settled in the truth, be blamed by everyone, I see which I would choose. Yet I wish that the approval of another did not even increase my joy at any good in me. But I admit it does increase it; and not only that, but blame diminishes it. And when I am troubled at this misery of mine, an excuse comes to me, of what worth, you, O God, know, for it leaves me uncertain. For since you have commanded us not only continence — that is, what to hold our love back from — but also righteousness, that is, where to bestow it, and have willed us to love not only you but our neighbor too, it often seems to me, when I am pleased by intelligent praise, that I am pleased at my neighbor's good sense or promise, or grieved at evil in him, when I hear him disparage either what he does not understand or what is good. For sometimes I am grieved at my own praise, either when things are praised in me which I dislike in myself, or when lesser and slight goods are valued more than they deserve. But again, how do I know whether I am thus affected because I do not want the one who praises me to differ from me about myself — not out of any concern for him, but because those same good things that please me in myself please me more when they please another as well? For in a way I am not praised, when my own judgment of myself is not praised; since either things are praised which displease me, or those more which please me less. Am I, then, in doubt about myself in this matter?

Look, Truth: in you I see that when I am praised, I ought to be moved not for my own sake, but for the good of my neighbor. Whether that is how it is with me, I do not know. In this, I know less of myself than I know of you. I beg you, my God: show me myself too, so that I can confess to my brothers, who will pray for me, whatever damage I discover in myself. Let me question myself again, more carefully. If, in my own praise, it is my neighbor's good that moves me, why am I stung less when another man is unjustly attacked than when I am? Why does an insult bite deeper when it is thrown at me than when, before my eyes and with the same injustice, it is thrown at someone else? Do I not know even this? Or does it come down, at last, to this — that I deceive myself, and do not do the truth before you, in my heart and on my tongue? Put such madness far from me, Lord — do not let my own mouth become the sinner's oil that makes my head glisten. I am poor and needy; and I am at my best when, in hidden groaning, I displease myself and seek your mercy — until what is broken in me is mended and made complete, into that peace which the eye of the arrogant does not know.

Behold, in you, O Truth, I see that I ought not to be moved by my own praises for my own sake, but for the good of my neighbor. And whether it is so with me, I do not know. For here I know less of myself than of you. I beg you now, O my God, show me to myself as well, that I may confess to my brothers, who are to pray for me, where I find myself crippled. Let me examine myself again, more carefully. If in my praise I am moved by my neighbor's good, why am I less moved if another is unjustly disparaged than if it is myself? Why am I more stung by an insult thrown at me than by one thrown, with equal injustice, at another in front of me? Do I not know this either? Or is it that at the last I deceive myself, and do not do the truth before you in heart and tongue? Put this madness far from me, O Lord, lest my own mouth be to me the sinner's oil to anoint my head. I am poor and needy, yet I am better while in hidden groanings I displease myself and seek your mercy, until what is lacking in my broken state is renewed and perfected, on to that peace which the eye of the proud does not know.

The word that leaves the mouth, and the deeds that people come to know of, carry with them a most dangerous temptation — the love of praise, which goes canvassing for compliments and collecting them, to prop up a private eminence of one's own. It tempts me even when I condemn it in myself — tempts me by the very fact of being condemned; and often a man preens more emptily on his very contempt for empty glory. And then it is no longer contempt for glory he is preening on: for no one despises what he is glorying in.

Yet the word that comes out of the mouth, and the deeds known to others, carry with them a most dangerous temptation through the love of praise, which, to establish a certain excellence of one's own, begs and gathers up the votes of men. It tempts even when it is reproved by me in myself, and on the very ground that it is reproved; and a man often glories more emptily over his very contempt of empty glory — so that it is no longer contempt of empty glory that he glories in, for he does not despise it when he glories.

Inside — inside us — lives another evil of the same family: the vanity of those who please themselves, however little they please anyone else, or however much they displease them, or however little they even care to please. But pleasing themselves, they deeply displease you — not only because they treat bad things as good, but because they treat your good things as their own; or admit them to be yours, but claim them as earned; or admit them to be unearned grace, and still refuse to rejoice in that grace with their brothers, envying it to others. In all these dangers and labors, and others like them, you see the trembling of my heart; and as for my wounds — I do not so much manage to stop dealing them as feel you healing them, again and again.

Within, too, within is another evil, arising from a like temptation, by which people grow vain, pleasing themselves in themselves, though they please no one else, or displease or do not care to please others. But pleasing themselves, they greatly displease you, taking pleasure not only in things that are not good as though they were good, but in your good things as though they were their own; or, even if as yours, then as though earned by their own merits; or, even if as from your grace, yet not with brotherly rejoicing, but begrudging that grace to others. In all these and the like perils and labors you see the trembling of my heart, and I feel my wounds healed by you rather than not inflicted by me.

Where have you not walked with me, O Truth — teaching me what to avoid and what to seek, whenever I laid before you the things I could see down here, and asked your counsel? With my outer senses I surveyed the world as far as I was able; I studied the life my body has from me, and these senses of mine. From there I went inward, into the storerooms of my memory — those manifold immensities, wondrously filled with uncountable riches — and I contemplated them and stood awestruck: of all that was there, I could make out nothing without you, and none of it was you. Nor was the finder you — I who went through it all, straining to distinguish each thing and value it according to its rank, taking some things as the senses reported them, questioning others I felt mixed into my very self, counting and sorting the reporters themselves, and in memory's broad treasury turning some things over, laying some away, drawing others out. Nor, when I was doing this, was the power that did it you: for you are the abiding Light that I kept consulting about them all — whether they were, what they were, what they were worth — and I heard you teaching and commanding. And I do this often now. It is my delight; whenever I can loosen the grip of necessary duties, I take refuge in this pleasure. And in all the things I range through as I consult you, I find no safe place for my soul except in you: there let what is scattered in me be gathered, and let nothing of me slip away from you. And sometimes you bring me, deep inside, to a feeling utterly unlike anything usual — a strange sweetness that, if it were made complete in me, would be something no longer this life, whatever it would be. But I fall back down under my miserable weights; the old ways swallow me again, and hold me; I weep hard, but I am held hard. So heavy is the baggage of habit! Here I can be, and do not want to be; there I want to be, and cannot — miserable in both.

Where have you not walked with me, O Truth, teaching me what to beware of and what to desire, when I referred to you what I could discover here below, and consulted you? With my outward senses, as best I could, I surveyed the world, and observed the life that my body has from me, and these my senses. From there I entered the recesses of my memory, those manifold and spacious chambers, wonderfully filled with countless stores; and I considered, and stood aghast, able to discern none of these things without you, and finding none of them to be you. Nor was I myself, who found these things out, who went over them all and labored to sort them and to value each according to its worth — taking some on the report of my senses, questioning others that I felt to be mingled with myself, numbering and distinguishing the reporters themselves, and in the great treasure-house of my memory turning over some things, storing up others, drawing out others. Nor was I myself when I did this — that is, that power of mine by which I did it — nor was it you; for you are the abiding light, which I consulted about all these things, whether they were, what they were, and how to be valued; and I heard you directing and commanding me. And this I often do; this delights me, and as far as I can be freed from necessary duties, to this pleasure I have recourse. Nor in all these things which I run over, consulting you, can I find a safe place for my soul except in you, into whom my scattered members may be gathered, and nothing of me depart from you. And sometimes you admit me to a feeling deep within, most unusual, rising to a strange sweetness, which, if it were perfected in me, would be I know not what that does not belong to the life to come. But through my wretched burdens I sink down again into these lower things, and am swept back by old habit, and held fast; and I weep much, but am much held. So heavily does the weight of bad habit press us down. Here I can stay, but would not; there I would be, but cannot; miserable both ways.

So I have looked over the diseases of my sins under the threefold lust, and I have called your right hand to my rescue. For with a wounded heart I saw your splendor, and, beaten back by the blaze, I said: “Who can reach it? I am flung away from before your eyes.” You are the Truth, presiding over all things; and I, in my greed, did not want to lose you — I wanted to hold a lie in the same hands with you, just as no one wants to lie so thoroughly that he no longer knows, himself, what is true. And that is how I lost you: you do not consent to be held alongside a lie.

So, then, I have considered the sicknesses of my sins in that threefold lust, and have called your right hand to my help. For with a wounded heart I have beheld your brightness, and, struck back, I said, "Who can reach there? I am cast away from before your eyes." You are the Truth, presiding over all; but I, in my greed, did not want to lose you, and yet wanted to possess a lie along with you — as no man wants to speak falsely in such a way as to be himself ignorant of the truth. And so I lost you, because you will not be possessed together with a lie.

Whom could I find to reconcile me to you? Should I have gone begging to angels? With what prayer? With what rites? Many who struggled to return to you, and could not do it by their own strength, have tried that road, I am told, and fallen into a hunger for exotic visions, and been found worthy of delusions. High-minded, they went looking for you with the pride of their learning, chests puffed out instead of beaten; and by the likeness of their hearts they drew to themselves the powers of the air, fellow conspirators in pride, who tricked them with magical powers. They were looking for a mediator to purify them, and it was not one. It was the devil, passing himself off as an angel of light — and it was a great lure to their proud flesh that he had no body of flesh himself. They were mortals, and sinners; you, Lord, with whom they proudly sought reconciliation, are immortal and without sin. A mediator between God and humanity had to have something like God and something like human beings: like humans in both, he would be far from God; like God in both, far from humans — and either way, no mediator. So that counterfeit mediator, by whom, in your secret judgment, pride earned its mockery, has one thing in common with human beings — sin — and pretends to another thing in common with God: since he wears no mortal flesh, he parades himself as immortal. But since the wages of sin is death, what he truly has in common with men is this: that with them, he is condemned to death.

Whom could I find to reconcile me to you? Was I to have recourse to angels? With what prayers, with what rites? Many, trying to return to you and unable of themselves, have, so I hear, attempted this, and fallen into a craving for strange visions, and been thought worthy only to be deluded. For, being high-minded, they sought you by the pride of learning, puffing out their chests rather than beating their breasts; and so, by the kinship of their hearts, they drew to themselves the powers of the air, their fellow conspirators in pride, by whom, through magical influences, they were deceived, seeking a mediator by whom they might be cleansed, and there was none. For it was the devil, transforming himself into an angel of light. And it greatly enticed proud flesh that he had no body of flesh. For they were mortal and sinners, but you, Lord, to whom they proudly sought to be reconciled, are immortal and without sin. But a mediator between God and man must have something like God and something like men; for if in both respects he were like man, he would be far from God, and if in both like God, too unlike man — and so not a mediator. That deceitful mediator, then, by whom in your secret judgments pride deserved to be deluded, has one thing in common with man, namely sin; and another thing he would seem to have in common with God, for, not being clothed with the mortality of flesh, he would vaunt himself as immortal. But since the wages of sin is death, this he has in common with men, that with them he should be condemned to death.

But the true Mediator — whom in your secret mercy you showed to the humble, and sent so that by his example they might learn humility itself — the Mediator between God and humanity, the man Christ Jesus, appeared between mortal sinners and the immortal Just One: mortal, as men are; just, as God is. And because the wage of justice is life and peace, he came so that, through a justice joined to God, he might cancel the death of the wicked he had justified — the death he willed to share with them. He was shown to the holy men of old, so that they might be saved through faith in his suffering still to come, as we are saved through faith in his suffering now past. For as man he is Mediator; but as Word he is not something in between, being equal to God, God with God, and with him one God.

But the true Mediator, whom in your secret mercy you have shown to the humble, and have sent so that by his example too they might learn that same humility — that Mediator between God and man, the man Christ Jesus, appeared between mortal sinners and the immortal Just One: mortal with men, just with God; so that, because the wage of righteousness is life and peace, he might, by a righteousness joined to God, cancel the death of sinners now made righteous, the death he willed to share with them. Through him he was shown forth to the holy men of old, that they, by faith in his Passion to come, as we by faith in it now past, might be saved. For as man he was Mediator; but as the Word he is not in the middle between God and man, because he is equal to God, and God with God, and together one God.

How you loved us, good Father — you did not spare your only Son, but handed him over for us, the godless! How you loved us — us, for whom he who did not think it robbery to be your equal was made subject even to death on a cross: he alone free among the dead, having power to lay down his life and power to take it up again. For us he stood before you as victor and victim — and victor because victim. For us he stood before you as priest and sacrifice — and priest because sacrifice. He made us sons to you instead of slaves, by being born of you and becoming our servant. With good reason my hope in him is strong: that you will heal all my diseases through him who sits at your right hand and intercedes with you for us. Otherwise I would despair. For my diseases are many and great — many, and great; but your medicine is greater. We might have thought your Word too remote to be joined to man, and despaired of ourselves, had he not become flesh and made his home among us.

How you have loved us, good Father, who did not spare your only Son, but gave him up for us ungodly ones! How you have loved us, for whom he, who thought it no robbery to be equal with you, was made subject even to the death of the cross — he, the only one free among the dead, having power to lay down his life and power to take it up again; for us to you both Victor and Victim, and therefore Victor because Victim; for us to you both Priest and Sacrifice, and therefore Priest because Sacrifice; making us, instead of servants, your sons, by being born of you and serving us. With reason, then, is my hope strong in him, that you will heal all my diseases through him who sits at your right hand and intercedes for us; otherwise I would despair. For many and great are my diseases, many and great; but your medicine is mightier. We might have thought your Word far removed from any union with man, and despaired of ourselves, had he not been made flesh and dwelt among us.

Terrified by my sins and by the dead weight of my misery, I had turned it over in my heart and resolved on flight into the wilderness. But you stopped me, and steadied me, saying: This is why Christ died for all — so that the living should live no longer for themselves, but for him who died for them. See, Lord: I throw my care on you, so that I may live; and I will contemplate the wonders of your law. You know my clumsiness and my weakness: teach me, and heal me. He — your only Son, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge lie hidden — has redeemed me with his blood. Let the proud not slander me: for I keep the price of my ransom in mind; I eat it and drink it and hand it out to others; and, poor myself, I long to be filled from it among those who eat and are filled — and they shall praise the Lord who seek him.

Terrified by my sins and the burden of my misery, I had turned it over in my heart and resolved to flee into the wilderness; but you forbade me, and strengthened me, saying: Therefore Christ died for all, that those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for him who died for them. See, Lord, I cast my care upon you, that I may live, and consider the wondrous things of your law. You know my unskillfulness and my weaknesses; teach me, and heal me. He, your only Son, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, has redeemed me with his blood. Let not the proud speak evil of me, because I meditate on my ransom, and eat and drink and share it abroad; and, poor, I desired to be filled from him among those who eat and are satisfied; and they shall praise the Lord who seek him.

Lord, since eternity is yours, are you ignorant of what I am saying to you? Do you see in time what happens in time? Then why am I laying out for you this long account of things? Not so that you can learn them from me, certainly, but to stir up my own heart toward you, and the hearts of my readers, so that all of us may say: Great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised. I have said it before and I will say it again: I do this out of love for your love. We pray, after all — and yet Truth has said, Your Father knows what you need before you ask him. So what we are opening to you is our affection: confessing to you our own miseries and your mercies upon us, so that you may finish setting us free, since you have begun; so that we may stop being wretched in ourselves and become blessed in you — for you have called us to be poor in spirit, and meek, and mourners, and hungry and thirsty for righteousness, and merciful, and pure in heart, and peacemakers. See, I have told you many things — what I could, what I wanted to — because you willed first that I confess to you, my Lord God: for you are good, and your mercy endures forever.

Lord, since eternity is yours, can you be ignorant of what I tell you? Or do you see in time what happens in time? Then why do I lay before you, one after another, so many accounts of myself? Surely not so that you might learn them through me — but to stir up my own devotion toward you, and my readers', so that together we may say: Great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised. I have said it already, and I will say it again: I do this for love of your love. For we pray, too, and yet the Truth has said, Your Father knows what you need before you ask. So it is our hearts we lay open to you, confessing our miseries and your mercies upon us, that you may set us wholly free — since you have already begun — that we may stop being wretched in ourselves and be blessed in you, for you have called us to become poor in spirit, and meek, and mourners, hungering and thirsting after righteousness, merciful, pure in heart, peacemakers. See, I have told you many things, as well as I could and as much as I wished, because you first willed that I should confess to you, Lord my God. For you are good, and your mercy endures forever.

But when could the tongue of my pen ever tell all your urgings and all your terrors, your comforts and your steerings, by which you brought me to preach your word and to serve your sacrament to your people? Even if I could tell them all in order — the drops of time are precious to me. For a long time now I have burned to meditate on your law and to confess to you, in its light, what I understand and what I do not: the first daybreak of your illumination, and the darkness still left in me, until weakness is swallowed up by strength. And I do not want anything else to siphon off the hours I find free — free from the needs of the body, the refreshment of the mind, and the service we owe to people, or do not owe, and pay anyway.

But how could I, with the pen for my tongue, ever utter all your urgings, all your warnings and comforts and guidings, by which you brought me to preach your Word and dispense your Sacrament to your people? And even if I could utter them in order, the drops of time are precious to me. For a long time I have burned to meditate on your law, and there to confess to you both my skill and my unskillfulness — the daybreak of your enlightening in me, and the leftover scraps of my darkness — until weakness is swallowed up in strength. I would not have anything else steal away the hours I find free of the needs of feeding my body and resting my mind, and of the service we owe to others, or that we pay even when we do not owe it.

O Lord my God, listen to my prayer; let your mercy hear my desire — a desire that burns not for myself alone, but wants to be useful to the brothers I love; and you see my heart, that it is so. Let me offer you the service of my thinking and my tongue, and give me something I can offer. For I am poor and needy; you are rich to all who call on you — you who, beyond the reach of care, care for us. Circumcise my lips, the inner and the outer, of all recklessness and all lying. Let your Scriptures be my chaste delight: let me not be deceived in them, and not deceive others out of them. Listen, Lord, and have mercy, O Lord my God, light of the blind and strength of the weak — and light of the seeing, too, and strength of the strong. Listen to my soul; hear it crying from the depths. For if your ears are not with us even in the depths, where can we go? Where can we cry? Yours is the day and yours is the night: at your nod the moments fly past. Grant me a space of them for meditating on the hidden places of your law; do not shut your law against those who knock. You did not will so many pages of dark secrets to be written for nothing; those forests are not without their deer, who take cover in them and gather strength — who walk and graze, lie down and chew it over. O Lord, perfect me, and open those pages to me. Look — your voice is my joy; your voice is better than a flood of pleasures. Give what I love; for I do love, and this love too is your gift. Do not abandon your own gifts; do not despise this green shoot of yours in its thirst. Let me confess to you whatever I find in your books; let me hear the voice of praise and drink you in and contemplate the wonders of your law — from the beginning, in which you made heaven and earth, all the way to the everlasting kingdom of your holy city with you.

Lord my God, give ear to my prayer, and let your mercy listen to my longing; for it is anxious not for myself alone, but would serve the love of my brothers — and you can see my heart, that this is so. Let me make a sacrifice to you of the work of my thought and my tongue; only give me what I may offer you. For I am poor and needy, and you are rich to all who call on you — you who are untouched by care, and yet care for us. Cut away from all rashness and all lying both my inner and my outer lips. Let your Scriptures be my pure delight; let me not be deceived in them, nor deceive out of them. Lord, listen and have pity, Lord my God, light of the blind, strength of the weak — and light of those who see, strength of the strong as well. Listen to my soul, and hear it crying out of the depths. For if your ears are not with us in the depths too, where shall we go? where cry out? The day is yours, the night is yours; at your nod the moments fly. Out of them grant us a space for meditating on the hidden things of your law, and do not shut it against us who knock. For it was not for nothing that you willed so many pages to be written with their shadowy secrets; those forests are not without their deer, which slip in among them and roam and walk, feed, lie down, and chew the cud. Make me whole, Lord, and unveil those secrets to me. Look — your voice is my joy; your voice outdoes a flood of pleasures. Give me what I love; for I do love, and this too you have given me. Do not forsake your own gifts, do not despise your green and thirsting blade of grass. Let me confess to you whatever I find in your books, and hear the voice of praise, and drink you in, and turn over the wonderful things in your law — from the very beginning, in which you made the heaven and the earth, all the way to the everlasting reign of your holy city with you.

Lord, have mercy on me, and hear my desire. For it is no desire for earthly things, I think — not for gold and silver and jewels, not for splendid clothes or honors or power, not for the pleasures of the flesh, not even for what the body needs in this pilgrim life of ours: all of that is added to those who seek your kingdom and your righteousness. See, O Lord my God, where my desire comes from. The wicked have told me tales of their delights — but they are nothing like your law, O Lord. See: there is my desire. Look, Father; look and see, and approve. Let it please your mercy that I find grace before your eyes, so that the inner rooms of your words may open to me when I knock. I beg it through our Lord Jesus Christ your Son, the man of your right hand, the Son of Man, whom you established for yourself as mediator between you and us — through whom you sought us when we were not seeking you, and sought us precisely so that we would seek you — your Word, through whom you made all things, and me among them; your only Son, through whom you called the people of believers into adoption, and me among them. Through him I beg you — through him who sits at your right hand and intercedes with you for us, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge lie hidden. Those are the treasures I am looking for in your books. Moses wrote of him: he says so himself; the Truth says so.

Lord, have mercy on me, and hear my longing. For it is not, I think, of the earth — not of gold and silver, precious stones, fine clothes, honors and offices, pleasures of the flesh, or even the necessities for the body and for this pilgrim life of ours: all these things shall be added to those who seek your kingdom and your righteousness. See, Lord my God, where my longing lies. The wicked have told me of their delights, but none like your law, Lord. See where my longing lies. Look, Father — look, and see, and approve; let it be pleasing in the sight of your mercy that I find grace with you, that the inner depths of your words may be opened to me as I knock. I beg you by our Lord Jesus Christ your Son, the Man at your right hand, the Son of man whom you have made strong for yourself as the mediator between you and us, through whom you sought us when we were not seeking you — sought us, so that we might seek you; your Word, through whom you made all things, and me among them; your Only-Begotten, through whom you called your believing people to adoption, and me among them. I beg you by him who sits at your right hand and pleads with you for us, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. These are the treasures I seek in your books. Of him Moses wrote; this he says himself; this says the Truth.

Let me hear and understand how in the beginning you made heaven and earth. Moses wrote this; he wrote it and passed on — passed from here, from you, to you — and he is not in front of me now. If he were, I would take hold of him and ask him, and beg him through you to unfold these things to me, and I would bend the ears of my body to the sounds breaking from his mouth. If he spoke Hebrew, the sound would knock at my senses for nothing; none of it would touch my mind. If he spoke Latin, I would know what he was saying. But how would I know whether what he said was true? And if I did know even that, would I know it from him? No: inside me, deep inside, in the house where my thinking lives, Truth — not Hebrew, not Greek, not Latin, not any foreign tongue, with no mouth, no tongue, no clatter of syllables — would say, "He is telling the truth," and at once, with confidence, I would say to that man of yours, "You are telling the truth." Since I cannot question him, then, I ask you — you, the Truth that filled him when he said true things — you, my God, I ask: pardon my sins, and as you gave your servant to say these things, give me to understand them.

I want to hear and understand how, in the Beginning, you made the heaven and the earth. Moses wrote this; he wrote and went on his way, passing from you to you; and he is not here before me now. For if he were, I would catch hold of him and ask him, and beg him by you to open these things to me, and lay the ears of my body to the sounds bursting from his mouth. But if he spoke Hebrew, it would strike my senses in vain — none of it would reach my mind; if Latin, I would know what he said. But how would I know whether he spoke the truth? And even if I knew that, would I know it from him? No — within me, deep within, in the chamber of my thoughts, Truth, which is neither Hebrew nor Greek nor Latin nor any foreign tongue, with no apparatus of voice or tongue, no sound of syllables, would say, It is true; and at once I would say, with all confidence, to that man of yours, You speak the truth. But since I cannot question him, it is you I beg — you, Truth, with whom he was full when he spoke truth — you, my God, I beg: forgive my sins; and you who gave your servant the gift of speaking these things, give me also the gift of understanding them.

Look: heaven and earth exist. They cry out that they were made, for they change and they vary — whereas whatever exists without having been made has nothing in it that was not there before, and having something in you that was not there before is what it means to change and vary. They cry out, too, that they did not make themselves: "We exist because we were made. We did not exist before we existed — how could we have made ourselves?" And the voice that says it is the plain evidence of their being there. It was you, then, Lord, who made them: you who are beautiful, for they are beautiful; you who are good, for they are good; you who are, for they are. But they are not beautiful, not good, and do not exist the way you their maker do; set beside you, they are not beautiful, not good — they are not, at all. We know this, and thanks be to you for it; and our knowledge, set beside your knowledge, is ignorance.

Look: the heavens and the earth exist; they cry out that they were created, for they change and vary. But whatever has not been made, and yet exists, has nothing in it that it did not have before — and to have such a difference is exactly what it means to change and vary. They cry out, too, that they did not make themselves: We exist, because we have been made; we did not exist before we existed, so as to give ourselves being. And the proof is the plain voice of the things that say it. You, then, Lord, made them — you who are beautiful, for they are beautiful; you who are good, for they are good; you who are, for they are. And yet they are not beautiful, not good, not even fully real, as you their Creator are: set beside you, they are neither beautiful nor good nor real at all. This we know — and thanks be to you for it. And our knowledge, set beside your knowledge, is ignorance.

But how did you make heaven and earth? What machinery did you use for a work so vast? You did not work like a human craftsman, who forms one body out of another as his mind directs — a mind that can somehow impose on matter the form it sees inside itself with its inner eye. And how could even that mind do it, unless you had made it? It imposes form on something that already exists and already has being — clay, or stone, or wood, or gold, or the like. And where would those come from, had you not appointed them to be? You made the craftsman his body; you made the mind that commands his limbs; you made the stuff he works from; you made the intelligence by which he masters his craft and sees within what he is making without; you made the body's senses, the interpreter through which he carries the work across from mind to material and reports back to the mind what has been done, so that the mind can consult the truth presiding within it and ask whether the work was done well. All these things praise you, the creator of all. But how do you make them? How, O God, did you make heaven and earth? Certainly it was not in heaven or on earth that you made heaven and earth; not in the air, not in the waters, for these belong to heaven and earth. Nor did you make the whole world inside the whole world, because before it was made there was no place for it to be made in. Nor were you holding something in your hand to make heaven and earth from — for where would you get what you had not made, to make anything with? What exists at all, except because you exist? So you spoke, and things were made; in your Word you made them.

But how did you make the heaven and the earth? What was the engine of so vast a work? You did not work as a human craftsman does, shaping one body out of another at the discretion of his mind, which can somehow cast over the new thing a form it sees within itself by its inward eye. And how would he be able to do even that, unless you had made his mind? He casts a form over what already exists and already has being — clay, or stone, or wood, or gold, or the like. And how would those exist, had you not appointed them? You made the craftsman his body; you made the mind that commands the limbs; you made the matter out of which he makes anything; you made the grasp by which he takes in his art and sees within what he is to do without; you made the senses of his body, by which, as by an interpreter, he carries over from mind to matter what he is making, and reports back to his mind what is done, so that the mind may consult within the Truth that presides over it, whether the thing is well done or not. All these praise you, the Creator of all. But how do you make them? How, God, did you make heaven and earth? Surely not in the heaven, nor in the earth, did you make heaven and earth; nor in the air or the waters, since these too belong to heaven and earth; nor in the whole world did you make the whole world, since there was no place to make it in, before it was made, that it might be. Nor did you hold anything in your hand out of which to make heaven and earth. For where would you have gotten this thing you had not yet made, to make anything from? For what is there at all, except because you are? So you spoke, and they were made; and in your Word you made them.

But how did you speak? Was it the way the voice came out of the cloud, saying, This is my beloved Son? That voice happened and was over; it began and it ended. The syllables sounded and passed away, the second after the first, the third after the second, and so on in order, until the last came after all the rest — and silence after the last. From this it is plain and obvious that the motion of a creature uttered it: something temporal, serving your eternal will. And those words of yours, made for a moment, the outer ear reported to the understanding mind, whose inner ear lies open to your eternal Word. And the mind compared those words sounding in time with your eternal Word in silence, and said: "It is different — utterly different. Those words are far below me. They do not even exist: they run away and pass. But the Word of my God stays above me forever." Now, if it was in sounding, passing words that you said heaven and earth should be made, and that is how you made heaven and earth, then some bodily creature already existed before heaven and earth, by whose motions in time that voice could run its course in time. But there was no body before heaven and earth — or if there was, then you had certainly made it without any passing voice, so that from it you could make the passing voice that said, Let heaven and earth be made. For whatever such a voice was made from, unless you had made it, it would not exist at all. So: to make the body from which those words could be made — by what word did you speak that?

But how did you speak? In the way the voice came out of the cloud, saying, This is my beloved Son? For that voice went by and went away — it began and ended; the syllables sounded and passed, the second after the first, the third after the second, and so on in order, until the last after all the rest, and silence after the last. From which it is perfectly plain that it was the motion of a creature that uttered it — a motion that is itself in time, in service to your eternal will. And these words of yours, made for a moment, the outward ear reported to the discerning soul, whose inward ear was listening to your eternal Word. But the soul compared these words sounding in time with that eternal Word of yours in its silence, and said: It is different — utterly different. These words are far beneath me; in fact they are not, for they flee and pass away; but the Word of my Lord abides above me forever. So if it was in sounding, passing words that you said heaven and earth should be made, and thus made heaven and earth, then there was some bodily creature before heaven and earth, by whose motions in time that voice could run its course in time. But there was no bodily thing before heaven and earth; or if there was, then surely you had created it — without any such passing voice — out of which to make the passing voice by which to say, Let the heaven and the earth be made. For whatever that was, out of which such a voice was made, unless you had made it, it could not have existed at all. By what Word, then, did you speak, so that a body might come to be, by which these words could in turn be made?

You are calling us, then, to understand the Word: God, God with you, spoken eternally — the Word in whom all things are spoken eternally. For it is not that one thing was said, and finished, so the next could be said, everything in sequence; no, everything is said at once and forever. Otherwise there is time, and change, and no true eternity, no true immortality. I know this, my God, and I give thanks. I know it, I confess it to you, Lord, and whoever is not ungrateful to certain truth knows it with me and blesses you with me. We know, Lord, we know: insofar as anything no longer is what it was, or now is what it was not, to that degree it dies and is born. So nothing of your Word ever steps aside or steps in to take another's place, because it is truly immortal and eternal. And that is why, in the Word coeternal with you, you say all that you say at once and eternally, and whatever you say shall be made, is made. You make in no other way than by speaking — and yet the things you make by speaking are not made all at once, nor made eternal.

So you call us to understand the Word, the God who is God with you, who is spoken eternally, and by whom all things are spoken eternally. For what is spoken is not spoken one thing after another, each finished so that the next may be spoken, but all things together and eternally. Otherwise we already have time and change — and not a true eternity, not a true immortality. This I know, my God, and I give thanks. I know it, I confess it to you, Lord; and along with me, anyone who is not ungrateful to certain Truth knows it and blesses you. We know it, Lord, we know it: insofar as a thing is not what it was, and is what it was not, just so far it dies and rises. Nothing of your Word, then, gives place or takes the place of another, because it is truly immortal and eternal. And so to the Word coeternal with you, you say all at once and eternally everything you say; and whatever you say shall be made, is made; nor do you make in any way except by speaking. And yet the things you make by speaking are not made all at once, and are not everlasting.

Why is that, I beg you, O Lord my God? I see it, after a fashion; but how to put it into words I do not know. Perhaps it is this: whatever begins to be, and ceases to be, begins at exactly the moment and ceases at exactly the moment when your eternal reason knows it should begin or cease — that reason in which nothing begins and nothing ceases. And that reason is your Word, which is also the Beginning, because it also speaks to us. So in the Gospel it speaks through flesh; it sounded in the outward ears of men so that it might be believed, and sought inwardly, and found in the eternal truth, where the good and only Teacher instructs all his disciples. It is there, Lord, that I hear your voice speaking to me — for whoever teaches us is speaking to us, and whoever does not teach us, whatever he says, is not speaking to us. And who teaches us now, except the unchanging Truth? Even when a changeable creature prompts us, it only leads us to the unchanging Truth, and there we truly learn: we stand and listen to him, and we are glad with a great gladness at the bridegroom's voice, giving ourselves back to the one we came from. He is the Beginning for this reason: if he did not stand fast while we strayed, there would be nowhere for us to come back to. And when we come back from wandering, we come back by knowing; and so that we may know, he teaches us — because he is the Beginning, and he speaks to us.

Why is this, I beg you, Lord my God? I see it after a fashion, but how to put it into words I do not know — unless it is this: that whatever begins to be, and stops being, begins and stops just then, when in your eternal Reason it is known that it ought to begin or to stop — in which Reason nothing begins or stops. This is your Word, which is also the Beginning, because it also speaks to us. So in the Gospel he speaks through the flesh, and this sounded outwardly in the ears of men, so that it might be believed and sought inwardly, and found in the eternal Truth, where the good and only Master teaches all his disciples. There, Lord, I hear your voice speaking to me; for the one who teaches us is the one who speaks to us, and the one who does not teach us, even when he speaks, does not speak to us. And who teaches us but the unchanging Truth? For even when we are warned through some changeable creature, we are only being led to the unchanging Truth, where we truly learn when we stand and listen to him and rejoice greatly because of the Bridegroom's voice, which gives us back to the One from whom we are. And therefore he is the Beginning: for unless he stayed fast, there would be, when we went astray, no place to return to. But when we return from our wandering, it is by knowing that we return; and so that we may know, he teaches us, because he is the Beginning, and speaks to us.

In this Beginning, O God, you made heaven and earth: in your Word, in your Son, in your power, in your wisdom, in your truth — speaking in a way beyond wonder, making in a way beyond wonder. Who can comprehend it? Who can put it into words? What is this that flashes through me and strikes my heart without wounding it — so that I shudder, and I catch fire? I shudder because I am so unlike it; I catch fire because I am so like it. It is Wisdom — Wisdom itself — flashing through me, cutting open my fog; and the fog closes over me again as I sink back, faint, into the dark my punishment piles upon me. For my strength has drained away into poverty, until I cannot carry even my own good — until you, Lord, who have been gracious to all my iniquities, heal all my diseases too. For you will redeem my life from the pit and crown me with kindness and mercy; you will satisfy my desire with good things, and my youth will be renewed like the eagle's. For in hope we are saved, and in patience we wait for your promises. Whoever can, let him listen to you speaking within. I will cry out boldly in the words you wrote: How wonderful are your works, O Lord; in Wisdom you have made them all. And that Wisdom is the Beginning, and in that Beginning you made heaven and earth.

In this Beginning, God, you made heaven and earth — in your Word, in your Son, in your Power, in your Wisdom, in your Truth — speaking in a wondrous way and making in a wondrous way. Who can grasp it? Who can tell it? What is this that flickers through me and strikes my heart without wounding it, so that I shudder and burn? I shudder, because I am unlike it; I burn, because I am like it. It is Wisdom — Wisdom herself — that flickers through me, parting the cloud over me, the cloud that mantles me again as I faint away from her, into the darkness that gathers on me for my punishment. For my strength has been worn down to nothing, so that I cannot bear my own blessings, until you, Lord, who have been gracious to all my wrongs, heal all my weaknesses. For you will redeem my life from ruin, and crown me with loving-kindness and tender mercy, and satisfy my longing with good things, because my youth shall be renewed like an eagle's. For in hope we are saved, and so we wait in patience for your promises. Let anyone who is able hear you speaking within him out of your own oracle. I will cry out boldly: How wonderful are your works, Lord; in Wisdom you have made them all. And this Wisdom is the Beginning, and in that Beginning you made heaven and earth.

Look at them — people still full of their old leaven, who say to us: "What was God doing before he made heaven and earth? If he was at leisure," they say, "and doing nothing, why didn't he stay that way forever, going on doing nothing as he had always done nothing before? If some new motion arose in God — a new will, to make a creature he had never made before — how is that true eternity, where a will springs up that was not there before? The will of God is not a creature; it comes before every creature, since nothing would be created unless the creator's will came first. God's will belongs to his very substance. And if something arose in God's substance that was not there before, then that substance cannot honestly be called eternal. But if God's will that creation exist is from eternity, why isn't creation from eternity too?"

Now look — are they not full of their old leaven, those who say to us: What was God doing before he made heaven and earth? For if (they say) he was idle and doing nothing, then why does he not stay idle from now on and forever, just as he did before? For if some new motion arose in God, and a new will to make a creature he had never made before, then how could that be a true eternity, in which a will arises that was not there before? For the will of God is no creature; it comes before any creature, since nothing could be created unless the Creator's will came first. So the will of God belongs to his very being. And if something arose in God's being that was not there before, then that being cannot truly be called eternal. But if it was God's will from eternity that the creature should exist, then why was the creature itself not from eternity?

People who say this do not yet understand you, O Wisdom of God, light of minds. They do not yet understand how things come to be that come to be through you and in you. They strain to taste eternity while their heart still flutters among the motions of things past and things to come — and it will not hold still. Who will take that heart and hold it, and fix it so that it stands steady for just a moment, and for just a moment catches the splendor of eternity, which stands forever; and sets it beside the times that never stand; and sees that there is no comparison? Then it would see that a long time gets its length only from many motions passing by, which cannot be stretched out side by side; that in the eternal nothing passes, but the whole is present — while no time is ever present whole; that everything past is driven back by what is coming, everything coming follows hard upon the past, and everything past and coming is created by, and flows out of, what is always present. Who will hold the human heart still, so that it can stand and see how eternity, standing still — neither future nor past — dictates times future and times past? Can my hand do that? Can the hand of my mouth, by mere talking, do a thing that size?

Whoever talks like this does not yet understand you, Wisdom of God, Light of minds; they do not yet understand how the things are made that are made through you and in you, and yet they strain to comprehend things eternal — while their heart flutters back and forth among the motions of past and future, and is still unsettled. Who will hold it still and fix it in place, so that it may stand still for a moment and catch, for a moment, the splendor of that ever-fixed Eternity, and set it beside the times that are never fixed, and see that there is no comparison? Who will make it see that a long time becomes long only out of many passing motions that cannot be stretched out all at once; that in the Eternal nothing passes, but the whole is present, whereas no stretch of time is ever wholly present at once; that all time past is driven on by time to come, and all that is to come follows on what is past, and all of it, past and future, is created and flows out of that which is always present? Who will hold still the heart of man, so that it may stand and see how the standing-still Eternity, which is neither past nor future, gives the orders to times past and to come? Can my hand do this — can the hand of my mouth, by speaking, bring about a thing so great?

Here, then, is my answer to the man who asks, "What was God doing before he made heaven and earth?" I will not answer as one man is said to have done, ducking the force of the question with a joke: "He was preparing hell for people who pry into deep matters." Seeing is one thing; sneering is another. That is not my answer. I would rather answer "I do not know" where I do not know than mock a man for asking a deep question and win applause for a false answer. Instead I say this: you, our God, are the creator of every creature; and if by "heaven and earth" we mean every creature, then I say it boldly: before God made heaven and earth, God was not making anything. If he was making something, what could it have been but a creature? And I wish I knew everything I want to know for my own good as surely as I know this — that no creature was made before any creature was made.

See, I answer the man who asks, What was God doing before he made heaven and earth? I do not answer the way someone is said to have done — dodging the force of the question with a joke — He was preparing hell for those who pry into deep things. It is one thing to answer a question, another to make sport of the questioner. So I will not answer that way. I would rather answer I do not know to what I do not know, than say something that earns a laugh at a man asking about deep things, and praise for a man giving false answers. No — I say that you, our God, are the Creator of every creature; and if by the name heaven and earth we mean every creature, then I say boldly: before God made heaven and earth, he was not making anything. For if he was making something, what would he have been making but a creature? And I wish I knew everything I want to know for my good as surely as I know this: that no creature was made before any creature was made.

But if some restless mind goes roving back through images of times before creation, and marvels that you — God almighty, all-creating, all-sustaining, architect of heaven and earth — sat out countless ages before undertaking so great a work: let him wake up and pay attention, because his marveling rests on a mistake. How could countless ages pass by that you had not made — you, the author and founder of all the ages? What times could there have been that you did not create?
