How could they pass, if they never existed? Since you are the maker of all times, then, if there was any time at all before you made heaven and earth, how can anyone say you were resting from work? You made that very time; no times could pass before you made times. And if there was no time before heaven and earth, why ask what you were doing then? Where there was no time, there was no "then."

But suppose some restless mind goes roving over the images of bygone times, and marvels that you, God Almighty, the All-creating and All-sustaining, the Maker of heaven and earth, held back from so great a work through countless ages before you would make it. Let such a mind wake up and see that it is marveling at things that are false. For how could countless ages pass by that you did not make, you the Author and Creator of all ages? What times could there be that were not made by you? And how could they pass by, if they never were? Since, then, you are the Creator of all times, if there was any time before you made heaven and earth, why do they say you were keeping back from work? That very time you made yourself, and no times could pass by before you made those times. But if before heaven and earth there was no time, why ask what you were doing then? For there was no then, when there was no time.

Nor is it in time that you go before times — or you would not go before them all. You precede everything past from the height of your ever-present eternity, and you outreach everything future, because the future is future, and once it comes it will be past; but you are the same, and your years do not run out. Your years neither come nor go; ours come and go, so that all of them may come. Your years all stand at once, because they stand: they are not shoved out by years arriving, because they never pass. Ours will all be, only when all of them are no more. Your years are one day, and your day is not day after day but today — for your today does not yield to a tomorrow, and it does not follow a yesterday. Your today is eternity: and so you begot the Coeternal, to whom you said, Today I have begotten you. You made all times, and before all times you are; and there was never a time when there was no time.

And you do not precede time by time — otherwise you would not precede all times. No, you precede all things past by the height of an ever-present eternity, and you outlast all things to come, because they are still to come, and once they have come they will be past; but you are the Same, and your years do not fail. Your years neither come nor go; ours both come and go, so that they may all come at last. Your years all stand together, because they stand still; the years coming on do not thrust out the years departing, because none of them pass away — but ours will all have been only when none of them are any longer. Your years are a single day; and your day is not a day-after-day, but Today, since your Today does not give way to a tomorrow, nor does it follow on a yesterday. Your Today is Eternity; and so you begot the Coeternal, to whom you said, Today I have begotten you. You made all things, and you are before all times; and there was no time in which there was no time.

So there was no time in which you were making nothing, since you made time itself. And no times are coeternal with you, because you stand fast — and if they stood fast, they would not be times. For what is time? Who can explain it briefly and easily? Who can even grasp it in thought clearly enough to say a word about it? Yet what do we mention in conversation more familiarly, more knowingly, than time? And we understand it when we speak of it; we understand it too when we hear someone else speak of it. What then is time? If no one asks me, I know; if I want to explain it to someone who asks, I do not know. Still, I can say with confidence that I know this much: if nothing passed away, there would be no past time; if nothing were coming, there would be no future time; if nothing existed, there would be no present time. Those two times, then, past and future — how can they be, when the past is no more and the future is not yet? And the present — if it were always present, and never passed into the past, it would not be time anymore; it would be eternity. So if the present becomes time only by passing into the past, how can we say that even it is — when its whole reason for being is that it will stop being? In truth we cannot say that time is, except because it is tending toward is not.

There was no time, then, in which you had not made anything, since time itself you made. And no times are coeternal with you, because you stand fast; whereas if they stood fast, they would not be times. For what is time? Who can explain it easily and briefly? Who can even grasp it in thought clearly enough to put it into words? And yet what do we mention in conversation more familiarly, more knowingly, than time? We understand it, surely, when we speak of it; we understand it, too, when we hear someone else speak of it. So what is time? If no one asks me, I know; if I want to explain it to someone who asks, I do not know. Yet I say boldly that I know this much: that if nothing passed away, there would be no past time; that if nothing were coming, there would be no future time; and that if nothing were, there would be no present time. Those two times, then — past and future — how can they be, when the past is now not, and the future is not yet? But the present, if it were always present and never slid away into the past, would not be time at all, but eternity. So if the present, in order to be time, comes into being only because it slips away into the past, how can we say that it is, when the very ground of its being is that it will not be — so that we cannot truly say that time is, except because it is tending not to be?

And yet we speak of "a long time" and "a short time" — though only of the past or the future. A hundred years back we call a long time past; a hundred years ahead, a long time to come. A short time past is, say, ten days ago; a short time to come, ten days from now. But how can something be long or short that does not exist? The past is no more; the future is not yet. So let us not say of the past, "it is long"; let us say "it was long," and of the future, "it will be long." My Lord, my light — will your truth not laugh at man even here? That long past time: was it long when it was already past, or before that, when it was still present? It could be long only while there was something that could be long. Once past, it no longer existed — and what did not exist at all could not be long. So let us not say "past time was long" either: we will find nothing there that was long, since from the moment it became past, it is not. Let us say instead, "that time was long while it was present," because while it was present, it was long. It had not yet gone off into nonexistence; there was something there that could be long. But the moment it passed, it stopped being long in the very act of stopping being.

And yet we say a long time and a short time, though only of the past or the future. A long time past, for instance, we call a hundred years ago; a long time to come, a hundred years from now. A short time past, say, ten days ago; a short time to come, ten days from now. But in what sense is that long or short, which does not exist? For the past is no longer, and the future is not yet. So let us not say it is long; let us say of the past, it has been long, and of the future, it will be long. My Lord, my Light — will not your Truth make a mockery of man here too? For that past time which was long: was it long when it was already past, or when it was still present? For it could only be long when there was something there that could be long; but once it was past, it no longer was, and so it could not be long, since it was not at all. Let us not say, then, time past has been long; for we will find nothing that has been long, since once it is past, it is no more. Let us say instead: that present time was long — because, while it was present, it was long. For it had not yet passed away into nonexistence, and so there was something that could be long. But once it was past, it stopped being long, because it stopped being.

Come then, human soul — you are the one given the power to sense and to measure stretches of time — let us see whether present time can be long. What is your answer? Are a hundred present years a long time? First look at whether a hundred years can be present at all. If the first of those years is running, it is present, and the other ninety-nine are future — so they are not yet. If the second year is running, one is already past, one is present, the rest are to come. Pick any year in the middle of the hundred as present: everything before it is past, everything after it future. So a hundred years cannot be present. Now look at whether even the one year that is running is present. If its first month is running, the rest are future; if the second, the first has already gone and the rest are not yet. So even the current year is not present whole — and if it is not present whole, the year is not present. A year is twelve months, and only the current month, whichever it is, is present; the rest are past or future. And even the current month is not present — only one day of it is: if the first day, the rest are future; if the last, the rest are past; if a middle day, it hangs between past days and future days.

Let us see, then, soul of man, whether present time can be long — for it is to you that the feeling and the measuring of length of time is given. What will you answer me? Are a hundred years, when present, a long time? But first see whether a hundred years can be present at all. If the first of those years is now running, it is present, but the other ninety-nine are still to come, and so are not yet. If the second year is running, one is already past, one present, the rest to come. And whatever middle year of the hundred we suppose to be present, all the years before it are past, all after it to come; so a hundred years cannot be present. But see at least whether the one year now running is itself present. If its first month is running, the rest are to come; if the second, the first is already past and the rest are not yet. So the year now running is not present as a whole; and if not present as a whole, then the year is not present. For twelve months make a year, and whichever month is running is present, while the rest are past or to come. Though in fact that running month is not present either, but only one day of it: if it is the first day, the rest are to come; if the last, they are past; if any day in between, then it stands between past and future.

Watch the present time — the only time we found we could call long — shrink to the span of scarcely a single day. And let us take even that apart, for not even one day is present whole. It is filled out by twenty-four hours of night and day: for the first hour, the rest are future; for the last, the rest are past; for any hour between, the hours before are past and the hours after are future. And that one hour itself runs off in fugitive particles: whatever has flown from it is past; whatever is left is future. If we can conceive a point of time that cannot be split into even the smallest particles of moments, that alone is what may be called present — and it flies from future to past so fast that it stretches over no interval at all. If it stretched at all, it would divide into past and future. The present has no extent. Where, then, is the time we can call long? The time to come? We do not say of it, "it is long," because there is nothing yet to be long; we say, "it will be long." When will it be long, then? If even then it is still to come, it will not be long, since what could be long does not yet exist. But if it will be long precisely then, when out of the future — which is not yet — it first begins to be, and becomes present, so that there is something that can be long: then the present time cries out, in the words we heard above, that it cannot be long.

See how the present time — the only one we found that could be called long — is shrunk to the length of barely a single day. But let us look even at that, because not even one day is present as a whole. For it is made up of twenty-four hours of night and day: the first hour has the rest still to come, the last has them all past, and any middle hour has those before it past and those after it to come. And that single hour itself is fleeing away in flying particles: whatever of it has flown off is past, whatever remains is to come. If we could conceive some instant of time that cannot be divided into even the smallest particles of moments, that alone is what could be called present — and yet it flies so fast from future into past that it cannot be stretched out with the least pause. For if it is stretched out, it is divided into past and future. The present has no length. Where, then, is the time we may call long? Is it the future? Of the future we do not say it is long, because it is not yet, so as to be long; we say it will be long. But when will it be? For if even then, while it is still to come, it shall not be long (because what can be long is not yet), and so it shall be long only when, out of the future that is not yet, it begins now to be and has become present — so that then there is something that can be long — then present time cries out, in the very words above, that it cannot be long.

And yet, Lord, we do perceive intervals of time; we compare them and call some longer, some shorter. We even measure how much longer or shorter this time is than that: we answer that this one is double or triple, that one single, or that the two are equal. But it is times in passing that we measure, and we measure them by perceiving them. Past times, which no longer are, or future times, which are not yet — who can measure those? Only someone bold enough to claim he can measure what does not exist. So while time is passing, it can be perceived and measured; once it has passed, it cannot, because it is not.

And yet, Lord, we do perceive intervals of time, and compare them, and say some are shorter, others longer. We even measure how much longer or shorter one time is than another, and we answer: this is double, or triple; that is just once over, or only just as long as the other. But it is times as they are passing that we measure, by perceiving them; for who can measure times past, which now are not, or times to come, which are not yet — unless someone dares to claim that what does not exist can be measured? So while time is passing, it can be perceived and measured; but once it is past, it cannot, because then it is not.

I am asking, Father, not asserting: my God, govern me and guide me. Who will tell me it is not so — that there are not three times, past, present, and future, as we learned as boys and have taught to boys, but only the present, because the other two do not exist? Or do they exist too — and does time come out of some hiding place when it turns from future to present, and go back into some hiding place when it turns from present to past? For where did those who foretold the future see it, if it does not yet exist? What does not exist cannot be seen. And those who recount the past could not recount it truly unless they saw it in their minds — and if past things were nothing at all, they could not be seen at all. Therefore future things and past things do exist.

I am asking, Father, not asserting: my God, rule me and guide me. Who will tell me there are not three times, the way we learned as boys and taught the boys after us — past, present, and future — but only the present, since the other two are not? Or are they too? And when the future becomes present, does it come out of some hidden place; and when it retreats, does present become past by going into hiding? For where did those who foretold things to come see them, if as yet they were not? What does not exist cannot be seen. And those who tell of things past could not tell of them if they did not somehow make them out in the mind; and if those things were nothing, they could in no way be made out. Things past, then, and things to come — they are.

Allow me, Lord, to push my search further. O my hope, do not let my attention snap. If future things and past things exist, I want to know where they are. If I cannot manage that yet, I still know this much: wherever they are, they are not there as future or as past, but as present. If the future is there as future, it is not there yet; if the past is there as past, it is there no longer. So wherever they are, whatever they are, they are only as present. When we tell the past truly, what comes out of memory is not the events themselves, which have passed, but words conceived from their images — images they planted in the mind like footprints as they passed through the senses. My boyhood, which no longer is, lies in past time, which no longer is; but its image, when I recall it and describe it, I am looking at right now, in the present, because it is still in my memory. Whether foretelling the future works the same way — images of things that do not yet exist, sensed in advance as already existing — I confess, my God, I do not know. But this I do know: we usually think out our future actions in advance, and that advance thinking is present, while the action we are planning does not yet exist, because it is future. Once we have set to it, and begun to do what we were planning, then the action will exist — because then it is not future but present.

Allow me, Lord, to search further. My hope, do not let my purpose be confounded. For if times past and future exist, I want to know where they are. And if I cannot grasp that, still I know this much: wherever they are, they are not there as future or as past, but as present. For if they are there as future, they are not yet there; if there as past, they are no longer there. Wherever they are, then, whatever they are, they are only as present. It is true that when we tell of past facts, what is drawn out of the memory is not the things themselves, which are gone, but words conceived from the images of those things — images they printed on the mind, in passing, by way of the senses, like footprints. My childhood, for instance, which now is not, lies in time past, which now is not; but when I call up its image and speak of it, I look on that image in the present, because it is still in my memory. Whether there is some like cause for the foretelling of things to come — so that images of things which as yet are not could be perceived beforehand, as already existing — I confess, my God, I do not know. This much I do know: that we generally think ahead about our future actions, and that this forethinking is present, but the action we are forethinking is not yet, because it is still to come. And once we have set about it and have begun to do what we were forethinking, then that action will be, because then it is no longer future but present.

However this hidden foresensing of the future works, then, nothing can be seen except what is. And what is now is not future but present. So when people speak of seeing the future, what they see is not the things themselves — which are not yet, being future — but perhaps their causes or their signs, which already exist. To the one seeing them, they are not future but present, and from them the mind conceives the future and foretells it. Those conceptions exist already too, and those who foretell are gazing at something present inside themselves. Let one example out of the whole teeming crowd of them speak for me. I watch the first light of dawn, and I announce in advance that the sun is going to rise. What I watch is present; what I announce is future — not the sun, which already exists, but its rising, which is not yet. And yet unless I pictured that rising in my mind, as I picture it now while speaking of it, I could not predict it. But the dawn glow I see in the sky is not the sunrise, though it runs ahead of it; and neither is the picture in my mind. Both of these are seen as present, so that the rising, which is future, can be told beforehand. Future things, then, are not yet; and if they are not yet, they are not; and if they are not, they cannot possibly be seen. But they can be foretold from present things, which already exist, and are seen.

Whatever the way may be, then, of this hidden fore-perceiving of things to come, nothing can be seen except what is. But what now is, is not future but present. So when things to come are said to be seen, it is not the things themselves that are seen — for as yet they are not — but perhaps their causes or signs, which already are. So they are not future to those who see them, but present; and out of them the future, conceived beforehand in the mind, is foretold. These conceptions, again, exist now; and those who foretell the things behold the conceptions present before them. Out of the countless variety of things, let one example serve me. I look at the daybreak; I announce that the sun is about to rise. What I look at is present; what I announce is to come. Not the sun, which already is, but its rising, which is not yet. And yet, unless I pictured that sunrise itself in my mind — as I do now while I speak of it — I could not foretell it. But neither is that daybreak which I make out in the sky the sunrise, though it goes before it; nor is the picture in my mind the sunrise: those two are seen now, in the present, so that the sunrise still to come may be foretold. Things to come, then, are not yet; and if they are not yet, they are not; and if they are not, they cannot be seen. Yet they can be foretold out of present things, which already are and are seen.

You, then, ruler of your creation — how is it that you teach souls what is to come? For you taught your prophets. How do you teach the future, you for whom nothing is future? Or do you rather teach present things about the future? For what does not exist certainly cannot be taught. That way of yours is far beyond my sight; it is too strong for me, and on my own I cannot reach it. But I will reach it from you, when you grant it — sweet light of my hidden eyes.

You, then, Ruler of your creation — by what way do you teach souls the things to come? For you did teach your prophets. By what way do you teach things to come, you to whom nothing is to come — or rather, out of things future, teach things present? For what does not exist cannot be taught. This way is too far beyond my sight; it is too mighty for me, I cannot reach it. But from you I can, when you grant it — sweet light of my hidden eyes.

But this much is now clear and evident: neither future nor past things exist. Strictly speaking, we cannot say, "There are three times: past, present, and future." Strictly, perhaps, we should say: there are three times — a present of things past, a present of things present, and a present of things future. These three do exist, somehow, in the soul; anywhere else, I do not see them. The present of things past is memory; the present of things present is sight; the present of things future is expectation. If we may speak this way, then I see three times, and I grant that there are three. Say too, then, "there are three times, past, present, and future," as loose custom puts it — say it. I do not mind; I raise no objection, no protest — provided we understand what is meant, and do not imagine that the future exists now, or the past. There are few things we say strictly, many things we say loosely; but what we mean gets understood.

What is clear and plain now is this: that neither things to come nor things past are. Nor is it strictly right to say there are three times, past, present, and to come. It might more strictly be said that there are three times: a present of things past, a present of things present, and a present of things future. For these three do exist, after a fashion, in the soul, and nowhere else do I see them: the present of things past is memory; the present of things present is direct sight; the present of things future is expectation. If we are allowed to speak this way, then I do see three times, and I admit there are three. Let it also be said, in our loose way, that there are three times, past, present, and to come. See, I do not object, I do not argue, I find no fault — provided that what is said is understood, that neither what is to be now is, nor what is past. For there are few things we say strictly; most things we say loosely, and still the meaning gets across.

I said a little while ago that we measure times as they pass — so that we can say this time is double that one, or equal to it, and report whatever else about the parts of time our measuring can report. So, as I said, we measure times as they pass; and if someone asks me, "How do you know?", I answer: I know because we do measure; because we cannot measure what does not exist; and because past and future do not exist. But how do we measure present time, when it has no extent? It is measured while it passes; when it has passed, it is not measured, for then there is nothing to measure. But from where, by what way, and to where does time pass while it is being measured? From where, but the future? By what way, but the present? To where, but the past? Out of what is not yet, then, through what has no extent, into what is no longer. Yet what do we measure, if not time over some extent? When we say single and double and triple and equal and everything else of the kind, we are naming extents of time. In what extent, then, do we measure time as it passes? In the future, which it comes out of? What is not yet, we cannot measure. In the present, which it passes through? What has no extent, we cannot measure. In the past, which it passes into? What is no more, we cannot measure.

I said just now that we measure times as they pass, so as to be able to say that this stretch of time is twice as long as that, or just as long as that, and so on for any measurable parts of time. So, as I said, we measure times as they pass. And if anyone should ask me, How do you know? I might answer, I know that we do measure them; and that we cannot measure what is not; and that things past and to come are not. But present time — how do we measure it, since it has no length? It is measured while passing; once it has passed, it is not measured, for then there will be nothing there to measure. But where does it come from, by what way does it go, and where does it go, while it is being measured? Where from, but the future? By what way, but the present? Where to, but the past? From that which is not yet, then, through that which has no length, into that which now is not. And yet what is it we measure, if not time in some kind of length? For we do not say single, double, triple, equal, or any other such thing of time, except of lengths of time. In what length, then, do we measure time as it passes? In the future, where it comes from? But what is not yet, we cannot measure. In the present, where it goes by? But a thing with no length we cannot measure. In the past, where it goes to? But what now is not, we cannot measure either.

My mind is on fire to solve this knotted riddle. Do not lock it away, Lord my God, good Father — through Christ I beg you — do not lock these things away from my desire, these things at once so ordinary and so hidden. Let my desire break through to them; let them shine out under your illuminating mercy, Lord. Whom else shall I ask about them? And to whom can I more usefully confess my ignorance than to you, who are not wearied by this zeal of mine, blazing over your Scriptures? Give what I love — for I do love, and that love is your gift. Give it, Father, you who truly know how to give good gifts to your children. Give it, because I have taken this knowing upon myself, and it is labor and trouble to me until you open the door. Through Christ I beg you, in the name of the Holy of Holies: let no one shout me down. I believed, and therefore I speak. This is my hope; for this I live: to gaze on the delight of the Lord. Look — you have made my days old, and they pass away, and how, I do not know. And we go on talking about time and time, times and times: "How long ago did he say this?" "How long since he did that?" "How long is it since I saw it?" "This syllable takes double the time of that short one." We say these things and hear them; we are understood, and we understand. They are the most obvious, most everyday things there are — and the same things are hidden too deep to reach, and finding them out would be a discovery.

My soul is on fire to know this tangled riddle. Do not lock it away, Lord my God, good Father — through Christ I beg you — do not lock these things, familiar and yet hidden, away from my longing, so that it is barred from breaking through to them; but let them dawn for me by your enlightening mercy, Lord. Whom shall I ask about these things? And to whom would it do me more good to confess my ignorance than to you, to whom these studies of mine, so fiercely kindled toward your Scriptures, are no trouble? Give me what I love; for I do love, and this love too you gave me. Give, Father — you who truly know how to give good gifts to your children — give, because I have set myself to know, and the labor is before me until you open the way. Through Christ I beg you, in his name, the Holy of holies: let no one interrupt me. For I have believed, and so I speak. This is my hope, this is what I live for: to contemplate the delights of the Lord. See, you have made my days a span of years, and they pass away, and how, I do not know. And we talk of time and time, of times and times — How long ago since he said this; how long since he did that; how long since I saw such a thing; and this syllable lasts twice as long as that single short one. These words we speak, and these we hear, and we are understood, and we understand. They are utterly plain and ordinary, and yet the same things are too deeply hidden, and the discovery of them would be something new.

I once heard a learned man say that time simply is the motion of the sun, moon, and stars. I did not agree. Why not the motions of all bodies, then? If the lights of heaven halted and a potter's wheel kept turning, would there be no time by which to measure its turns — no way to say that it was spinning at even intervals, or, if it ran now slower and now faster, that some turns took longer and some shorter? And while we were saying all this, wouldn't we be speaking in time? Wouldn't some syllables in our words be long and some short — for no other reason than that some sounded for a longer time and some for a shorter? God, grant men to see in a small thing the laws common to things small and great. The stars and the lamps of the sky are for signs and for seasons, for years and for days — yes, they are. But I would no more say that one turn of that little wooden wheel makes a day, than that learned man could say it therefore makes no time.

I once heard from a learned man that the motions of the sun, moon, and stars are what time is — and I did not agree. For why should the motions of all bodies, rather, not be time? Suppose the lights of heaven were to stop, and a potter's wheel went on turning: would there be no time by which to measure its turnings, and say that it turned at even intervals, or, if it ran sometimes slower and sometimes faster, that some rounds took longer and others less? And while we were saying this, would we not ourselves be speaking in time? And would there not be in our words some syllables short, some long — short because they sounded in a shorter time, long because in a longer? God, grant to men to see, in a small thing, what holds true of things great and small alike. There are stars and lights of heaven for signs and seasons, for years and days; there they are. Yet I would not say that the turning of that wooden wheel was a day, nor would he be right to say it was therefore no time at all.

What I long to know is the force and the nature of time, by which we measure the motions of bodies and say, for instance, that this motion lasts twice as long as that one. I ask this: since "day" means not only the sun's hours above the earth — day as opposed to night — but also its whole circuit from the east around to the east again (as when we say "so many days passed," the nights counted in), and since a day is completed by the sun's motion, its circuit from east to east — I ask whether the day is the motion itself, or the interval the motion takes, or both. If the motion were the day, then we would have a day even if the sun completed its whole course in a stretch as short as one hour. If the interval, then there would be no day if from one sunrise to the next were only as long as an hour: the sun would have to circle twenty-four times to complete a single day. If both, then it could not be called a day if the sun ran its whole round in an hour; nor could it, if the sun stopped and as much time passed as the sun usually spends on its whole circuit, morning to morning. So I will not ask now what it is we call a day; I ask what time is — the time by which we would measure the sun's circuit and say it was completed in half its usual interval, if it were completed in a stretch like twelve hours; the time by which we could compare the two intervals and call one single and the other double, even if the sun sometimes ran from east to east in the single and sometimes in the double. So let no one tell me that times are the motions of the heavenly bodies. When at one man's prayer the sun stood still, so that he could finish his battle in victory, the sun stood — but time went on. That battle was fought and ended in its own tract of time, as much as it needed. I see, then, that time is some kind of stretching-out. But do I see it, or do I only seem to see it? You will show me, Light; you will show me, Truth.

I want to know the force and nature of time, by which we measure the motions of bodies and say, for instance, this motion is twice as long as that. For here is my question. A day does not mean only the sun's stay above the earth — by which day is one thing and night another — but also its whole circuit from east round to east again, by which we say so many days have passed, the nights included when we say so many days, and not counted apart. Since, then, a day is completed by the sun's motion, by its circuit from east round to east, I ask: is it the motion alone that makes the day, or the stretch of time in which that motion is completed, or both? If the first, then we would have a day even if the sun finished that course in as small a space as one hour. If the second, then it would not make a day if there were only as short a stay as one hour between one sunrise and the next, but the sun would have to go round twenty-four times to complete a single day. If both, then it could not be called a day either if the sun ran its whole round in the space of one hour, nor if, while the sun stood still, as much time went by as the sun usually takes to make its whole course from one morning to the next. So I will not ask now what it is that we call a day, but what time itself is — that time by which, measuring the sun's circuit, we could say it was finished in half the usual time, if it ran its course in as small a space as twelve hours; and, comparing the two times, could call this one a single time and that a double — even supposing the sun ran its round from east to east sometimes in the single time, sometimes in the double. So let no one tell me that the motions of the heavenly bodies are time, since once, at one man's prayer, the sun stood still until he could win his battle: the sun stood still, but time went on. For in its own allotted span of time that battle was fought and finished. I see, then, that time is a kind of stretching-out. But do I really see it, or only seem to? You, my Light and my Truth, will show me.

Do you command me to agree if someone defines time as the motion of a body? You do not. That no body moves except in time — that I hear; you say it. But that the motion of a body is time — that I do not hear; you do not say it. When a body moves, it is by time that I measure how long it moves, from when it begins until it stops. If I did not see it begin, and it keeps on so that I never see it stop, I cannot measure — except from the moment I began to watch until I stopped watching. If I watch a long while, all I can report is that it was a long time, not how long; because when we say how long, we say it by comparison: "as long as that," "twice as long as that," and so on. But if we can mark the places a moving body goes from and comes to — or the places its parts pass through, if it is turning like a lathe — then we can say exactly how much time the motion of the body, or of its part, took from this place to that. So a body's motion is one thing, and what we measure its duration by is another — and given that, who can fail to see which of the two better deserves the name of time? A body may sometimes move and sometimes stand still, and we measure not only its motion but its rest, and measure both by time: we say "it stood as long as it moved," or "it stood two or three times as long as it moved," or whatever else our measuring has fixed exactly or roughly guessed — more or less, as we say. Time, therefore, is not the motion of a body.

Do you tell me to agree, if someone defines time as the motion of a body? You do not. For that no body is moved except in time, I hear — this you say; but that the motion of a body is time, I do not hear; this you do not say. For when a body is moved, it is by time that I measure how long it moves, from when it began until it stopped. And if I did not see where it began, and it kept moving so that I did not see when it stopped, I cannot measure it — except, perhaps, from the time I began watching until I stopped. And if I watch long, I can only say it is a long time, not how long; for when we say how long, we say it by comparison: this is as long as that, or twice as long as that, and the like. But when we can mark the distances of the places the moving body goes from and to — or the distances its parts go, if it turns like a wheel on a lathe — then we can say exactly in how much time the motion of that body, or of its part, from this place to that, was finished. Since, then, the motion of a body is one thing, and that by which we measure how long the motion is, another, who does not see which of the two ought rather to be called time? For if a body is sometimes moving and sometimes standing still, we measure by time not only its motion but its standing still as well, and say it stood still as long as it moved, or twice or three times as long as it moved, or whatever other length our measuring has fixed, or guessed at — more or less, as we say. Time, then, is not the motion of a body.

And I confess to you, Lord, that I still do not know what time is. And yet again I confess to you, Lord, that I know I am saying this in time; that I have been talking about time for a long while now; and that this "long while" is only a long while because of some duration of time. How do I know that, when I do not know what time is? Or maybe I do not know how to say what I do know? What a state I am in — I do not even know what I do not know! See me, my God: I stand before you, and I am not lying. As my words are, so is my heart. It is you who will light my lamp; you, O Lord my God, will turn my darkness into light.

And I confess to you, Lord, that I still do not know what time is. And again I confess to you, Lord, that I know I am saying this in time, and that I have been speaking of time for a long while, and that this very long while is long only by the passing of time. So how do I know this, when I do not know what time is? Or is it perhaps that I do not know how to put into words what I do know? How wretched I am, that I do not even know what I do not know! See, my God, I do not lie before you: as I speak, so is my heart. You will light my lamp; you, Lord my God, will brighten my darkness.

Does not my soul confess to you, and confess truly, that I do measure times? So it is, my God: I measure, and I do not know what I am measuring. I measure the motion of a body by time. Then am I not measuring time itself? Could I really measure how long a body moves, and how long it takes to get from here to there, without measuring the time it moves in? So how do I measure time itself? Do we measure a longer time by a shorter, the way we measure a beam by the length of a cubit? That does seem to be how we measure the span of a long syllable by the span of a short one and call it double; how we measure the length of a poem by the lengths of its lines, the lengths of the lines by the lengths of the feet, the lengths of the feet by the lengths of the syllables, and the long syllables by the short — not measuring on the page (that way we would be measuring space, not time), but as the words go past in the speaking: "A long poem — it is built of so many lines; long lines — they run so many feet; long feet — they stretch across so many syllables; a long syllable — it is double a short one." But even so we get no fixed measure of time, because a shorter line, spoken with a drawl, can fill more time than a longer one rattled off. So with a whole poem, so with a foot, so with a syllable. From all this it began to seem to me that time is nothing other than a stretching-out — but of what, I do not know. And I would be surprised if it were not of the mind itself. For what, I beg you, my God, am I measuring when I say, loosely, "this time is longer than that," or even, precisely, "this is double that"? That I am measuring time, I know. But I am not measuring the future — it is not yet; nor the present — it stretches over no extent; nor the past — it is no more. What am I measuring, then? Times passing, not past? So I said earlier.

Does not my soul confess to you, most truly, that I do measure times? And so, my God, I measure, and I do not know what I am measuring? I measure the motion of a body by time — and time itself, do I not measure that? But could I really measure how long a body moves, and in how long a stretch of time it goes from this place to that, without measuring the time in which it moves? So this time itself, how do I measure it? Do we measure a longer time by a shorter, as we measure the length of a beam by the length of a forearm? For that does seem to be how we measure the length of a long syllable by a short one, and say it is double. In just this way we measure the length of a stanza by the lengths of its lines, the lengths of the lines by the lengths of the feet, the lengths of the feet by the lengths of the syllables, the lengths of long syllables by the lengths of short — not measuring by pages (for that way we measure spaces, not times), but as the words are uttered and pass by, when we say: it is a long stanza, because made of so many lines; long lines, because made of so many feet; long feet, because drawn out by so many syllables; a long syllable, because double a short one. But not even this way do we get any sure measure of time, because it may happen that a shorter line, pronounced slowly, takes up more time than a longer one rushed through — and the same for a foot, a syllable. From all this it seemed to me that time is nothing other than a stretching-out — but of what, I do not know, and I would be amazed if it were not a stretching of the mind itself. For what is it, I beg you, my God, that I measure, when I say, vaguely, this time is longer than that, or, exactly, this is double that? That I measure time, I know; and yet I do not measure the future, for it is not yet; nor the present, because it has no length; nor the past, because it now is not. What, then, do I measure? Times as they pass, not times that have passed? For so I said.

Hold on, my mind, and press hard. God is our help; he made us, and not we ourselves. Press on toward the place where truth is beginning to dawn. Suppose a physical voice begins to sound — sounds, goes on sounding — and now stops: silence; the voice is past; there is no voice anymore. Before it sounded, it was future and could not be measured, because it did not yet exist; and now it cannot be measured, because it no longer exists. It could be measured, then, while it was sounding, because then there was something there to measure. But even then it was not standing still: it was going, going away. Is that what made it measurable? For in passing it was being stretched out across some interval of time in which it could be measured — since the present has no extent. If it could be measured then, look: suppose another voice has begun to sound and is sounding still, one continuous unwavering tone. Let us measure it while it sounds; when it falls silent, it will be past, with nothing left to measure. Let us measure it exactly, then, and say how long it is. But it is still sounding — and it can only be measured from its beginning, where it started, to its end, where it stops. What we measure is precisely the interval between some beginning and some end. So a voice that has not yet ended cannot be measured; no one can say how long or short it is, or call it equal to another, or single, or double, or anything of the kind. But once it has ended, it will no longer exist. How, then, can it be measured? And yet we do measure times. Not times that are not yet, not times that are no longer, not times stretched over no duration, not times without end points. Not future times, then, nor past, nor present, nor passing — and yet we measure times.

Courage, my mind, and press on hard. God is our helper; he made us, and not we ourselves. Press on where the truth begins to dawn. Suppose the sound of a voice begins, and sounds, and goes on sounding, and then — listen — it stops; now there is silence, and the voice is past, and is no longer a voice. Before it sounded, it was to come, and could not be measured, because as yet it was not; and now it cannot be measured, because it no longer is. So while it was sounding it could be, because then there was something that could be measured. But even then it was not standing still, for it was passing on and passing away. Was it the more measurable for that? For as it passed, it was being stretched out into some length of time, so that it could be measured, since the present has no length. So if it could be measured then — see, suppose another voice has begun, and is still sounding on in one unbroken stretch without a break. Let us measure it while it sounds; for once it has stopped sounding it will be past, and there will be nothing left to measure. Let us measure it, then, and say how long it is. But it is still sounding, and it cannot be measured except from where it began to where it left off. For the very interval between is the thing we measure — from some beginning to some end. So a voice that is not yet ended cannot be measured, in such a way that one could say how long or short it is, or call it equal to another, or double a single one. But once it is ended, it no longer is. How, then, can it be measured? And yet we do measure times — not those which are not yet, nor those which no longer are, nor those that are not stretched out by any pause, nor those that have no bounds. We measure neither times to come, nor past, nor present, nor passing; and still we do measure times.

"Deus creator omnium" — "God, creator of all things." The line runs eight syllables, short and long alternating: the four short — first, third, fifth, seventh — are single against the four long — second, fourth, sixth, eighth. Each long takes double the time of each short. I pronounce them and report it, and it is so, as plain hearing tells. As far as plain hearing goes, then, I measure the long syllable by the short, and I feel it holding the short twice over. But since one sounds only after the other — the short first, the long after — how do I keep hold of the short one? How do I lay it against the long as a measure, to find that the long has it twice, when the long does not begin to sound until the short has stopped sounding? And the long itself — am I measuring it as present, when I cannot measure it before it ends? Its ending is its passing away. What is it, then, that I am measuring? Where is the short syllable I measure with? Where is the long syllable I measure? Both have sounded, flown, passed away; they are no more. And still I measure, and I answer with confidence — as far as a practiced ear can be trusted — that in span of time the one is single, the other double. And I could not do it unless they had already passed and ended. So it is not the syllables themselves I measure, for they no longer exist, but something in my memory that stays fixed there.

Deus Creator omnium — God, Creator of all: this verse of eight syllables alternates between short and long. The four short ones, the first, third, fifth, and seventh, are single, against the four long, the second, fourth, sixth, and eighth; each of these long ones takes double the time of each short one. I pronounce them, I report on them, and I find it so, as plain hearing perceives. By plain hearing, then, I measure a long syllable by a short, and I plainly find it to last twice as long. But when one sounds after the other — the short one first, the long one after — how am I to hold on to the short one, and how, in measuring, am I to lay it against the long one, so as to find that the long has twice as much, seeing that the long does not begin to sound until the short has stopped? And that long syllable itself — do I measure it while it is present, when I do not measure it until it is ended? And its ending is its passing away. So what is it I measure? Where is the short syllable I measure by? Where the long one I measure? Both have sounded, have flown off, have passed away, are gone; and yet I measure, and I answer with confidence — as far as a practiced ear can be trusted — that this syllable is single, that one double, in length of time. And I could not do this unless they were already past and ended. So it is not the syllables themselves, which now are not, that I measure, but something that stays fixed in my memory.

It is in you, my mind, that I measure times. Do not shout me down — I mean, do not shout yourself down with the mob of your own impressions. In you, I say, I measure times. The impression that passing things make in you stays in you when they have passed; that impression, still present, is what I measure — not the things that passed in making it. That is what I measure when I measure times. So either that is what times are, or I do not measure times at all. What about when we measure silences, and say that this silence lasted as long as that voice did? Do we not stretch our thought out to the measure of the voice, as though it were still sounding, so as to report something about the intervals of silence within a span of time? With voice and mouth entirely still, we run through poems in thought — lines, whole speeches, the dimensions of any motion — and we report on spans of time, how long this took against that, exactly as if we were saying it all aloud. Suppose a man decides to utter a longish sound and fixes in advance, in thought, how long it will last. He has already gone through that interval of time in silence; he commits it to memory, then begins to utter the sound, and it sounds until it reaches the end he set for it. Or rather: it has sounded and it will sound — for the part of it already done has sounded, and the rest will sound. And so the thing is carried through, as the mind's present attention hauls the future over into the past — the past growing as the future shrinks, until the future is used up and everything is past.

It is in you, my mind, that I measure times. Do not interrupt me — that is, do not interrupt yourself with the uproar of your own impressions. In you I measure times. The impression that things make on you as they pass remains when they are gone; it is this present impression that I measure, not the things that passed by to make it. This is what I measure when I measure times. So either this is time, or I am not measuring time at all. And what of when we measure silence, and say this silence lasted as long as that voice did? Do we not stretch out our thought to the measure of the voice, as if it were sounding, so as to be able to report on the intervals of silence in a given length of time? For though voice and tongue are still, in thought we go over poems and verses and any other discourse, and over the spans of any motions, and we report on their lengths of time, how much this is in relation to that, exactly as if we were uttering them aloud. If a man wants to make a long sound, and has settled in thought how long it is to be, that man has already gone through a length of time in silence, and, committing it to memory, he begins to utter the sound, which goes on sounding until it is brought to the end he set for it. Indeed it has sounded, and it will sound; for as much of it as is finished has already sounded, and the rest will sound. And so it goes on, until present attention carries the future over into the past, the past growing as the future shrinks, until, when the future is wholly used up, the whole is past.

But how can the future shrink or be used up, when it does not yet exist? How can the past grow, when it no longer exists? Only because in the mind, which does all this, there are three acts. The mind expects, it attends, and it remembers: what it expects passes, through what it attends to, into what it remembers. Who denies that the future does not yet exist? Yet an expectation of the future already exists in the mind. Who denies that the past no longer exists? Yet a memory of the past still exists in the mind. Who denies that the present has no extent, since it passes in an instant? Yet attention lasts — and through attention what is arriving is carried off into absence. So it is not the future, which does not exist, that is long: a long future is a long expectation of the future. And it is not the past, which does not exist, that is long: a long past is a long memory of the past.

But how is that future shrunk or used up, when it is not yet? And how is the past made to grow, when it is no longer? Only because, in the mind that does all this, there are three things going on. For it expects, and it attends, and it remembers, so that what it expects passes, by way of what it attends to, into what it remembers. Who would deny that things to come are not yet? And yet there is in the mind an expectation of things to come. Who would deny that things past are now no longer? And yet there is still in the mind a memory of things past. And who would deny that the present time has no length, since it passes away in an instant? And yet attention lasts on, and through it what shall be present goes on its way to become no longer present. So it is not future time that is long, for it is not yet; a long future is a long expectation of the future. Nor is it past time that is long, for it now is not; a long past is a long memory of the past.

Say I am about to recite a psalm I know. Before I begin, my expectation reaches across the whole of it. Once I have begun, whatever I have plucked off it and dropped into the past is stretched along my memory instead — and the life of this act of mine is stretched two ways: into memory, because of the part I have said, and into expectation, because of the part I am about to say. Yet all the while my attention is present, and through it what was future is carried across into what is past. And the further the act proceeds, the shorter grows expectation and the longer memory, until the whole of expectation is used up, the whole act is finished, and it has passed entire into memory. And what happens in the psalm as a whole happens in each of its parts, and in each of its syllables; it happens in the longer performance of which that psalm may be one small part; it happens in the whole of a human life, whose parts are all of a person's acts; it happens in the whole age of the children of men, whose parts are all human lives.

I am about to recite a psalm I know. Before I begin, my expectation reaches out over the whole; but once I have begun, whatever I pluck off from it into the past reaches out along my memory; and so the life of this act of mine is stretched two ways — into memory, as to what I have already said, and into expectation, as to what I am about to say. But attention is present all the while, and through it what was future is carried over to become past. And the more this goes on and on, the more expectation is shortened and memory is lengthened, until the whole expectation is used up, when the whole act is finished and has passed over into memory. And what happens in the whole psalm happens also in each of its parts and each of its syllables; it happens in the longer action of which this psalm may be a part; it happens in the whole life of a man, of which all his actions are parts; it happens across the whole age of the sons of men, of which all the lives of men are parts.

But because your mercy is better than lives, look at mine: my life is a stretching-apart — pulled many ways at once. And your right hand took hold of me in my Lord, the Son of Man, mediator between you, the One, and us, the many — the many, pulled many ways among many things — so that through him I might lay hold of him who has laid hold of me; that I might be gathered in from my old days to follow the One; forgetting what is behind, strained not apart toward the things that will come and pass away, but forward toward what lies ahead — moving not by distension but by intention — I press on toward the prize of the call from above, where I will hear the voice of your praise and gaze on your delight, which neither comes nor passes. But for now my years go by in groaning, and you are my comfort, Lord — my Father, everlasting — while I have flown apart into times whose order I do not know. My thoughts, the innermost guts of my soul, are torn to shreds by the noisy crowds of change, until the day I flow together into you, refined and melted clean in the fire of your love.

But because your loving-kindness is better than all our lives, see, my life is nothing but a being-pulled-apart; and your right hand has held me up, in my Lord the Son of man, the Mediator between you, the One, and us the many — many, and scattered too among many things. Through him may I lay hold of the One in whom I have been laid hold of, and be gathered up out of my old days, to follow the One — forgetting what lies behind, and not stretched out and torn between what shall be and what shall pass away, but reaching toward the things that are before me, and not by being pulled apart but by straining forward, I press on for the prize of my heavenly calling, where I may hear the voice of your praise and contemplate your delight, which neither comes nor passes away. But now my years are spent in mourning, and you, Lord, are my comfort, my Father everlasting; while I have been broken apart among times whose order I do not know, and my thoughts, the very inmost depths of my soul, are torn and mangled with their tumult of changes, until I flow together into you, refined and melted down in the fire of your love.

And now I will stand and grow firm in you, in the mold of me that is your truth. I will not put up with the questions of men whose sickness is its own punishment — who thirst for more than they can hold and ask, "What was God doing before he made heaven and earth?" or, "How did it ever occur to him to make something, when he had never made anything before?" Grant them, Lord, to think well about what they are saying, and to discover that where there is no time, there is no "never." To say that someone "never made" something is simply to say that he made it "at no time." Let them see, then, that without creation there can be no time — and let them stop talking that emptiness. Let them too be stretched forward to what lies ahead, and understand that you are before all times, the eternal creator of all times; that no times are coeternal with you, and no creature either — even if there is some creature above all times.

And then I will stand still, and grow firm in you — in my mould, your truth; and I will not put up with the questions of men who, by a sickness they have earned, thirst for more than they can hold, and say: What was God doing before he made heaven and earth? Or, How did it come into his mind to make something, when he had never made anything before? Grant them, Lord, to think hard about what they are saying, and to find that never cannot be said where there is no time. To say that he never made anything — what is that but to say that he made it in no time? Let them see, then, that there can be no time without a created world, and let them stop talking that empty talk. Let them too be stretched toward the things that are before; let them understand that you are before all times, the eternal Creator of all times, and that no times are coeternal with you, and no creature either, even if there is some creature before all times.

O Lord my God, how deep is the fold of your secret, and how far from it the consequences of my sins have flung me! Heal my eyes, and let me rejoice with your light. Certainly, if there were a mind of such vast knowledge and foreknowledge that it knew all things past and all things future the way I know one well-known psalm, that mind would be a wonder past belief — astonishing to the point of dread — since nothing done in all the ages gone by, and nothing in all the ages remaining, would be any more hidden from it than, while I sang that psalm, it was hidden from me what and how much of it had passed since the beginning, and what and how much remained until the end. But far be it from us to think that you, creator of the universe — creator of souls and bodies — know all things future and past merely like that. Far, far more wonderfully do you know them, and far more secretly. When someone sings a well-known song, or listens to one, his feelings are swung and his attention pulled apart between expecting the sounds to come and remembering the sounds gone by. Nothing of the kind happens to you — the unchangeably eternal, that is, the truly eternal creator of minds. So then: as you knew heaven and earth in the beginning without any variation in your knowledge, so you made heaven and earth in the beginning without any stretching-apart of your action. Let whoever understands this confess to you, and let whoever does not understand it confess to you. Oh, how high you are — and the humble in heart are your house! For you raise up the downcast, and those whose high place is you do not fall.

Lord my God, what a depth is this hidden recess of your mysteries — and how far from it the consequences of my sins have flung me! Heal my eyes, that I may share in the joy of your light. Surely, if there is a mind so richly gifted with knowledge and foreknowledge that it knows all things past and to come as well as I know one familiar psalm, that mind is wonderful past all telling, dreadful and astonishing — since nothing of the past, nothing of the ages to come, is any more hidden from it than, when I sang that psalm, it was hidden from me what and how much of it had passed away from the start, and what and how much remained until the end. But far be it that you, the Creator of the universe, the Creator of souls and bodies — far be it that you should know all things past and to come in such a way as that. Far, far more wonderfully, far more mysteriously, do you know them. For with the man who sings a song he knows, or hears a familiar one, his feelings vary, and his senses are divided, by his expecting the words to come and remembering the words gone by; but nothing of the sort happens to you, unchangeably eternal, the truly eternal Creator of minds. And so, just as in the Beginning you knew heaven and earth without any change in your knowing, so in the Beginning you made heaven and earth without any pulling-apart of your action. Let whoever understands this confess to you; and whoever does not understand it, let him confess to you too. Oh, how high you are — and yet the humble in heart are your dwelling place; for you lift up those who are bowed down, and they do not fall, whose lifting-up is you.

sections.title: The Heaven of Heavens
Heaven of Heavens, Formless Earth, and the Many Truths of Moses

segments.text: My heart is busy with many things, Lord — prodded by the words of your holy Scripture in the middle of this poor life of mine. That is why the poverty of human understanding usually runs long in words: searching has more to say than finding, asking takes longer than getting, and the hand that knocks works harder than the hand that receives. But we hold the promise — who can break it? If God is for us, who can be against us? Ask, and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. Everyone who asks receives; whoever seeks finds; to the one who knocks, it will be opened. These are your own promises — and who fears being deceived when Truth is the one who promises?

O Lord, my heart is busy over the words of your holy Scripture, here in the poverty of my life. And this is why, most of the time, the poverty of human understanding runs on in so many words: because asking has more to say than finding, and the knocking lasts longer than the opening, and the hand that knocks has more work to do than the hand that receives. Yet we hold your promise; who shall cancel it? If God is for us, who can be against us? Ask, and you shall be given; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it shall be opened. These are your own promises; and who could fear to be cheated, when the Truth is the one who promises?

The lowliness of my tongue confesses to your highness: you made heaven and earth — this heaven I see, this earth I walk on, the earth I carry about in this body. You made them. But where, Lord, is that heaven of heavens we hear of in the words of the Psalm: The heaven of heavens is the Lord's, but the earth he has given to the children of men? Where is the heaven we cannot see, beside which everything we can see is earth? For this bodily universe, which is nowhere whole all at once, has received its portion of beauty in these lower parts, and the lowest of them is our earth; but next to that heaven of heavens, even the heaven over our earth is only earth. Yes, both of these great bodies may fairly be called earth beside that unknown heaven, which is the Lord's and not the sons of men's.

From the lowliness of my tongue I confess to your highness that you made heaven and earth — this heaven I see, and this earth I tread on, the earth I carry about in my own body: you made it. But where, O Lord, is that heaven of heavens we hear of in the words of the Psalm, the heaven of heavens is the Lord's, but the earth he has given to the children of men? Where is that heaven we cannot see, the one to which everything we can see is only earth? For this whole bodily world is not present everywhere at once; it has received its measure of beauty even down here in these lower regions, of which the very lowest is this earth of ours. But set beside that heaven of heavens, even the sky over our earth is only earth; and it is not absurd to call both of these great bodies earth, compared with that unknown heaven which is the Lord's and not the sons' of men.

And this earth, surely, was invisible and formless — some unfathomable deep of abyss with no light above it, because it had no shape. So you commanded it to be written that darkness was upon the face of the deep — and what is that but the absence of light? If light had been there, where would it have been but overhead, above everything, filling it all with light? So where light was not yet, what was the presence of darkness but the absence of light? Darkness lay over it because light did not lie over it — just as silence is wherever sound is not. And what is it for silence to be there, except for sound not to be there? Haven't you, Lord, taught this soul what it confesses to you? Haven't you taught me, Lord, that before you formed this formless matter and sorted it into distinct things, there was nothing at all — no color, no shape, no body, no spirit? And yet not absolutely nothing: there was a certain formlessness, with no beauty in it.

Now this earth was invisible and unformed, and there was some unfathomable depth, an abyss with no light upon it, because it had no shape. That is why you commanded it to be written that darkness was upon the face of the deep. And what is darkness but the absence of light? For had there been light, where would it have been but up over everything, shining down? Where light was not, then, what was the presence of darkness but the absence of light — just as where there is no sound, there is silence, and to have silence in a place is simply to have no sound in it? Have you not taught this, O Lord, to the soul that confesses to you? Have you not taught me, Lord, that before you formed and shaped this formless matter, there was nothing — no color, no figure, no body, no spirit? And yet not altogether nothing: there was a certain formlessness, without any beauty at all.

Then what should it be called, so that even slower minds could take some hold of it, if not by a familiar word? And what can be found anywhere in the world closer to utter formlessness than earth and the deep? They occupy the lowest rung, and they are less beautiful than the higher regions, which are translucent and shining, all of them. So why shouldn't I take earth invisible and formless as the fitting way to suggest to human beings that formlessness of matter — the matter you had created without beauty, in order to make from it this beautiful world?

What should it be called, then, so that it could be conveyed in some measure even to slower minds, except by some ordinary word? And among all the parts of the world, what comes nearer to sheer formlessness than earth and the deep? Lying at the lowest level, they are less beautiful than the higher parts, which are all transparent and shining. So why may I not take it that the formlessness of matter — which you had made without beauty, that you might make this beautiful world out of it — was fittingly hinted to us under the name of earth invisible and unformed?

So when thought looks for what the senses might find underneath that name, it says to itself: 'This is no intelligible form, like life or like justice, because it is the stuff of bodies; and it is nothing the senses can perceive, because in the invisible and the formless there is nothing to see and nothing to sense.' And while human thought talks this way to itself, let it attempt one of two things: to know it by not knowing it, or not to know it by knowing it.

So when thought goes looking for what the senses might lay hold of under this name, and says to itself, It is no intelligible form, like life or justice, since it is the stuff of bodies; and it is no object of the senses either, since, being invisible and unformed, there was in it nothing to see or to feel — while a man's thought says this to itself, it can only try either to know it by being ignorant of it, or to be ignorant of it by knowing it.

But I, Lord — if I am to confess to you, with tongue and pen, everything you have taught me about this matter — the truth is that I heard its very name before I understood it, from people who spoke of it without understanding it themselves; and I pictured it with countless forms of every kind, which is to say I did not picture it at all. My mind churned up foul and hideous forms, everything out of order — but forms still — and I called what I saw 'formless' not because it lacked form, but because its form was such that, had it actually appeared, my senses would have recoiled from it as something freakish and wrong, and my human weakness would have been shaken. Even then, what I was imagining was formless not because every form had been stripped from it, but only in comparison with lovelier forms. And true reason kept persuading me that if I meant to conceive the truly formless, I must peel away every last remnant of form whatsoever — and I could not do it. I found it easier to suppose that a thing stripped of all form simply was not, than to conceive of something between form and nothing — neither formed nor nothing: formless, almost nothing. So my mind gave up interrogating my own spirit about it, stuffed as that spirit was with images of formed bodies, which it shuffled and varied at will; and I turned to bodies themselves, and looked more deeply into their changeableness — the way they cease to be what they were and begin to be what they were not. And this crossing from form to form, I began to suspect, passes through something formless, not through sheer nothing. But I wanted to know it, not just suspect it. — Now, if my voice and pen were to confess to you the whole of it, every knot you untied for me in this question, which of my readers would hold out long enough to take it all in? But my heart will not, for that, stop giving you honor, and a song of praise for the things it has no way to say. For the changeableness of changeable things is itself the capacity for all the forms into which changeable things change. And this changeableness — what is it? Soul? Body? Some mode of soul or body? If one could say 'a nothing-something,' or 'an is that isn't,' that is what I would call it. And yet even then it in some way was, since it could receive these visible, composite appearances.

But, Lord, if I were to confess to you with my tongue and my pen the whole of whatever you have taught me about that matter — I, who used to hear the very name before I understood it, when those who did not understand it told me of it, and so I pictured it as having countless different forms, and therefore did not picture it at all, my mind tossing up foul and horrible shapes, all out of order, but still shapes; and I called it formless not because it lacked all form, but because it had the sort my mind would turn away from if it met them, as strange and jarring, the sort that would trouble human frailty. And even what I did picture was formless not because it was stripped of every form, but only by comparison with more beautiful forms. True reason kept persuading me that I must strip off every last remnant of form whatsoever, if I wanted to conceive matter utterly without form — and I could not. Sooner could I judge that a thing deprived of all form simply did not exist, than conceive something halfway between form and nothing, neither formed nor nothing, a formless almost-nothing. So my mind gave up questioning my own spirit about it, for my spirit was filled with the images of formed bodies, shifting and varying them as it pleased; and I turned instead to bodies themselves and looked more deeply into their changeableness, by which they cease to be what they were and begin to be what they were not. And this very passing from one form to another I suspected took place through some formless state, and not through sheer nothing — though I longed to know this, not merely to suspect it. If, then, my voice and my pen were to confess to you the whole of every knot you untied for me in this question, what reader could hold on to take it all in? And yet my heart will not for that reason stop giving you honor and a song of praise for the things it cannot put into words. For the changeableness of changeable things is itself capable of taking on all the forms into which changeable things are changed. And this changeableness — what is it? Is it soul? Is it body? Is it some likeness of soul or body? If one could say a nothing-something, an is-and-is-not, I would say it was this; and yet in some way it already was, since it was capable of receiving these visible, composite shapes.

And where did it get even that degree of being, if not from you, from whom all things are, insofar as they are? But a thing stands the further from you the less like you it is — and I am not speaking of distance in space. So you, Lord — you who are not one thing in one place and another thing in another, but the Selfsame, and the Selfsame, and the Selfsame: Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God Almighty — you, in the Beginning, which is from you, in your Wisdom, which was born of your substance, made something, and made it from nothing. For you made heaven and earth, and not out of yourself: had they been out of yourself, they would have been equal to your only-begotten Son, and through him to you; and nothing could rightly be your equal that was not of you. And there was nothing else besides you from which you might make them, God — one Trinity, threefold Unity — and therefore you made heaven and earth out of nothing: a great thing and a small thing, since you are almighty and good, and make all things good — the great heaven and the little earth. You were; nothing else was; and out of nothing you made heaven and earth: two things, one near to you, the other near to nothing; one with only you above it, the other with nothing at all below it.

But where did it get even this much of being, except from you, from whom all things have being insofar as they are at all? Only the more unlike you a thing is, the further from you — and not by any distance of place. So you, Lord, who are not one thing here and another thing there, but the Selfsame, the Selfsame, the Selfsame, Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God Almighty — in the Beginning, which is from you, in your Wisdom, which was born of your own substance, you made something, and made it out of nothing. For you made heaven and earth, but not out of yourself; otherwise they would have been equal to your only-begotten Son, and so to you as well, and it could never be right that anything should be equal to you which was not from you. And there was nothing else besides you out of which you might make them, O God, one Trinity and threefold Unity; and so out of nothing you made heaven and earth, a great thing and a small thing, for you are almighty and good, able to make all things good — the great heaven and the little earth alike. You were, and nothing else was, out of which you made heaven and earth: two kinds of thing, one near to you, the other near to nothing; one with you alone above it, the other with nothing below it.

But that heaven of heavens is yours, Lord; while the earth you gave to the sons of men to see and touch was not yet the earth we now see and touch. It was invisible, formless; there was a deep, and no light over it — or rather, darkness was over the deep, meaning more darkness than there was in the deep. For this deep of waters we see now has, even down in its depths, a light proper to its kind, sensed in some fashion by the fish and the creatures that crawl on the bottom. But that whole deep was almost nothing, because it was still altogether formless — and yet already there was something there that could be formed.
