For you, Lord, made the world out of formless matter, and that matter you made out of nothing: you made it next to nothing, in order to make from it the great things that we sons of men wonder at. Truly wonderful is this bodily heaven, the firmament between water and water, which you made on the second day, after the creation of light, saying, Let it be made — and it was made. That firmament you called heaven: heaven, that is, relative to this earth and sea, which you made on the third day, when you gave visible shape to the formless matter you had made before there was any day. For you had already made a heaven before any day — but that was the heaven of this heaven, because in the beginning you had made heaven and earth. And the earth you had made then was this formless matter, because it was invisible and formless, and darkness was over the deep. Out of that invisible, formless earth — out of that formlessness, that almost-nothing — you were to make all the things this changeable world consists of, consists and never holds still; the world whose very changeableness shows itself in this, that times can be noticed in it and counted. For times are made by the changing of things, as the shapes whose matter is that invisible earth are varied and turned.

But that heaven of heavens was for yourself, O Lord. The earth, though — the earth you gave to the sons of men to be seen and touched — was not yet the earth we now see and touch. For it was invisible and unformed, and there was a deep over which there was no light; or rather, darkness was over the deep, that is, more than merely in the deep. For the deep of waters we now see has, even in its depths, a light suited to its nature, perceived in some degree by the fish and the creeping things at the bottom of it. But that whole deep was almost nothing, since up to then it was wholly without form; and yet there was already that which could be formed. For you, Lord, made the world out of formless matter, and that matter you made out of nothing — next to nothing — to make from it the great things we sons of men marvel at. For this bodily heaven is a wonder indeed, this firmament between water and water which, on the second day, after the making of light, you said, Let it be made, and it was made. This firmament you called heaven — the heaven of this earth and sea, which you made on the third day by giving a visible shape to the formless matter you had made before any day. For you had already made a heaven before all days, but that was the heaven of this heaven; because In the beginning you had made heaven and earth. But this earth that you made was formless matter, since it was invisible and unformed and darkness was upon the deep; and out of this invisible and unformed earth, out of this formlessness, this almost-nothing, you were to make all these things of which this changing world consists — though it has no firm standing, for its very changeableness shows itself in this, that times can be marked and counted in it. For times are made by the alterations of things, as the shapes are varied and turned, whose underlying matter is that invisible earth.

That is why the Spirit, the teacher of your servant, in recounting that in the Beginning you made heaven and earth, says nothing about times and nothing about days. For that heaven of heavens which you made in the Beginning is some intellectual creature which, though in no way coeternal with you, the Trinity, still shares in your eternity: through the sweetness of gazing on you in perfect happiness, it holds its own changeableness firmly in check; and clinging to you without one lapse since the moment it was made, it stands beyond the whole rolling turn of times. Nor is that formlessness, the earth invisible and formless, counted among the days either. Where there is no shape and no order, nothing comes and nothing goes; and where nothing comes or goes, there are plainly no days, and no succession of one stretch of time after another.

And so the Spirit, the teacher of your servant, when it tells how In the Beginning you created heaven and earth, says nothing of times, nothing of days. For truly that heaven of heavens which you created in the Beginning is some intelligent creature, which, though in no way coeternal with you, the Trinity, still has a share in your eternity, and through the sweetness of that most happy contemplation of you holds its own changeableness firmly in check; and, never having fallen since it was first made, clinging close to you, it stands beyond all the rolling change of times. And neither is that very formlessness of the earth — invisible and unformed — reckoned among the days. For where there is no shape and no order, nothing comes and nothing goes; and where this is so, there plainly are no days, no turning round of stretches of time.

O let Truth, the light of my heart, speak to me — not my own darkness! I slid down into that darkness and was darkened; but even from there, even from there, I loved you. I lost my way, and I remembered you. I heard your voice behind me calling me back, and I could barely hear it through the uproar of those who have no peace. And now, look — I come back, burning and gasping, to your fountain. Let no one bar my way: I will drink from this, and I will live from this. Let me not be my own life. Out of myself I lived badly — I was death to myself; in you I come alive again. Speak to me; talk with me. I have believed your books, and their words are deep mystery.

O let the Light, the Truth, the Light of my heart, and not my own darkness, speak to me. I slipped down into that darkness and was darkened; but even from there, even from there I loved you. I went astray, and remembered you. I heard your voice behind me, calling me to return, and I scarcely heard it through the uproar of the enemies of peace. And now, look, I am coming back, gasping and panting after your fountain. Let no one keep me from it. From this I will drink, and so I will live. Let me not be my own life; out of myself I lived badly, I was death to myself; in you I come alive again. Speak to me, talk with me. I have believed your Books, and their words are full of mystery.

You have already told me, Lord, with a strong voice in my inner ear, that you are eternal — you who alone have immortality — since no shape and no motion changes you, and your will does not vary with the times; for no will that shifts is immortal. In your sight this is clear to me; let it grow clearer and clearer, I beg you, and in that light let me stay sober under your wings. You have told me too, Lord, with a strong voice in my inner ear, that you made all natures and all substances — the things that are not what you are, and yet are. Only what is not comes not from you: that, and the movement of the will away from you, who are, toward what is in a lesser degree — for that movement is transgression and sin. And you have told me that no one's sin harms you, or disturbs the order of your rule, at the highest point or the lowest. In your sight this is clear to me; let it grow clearer and clearer, I beg you, and in that light let me stay sober under your wings.

Already, Lord, you have told me with a strong voice, in my inner ear, that you are eternal, you who alone have immortality; since you cannot be changed in shape or in motion, and your will is not altered by the passing of time — for no will that varies is immortal. This is clear to me in your sight; let it be made clearer and clearer to me, I beg you, and in that unveiling let me rest soberly under your wings. You have told me also with a strong voice, in my inner ear, that you have made all natures and all substances which are not what you yourself are, and yet are; and that the only thing not from you is what has no being at all, and the swerving of the will away from you, who are, toward something that is to a lesser degree — for that swerving is transgression and sin. And no one's sin either harms you or disturbs the order of your rule, first or last. This too is clear to me in your sight; let it be made clearer and clearer to me, I beg you, and in that unveiling let me rest soberly under your wings.

You have told me too, with a strong voice in my inner ear, that not even that creature is coeternal with you whose only joy is you — the creature that drinks from you with the most persevering purity, and nowhere and never lets go into its own changeableness; with you present to it always, holding itself to you with its whole affection, having no future to wait for and nothing to carry over into a past it remembers, it is neither altered by any change nor stretched out into time. O happy creature, if such a creature exists — happy in clinging to your happiness; happy in you, its everlasting inhabitant, its light! I cannot find a better name for the heaven of heavens that is the Lord's than your house — the house that contemplates your delight without ever tiring of it, without ever leaving it for anything else: one pure mind, made harmoniously one by the settled peace of holy spirits, the citizens of your city in the heavens above these heavens we see.

You have told me also with a strong voice, in my inner ear, that not even that creature is coeternal with you whose whole happiness is you alone, and which, drinking its nourishment from you with a most steadfast purity, nowhere and at no time lets its natural changeableness break out; for, with you ever present to it, to whom it holds with its whole love, it has no future to wait for and carries nothing it remembers off into the past, and so it is neither altered by any change nor pulled apart into times. O blessed creature — if such there is — for clinging to your blessedness; blessed in you, its eternal dweller and its light! I can find no better name for that heaven of heavens which is the Lord's than your house — the house that contemplates your delight without ever lapsing into a turning-away toward something else; one pure mind, knit together in the most perfect oneness by the settled peace of holy spirits, the citizens of your city in the heavenly places, far above these heavenly places that we can see.

From this the soul whose pilgrimage has carried her far away may understand — if she now thirsts for you, if her tears have become her bread while day after day they say to her, Where is your God?, if she now asks one thing of you and seeks only that: to dwell in your house all the days of her life (and what is her life, if not you? and what are your days, if not your eternity — like your years, which do not fail, because you are always the same?) — from this, then, let the soul that is able understand how far above all times you are, eternal: since your house, which has never gone abroad to a far country, though it is not coeternal with you, suffers no vicissitude of time, because it clings to you continually and without failing. In your sight this is clear to me; let it grow clearer and clearer, I beg you, and in that light let me stay sober under your wings.

By this the soul whose pilgrimage has carried it long and far away may understand — if by now it thirsts for you, if by now its tears have become its bread while day after day they say to it, Where is your God? — if by now it asks one thing of you and longs for it, that it may dwell in your house all the days of its life. And what is its life but you? And what are your days but your eternity, your years that do not fail, because you are always the same? By this, then, the soul that is able may understand how far above all times you are, eternal; seeing that your house, which has never gone off into any far country, though it is not coeternal with you, yet by clinging to you ceaselessly and without failing, suffers no changeableness of times. This is clear to me in your sight; let it be made clearer and clearer to me, I beg you, and in that unveiling let me rest soberly under your wings.

And look — there is some formlessness or other in the changes of these last and lowest things. Who will tell me — unless it is a man wandering and tossing among his own fantasies out of the emptiness of his heart — who but such a man would tell me that if all shape were so worn down and eaten away that only formlessness remained, the formlessness through which a thing was changed and turned from one shape to another, that formlessness could by itself exhibit the changes of time? Plainly it could not. Without a variety of motions there are no times; and there is no variety where there is no shape.

There is, I confess, some formlessness or other in these changes of the lowest and last of creatures. And who shall tell me — unless it be some empty-hearted man, who wanders and tosses himself up and down among his own fancies — who but such a one would tell me that, if every shape were so worn and consumed away that only that formlessness remained, through which a thing was changed and turned from one shape to another, this could still display the turning of times? It plainly could not, because without a variety of motions there are no times, and there is no variety where there is no shape.

Weighing all this — as much as you grant, my God, as much as you rouse me to knock, and as much as you open to me when I knock — I find two things you have made that stand outside time, though neither is coeternal with you. One is so formed that without any lapse in its contemplation, without any interval of change — changeable, yet never changed — it enjoys your eternity and your unchangeableness to the full. The other was so formless that it had nothing in it that could be changed from one form to another, in motion or at rest, and so nothing by which it could become subject to time. But you did not leave it formless: before there was any day, in the Beginning you created heaven and earth — the two things I have been speaking of. And the earth was invisible and formless, and darkness was over the deep. Those words convey the formlessness to us — so that minds may be drawn along by degrees which cannot yet conceive a total absence of form that still stops short of nothing — the formlessness out of which another heaven was to be created, and an earth visible and well formed, and waters in their beautiful order, and whatever else the making of this world records as created not without days; because such things are of a kind in which the successions of time can happen, through the ordered alterations of their motions and their forms.

Having considered these things, as much as you give me to, O my God, as much as you stir me up to knock, and as much as you open to me when I knock, I find two things you have made that are not within the reach of time, though neither is coeternal with you. One is so formed that, without any break in its contemplation, without any interval of change — changeable, yet not changed — it fully enjoys your eternity and your unchangeableness. The other was so formless that it had nothing in it that could be changed from one form to another, neither in motion nor in rest, so as to be subject to time. But you did not leave this one formless, for before any day, in the Beginning, you created Heaven and Earth — the two things I have been speaking of. But the Earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was upon the deep. In these words the formlessness is conveyed to us — so that minds unable to conceive an utter absence of all form, short of arriving at nothing, may be led on by degrees — the formlessness out of which another Heaven was to be made, together with a visible and well-formed earth, and the waters set in their different orders, and whatever else is recorded to have been made, not without days, in the forming of the world; things of such a nature that the successive changes of times can take place in them, since they are subject to their appointed alterations of motion and of form.

This, then, is what I understand, my God, when I hear your Scripture say, In the beginning God made heaven and earth; and the earth was invisible and formless, and darkness was over the deep — and does not say on what day you made them. I understand it this way because of the heaven of heavens — that intellectual heaven, where it belongs to intellect to know all at once: not in part, not in a riddle, not through a mirror, but whole, out in the open, face to face; not this thing now and that thing later, but — as I said — all at once, with no succession of times. And because of the earth invisible and formless, which likewise has no succession of times, no 'this now and that later,' since where there is no form there is no distinguishing this from that. Because of these two, then — one formed from the very first, the other utterly formless; the one heaven, but the heaven of heavens, the other earth, but the earth invisible and formless — because of these two, as I understand it, your Scripture said, without mention of days, In the beginning God made heaven and earth. For it added at once which earth it meant. And when the firmament is recorded as made on the second day and called heaven, it points us back to which heaven was meant before, when no days were yet named.

This, then, is what I take it to mean, O my God, when I hear your Scripture say, In the beginning God made Heaven and Earth, and the Earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was upon the deep — and it names no day on which you made them. This is what I take it to mean: that because of the Heaven of heavens, that intelligible Heaven whose minds know all at once — not in part, not darkly, not through a glass, but as a whole, openly, face to face; not this thing now and that thing next, but, as I said, all at once, with no succession of times — and because of the earth invisible and unformed, which likewise has no succession of times, for succession is what gives us this thing now and that thing next, and where there is no form there is no marking off of one thing from another — because of these two, a thing first formed and a thing first formless, the one heaven but the Heaven of heaven, the other earth but the earth invisible and unformed, because of these two, your Scripture said, without mentioning days, In the Beginning God created Heaven and Earth. For at once it added which earth it meant; and since the Firmament is recorded as made on the second day and called Heaven, this tells us which Heaven it had spoken of before, without mention of days.

The wondrous depth of your words! Look — their surface lies before us, smiling on little ones; but the depth is wondrous, my God, a wondrous depth. To look into it makes one shudder — a shudder of reverence, a trembling of love. Its enemies I hate with a vehement hatred: oh, that you would slay them with your two-edged sword, so that they would be its enemies no longer! For this is how I love them slain: slain to themselves, so that they may live to you. But look — here are others, not fault-finders but praisers of the book of Genesis, who say: 'The Spirit of God, who wrote these things through his servant Moses, did not want these words understood the way you read them. He did not mean what you say; he meant what we say.' To them, God of us all, with you as judge, I make this answer.

What a marvelous depth there is in your words! Their surface, look, lies open before us, inviting the little ones; and yet, what a marvelous depth, O my God, a marvelous depth! It strikes awe to look into it — the awe of honor, the trembling of love. Its enemies I hate fiercely; oh that you would slay them with your two-edged sword, that they might be its enemies no longer! For this is how I love to have them slain to themselves: that they may live to you. But look, there are others who do not find fault with the book of Genesis but praise it, and yet they say: The Spirit of God, who wrote these things through his servant Moses, did not mean those words to be understood as you say, but otherwise, as we say. To them, with you as judge over us all, my God, this is how I answer.

'Will you call it false, what Truth tells me with a strong voice in my inner ear about the real eternity of the Creator — that his substance changes in no way through time, and that his will is nothing apart from his substance? Which is why he does not will one thing now and another thing later: whatever he wills, he wills once, and all at once, and always. Not again and again, not now this and now that; he does not later will what he did not will before, or unwill what he willed — because a will like that is changeable, and nothing changeable is eternal; but our God is eternal. And this too, which he tells me in my inner ear: the expectation of things to come turns into sight when they come, and sight turns into memory when they have passed. All attention that varies like that is changeable — and nothing changeable is eternal; but our God is eternal.' These things I gather up and put together, and I find that my God, the eternal God, did not found creation by some new act of will, and that his knowledge admits nothing that merely passes. 'What will you say to that, you objectors? Are these things false?' 'No,' they say. 'What then? Is it false that every nature already formed, and every matter capable of form, is only from him who is supremely good, because he supremely is?' 'We do not deny that either,' they say. 'What then — do you deny that there is a certain sublime creature which clings with so chaste a love to the true and truly eternal God that, although it is not coeternal with him, it never detaches itself from him, never spills away into the variety and vicissitude of times, but rests in the utterly true contemplation of him alone?' For you, God, show yourself to whoever loves you as much as you command, and you are enough for him; and this is why he does not swerve from you — not even toward himself. This is the house of God: not earthly, not made of any heavenly mass of body, but spiritual, and a sharer in your eternity, because it is without blemish forever. You have set it fast for ever and ever; you have given it a law, and that law shall not pass away. And yet it is not coeternal with you, God, because it is not without a beginning: it was made.

Will you call it false, what Truth tells me with a strong voice in my inner ear about the eternity of the Creator — that his substance is in no way changed by time, and his will is not separate from his substance? Therefore he does not will one thing now and another thing next, but once, and all at once, and forever, he wills everything that he wills; not again and again, not now this and now that, nor does he will afterward what before he did not, nor stop willing what before he willed; for a will like that is changeable, and nothing changeable is eternal — but our God is eternal. And again, what Truth tells me in my inner ear: that the looking-forward to things to come becomes the seeing of them when they are here, and this same seeing becomes memory when they are past; and all thought that varies in this way is changeable, and nothing changeable is eternal — but our God is eternal. These things I gather and put together, and I find that my God, the eternal God, did not make any creature by some new act of will, nor does his knowledge take in anything passing. What will you say, then, you who contradict me? Are these things false? No, they say. What then? Is it false, that every nature already formed, and every matter capable of form, has its being only from him who is supremely good, because he supremely is? No, we do not deny that either, they say. What then? Do you deny that there is a certain lofty creature which clings with so chaste a love to the true and truly eternal God that, though not coeternal with him, it is never torn away from him, never dissolved into the variety and changing of times, but rests in the most true contemplation of him alone? For you, O God, show yourself and are enough for the one who loves you as much as you command; and so he does not turn away from you, nor toward himself. This is the house of God, not made of earthly stuff, nor of any heavenly bulk of body, but spiritual, and a sharer in your eternity, because it is forever without lapse. For you have made it firm forever and ever; you have given it a law it shall not overstep. And yet it is not coeternal with you, O God, because it is not without a beginning — for it was made.

For though we find no time before it — since wisdom was created before all things — this is certainly not that Wisdom fully coeternal and equal with you, our God, its Father, the Wisdom through whom all things were created, the Beginning in whom you made heaven and earth. It is the wisdom that is created: the intellectual nature, which is light because it contemplates the light. For this too, though created, is called wisdom. But whatever the difference between the light that gives light and the light that receives it, that is the difference between the Wisdom that creates and the wisdom that is created — as between the Righteousness that justifies and the righteousness that justification makes. For we too are called your righteousness; as a certain servant of yours says, that we might become the righteousness of God in him. So a certain created wisdom was created before all things: the rational and intellectual mind of your chaste city, our mother, which is above, and is free, and is eternal in the heavens — and in what heavens, if not the heavens that praise you, the heaven of heavens? for this too is the heaven of heavens for the Lord. And though we find no time before it — because what was created before all things precedes even the creature called time — still, before it stands the eternity of the Creator himself, from whom, when it was made, it took its beginning: not a beginning in time, for time did not yet exist, but the beginning of its own creation.

For although we find no time before it, since wisdom was created before all things — not that Wisdom which is altogether equal and coeternal with you, our God, its Father, by whom all things were made, in whom, as the Beginning, you made heaven and earth, but a created wisdom, that is, the intelligent nature which becomes light by contemplating the Light. For this, though created, is also called wisdom. But the difference between the Light that gives light and the light that receives it is the same as the difference between the Wisdom that creates and the wisdom that is created, as between the Righteousness that justifies and the righteousness made by justification. For we too are called your righteousness, since one of your servants says, That we might be made the righteousness of God in him. Since, then, a certain created wisdom was created before all things — the rational and intelligent mind of that chaste city of yours, our mother who is above and is free and eternal in the heavens (in what heavens, if not in those that praise you, the Heaven of heavens? for this also is the Heaven of heavens that belongs to the Lord) — though we find no time before it, because what was created before all things comes before time's own creatures too, yet the Eternity of the Creator himself is before it, the Creator from whom, being made, it took its beginning — not a beginning in time, for time itself was not yet, but the beginning of its being created.

So it comes from you, our God, but in such a way as to be wholly other than you — not the Selfsame. Though we find time neither before it nor within it — because it is fitted to see your face forever and is never drawn away from it, and therefore is never varied by any change — still the possibility of change is in it; and it would grow dark and cold, if it did not cling to you with a great love and shine and glow from you like perpetual noon. O house full of light and beauty! I have loved your loveliness, and the place where the glory of my Lord dwells — my Lord, your builder and your possessor. Let my wandering sigh for you. I say to him who made you: let him possess me too, in you, since he made me too. I have strayed like a lost sheep; but on the shoulders of my shepherd, your builder, I hope to be carried home to you.

And so it is from you, our God, in such a way as to be altogether other than you, and not the Selfsame. For although we find no time before it, nor even in it, since it is fit ever to behold your face and is never drawn away from it, and so is never varied by any change, yet there is in it a liability to change, by which it would grow dark and cold, were it not that, clinging to you with a strong love like a perpetual noon, it shines and glows from you. O house full of light, full of delight! I have loved your beauty, and the place where the glory of my Lord dwells, your builder and possessor. Let my wandering sigh after you; and I say to him who made you, let him take possession of me too in you, since he made me as well. I have gone astray like a lost sheep; yet upon the shoulders of my Shepherd, your builder, I hope to be carried back to you.

What do you say to me now, you objectors I was addressing — you who still believe that Moses was the devoted servant of God and that his books are oracles of the Holy Spirit? Is this house of God not — though not coeternal with God — in its own measure eternal in the heavens, where you look for changes of time in vain, because you will not find them? For that to which it is always good to hold fast to God outstrips every stretching-out and every rolling span of time. 'It is,' they say. 'Then which part of what my heart cried out to my God, when inwardly it heard the voice of his praise — which part of that do you call false? That the matter was formless, and that where there is no form there is no order? But where there was no order, there could be no vicissitude of times; and yet this almost-nothing, since it was not absolutely nothing, was certainly from him from whom is whatever is, in whatever degree it is.' 'That too,' they say, 'we do not deny.'

What do you say to me, you who contradict me, you to whom I was speaking — you who do, after all, believe Moses to have been the holy servant of God, and his books the oracles of the Holy Spirit? Is not this house of God — not coeternal with God, indeed, but in its own measure eternal in the heavens — a place where you look in vain for changes of times, because you will not find them? For that to which it is always good to cling fast to God rises above all stretching-out and all the revolving cycles of time. It is, they say. Then what of all that my heart cried aloud to my God, when inwardly it heard the voice of his praise — what part of it do you call false? Is it that the matter was without form, in which, because there was no form, there was no order; and where there was no order, there could be no turning of times — and yet this almost-nothing, since it was not altogether nothing, was certainly from him, from whom is whatever is, in whatever degree it is? This too, they say, we do not deny.

With these people I want to talk a little now in your presence, my God — with those who grant that everything your Truth whispers within my soul is true. As for those who deny it — let them bark as loud as they like, and deafen themselves. I will keep trying to calm them, to open in them a way for your word. But if they refuse and push me off, I beg you, my God, do not you be silent to me. Speak truly in my heart — only you speak that way — and I will leave them outside, blowing on the dust and kicking the dirt up into their own eyes, and I will go into my inner room and sing you love songs there: groaning, on my pilgrimage, with groans that words cannot carry; remembering Jerusalem, my heart stretched upward toward her — Jerusalem my homeland, Jerusalem my mother — and remembering you who rule over her: her light, her father, her guardian, her husband; her delight, pure and strong; her solid joy and all her good things past telling, all of them at once, because you are the one supreme and true Good. And I will not be turned aside until you gather everything that I am out of this scattered and broken condition into the peace of that dearest mother — where the firstfruits of my spirit already are, and from which all this is certain to me — and shape it, and set it firm forever, my God, my Mercy. But to those who do not call all these truths false — who honor your holy Scripture given through holy Moses, and set it, as we do, at the summit of authority to be followed — and yet contradict me on some point, I answer this: judge for yourself, our God, between my confessions and their contradictions.

With these men I will now talk a little while in your presence, O my God — these men who grant that all these things are true, which your Truth whispers to my soul. For those who deny them, let them bark and deafen themselves as much as they please; I will try to coax them into quiet and to open in them a way for your word. But if they refuse and turn me away, then I beg you, my God, do not be silent to me. Speak truly in my heart, for only you speak so; and I will leave them outside, blowing on the dust and raising it up into their own eyes, and I will go into my room and there sing a song of love to you, groaning with groans beyond words on my pilgrimage, remembering Jerusalem with my heart stretched up toward it — Jerusalem my homeland, Jerusalem my mother, and you who rule over it, the Light-giver, the Father, the Guardian, the Husband, the pure and strong delight, the solid joy, and all good things beyond speech, all of them at once, because you are the one sovereign and true Good. And I will not be turned aside until you gather all of me, out of this scattered and disordered state, into the peace of that mother most dear, where the first-fruits of my spirit already are, and from which I am made sure of these things, and you shape me and make me firm forever, O my God, my Mercy. But to those who do not call all these truths false, who honor your holy Scripture set forth by holy Moses, placing it, as we do, at the very summit of authority to be followed, and yet contradict me on some point, I answer this: be yourself the judge, O our God, between my confessions and these men's contradictions.

For they say: 'All this may be true; but Moses did not have those two things in view when, by the Spirit's revelation, he said, In the beginning God created heaven and earth. Under the name of heaven he did not signify that spiritual or intellectual creature that beholds God's face forever; nor, under the name of earth, that formless matter.' What then? 'That man of God,' they say, 'meant what we say. That is what he declared by those words.' And what is that? 'By the words heaven and earth,' they say, 'he wished first to signify, universally and compactly, this whole visible world — so that afterward, through the numbering of the days, he could lay everything out in detail, piece by piece as it were, everything the Holy Spirit chose to declare in this way. For the people he spoke to were so rough and carnal that he judged only the visible works of God fit to be entrusted to them.' They agree, though, that the earth invisible and formless, and that darksome deep — out of which, as the sequel shows, all these visible things known to everyone were made and set in order through those days — may without any strain be understood as this formless first matter.

For they say: Even if these things are true, still Moses did not have those two in mind when, by revelation of the Spirit, he said, In the beginning God created heaven and earth. He did not mean, under the name of heaven, that spiritual or intelligible creature which always beholds the face of God; nor, under the name of earth, that formless matter. What then? That man of God, they say, meant what we say; this is what he declared by those words. What is that? By the name of heaven and earth, they say, he first meant to signify, all together and in brief, this whole visible world, so that afterward, by listing the several days, he might lay out in detail, piece by piece, all those things which it pleased the Holy Spirit to set forth in this way. For that rough and earthbound people he spoke to was such that he judged them fit to be told only of those works of God that could be seen. They do agree, however, that under the words earth invisible and unformed, and that dark deep — out of which, it is afterward shown, all these visible things we know were made and set in order during those days — one may, not unfittingly, understand this formless first matter.

And now what if another man says that this same formless, jumbled matter was put first under the name of heaven and earth because out of it was created and completed this visible world, with all the natures that appear so plainly in it — this whole which is so often called by the name of heaven and earth? And what if yet another says that invisible and visible nature together are not unfittingly called heaven and earth, so that the whole creation which God made in his Wisdom — that is, in the Beginning — is comprehended under those two words? But since all things were made not from God's substance but out of nothing — because they are not the same as God, and a certain changeableness is in them all, whether they abide, like the eternal house of God, or change, like the soul and body of man — the common matter of all things invisible and visible, still formless but certainly formable, out of which heaven and earth were to be created (that is, the invisible and the visible creature, each now formed) was called by the same names given to the earth invisible and formless and the darkness over the deep; with this distinction, that the earth invisible and formless means corporeal matter before it had any quality of form, and the darkness over the deep means spiritual matter before its unbounded fluidness was reined in, and before Wisdom gave it any light.

What now if someone else should say that this same formlessness and confusion of matter was first set down under the name of heaven and earth for this reason: that out of it was made this visible world, with all the natures that most plainly appear in it, the world that is so often itself called by the name heaven and earth, once it is made and finished? Or what if another should say that the invisible and the visible nature are not inaptly called heaven and earth, and so the whole creation, which God made in his Wisdom — that is, in the Beginning — was gathered up under those two words; but since all things are made not out of the substance of God but out of nothing, because they are not the same as God is, and there is a changeable nature in them all, whether they abide, as the eternal house of God does, or are changed, as the soul and body of a man are — that therefore the common matter of all things visible and invisible, still unformed but capable of form, out of which both heaven and earth were to be made (that is, the invisible and the visible creation once formed), was named by the very same names given to the earth invisible and unformed and to the darkness upon the deep, but with this difference: that by the earth invisible and unformed is meant bodily matter before it took on any form, and by the darkness upon the deep, spiritual matter before any check was put on its unbounded fluidity, before it received any light from Wisdom?

There is still room for a man to say, if he likes, that the already finished and formed natures, visible and invisible, are not what the words heaven and earth signify when we read, In the beginning God made heaven and earth; rather, the still unformed beginning of things, the stuff apt for forming and making, was called by those names — because in it, jumbled together, not yet distinguished by their qualities and forms, lay all the things that now, arranged each in its own order, are called heaven and earth: the one the spiritual creation, the other the corporeal.

And there is still room for a man to say, if he likes, that the already finished and formed natures, visible and invisible, are not what is meant under the name of heaven and earth when we read, In the beginning God made heaven and earth, but rather that the still-unformed first stage of things, the stuff fit to take on form and making, was called by these names, because in it were held together, all confused, not yet sorted out by their qualities and forms, all those things which, now arranged in order, are called Heaven and Earth — the one the spiritual, the other the bodily creation.

Having heard and weighed all of this, I will not fight over words: that is good for nothing but the ruin of the listeners. But the law is good for building up, if a man uses it lawfully; for its end is love out of a pure heart and a good conscience and unfeigned faith. And our Master knew well which two commandments he hung all the Law and the Prophets on. And if I confess all this with burning zeal, my God, light of my eyes in secret, what harm does it do me that these words can be understood in several ways — all of them true? What harm does it do me if I take the writer to have thought something different from what someone else takes him to have thought? All of us who read are certainly straining to track down and grasp the meaning of the man we are reading; and since we believe he speaks the truth, we do not dare suppose he said anything we know or think to be false. So while each of us is trying to understand, in the holy Scriptures, the same thing the writer understood, what is the harm if a man understands what you — the light of every truthful mind — show him to be true, even if the author he is reading did not understand this, since the author too understood a truth, though not this one?

Having heard and weighed all this, I have no wish to fight about words, which is good for nothing but the ruin of those who listen. The law, though, is good for building up, if a man uses it lawfully, for its end is charity, out of a pure heart and a good conscience and faith unfeigned. And our Master knew well on which two commandments he hung all the Law and the Prophets. So what does it matter to me, O my God, light of my eyes in their secret place, while I confess these things in earnest — since many things, all of them true, may be understood under these words — what, I say, does it harm me if I think the writer meant one thing where another thinks he meant something else? All of us who read are truly trying to track down and grasp the meaning of the one we read; and since we believe he spoke the truth, we dare not imagine him to have said anything we ourselves know or believe to be false. So while each one is straining to understand in the holy Scriptures the very thing the writer understood, what harm is there if a man understands something that you, the light of all truth-speaking minds, show him to be true — even if the one he reads did not understand this particular truth, seeing that he too understood a truth, though not this truth?

For it is true, Lord, that you made heaven and earth. And it is true that the Beginning is your Wisdom, in which you made all things. And it is true, again, that this visible world has as its greatest parts the heaven and the earth — a short way of comprehending the whole of made and established nature. And it is true that whatever changes points us to a certain formlessness in it, by which it receives form, or is changed, or turned. It is true that what clings so fast to the unchangeable Form that, although changeable, it is never changed, undergoes no times. It is true that the formlessness which is almost nothing cannot have alternations of time. It is true that what a thing is made of can, by a certain manner of speech, be called by the name of the thing made from it — so the formlessness out of which heaven and earth were made could itself be called 'heaven and earth.' It is true that of all things having form, nothing is nearer to the formless than earth and the deep. It is true that not only everything created and formed, but everything capable of being created and formed, was made by you, from whom all things are. It is true that whatever is formed out of the formless was formless before it was formed.

For it is true, O Lord, that you made heaven and earth; and true that the Beginning is your Wisdom, in which you made all things; and true again that this visible world has for its greater parts the heaven and the earth, which in two words take in all made and created natures. And true that whatever is changeable gives us to understand a certain lack of form, by which it takes on a form, or is changed, or turned. And true that whatever clings to the unchangeable Form in such a way that, though it could be changed, it is never changed, is subject to no times. True that the formlessness which is almost nothing cannot be subject to the change of times. True that the thing a thing is made from may, by a certain way of speaking, be called by the name of the thing made from it; and so that formlessness, out of which heaven and earth were made, might be called heaven and earth. True that of all things having form, none is nearer to having no form than the earth and the deep. True that not only every created and formed thing, but whatever is even capable of being created and formed, you made, you from whom are all things. And true that whatever is formed out of what had no form was unformed before it was formed.

Out of these truths — which none of them doubt whose inner eye you have opened to see such things, and who believe unshakably that your servant Moses spoke in the Spirit of truth — out of all these, one man takes one for himself, and says: In the beginning God made heaven and earth means 'in his Word, coeternal with himself, God made the intelligible and the sensible creation — the spiritual and the corporeal.' Another takes another: In the beginning God made heaven and earth means 'in his Word, coeternal with himself, God made the whole mass of this corporeal world, with all the evident and familiar natures it contains.' Another: 'in his Word, coeternal with himself, God made the formless matter of creation, spiritual and corporeal alike.' Another: 'in his Word, coeternal with himself, God created the formless matter of corporeal creation, in which heaven and earth still lay mingled together — the heaven and earth we now see, distinguished and formed, in the mass of this world.' And another: 'at the very outset of making and working, God made a formless matter that contained heaven and earth confusedly within itself; and out of it, once they were formed, they now stand forth, plain to see, with everything that is in them.'

Out of these truths, which they do not doubt whose inner eye you have enabled to see such things, and who unshakably believe your servant Moses spoke in the Spirit of truth — out of all of these, one man takes this one, who says, In the Beginning God made heaven and earth, meaning, in his Word coeternal with himself God made the intelligible and the sensible, that is, the spiritual and the bodily creation. Another takes this: In the Beginning God made heaven and earth, meaning, in his Word coeternal with himself God made the whole bulk of this bodily world, with all the plain and familiar creatures it holds. Another: In the Beginning God made heaven and earth, meaning, in his Word coeternal with himself God made the formless matter of the spiritual and bodily creatures. Another: In the Beginning God created heaven and earth, meaning, in his Word coeternal with himself God created the formless matter of the bodily creation, in which heaven and earth still lay confused together, the same heaven and earth that, now sorted out and formed, we see today in the bulk of this world. And another, who says: In the Beginning God made heaven and earth, meaning, in the very beginning of his creating and working God made that formless matter, holding confusedly within itself both heaven and earth, out of which, now that they are formed, they stand out and are plain to see, with all that is in them.

And so too with the understanding of the words that follow. Out of all those truths, one man chooses one for himself, and says: But the earth was invisible and formless, and darkness was over the deep — meaning, 'the corporeal thing God made was still only the formless matter of corporeal things, without order, without light.' Another says: The earth was invisible and formless, and darkness was over the deep — meaning, 'this whole, which is called heaven and earth, was still formless, dark matter, out of which were to be made the corporeal heaven and the corporeal earth, with everything in them that our bodily senses know.' Another: 'this whole called heaven and earth was still formless, dark matter, out of which were to be made both the intelligible heaven — elsewhere called the heaven of heavens — and the earth, meaning the whole of corporeal nature, a name that takes in this bodily sky as well: in short, the matter out of which every creature, visible and invisible, was to be created.' Another: 'Scripture did not call that formlessness by the name of heaven and earth. The formlessness already existed, and it is what Scripture called the earth invisible and formless and the darkness over the deep; and Scripture had already said of it that God made heaven and earth — namely, the spiritual and the corporeal creature.' And another: 'a certain formlessness already existed as matter, and of it Scripture had already said that God made heaven and earth — namely, the whole corporeal bulk of the world, divided into its two greatest parts, upper and lower, with all the common and familiar creatures in them.'

And as for the understanding of the words that follow, out of all those truths one man chooses for himself this one, who says, But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was upon the deep, meaning that the bodily thing God made was as yet a formless matter of bodily things, without order, without light. Another says, The earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was upon the deep, meaning that this whole, called heaven and earth, was still a formless and dark matter, out of which the bodily heaven and the bodily earth were to be made, with all the things in them that our bodily senses know. Another says it meaning that this whole, called heaven and earth, was still a formless and dark matter, out of which were to be made both that intelligible heaven, elsewhere called the Heaven of heavens, and the earth, that is, the whole bodily nature, under which name this bodily sky too is taken in — in a word, out of which every visible and invisible creature was to be created. Another says it meaning that Scripture did not call that formlessness by the name of heaven and earth, but that the formlessness already existed, which he called the earth invisible and unformed, and darkness upon the deep, of which it had been said just before that God made heaven and earth, namely the spiritual and bodily creation. And another says it meaning that there already was a certain formless matter, of which Scripture had said before that God made heaven and earth, namely the whole bodily bulk of the world, split into two great parts, the upper and the lower, with all the common and familiar creatures in them.

Suppose someone tried to argue against these last two opinions like this: 'If you will not allow that this formlessness of matter is what the name of heaven and earth signifies, then there was something God had not made, out of which he made heaven and earth. For Scripture nowhere tells us that God made this matter — unless we understand it to be signified by the phrase heaven and earth, or by earth alone, when it is said, In the beginning God made heaven and earth. So in what follows — and the earth was invisible and formless, even though it pleased him to name the formless matter that way — we may understand no other matter than the very matter of which it is written above, God made heaven and earth.' The holders of those two last opinions, hearing this, will answer: 'We do not at all deny that this formless matter was made by God — the God from whom all things are, and are very good; for as we call what is created and formed a greater good, so we grant that what is made capable of creation and form is a lesser good — but still a good. Scripture simply did not record that God made this formlessness, just as it has not recorded many other things — the Cherubim, and the Seraphim, and those the Apostle names one by one: Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, Powers. That God made all of these is perfectly plain. Or if everything is included in the words He made heaven and earth, what shall we say of the waters, over which the Spirit of God moved? If they are included under the word earth, how can that word mean formless matter, when we see the waters, and they are so beautiful? Or if we do take it so, why is it written that out of this formlessness the firmament was made, and called heaven — and not written that the waters were made? For the waters have not stayed formless and invisible: we watch them flow, and how lovely their flowing is. And if they received that beauty when God said, Let the waters under the firmament be gathered together — the gathering itself being their forming — what will be said of the waters above the firmament? If they were formless, they would hardly have deserved so honorable a seat; and yet no word is written by which they were formed. So if Genesis is silent about God making something which neither sound faith nor sure understanding doubts that God made — and no sober teaching will dare to say that those waters are coeternal with God merely because we hear them mentioned in the book of Genesis and never find when they were created — then why, with truth to teach us, should we not understand that this formless matter too, which this Scripture calls the earth invisible and formless and the darksome deep, was made by God out of nothing, and therefore is not coeternal with him, even though the narrative leaves out when it was made?'

Now suppose someone should try to argue against these last two opinions like this: If you will not allow that this formlessness of matter seems to be called by the name of heaven and earth, then there was something God had not made, out of which to make heaven and earth; for Scripture has not told us that God made this matter, unless we take it to be signified by the name of heaven and earth, or of earth alone, where it is said, In the Beginning God made heaven and earth — so that in what follows, and the earth was invisible and unformed (even granting that it pleased him to call the formless matter by this name), we are to understand no other matter than the one God made, of which it was written just above, God made heaven and earth. To this the defenders of either of those last two opinions, when they hear it, will answer: We do not at all deny that this formless matter was created by God, the God from whom are all things, very good; for just as we hold that to be a greater good which is created and formed, so we confess that to be a lesser good which is only made capable of creation and form — yet still good. But we say that Scripture has not set down that God made this formlessness, just as it has not set down many other things, such as the Cherubim and Seraphim, and those the Apostle names so distinctly, Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, Powers — all of which, plainly, God made. Or if in the words, He made heaven and earth, everything is taken in, then what shall we say of the waters, over which the Spirit of God moved? If they are included in the word earth, how then can formless matter be meant by the name of earth, when we see the waters so beautiful? Or if it is so taken, why then is it written that out of the same formlessness the firmament was made and called heaven, while it is not written that the waters were made? For the waters do not remain formless and invisible — we behold them flowing in so lovely a way. But if they received that beauty when God said, Let the waters under the firmament be gathered together, so that the gathering is itself their forming, what shall be said of those waters above the firmament? For if they were formless they would not have been worthy of so honorable a seat, and it is not written by what word they were formed. So if Genesis is silent about God's making of something which God nonetheless did make, as neither sound faith nor sound understanding doubts — and no sober teaching would dare to call these waters coeternal with God, just because we find them named in the book of Genesis while we do not find when they were created — then why, since truth teaches us, should we not understand that the formless matter, which this Scripture calls the earth invisible and unformed and the dark deep, was created by God out of nothing, and so is not coeternal with him, even though this history has left out telling when it was created?

Having heard all this and taken it in, as far as the weakness of my capacity allows — a weakness I confess to you, Lord, though you know it already — I see that two kinds of disagreement can arise when honest reporters tell of something in words: one about the truth of the things themselves, the other about the intention of the one who tells them. It is one question to ask what is true about the making of the creation, and another to ask what Moses, that excellent servant of your faith, wanted his reader and hearer to understand by those words. As for the first kind — away from me, all who imagine they know as truth what is in fact false. As for the second — away from me too, all who imagine Moses wrote what is false. But let me be joined in you, Lord, with the others, and take my delight in you with them — with those who feed on your truth in the wide field of charity. Let us come together to the words of your book, and seek in them your meaning through the meaning of your servant, by whose pen you dispensed them.

Having heard and grasped these things, as far as my small capacity allows — which I confess to you, O Lord, you who know it — I see that two sorts of disagreement may arise when something is related in words by truthful reporters: one about the truth of the things themselves, the other about the meaning of the one who reports them. For we ask one question about the making of the creation, what is true; and another about what Moses, that excellent minister of your faith, would have his reader and hearer understand by those words. As for the first sort, away with all those who imagine they know as true what is in fact false; and as for the second, away with all those too who imagine Moses wrote things that are false. But let me be joined, O Lord, in you, with these others, and let me delight myself in you together with those who feed on your truth in the broad room of charity; and let us draw near together to the words of your book and seek in them your meaning through the meaning of your servant, by whose pen you have dealt them out to us.

But among so many truths that offer themselves to inquirers in those words, understood now one way and now another — which of us can single out the one meaning and say, 'This is what Moses thought; this is what he wanted understood in that account,' with the same confidence he would say, 'This is true' — whether Moses thought it or something else? Look at me, my God — I, your servant, who have vowed in this book a sacrifice of confession to you, and who pray that by your mercy I may pay my vow. Look: can I say, with the same confidence with which I say that in your unchangeable Word you created all things, visible and invisible, that Moses meant nothing else than this when he wrote, In the beginning God made heaven and earth? No. For I do not see into his mind and see that he was thinking this when he wrote it — the way I do see, in your Truth, that the thing itself is certain. He might have had his thought on the mere start of creating, when he said in the beginning; he might have wanted heaven and earth in this place to mean no formed and finished nature, whether spiritual or corporeal, but both of them begun, and still formless. I can see that whichever of these had been said, it could have been said truly; but which of them he had in mind in these words, I do not see in the same way. Yet whether it was one of these, or some other meaning I have not mentioned here, that this great man saw in his mind when he brought out these words, I have no doubt that he saw it truly, and expressed it aptly.

But which of us, among all those many truths that come to mind in those words as they are differently understood, can so single out that one meaning as to declare, This is what Moses thought, this is what he meant to be understood in that history, with the same confidence he would say, This is true, whether Moses thought it or not? For look, O my God, I your servant, who in this book have vowed a sacrifice of confession to you, and pray that by your mercy I may pay my vows to you — can I, with the same confidence with which I declare that in your unchangeable Word you made all things visible and invisible, also declare that Moses meant nothing other than this when he wrote, In the Beginning God made heaven and earth? No. Because I do not see it in his mind, that he was thinking of this when he wrote these things, as I do see it to be certain in your truth. For he might have had his thoughts on God's first act of creating when he said In the beginning; and by heaven and earth, here, he might have meant no formed and finished nature, whether spiritual or bodily, but both of them just begun and still formless. For I see that whichever of the two had been said, it could have been truly said; but which of the two he had in mind when he wrote these words, I do not so plainly see. And yet, whether it was one of these, or some other sense I have not mentioned here, that so great a man saw in his mind when he uttered these words, I do not doubt that he saw it truly and put it aptly.

So let no one badger me now by saying, 'Moses did not think what you say; he thought what I say.' If he asked me, 'How do you know Moses thought what you draw out of his words?' — I ought to take that calmly, and I would answer, perhaps, what I have answered above, or somewhat more fully if he were stubborn. But when he says, 'Moses did not mean what you say but what I say,' while not denying that what each of us says is true — then, O my God, life of the poor, in whose breast there is no contradiction, rain a softness down into my heart, so that I can bear such people patiently. They say this to me not because they are seers who have looked into the heart of your servant and found what they assert; they say it because they are proud. They do not know Moses' opinion; they love their own — not because it is true, but because it is theirs. Otherwise they would love another true opinion just as much, the way I love what they say when they say what is true: not because it is theirs, but because it is true — and precisely because it is true, it is by that fact not theirs. But if they love it because it is true, then it is theirs and mine alike, the common property of all lovers of truth. Their insistence that Moses meant not what I say but what they say — that I refuse; that I do not love. Even if it were so, their boldness belongs not to knowledge but to recklessness: not sight but swollen pride gave it birth. This, Lord, is why your judgments must make us tremble: because your truth is not mine, not his, not anyone's, but belongs to all of us whom you call openly to share in it — warning us, in words of terror, not to hold it as private property, or we will lose it. For whoever claims as his own what you offer to all for their enjoyment, and wants what belongs to everyone to be his alone, is driven from what is common to what is merely his own — that is, from truth to a lie. For he who speaks a lie speaks out of what is his own.

Let no one badger me, then, by saying, Moses did not think as you say, but as I say. For if he were to ask me, How do you know that Moses thought what you draw out of his words? I ought to take it in good part, and would answer perhaps as I have above, or more fully if he kept pressing. But when he says, Moses did not mean what you say, but what I say — and yet does not deny that what each of us says may both be true — then, O my God, life of the poor, in whose bosom there is no contradiction, pour down a softening dew into my heart, that I may bear patiently with those who say this to me. They say it not because they are godly men and have seen in the heart of your servant what they claim, but because they are proud; they do not know Moses' meaning, but love their own — not because it is true, but because it is theirs. Otherwise they would love another true opinion just as much, the way I love what they say when they say something true, not because it is theirs but because it is true, and on that very account no longer theirs, because it is true. But because they insist Moses meant not what I say but what they say, this I do not like, do not love; for even were it so, that rashness of theirs comes not from knowledge but from sheer boldness, and not insight but vanity is its parent. And so, O Lord, your judgments are to be feared, since your truth is not mine, nor his, nor anyone's, but belongs to us all, whom you call openly to share in it, warning us terribly not to treat it as our own private property, or we will be cut off from it. For whoever lays claim to as his own what you set before all to enjoy, and wants for himself alone what belongs to all, is driven out of what is held in common into what is his own — that is, out of truth into a lie. For whoever speaks a lie speaks from what is his own.

Listen, God, best of judges — Truth itself — listen to what I will say to this objector. Listen: I say it before you, and before my brothers who use the law lawfully, aiming it at the end of charity. Listen and see, if it pleases you, what I say to him. For this is the brotherly, peace-making word I return to him: if we both see that what you say is true, and we both see that what I say is true — where, I ask, do we see it? Not I in you, nor you in me: both of us see it in the unchangeable Truth itself, which stands above our minds. Since we do not quarrel, then, about the very light of the Lord our God, why do we quarrel about the thought of our neighbor, which we cannot see the way unchangeable Truth is seen? If Moses himself appeared to us and said, 'This is what I meant,' even then we would not see his meaning — we would believe him. So let us not be puffed up, one on behalf of one man against another, beyond what is written. Let us love the Lord our God with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our mind, and our neighbor as ourselves. Unless we believe that whatever Moses meant in those books, he meant it with a view to those two commandments of charity, we make the Lord a liar — supposing about our fellow servant's mind something other than what he taught. See now how foolish it is, in such an abundance of utterly true meanings that can be drawn from those words, to rush to assert which of them Moses chiefly intended — and, by quarrels that destroy, to offend against charity itself, the very thing for whose sake he said every word we are laboring to expound.

Listen, O God, best of judges, Truth itself, listen to what I say to this man who contradicts me — listen, for I speak before you and before my brothers, who use your law lawfully, to the end of charity. Listen and look, if it please you, at what I say to him. For this is the brotherly and peaceful word I give him back: If we both see that what you say is true, and both see that what I say is true, where, I ask you, do we see it? Surely not I in you, nor you in me, but both of us in the unchangeable Truth itself, which is above our minds. Since, then, we are not quarreling over the very light of the Lord our God, why do we quarrel over the thoughts of our neighbor, which we cannot see as the unchangeable Truth is seen? For even if Moses himself appeared to us and said, This is what I meant, we would not see it, but would only believe it. Let us not, then, be puffed up one against another beyond what is written; let us love the Lord our God with all our heart, all our soul, and all our mind, and our neighbor as ourselves. And with these two precepts of charity in view, unless we believe that Moses meant whatever in those books he did mean, we shall make God a liar, by imagining our fellow servant's mind to be other than what God has taught us. See, then, how foolish it is, amid such a wealth of perfectly true meanings as can be drawn out of those words, to assert rashly which of them Moses chiefly meant, and with ruinous quarrels to wound charity itself — the very thing for whose sake he said everything we are trying to expound.

And yet I, my God — you height of my lowliness and rest of my labor, you who hear my confessions and forgive my sins — since you command me to love my neighbor as myself, I cannot believe you gave Moses, your most faithful servant, a lesser gift than I would have wished and wanted from you for myself, had I been born in his time and had you set me in his place: to dispense, by the service of my heart and tongue, those books which were to profit all the nations for so long afterward, and from such a height of authority to overtop, throughout the whole world, the words of every false and arrogant teaching. Had I been Moses then — and we all come from the same lump, and what is man, that you are mindful of him? — had I been then what he was, and had you charged me with writing the book of Genesis, I would have wished to be given such a power of expression, and such a way of weaving speech, that not even those who cannot yet understand how God creates would reject the words as beyond their strength; that those who already can understand would find whatever true opinion their thought had reached not left out of your servant's few words; and that if another man, in the light of truth, had seen some further truth, that too would not fail to be found in those same words.

And yet I, O my God — you who lift up my lowliness and are the rest of my labor, you who hear my confessions and forgive my sins — since you command me to love my neighbor as myself, I cannot believe that you gave a smaller gift to Moses, your faithful servant, than I would have wished or longed for you to give me, had I been born in his time and had you set me in that office, that through the service of my heart and tongue those books might be handed down which were for so long after to do good to all nations, and from such a height of authority were to overtop all the sayings of false and proud teachings. I should truly have wished, had I then been Moses — for we all come from the same lump, and what is man, unless you are mindful of him? — I would then, had I been what he was, and been charged by you to write the book of Genesis, have wished for such power of expression and such a way of writing to be given me that neither those who cannot yet understand how God creates would reject the words as beyond their reach, nor those who could understand would find any true opinion they had reached by their own thought passed over in those few words of your servant; and that if another man, by the light of truth, had found yet another meaning, that too should not fail to be found in those same words.

For as a spring in its narrow basin is more abundant, and feeds more streams across wider country than any one of those streams, however far it runs from that same source — so the account given by your steward, destined to serve so many future expounders, pours out of a small measure of words whole rivers of clear truth; and from those rivers each man draws off for himself what truth he can about these things — one man one truth, another man another — through longer windings of speech. For some people, when they read or hear these words, picture God like a man, or like some mass endowed with enormous power, who by a new and sudden decision made heaven and earth outside himself, at a certain distance as it were — two great bodies, one above and one below, with everything packed inside them. And when they hear, God said, Let it be made, and it was made, they picture words that began and ended, sounding through time and passing away — and the moment they passed, the thing commanded to exist existed; and whatever else of that sort their familiarity with the world of flesh suggests to them. In such people — little ones still, and carnal — while their weakness is carried along by this humblest style of speech as in a mother's arms, faith is being built up soundly: the faith by which they hold it certain that God made all the natures their eyes see around them in astonishing variety. But if any one of them scorns those words as cheap, and in proud weakness stretches himself out beyond the nest that reared him — alas, the wretch will fall. Have pity, Lord God: do not let the passers-by trample the unfledged chick. Send your angel to set it back in the nest, and let it live there until it can fly.

For just as a spring within a narrow space is more abundant, and feeds streams over wider ground than any one of the streams that flows, after a long way, from that same spring, so the account of that steward of yours, meant to benefit many who would discourse upon it, overflows out of a small measure of language into streams of the clearest truth, from which each one may draw out for himself such truth as he can on these matters — one this truth, another that — by longer roundabout ways of speaking. For some, when they read or hear these words, imagine that God, like a man or some mass endowed with boundless power, by some new and sudden decision made heaven and earth outside himself, as it were at a certain distance, two great bodies above and below, in which all things were to be contained. And when they hear, God said, Let it be made, and it was made, they imagine words that began and ended, sounding in time and passing away, after whose passing the thing came into being that had been commanded to be — and whatever else of this kind their acquaintance with the material world would suggest. In such people, still little ones and earthbound, while their weakness is carried along by this humble manner of speech as in a mother's lap, their faith is wholesomely built up, so that they hold it sure that God made all the natures their eyes behold around them in such marvelous variety. But if any of them, scorning these words as too simple, should in proud weakness stretch himself out beyond the sheltering nest, then — alas — he will fall miserably. Have pity, O Lord God, lest those who pass by trample the unfledged bird, and send your angel to put it back in the nest, that it may live until it can fly.

But there are others for whom these words are no longer a nest but a shaded orchard: they see the fruit hidden in the leaves, and they fly about it rejoicing, and search it out, chattering, and pluck it. For when they read or hear these words, they see that all times, past and future, are outstripped by your eternal, stable permanence — and yet that there is no creature in time that you did not make. They see that your will, because it is the very thing you are, made all things without any alteration in itself, without the rising of any will that was not there before; and that you made them not out of yourself, in your own likeness — the likeness that is the form of all things — but out of nothing: a formless unlikeness, to be formed by your likeness and drawn back to you, the One, each thing according to its appointed capacity, so far as is given to each in its kind; and that all things were made very good, whether they stay close around you or, ranged at their distances through times and places, work or undergo the beautiful changes of the universe. These things they see, and they rejoice in the light of your truth, in the small measure that is possible here.

But there are others to whom these words are no longer a nest but a deep, shady orchard; they see the fruit hidden in it, fly joyously around, and with cheerful cries seek it out and pick it. For when they read or hear these words, they see that all times past and to come are surpassed by your eternal and steadfast abiding, and that even so there is no creature formed in time that is not of your making. They see that your will, because it is the very thing you are, made all things by no change of will, by no will that before was not; and that these things were made not out of yourself, in your own likeness, which is the form of all things, but out of nothing, a formless unlikeness, to be formed by your likeness — returning, each to your Unity, according to the measure appointed to it, as far as is granted to each thing in its kind — and all to be made very good, whether they remain close around you or, removed by degrees in time and place, make or undergo the beautiful changes of the universe. These things they see, and they rejoice, in the small measure they can here, in the light of your truth.

One of them fastens on the words, In the beginning God made heaven and earth, and sees the Beginning as Wisdom — because Wisdom also speaks to us. Another fastens on the same words and takes 'beginning' as the start of things created: In the beginning he made, as if to say, at first he made. Among those who take 'in the Beginning' to mean 'in your Wisdom you made heaven and earth,' one believes 'heaven and earth' names the matter out of which heaven and earth were to be created; another, natures already formed and distinct; another, one formed nature — the spiritual, under the name of heaven — and one formless nature, corporeal matter, under the name of earth. And those who take the names heaven and earth to mean matter still formless, out of which heaven and earth were to be formed, do not take even that in one way: for one, it is the matter from which both the intelligible and the sensible creation were to be completed; for another, only the matter of this sensible, bodily mass, holding in its vast lap all these visible and ready-to-hand natures. Nor do those who believe heaven and earth here means the creation already ordered and arranged read it alike: one takes it as the invisible and the visible both; another, the visible only, in which we look up at the luminous sky and down at the dark earth, and at all the things they contain.

Another bends his mind on what is said, In the Beginning God made heaven and earth, and sees in the Beginning Wisdom, because it also speaks to us. Another likewise bends his mind on the same words, and by Beginning understands the mere starting of things created — In the beginning he made, as if it were said, He at first made. And among those who understand In the Beginning to mean, In your Wisdom you made heaven and earth, one believes that the matter out of which heaven and earth were to be made is what is here called heaven and earth; another, natures already formed and distinct; another, one formed nature, and that a spiritual one, under the name Heaven, and the other formless, a bodily matter, under the name Earth.
