And those who by the names heaven and earth understand matter still formless, out of which heaven and earth were to be formed, do not all understand it in one way either: one means the matter out of which both the intelligible and the sensible creation were to be perfected, another only the matter out of which this sensible bodily mass was to be made, holding in its vast bosom these visible and ordinary natures. Nor do those who believe the creatures already ordered and arranged are here called heaven and earth understand it the same: one means both the invisible and the visible, another only the visible, in which we behold this bright sky and this dark earth, with the things they contain.

But whoever takes In the beginning he made simply as at first he made has no true way to understand heaven and earth except as the matter of heaven and earth — that is, of the entire creation, intelligible and corporeal. For if he tries to take it as the universe already formed, he can rightly be asked: 'If God made this first, what did he make afterward?' After the universe he will find nothing — and then, like it or not, he must hear: 'How is this first, if there is nothing after?' But when he says that God made matter first formless and then formed, he says nothing absurd — provided he is able to tell what comes before what: what by eternity, what by time, what by choice, and what by origin. By eternity, as God is before everything; by time, as the flower is before the fruit; by choice, as the fruit is before the flower; by origin, as the sound is before the song. Of these four, the first and the last are grasped only with great difficulty; the middle two, very easily. For it is a rare and lofty vision, Lord, to behold your eternity making changeable things without changing, and so standing before them. And who has a mind sharp enough to make out, without hard labor, how the sound is before the song? The song is formed sound; and a thing not yet formed can exist, but what does not exist cannot be formed. In this way the matter is before what is made from it — not before because it makes it, for the matter is what is made into it rather than what makes; and not before by any interval of time. We do not first, at one moment, emit formless noises that are not yet song, and later adapt them and hammer them into the shape of a song, the way wood is worked into a chest or silver into a dish; materials of that kind do precede, in time, the forms of the things made from them. But with a song it is not so. When a song is sung, its sound is heard then: there is not first a formless sounding which is afterward formed into a song. Each sound, the moment it sounds, passes away, and you will find nothing of it to gather back and set in order by art. So the song is carried in its own sound, and its sound is its matter — and that very sound is formed so that it may be a song. This is why, as I was saying, the matter of the sounding is prior to the form of the singing: prior not by any power of making the song, for the sound is no craftsman of the song; it is supplied from the body to the singer's soul, for the soul to make a song of it. Not prior in time, either: it is poured out together with the song. Not prior in choice: sound is not better than song, since a song is not merely sound but beautiful sound. But it is prior in origin, because a song is not formed in order to become sound; sound is formed in order to become a song. By this example, let anyone who can, understand how the matter of things was made first, and was called heaven and earth because heaven and earth were made out of it — and yet was not made first in time, since it is the forms of things that give rise to time. That matter was formless; now, in time, it is perceived only along with its form. And still, nothing can be said about that matter except as if it were first in time — though in worth it stands last, since formed things are certainly better than formless ones — and it is preceded by the eternity of the Creator: so that out of nothing there might be that out of which something could be made.

But the one who understands In the Beginning he made no otherwise than as if it were said, At first he made, can only truly understand heaven and earth as the matter of heaven and earth, that is, of the whole intelligible and bodily creation. For if he wished to understand by it the universe already formed, it could rightly be asked of him, If God made this first, what did he make afterward? And after the universe he will find nothing; whereupon, against his will, he must hear another question: How did God make this first, if nothing came after? But when he says, God made matter first formless, then formed, there is no absurdity, provided he is able to tell apart what comes before by eternity, what by time, what by choice, and what in origin. By eternity, as God is before all things; by time, as the flower before the fruit; by choice, as the fruit before the flower; by origin, as the sound before the tune. Of these four, the first and the last are understood only with great difficulty, the two middle ones easily. For it is a rare and lofty sight, O Lord, to behold your Eternity, unchangeably making things changeable, and so being before them. And who, again, is sharp-sighted enough to discern without great labor how the sound is therefore before the tune — because a tune is a formed sound, and a thing not formed can exist, whereas a thing that does not exist cannot be formed? Just so the matter is before the thing made from it: not because it makes that thing, since rather it is itself made; nor before it by any interval of time. For we do not first utter formless sounds without singing, and afterward shape and fit them into the form of a chant, as wood or silver out of which a chest or a vessel is made. For such materials do precede in time the forms of the things made from them; but in singing it is not so, for when it is sung, its sound is heard at once: there is not first a formless sound, afterward formed into a chant. For every sound, as soon as it is made, passes away, and you can find nothing to call back and by art to compose. So the chant is held together in its sound, which sound is its matter. And this is indeed formed, that it may be a tune; and therefore, as I said, the matter of the sound is before the form of the tune — not before it by any power to make it, for a sound is in no way the maker of the tune, but is something bodily, put under the soul that sings, out of which to make a tune; nor first in time, for it is given out together with the tune; nor first in choice, for a sound is no better than a tune, since a tune is not merely a sound but a beautiful sound. But it is first in origin, because a tune does not receive form in order to become a sound, but a sound receives form in order to become a tune. By this example let the one who is able understand how the matter of things was first made and called heaven and earth, because heaven and earth were made from it — and yet it was not made first in time, since it is the forms of things that give rise to time, while that matter was without form, and only now, in time, is an object of the senses together with its form. And yet nothing can be told of that matter except as though it came earlier in time, while in worth it comes last, because formed things are higher than things without form; and it is preceded by the Eternity of the Creator, so that out of nothing there might be something from which something could be made.

In this diversity of true opinions, let Truth herself bring forth concord; and may our God have mercy on us, so that we may use the law lawfully — for the end of the commandment, which is pure charity. And so, if anyone asks me which of these your servant Moses meant, this book is not my confessions unless I confess to you: I do not know. Yet I do know that those readings are true — apart from the carnal ones, about which I have said what seemed needed. And even the hopeful little ones who read that way are not frightened by the words of your Book, which speak high things humbly and say much in few words. But all of us who, I acknowledge, see and speak truth in those words — let us love one another, and together love you, our God, fountain of truth, if truth is what we are thirsty for and not vanity. And let us so honor this servant of yours, the dispenser of this Scripture, filled with your Spirit, as to believe that when he wrote these things by your revelation, his mind was fixed on whatever in them most excels — in the light of truth, and in the fruit of profit.

In this variety of true opinions, let Truth herself bring forth concord; and let our God have mercy on us, that we may use the law lawfully, to its end, the pure charity of the commandment. By this, if anyone asks me, Which of these was the meaning of your servant Moses? — this would not be the language of my Confessions, if I did not confess to you, I do not know. And yet I know that those senses are true, except for the earthbound ones, of which I have said what seemed necessary. And even those hopeful little ones who think in that earthbound way have this benefit, that the words of your Book do not frighten them, since they utter high things in a lowly way, a rich meaning in few words. And all of us who, I confess, see and speak the truth set down in those words — let us love one another, and together love you, our God, the fountain of truth, if we are truly thirsting for it and not for empty things. And let us so honor this servant of yours, the dispenser of this Scripture, full of your Spirit, as to believe that, when by your revelation he wrote these things, he had in view whichever meaning among them most excels both for light of truth and for richness of profit.

So when one man says, 'Moses meant what I mean,' and another, 'No — what I mean,' I think it more reverent to say: why not both, if both are true? And if there is a third truth, and a fourth, and if anyone sees any other truth in those words, why not believe that he saw them all — that great man through whom the one God tempered the sacred writings to the minds of many readers, who would see in them things true and diverse? For my part — and I say it fearlessly, from my heart — if I were writing anything that was to carry supreme authority, I would rather write in such a way that my words carried whatever truth anyone could grasp on these matters, than set down one true opinion so plainly that it shut out the rest — readings with no falsehood in them to offend me. I will not, then, my God, be so rash as to believe that you granted less than this to that great man. When he wrote those words, he perceived and had in mind whatever truth we have managed to find in them — and whatever truth we have not managed to find, or not yet, though it lies in them, waiting to be found.

So when one man says, Moses meant as I do, and another, No, but as I do, I think I speak more reverently when I say, Why not as both, if both are true? And if there is a third, or a fourth, indeed if anyone sees yet another truth in those words, why may he not be believed to have seen all of them — he through whom the one God shaped the holy Scriptures to fit the understandings of many, who would see in them things true but different? For I, at least — and I say it from my heart without fear — were I to write anything to have the highest authority, I would rather write so that whatever truth anyone could grasp on these matters might be conveyed by my words, than set down one meaning of my own so plainly as to shut out the rest, which, not being false, could give me no offense. I will not, then, O my God, be so rash as not to believe that you granted as much to that great man. He, beyond doubt, when he wrote those words, perceived and had in mind whatever truth we have been able to find in them, and whatever we have not been able to find, and are not yet able to, but which may still be found in them.

Last of all, Lord — you who are God, and not flesh and blood — even if a man saw less than the whole, could anything be hidden from your good Spirit, who will lead me into the land of uprightness — anything you yourself were going to reveal through those words to readers still to come, even if the man through whom they were spoken had in mind, perhaps, only one of the many true meanings? If that is how it is, then let the meaning he had in mind stand higher than all the rest. But to us, Lord, show either that same meaning or any other true one you please; so that whether you disclose to us what you disclosed to your servant, or some other meaning by the occasion of those same words, still it is you who feed us, and not error that mocks us. See, Lord my God, how much we have written on a few words — how much! At this rate, what strength of ours, what stretch of ages, would be enough for all your books? Let me then confess to you more briefly in them, and choose some one meaning — true, certain, and good — that you inspire, even where many offer themselves and many may; with this as the good faith of my confession: that if I say what your minister meant, that is right and best, and that is what I must strive for; but if I fail of it, let me still say what your Truth willed to tell me through his words — the same Truth that told him, too, whatever it willed.

Lastly, O Lord, you who are God and not flesh and blood — if a man saw less, could anything be hidden from your good Spirit, who shall lead me into the land of uprightness, anything that you yourself were about to reveal, by those very words, to readers in times to come, even though the one through whom they were spoken perhaps had in mind, among many true meanings, only some single one? And if that is how it is, then let the one he had in mind be the highest of all. But to us, O Lord, either reveal that same meaning, or any other true one that pleases you, so that whether you uncover to us the same as to your servant, or some other by occasion of those words, you may still feed us, and no error deceive us. Look, O Lord my God, how much we have written on a few words — how much, I beg you! What strength of ours, what ages, would be enough for all your books at this rate? Let me, then, confess to you in these things more briefly, and choose some one true, certain, and good sense that you shall inspire, even where many present themselves, where many may; this being the law of my confession: that if I should say what your minister meant, that is right and best, and that is what I should strive for; and if I should not reach it, then I should still say what your Truth willed to tell me by his words — your Truth, which told him too what it willed.

sections.label: Book XIII
sections.title: The Sabbath Without Evening
Creation, the Spirit on the Waters, and the Sabbath That Has No Evening

segments.text: I call on you, my God, my mercy, who made me, and who did not forget me when I forgot you. I call you into my soul, which you are making ready to receive you by the very longing you breathe into it. Do not desert me now that I am calling — you who came ahead of my calling, who pressed me over and over with calls of every kind, so that I would hear you from far off, and turn, and call back to you who were calling me. For you, Lord, wiped out everything I had earned by my evil, not paying back into these hands the wages of the deeds by which I fell away from you; and you came ahead of everything I could earn by my good, to repay the work of your own hands, the hands that made me. Before I was, you were; I was nothing — nothing that could be owed existence. And yet here I am, out of your goodness, which came before all this that you have made me and all this you have made me from. You did not need me. I am not some good that is useful to you, my Lord and my God. It is not that serving you would spare you weariness in your working, or that your power would be less without my service; not that I tend you the way a man tends a field, as if you would go uncultivated unless I cultivated you. No — I serve you and worship you so that it may be well with me, from you: from you, from whom I have even this, that I am a being with whom it can be well.

I call on you, my God, my mercy, who made me and did not forget me even when I was forgetting you. I call you into my soul, which you are making ready for yourself by the longing you breathe into her. Do not abandon me now, as I call on you — you who came before my call and pressed me with so many repeated invitations, in so many forms, that I might hear you from far off and turn back and call on you in turn, you who had been calling after me all along. For you, Lord, wiped out all my deserving of punishment, so as not to repay into my hands what I did when I fell from you; and you came before all my deserving of reward, so as to repay the work of your own hands by which you made me. Because before I existed, you were; and I was nothing at all, to which you might grant existence. And yet, here I am, out of your goodness — your goodness which came before everything you made me out of and everything you made me to be. For you had no need of me. I am not a good of the kind that could be of any use to you, my Lord and my God: not as if you would tire at your work and need my service to spare you, nor as if your power would be diminished without my help, nor as if you were a field that must lie fallow unless I tended you. No — I serve and worship you so that good may come to me from you, from whom it comes that I have a being capable of receiving good at all.

It is from the fullness of your goodness that your creation exists at all — so that a good which could do you no good, and which was not of your own substance, as though it were your equal, might still exist, since it could be made by you. What claim did heaven and earth, which you made in the beginning, ever have on you? Let the spiritual and bodily natures you made in your Wisdom say what they did to deserve you. On you they depended even in their raw and formless state, spiritual or bodily, each ready to slide off into disorder and into a far unlikeness to you — the spiritual, though formless, higher than any formed body; the bodily, though formless, better than sheer nothing. And formless they would have hung upon your Word forever, had not that same Word called them back to your oneness and given them form, so that from you, the one supreme Good, they were all made very good. What did they do to deserve even formlessness, when they would not have been even that, except from you?

For it is out of the fullness of your goodness that your creation holds together — so that a good which could in no way profit you, and was not made out of you (lest it be your equal), might still exist, since it could be made by you. For what claim did heaven and earth have on you, which you made in the Beginning? Let those natures, spiritual and bodily, which you made in your Wisdom, tell what they did to deserve you — even in their first unfinished, formless state, whether spiritual or bodily, on the verge of sliding away into a wild lawlessness, into a likeness to you grown faint and far. (The spiritual, even without form, is higher than the bodily even when formed; and the bodily, even without form, is better than it would be if it were nothing at all.) So they hung upon your Word, formless, unless by that same Word they were called back to your unity and given form, and out of you, the one Sovereign Good, were all made very good. What did they do to deserve from you even to be formless, when they would not have been even this, except from you?

What did bodily matter do to deserve even its invisible, formless state? It was not even that, except that you made it; and since it did not exist, it could not deserve to be made. And what did the raw beginning of the spiritual creation do to deserve even its dark drifting, like the deep — so unlike you? It was the Word that turned it toward the Word that made it; the Word lit it and made it light — not the Light's equal, but formed to the likeness of the Form that is equal to you. For a body, to exist is not the same as to be beautiful; otherwise nothing could be ugly. In the same way, for a created spirit, to live is not the same as to live wisely; otherwise its wisdom could never be lost. Its good is to hold fast to you, always — otherwise the light it gained by turning toward you it loses by turning away, and it slides back into the life that is like the dark deep. We ourselves, who in our souls are spiritual creation, turned away from you, our light; in that life we were once darkness, and we labor still among the remnants of our darkness, until in your Only Son we become your righteousness, like the mountains of God. For we were once your judgments, which are like the great deep.

What claim did bodily matter have on you, even to be invisible and without form? It would not have been even this, had you not made it; and since it was not, it could not deserve from you to be made at all. And the spiritual creature in its first beginning — how could it deserve from you even to drift darkly to and fro like the deep, so unlike you, unless by the same Word it had been turned to the One who created it, and lit by him, become light, though not as his equal, yet shaped to that Form which is your equal? For just as, in a body, to exist is not the same as to be beautiful — or else it could never be deformed — so likewise, for a created spirit, to live is not the same as to live wisely, or else it would be wise unchangeably. But its good is to hold fast to you always; otherwise it loses, by turning away, whatever light it gained by turning to you, and slips back into a life like the dark deep. For we too, who as to the soul are a spiritual creature, when we turned away from you our light, were in that life once darkness; and we still labor among the remnants of our darkness, until in your Only Son we become your righteousness, like the mountains of God. For we have been your judgments, which are like the great deep.

What you said at the beginning of creation — Let there be light, and there was light — I take, not unreasonably, to mean the spiritual creation, because there was already a kind of life there for you to light. But just as it had no claim on you to be the sort of life that could be lit, so, once it existed, it had no claim on you to be lit in fact. Its formlessness could not have pleased you unless it became light — and it became light not by merely existing, but by turning to face the Light that lights it, and holding fast. That it lives at all, and lives in happiness, it owes to nothing but your grace: it was turned, by a change for the better, toward that which can never change for better or worse — toward you; for you alone simply are, and for you, to live is the same as to live in blessedness, because you are your own blessedness.

When you said at the beginning of creation, Let there be light, and there was light, I think it is fair to understand this of the spiritual creature: for there was already a kind of life, which you could illuminate. But just as it had no claim on you for the very life that could be enlightened, so now that it existed, it had no claim to be enlightened either. For its formless state could not have pleased you unless it became light — and not by simply existing, but by gazing on the light that gives light, and clinging to it. That it lived, and lived in happiness, it owes to nothing but your grace, having been turned by a change for the better toward the One who cannot be changed for worse or for better — which you alone are, because you alone simply are. For you, to live and to live blessedly are not two things, since you are your own blessedness.

And what would have been missing from your good — the good that you are to yourself — even if none of this had ever existed, or had stayed formless? You made it not out of any need but out of the overflow of your goodness, reining it in and turning it toward form — not as though your joy were incomplete without it. Your perfection is displeased by imperfection, and so these things were perfected by you, and please you — not as though you were imperfect and needed their perfection to complete your own. For your good Spirit was borne over the waters; the waters did not bear him up, as if he rested his weight on them. When your Spirit is said to rest on people, it is he who makes them rest in him. Your incorruptible and unchangeable will, sufficient in itself and to itself, was borne over the life you had made — the life for which living is not the same as living happily, because it goes on living even while it drifts in its own darkness. What remains for it is to turn to the one who made it, and to live nearer and nearer to the fountain of life; to see light in his light, and be perfected, and lit, and made beautiful.

What, then, could your good be lacking — that good which you yourself are — even if these things had never existed at all, or had stayed without form? You made them not out of any want, but out of the fullness of your goodness, holding them in and turning them into form, not as though your joy needed completing by them. For to you, who are perfect, their imperfection is displeasing, and so they were perfected by you, and please you — not as though you were imperfect and had to be perfected by perfecting them. For your good Spirit was borne above the waters, not borne up by them, as if he rested upon them. For those upon whom your good Spirit is said to rest, he causes to rest in himself. But your incorruptible and unchangeable will, in itself all-sufficient to itself, was borne above that life which you had created — a life for which living and living happily are not one and the same, since it goes on living even while it ebbs and flows in its own darkness; and what remains for it is to be turned back to the One by whom it was made, and to live more and more by the fountain of life, and in his light to see light, and to be perfected, enlightened, and made beautiful.

And look — the Trinity appears to me, in a riddle, in a glass darkly; and the Trinity is you, my God. You, Father, created heaven and earth in the Beginning of our wisdom — in your Wisdom, born of you, equal to you and coeternal with you: that is, in your Son. We have said much already about the heaven of heavens, and the earth invisible and formless, and the dark deep — dark with the drifting instability of spiritual formlessness, until it turned to him from whom it had whatever life it had, and in his light became a life of beauty: the heaven of that heaven which was afterward set between water and water. In the name God, I now recognized the Father, who made these things; in the name Beginning, the Son, in whom he made them; and believing my God to be Trinity, I searched further in his holy words — and there it was: your Spirit was moving over the waters. There is the Trinity, my God: Father and Son and Holy Spirit, creator of all creation.

And now, look — the Trinity appears to me in a glass, darkly, and that Trinity is you, my God. For you, O Father, in him who is the Beginning of our wisdom, which is your Wisdom, born of you, equal to you and coeternal — that is, in your Son — created heaven and earth. Much we have said already of the Heaven of heavens, and of the earth invisible and without form, and of the dark deep, with its restless wandering of spiritual deformity, which would have stayed so unless it had been turned to the One from whom it had whatever life it then had, and by his light become a beautiful life, the heaven of that heaven which was afterward set between the waters and the waters. Under the name of God I now held the Father, who made these things; and under the name of Beginning, the Son, in whom he made them; and believing, as I did, that my God is the Trinity, I searched on in your holy words, and look — your Spirit moved upon the waters. Behold the Trinity, my God: Father, and Son, and Holy Spirit, the Creator of all that is created.

But why, O Light who speak the truth? To you I lift up my heart — do not let it teach me empty things; scatter its darkness and tell me — I beg you by charity, our mother, I beg you, tell me — why does your Scripture wait until it has named heaven, and the invisible formless earth, and darkness over the deep, and only then name your Spirit? Was it because he had to be introduced as borne above — and that could not be said until something had been named that he could be understood to be borne above? He was not borne above the Father, nor above the Son; and he could not rightly be said to be borne above if he were borne above nothing. First, then, the thing he was borne above had to be named; then he, who had to be named in no other way than as borne above it. But why was it fitting that he be introduced in no other way than as borne above?

But what was the reason, O Light that speaks the truth? To you I lift up my heart; let it not teach me empty things. Scatter its darkness, and tell me, I beg you — by our mother, charity, I beg you — tell me the reason why, after the mention of heaven, and of the earth invisible and without form, and of darkness upon the deep, your Scripture should then at last name your Spirit. Was it because it was fitting that knowledge of him should be conveyed as one who is borne above — and this could not be said until first there was named the thing over which your Spirit may be understood to have been borne? For he was not borne above the Father, nor above the Son, nor could he rightly be said to be borne above if he were borne over nothing. First, then, that had to be spoken of over which he might be borne; and then he, of whom it was fitting to speak only as one borne above. But why was it fitting to convey knowledge of him in no other way than as one borne above?

From here, let whoever can follow your apostle with understanding, when he says that your love is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us; and when, teaching about the gifts of the Spirit, he shows us a way that surpasses them all — the way of love; and when he bends his knee to you on our behalf, that we may know the knowledge of the love of Christ, which surpasses knowledge. From the beginning, that surpassing love was borne above the waters. To whom can I say this, and how? How do I speak of the weight of evil desire, dragging down into the sheer drop of the abyss — and of the love that lifts us back up through your Spirit, who was borne above the waters? To whom do I say it? How do I say it? It is not space we sink into and climb out of. What could be more like it — and what less? They are affections; they are loves: the uncleanness of our own spirit, flowing downward under its load of anxious cares, and the holiness of yours, lifting us upward in love of the peace that is past all worry — so that we lift our hearts to you, where your Spirit is borne above the waters, and come at last to the rest that surpasses everything, when our soul has passed through the waters that give no footing.

Let anyone who can follow your Apostle with his understanding, where he says, Because your love is poured out in our hearts by the Holy Spirit who is given to us; and where, speaking of spiritual gifts, he teaches and shows us a still more excellent way, the way of charity; and where he bends his knee to you on our behalf, that we may know the surpassing knowledge of the love of Christ. And so, from the beginning, the Spirit was borne surpassingly above the waters. To whom shall I say this? How put into words the weight of evil desires, dragging down into the steep abyss, and how charity lifts us up again by your Spirit who was borne above the waters? To whom shall I say it? How say it? For it is not in any space that we sink and surface. What could be more alike, and yet what less? These are feelings; these are loves: the uncleanness of our spirit flowing away downward with the love of cares, and the holiness of your Spirit raising us upward by the love of an untroubled rest — that we may lift up our hearts to you, where your Spirit is borne above the waters, and come at last to that surpassing rest, when our soul has passed through the waters that give no foothold.

The angels fell; the human soul fell; and their falling showed how deep the abyss goes — the dark abyss that stood waiting for the whole spiritual creation, if you had not said at the beginning, Let there be light — and there was light, and every obedient intelligence of your heavenly city held fast to you, and rested in your Spirit, who is borne unchangeably above everything that changes. Otherwise even the heaven of heavens would have been, in itself, a dark deep; but now it is light in the Lord. Even in the miserable restlessness of the spirits who fell, who showed their darkness the moment your light no longer clothed them, you make it plain how noble you made your rational creation: nothing less than you will ever be enough to give it rest and happiness — not even itself. For it is you, our God, who will light our darkness; from you comes our garment of light, and then our darkness will be like noon. Give me yourself, my God — give yourself back to me. Look: I love you; and if that is too little, let me love more strongly. I cannot measure my love, to know how far it still falls short of enough — enough for my life to run into your embrace and not turn away again until it is hidden in the hiding place of your face. This much I know: apart from you it goes badly with me — not only around me but inside me; and every abundance that is not my God is, to me, poverty.

Angels fell away, the soul of man fell away, and so they showed how deep the abyss was in that dark depth, ready to swallow the whole spiritual creation, had you not said from the beginning, Let there be light, and there was light, and had not every obedient mind of your heavenly City clung to you and rested in your Spirit, who is borne unchangeably over everything that changes. Otherwise the very heaven of heavens would have been in itself a dark deep; but now it is light in the Lord. For even in that wretched restlessness of the spirits who fell away and discovered their own darkness, once stripped of the garment of your light, you show clearly enough how noble you made the rational creature: nothing less than you will satisfy it for a happy rest — and so, not even itself. For you, O our God, will light up our darkness; from you comes our garment of light, and then our darkness shall be like the noonday. Give yourself to me, my God; restore yourself to me. See, I love you; and if it is too little, let me love more strongly. I cannot measure it well enough to know how much love is still lacking in me, before my life can run into your embrace and not turn away until it is hidden in the hidden place of your presence. This much only I know: that it goes ill with me except in you — not only outside myself but within me too; and all abundance that is not my God is emptiness to me.

But were not the Father and the Son also borne above the waters? If we mean above in space, the way a body is, then not even the Spirit was. But if we mean the unchangeable supremacy of God above everything changeable, then Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were all borne above the waters. Why, then, is it said only of your Spirit? Why only of him — as if he were in a place, who is in no place — of whom alone it is written that he is your Gift? In your Gift we rest; there we enjoy you. Our rest is our place. Love lifts us there, and your good Spirit raises our lowliness up from the gates of death. In your good will is our peace. A body strains by its own weight toward its own place. Weight does not pull only downward; it pulls toward a thing's own place. Fire strains upward, a stone downward: driven by their own weights, they seek their own places. Oil poured in under water rises up above the water; water poured on top of oil sinks down beneath the oil: driven by their own weights, they seek their own places. Out of their place, things are restless; set in their place, they rest. My weight is my love; wherever I am carried, it is love that carries me. By your Gift we catch fire, and we are carried upward; we burn inwardly, and we go. We climb the ascents that are in the heart, and we sing the song of ascents. With your fire — your good fire — we burn, and we go: for we are going up, to the peace of Jerusalem, for I was glad when they said to me, Let us go up to the house of the Lord. There a good will shall set us down, and we shall want nothing else, forever, but to stay there.

But was not the Father, or the Son, also borne above the waters? If this means borne in space, like a body, then neither was the Holy Spirit. But if it means the unchangeable height of the Godhead above all changeable things, then Father and Son and Holy Spirit were all borne above the waters. Why, then, is it said of your Spirit only? Why said of him alone — as if he had been in a place, who is not in any place, of whom alone it is written that he is your Gift? In your Gift we rest; there we enjoy you. Our rest is our place. Love lifts us up there, and your good Spirit lifts our lowliness from the gates of death. In your good pleasure is our peace. A body strives by its own weight toward its own place. Weight does not pull only downward, but toward its own place. Fire tends upward, a stone downward; they are driven by their own weight, they seek their own places. Oil poured under water rises above the water; water poured on oil sinks below the oil: they are driven by their own weights to seek their own places. When they are out of order, they are restless; restored to order, they are at rest. My weight is my love; by it I am carried, wherever I am carried. By your Gift we are kindled and carried upward; we catch fire and go. We climb the ascents that are in our heart, and sing a song of degrees. With your fire, your good fire, we glow, and we go — because we are going upward, to the peace of Jerusalem; for I was glad in those who said to me, We will go up to the house of the Lord. There your good pleasure has set us, so that we may want nothing else but to stay there forever.

Happy the creature that has never known anything else — though it might itself have been something else, had it not been lifted, the moment it was made, with no interval at all, by your Gift, who is borne above everything changeable: lifted by the call in which you said, Let there be light — and there was light. In us the two things happen at separated times: we were darkness, and we are being made light. But of that creature the text says only what it would have been if it had not been lit; and it speaks as though the creature had first been fluid and dark, so that the cause of its being otherwise would stand out — the cause being that it was turned to the unfailing Light, and became light. Whoever can grasp this, let him grasp it; let him ask it of you. Why trouble me about it — as if I were the one who lightens every man who comes into this world?

Blessed is that creature which, being other than you, has known no other condition than this: that as soon as it was made, it was — without any interval — by your Gift, which is borne above everything changeable, caught up by that call in which you said, Let there be light, and there was light. Whereas in us this happens at different times, in that we were darkness and are made light; but of that creature it is said only what it would have been, had it not been enlightened. It is spoken of as if it had been unsettled and dark before, so that the reason it became otherwise might be made plain — namely, that by being turned to the Light that does not fail, it became light. Let whoever can, understand this; and let him ask it of you. Why should he trouble me, as if I could enlighten any man who comes into this world?

Who comprehends the almighty Trinity? And yet who does not talk about it — if it really is the Trinity he is talking about? Rare is the soul that knows what it is speaking of when it speaks of that. Men argue and fight about it; and no one sees that vision without peace. I wish they would consider three things inside themselves — three things far other than the Trinity, but worth naming as a place where they can test themselves and feel how far away they are. I mean these three: being, knowing, willing. For I am, and I know, and I will: I am a being that knows and wills; I know that I am and that I will; and I will to be and to know. Let anyone who can see how inseparable a life is in these three — one life, one mind, one essence — and yet how inseparable a distinction: distinction, and yet inseparable. A man has it right in front of him: let him look into himself, and see, and tell me. But when he has found something in these three and said what he can, let him not think he has found the Unchangeable that is above them — that which is, unchangeably; and knows, unchangeably; and wills, unchangeably. Whether God is Trinity because of these three; or whether all three are in each Person, so that each possesses all; or both at once — wondrously simple and wondrously manifold, its own boundary within itself and yet boundless, by which it is, and is known to itself, and suffices to itself, unchangeably the selfsame in the overflowing greatness of its unity — who can easily conceive it? Who can find any words for it at all? Who would dare, in any way, to pronounce on it rashly?

Which of us grasps the Almighty Trinity? And yet which of us does not speak of it — if indeed it is of it that he speaks? Rare is the soul that, while it speaks of the Trinity, knows what it is speaking of. People argue and contend, yet no one sees that vision without peace. I wish people would consider three things that are in themselves. These three are something altogether different from the Trinity; I only point out where they may test themselves, and prove and feel how far apart the two are. The three I mean are these: to be, to know, and to will. For I am, and I know, and I will. I am one who knows and wills; and I know that I am and that I will; and I will to be and to know. In these three, let whoever can, discern how inseparable a life there is — yes, one life, one mind, one essence — and yet how inseparable a distinction, and still a distinction. A man has it before him; let him look into himself and see, and tell me. But when he has found and can say something of these three, let him not therefore think he has found that which is above them — the Unchangeable, which unchangeably is, and unchangeably knows, and unchangeably wills. Whether, because of these three, there is in God too a Trinity; or whether all three are in each, so that all three belong to each; or whether both at once, in a way past wonder, simply and yet manifoldly, itself a bound to itself within itself, and yet unbounded — by which it is, and is known to itself, and is sufficient to itself, unchangeably the Selfsame, in the overflowing greatness of its unity — who can readily conceive this? Who could in any way put it into words? Who would dare to pronounce on it rashly?

Go forward in your confession, my faith; say to the Lord your God: Holy, holy, holy, Lord my God — in your name we were baptized, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; in your name we baptize, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. For among us too, in his Christ, God made a heaven and an earth: the spiritual and the fleshly members of his Church. And our earth, before it received the form that teaching gives, was invisible and unformed, and we were covered by the darkness of ignorance — for you disciplined man for his sin, and your judgments were like the great deep over him. But because your Spirit was borne above the waters, your mercy did not abandon our misery, and you said: Let there be light. Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near. Repent: let there be light. And because our soul was troubled within us, we remembered you, Lord, from the land of Jordan, and from the mountain that is high as you are, and became small for our sake; our darkness disgusted us, and we turned to you — and there was light. And look: we were once darkness, and now we are light in the Lord.

Go on, then, with your confession, O my faith; say to the Lord your God, Holy, Holy, Holy, O Lord my God. In your name we have been baptized, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; in your name we baptize, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; because among us too, in his Christ, God made heaven and earth — that is, the spiritual and the carnal people of his Church. And our earth, before it received the form of teaching, was invisible and without form, and we were covered with the darkness of ignorance. For you corrected man for his sin, and your judgments were a great deep to him. But because your Spirit was borne above the waters, your mercy did not abandon our misery, and you said, Let there be light. Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand. Repent: let there be light. And because our soul was troubled within us, we remembered you, O Lord, from the land of Jordan, and from that mountain equal to yourself but made small for our sakes; and our darkness displeased us, and we turned to you, and there was light. And behold, we were once darkness, but now we are light in the Lord.

But still by faith, not yet by sight; for by hope we are saved, and hope that is seen is not hope. Still deep calls to deep — but now in the voice of your waterfalls. Still even the one who said, I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as people of flesh — even he does not consider that he has taken hold of it: he forgets what is behind and strains toward what is ahead; he groans under the weight; his soul thirsts for the living God as the deer thirsts for the springs of water, and he says, When shall I come? He longs to be clothed with his dwelling from heaven; and he calls down to the deep below: Do not be shaped by this world — be transformed by the renewing of your mind. And: Do not be children in your thinking; in malice be infants, so that in thinking you may be grown. And: You foolish Galatians — who has bewitched you? But by now it is not his own voice. It is yours — you who sent your Spirit down from on high, through him who ascended on high and threw open the floodgates of his gifts, so that the rushing of the river might gladden your city. For him the friend of the Bridegroom sighs — he who has the firstfruits of the Spirit already, laid up with him — and still he groans within himself, waiting for the adoption, the redemption of his body. For him he sighs, being a member of the Bride; for him he is jealous, being the friend of the Bridegroom — jealous for him, not for himself. For it is in the voice of your waterfalls, not in his own voice, that he calls to that other deep — the deep he trembles for in his jealousy, afraid that just as the serpent seduced Eve with its cunning, so their minds too might be corrupted away from the purity that is in our Bridegroom, your only Son. And what a light of beauty that will be, when we shall see him as he is — when these tears are gone that have been my bread day and night, while every day they say to me: Where is your God?

But as yet by faith and not by sight; for by hope we are saved, and hope that is seen is not hope. As yet deep calls to deep, but now in the voice of your waterfalls. As yet the one who said, I could not speak to you as to spiritual people, but as to carnal — even he does not yet count himself to have laid hold of it, but forgets the things behind and reaches out to the things ahead, and groans under his burden, and his soul thirsts for the living God as the deer thirsts for the streams of water, and he says, When shall I come? — longing to be clothed over with his dwelling that is from heaven. And he calls out to this lower deep, saying, Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind; and, Do not be children in understanding, but in malice be children, so that in understanding you may be grown; and, O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you? But now no longer in his own voice — in yours, who sent your Spirit from above, through him who ascended on high and threw open the floodgates of his gifts, that the rush of his streams might gladden the city of God. For him this friend of the Bridegroom sighs, holding now the first fruits of the Spirit laid up with him, yet still groaning within himself, waiting for the adoption, that is, the redemption of his body. For him he sighs, a member of the Bride; for him he is jealous, as a friend of the Bridegroom; for him he is jealous, not for himself; because it is in the voice of your waterfalls, and not in his own, that he calls to that other deep, over which, being jealous, he is afraid — afraid that, as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so their minds may be corrupted from the purity that is in our Bridegroom, your only Son. Oh, what a light of beauty that will be, when we shall see him as he is, and those tears have passed away that have been my food day and night, while they say to me all day long, Where is your God now?

Look — I too say it: My God, where are you? There you are — there. In you I catch my breath a little, when I pour out my soul beyond myself in the voice of joy and praise, the sound of a crowd keeping festival. And still the soul turns sad again, because it slips back and becomes a deep — or rather, feels that it is a deep still. My faith speaks to it, the faith you kindled to light my feet in the night: Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in the Lord; his word is a lamp to your feet. Hope, and hold on, until the night passes — the mother of the wicked; until the anger of the Lord passes. We were children of that anger once; we were darkness once, and we carry its remnants around in this body, dead because of sin — until the day breathes, and the shadows slip away. Hope in the Lord. In the morning I will stand in your presence and keep watch; I will confess to you forever. In the morning I will stand in your presence, and I will see the saving health of my face — my God, who will bring even our mortal bodies to life through the Spirit who lives in us, because in mercy he has been borne above the dark drifting deep inside us. From him, on this pilgrimage, we have received the pledge that we are already light. Still we are saved by hope; but we are children of light and children of the day, not children of night and darkness — though we were that, once. Between them and us, in this half-light of human knowledge, only you can divide — you who test our hearts, and call the light day and the darkness night. Who can tell us apart, if not you? And what do we have that we did not receive from you — we, vessels made for honor from the same lump out of which others are made for dishonor?

Behold, I too say it: O my God, where are you? See where you are! In you I breathe a little, when I pour out my soul above myself in the voice of joy and praise, the sound of one who keeps a festival. And yet again it is sad, because it slips back and becomes a deep — or rather, perceives that it is still a deep. To it my faith speaks, the faith you have kindled to light my feet in the night: Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in the Lord; his word is a lamp to your feet. Hope and endure, until the night is over — the night, the mother of the wicked — until the wrath of the Lord is past, whose children we too once were, we who were sometimes darkness, and whose remnants we still carry about in our body, dead because of sin, until the day breaks and the shadows flee away. Hope in the Lord: in the morning I shall stand in your presence and gaze on you; I shall confess to you forever. In the morning I shall stand in your presence and shall see the salvation of my face, my God, who will also give life to our mortal bodies by the Spirit who dwells in us, because in mercy he was borne above our inner deep, dark and adrift. From him we have received, on this pilgrimage, a pledge that we should now be light, while we are saved by hope and are children of the light and children of the day — not children of the night, nor of the darkness, which yet we once were. Between them and us, in this uncertainty of human knowledge, you alone divide; you, who test our hearts and call the light day, and the darkness night. For who tells us apart but you? And what do we have that we have not received from you — out of the same lump, vessels made for honor, of which others also are made for dishonor?

And who but you, our God, made over us a firmament of authority — your divine Scripture? For the heaven will be folded up like a scroll; but now it is stretched over us like a skin. Your divine Scripture carries an authority all the higher now that the mortal men through whom you dispensed it to us have died their mortal deaths. And you know, Lord, you know how you clothed human beings in skins when by sin they became mortal. So you stretched out the firmament of your book like a skin — your words, so deeply in harmony with one another, which you spread over us through the ministry of mortal men. By their very deaths, the solid firmament of authority in the words you spoke through them was raised higher, stretched above everything beneath it — higher than it was ever raised while they still lived here. You had not yet stretched out the heaven like a skin; you had not yet spread the fame of their deaths to every side.

Or who but you, our God, made for us that firmament of authority over us in your divine Scripture? For it is said, Heaven shall be folded up like a scroll; and now it is stretched over us like a skin. Your divine Scripture has a more eminent authority because the mortals through whom you dispensed it to us have passed through death. And you know, Lord, you know how you clothed men with skins when they became mortal by sin. So you have stretched out the firmament of your Book like a skin — your words in their harmony, which you spread over us by the ministry of mortal men. For by their very death the solid firmament of authority in the words you set forth through them was stretched more eminently over all who are beneath it than while they lived here. As long as they were alive, it was not stretched so eminently. You had not yet spread out the heaven like a skin; you had not yet enlarged in every direction the glory of their deaths.

Let us look, Lord, at the heavens, the work of your fingers. Clear from our eyes the fog you have spread beneath them. There stands your testimony, which gives wisdom to little ones. My God, perfect your praise out of the mouths of babies and nursing infants. We know no other books that so tear down pride — that so tear down the enemy, the self-defender who resists reconciliation with you by defending his own sins. I know no other words so pure, Lord — none that so persuade me to confess, that so gentle my neck to your yoke and invite me to serve you for nothing. Let me understand them, good Father. Grant that to me, who am placed beneath them; for it was for those beneath them that you made them firm.

Let us look, O Lord, on the heavens, the work of your fingers; clear from our eyes the cloud you have spread beneath them. There is your testimony, which gives wisdom to little ones: perfect your praise, my God, out of the mouths of babes and infants at the breast. For we know no other books that so demolish pride, that so destroy the enemy and the defender, who resists your reconciliation by defending his own sins. I know of no others, Lord, I know of no other words so pure, which so persuade me to confess, and make my neck supple to your yoke, and invite me to serve you for nothing in return. Let me understand them, good Father; grant me this, set as I am beneath them — for it is for those set beneath them that you established them.

There are other waters above this firmament — immortal, I believe, and kept clear of earthly decay. Let them praise your name — the peoples above the heavens, your angels, who have no need to look up at this firmament, no need of reading to know your Word. They behold your face always, and there they read, without syllables sounding in time, what your eternal will wills. They read it; they choose it; they love it. They are reading always, and what they read never passes away; for by choosing and by loving they read the very unchangeableness of your counsel. Their book is never closed; their scroll is never rolled up — for you yourself are their book, and are so eternally. You ranked them above this firmament, which you made firm over the weakness of the peoples below, so that we might look up and learn your mercy there — your mercy, announcing in time the one who made time. For your mercy, Lord, is in the heavens, and your faithfulness reaches to the clouds. The clouds pass; the heaven remains. The preachers of your word pass out of this life into the next; your Scripture stays stretched out over the peoples to the end of the age. Heaven and earth too will pass away, but your words will not pass away: the scroll will be rolled up, and the grass over which it was stretched will wither, and its glory with it — but your Word remains forever. Now he appears to us not as he is, but in the riddle of clouds and through the mirror of heaven; for we too, though your Son loves us, what we shall be has not yet appeared. He looks at us through the lattice of our flesh; and he spoke tenderly, and set us on fire, and we run after his fragrance. But when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. To see him as he is, Lord — that seeing is ours, but not yet.

There are other waters above this firmament, immortal, I believe, and kept apart from earthly corruption. Let them praise your name; let them praise you, the people above the heavens, your angels, who have no need to look up at this firmament, or to learn your Word by reading. For they always behold your face, and there they read, without any syllables of time, what your eternal will wills. They read, they choose, they love. They are forever reading, and what they read never passes away; for by choosing and by loving they read the very unchangeableness of your counsel. Their book is never closed, nor their scroll rolled up, for you yourself are this to them, and are so eternally — because you have set them above this firmament, which you have fixed firmly over the weakness of the lower people, where they might look up and learn your mercy, which announces in time the One who made the times. For your mercy, O Lord, is in the heavens, and your truth reaches to the clouds. The clouds pass away, but the heaven abides. The preachers of your word pass from this life into another, but your Scripture is spread abroad over the people, even to the end of the world. Yet heaven and earth too shall pass away, but your words shall not pass away. Because the scroll shall be rolled together, and the grass over which it was spread shall pass away with all its beauty; but your Word remains forever — which now appears to us under the dark image of the clouds, and through the mirror of the heavens, not as it is. For even though we are the beloved of your Son, it has not yet appeared what we shall be. He looks through the lattice of our flesh, and he spoke us tenderly, and kindled us, and we ran after his fragrance. But when he appears, then we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is. As he is, Lord — such will our seeing be.

For as you are — altogether — only you know; you who are unchangeably, and know unchangeably, and will unchangeably. Your being knows and wills unchangeably; your knowing is and wills unchangeably; your willing is and knows unchangeably. And it does not seem right in your eyes that the unchangeable Light should be known by the lit and changeable creature the way that Light knows itself. So my soul is like dry ground with no water before you: as it cannot light itself from its own resources, it cannot satisfy itself from its own resources either. For with you is the fountain of life — and it is in your light that we shall see light.

For altogether, as you are, you alone know — you who unchangeably are, and unchangeably know, and unchangeably will. Your Essence knows and wills unchangeably; your Knowledge is and wills unchangeably; your Will is and knows unchangeably. Nor does it seem right in your sight that, as the unchangeable Light knows itself, so it should be known by the thing it enlightens, which is changeable. Therefore my soul is like a land where there is no water; for just as it cannot of itself give itself light, so neither can it of itself satisfy itself. For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light.

And who gathered the embittered into one fellowship? They all share one end: a temporal, earthly happiness. Everything they do, they do for that, however they pitch and toss on a countless variety of cares. Who gathered them, Lord, if not you — you who said: Let the waters be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear, the land that thirsts for you? For the sea too is yours; you made it, and your hands formed the dry land. It is not the bitterness of wills that is called sea, but the gathering of the waters. You rein in even the evil cravings of souls; you fix the limits of how far the waters may advance, so that their waves break against each other — and so you make a sea of them, by the order of your rule over all things.

Who gathered the embittered into one society? For they all have one aim — a happiness that is temporal and earthly — and for the sake of it they do everything they do, though they toss up and down in a countless variety of cares. Who, Lord, but you said, Let the waters be gathered together into one place, and let the dry land appear, which thirsts for you? For the sea also is yours, and you made it, and your hands shaped the dry land. It is not the bitterness of men's wills, but the gathering of the waters, that is called the sea; for you restrain the wicked desires of men's souls and set them their bounds, how far they may be allowed to go, so that their waves break against one another. And so you make it a sea, by the order of your dominion over all things.

But the souls that thirst for you, and appear before you, set apart from the fellowship of the sea by another boundary — these you water from a sweet hidden spring, so that the earth may give its fruit. And it gives it: at the command of its Lord and God, our soul buds with works of mercy, each after its kind, loving our neighbor in the relief of his bodily needs — works that hold seed in themselves, after their likeness, since it is from feeling our own weakness that compassion moves us to help the needy the way we would want to be helped if we stood in the same want. And not only in the easy things, like the green herb bearing seed, but in the strong shelter of real help, like the tree that bears fruit: the good work of rescuing a wronged man from the hand of the powerful, and stretching over him the shade of protection — the solid strength of just judgment.

But the souls that thirst for you and stand before you, marked off by other boundaries from the company of the sea — these you water with a sweet spring, so that the earth may bring forth its fruit. And, at your command, O Lord God, our soul may put forth works of mercy after their kind, loving our neighbor in the relief of his bodily needs, having seed in itself after its likeness; when, out of a sense of our own weakness, we feel for the needy so as to help them, helping them as we would want to be helped if we were in like need — and not only in easy things, like the herb that yields seed, but in the protection we give with our utmost strength, like the tree that yields fruit: that is, doing good by rescuing one who suffers wrong from the hand of the powerful, and giving him the shelter of protection by the strong force of just judgment.

So, Lord, so — I beg you: let it rise as you make it rise, as you give joy and strength; let truth spring up from the earth, and righteousness look down from heaven, and let there be lights in the firmament. Let us break our bread with the hungry and bring the homeless poor under our roof; let us clothe the naked, and not turn away from our own flesh and blood. When these fruits have sprung from the earth, look and see that it is good; and let our light, the light of this brief season, break forth — so that rising from this lower harvest of action to the delights of contemplation, holding fast the Word of Life above us, we may appear like lights in the world, fastened to the firmament of your Scripture. For there you teach us to divide between the things of the mind and the things of the senses as between day and night — or between souls given to the mind and souls given to the senses. Once, before the firmament was made, you alone divided light from darkness, in the secret of your judgment; but now your spiritual children too, set and ranked in that same firmament — now that your grace shines out across the world — give light over the earth, and divide day from night, and stand as signs of the times: for the old things have passed away, and look, all is made new; and our salvation is nearer now than when we first believed; and the night is far gone, and the day is near; and you crown your year with blessing, sending laborers of your goodness into your harvest, where the sowing was other men's labor — and sending them out to another sowing too, whose harvest will come at the end. You grant the prayers of the one who asks; you bless the years of the righteous. But you are the same; and in your years, which do not fail, you build a granary for our years as they pass. By an eternal counsel you bestow the goods of heaven on the earth, each in its proper season. To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom — like the greater light, for those who delight in the light of truth seen clear, as at the break of day; to another the word of knowledge through the same Spirit — like the lesser light; to another faith; to another the gift of healing; to another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another the discerning of spirits; to another kinds of tongues — and all these like stars. For one and the same Spirit works them all, giving to each his own portion as he wills, and making stars appear openly, for the good of all. But the word of knowledge, which holds all the sacraments in it and varies with its seasons like the moon, and those other gifts, counted off in turn like stars — they fall short of the brightness of wisdom that gladdens the day, and by just that much they stand at the beginning of the night. Yet they are necessary — necessary for those to whom your most prudent servant could not speak as to spiritual people, but as to people of flesh — he who speaks wisdom among the mature. The natural man, like a baby in Christ still drinking milk, until he grows strong enough for solid food and his eye is steady enough to look at the sun — let him not live in a night stripped of all light; let him be content with the light of the moon and the stars. You reason all this with us, our God, all-wise, in your book — your firmament — so that we may learn to see all things in wondering contemplation, though still among signs and seasons and days and years.

So, Lord, so, I beg you — let it spring up, as you do it, as you give cheerfulness and ability: let truth spring out of the earth, and righteousness look down from heaven, and let there be lights in the firmament. Let us break our bread for the hungry, and bring the homeless poor under our roof; let us clothe the naked, and not despise our own flesh and blood. When these fruits have sprung from the earth, see that it is good; and let our short-lived light break forth, and let us, rising from this lower fruitfulness of action to the delight of contemplation, take hold of the Word of life above, and appear like lights in the world, fixed in the firmament of your Scripture. For there you teach us to divide between things of the mind and things of the senses, as between day and night, or between souls given to one or to the other; so that now it is not you alone who, in the secret of your judgment, divide between light and darkness as you did before the firmament was made, but your spiritual children too, set and ranked in that same firmament — now that your grace is laid open throughout the world — may give light upon the earth, and divide the day from the night, and serve as signs of the seasons: that the old things have passed away and, behold, all things have become new; that our salvation is nearer than when we first believed; that the night is far spent and the day is at hand; and that you will crown your year with blessing, sending the laborers of your goodness into your harvest, in the sowing of which others have labored, and sending them too into another field, whose harvest will be at the end. So you grant the prayers of the one who asks, and bless the years of the just; but you are the same, and in your years that do not fail you prepare a storehouse for our passing years. For by an eternal counsel you bestow on the earth, in their proper seasons, your heavenly blessings. For to one is given by the Spirit the word of wisdom, like the greater light, for those who delight in the clear shining of truth, as for the rule of the day; to another the word of knowledge by the same Spirit, like the lesser light; to another faith; to another the gift of healing; to another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another the discerning of spirits; to another different kinds of tongues — and all these, as it were, the stars. For one and the same Spirit works all of them, distributing to each his own as he wills, and making the stars appear plainly for our profit. But the word of knowledge, in which all the sacraments are contained — varied in their seasons like the moon — and the other gifts reckoned up as if they were stars, in that they fall short of that brightness of wisdom which gladdens the day already spoken of, are only for the rule of the night. For they are needed by those whom your most prudent servant could not address as spiritual, but only as carnal — he who yet speaks wisdom among the perfect. But the natural man, a babe in Christ and fed on milk until he is strong enough for solid food and his eye is able to bear the Sun, let him not dwell in a night forsaken of all light, but be content with the light of the moon and the stars. So you speak to us, our All-wise God, in your Book, your firmament, that we may discern all things in a wonderful contemplation — though still in signs, and seasons, and days, and years.

But first: wash yourselves; be clean. Put wickedness away from your souls and away from the sight of my eyes — so that the dry land may appear. Learn to do good; give the orphan justice; take up the widow's cause — so that the earth may bring forth the green herb for food, and the tree that bears fruit. And come, let us reason together, says the Lord — so that there may be lights in the firmament of heaven, and they may shine upon the earth. That rich man asked the good Master what he should do to lay hold of eternal life. Let the good Master tell him — the Master he took for a man and nothing more; but he is good because he is God — let him tell him that if he wants to come into life, he must keep the commandments: put away the bitterness of malice and wickedness; do not kill, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not bear false witness — so that the dry land may appear, and bring forth the honoring of father and mother, and the love of neighbor. All these, he says, I have kept. Then where do all these thorns come from, if the land is fruitful? Go, tear out the tangled scrub of greed: sell what you have, be loaded with fruit by giving to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and follow the Lord, if you want to be perfect — in the company of those among whom he speaks wisdom, he who knows what to assign to the day and what to the night — so that you too may know it, and for you too there may be lights in the firmament of heaven. And that will not happen unless your heart is there; and your heart will not be there unless your treasure is there, as you heard from the good Master. But the barren earth was grieved, and the thorns choked the word.

But first wash yourselves, be clean; put away evil from your souls and from before my eyes, that the dry land may appear. Learn to do good, defend the orphan, plead for the widow, that the earth may bring forth the green herb for food, and the tree that bears fruit; and come, let us reason together, says the Lord, that there may be lights in the firmament of heaven, and that they may shine upon the earth. That rich man asked the good Master what he should do to gain eternal life. Let the good Master tell him — whom he took for no more than a man, though he is good because he is God — let him tell him that, if he would enter into life, he must keep the commandments; let him put from himself the bitterness of malice and wickedness; let him not kill, not commit adultery, not steal, not bear false witness, that the dry land may appear and bring forth the honoring of father and mother and the love of neighbor. All these, he says, I have kept. Where, then, do so many thorns come from, if the earth is fruitful? Go, root up the spreading thickets of greed; sell what you have, and be filled with fruit by giving to the poor, and you shall have treasure in heaven; and follow the Lord, if you would be perfect, joining the company of those among whom he speaks wisdom, he who knows what to apportion to the day and to the night, that you too may know it, and that for you there may be lights in the firmament of heaven — which there will not be, unless your heart is there; nor will your heart be there, unless your treasure is there, as you have heard from the good Master. But that barren earth was grieved, and the thorns choked the word.

But you, chosen race, you weak things of the world, who have left everything to follow the Lord: go after him, and put the strong to shame; go after him, you beautiful feet, and shine in the firmament, so that the heavens may declare his glory — dividing between the light of the mature, who are not yet like the angels, and the darkness of the little ones, who are not beyond hope. Shine over all the earth; and let the day, blazing with the sun, speak to day the word of wisdom, and the night, glowing with the moon, show to night the word of knowledge. The moon and the stars shine for the night, but the night does not darken them; they light it, in its measure. For look — as though God were saying, Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven — suddenly there came a sound from heaven, like the rush of a violent wind, and tongues appeared, divided as if of fire, and one settled on each of them. And there were made lights in the firmament of heaven, holding the word of life. Run everywhere, holy fires, beautiful fires! You are the light of the world, and you are not shut under a basket. He to whom you hold fast has been lifted high, and he has lifted you high. Run everywhere; be known to all the nations.

But you, chosen generation, you weak things of the world, who have left everything to follow the Lord — go after him, and put the mighty to shame; go after him, you beautiful feet, and shine in the firmament, that the heavens may declare his glory, dividing between the light of the perfect (though not yet as the angels) and the darkness of the little ones (though not to be despised). Shine over the earth; and let the day, lit by the sun, pour out to the day a speech of wisdom, and the night, glowing with the moon, show to the night the word of knowledge. The moon and the stars shine for the night, yet the night does not dim them, since they give it light in its measure. For behold, when God said, as it were, Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, suddenly there came a sound from heaven, as of a rushing mighty wind, and there appeared tongues as of fire, divided, and it sat upon each of them; and there were made lights in the firmament of heaven, having the word of life. Run to and fro everywhere, you holy fires, you beautiful fires; for you are the light of the world, and you are not put under a basket. He to whom you cling is lifted high, and has lifted you high. Run to and fro, and be made known to all the nations.

And let the sea too conceive and give birth to your works; let the waters bring forth the creeping creature that has a living soul. For you who divide the precious from the worthless have become the mouth of God, and through you he said: Let the waters bring forth — not the living soul, which the earth will bring forth, but the creeping creature that has a living soul, and the birds that fly over the earth. For your sacraments, O God, carried by the work of your holy ones, have made their way through the middle of the waves of this world's temptations, to steep the nations in your name, in your baptism. And as they went, great wonders were worked, like the great whales; and the voices of your messengers flew above the earth, close under the firmament of your book — for that was set over them as the authority under which they were to fly, wherever they went. For there is no speech, no language, where their voice is not heard; their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the end of the world — because you, Lord, blessed them and multiplied them.

Let the sea also conceive and bring forth your works; let the waters bring forth the moving creature that has life. For you, separating the precious from the worthless, are made the mouth of God, by which he says, Let the waters bring forth — not the living creature that the earth brings forth, but the moving creature that has life, and the birds that fly above the earth. For your sacraments, O God, by the ministry of your holy ones, have moved amid the waves of the world's temptations, to hallow the nations in your name, in your Baptism. And in the midst of this, many great wonders were worked, like great whales; and the voices of your messengers flew above the earth, in the open firmament of your Book, set over them as the authority under which they were to fly wherever they went. For there is no speech nor language where their voice is not heard, since their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the end of the world, because you, Lord, multiplied them by your blessing.

Am I lying? Am I mixing things together, failing to distinguish between the clear knowledge of these realities in the firmament of heaven and the bodily works done in the surging sea, beneath that firmament? There are things whose knowledge is solid and complete, not growing generation by generation — lights, as it were, of wisdom and of knowledge; and yet these same things are worked out bodily in many changing ways, and one thing grows from another, and they multiply under your blessing, O God. You have relieved the weariness of our mortal senses, letting one thing, grasped once by the understanding of the mind, be figured and voiced in many ways through the motions of the body. The waters brought these forth — but in your Word.
