The needs of peoples estranged from the eternity of your truth brought them forth — but in your Gospel; for it was the waters themselves that cast them up, and the diseased bitterness of those waters was the very reason they issued forth in your Word.

Am I speaking falsely? Or am I confusing things and failing to distinguish between the clear knowledge of these matters in the firmament of heaven, and the bodily works in the surging sea and beneath the firmament of heaven? For there are things whose knowledge is fixed and defined, with no increase by generation — like the lights of wisdom and knowledge — and yet even of these the bodily workings are many and various; and one thing growing out of another, they are multiplied by your blessing, O God, who have refreshed the weariness of mortal senses, so that one thing in the understanding of our mind may, through the motions of the body, be set out and expressed in many ways. These sacraments the waters have brought forth — but in your Word. The needs of the people estranged from the eternity of your truth have brought them forth — but in your Gospel; because the waters themselves cast them up, the diseased bitterness of those waters being the very reason they were sent forth in your Word.

And everything you have made is beautiful — and look, you who made everything are more beautiful than words can say. If Adam had not fallen away from you, the salt brine of the sea would never have poured out of him — the human race: so deeply curious, so stormily swollen, so restlessly rolling up and down. There would then have been no need for your dispensers to work bodily, among many waters, through the senses — their mysterious acts and sayings. For that is what those creeping and flying creatures now suggest to me: people brought in and consecrated by bodily sacraments will get no further unless their soul comes alive at a spiritual depth — unless, after the word of admission, it looks ahead toward completion.

Now all things you have made are fair; but behold, you yourself, who made them all, are unutterably fairer. Had Adam not fallen, the brackishness of the sea would never have flowed out of him — that is, the human race so deeply curious, so stormily swelling, so restlessly tossing up and down — and then there would have been no need for your stewards to work in many waters, in a bodily and sensible way, at mysterious doings and sayings. For so those moving and flying creatures now seem to me to mean: that people, once initiated and consecrated by bodily sacraments, should make no further progress, unless their soul came alive with a spiritual life, and after the word of admission looked forward to perfection.

And so, in your Word, it is not the depth of the sea but the earth, set apart from the bitterness of the waters, that brings forth — not the creeping creature with a living soul, but the living soul itself. For that soul no longer needs baptism, as the heathen need it, as it needed it itself when the waters still covered it — there is no other entrance into the kingdom of heaven, since you appointed this one. It no longer demands marvels and miracles to make it believe; it is not the kind that will not believe unless it sees signs and wonders — for the believing earth now stands separated from the waters that are bitter with unbelief, and tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers. Nor does the earth you founded upon the waters have any need of the flying kind that the waters brought forth at your word. Send your word into it by your messengers. We tell of their working, but it is you who work in them, so that in it they may work a living soul. The earth brings it forth, because the earth is the reason they work this in the soul — just as the sea was the reason they worked upon the creeping creatures and the birds that fly under the firmament of heaven. Of these the earth has no more need — though it feeds on the Fish that was drawn from the deep, at the table you have set before the eyes of believers: he was drawn from the deep in order to feed the dry land. And the birds, though the sea bred them, still multiply upon the earth: the first preachings of the evangelists were called forth by man's unbelief, but the faithful too are urged and blessed by them in a thousand ways, day after day. The living soul, though, takes its beginning from the earth: for only those already faithful profit by holding themselves back from the love of this world, so that their soul may live to you — the soul that was dead while it lived in pleasures. Death-dealing pleasures, Lord; for you, Lord, are the life-giving delight of the pure heart.

And so, in your Word, it is not the depth of the sea but the earth, separated from the bitterness of the waters, that brings forth — not the moving creature that has life, but the living soul. For now this soul has no more need of baptism, as the heathen have, and as it had itself when it was covered with the waters (for there is no other entrance into the kingdom of heaven, since you have appointed this to be the entrance); nor does it look for the wonder of miracles to make it believe, for it is not of the kind that will not believe unless it sees signs and wonders, now that the faithful earth is parted from the waters that were bitter with unbelief. And tongues are a sign, not for those who believe, but for those who do not believe. Nor does that earth which you have founded upon the waters need the flying kind which the waters brought forth at your word. Send your word into it by your messengers; for it is their working we speak of, yet it is you who work in them, that they may bring about a living soul in it. The earth brings it forth, because the earth is the reason they do this in the soul — just as the sea was the reason they worked upon the moving creatures that have life, and the birds that fly under the firmament of heaven, which the earth has no need of; though it feeds on that Fish which was drawn up from the deep, on that table which you have prepared in the presence of those who believe. For he was drawn from the deep for this very purpose: that he might feed the dry land. And the bird, though bred in the sea, is yet multiplied upon the earth. For the unbelief of men was the cause of the first preaching of the evangelists; yet the faithful too are exhorted and blessed by them in many ways, day after day. But the living soul takes its beginning from the earth; for it profits only those already among the faithful to hold themselves back from the love of this world, so that their soul may live to you — the soul that was dead while it lived among pleasures, deadly pleasures, Lord; for you, Lord, are the life-giving delight of the pure heart.

So let your ministers work now upon the earth — not as they worked on the waters of unbelief, preaching and proclaiming through miracles and sacraments and mystic words, where ignorance, the mother of wonder, is held rapt in awe of hidden signs — for that is how faith's entrance comes to the sons of Adam who have forgotten you, while they hide themselves from your face and become a dark deep. Let your ministers work now as on the dry land, standing clear of the whirlpools of the abyss; let them be a pattern for the faithful, by living in front of them and rousing them to imitation. Then people listen not just to hear, but to do. Seek God, and your soul will live — so that the earth may bring forth the living soul. Do not be shaped by this world; hold yourselves back from it. The soul lives by avoiding the very things it dies by desiring. Hold yourselves back from the savage wildness of pride, the sluggish pleasure of self-indulgence, and the false name of knowledge — so that the wild beasts may be tamed, the cattle broken to the yoke, the serpents made harmless. In the allegory, these are the motions of the mind: the haughtiness of pride, the delight of lust, and the poison of curiosity are the motions of a dead soul. For the soul does not die by losing all motion; it dies by leaving the fountain of life — and then this passing world picks it up, and it is shaped to the world's likeness.

Now, then, let your ministers work upon the earth — not as upon the waters of unbelief, by preaching and speaking through miracles and sacraments and mysterious words, where ignorance, the mother of wonder, might fasten on them out of reverence for those secret signs. For such is the way into the faith for the sons of Adam, forgetful of you, while they hide themselves from your face and become a dark deep. No — let your ministers now work as on dry land, parted from the whirlpools of the great deep; and let them be a pattern to the faithful by living before them, and stirring them to imitate. For this is how people listen so as not only to hear but to act. Seek the Lord, and your soul shall live, that the earth may bring forth the living soul. Do not be conformed to the world; hold yourselves back from it; the soul lives by avoiding what it dies by loving. Hold yourselves back from the runaway wildness of pride, the dull pleasure of self-indulgence, and the so-called knowledge that is no knowledge — so that the wild beasts may be tamed, the cattle broken to the yoke, and the serpents made harmless. For these are the motions of our mind under an image: the arrogance of pride, the delight of lust, and the poison of curiosity are the motions of a dead soul; for the soul does not die so as to lose all motion, but it dies by deserting the fountain of life, and so is caught up by this passing world and conformed to it.

But your word, O God, is the fountain of eternal life, and it does not pass away. So the soul's drifting away is checked by your word, when it says to us, Do not be shaped by this world — so that the earth, at the fountain of life, may bring forth a living soul: a soul that keeps itself whole, by your word carried through your evangelists, by imitating the imitators of your Christ. That is what after its kind means; for a man models himself on his friend. Become as I am, he says, because I too became as you are. So in this living soul there will be good beasts, gentle in what they do — for you have commanded: Carry out your work in meekness, and you will be loved by all men — and good cattle, which are not glutted if they eat and do not go hungry if they do not eat; and good serpents, not dangerous for doing harm, but shrewd for taking care — probing this temporal nature only as far as is needed for eternity to be seen clearly, understood through the things that are made. For these creatures obey reason when they are held back from their deadly advance; then they live, and they are good.

But your Word, O God, is the fountain of life eternal, and does not pass away; and so this departure of the soul is held back by your Word, when it is said to us, Do not be conformed to this world — that the earth may bring forth, in the fountain of life, a living soul: a soul made self-controlled in your Word, by your evangelists, by following the followers of your Christ. For this is after its kind, since a man is apt to imitate his friend. Be as I am, he says, for I too am as you are. So in this living soul there shall be good beasts, in gentleness of action — for you have commanded, Carry on your business in gentleness, so you will be loved by all men — and good cattle, which neither have too much if they eat, nor go without if they do not; and good serpents, not dangerous to do harm, but wise to be on guard, searching into this temporal nature only so far as is enough that your eternity may be clearly seen, understood through the things you have made. For these creatures obey reason, when, held back from the deadly hold they would have on us, they live and are good.

For look, Lord our God, our creator: when our affections have been reined back from the love of the world — the love we were dying of, as we lived badly — and the living soul has begun to live, by living well; when the word you spoke through your apostle has come true in us, Do not be shaped by this world — then follows what you added at once: But be transformed by the renewing of your mind. This is no longer after your kind, as though you copied the neighbor who went just ahead of you, or lived on the authority of some better man. You did not say, Let man be made after his kind, but: Let us make man in our image and likeness — so that we might test for ourselves what your will is. That is why your steward, who begot children through the Gospel and did not want to keep them babies forever, nursed on milk and tended like a wet nurse's charges — that is why he said: Be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may test what the will of God is — what is good, and pleasing, and perfect. So you do not say, Let man be made, but Let us make man; not after his kind, but in our image and likeness. For a man renewed in his mind, who sees your truth and understands it, needs no other man to point the way, copying his own kind; by your direction he tests for himself what your will is — what is good, and pleasing, and perfect. And you teach him, now that he is able, to see the Trinity of the Unity and the Unity of the Trinity. So after the plural, Let us make man, comes the singular, And God made man; and after the plural, in our likeness, the singular, in the image of God. So man is renewed in the knowledge of God, according to the image of his creator; and having become spiritual, he judges all things — all things, that is, that are his to judge — and is himself judged by no one.

For behold, O Lord our God, our Creator, when our affections have been held back from the love of the world by which we were dying through evil living, and have begun to be a living soul through good living, and your word which you spoke through your apostle is fulfilled in us — Do not be conformed to this world — there follows that other thing which you went on to add, saying, But be transformed by the renewing of your mind: not now after your kind, as if following a neighbor who went before you, nor living after the example of some better man. For you did not say, Let man be made after his kind, but, Let us make man after our own image and likeness — that we might prove for ourselves what your will is. For this is why that steward of yours, who fathered children by the Gospel, would not have them remain forever babes whom he must feed with milk and cherish as a nurse: Be transformed, he says, by the renewing of your mind, that you may prove what is that good and acceptable and perfect will of God. And so you say, not Let man be made, but Let us make man; nor did you say after his kind, but after our image and likeness. For man, renewed in his mind and beholding and understanding your truth, has no need of another man as his guide so as to follow after his kind; but under your guidance he proves what is that good, acceptable, and perfect will of yours. Indeed you teach him, now made able, to discern the Trinity in the Unity and the Unity in the Trinity. And so, to what was said in the plural, Let us make man, there is added in the singular, And God made man; and to what was said in the plural, after our likeness, there is added in the singular, after the image of God. Thus is man renewed in the knowledge of God, after the image of the One who created him; and being made spiritual, he judges all things — all things that are to be judged — yet he himself is judged by no one.

Now, he judges all things — this answers to his dominion over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air, over all cattle and wild beasts, over all the earth and every creeping thing that creeps upon it. And he exercises it by the understanding of his mind, through which he perceives the things of the Spirit of God. Without that, man, set in a place of honor, has no understanding; he is ranked with the mindless beasts, and becomes like them. So in your Church, our God, according to the grace you have given it — for we are your workmanship, created for good works — the spiritual are not only those who preside spiritually but also those who are spiritually subject to the ones presiding; for this too is how you made man male and female, in your spiritual grace, where by bodily sex there is neither male nor female, as there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free. Spiritual persons, then, whether they preside or obey, judge spiritually. But they do not judge the spiritual knowledge that shines in the firmament — it is not for them to sit in judgment over so high an authority. Nor do they judge your book itself, even where something in it does not shine clear: we bow our understanding beneath it, and hold it certain that even what is closed to our sight is said rightly and truly. A man, though spiritual and renewed in the knowledge of God after the image of his creator, must be a doer of the law, not its judge. Nor does he judge that division between spiritual and fleshly men which is known to your eyes, our God, and has not yet shown itself to us in works, so that we might know them by their fruits; you, Lord, know them already — you divided them and called them in secret, before the firmament was made. Nor does he, spiritual as he is, judge the restless peoples of this world. What business is it of his to judge those outside, when he cannot know who will come in from there to the sweetness of your grace, and who will stay out in the enduring bitterness of godlessness?

But that he judges all things answers to his having dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the air, and over all cattle and wild beasts, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth. For this he does by the understanding of his mind, by which he perceives the things of the Spirit of God; whereas otherwise man, set in honor, had no understanding, and is compared to the brute beasts, and has become like them. In your Church, then, our God, according to the grace you have given it — for we are your workmanship, created for good works — not only those who are spiritually set over others, but those also who are spiritually subject to those set over them. For in this way you made man male and female: in your spiritual grace, where, as to the body's sex, there is neither male nor female, because there is neither Jew nor Greek, neither slave nor free. Spiritual persons, then, whether those set over others or those who obey, judge spiritually — not concerning that spiritual knowledge which shines in the firmament, for they ought not to judge of so supreme an authority; nor may they judge of your Book itself, even where something in it does not shine clearly, for we submit our understanding to it, and hold for certain that even what is closed to our sight is rightly and truly spoken. For so a man, though now spiritual and renewed in the knowledge of God after the image of the One who created him, ought to be a doer of the law, not a judge of it. Neither does he judge of that distinction between spiritual and carnal men, which is known to your eyes, our God, but has not yet disclosed itself to us by works, that by their fruits we might know them. But you, Lord, already know them, and have divided them and called them in secret, before the firmament was made. Nor does he, though spiritual, judge the restless people of this world; for what has he to do with judging those who are outside, not knowing which of them will hereafter come into the sweetness of your grace, and which will remain in the everlasting bitterness of ungodliness?

So man, whom you made in your image, did not receive dominion over the lights of heaven, nor over the hidden heaven itself, nor over the day and the night, which you named before any heaven was founded, nor over the gathering of the waters, which is the sea. He received dominion over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air, over all cattle, over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth. For he judges — approving what he finds right, disapproving what he finds wrong — whether in the celebration of the sacraments by which those people are initiated whom your mercy searches out through many waters; or in that celebration in which the Fish is set forth — the Fish drawn from the deep, on which the devout earth feeds; or in the significations and soundings of words, subject to the authority of your book, like birds flying under that firmament: interpreting, expounding, discoursing, disputing, blessing you and calling upon you — the signs bursting from the mouth and ringing out, so that the people may answer: Amen. That all these words must be spoken aloud in the body has its cause in the deep of this world and the blindness of the flesh: thoughts cannot be seen, so they must be sounded in the ears. And so, though the flying birds multiply upon the earth, they still draw their beginning from the waters. The spiritual man also judges by approving what he finds right and disapproving what he finds wrong in the works and morals of the faithful — in their almsgiving, like the earth bearing fruit; and he judges the living soul, made living by the taming of its affections, in chastity, in fasting, in holy reflection; and he judges the things perceived through the senses of the body. In all these he is now said to judge — in all of them, he also holds the power to set right.

Man, then, whom you made after your own image, did not receive dominion over the lights of heaven, nor over that hidden heaven itself, nor over the day and the night which you named before the foundation of the heaven, nor over the gathering of the waters which is the sea; but he received dominion over the fish of the sea, and the birds of the air, and over all cattle, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth. For he judges and approves what he finds right, and disallows what he finds amiss — whether in the celebration of those sacraments by which they are initiated whom your mercy searches out in many waters; or in that in which the Fish is set forth, drawn from the deep, on which the devout earth feeds; or in the expressions and signs of words, subject to the authority of your Book — signs such as come from the mouth and sound forth, flying as it were beneath the firmament, by interpreting, explaining, discoursing, disputing, blessing, calling upon you, so that the people may answer, Amen. The vocal pronouncing of all these words is occasioned by the deep of this world and the blindness of the flesh, which cannot see thoughts, so that there is need to speak aloud into the ears; and so, although the flying birds are multiplied upon the earth, they still take their beginning from the waters. The spiritual man judges also by approving what is right and disallowing what he finds amiss in the works and lives of the faithful — their almsgiving, like the earth bringing forth fruit; and the living soul, made alive by taming its affections, in chastity, in fasting, in holy meditations; and those things perceived by the senses of the body. Over all these he is now said to judge, and in them he also has the power of correction.

But what is this — what kind of mystery is this? Look, Lord: you bless human beings so that they may increase and multiply and fill the earth. Are you not hinting that we should notice something? Why did you not also bless the light, which you called day, or the firmament of heaven, or the sun and moon, or the stars, or the earth, or the sea? I might have said that you, our God, who created us in your image, had chosen to keep this blessing for man alone — except that you blessed the fish and the whales in the same way, to increase and multiply and fill the waters of the sea, and the birds, to be multiplied over the earth. And I might have said the blessing belonged to every kind that propagates its own line, if I had found it given to the fruit trees and the plants and the beasts of the earth. But Increase and multiply is not said to the plants or the trees or the beasts or the serpents — though all of these, just like the fish and the birds and mankind, increase by generation and preserve their kind.

But what is this, and what kind of mystery? Behold, you bless mankind, O Lord, that they may increase and multiply and fill the earth. Do you not by this give us a hint to understand something? Why did you not likewise bless the light, which you called day; nor the firmament of heaven, nor the lights, nor the stars, nor the earth, nor the sea? I might say that you, O God, who created us after your image, were pleased to give this blessing to man alone — had you not in the same way blessed the fish and the whales, that they should increase and multiply and fill the waters of the sea, and that the birds should be multiplied upon the earth. I might likewise say that this blessing belonged properly to such creatures as are bred of their own kind — had I found it given to the fruit trees and the plants and the beasts of the earth. But now it is not said to the herbs, nor the trees, nor the beasts, nor the serpents, Increase and multiply — even though all these, as well as the fish, the birds, and men, do by generation increase and continue their kind.

What shall I say then, O Truth, my Light? That it was empty — said for nothing? Surely not, Father of piety; far be it from a servant of your word to say that. And if I do not understand what you mean by this phrase, let my betters — those with more understanding than I — make better use of it, each as you have given him to understand. But let my confession too be pleasing in your eyes, when I confess to you, Lord, my belief that you did not speak this way for nothing; and I will not pass over in silence what this passage stirs in me. For it is true, and I do not see what should stop me from reading the figurative sayings of your books this way. I know that what the mind understands in only one way can be given body in many kinds of signs; and that what the mind understands in many ways can be given body in only one kind of sign. Look at the single love of God and of our neighbor: how many sacraments give it body, how many countless languages, and in every language how many countless turns of phrase! So do the offspring of the waters increase and multiply. And look again, whoever you are who read this: Scripture delivers it in one way only, the voice sounds it in one way only — In the beginning God created heaven and earth — and yet is it not understood in many ways? Not by the deceit of error, but by many kinds of true reading. So do the offspring of man increase and multiply.

What, then, shall I say, O Truth, my Light? That it was said idly, with no meaning? Not so, O Father of mercy; far be it from a minister of your word to say so. And if I do not understand what you mean by that phrase, let my betters — those of greater understanding than I — make better use of it, according as you, my God, have given to each man to understand. But let my confession also be pleasing in your eyes, in which I confess to you that I believe, O Lord, you did not speak so in vain; nor will I suppress what this passage suggests to me. For it is true; nor do I see what should keep me from thus understanding the figurative sayings of your Scripture. For I know that a thing understood one way by the mind can be signified in many ways by bodily expressions, and that a thing signified one way by bodily expression can be understood in many ways in the mind. Behold the single love of God and of neighbor — by how many sacraments and countless languages, and in each language by how many countless ways of speaking, it is bodily expressed. So do the offspring of the waters increase and multiply. Observe again, whoever you are who read this: behold, what Scripture sets down and the voice utters in one way only — In the Beginning God created heaven and earth — is it not understood in many ways, not through any deceit of error, but through various kinds of true meanings? So do the offspring of man increase and multiply.

So if we think of the natures of things themselves, literally and not allegorically, then increase and multiply fits everything that comes from seed. But if we take the words as figurative — and I rather think this is what Scripture intends, since surely it does not confine this blessing, for no reason, to the offspring of water-creatures and of man — then multitudes are everywhere: in the spiritual and the bodily creations, as in heaven and earth; in righteous and unrighteous souls, as in light and darkness; in the holy authors who ministered the Law to us, as in the firmament made firm between the waters and the waters; in the fellowship of peoples still in their bitterness, as in the sea; in the ardor of holy souls, as in the dry land; in the works of mercy of this present life, as in the herbs bearing seed and the trees bearing fruit; in the gifts of the Spirit, set shining for our profit, as in the lights of heaven; in affections formed to temperance, as in the living soul. In all of these we meet multitude, abundance, increase. But something that increases and multiplies in such a way that one thing is said in many ways, and one saying is understood in many ways — this we find only in signs given bodily form, and in things conceived by the mind. Signs bodily uttered are the generations of the waters, made necessary by the depth of the flesh; things conceived by the mind are the generations of men, because of the fruitfulness of reason. So we believe, Lord, that to both these kinds you said: Increase and multiply. In this blessing, I understand you to have granted us the power and the faculty both to say in many ways what we understand in one, and to understand in many ways what we read stated darkly in one. So the waters of the sea are filled — waters moved only by their many meanings; and so the earth too is filled with the offspring of men — the dry land whose thirst shows in its longing, and which reason rules.

If, then, we think of the natures of the things themselves, not allegorically but literally, then the phrase increase and multiply fits all things that come from seed. But if we take the words as figuratively spoken — which I rather suppose is the purpose of Scripture, which surely does not for nothing reserve this blessing to the offspring of the water creatures and of man alone — then we find that multitude belongs to spiritual as well as bodily creatures, as in heaven and earth; and to the righteous and the unrighteous, as in light and darkness; and to the holy authors who have been the ministers of the Law to us, as in the firmament set between the waters and the waters; and to the society of people still in the bitterness of unbelief, as in the sea; and to the zeal of holy souls, as in the dry land; and to works of mercy belonging to this present life, as in the herbs bearing seed and the trees bearing fruit; and to spiritual gifts set forth for building up, as in the lights of heaven; and to affections shaped to temperance, as in the living soul. In all these we meet with multitudes, abundance, increase. But what shall increase and multiply in such a way that one thing may be expressed in many ways, and one expression understood in many ways — this we find only in signs bodily expressed, and in things mentally conceived. By signs bodily uttered we understand the generations of the waters, made necessary by the depth of the flesh; by things mentally conceived, the generations of men, on account of the fruitfulness of reason. And it is for this end that we believe you, Lord, said to these kinds, Increase and multiply. For in this blessing I take it that you granted us a power and a faculty both to express in several ways what we understand as one, and to understand in several ways what we read as set down obscurely in one. Thus are the waters of the sea filled, which are not stirred but by various meanings; and thus, by the increase of men, the earth too is filled, whose dryness appears in its longing, and over which reason rules.

I want to say, too, Lord my God, what the next words of your Scripture press on me; and I will say it and not be afraid. For I will speak the truth, with you breathing into me what you willed me to say out of those words; and I believe I can speak the truth by no breath but yours, since you are the Truth, and every man a liar — so whoever speaks a lie speaks from what is his own. Therefore, to speak truth, I will speak from what is yours. Look: you have given us for food every herb bearing seed on the face of all the earth, and every tree that carries in itself the fruit of a tree bearing seed — and not to us alone, but to all the birds of the air, and to the beasts of the earth, and to all creeping things; but not to the fish and the great whales. We were saying that these fruits of the earth signify, in the allegory, the works of mercy that the fruitful earth supplies for the needs of this life. Such an earth was the devout Onesiphorus, to whose household you gave mercy, because he often refreshed your Paul and was not ashamed of his chain. So were the brothers, and such was the fruit they bore, who supplied out of Macedonia what he lacked. But how he grieves over certain trees that did not give him the fruit they owed him, where he says: At my first defense, no one stood by me; everyone deserted me. May it not be counted against them. For these fruits are owed to those who minister the teaching of the Spirit to us out of their understanding of the divine mysteries; owed to them as men. And they are owed to them as the living soul, since they offer themselves as a pattern in every kind of self-mastery. And owed to them again as flying creatures, because of their blessings which are multiplied upon the earth — for their sound has gone out into all lands.

I would also say, O Lord my God, what the next part of Scripture reminds me of; yes, I will say it, and not be afraid. For I will speak the truth, with you breathing into me what you willed me to draw out of those words. By no other inspiration than yours do I believe myself to speak truth, since you are the Truth, and every man a liar. He, therefore, who speaks a lie speaks of his own; and so that I may speak the truth, I will speak of yours. Behold, you have given us for food every herb bearing seed that is upon all the earth, and every tree in which there is the fruit of a tree yielding seed; and not to us alone, but also to all the birds of the air, and to the beasts of the earth, and to all creeping things — but not to the fish and the great whales. Now we said that by these fruits of the earth were signified, figured in an allegory, the works of mercy provided for the needs of this life out of the fruitful earth. Such an earth was the devout Onesiphorus, on whose house you had mercy, because he often refreshed your Paul and was not ashamed of his chains. So did the brethren too bear such fruit, who out of Macedonia supplied what was lacking to him. But how grieved he is over certain trees that did not yield him the fruit due to him, where he says, At my first defense no one stood by me, but all forsook me — I pray it may not be charged against them. For these fruits are due to those who minister the spiritual teaching to us out of their understanding of the divine mysteries; and they are due to them as men; yes, and due to them also as the living soul, which gives itself as an example in all self-control; and due to them also as flying creatures, for their blessings multiplied upon the earth, because their sound went out into all lands.

Only those are fed by these fruits who find their joy in them; and those whose god is their belly find no joy in them. For even in the givers, the fruit is not the thing given but the heart in which it is given. So I can see plainly why he rejoiced — the man who served God, not his belly. I see it, and I rejoice with him. He had received from the Philippians what they had sent by Epaphroditus; and still I see why he rejoiced. What he rejoiced over, he fed on; for he says — and he speaks the truth — I rejoiced greatly in the Lord that now at last your care for me has flowered again: you did care, but the caring had grown weary. So the Philippians, under a long weariness, had dried up — withered, as it were, for bearing this fruit of good work; and Paul rejoices for them, that they have flowered again — not for himself, that they met his need. So he goes on: I am not saying this out of want, for I have learned to be content in whatever state I am. I know how to be brought low, and I know how to abound. In anything, and in everything, I have been schooled to be full and to be hungry, to abound and to suffer need. I can do all things in him who strengthens me.

But those are fed by these fruits who are gladdened by them; and they are not gladdened by them whose god is their belly. For neither in those who yield the fruits is the thing yielded the real fruit, but the mind with which they yield it. He, then, who served God and not his own belly — I see plainly why he rejoiced; I see it, and I rejoice with him. For he had received from the Philippians what they had sent by Epaphroditus to him; and yet I see why he rejoiced. For he fed on the very thing for which he rejoiced; for, speaking the truth, I rejoiced greatly in the Lord, he says, that now at last your care for me has flowered again, in which you were indeed concerned, but it had grown wearisome to you. These Philippians, then, had dried up under a long weariness, and withered, as it were, in the bearing of this fruit of a good work; and he rejoices for them, that they flowered again — not for himself, that they relieved his need. And so he adds, Not that I speak in respect of want, for I have learned, in whatever state I am, to be content. I know how to be brought low, and I know how to abound; in everything and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need. I can do all things in him who strengthens me.

What are you rejoicing over, then, great Paul? What is your joy? What are you fed by — you, a man renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of your creator, a living soul in such command of itself, a tongue like the flying birds, speaking mysteries? For to such living beings this food is owed. What is it that feeds you? Joy. Hear what comes next: Still, you have done well to share in my affliction. That is his joy; that is his food: that they did well — not that his own strain was eased. For he says to you, In my distress, you gave me room; he knew how to abound and how to suffer want, in you who strengthened him. You Philippians know, he says, that in the early days of the Gospel, when I set out from Macedonia, no church shared with me in the account of giving and receiving except you alone; even in Thessalonica you sent, once and then a second time, for my need. Now his joy is that they have come back to these good works: he is glad that they have flowered again, the way a fruitful field is glad when it turns green once more.

At what, then, do you rejoice, great Paul? At what do you rejoice? On what do you feed, O man, renewed in the knowledge of God after the image of the One who created you, you living soul of such self-control, you tongue like the flying birds, speaking mysteries? For to such creatures is this food due. What is it that feeds you? Joy. Let us hear what follows: Nevertheless, you have done well, that you shared in my affliction. At this he rejoices, on this he feeds — because they had done well, not because his hardship was eased; he who says to you, You have set me free when I was in distress. For he knew how to abound and how to suffer want, in you who strengthen him. For you Philippians also know, he says, that in the beginning of the Gospel, when I left Macedonia, no church shared with me in the matter of giving and receiving but you only; for even in Thessalonica you sent once and again to my need. He now rejoices that they have come back to these good works, and is glad that they have flowered again, as a fruitful field puts on its green once more.

Is it for his own needs, then, since he said, you sent for my need? Does he rejoice over that? No — not over that. And how do we know? Because he says at once: Not that I seek the gift; I seek the fruit. From you, my God, I have learned to tell a gift from fruit. The gift is the thing itself, given by the one who shares these necessities: money, food, drink, clothing, shelter, help. The fruit is the good and right will of the giver. For the good Master did not only say, Whoever receives a prophet — he added, in the name of a prophet; and he did not only say, Whoever receives a righteous man — he added, in the name of a righteous man: for so the one will receive a prophet's reward, and the other the reward of a righteous man. And he did not only say, Whoever gives one of my little ones a cup of cold water to drink — he added, in the name of a disciple, and concluded: Truly I tell you, he shall not lose his reward. The gift is receiving the prophet, receiving the righteous man, handing the disciple the cup of cold water; the fruit is doing it in the name of a prophet, in the name of a righteous man, in the name of a disciple. Elijah was fed with fruit by the widow, who knew she was feeding a man of God, and fed him because of that; by the raven he was fed only with a gift. And it was not the inner Elijah who was fed by that, but only the outer man — the man who could have starved for want of such food.

Was it for his own needs, because he said, You sent to my need? Does he rejoice for that? Truly not for that. And how do we know? Because he says at once, Not that I seek a gift, but I seek fruit. I have learned from you, my God, to tell the difference between a gift and fruit. A gift is the thing itself which a man gives who provides us these necessaries — money, food, drink, clothing, shelter, help. But the fruit is the good and right will of the giver. For the good Master did not say only, He who receives a prophet, but added, in the name of a prophet; nor did he say only, He who receives a righteous man, but added, in the name of a righteous man; so that the one shall surely receive the reward of a prophet, the other the reward of a righteous man. Nor did he say only, He who gives a cup of cold water to one of my little ones, but added, in the name of a disciple; and so he concludes, Truly I tell you, he shall not lose his reward. The gift is to receive a prophet, to receive a righteous man, to give a cup of cold water to a disciple; but the fruit is to do this in the name of a prophet, in the name of a righteous man, in the name of a disciple. With fruit was Elijah fed by the widow who knew she was feeding a man of God, and fed him for that reason; but by the raven he was fed with a gift only. Nor was the inner man of Elijah fed in that way, but the outer man only — which might also, for want of such food, have perished.

So I will say what is true in your sight, Lord. When unbelievers and people of the flesh — those for whose winning and initiation the sacraments of entry and the great workings of miracles are necessary, the ones I take to be signified by the names fishes and whales — when such people take up the bodily care of your servants, or help them in something useful to this present life, without knowing why it should be done or to what end, they do not really feed your servants, and your servants are not really fed by them. For the one side does not act from a holy and right will, and the other finds no joy in gifts whose fruit it cannot yet see; and the mind is fed by what it rejoices in. That is why the fishes and the whales do not feed on the foods that only the earth brings forth — the earth set apart, at last, from the bitterness of the waves of the sea.

I will say, then, what is true in your sight, O Lord, that when carnal men and unbelievers — for whose gaining and initiation the initiatory sacraments and the great workings of miracles are needed, which we take to be signified by the names of fish and whales — undertake the bodily refreshment of your servant, or otherwise help him with something useful for this present life, while yet they are ignorant why this is to be done, and to what end, then neither do they feed these servants, nor are these fed by them. For the one do not do it out of a holy and right intent, and the others do not rejoice in their gifts, whose fruit they do not yet see. For the mind is fed by that in which it is glad. And so the fish and the whales do not feed on such food as the earth does not bring forth until after it has been separated and divided from the bitterness of the waves of the sea.

And you, God, saw everything that you had made, and look: it was very good. We too see it all — and look, it is all very good. Kind by kind of your works, when you had said, Let them be, and they were, you saw each one, that it was good. Seven times, by my count, it is written that you saw that what you made was good; and the eighth time, you saw everything that you had made, and look — it was not only good but very good: all of it, now, together. Taken one by one, they were only good; taken all together, they were both good and very good. Every beautiful body says the same: a body whose members are all beautiful is far more beautiful than the members are separately; the whole is completed by their well-ordered joining, though each member is beautiful by itself as well.

And you, O God, saw everything that you had made, and behold, it was very good. Yes, we too see the same, and behold, all things are very good. As you finished each kind of your works, having said, Let them be, and they were, you saw of each that it was good. Seven times I have counted it written that you saw what you made was good; and this is the eighth, that you saw everything you had made, and behold, it was not only good, but very good — being now all together. For taken separately they were only good; but all together, both good and very good. All beautiful bodies say the same: a body made up of members all beautiful is far more beautiful than those same members are by themselves, by whose well-ordered blending the whole is perfected — even though the members one by one are also beautiful.

And I looked hard at the text, to find whether it was seven times or eight that you saw your works were good, when they pleased you; and in your seeing I found no times at all — nothing to make me understand that you saw what you made so many times over. And I said: Lord, surely this Scripture of yours is true, for you are truthful — you are Truth itself — and you set it forth. Why then do you tell me there are no times in your seeing, while this Scripture of yours tells me that on each day you saw that what you made was good — and when I counted, I found how many times? And you answer me, for you are my God, and you say it to your servant with a strong voice in his inner ear, breaking through my deafness, crying: Man, what my Scripture says, I say. But Scripture speaks in time, and time does not touch my Word, which stands with me, equal, in eternity. What you see through my Spirit, I see — just as what you say through my Spirit, I say. But when you see these things in time, I do not see them in time; and when you say these things in time, I do not say them in time.

And I looked closely to find whether you saw your works to be good seven times or eight, when they pleased you; but in your seeing I found no times, by which I might understand that you saw so many times over what you made. And I said: Lord, is not this your Scripture true, since you are true, and being Truth, have set it forth? Why, then, do you tell me that in your seeing there are no times, while this Scripture of yours tells me that what you made on each day, you saw that it was good — and when I counted, I found how often? To this you answer me, for you are my God, and with a strong voice you tell your servant in his inner ear, breaking through my deafness and crying: O man, what my Scripture says, I say; and yet Scripture speaks in time, while time has no bearing on my Word, because my Word stands in eternity, equal with myself. So the things you see through my Spirit, I see, just as what you speak by my Spirit, I speak. And so, when you see those things in time, I do not see them in time, just as, when you speak in time, I do not speak them in time.

And I heard, Lord my God — I licked up a drop of sweetness from your truth — and I understood. There are people who dislike your works. They say you made many of them under the squeeze of necessity — the fabric of the heavens, for instance, and the composition of the stars — and not from what was yours, but from material already created elsewhere, out of some other source, which you merely gathered and fitted and joined together, building the ramparts of the universe out of your conquered enemies, so that, bound down in that structure, they could never rise against you again. And other things, they say, you neither made nor even assembled — all flesh, and all the smallest living creatures, and everything that grips the earth by its roots. These, they say, a mind hostile to you begot and shaped in the lower stories of the world — an alien nature, not created by you and set against you. They are out of their minds who say so, because they do not see your works through your Spirit, and do not recognize you in them.

And I heard, O Lord my God, and drank up a drop of sweetness from your truth, and I understood that there are certain men who dislike your works and say that you made many of them under the force of necessity — such as the structure of the heavens and the order of the stars — and that you made them not out of what was yours, but out of what was created elsewhere and from other sources, for you to gather and fit and join together, when out of your conquered enemies you raised up the walls of the universe, so that they, bound down by the structure, might not be able to rebel against you again. And other things, they say, you neither made nor even fitted together — all flesh, and all tiny creatures, and whatever has its root in the earth — but that a mind at war with you, and another nature not created by you and contrary to you, begot and framed these things in the lower stages of the world. Frenzied are they who say this, because they do not see your works by your Spirit, nor recognize you in them.

But those who see these things through your Spirit — it is you who see, in them. When they see that these things are good, you are seeing that they are good; whatever pleases them for your sake — it is you who please them in it; and whatever pleases us through your Spirit pleases you, in us. For who among men knows the things of a man, except the spirit of the man that is in him? In the same way, no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God. Now we, he says, have received not the spirit of this world but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know what God has given us. And I am pressed to say: Truly, no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God; how then do we also know what God has given us? The answer comes back to me: even the things we know through his Spirit, no one knows except the Spirit of God. For just as it was rightly said to those who would speak through the Spirit of God, It is not you who speak, so it is rightly said to those who know through the Spirit of God, It is not you who know — and no less rightly to those who see through the Spirit of God, It is not you who see. Whatever they see through the Spirit of God to be good — it is not they who see that it is good, but God. It is one thing, then, for a man to think that what is good is bad, like the people I named. It is another for a man to see that what is good is good — for your creation pleases many because it is good, and yet you do not please them in it, because they would rather enjoy it than enjoy you. And it is another thing again that, when a man sees that something is good, God in him should be seeing that it is good — so that God is loved in what he made; and he cannot be loved except through the Holy Spirit he has given, because the love of God is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit given to us. Through him we see that whatever is, in any degree at all, is good; for it comes from him who does not exist in degrees, but is what he is.

But those who see these things by your Spirit, it is you who see in them. So when they see that these things are good, it is you who see that they are good; and whatever things please for your sake, it is you who are pleasing in them; and what pleases us through your Spirit, it is you who are pleasing in us. For what man knows the things of a man, except the spirit of the man that is in him? Even so, no one knows the things of God but the Spirit of God. Now we, he says, have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we might know the things freely given us by God. And I am reminded: Truly, no one knows the things of God but the Spirit of God; how, then, do we also know what things are given us by God? The answer is made to me: because the very things we know by his Spirit, even these no one knows but the Spirit of God. For as it was rightly said to those who were to speak by the Spirit of God, It is not you who speak, so it is rightly said to those who know through the Spirit of God, It is not you who know; and no less is it rightly said to those who see through the Spirit of God, It is not you who see. So whatever they see, through the Spirit of God, to be good, it is not they but God who sees that it is good. It is one thing, then, for a man to think that to be bad which is good, as the people just spoken of do; another, for a man to see that what is good is good, as your creatures please many because they are good, in whom yet you are not pleasing, when they would rather enjoy the creatures than you; and another still, that when a man sees a thing to be good, God in him sees that it is good — so that he may be loved in what he made, who cannot be loved except by the Holy Spirit whom he has given. Because the love of God is poured out in our hearts by the Holy Spirit who is given to us; by whom we see that whatever in any degree is, is good. For it is from him who is not in any degree, but who Is what He Is.

Thanks be to you, Lord! We see heaven and earth — whether that means the higher and the lower bodily regions, or the spiritual and the bodily creation; and for the adorning of these parts, which make up either the whole mass of the world or the whole of creation altogether, we see light made, and divided from the darkness. We see the firmament of heaven — whether that first body of the world, between the spiritual waters above and the bodily waters below, or this stretch of air, which is also called heaven, through which the birds of heaven wander — between the waters carried above it in vapor, falling as dew on clear nights, and the heavy waters that run along the ground. We see the beauty of waters gathered across the plains of the sea; and the dry land, first bare, then formed, made visible and set in order, the mother of plants and trees. We see the lights shining from above — the sun sufficing for the day, the moon and the stars consoling the night — and time marked and signified by them all. We see on every side the wet element, teeming with fish and beasts and birds — for the thickness of the air that bears up the flight of birds condenses out of the rising vapor of the waters. We see the face of the earth arrayed with its land animals; and man, made in your image and likeness, set over all the unreasoning animals by that very image and likeness — that is, by the power of reason and understanding. And as in his soul there is one power that rules by taking thought and another made subject, so that it obeys, so bodily too a woman was made for the man: in the mind of her rational understanding, equal in nature; in the sex of her body, subject to the man's sex, the way the impulse to act is subject to the mind's reasoned skill in acting rightly. We see these things: each of them is good, and all of them together are very good.

Thanks be to you, O Lord. We behold heaven and earth, whether the bodily part, higher and lower, or the spiritual and bodily creation; and in the ordering of these parts, of which the whole frame of the world — or rather the whole of creation — is made up, we see light made and divided from the darkness. We see the firmament of heaven, whether that first body of the world, between the spiritual upper waters and the lower bodily waters, or — since this too is called heaven — this stretch of air through which the birds of heaven wander, between those waters that are borne above them in vapor and on clear nights distill down as dew, and those heavier waters that flow along the earth. We behold a face of waters gathered together in the fields of the sea; and the dry land both bare, and shaped so as to be visible and ordered, and the matter of herbs and trees. We behold the lights shining from above, the sun to suffice for the day, the moon and the stars to cheer the night, and that by all of these the seasons should be marked and signified. We behold on every side a moist element, filled with fish and beasts and birds, because the thickness of the air, which bears up the flight of birds, thickens itself by the rising vapor of the waters. We behold the face of the earth decked with earthly creatures, and man, made after your image and likeness, set over all the irrational creatures by that very image and likeness of yours — that is, the power of reason and understanding. And as in his soul there is one power that rules by directing, and another made subject so that it might obey, so for the man, bodily too, a woman was made, who in the mind of her reasoning understanding should have an equal nature, but in the sex of her body should be subject in like manner to the sex of her husband — as the impulse to act is fain to conceive, from the reason of the mind, the skill of acting rightly. These things we behold, and they are good each by each, and all together very good.

Let your works praise you, so that we may love you; and let us love you, so that your works may praise you. In time they have their beginning and their end, their rising and their setting, their growth and their decay, their form and their loss of form. They have, then, their morning and their evening, in succession — partly hidden, partly plain. For they were made from nothing, by you: not out of you, not out of any matter not your own or existing beforehand, but out of matter created together with them — created, that is, by you at the same time, since you gave form to its formlessness with no interval of time between. The matter of heaven and earth is one thing, the form of heaven and earth another; yet you made the matter out of nothing at all, and the form of the world out of the formless matter — and both at once, so that form followed matter with no pause and no delay.

Let your works praise you, that we may love you; and let us love you, that your works may praise you — works which have their beginning and ending in time, their rising and setting, their growth and decay, their form and their want of form. So they have their succession of morning and evening, partly hidden, partly plain to see; for they were made out of nothing, by you, not out of you; not out of any matter not yours, or already in being, but out of matter created together with them — that is, made by you at the same time — because to their unformed state you gave form without any interval of time. For though the matter of heaven and earth is one thing, and the form another, you made the matter out of nothing at all, and the form of the world out of the matter without form; yet both together, so that the form should follow the matter with no interval of delay.

We have also looked into what you meant to prefigure by making these things — or by having them told — in just this order. And we have seen that they are good one by one, and all together very good, in your Word, in your Only-Begotten: heaven and earth, the Head and the body of the Church, predestined before all times, with no morning and no evening. But then you began to carry out in time what you had predestined — to reveal what was hidden and to set straight what was disordered in us; for our sins hung over us, and we had sunk away from you into the dark deep, and your good Spirit was borne above us, to come to our help in due season. You justified the ungodly and divided them from the wicked; you made firm the authority of your book, a firmament between those above, who would be teachable under you, and those beneath, who would be subject to them. You gathered the fellowship of the unbelieving into a single mass, so that the ardor of the faithful might stand out, and they might bring forth for you works of mercy — giving away even their earthly riches to the poor, to gain the riches of heaven. Then you kindled certain lights in the firmament — your holy ones, holding the word of life and shining with an authority lifted high by the gifts of the Spirit. Then, for the initiation of the unbelieving nations, you brought forth out of bodily matter the sacraments and the visible miracles and the sounding voices of words, according to the firmament of your book — and by these the faithful too are blessed and multiplied. Next you formed the living soul of the faithful, its affections set in order by the strength of continence. Then the mind subject to you alone, needing no human authority to copy — you renewed it in your image and likeness; you subjected its rational action to the higher rule of the understanding, as woman to man; and to all your ministries, needed for perfecting the faithful in this life, you willed that the same faithful give good things for temporal use, bearing fruit for the time to come. All these things we see, and they are very good — because you see them in us: you, who gave us the Spirit by which we see them, and in them love you.

We have also examined what you willed to be foreshadowed, whether by the creating of things, or by the relating of them in such an order. And we have seen that things singly are good, and all together very good, in your Word, in your Only-Begotten — both heaven and earth, the Head and the body of the Church — in your predestination before all times, without morning and evening. But when you began to carry out in time the things you had foreordained, so that you might reveal hidden things and set our disorders right — for our sins hung over us, and we had sunk into the dark deep, and your good Spirit was borne above us to help us in due season — you justified the ungodly and divided them from the wicked; and you made the firmament of the authority of your Book between those set above, who were to be teachable before you, and those below, who were to be subject to them; and you gathered the society of unbelievers into one conspiracy, that the zeal of the faithful might appear, and that they might bring forth works of mercy, even handing over their earthly riches to the poor, to gain what is heavenly. And after this you kindled certain lights in the firmament — your holy ones, having the word of life and shining with an eminent authority set on high through spiritual gifts. And after that again, for the initiation of the unbelieving nations, you brought forth out of bodily matter the sacraments, and visible miracles, and forms of words according to the firmament of your Book, by which the faithful should be blessed and multiplied. Next you formed the living soul of the faithful, through affections well ordered by the strength of self-control. And after that you renewed, after your own image and likeness, the mind subjected to you alone and needing no human authority to imitate; and you made its rational actions subject to the excellence of the understanding, as the woman to the man. And to all the offices of your ministry, needed for perfecting the faithful in this life, you willed that good things — fruitful to those same faithful in the time to come — should be given by them for their temporal uses. All these we see, and they are very good, because you see them in us, you who have given us your Spirit, by which we might see them, and in them love you.

Lord God, give us peace — for you have given us everything else — the peace of rest, the peace of the sabbath: peace without an evening. All this order of things — so beautiful, so very good — will pass away when its measures have been fully run; for in these things there was made a morning, and an evening.

O Lord God, give us peace — for you have given us all things — the peace of rest, the peace of the Sabbath, the Sabbath that has no evening. For all this most lovely array of things very good, when their courses are finished, is to pass away; for in them there was morning and evening.

But the seventh day has no evening, and it has no setting, because you sanctified it to endure forever. After all your works, which were very good, you rested on the seventh day — though you made them all in unbroken rest — so that the voice of your book might tell us in advance: we too, after our works — very good only because you have given them to us — will rest in you, in the sabbath of eternal life.

But the seventh day has no evening, and has no setting, because you have hallowed it to last forever; so that what you did after your works that were very good, resting on the seventh day — though you made them in unbroken rest — this the voice of your Book may foretell to us: that we too, after our works, which are therefore very good because you have given them to us, shall rest in you on the Sabbath of life eternal.

For then you will rest in us, as now you work in us; and that rest will be your rest through us, as these works are your works through us. But you, Lord, are always working and always at rest. You do not see in time, or move in time, or rest in time — and yet you make the things that are seen in time, and time itself, and the rest that comes when time is done.

For then you will rest in us, as now you work in us; and so that will be your rest through us, as these are your works through us. But you, Lord, are always at work and always at rest. You do not see in time, nor are you moved in time, nor do you rest in any time; and yet you make the things that are seen in time, yes, the very times themselves, and the rest that comes after time.

So we see the things you have made, because they are; and they are, because you see them. We see, outside us, that they are; and inside us, that they are good. But you saw them made in the very place where you saw them yet to be made. We were moved to do good at a later time, once our heart had conceived by your Spirit; at the earlier time we were moved to do evil, and we abandoned you. But you, the one good God, have never stopped doing good. Some of our works are indeed good, by your gift, but they are not forever; after them, we hope to rest in your great hallowing. But you, the Good that needs no good, are at rest always, because your rest is you yourself. And what man will give another man to understand this? What angel will give it to an angel? What angel to a man? Let it be asked of you, sought in you, knocked for at your door: so, so it will be received; so it will be found; so it will be opened. Amen.
Thanks be to you, Lord.

We therefore see these things which you made, because they are; but they are, because you see them. And we see, outwardly, that they are, and inwardly, that they are good; but you saw them as made, there where you saw them still to be made. And at a later time we were moved to do well, after our hearts had conceived of your Spirit; though in the earlier time we were moved to do evil, deserting you. But you, the one good God, never ceased to do good. And we too have some good works, by your gift, though they are not eternal; and after them we hope to rest in your great holiness. But you, being the Good that needs no good, are always at rest, because your rest is yourself. And what man can teach another man to understand this? What angel, another angel? What angel, a man? It must be asked of you, sought in you, knocked for at you; so, and only so, will it be received; so will it be found; so will it be opened. Amen.
